chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human
chunks.text: 01 300,000–70,000 years ago Many Kinds of Human For most of our species' history we shared the Earth with other humans, and some of them built, decorated and may have crossed the sea. ↕ Rise and fall. How capable were the other humans, and how much of their world has vanished? The claim on the scales Humans other than Homo sapiens were capable of planned construction and symbolic behaviour long before 70,000 years ago. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established The Bruniquel structures are securely dated by uranium-series methods and were clearly built, not natural. Neanderthal use of pigments, shells and bird feathers is documented at several sites by different teams. What remains open is the edge of the claim: whether Neanderthals made cave paintings, whether naledi buried its dead, and whether anyone crossed to Crete. The core claim of capable cousins is strong; the most dramatic individual cases are still contested. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Older textbooks were overconfident: they presented Neanderthals as dim evolutionary dead ends and symbolic behaviour as a sapiens monopoly, on thin evidence from a few excavated caves. Newer museum labels have largely caught up. Where they now risk overreaching is the other way, presenting contested cases such as naledi burials as fact. What is solid Fossils with modern-looking faces from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, date to c. 315,000 years ago and are counted as early Homo sapiens. Richter et al. 2017; Hublin et al. 2017 Around 100,000 years ago at least four kinds of human were alive: our species, Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo floresiensis, and probably Homo luzonensis too. Sutikna et al. 2016; Slon et al. 2018; Détroit et al. 2019 Neanderthals broke off about 400 stalagmite pieces (c. 2.2 t) and built two rings and four stacks deep in Bruniquel Cave, dated to 176,500 ± 2,100 years ago. Jaubert et al. 2016 The different kinds of human met and had children together: a girl from Denisova Cave, c. 90,000 years ago, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Slon et al. 2018 People made a cross-hatched drawing in ochre on a stone flake at Blombos Cave, South Africa, c. 73,000 years ago. Henshilwood et al. 2018 What is disputed Whether small-brained Homo naledi buried its dead and engraved cave walls in the Rising Star system (Berger et al. 2025 versus Martinón-Torres et al. 2024). Whether stone tools near Plakias on Crete, argued to be at least 130,000 years old from their geological setting, show that pre-sapiens humans crossed open sea to the island. Whether the

chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human: 01 A crowded planet
chunks.text: Picture the world 100,000 years ago and count the humans. In North and East Africa, people with faces much like ours. In Europe and western Asia, stocky Neanderthals. Across Asia, the Denisovans, a population we know mostly from DNA. On the island of Flores, people about 1.1 m tall. On Luzon, another small island people. For almost all of our species' existence, being human did not mean being the only kind. The textbook picture many of us grew up with was a ladder: primitive cousins on the lower rungs, then us, clever and alone. This age is where that ladder breaks. The evidence now points to a crowded, overlapping world in which several kinds of human made tools, used fire, mixed with one another and, in at least one case, built something strange in the dark. For almost all of our species' existence, being human did not mean being the only kind.

chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: Some things here rest on several independent lines of evidence. The Jebel Irhoud fossils from Morocco, dated by luminescence to c. 315,000 years ago, have a modern face on a longer, lower braincase. Our species seems to have assembled itself across Africa over a long time rather than in one cradle. Genomes read from bones show that Neanderthals and Denisovans split from our lineage more than half a million years ago and from each other a little later, and that the groups met and had children together. Step 1 of 4. The lineages. Solid bars show where fossils or DNA exist; dashed lines are inferred ancestry and gaps. The lineages. Solid bars show where fossils or DNA exist; dashed lines are inferred ancestry and gaps. Slice the tree at 100,000 years ago: at least four kinds of human are alive at once, probably five or six. They meet and mix: Denny around 90,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens with Neanderthals and Denisovans around 50,000–44,000 years ago. By about 40,000 years ago only one kind is left in the fossil record. The Denisovans' end is unknown. A timeline chart with seven horizontal rows for Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo erectus, Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and Homo naledi, running from 800,000 years ago to today with the scale stretched after 200,000. Solid bars show fossil or DNA evidence and dashed lines show inferred lineages joining sapiens to the Neanderthal and Denisovan branch. Step 2 adds a vertical band at 100,000 years ago with dots on the sapiens, Neanderthal, Denisovan and floresiensis rows and open rings for erectus and luzonensis. Step 3 adds curved arrows for interbreeding. Step 4 adds crosses where lineages end, leaving only Homo sapiens. The clearest single case is Denisova 11, nicknamed Denny, a girl who lived in a Siberian

chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human: 03 Builders in the dark
chunks.text: In 1990 cavers broke into a sealed passage of Bruniquel Cave in southern France. About 336 m from the entrance they found rings of broken stalagmites on the floor. When a team led by Jacques Jaubert dated the calcite that had regrown over the pieces, the answer was 176,500 ± 2,100 years. No Homo sapiens is known in Europe anywhere near that early. The builders were almost certainly early Neanderthals. A strip at the top shows a long cave passage 336 metres from entrance to structures. Below, a plan drawn to scale shows a large oval ring 6.7 by 4.5 metres made of two rows of short stalagmite pieces, a small ring 2.2 by 2.1 metres, and two circular stacks 0.55 and 2.6 metres across, with a 2 metre scale bar. Orange dots mark pieces with traces of fire. A note gives the date 176,500 plus or minus 2,100 years ago. The numbers are not casual. About 400 pieces with a total length of 112 m, of fairly even length, laid in rings up to 6.7 m across, in places stacked several layers high and wedged with small props. Many carry traces of fire: reddened, blackened and cracked calcite, and at least one burnt bone. Nobody knows what the rings were for. Shelter, ritual, storage, something we have no word for. But someone planned it, carried light deep underground and worked as a group. Stalagmites grow by adding calcite. When a piece is broken off and laid down, new calcite starts to grow on it. Uranium-series dating measures how long that new growth has been accumulating, so the regrowth on the cut pieces gives the time since they were moved. The team dated both the stumps left in the floor and the regrowth on the placed pieces, and the two agree.

chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human: 04 Beads, pigment and a drawing
chunks.text: In Africa the symbolic record thickens through this age. At Bizmoune Cave in Morocco, perforated sea snail shells, apparently worn as beads, date to c. 142,000–150,000 years ago. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people mixed ochre in abalone shells c. 100,000 years ago and, c. 73,000 years ago, drew a red cross-hatched pattern on a stone flake. Beads say something about identity: who you are, whose group you belong to. The most contested case is Homo naledi, a small-brained species that lived in South Africa c. 335,000–236,000 years ago. Its discoverers argue that bodies were deliberately buried deep in the Rising Star cave system and that nearby wall marks are engravings. Critics reply that the burial pits are not demonstrated and the marks are undated. Both sides agree something unusual happened there; the verdict on what remains open. Absence of beads in a cave nobody has dug is not evidence that nobody wore them.

chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human: 05 Sailors before us?
chunks.text: Flores has been an island throughout human history, and hominins were there by c. 700,000 years ago. On Luzon, butchered rhinoceros bones date to c. 709,000 years ago, long before Homo sapiens existed. However they arrived, on rafts, drifting on storm debris or on purpose, water was crossed by people who were not us. Crete is the boldest claim. In 2008 and 2009 a survey led by Thomas Strasser found quartz handaxes in terraces near Plakias and argued, from the geology, that they are at least 130,000 years old. Crete has been separated from the mainland for millions of years, so the claim implies deliberate seafaring in the Mediterranean. Sceptics point out that the age comes from the geological setting of the finds rather than from direct dating. It remains open, and it is exactly the kind of result that a few well-dated excavations could settle.

chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human: 06 The Toba question
chunks.text: About 74,000 years ago Toba in Sumatra erupted, the largest eruption of the last few hundred thousand years, spreading ash from the South China Sea to Lake Malawi. In 1998 anthropologist Stanley Ambrose proposed that its volcanic winter crashed human numbers to a few thousand. It is a great story, and it seemed to fit genetic hints of an old bottleneck. The field tested it, which is to the credit of everyone involved. In India, stone tools at Jwalapuram continue above and below the ash. At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, where tiny glass shards from Toba were found in the layers, people carried on through the eruption. At Shinfa-Metema in Ethiopia, a 2024 study found people adapting to drought and following seasonal rivers across the Toba horizon. The catastrophe version now looks unlikely for people in Africa; regional effects in South and Southeast Asia are less studied.

chunks.heading: Many Kinds of Human: 07 What time has taken
chunks.text: This age is our deepest look at a real pattern: many experiments in being human, most of which ended. Several of those endings are genuine mysteries. Why did naledi, erectus, the Flores and Luzon people and eventually the Neanderthals disappear, while one lineage spread everywhere? Small populations and climate swings are strong candidates, but for most of these groups we have a handful of sites. And the most human-friendly land of the cold phases, the lowland coasts, is now seabed. What would change the picture: dated underwater surveys of Pleistocene shorelines, direct dates on the Plakias tools, more Denisovan skeletons and securely dated naledi remains. Until then the honest summary is that the cousins were cleverer than we were taught, and much of their story is still buried.

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening
chunks.text: 02 70,000–30,000 years ago The Great Awakening Our species spreads across the world, paints the oldest pictures we know, and absorbs the last of the other humans. ▲ Rise. Did the human mind switch on in Europe 40,000 years ago, or much earlier elsewhere? The claim on the scales People reached Sahul (Australia and New Guinea) by about 65,000 years ago. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established Madjedbebe's luminescence dates are internally consistent, a 2025 genetic study of nearly 2,500 mitochondrial genomes lands near 60,000 years, and the 2026 Sulawesi date shows people on the island route by 67,800 years ago. Against it: sandy sites can move artefacts downward, other sites are younger, and the Neanderthal mixing window (50,500–43,500 years ago) sits awkwardly with an earlier arrival unless those genes came in later. The earlier date is now well supported but not settled. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact The confidence depends on where you read. Many international textbooks state 'about 50,000 years', while Australian public institutions often present 65,000 years as fact. Both sound more settled than the evidence, which consists of a few key sites and conflicting genetic arguments. On the rise of art, older textbooks were overconfident in a European 'creative explosion' that the Sulawesi dates have overturned. What is solid A hand stencil on Muna Island off Sulawesi is at least 67,800 years old, the oldest dated rock art known; a painted scene of people and a pig on Sulawesi is at least 51,200 years old. Oktaviana et al. 2026; Oktaviana et al. 2024 Everyone with ancestry outside Africa carries c. 1.5–2.1% Neanderthal DNA, mostly from one long episode of mixing c. 50,500–43,500 years ago. Prüfer et al. 2014; Iasi et al. 2024 Modern humans were at Grotte Mandrin in France c. 54,000 years ago, far earlier than the old picture allowed. Slimak et al. 2022 People were in Australia by at least c. 45,000–40,000 years ago; the burials at Lake Mungo date to c. 40,000 years. Bowler et al. 2003; O'Connell et al. 2018 Neanderthal sites across Europe end c. 41,000–39,000 years ago, after thousands of years of overlap with modern humans. Higham et al. 2014 What is disputed Whether people reached Sahul by c. 65,000 years ago (Madjedbebe; mitochondrial genomes, 2025) or only after c. 50,000 (the 'short chronology'). Why the Neanderthals disappeared: competition, absorption, small numbers, climate, disease, or a mix. Whether the Laschamps magnetic excursion c. 42,000 years ago had any effect on people, as Cooper et al. 2021 proposed.

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening: 01 A hand on the wall
chunks.text: On Muna, a small island off southeast Sulawesi, someone pressed a hand against a limestone wall at least 67,800 years ago and blew red pigment around it. Then, it seems, they reworked the outline so the fingertips look narrow and pointed, almost like claws. It is the oldest dated rock art on Earth, and it is not in Europe, where the story of human creativity used to begin. This age is the one most textbooks call the great awakening: art, ornaments, musical instruments, long-distance travel. The evidence now suggests the awakening was not a sudden switch in one place but lights coming on across a vast region, most of them in places archaeologists visited late. The awakening looks less like a switch in Europe and more like lights coming on across half the world.

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening: 02 Out of Africa, again
chunks.text: Homo sapiens had left Africa before, into the Levant and perhaps beyond, but those earlier groups left little or no trace in living people. The dispersal that counts genetically happened roughly 60,000–50,000 years ago. From there people moved fast: into South and Southeast Asia, across the sea to Sahul, and into Europe. At Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley, a tooth and distinctive stone points place modern humans in France c. 54,000 years ago, apparently a pioneer group that did not last. Much of that journey probably ran along coasts. During this age the sea stood tens of metres below today, so the beaches, estuaries and shell middens of the southern route now lie offshore. Its best evidence is underwater.

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening: 03 Mixing with the cousins
chunks.text: Ancient genomes have turned a debate into a record. Everyone with ancestry outside Africa carries roughly 1.5–2.1% Neanderthal DNA. Genomes from Ranis in Germany and Zlatý kůň in Czechia, and a 2024 study of many ancient individuals, place most of that mixing in one long episode c. 50,500–43,500 years ago. People in New Guinea and Aboriginal Australians carry additional Denisovan ancestry, from encounters somewhere in Asia or Wallacea. Some of these genes still matter. A Denisovan-derived gene variant helps many Tibetans cope with high altitude. The other humans did not simply vanish; part of them is in us.

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening: 04 The oldest art is not where we looked
chunks.text: European caves gave the world its first image of Ice Age art: the lions and rhinos of Chauvet, painted c. 36,000 years ago, the ivory lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel, bone flutes from the Swabian Jura. For a century these were treated as the beginning. Then a team working in Sulawesi began dating the thin mineral crusts that grow over paintings there. Step 1 of 5. An artist blows pigment around a hand pressed to the rock, leaving a stencil. On Muna the fingertips were reshaped to look pointed. An artist blows pigment around a hand pressed to the rock, leaving a stencil. On Muna the fingertips were reshaped to look pointed. Over thousands of years, water seeping down the wall leaves thin films of calcite that build up into a crust over the paint. Researchers scrape tiny samples from the crust, layer by layer, down towards the paint. Water brings in uranium but almost no thorium. Uranium decays into thorium-230 at a known rate, so the ratio of the two gives each layer's age. The deepest crust over the Muna stencil is at least 67,800 years old, so the painting beneath is older still. Left: a cave wall with a red sprayed stencil of a hand whose fingertips are narrowed to points. A magnifying circle on the stencil's edge links to a magnified cross-section on the right: limestone at the bottom, a thin red paint layer, and above it four bands of calcite crust. Step 3 adds small sample boxes cut from each band. Step 4 adds bars comparing uranium and thorium in each sample, with more thorium in deeper layers. Step 5 marks the layer just above the paint as at least 67,800 years old and the top as younger. The results arrived in steps. A painted pig at Leang Tedongnge, at least 45,500 years old. A scene of human-like figures and a pig at Leang Karampuang, at least 51,200 years old,

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening: 05 When did people reach Australia?
chunks.text: Reaching Sahul needed boats and open-water crossings, even at low sea level. At Madjedbebe, a rock shelter in Arnhem Land, excavators in 2017 dated the lowest dense layer of stone tools, ground ochre and grinding stones to c. 65,000 years ago. Critics, notably James O'Connell and Jim Allen, argue that artefacts can sink through sandy deposits and that most reliably dated sites are younger than c. 50,000 years. In 2025 they added a genetic argument: the Neanderthal DNA shared by all non-Africans was acquired no earlier than about 50,500 years ago, so Sahul's first settlers, they reason, arrived after that. A horizontal time axis from 80,000 to 35,000 years ago with seven rows. Madjedbebe: a bar from about 70,700 to 59,300 with a point at 65,000. Sulawesi hand stencil: a point at 67,800 with an arrow pointing older. Mitochondrial genomes: a point at about 60,000. Sulawesi painted scene: a point at 51,200 with an arrow pointing older. Neanderthal mixing: a bar from 50,500 to 43,500, also shaded as a vertical band. Short chronology: a bar from about 50,000 to 45,000. Lake Mungo burials: a bar around 40,000 years. The same year a study of nearly 2,500 mitochondrial genomes from Aboriginal Australians and New Guineans estimated first settlement at about 60,000 years ago, by two routes. And the Muna date shows people on the island chain leading toward Australia by 67,800 years ago. Many Aboriginal communities hold that they have always been on Country; science cannot test 'always', but it increasingly supports a very deep presence.

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening: 06 The last of the others
chunks.text: By c. 41,000–39,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone from the record across Europe, after thousands of years of overlap with incoming modern humans. Homo floresiensis disappears c. 50,000 years ago, not long after modern humans reached the region. In Australia, giant marsupials, birds and reptiles vanish roughly 45,000–40,000 years ago. The timing is suggestive; the mechanism is still argued over. Competition and absorption, fire, hunting and a jittery climate all play a part in current models. Some researchers point to extra shocks: the Campanian Ignimbrite super-eruption near Naples c. 40,000 years ago, and the Laschamps excursion c. 42,000 years ago, when Earth's magnetic field weakened drastically. A 2021 study linked the latter to environmental crisis and even to cave use; critics find the human connections unproven.

chunks.heading: The Great Awakening: 07 What time has hidden
chunks.text: The pattern here is a rise, but a rise seen through a keyhole. The coasts are drowned, the boats have rotted, and tropical paint weathers. The Sulawesi dates came from a handful of caves; most walls in Southeast Asia, India and Arabia have never been sampled. Every time a new region is examined carefully, the story gets older. What would settle the big questions: more dated sites in Wallacea and northern Australia with sealed layers, Denisovan skeletons, submerged coastal surveys along the Arabian and Indian shelves, and uranium-series dating of rock art far beyond Sulawesi.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age World
chunks.text: 03 30,000–14,700 years ago The Ice Age World With the sea some 130 m lower, a lost world of coasts, plains and river valleys lay open, and people walked into the Americas. ↕ Rise and fall. Who lived on the Ice Age coasts that are now under the sea? The claim on the scales A civilisation with monumental architecture flourished on the ice-age coasts and was lost when the sea rose. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The premise is sound: vast coastal land was drowned and is largely unexplored. But no artefact, structure, domesticated plant or genetic trace of a complex ice-age society has been found, including on shelves that have been dredged, trawled and surveyed, such as the North Sea. The Gunung Padang construction claim was retracted in 2024 because the dated soil showed no link to human activity. The idea awaits evidence rather than being ruled out. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks are right that every excavated ice-age site shows hunter-gatherers, but they rarely mention that the likeliest places for larger coastal settlements were never excavated. On the Americas they were badly overconfident: 'Clovis first', about 13,000 years ago, was taught as settled for decades before sites such as Monte Verde and White Sands pushed arrival much earlier. What is solid Global sea level stood about 134 m below today at the height of the last glaciation, c. 21,000 years ago. Lambeck et al. 2014 Sundaland, the dry Sunda Shelf joining Malaysia, Sumatra, Java and Borneo, covered about 1.8 million km², roughly twice the land there today. Hanebuth et al. 2000; Bird et al. 2005 Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, are c. 23,000–21,000 years old, confirmed by seeds, pollen, quartz and lake-sediment dating. Bennett et al. 2021; Pigati et al. 2023; Holliday et al. 2025 Cosquer Cave near Marseille holds Ice Age paintings and engravings; its entrance is now 37 m under the sea. Clottes & Courtin 1996 Beringia, the land between Siberia and Alaska, was up to about 1,000 km wide from north to south. Hoffecker et al. 2014 What is disputed How the first Americans arrived: along the Pacific coast by boat, through an inland route, or earlier than anyone has shown. Whether any society on the drowned shelves was more complex than the hunter-gatherers known from inland sites. Whether Gunung Padang in Java hides construction c. 27,000 years old; the 2023 paper claiming it was retracted in 2024. What time has hidden The ice-age coastline itself: a strip of land that ran around every continent now lies 40–130 m under water

chunks.heading: The Ice Age World: 01 A world with the plug pulled
chunks.text: Twenty-one thousand years ago you could have walked from England to Denmark, from Siberia to Alaska and from Malaysia to Borneo without getting your feet wet. So much water was locked in ice sheets up to 3 km thick that the oceans stood about 130 m lower than today. The world's coastlines lay far out on what is now seabed, and a strip of land larger than many countries edged every continent. This is the age of the Last Glacial Maximum. Textbooks show it as a hard time of mammoth hunters in fur. That is true inland. But it was also a world of broad coastal plains, estuaries and lagoons, perhaps the richest real estate on Earth, and nearly all of it is now underwater. The best land of the Ice Age is exactly the land nobody can dig.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age World: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The physical numbers are well constrained. Ice sheets reached their greatest extent c. 26,500–19,000 years ago. Coral reefs, drowned beaches and ice-volume models put global sea level about 134 m below today around 21,000 years ago. Then the melt began, first slowly and later in dramatic pulses, and the sea climbed back over the land, reaching roughly its modern level only some 7,000 years ago. Step 1 of 6. 21,000 years ago: sea level about 134 m below today. The whole shelf is dry land with rivers, lagoons and camps. 21,000 years ago: sea level about 134 m below today. The whole shelf is dry land with rivers, lagoons and camps. 14,500 years ago: the melt is under way and the sea has climbed to about 100 m below today. 14,000 years ago: Meltwater Pulse 1A has added about 20 m in roughly 500 years. The outer camps are gone. 11,700 years ago, the start of the Holocene: the sea is near 58 m below today. 8,200 years ago: the sea is about 12 m below today. Doggerland is almost gone. Today: the ice-age coast lies far offshore, and every camp is on the seabed. A cross-section of land sloping gently from a hill on the left down a wide continental shelf to a steep shelf edge at the right, with depth marks at 0, 50, 100 and 150 metres below today's sea level. Three camps sit on the shelf. In step 1 the sea level is at minus 134 metres and the shelf is dry. In each later step the water rises: minus 100 metres, minus 80 after Meltwater Pulse 1A, minus 58 at the start of the Holocene, minus 12 at 8,200 years ago, and finally today's level, when all three camps are under water. Some of the lost lands were enormous. Sundaland in Southeast Asia covered about 1.8 million km².
