chunks.heading: The Ice Age World: 03 Proof that sites went under
chunks.text: In 1985 the diver Henri Cosquer found a narrow tunnel in the sea cliffs near Marseille. Its entrance is now 37 m underwater. It leads up into chambers above the waterline, painted and engraved during the Ice Age with horses, bison, seals, penguin-like great auks and hand stencils. When the art was made, the entrance opened onto dry land several kilometres from the shore. Cosquer is the rule made visible. Wherever people lived close to the Ice Age sea, their traces are now either underwater or scoured away. A few projects map drowned landscapes, notably in the North Sea, where trawlers have brought up bone tools and animal remains for a century. But for most of the world's lost coast, no one has looked at all.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age World: 04 Footprints that broke a rule
chunks.text: For much of the 20th century, American textbooks taught 'Clovis first': people arrived c. 13,000 years ago, walked down an ice-free corridor and spread with their distinctive spear points. Sites that seemed older were dismissed. Monte Verde in Chile, c. 14,500 years old, won acceptance only in 1997 after a long fight. White Sands pushed the date far back. In the gypsum basin of New Mexico, footprints of adults, teenagers and children cross ancient lake-shore mud, alongside tracks of mammoth and giant ground sloth. In 2021 seeds of a water plant in the layers gave ages of c. 23,000–21,000 years. Critics argued the seeds could hold 'old' carbon from the lake water. So teams dated conifer pollen and quartz grains, and later the lake's own sediments. The answers agreed. A layered block of lake sediments beneath gypsum dunes. Three dashed lines inside mark footprint surfaces with small dark footprints on them. An arrow on the left shows older at the bottom and younger at the top. Small symbols in the layers mark sampled seeds, pollen grains and quartz grains, with leader lines to labels on the right: ditchgrass seeds dated by radiocarbon to about 23,000 to 21,000 years, conifer pollen with the same age range, quartz grains dated by luminescence to at least about 21,000 years, and old lake beds whose chronology agrees. Radiocarbon measures the decay of carbon-14 in once-living things, such as seeds and pollen. Luminescence measures how long quartz grains have been buried out of sunlight. The two methods rely on different physics and different materials, so when they agree, a shared error becomes much less likely.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age World: 05 Art in the deep cold
chunks.text: In Europe, people pulled back into warmer refuges in Iberia, southern France, Italy and the Balkans. Life there was not merely survival. The Lascaux paintings, usually dated to c. 17,000–22,000 years ago, include nearly 6,000 figures, among them hundreds of horses and a famous shaft scene with a bird-headed man. Eyed bone needles made tailored clothing possible, and on the Russian and Ukrainian plains people built dwellings from mammoth bones. In the Americas the puzzle is how anyone got south of the ice so early. The inland corridor between the great North American ice sheets was probably closed, or too barren to cross, around 23,000 years ago. Many researchers therefore favour a route down the Pacific coast by boat, following shorelines rich in kelp, fish and seals, an idea championed by Jon Erlandson as the 'kelp highway'. Genetic studies suggest the ancestors of Native Americans were isolated for several thousand years, perhaps in Beringia, before spreading south. White Sands forces that clock earlier, and the coastal sites that could show the route are, once again, underwater.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age World: 06 A lost civilisation on the shelves?
chunks.text: Graham Hancock's argument, developed in Underworld (2002) and later books, starts from a real gap. If the most attractive land was drowned, then perhaps a more advanced ice-age society lived there, and all we see inland are its hunter-gatherer neighbours. Danny Hilman Natawidjaja has argued that Gunung Padang, a terraced hilltop site in West Java, contains buried construction phases going back c. 27,000 years. The test is what has been found. Dredging and trawling on the North Sea and other shelves have produced ice-age animal bones, stone tools and hunter-gatherer camps, but no masonry, metal, pottery or crops. Genetics shows no population with the signature of an early farming civilisation. In 2024 the Gunung Padang paper was retracted by its journal because the radiocarbon-dated soil had no demonstrated link to human work. The drowned-coast idea is a fair question; it is not yet a finding.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age World: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The answer lies under the sea. Systematic surveys of drowned river valleys and shorelines at depths of 40–130 m, cores through submerged sediments, and targeted underwater excavation would reveal what kind of people lived on the lost coasts. In the Americas, older sealed sites on the Pacific coast route would show how the first Americans arrived. Until then, the Ice Age holds the largest unexplored archive of human history. It is worth being clear about both halves of the verdict. The lost coasts are real, vast and almost untouched by archaeology. The lost civilisation is, so far, a hypothesis without a single artefact. Both statements can be true at once, and only fieldwork on the seabed will move either of them.

chunks.heading: The Great Melt
chunks.text: 04 14,700–12,900 years ago The Great Melt Greenland warmed by around 9 °C within decades, the sea surged, and in the Levant people settled into the first villages. ▲ Rise. Could people have watched the coast move within a single lifetime? The claim on the scales During Meltwater Pulse 1A the sea rose fast enough for people on low coasts to see their shoreline move within a single lifetime. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established At c. 40 mm a year, the sea rose about 2.4 m in 60 years. On very flat shelves such as the Sunda Shelf, a metre of rise can move the shore hundreds of metres to kilometres inland, so the change would have been visible within one life. The physical numbers come from independent coral, sediment and model records. What cannot be tested directly is whether anyone remembered it. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Popular accounts still describe the end of the Ice Age as a slow, steady warming and a gradual rise of the sea. The evidence shows steps and jolts: warmings of several degrees within decades and sea-level pulses ten times faster than today's. On this point the textbooks sound calmer and more certain than the evidence allows. What is solid Central Greenland warmed by about 9 ± 3 °C within a few decades at the start of the Bølling, c. 14,700 years ago. Severinghaus & Brook 1999 Meltwater Pulse 1A raised global sea level by roughly 14–20 m within a few centuries, at rates of c. 40 mm a year or more. Deschamps et al. 2012; Lambeck et al. 2014 Natufian foragers at Shubayqa 1 in Jordan baked a flatbread-like food c. 14,400 years ago, some 4,000 years before farming. Arranz-Otaegui et al. 2018 People were in the Americas well before Clovis: Monte Verde in Chile c. 14,500 years ago, Page-Ladson in Florida c. 14,550, Paisley Caves in Oregon c. 14,300. Dillehay et al. 2015; Halligan et al. 2016; Gilbert et al. 2008 Giant ice-age floods from glacial Lake Missoula repeatedly scoured the Channeled Scablands of Washington State near the end of the Ice Age. Bretz 1923; Baker 2009 What is disputed Where Meltwater Pulse 1A's water came from: mostly Antarctica, mostly North America, or both. Whether residues in 13,000-year-old stone mortars at Raqefet Cave show brewing of beer. Whether any myths preserve memories of this particular surge of the sea, as opposed to later, slower rises. What time has hidden The coastlines people knew at the start of this age were drowned by its end; coastal Natufian and pre-Clovis sites would now be offshore. Wooden boats, nets and basketry that would show how people m

chunks.heading: The Great Melt: 01 The thaw that was not gradual
chunks.text: About 14,700 years ago the North Atlantic world switched climate. Gases trapped in bubbles in the Greenland ice show that the air above the ice sheet warmed by about 9 °C within a few decades. Forests pushed north into tundra, lakes filled, rainfall returned to the eastern Mediterranean. Scientists call the warm period that followed the Bølling-Allerød; it lasted, with wobbles, until c. 12,900 years ago. For people alive at the time, this was not a slow trend visible only to geologists. A grandchild could grow up in a different landscape from the grandparent. And on the coasts, something even more dramatic was under way. A grandchild could grow up in a different landscape from the grandparent.

chunks.heading: The Great Melt: 02 Seas on the move
chunks.text: As the ice sheets collapsed, the sea surged. Drowned coral reefs off Tahiti, drilled in 2005 and dated with uranium-series methods, record a rise of about 14–18 m between c. 14,650 and 14,310 years ago. Global reconstructions put the jump at about 20 m in roughly 500 years, at c. 40 mm a year or more. Today the sea rises by a few millimetres a year and it is front-page news. A line chart of global sea level from 17,000 to 11,500 years ago, rising from about 124 metres below today to about 58 metres below. A shaded band between 14,500 and 14,000 years ago marks Meltwater Pulse 1A, where the line steepens and rises about 20 metres. A dashed line marks the Bølling warming at 14,700 years ago. To the right, a blue column 20 metres tall stands beside a 1.7 metre person and is compared to a six-storey building. What did that mean on the ground? At 40 mm a year, the sea climbs about 2.4 m in 60 years. On a very flat shelf, such as much of Sundaland, where the seabed may drop only about a metre per kilometre, that is kilometres of lost land in one lifetime. Hunting grounds, fresh-water springs and burial places would have gone under within memory. The water came from shrinking ice sheets, but which ones is still debated: Antarctica, North America and Scandinavia all have their advocates.

chunks.heading: The Great Melt: 03 The first villagers
chunks.text: In the Levant, the warm, wet centuries helped a remarkable culture flourish. The Natufians, named after Wadi en-Natuf in the Judean hills, built hamlets of round, semi-sunken stone houses at sites such as Ain Mallaha (Eynan) in the Jordan Valley. They harvested wild cereals with sickles of flint set in bone handles, pounded them in stone mortars, stored food and buried their dead beneath their floors. They were not farmers. They were foragers who stayed put, and their lives look surprisingly familiar. At Shubayqa 1 in northeast Jordan, charred crumbs show that people were baking a flatbread-like food c. 14,400 years ago. At Raqefet Cave near Mount Carmel, residues in stone mortars c. 13,000 years old have been read as traces of brewing, though others doubt it. Dogs were already companions. At Bonn-Oberkassel in Germany, a young dog buried with two people c. 14,200 years ago had survived a serious illness, which suggests it was cared for. At Ain Mallaha, c. 12,000 years ago, an elderly person was buried with a hand resting on a puppy. Charred plant remains survive when food falls into a fire. Under the microscope, bread crumbs show the porous structure left by gas bubbles in dough and the fragments of ground grain, which distinguishes them from roasted whole seeds. At Shubayqa 1 these were found in a hearth together with the radiocarbon-dated charcoal.

chunks.heading: The Great Melt: 04 Everywhere in the Americas
chunks.text: Across the Americas, this age now has people in it, which is itself a revolution in the textbooks. At Monte Verde in southern Chile, a waterlogged camp c. 14,500 years old preserved wooden foundations, hide scraps and medicinal plants. At Page-Ladson in Florida, divers recovered stone tools and a butchered mastodon tusk c. 14,550 years old from a sinkhole river. In the Paisley Caves in Oregon, dried human faeces c. 14,300 years old contain human DNA. At the Friedkin site in Texas, thousands of stone artefacts lie beneath the Clovis layer, dated c. 15,500 years ago. Clovis itself, with its elegant fluted spear points, appears only near the end of this age, c. 13,050 years ago. It was a successful technology spreading through a continent that was already inhabited, not the first footprint.

chunks.heading: The Great Melt: 05 The catastrophists' case
chunks.text: Randall Carlson and Graham Hancock read this age as a time of catastrophe, and they have a strong precedent. In 1923 geologist J Harlen Bretz argued that the bizarre landscape of eastern Washington, with its dry waterfalls, giant ripples and canyons cut into basalt, was carved by a colossal flood. Geology at the time rejected sudden catastrophes on principle, and Bretz was dismissed for decades. Once the source was identified, glacial Lake Missoula, repeatedly bursting through its ice dam, he was vindicated and, in 1979, awarded geology's Penrose Medal. The megafloods, the rapid warmings and the sea-level pulses are all real. Where the catastrophists go further, arguing that these events wiped out an advanced culture or that specific myths describe them, the evidence is thinner. The lesson Bretz teaches cuts both ways: geology was wrong to rule catastrophe out in advance, and it came round because the physical evidence was overwhelming.

chunks.heading: The Great Melt: 06 What the melt erased
chunks.text: By the end of this age the sea had risen roughly 60 m from its lowest point, and the coasts people had used for thousands of years were gone. That means the Natufian and pre-Clovis worlds we know are the inland halves of those worlds. The coastal halves, where boats were launched and shellfish gathered, are offshore. Could anyone have remembered? In Australia, geographer Patrick Nunn and linguist Nicholas Reid gathered Aboriginal stories from 21 places around the coast that describe the sea rising and drowning land that was once walked on. They argue that some of these accounts are more than 7,000 years old. Those memories, if they are memories, would belong to the later and slower stages of the rise, not to this pulse. But they show that the loss of land to the sea is exactly the kind of event people pass on. What would settle the open questions: dated drowned shorelines at the depths of the pre-pulse coast, better fingerprinting of where Meltwater Pulse 1A's water came from, and more sealed early sites in the Americas. Then, around 12,900 years ago, the warm world stopped.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset
chunks.text: 05 12,900–11,700 years ago The Younger Dryas Reset Just as the world warmed, the north plunged back into near-glacial cold for 1,200 years, then leapt out of it within decades. ↺ Reset. What flipped the climate back to the Ice Age, and what did it cost people? The claim on the scales A cosmic airburst or impact c. 12,800 years ago triggered the Younger Dryas cooling, the megafauna extinctions and the collapse of Clovis. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established After nearly two decades, the key markers have not been consistently reproduced by independent teams, several are common in ordinary sediments, and no crater of the right age is known. A 2025 study attributes the Greenland platinum spike to Icelandic eruptions, and the timing does not match an impact. In 2025 and February 2026, three papers by the group were retracted, citing problems with dating, sampling and data. The weakening of Atlantic circulation explains the cooling without an impact, though its trigger is still discussed. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks present the meltwater-and-ocean-current explanation as settled. It is well supported but not closed: the meltwater route, its timing and whether the Younger Dryas was one of several natural oscillations are still researched. The popular impact story is presented in documentaries far more confidently than the evidence justifies, which is the larger gap today. What is solid The Younger Dryas began 12,896 ± 138 years before 2000 CE in the Greenland ice and ended 11,703 years before 2000 CE, the formal start of the Holocene. Rasmussen et al. 2006; Walker et al. 2009 Central Greenland fell back to near-glacial temperatures, about −46 to −50 °C, then warmed by about 8 °C within a century at the end. Alley 2000 The Clovis tool tradition dates to c. 13,050–12,750 years ago and ends near the Younger Dryas onset. Waters et al. 2020 About 35 genera of large mammals disappeared from North America at the end of the Ice Age, many of them near this time. Faith & Surovell 2009 A dark organic 'black mat' layer caps Clovis-age deposits at many North American sites. Haynes 2008 What is disputed Whether a cosmic impact or airburst c. 12,800 years ago triggered the cold, fires and extinctions (the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis). Exactly where the meltwater went (east through the St Lawrence or north through the Mackenzie River to the Arctic), and whether meltwater alone explains the timing. How much hunting, climate and habitat change each contributed to the megafauna extinctions. Whether melted glass at A

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset: 01 The world slips back
chunks.text: Imagine being a Natufian grandmother on the Euphrates c. 12,900 years ago. For as long as anyone can remember, the valley has been generous: oak and pistachio on the slopes, wild rye and einkorn in the steppe, gazelle every spring. Then, within a few decades, the winters bite harder, the rains fail more often, the wild stands thin. No one alive has seen anything like it, and no one alive will see it end. This is the Younger Dryas, named after a small Arctic flower, Dryas octopetala, whose leaves turn up in European lake muds of this time. It is the most famous reversal in the story of the end of the Ice Age, and, since 2007, one of its fiercest debates. No one alive has seen anything like it, and no one alive will see it end.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset: 02 What the ice remembers
chunks.text: Greenland's ice sheet stores a year-by-year archive. Counting annual layers places the onset of the cold at 12,896 ± 138 years before 2000 CE and its end at 11,703. Reconstructed temperatures at the GISP2 drill site show the summit dropping from around −41 °C to near −49 °C within about 160 years, staying at −46 to −50 °C for some twelve centuries, then jumping by about 8 °C in less than a century. Step 1 of 5. Bølling warming, c. 14,700 years ago: the Greenland summit warms by about 11 °C in about 160 years. Bølling warming, c. 14,700 years ago: the Greenland summit warms by about 11 °C in about 160 years. Allerød: a slow, bumpy cooling over about 1,600 years, with short cold dips. The plunge, c. 12,900 years ago: about 8 °C of cooling in roughly 160 years. The Younger Dryas: about 1,200 years at −46 to −50 °C, near full glacial cold. The Holocene jump, 11,700 years ago: about 8 °C of warming in less than a century. A line chart of temperature in central Greenland from 15,700 to 10,000 years ago, on a scale from minus 50 to minus 30 degrees Celsius, with a dashed line at minus 31.6 for the most recent value in the core. Step 1 highlights a jump of about 11 degrees at 14,700 years ago. Step 2 shows a bumpy slide through the Allerød. Step 3 shows a plunge of about 8 degrees around 12,900 years ago. Step 4 shades the 1,200-year Younger Dryas with temperatures between minus 46 and minus 50. Step 5 shows a rise of about 8 degrees within a century at 11,700 years ago and the warm Holocene after it. Three independent signals in the ice agree. The ratio of heavy to light oxygen in the ice tracks temperature. Nitrogen and argon isotopes in trapped air bubbles record how steep the temperature gradient in the snow was, giving the size of abrupt changes. And annual layers in dust

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset: 03 Losses in the Americas
chunks.text: In North America the Clovis tool tradition, with its fluted points, ends c. 12,750 years ago. Mammoths, mastodons, native horses and camels, giant ground sloths and sabre-toothed cats disappear around the same broad window; in all about 35 genera of large mammals were lost at the end of the Ice Age. People did not vanish: Folsom and other traditions followed. But a way of life built around big game ended. A cross-section of layered ground. At the bottom, older stream sands and silts. Above them, a layer holding mammoth bones, a tusk and a Clovis spear point. Directly on top, a dark band labelled the black mat. Above that, later Holocene sediments and a grassy surface. Labels on the right describe the black mat as a wet-ground soil found at dozens of sites near the Younger Dryas onset, the impact claim that its base holds microspherules, nanodiamonds, platinum and iridium, and the counter-evidence that the markers are often not reproduced and black mats form at other times too. At many sites a thin, dark 'black mat' lies directly over Clovis-age deposits. At Murray Springs in Arizona, mammoth bones and Clovis points lie right beneath it and none are found above it. It is one of the most dramatic lines in American archaeology, and both sides of the impact debate have read it differently.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset: 04 The impact hypothesis at its strongest
chunks.text: In 2007 Richard Firestone and a large team proposed in PNAS that a comet or its fragments exploded over North America c. 12,900 years ago. At the base of the black mat and similar layers, they reported magnetic microspherules, nanodiamonds, carbon spherules and soot. The group, later known as the Comet Research Group, has since reported similar markers from Europe, Syria and South America, and argued that fires burned across continents. In 2013 a separate team found a sharp platinum spike in the GISP2 ice core near the onset. Martin Sweatman has argued that carvings at Göbekli Tepe record the event, and Graham Hancock's Magicians of the Gods (2015) made the airburst the destroyer of a lost ice-age civilisation. At its best, the argument is about coincidence in time: abrupt cooling, the end of Clovis, extinctions and a platinum spike, all near 12,800 years ago.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset: 05 The case against, and the retractions
chunks.text: Independent tests have repeatedly failed to confirm the markers. A 2009 study could not reproduce the reported microspherule peaks at several sites, including some the group had sampled. A 2010 study found no nanodiamonds of the kind described. Carbon spherules turned out to include fungal bodies and insect droppings. A 2011 review called for the hypothesis to be set aside, and in 2023 a team of 13 specialists, from archaeologists to impact physicists, published a detailed rebuttal. Black mats, they note, formed repeatedly through time when groundwater rose, not at one moment. In April 2025 Scientific Reports retracted the group's paper claiming an airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam in Jordan. In September 2025 a PLOS One study argued the Greenland platinum spike begins about 45 years after the cooling began and lasted 14 years, pointing to Icelandic fissure eruptions. On 11 February 2026 PLOS One retracted two 2025 papers by the group, on shocked quartz and on Baffin Bay sediments, citing problems with age models and sampling. Most of the authors disagreed with the retractions.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset: 06 Abu Hureyra: a village through the cold
chunks.text: Abu Hureyra, on the Euphrates in Syria, was a village before, during and after the Younger Dryas. Andrew Moore excavated it in 1972 and 1973 in a race against the Tabqa Dam; the site now lies under Lake Assad. Plant remains suggested that villagers leaned harder on hardy wild plants as the cold set in, and one team argued they began to cultivate rye, a claim others dispute. In 2020 Moore and colleagues reported melted glass with minerals formed above 2,200 °C, which they read as an airburst over the village. Critics had earlier argued that similar glassy droplets in Syrian sites formed when buildings and plant material burned. Because the site is drowned, the samples collected half a century ago are all there is.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Reset: 07 The sudden spring
chunks.text: The end was as dramatic as the start. At 11,703 years before 2000 CE, Greenland warmed by several degrees within decades, and some ice indicators flipped within one to three years. That moment is the official beginning of the Holocene, the age we still live in. The leading explanation for both switches is a stall and restart of the Atlantic's overturning circulation, set off by meltwater from the North American ice sheet. It is well supported, though the meltwater's route and timing are still debated. Ancient writers sensed that the world moves in cycles of catastrophe and renewal. In Plato's Timaeus, an Egyptian priest tells the Athenian Solon that his people's memory is short because it has been repeatedly wiped out: There have been, and will be again, many destructions of mankind arising out of many causes; the greatest have been brought about by the agencies of fire and water, and other lesser ones by innumerable other causes. The Younger Dryas shows that at least the climate half of that idea is real: the world can reset within a lifetime. Whether fire from the sky played a part remains, on present evidence, unsupported but not beyond testing. Finely dated sediment cores, blind tests of markers by independent labs and a crater or airburst signature of the right age would settle it.

chunks.heading: The First Monuments
chunks.text: 06 11,700–9,000 years ago The First Monuments As the climate steadied, people who were not yet farmers raised carved stone pillars, a stone tower and the first domesticated crops. ▲ Rise. Did monuments come before farming, and why build them at all? The claim on the scales Göbekli Tepe's builders inherited their astronomy and engineering from survivors of a lost ice-age civilisation. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Everything found so far points to local roots: the flint and limestone come from the plateau, the tools are regional Pre-Pottery Neolithic types, the animals carved are the local fauna, and the building tradition develops over centuries at a dozen neighbouring sites, with earlier Natufian and Epipalaeolithic precedents. The site's excavators reject the comet reading of Pillar 43. No foreign material or technology has appeared. The inheritance idea awaits evidence. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Before the 1990s, textbooks confidently taught that farming came first and monuments followed. They were wrong, and the correction came from Göbekli Tepe. Today's labels have caught up on the date but often still call it 'the world's first temple', a label its current excavators question now that houses, cisterns and everyday tools have been found there. What is solid Göbekli Tepe's monumental enclosures, with T-shaped pillars up to c. 5.5 m tall, were built from c. 9500 BCE by people without domesticated crops or animals. Dietrich et al. 2012; Schmidt 2012 A related site, Karahan Tepe, has a room cut into the bedrock with pillars and a carved human head, part of a cluster of similar sites in the Şanlıurfa region. Karul 2021 The Tower of Jericho, 8.5 m tall with an internal stair of 22 steps, was built c. 8000 BCE, before pottery. Kenyon 1957; Barkai & Liran 2011 Domesticated cereals appear in the Fertile Crescent by c. 10,500 years ago, and goats were being herded in the Zagros by c. 10,000 years ago. Zeder 2011; Zeder & Hesse 2000 The Holocene began 11,700 years before 2000 CE, and sea level rose about 15 m per thousand years through most of this age. Walker et al. 2009; Lambeck et al. 2014 What is disputed Whether Göbekli Tepe was mainly a ritual centre where few people lived, or a settlement where ritual and daily life mixed. Whether carvings on Pillar 43, the 'Vulture Stone', record a comet strike or an astronomical calendar (Sweatman) or depict myth and funerary imagery (the excavators). Whether the Tower of Jericho was defensive, communal-symbolic or aligned with the midsummer sunset. Whethe

chunks.heading: The First Monuments: 01 Stone before seed
chunks.text: On a limestone ridge above the Harran plain in southeastern Türkiye, c. 11,500 years ago, people are cutting a pillar out of the bedrock. They have stone tools, rope, wood and many hands, and no domesticated plants or animals at all. When the T-shaped pillar stands, it gets arms, hands, a belt and a fox-pelt loincloth: a stylised giant in stone. Around it, foxes, boars, snakes and vultures are carved in relief. The climate had just steadied after the Younger Dryas. The world was warmer, wetter and, for the first time in a hundred thousand years, reliably so. In this age, the first known monuments rose, the first crops were tamed, and the sea kept climbing over the old coasts. Göbekli Tepe was built by foragers. The textbooks had the order backwards.

chunks.heading: The First Monuments: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: Radiocarbon dates put Göbekli Tepe's great enclosures at c. 9500 BCE and later. The central pillars of Enclosure D stand about 5.5 m high and the largest may weigh about 10 t. The builders were hunter-gatherers who processed wild cereals on a huge scale, with thousands of grinding stones, and feasted on gazelle and wild cattle. Since 2021 the Taş Tepeler project has revealed a whole landscape of related sites. At Karahan Tepe, some 46 km away, a room cut into the bedrock is filled with pillars and watched by a human head carved from the wall. The discovery overturned a settled idea. For most of the 20th century it was taught that monumental building needed farming surpluses, towns and rulers. Göbekli Tepe shows the reverse order in this region: gathering and building came first, and domestication followed in the same area. Genetic studies trace domesticated einkorn wheat to wild stands on Karacadağ, a volcanic mountain in the same region.

chunks.heading: The First Monuments: 03 A tower at Jericho
chunks.text: In the Jordan Valley, c. 8000 BCE, the people of Jericho built a stone tower 8.5 m high, about 9 m across at its base, with a stair of 22 steps inside. It is more than 5,000 years older than the Great Pyramid. Kathleen Kenyon, who excavated it in the 1950s, saw a fortification; later researchers doubted that, since no enemy is known. A side section of a tapering stone tower, 8.5 metres tall, about 9 metres wide at the base and 7 at the top, built of horizontal stone courses. A diagonal staircase of 22 steps rises inside from an entrance at the base to the top. To the right, a lower town wall and a 1.7 metre person give scale. Top left, a sun with a dashed line to the tower top is labelled midsummer sunset, proposed alignment. A note says it was built with stone tools, before pottery, around 8000 BCE. In 2011 Ran Barkai and Roy Liran argued that on the midsummer evening the shadow of a nearby mountain first falls on the tower and then spreads over the town, and suggested it was a communal monument meant to bind people together. That reading is possible but hard to test. What is solid is the effort: a large, organised project, in a pre-pottery village.

chunks.heading: The First Monuments: 04 The slow taming of wheat
chunks.text: Farming did not arrive as a sudden invention. Wild einkorn, barley and emmer drop their seeds when ripe. Harvesting and replanting slowly favoured rare plants whose ears stay whole, and plant remains from sites across the Fertile Crescent show those plants taking over across two to three thousand years. By c. 10,500 years ago domesticated cereals are clear; by c. 10,000 years ago goats were being herded in the Zagros mountains of Iran. Step 1 of 4. Wild einkorn: when ripe, the ear shatters and the grains fall to the ground and sow themselves. Wild einkorn: when ripe, the ear shatters and the grains fall to the ground and sow themselves. Harvesters cutting ripe stands take home the rare plants whose ears stay whole; the rest has already fallen. Sowing saved grain year after year lets the tough-eared plants spread through the fields. After two to three thousand years the crop is domesticated: its ears wait for the farmer, and it depends on people to be sown. Left, plants of einkorn wheat standing on soil. Step 1 shows a wild ear dropping its grains. Step 2 shows a shattered wild ear beside a rare ear that keeps its grains, with a curved sickle over it. Step 3 shows a field of mostly whole ears with a few shattering ones. Step 4 shows a field where every ear is whole. Right, a bar chart of the share of tough ears grows from almost none to nearly all across four stages labelled wild, first, centuries and millennia. People also moved plants and animals by sea. Farmers reached Cyprus in this age, carrying cattle, goats, pigs and deer across tens of kilometres of open water. At Shillourokambos, c. 9,500 years ago, a person was buried with a cat, the oldest known burial of the kind.

chunks.heading: The First Monuments: 05 Inheritance from a lost world?
chunks.text: Graham Hancock sees Göbekli Tepe as too sophisticated to be a first attempt. In his reading it appears soon after the Younger Dryas catastrophe, perhaps built with help or knowledge from survivors of a lost ice-age civilisation. Martin Sweatman argues that the carvings of Pillar 43 encode the date of a comet impact. Robert Schoch, a geologist, argues that deep weathering of the Sphinx enclosure at Giza points to an age far older than the 4th Dynasty. These are real questions, fairly asked, but the evidence so far points inward. The Göbekli builders used local flint and limestone, made regional tool types and carved local animals. Their building tradition can be traced developing across a dozen neighbouring sites and back into Natufian round houses. The excavators interpret the Pillar 43 carvings as myth and funerary imagery. Sophistication, the finds suggest, was home-grown.

chunks.heading: The First Monuments: 06 Rising seas and stories of the flood
chunks.text: Through this age the sea rose by around 35–40 m. The floor of the Persian Gulf, a broad river valley during the Ice Age, was progressively flooded, and reached roughly its modern shoreline only about 6,000 years ago. Lowlands from the North Sea to Sundaland went under. Stories of a great flood are among the most widespread in human tradition. In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened. Then We opened the gates of the heaven with rain pouring down. And caused the earth to burst with springs, and the waters met for a matter already predestined. Believers read these accounts as sacred history with moral meaning, and many scholars read the Mesopotamian flood stories, including Gilgamesh, as rooted in real river floods. What can be tested is narrower: did people live through seas that drowned their land? Yes, repeatedly, and within living memory. Whether any specific text remembers post-glacial sea rise, a later local flood, or something else is open. It is a question to hold with care rather than a finding.

chunks.heading: The First Monuments: 07 What is still buried
chunks.text: Only a small part of Göbekli Tepe has been excavated, and most Taş Tepeler sites have barely been touched. Geophysical surveys hint at more enclosures and buildings under the mound. The coasts of this age, where the richest fishing and gathering sites probably were, are 20–60 m underwater. And the meanings of the pillars' animals, the reasons for filling in enclosures, the songs sung at the gatherings, are gone. What would change the picture: full excavation of more Taş Tepeler sites, underwater survey of the early Holocene coasts of the Gulf and eastern Mediterranean, and further scientific dating of the Sphinx enclosure's weathering. This age marks a rise, but a rise built on older foundations that we are only beginning to see.

chunks.heading: The Green Sahara
chunks.text: 07 c. 9,000–5,500 years ago The Green Sahara The world's biggest hot desert held lakes, hippos and painters, until the rains moved south and a whole people walked toward the Nile. ↕ Rise and fall. When the Sahara dried, did its refugees help make Egypt? The claim on the scales As the Green Sahara dried, its people moved toward the Nile and the Sahel, and their herding culture helped shape early Egypt. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The first half of the claim is strongly supported: hundreds of radiocarbon dates track people leaving the drying eastern Sahara for the Nile valley, oases and the south between about 5300 and 3500 BCE. The second half is harder to test. Cattle burials and cattle symbolism at Nabta Playa and in early Egyptian art are suggestive, and Egypt's own population was mixed, but no single line of evidence traces particular beliefs from desert herders into Pharaonic religion. So the whole claim rates as plausible, not strong. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact School histories of Egypt still often begin on the Nile, as if the desert had always been empty; that is underconfident about a well-evidenced Saharan prelude. Popular accounts go the other way on timing, presenting a single abrupt 'switch' 5,500 years ago as settled. The records disagree: some show an abrupt end, others a slow fade, and the end came earlier in the north than in the south. What is solid Much of the Sahara was wetter and greener during the African Humid Period, roughly 11,000 to 5,500 years ago, with lakes, grassland and savanna animals. deMenocal et al. 2000; Tierney et al. 2017 Lakeside cemeteries at Gobero, Niger, hold about 200 burials from two cultures, with bones of fish, crocodiles and hippos. Sereno et al. 2008 Radiocarbon-dated sites show people leaving the eastern Sahara for the Nile valley and the Sahel as the rains failed, with the Egyptian Sahara largely abandoned outside oases by about 3500 BCE. Kuper and Kröpelin 2006 A sharp cold event about 8,200 years ago is recorded in ice cores and across the Northern Hemisphere, and it marks the start of the Northgrippian Age of the Holocene. Alley et al. 1997; Walker et al. 2019 The Black Sea was once a lake that the Mediterranean reconnected with in the early Holocene. Ryan et al. 1997; Yanko-Hombach et al. 2007 What is disputed Whether the Green Sahara ended abruptly around 5,500 years ago or drained away gradually over two millennia, and whether that timing differed from north to south. Whether the Black Sea filled in a catastrophic deluge in months, or rose over d

chunks.heading: The Green Sahara: 01 Hippos in the Ténéré
chunks.text: Stand at Gobero, in the Ténéré desert of Niger, and the horizon is sand in every direction. In 2000 a team led by palaeontologist Paul Sereno, out looking for dinosaurs, found something stranger: human skeletons weathering out of the dunes beside the bones of large fish, crocodiles and hippos. About 200 graves turned up, left by two peoples. The Kiffian people fished a lake here from roughly 9,700 to 8,200 years ago. After a dry gap, the Tenerian people buried their dead in the same spot from about 7,200 to 4,500 years ago. One Tenerian grave holds a woman and two children laid close together, and pollen in the grave hints that flowers were placed with them. This is the African Humid Period, the Green Sahara. For thousands of years the world's largest hot desert was a patchwork of grassland, scrub, wetlands and lakes. It is one of the clearest cases on Earth of a landscape that looks eternal and is not, and it sets up this age's question: when the water left, where did the people go, and what did they carry with them? The emptiest place on the map was once a lakeshore with fishermen, hippos and funerals.

chunks.heading: The Green Sahara: 02 Reading a vanished monsoon
chunks.text: The cause was astronomical. Earth's axis wobbles on a cycle of about 23,000 years, and around 11,000 years ago that wobble gave the Northern Hemisphere its strongest summer sunshine. North Africa heated up, pulled in moist Atlantic air, and the West African monsoon pushed hundreds of kilometres further north than it reaches today. Leaf waxes in marine sediments suggest that parts of the western Sahara received many times today's rainfall. The lakes were the most spectacular result. Ancient shorelines show that Lake Chad, today a shrinking wetland, swelled into Lake Mega-Chad, which by some estimates covered around 350,000 km², roughly the area of Germany. Smaller lakes filled in the Fezzan of Libya, in northern Chad and in the Nubian desert of Sudan. Painters on the Tassili plateau recorded giraffes, elephants and, later, herds of spotted cattle. Step 1 of 4. Today: the Sahara, with the desert's southern edge near 15° north and a small Lake Chad. Today: the Sahara, with the desert's southern edge near 15° north and a small Lake Chad. c. 9,000–6,000 years ago: a stronger monsoon brings grassland far north and fills great lakes. People: fishers at Gobero, painters at Tassili and Sefar, herders at Nabta Playa. From c. 5300 BCE: the rains retreat south, lakes shrink, and people move toward the Nile and the Sahel. A map of North Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. Step one shows today's desert with the Sahel edge near 15 degrees north and a small Lake Chad. Step two adds green grassland reaching far north and large lakes: Mega-Chad, lakes in the Fezzan and the West Nubian palaeolake. Step three marks people: Gobero, Tassili and Sefar, Wadi Sura and Nabta Playa. Step four shows the lakes shrinking to dashed outlines, the green belt retreating south, and arrows of people

chunks.heading: The Green Sahara: 03 The cold snap of 8,200 years ago
chunks.text: Even in the green millennia the climate could lurch. Around 8,200 years ago, giant meltwater lakes left by the North American ice sheet drained into the North Atlantic. The fresh water appears to have weakened the ocean currents that carry heat north. Greenland ice records a cooling of about 3.3 °C in under 20 years, with the coldest spell lasting a few decades and the whole event about a century and a half. The shock is so widely recorded that geologists now use it to mark the start of a formal slice of time, the Northgrippian Age. Much of the Northern Hemisphere turned drier. In Anatolia, the famous town of Çatalhöyük, home to perhaps a few thousand people who walked across the rooftops and climbed down ladders into their houses, reorganised around this time, and by about 6000 BCE its people had moved to a new mound across the river. Whether the cold snap pushed them, or merely coincided with changes already under way, is still argued. Some villages in the Near East show disruption; others, such as Tell Sabi Abyad in Syria, carried on.

chunks.heading: The Green Sahara: 04 Did the sea break into the Black Sea?
chunks.text: In 1997 two marine geologists at Columbia University, William Ryan and Walter Pitman, made a thrilling proposal. At the end of the Ice Age, they argued, the Black Sea was a freshwater lake lying far below the level of the rising Mediterranean. Around 7,600 years ago (a date later revised to about 8,800) the sea topped the Bosporus sill and poured in. By their estimate about 50 km³ of water rushed through every day for at least 300 days, drowning roughly 100,000 km² of shoreline. Farmers who fled, they suggested, carried the memory of a world lost to water into the flood stories of Mesopotamia and beyond. Their strongest evidence came from the seabed: freshwater mollusc shells abruptly replaced by Mediterranean species, and drowned beaches and dunes far below today's water line. In 1999 an expedition led by Robert Ballard reported an ancient shoreline about 150 metres down off Sinop in Türkiye. Critics pushed back hard. Ali Aksu, Richard Hiscott and colleagues argued from cores near the Bosporus that the Black Sea had been flowing out into the Mediterranean, not the other way, which would rule out a waterfall. Valentina Yanko-Hombach and others reported no archaeological sign of a catastrophic submergence of settlements. Today many researchers accept a real reconnection and a rise in the Black Sea, but argue over its speed, with estimates ranging from a months-long deluge to a 'fast transgression' over decades or a couple of centuries. The flood case weighs the memory question in detail. A real sea did rise over real land. What remains open is whether it came as a deluge anyone would remember.

chunks.heading: The Green Sahara: 05 Turning off the tap
chunks.text: As summer sunshine weakened, the monsoon slowly retreated south. How fast the Sahara then dried is a live argument. The dust record off Mauritania shows a sharp switch around 5,500 years ago. But when Stefan Kröpelin's team cored Lake Yoa in northern Chad, one of the few Saharan lakes that never dried, they found a gradual change in its pollen over about two thousand years. A 2015 study concluded that the end was time-transgressive: earlier in the north, later in the south. People followed the water. Kuper and Kröpelin compiled radiocarbon dates from archaeological sites across the eastern Sahara and found occupation retreating from about 5300 BCE onward, toward the Sudanese Sahel, the oases and the Nile. By about 3500 BCE the Egyptian Sahara was largely empty, and the valley was filling with the villages that would, within a few centuries, become a unified kingdom. At Nabta Playa in southern Egypt, herders had already buried cattle in stone-covered tombs and set up a small ring of standing stones. Some scholars see a line from that cattle-centred world to the cow goddesses of Pharaonic Egypt. It is a fair suggestion, not yet a demonstration. Arabia went through the same cycle. Its own humid phase filled lakes in the Nefud before the rains failed, which is worth remembering whenever old stories speak of lost peoples and cities in the sands, such as the tradition weighed in the case of Iram of the pillars.

chunks.heading: The Green Sahara: 06 What the sand keeps, and what it erased
chunks.text: The Green Sahara is a textbook example of evidence destroyed by time. Wind has stripped away many lakeshore camps; dunes have buried others. Rock paintings rarely contain anything that can be radiocarbon dated, so their ages rest on style sequences and on dates from nearby deposits, and some famous copies made in the 1950s were later exposed as embellished or even invented. The drowned Black Sea shelf, where any flooded farming villages would lie, has scarcely been searched. Directly dated pigments or mineral crusts on Round Head paintings would anchor the art to the climate record. Systematic survey of the drowned Black Sea shelf, below 50 metres, could find or rule out flooded villages. Ancient DNA from Saharan burials such as Gobero, compared with early Nile valley genomes, could test whether desert herders fed into Egypt's population. The lesson of this age is the one this whole timeline keeps teaching. A desert can be a garden, a lake can be a sea, and an empty map can hide a crowded past.

chunks.heading: First Cities and Writing
chunks.text: 08 c. 5,500–4,200 years ago First Cities and Writing In a few centuries, on four continents, people built cities, pyramids and scripts, and one of those scripts still refuses to be read. ▲ Rise. Did civilisation start here, or is something older hiding underneath? The claim on the scales The core of the Great Sphinx was carved thousands of years before Khafre, by an older, forgotten culture. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The weathering pattern is real and Schoch is a serious geologist. But other geologists explain it through salt crystallisation, softer limestone members and the rains that still fell in the early third millennium BCE. The archaeology points one way: the Sphinx Temple was built from blocks cut out of the Sphinx ditch, the enclosure sits against Khafre's causeway, and no tools, pottery, hearths or buildings of an older culture have been found on the plateau. A dated older layer would change this rating. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Museum labels state flatly that Khafre built the Sphinx. That is the best reading, but it rests on context, not an inscription: no contemporary text names him as its builder. The textbooks are slightly overconfident about the attribution, and too dismissive of the fact that the weathering question was raised by a qualified geologist. The challenger case, though, still lacks any artefact from the supposed older culture. What is solid Proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk date to about 3300–3100 BCE, and most record administration rather than stories. Englund 1998; Woods 2010 Writing was invented independently at least three times: in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably also in Egypt. Woods 2010 The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu around 2560 BCE, and a logbook by an official named Merer records limestone deliveries to it. Lehner 1997; Tallet and Lehner 2021 Mohenjo-daro covered about 250 hectares, with hundreds of wells and street drains, at its height around 2500 BCE. Kenoyer 1998 Caral in Peru was a planned monumental centre by about 2600 BCE, without pottery and without known fortifications. Shady Solís et al. 2001 What is disputed Whether the Indus script records a spoken language at all, and which one. How the Great Pyramid's blocks were raised, and how large the workforce was. Whether the Great Sphinx was carved under Khafre around 2500 BCE or reworked from a much older monument. Whether Egyptian writing was inspired by Mesopotamian contact or invented on its own. What time has hidden Most early writing was on perishable media (papyrus, wo

chunks.heading: First Cities and Writing: 01 Somebody needed to count the barley
chunks.text: Uruk, southern Iraq, around 3200 BCE. The city is enormous for its time, with perhaps tens of thousands of people, temple precincts faced with mosaics of coloured clay cones, and canals branching off the Euphrates. In a storeroom an official wets a lump of clay, flattens it, and presses a reed into it: a sign for barley, marks for quantities, a sign group that may be a name or a job title. About 85% of the earliest tablets are records like this, of rations, sheep, workers and beer. Nobody here thinks they are inventing history. They are trying not to lose track of the grain. Within a few centuries of this moment, the world changes shape. Cities, kings, scripts, standard weights and monuments appear in Mesopotamia, then Egypt, the Indus valley, China's Yangtze delta and the desert coast of Peru. It looks like a starting gun. The question for this age is whether it really was one, or whether we are seeing only the first chapter that happened to be written on clay and stone. Writing was not invented for poetry. It was invented because a city could no longer remember its own accounts.

chunks.heading: First Cities and Writing: 02 Four starts, not one
chunks.text: The striking thing about this age is that it happened more than once. Egypt's earliest hieroglyphs, on small bone and ivory labels from a tomb at Abydos, date to about 3250 BCE, and around 3100 BCE the Nile valley was united under one king. Writing was invented independently at least three times in world history, in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably in Egypt as well. A timeline from 3600 to 1800 BCE with six horizontal lanes. Mesopotamia's bar starts about 3500 BCE with the first tablets at 3300 BCE. Egypt's begins with unification at 3100 BCE and marks the Great Pyramid at 2560 BCE, then breaks at 2181 BCE. The Indus bar runs from 2600 to 1900 BCE. China's Liangzhu runs from 3300 to 2300 BCE with dams about 3100 BCE. Peru's Caral runs from 2600 to 2000 BCE. Britain's Stonehenge runs from 3000 BCE with the sarsen circle at 2500 BCE. A shaded band at 2200 BCE marks the 4.2 kiloyear drought. In the Indus valley, cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa reached their mature form around 2600 BCE. Mohenjo-daro covered about 250 hectares and housed perhaps 40,000 people. Its builders used bricks of standard proportions, sank more than 700 wells, and ran covered drains along the streets, a level of municipal plumbing many European towns did not match until the 19th century. The Great Bath, a waterproofed brick pool about 12 by 7 metres and 2.4 metres deep, still has its steps. On the other side of the world, in Peru's Supe valley, Caral was a planned centre of platform mounds and sunken circular plazas by about 2600 BCE, as radiocarbon dates published in Science in 2001 showed. Its people had no pottery and, as far as excavators can tell, no walls, weapons or massacre graves. In China, the Liangzhu culture built a system of earthen dams more than 5,000 years ago

chunks.heading: First Cities and Writing: 03 Pyramids and the paperwork of Khufu
chunks.text: Egypt's builders moved from mud-brick tombs to Djoser's Step Pyramid around 2650 BCE, and within a century to the Great Pyramid of Khufu, finished around 2560 BCE at about 146.6 metres tall. It stayed the tallest human-made structure for around 3,800 years. In 2013, at the Red Sea harbour of Wadi al-Jarf, Pierre Tallet's team found the oldest inscribed papyri yet known: the logbook of an inspector named Merer, whose crew of about 40 men shipped white limestone from the Tura quarries to Giza. In 2024 satellite radar and sediment cores revealed a buried branch of the Nile running beside 31 pyramids, which probably served as their transport canal. Merer's diary gives the building in the words of someone who was there: dates, sailing times, a basin called the 'Lake of Khufu' near the site. It confirms an organised, provisioned workforce, not slaves under whips. It does not tell us how the blocks were lifted; that remains one of the most argued questions in archaeology.

chunks.heading: First Cities and Writing: 04 The script that will not speak
chunks.text: About 5,000 Indus inscriptions are known, mostly on small stone seals carved with animals such as the 'unicorn' bull. They average about five signs each, and scholars count somewhere between 400 and 700 distinct signs. Dozens of decipherments have been announced; none has produced readings that others can check against new finds. A 2009 statistical study argued the sign sequences behave like language, while critics argue the inscriptions are too short to tell. In 2025 the government of Tamil Nadu offered a prize of US$1 million to anyone who can crack it. This is a reminder of how fragile knowledge is. A whole civilisation of perhaps a million or more people across an area larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined left us thousands of messages, and we cannot read one of them.

chunks.heading: First Cities and Writing: 05 The Sphinx question
chunks.text: Here the challengers have a real argument. In 1991 geologist Robert Schoch, encouraged by the writer John Anthony West, told the Geological Society of America that the walls of the Sphinx enclosure look rain-weathered: deep vertical fissures and a rounded, rolling profile. Long periods of rainfall, he argued, point to a time before the Old Kingdom, when Egypt was wetter. Graham Hancock and others took this as a clue that the dynastic Egyptians inherited a much older monument from a forgotten culture. The mainstream reply, led by Egyptologist Mark Lehner and geologists such as K. Lal Gauri and James Harrell, is that the limestone layers of the enclosure are of very different hardness, that salts drawn up from the ground and dissolved by dew crumble the rock quickly, and that occasional heavy rains still fell in the third millennium BCE. The archaeological context is harder to wave away: the blocks of the Sphinx Temple were quarried from the Sphinx ditch itself, and the enclosure respects the line of Khafre's causeway. After a century of digging on the plateau, no pottery, tools or hearths of an older culture have been found. The weathering question was fair to ask. What the older-Sphinx theory still lacks is a single object left by the people who supposedly carved it.

chunks.heading: First Cities and Writing: 06 What the clay does not show
chunks.text: This age may look like the beginning mainly because clay and stone survive. Papyrus, wood, textiles and bamboo usually do not. The deepest levels of Uruk and Mohenjo-daro sit at or below the water table and have barely been reached, and the Nile's floodplain has buried its earliest towns under metres of silt. Caral itself was dismissed as a late site until radiocarbon dates showed it was as old as the pyramids. And earlier chapters did exist: Göbekli Tepe's enclosures were already 6,000 years old when Uruk's scribes pressed their first signs, and Çatalhöyük housed thousands of people long before any king. The first cities were not a bolt from the blue. They were the part of a much longer story that started keeping records.

chunks.heading: The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse
chunks.text: 09 c. 4,300–3,900 years ago The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse Dust storms, failed floods and empty cities: the first recorded age of collapse is so clear that geologists named an age after it. ▼ Fall. Did one megadrought bring down the first empires? The claim on the scales A global megadrought around 4,200 years ago caused the fall of the Akkadian empire, Egypt's Old Kingdom and the Indus cities. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established Part of this holds up well: many records from the eastern Mediterranean to India show a sharp dry, dusty phase, and its timing fits the end of Akkad and the Old Kingdom closely. Other parts do not: the Indus cities declined some three centuries later and gradually, Liangzhu fell earlier and apparently to floods, and in Egypt the Old Kingdom was already fragmenting. Drought looks like a powerful stress on fragile states, not a single global switch. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Older textbooks blamed Akkad's fall on invading Gutians, repeating a Mesopotamian poem, and treated Egypt's First Intermediate Period as purely political. Newer popular accounts swing to the opposite certainty, a planet-wide drought toppling empires. The evidence sits between: a real, regionally severe drying whose effects depended on how each society was already organised. Both versions have been more confident than the record allows. What is solid A climate shift around 4,200 years ago is recorded widely enough that it marks the start of the Meghalayan Age, the latest formal slice of the Holocene, from 4,250 years before 2000 CE. Walker et al. 2018; Walker et al. 2019 Tell Leilan in northeast Syria was abandoned around 2200 BCE, and its abandonment layer is covered by windblown silt. Weiss et al. 1993 Egypt's Old Kingdom ended around 2181 BCE, followed by roughly 125 years of divided rule. Shaw (ed.) 2000 Drier or dustier conditions around this time are recorded in caves, lakes and marine cores from the eastern Mediterranean to India. Bini et al. 2019; Carolin et al. 2019 What is disputed Whether the drought caused the collapses, or struck states already failing for political reasons. How global the event was: some regions show drying, some show wetter conditions, and the timing differs by up to centuries. Whether the Indus decline around 1900 BCE belongs to the same event at all. Whether the Egyptian 'lament' texts describe this period or were written generations later as literature. What time has hidden Most farming villages of the period were mud-brick and have eroded or lie under later towns, so we see co

chunks.heading: The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse: 01 The first great crash
chunks.text: Around 2200 BCE the world's first empires were at a peak. Akkad, founded by Sargon, ruled from the Gulf to the upper Euphrates. Egypt's pharaohs had been building pyramids for four centuries. The Indus cities traded seals and beads as far as Mesopotamia. Within a few generations the Akkadian empire had dissolved, Egypt had split into rival lordships, and the dry-farming towns of northern Syria stood empty. A few centuries later the great Indus cities were emptying too. Ancient writers remembered it as a time of chaos. A Sumerian poem blamed Akkad's fall on a god's anger and on the Gutians, mountain people it described in unflattering terms. Modern scientists have found something the poets could only feel: dust in the caves, silt in the ruins, and a failing monsoon. As if it had been before the time when cities were built and founded, the large arable tracts yielded no grain

chunks.heading: The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse: 02 Dust on the floors of Tell Leilan
chunks.text: In 1993 Harvey Weiss and his colleagues published a paper in Science that changed the debate. At Tell Leilan, a walled city on the rain-fed plains of northeast Syria, the last Akkadian-period floors were covered by a layer of fine windblown silt, with no sign of people for about three centuries. Nearby towns showed the same pattern. Weiss argued that an abrupt drought had wrecked rain-fed farming and sent people south toward the irrigated river valleys, where the next rulers built walls to keep newcomers out. Later work filled in the climate side. A marine core from the Gulf of Oman showed a spike of dust blown from Mesopotamia. A stalagmite from Gol-e Zard cave in northern Iran, dated precisely with uranium series, recorded a surge in dust from about 4,260 to 3,970 years ago, a dry spell lasting roughly 290 years. Caves in Israel, lakes in Turkey and Italy and even the ice of Kilimanjaro record changes around the same time. Step 1 of 3. The records: dust, silt, low Nile floods and a weaker monsoon around 4,200 years ago. The records: dust, silt, low Nile floods and a weaker monsoon around 4,200 years ago. The societies: Akkad, Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Indus cities and Liangzhu. The caveats: different timings, a flood not a drought in China, and states already under strain. A map from West Africa to China. Step one marks climate records: Tell Leilan in Syria with windblown silt, Gol-e Zard cave in Iran with a dust peak, a Gulf of Oman core with a dust spike, low Nile floods, weaker monsoon in the Indus region, the Mawmluh Cave stalagmite in India, Kilimanjaro's dust layer, and Liangzhu in China marked as wetter. Step two names the societies: the Akkadian empire, Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Indus cities and Liangzhu. Step three adds caveats: some towns carried on, Egypt was

chunks.heading: The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse: 03 A golden spike in a cave
chunks.text: In 2018 the International Union of Geological Sciences made the event official. The Holocene, our current epoch, was divided into three ages, and the youngest, the Meghalayan, begins 4,250 years before 2000 CE. Its reference point is a layer in a stalagmite from Mawmluh Cave in Meghalaya, northeast India, where oxygen isotopes record a weakening of the monsoon. An ice core from Mount Logan in Canada serves as a backup. Stalagmites grow in thin layers from dripping cave water. The ratio of oxygen isotopes in each layer tracks rainfall, and tiny amounts of uranium decaying into thorium date the layers, often to within a few decades. Dust, pollen and lake levels add independent lines. When several of these move together in different places, a regional event becomes hard to doubt. Not everyone was happy. Some scientists criticised building a worldwide time boundary on one stalagmite and on an event that looks different from place to place. Jessica Tierney and others have argued that studies sometimes lumped together droughts and wet spells centuries apart and called them one event.

chunks.heading: The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse: 04 Egypt: when the Nile ran low
chunks.text: Egypt's Old Kingdom ended around 2181 BCE, after the very long reign of Pepi II. Sediments from the Nile delta suggest weak floods at this time, and tomb inscriptions of provincial governors from the following decades boast of feeding their people during famines. The most vivid, in the tomb of Ankhtifi at Mo'alla, claims that all of Upper Egypt was starving. Egyptologists note that such boasts were a standard way for a governor to praise himself, but the theme is persistent. Here care is needed with a famous text. The Admonitions of Ipuwer, a lament of a land turned upside down, contains the line usually translated as 'the river is blood'. It was long read as an eyewitness account of this collapse, and some writers have linked it to the plagues of the Exodus. But the only copy, Papyrus Leiden I 344, was written around 1250 BCE, and scholars such as Harco Willems and Stephen Quirke date its composition no earlier than the late 12th Dynasty, centuries after the Old Kingdom fell. It is best read as literature about chaos, perhaps shaped by memory of this age, not as a report from it.

chunks.heading: The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse: 05 Not one switch, but many stresses
chunks.text: The strongest objection to a single global megadrought is timing. The Indus cities did not fall around 2200 BCE. They thinned out gradually from about 1900 BCE, as people moved east toward the Ganga plain and into smaller villages, perhaps as monsoon rivers became less reliable. Liangzhu, in the Yangtze delta, collapsed around 2300 BCE, and a 2021 cave study points to extreme rainfall and flooding, not drought. In Egypt, provincial governors had been growing more powerful for generations. The geographer Karl Butzer argued that collapse happens when environmental shocks hit societies that have lost the ability to adapt: rigid elites, overstretched armies, broken trade. By that reading, the 4.2 kiloyear event was the hammer, but the empires were already cracked. Harvey Weiss's challenge was right in forcing climate into the story. The critics are right that climate alone does not write it. The drought was real. Whether it toppled empires depended on how brittle each empire already was.

chunks.heading: The 4.2 Kiloyear Collapse: 06 What we still cannot see
chunks.text: Much of this age is invisible. Village houses of mud brick have melted back into the plain, and most excavations target the big mounds. The absolute dates of the Akkadian kings shift by decades depending on which chronology is used. Few climate archives sit right beside the sites whose fate they are asked to explain, so the link is often a matter of 'about the same time, some hundreds of kilometres away'. More stalagmite and lake records beside the collapsed sites themselves, especially in Syria, Egypt and Sindh. Radiocarbon series from the final floors of many towns, not just a few famous ones, to test whether abandonment was sudden and simultaneous. Ancient DNA and isotopes from cemeteries before and after, to see who moved and who stayed. Old stories of cities destroyed by wind and drought, from Mesopotamia to Arabia, may carry distant echoes of ages like this. The Iram case looks at one of them.

chunks.heading: The Bronze Age World and its Collapse
chunks.text: 10 c. 3,600–3,150 years ago The Bronze Age World and its Collapse Kings called each other 'brother', ships carried copper from Cyprus and tin from Central Asia, then in about fifty years almost all of it burned. ▼ Fall. What brought down the first globalised world? The claim on the scales Invading Sea Peoples destroyed the Late Bronze Age civilisations. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established The Sea Peoples are real: Egyptian reliefs show their ships and captives, and Ugarit's last letters describe enemy fleets. But tree rings show a severe drought, some destructions may be earthquakes or revolts, and several cities fell without any sign of foreign attackers. Most specialists now see a cascade in which drought, famine, raids, rebellion and broken trade fed one another, with the Sea Peoples as one strand, and partly as displaced people themselves. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact For much of the 20th century textbooks told a crisp story of barbarian invaders from the sea. That was overconfident: it rested mostly on Egyptian royal propaganda. Newer textbooks present a multi-causal collapse, which fits the evidence better, but they can make it sound more settled than it is. The order and weight of the causes still differ from site to site and remain open. What is solid The Uluburun ship, wrecked off southern Türkiye around 1300 BCE, carried about 10 tonnes of copper and 1 tonne of tin, plus glass, ivory and ebony from several lands. Pulak 1998 About two-thirds of Uluburun's tin came from Kestel in Anatolia and about a third from Mušiston in Central Asia, thousands of kilometres away. Powell et al. 2022 Hattusa, Ugarit, Pylos, Mycenae and Troy VIIa were destroyed or abandoned within a few decades of 1200 BCE. Cline 2014; Knapp and Manning 2016 Linear B, deciphered as Greek by Michael Ventris in 1952, disappears with the palaces; Greek was next written in an alphabet from about the 8th century BCE. Chadwick 1958; Cline 2014 A severe three-year drought hit central Anatolia around 1198–1196 BCE. Manning et al. 2023 What is disputed Who the Sea Peoples were, where they came from, and whether they were a cause of the collapse or refugees from it. When Thera erupted: radiocarbon on an olive branch favours c. 1600 BCE, tree-ring calibrations and a 2023 olive shrub favour the mid-16th century, and some archaeologists prefer c. 1500 BCE. Whether earthquakes caused several destructions, or whether burned layers are the work of enemies. Whether the Trojan War of Greek epic remembers a real war over Wilusa (Troy). What time has h

chunks.heading: The Bronze Age World and its Collapse: 01 Metal biscuits with ears
chunks.text: In 1982 a young Turkish sponge diver told archaeologists he had seen 'metal biscuits with ears' on the sea floor off Cape Uluburun. They were copper ingots in the shape of an ox hide, and they belonged to a ship that sank around 1300 BCE. Over eleven summers of diving, a team led by George Bass and Cemal Pulak raised the Bronze Age in miniature: about ten tonnes of copper in 354 ingots, about a tonne of tin, 175 ingots of blue and turquoise glass, logs of African ebony, hippo and elephant ivory, amber, and a gold scarab with the name of Queen Nefertiti. Copper plus tin at about ten to one makes bronze, and that ship carried enough for roughly eleven tonnes of it. A 2022 study traced about two-thirds of its tin to Kestel in Anatolia and a third to Mušiston in Central Asia, thousands of kilometres from any sea. This was a connected world, and connected worlds have a weakness: they can fall together. One wreck held the raw materials of a whole civilisation, gathered from three continents.

chunks.heading: The Bronze Age World and its Collapse: 02 A club of great kings
chunks.text: Between about 1600 and 1200 BCE the eastern Mediterranean was run by a handful of powers that knew each other well. The Amarna letters, 382 clay tablets found in Egypt, preserve their correspondence from the 14th century BCE: the kings of Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti and Assyria write to Pharaoh as 'my brother', ask for gold, send horses, and negotiate royal marriages. After the great chariot battle at Kadesh, Egypt and the Hittites signed a peace treaty around 1259 BCE whose text survives in both Egyptian and Akkadian versions. On Crete the Minoans had built palaces with light wells, drains and painted walls, and wrote in Linear A, still unread. On Thera, the island now called Santorini, a whole town was buried by one of the largest eruptions of the last ten thousand years. When exactly is fiercely argued: radiocarbon on a buried olive branch favours about 1600 BCE, while tree-ring calibrations and an olive shrub published in 2023 favour the middle of the 16th century. The Atlantis case examines whether Plato's story could remember it. After about 1450 BCE Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos and wrote their accounts in Linear B, an early form of Greek. Step 1 of 5. c. 1300 BCE: a network of palaces and great kings; the Uluburun ship carries copper and tin. c. 1300 BCE: a network of palaces and great kings; the Uluburun ship carries copper and tin. c. 1200 BCE: stresses pile up: drought in Anatolia, earthquakes, raiders at sea. c. 1200–1180 BCE: palaces burn or are abandoned, and the links break. c. 1177 BCE: Ramesses III fights the Sea Peoples on Egypt's border. After c. 1150 BCE: survivors and a long quiet; Greece loses writing for about 400 years. chunks.heading: The Bronze Age World and its Collapse: 03 The fifty years that ended an age
chunks.text: Then, in the decades around 1200 BCE, almost every palace in the network was destroyed or abandoned. Pylos burned, preserving its clay archive by baking it. Mycenae's citadel was damaged and later abandoned as a seat of power. Hattusa, the Hittite capital, was emptied. Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, was destroyed around 1185 BCE and never rebuilt. Troy VIIa burned. In Egypt, Ramesses III recorded on his temple at Medinet Habu how in his 8th year, around 1177 BCE, he defeated a coalition of peoples from the sea. My father, behold, the enemy's ships came (here); my cities (?) were burned, and they did evil things in my country. For decades that was the whole story: barbarians from the sea. The evidence now shows a more tangled picture. Tree rings from Gordion show three consecutive severe drought years around 1198–1196 BCE. Letters from Ugarit and Hatti beg for grain shipments. Some ruins look like earthquake damage. Some cities were burned with no weapons in the streets, which could mean revolt. The archaeologist Eric Cline calls it a 'perfect storm': a system so interconnected that when several stresses hit at once, each failure made the next more likely.

chunks.heading: The Bronze Age World and its Collapse: 04 The challenger: a Luwian world war?
chunks.text: Geoarchaeologist Eberhard Zangger argues that historians have missed a whole civilisation. Western Anatolia, he points out, was home to Luwian-speaking kingdoms such as Arzawa, the Seha River Land and Wilusa (Homer's Ilios), and it is dotted with hundreds of large settlement mounds that have never been excavated. His thesis is that wars launched by these states, a 'World War Zero', were the core of the collapse, and that the Sea Peoples were largely their fleets. The geographical point is fair, and Hittite texts do show powerful western kingdoms. But the case suffered a blow when a long hieroglyphic Luwian inscription that Zangger and a colleague published in 2017 turned out to rest entirely on drawings left by the late James Mellaart; in 2019 Zangger himself reported evidence that Mellaart had fabricated material. Without excavation, the world-war scenario remains a hypothesis. Its useful demand stands, though: dig the mounds.

chunks.heading: The Bronze Age World and its Collapse: 05 Four hundred years without writing
chunks.text: The most striking loss was knowledge itself. Linear B was a palace tool, used by scribes to count sheep, bronze and perfumed oil. When the palaces fell, so did the need for it, and Greece became illiterate. When Greeks wrote again, from around the 8th century BCE, they used an alphabet borrowed from the Phoenicians, and they remembered their Bronze Age only through poetry: heroes, a war at Troy, a palace with a labyrinth. When Michael Ventris showed in 1952 that Linear B was Greek, the tablets turned out to be mostly inventories, not epics. Egypt survived but shrank, losing its empire in Canaan and, after about 1070 BCE, its unity. Assyria endured. Phoenician cities such as Tyre and Sidon recovered fastest and spread a new, simpler way of writing that most alphabets descend from. Iron, available locally in many places, gradually replaced bronze, which had depended on long trade routes. A whole civilisation forgot how to write, and remembered its past only as a story of heroes.

chunks.heading: The Bronze Age World and its Collapse: 06 What the fire kept and what it took
chunks.text: Ironically, destruction preserved our best evidence. Clay tablets survive because burning buildings baked them hard, so we read the last weeks of Ugarit and Pylos in detail and know far less about the years before. Wooden writing boards, mentioned in texts and found at Uluburun, have almost all rotted away. Western Anatolia, the key region for the Sea Peoples question, is still largely unexcavated. Excavating large western Anatolian mounds would test the Luwian hypothesis directly. More annually dated tree-ring and cave records from Greece, Cyprus and the Levant would show how far the drought reached. A decipherment of Linear A or Cypro-Minoan would give Crete and Cyprus their own voice.

chunks.heading: The Axial and Classical Age
chunks.text: 11 c. 800 BCE–400 CE The Axial and Classical Age Philosophers, prophets, a bronze computer, self-healing concrete and a library that tried to hold every book, and most of what they wrote is gone. ▲ Rise. How much did the ancients know that we later lost? The claim on the scales Hellenistic science reached a nearly modern level and was then lost for more than a thousand years. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established The loss was real and large: most scientific works vanished, and nothing as complex as the Antikythera mechanism survives for over a millennium. But 'lost' is too strong. Euclid, Ptolemy, Galen and Archimedes were preserved in Greek in Byzantium and translated and extended in Arabic, and that relay fed Europe's revival. And 'nearly modern' overstates: systematic experiment and physics built on it did not develop in antiquity in the way it did later. Half of the claim fits the evidence well. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact School histories tend to present classical knowledge as having been passed down, dimmed in a 'Dark Age' and then revived. That story is too tidy in two directions. It understates how much was lost (for many authors, well under a tenth of their work) and it overstates the darkness, ignoring the Greek East and the Arabic translators who kept and extended the sciences. What is solid Eratosthenes estimated the Earth's circumference around 240 BCE from shadow angles at Syene and Alexandria. Cleomedes, On the Heavens 1.7 The Antikythera mechanism, from a wreck of about 70–60 BCE, used around 30 surviving bronze gears to model the Sun, Moon and eclipse cycles. Freeth et al. 2006; Freeth et al. 2021 Roman concrete contains lime clasts from hot mixing that can reseal cracks, and the Pantheon's 43.3-metre dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome. Whether the Antikythera mechanism was a one-off masterpiece or one of many lost instruments.
