chunks.heading: The Axial and Classical Age: 01 A computer on the sea floor
chunks.text: In 1901 sponge divers working a Roman-era wreck off the Greek island of Antikythera brought up statues, glass, coins and a lump of corroded bronze. It later cracked open to reveal gear teeth. Over the following century, and especially since X-ray tomography in the 2000s, researchers have shown that the Antikythera mechanism was a hand-cranked model of the heavens: around 30 surviving bronze gears tracked the Sun and Moon, the Moon's phases and a cycle of eclipses, and inscriptions refer to the planets. The ship sank around 70–60 BCE. Nothing of comparable complexity survives from the next thousand years; simpler geared calendars are known from Byzantium around 500 CE and from the writings of al-Biruni in the 11th century. It is the single best object for this age's big question. The Classical world was not just temples and poetry. It had mathematics, instruments and engineering that were later forgotten, at least in part. How much, and how completely, is the argument. The Antikythera mechanism is a message from a technical tradition whose other products have simply vanished.

chunks.heading: The Axial and Classical Age: 02 An age of big questions
chunks.text: In 1949 the philosopher Karl Jaspers noticed something strange. Between roughly 800 and 200 BCE, in lands with little contact, people began asking new questions about justice, suffering and how to live. Greek philosophers argued about the nature of the world; Hebrew prophets preached justice for the poor; the Upanishads explored the self; the Buddha taught a path out of suffering; Confucius and the Daoist thinkers debated order and virtue. Jaspers called it the Axial Age. When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it Whether it was one connected turning point is debated. A 2018 study using a global historical database found that the key changes were spread over a longer period and appeared earlier in some places than others. Dates for several founders, including the Buddha and Zarathustra, are uncertain by a century or more. But the explosion of recorded thought is real, and much of the world's religious and philosophical vocabulary still comes from it.

chunks.heading: The Axial and Classical Age: 03 Measuring the world
chunks.text: The Greek-speaking scientists of Alexandria did astonishing things with simple tools. Around 240 BCE Eratosthenes compared the Sun's angle at Syene and at Alexandria at noon and worked out the Earth's circumference; depending on the length of his stade, his answer was somewhere between about 2% and 16% off the true value. Aristarchus of Samos proposed that the Earth goes round the Sun. Hipparchus catalogued stars and discovered the slow shift of the equinoxes. Hero of Alexandria described a steam-driven spinning ball and automated theatres. In Rome, builders mixed quicklime with volcanic ash and water while hot, creating concrete with lime clasts that can reseal cracks when water seeps in, a trick rediscovered by researchers in 2023. The Pantheon's dome, 43.3 metres across and finished around 125 CE, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. In Han China, officials counted 57.7 million people in 2 CE, papermaking was reported to the court in 105 CE, and the astronomer Zhang Heng built a device to detect distant earthquakes in 132 CE. Vesuvius buried a library at Herculaneum in 79 CE, carbonising about 1,800 scrolls too fragile to unroll. In 2023–2024 the Vesuvius Challenge used X-ray scans and machine learning to read more than 2,000 characters from inside one of them, a philosophical text on pleasure, and in 2025 researchers read the title of another as a work by Philodemus. Whole lost books may still be waiting inside.

chunks.heading: The Axial and Classical Age: 04 The great copying bottleneck
chunks.text: Here is the uncomfortable number at the heart of classical history: most of it is gone. Ancient books existed only as handwritten copies on papyrus, which rots in damp climates. A text survived only if, generation after generation, someone chose to copy it again. When the school curriculum narrowed in late antiquity and papyrus rolls gave way to parchment books, anything not being actively read was left behind. A horizontal bar chart. Aeschylus wrote about 70 to 90 plays and 7 survive. Sophocles wrote 123 and 7 survive. Euripides wrote about 90 and 18 survive. Menander wrote over 100 comedies and 1 survives nearly complete. Livy wrote 142 books of history and 35 survive. Polybius wrote 40 books and 5 survive complete. Diodorus wrote 40 books and 15 survive. The Library of Alexandria has become the symbol of this loss, but the evidence suggests it faded over centuries through lost royal funding, a purge of scholars in 145 BCE, fire during Caesar's war in 48 BCE and civil wars in the 3rd century CE, rather than in one great blaze. Ancient estimates of its size range from 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls, and nobody knows which is closer. The Library case weighs the famous culprits.

chunks.heading: The Axial and Classical Age: 05 A forgotten revolution?
chunks.text: The physicist Lucio Russo argues that we have misjudged the Hellenistic age. In his book The Forgotten Revolution he makes the case that scientists in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE built true theoretical science, deducing results from definitions and testing them against measurement, and applied it in engineering, optics, anatomy and hydraulics. After Rome's conquests broke up the Hellenistic kingdoms, he argues, that culture collapsed; later writers copied summaries they no longer fully understood, and Europe had to reinvent the method more than 1,500 years later. His strongest exhibit is the Antikythera mechanism itself: gearing of comparable complexity does not reappear in the surviving record until the astronomical clocks of medieval Europe. Critics reply that ancient science rarely used controlled experiment, and that 'lost' is not quite right, because much Greek science was copied in Byzantium and translated, corrected and extended in Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba, as the next age shows. The ancients knew more than their surviving books show. Where the knowledge went next is its own adventure.

chunks.heading: The Axial and Classical Age: 06 What might still come back
chunks.text: Some of what this age lost is not destroyed, only hidden. Charred scrolls at Herculaneum, reused parchments whose original writing was scraped off (like the Archimedes Palimpsest, which preserved his otherwise lost Method), papyrus scraps in the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus, and the unexcavated parts of the Villa of the Papyri may still hold lost works. Other losses, such as most of Aristotle's published dialogues or Eratosthenes' own account of his measurement, are probably gone for good. Excavating the unexplored lower floors of the Villa of the Papyri could recover a larger Latin or Greek library. Scanning more palimpsests with multispectral imaging keeps revealing erased texts. Finding a second geared instrument would settle whether Antikythera was unique.

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay
chunks.text: 12 536–c. 1000 CE The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay A dimmed sun and a new plague, then a faith whose first word was 'Read!' and a relay carrying science from Alexandria to Baghdad to Toledo. ↕ Rise and fall. Did a volcanic winter help end the ancient world? The claim on the scales A volcanic 'dust veil' from 536 and the plague that followed helped end the ancient world and opened the way for new powers. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The eruptions, the cold and the plague are all firmly established, and their timing lines up with famine, the failure of Justinian's reconquest and the exhaustion of Rome and Persia before the Arab conquests. What remains hard is measuring cause: some studies find the plague's long-term footprint smaller than the texts suggest, and politics, war and religion had their own momentum. Baillie's comet adds nothing the ice cores require; the sulphate is volcanic, so that variant awaits evidence. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks still often call this the 'Dark Ages' with confidence, a label that fits parts of western Europe but not Byzantium, the Islamic world, India or China. They usually leave out 536 and the Late Antique Little Ice Age entirely, and describe Islamic scholars as 'preserving' Greek science when they also corrected and extended it. Overconfident framing, underplayed evidence. What is solid Contemporary writers in 536 describe a dim sun for about a year, and ice cores record the volcanic sulphate that explains it. Procopius, Wars 4.14.5; Sigl et al. 2015 Yersinia pestis caused the first plague pandemic, which reached Pelusium in Egypt in 541 and Constantinople in 542. Wagner et al. 2014; Keller et al. 2019 Two leaves of a Quran manuscript at the University of Birmingham were radiocarbon dated to 568–645 CE (95.4% probability). University of Birmingham 2015 Baghdad's scholars translated much of Greek science and philosophy into Arabic between the 8th and 10th centuries, then corrected and extended it. Gutas 1998 Twelfth-century translators in Toledo turned Arabic scientific works, including Ptolemy's Almagest, into Latin. Burnett 2001 What is disputed How deadly the first plague pandemic was across the whole Mediterranean: a quarter or more, or much less. Whether the cold of 536–660 helped drive migrations, wars and the fall of empires, or merely coincided with them. Whether 'Dark Ages' is a fair name even for western Europe, given continuity in Byzantium and the flowering of the Islamic world. Which volcanoes erupted in 536 and 540; candidates in Iceland and

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay: 01 The year the sun went dim
chunks.text: In 536 CE the historian Procopius, travelling with the Byzantine army, recorded something that frightened everyone who saw it. For a whole year the sun seemed weak and pale. Irish annals record a 'failure of bread'. Chinese chronicles report a yellow dust falling from the sky, unusual cold and famine. The medieval historian Michael McCormick later called 536 the beginning of one of the worst periods to be alive, if not the worst year. For the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, during this whole year, and it seemed exceedingly like the sun in eclipse. For centuries this read like exaggeration. Then the science caught up. Greenland and Antarctic ice cores hold layers of volcanic sulphate from a large eruption in 536 and another around 540, followed by a third in 547. Tree rings across the Northern Hemisphere go narrow, and a 2016 study defined a Late Antique Little Ice Age lasting from 536 to about 660. A horizontal strip of wood showing tree rings from 526 to 560 CE. Rings are wide in the 520s and early 530s, then suddenly narrow in 536, stay narrow through the early 540s with a second dip at 540 and a third at 547, and recover only slowly. Labels mark the 536 eruption, the eruption around 540, the arrival of plague in Egypt in 541 and the eruption of 547, and an arrow notes that cool conditions continued to about 660.

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay: 02 Plague, and the end of an old world
chunks.text: In 541 a new disease arrived by ship at Pelusium in Egypt. It reached Constantinople the next year, where Procopius claims that at the peak ten thousand people died each day. Ancient DNA from 6th-century graves in Bavaria and, in 2025, from a mass grave at Jerash in Jordan confirms the killer as Yersinia pestis, the bacterium of the later Black Death. Waves returned for two centuries. How deadly it was overall is argued: some historians estimate a quarter or more of the Mediterranean population, while a 2019 review of papyri, coins, laws and pollen found little sign of a lasting collapse in many places. In the former Western Roman provinces, the change was already deep. The last western emperor had been deposed in 476, and Justinian's long wars to reconquer Italy, fought through the cold years, ruined much of what remained. Archaeologist Bryan Ward-Perkins has documented the result: fewer coins, cruder pottery, fewer tiled roofs, and even smaller cattle. Byzantium survived, and built Hagia Sophia, but it and Persia fought each other almost to exhaustion in the early 7th century.

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay: 03 'Read!': a new faith in Arabia
chunks.text: Into that exhausted world came a message from western Arabia. Muslim tradition holds that around 610 Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca then about forty, was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira when the angel Gabriel brought the first words of the Quran. They are a command to read, and a praise of the pen and of learning, which is worth remembering given what followed. Read! In the name of your Lord who created: He created man from a clinging form. Read! Your Lord is the Most Bountiful One who taught by [means of] the pen, who taught man what he did not know. The early community migrated to Medina in 622, the year from which the Islamic calendar counts. The Quran also speaks to events of its own day. A passage that tradition dates to the years of Persian victory opens: 'The Byzantines have been defeated in a nearby land. They will reverse their defeat with a victory in a few years' time.' The history fits well: the Persians took Antioch in 613 and Jerusalem in 614, and from 622 the emperor Heraclius counter-attacked, crushing a Persian army near Nineveh in 627 and forcing a peace in 628. Believers read this as a fulfilled prophecy; historians note how closely the text tracks the war. The physical record of the text is early too: in 2015, two leaves at the University of Birmingham were radiocarbon dated to between 568 and 645, within or close to the Prophet's lifetime. A civilisation that began with the command 'Read!' became, within two centuries, the world's great translator.

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay: 04 The relay: Alexandria to Baghdad to Toledo
chunks.text: Within a century of Muhammad's death in 632 the caliphate reached from Iberia to the Indus. In 762 the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad, and over the next two centuries its patrons paid for one of the great intellectual projects in history: translating the science and philosophy of Greece, Persia and India into Arabic. Hunayn ibn Ishaq and his circle translated Galen's medicine; Euclid, Ptolemy and Aristotle followed. Indian astronomy and the decimal place-value numerals arrived with Sanskrit texts. Paper, made in Baghdad from the late 8th century, made books cheaper. Step 1 of 5. Greek science in Athens and Alexandria; Syriac Christian scholars keep and translate it. Greek science in Athens and Alexandria; Syriac Christian scholars keep and translate it. 8th–10th centuries: Greek, Persian and Indian learning converges on Baghdad. New work: al-Khwarizmi's algebra, al-Biruni's measurements, Ibn al-Haytham's optics. West through al-Andalus: Córdoba's libraries and Toledo's translators (12th century). Into Latin Europe: new numerals, Ptolemy, Galen and optics in the universities. A map from Iberia to India. Step one marks Athens and Alexandria with Greek science, and Syriac translators at Edessa and Gundeshapur. Step two shows arrows from Alexandria, Gundeshapur and India converging on Baghdad, the House of Wisdom, in the 8th to 10th centuries. Step three marks new work: al-Khwarizmi in Baghdad around 820, Ibn al-Haytham in Cairo around 1011 to 1021 and al-Biruni in Ghazni. Step four shows the westward route to Córdoba and Toledo, where 12th-century translators produced Latin versions. Step five shows arrows into Latin Europe, to Pisa, where Fibonacci popularised Hindu-Arabic numerals in 1202, and to Oxford. Translation turned into discovery. Around 820 Muhammad ib

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay: 05 Drought in the Maya forest
chunks.text: Across the Atlantic, the great Classic Maya cities of the southern lowlands were emptying. Between about 800 and 950, cities such as Tikal and Calakmul stopped raising dated monuments; the last known Long Count date was carved in 909. Sediment cores from Lake Chichancanab show annual rainfall 41 to 54% lower than before during this period, with deeper falls in the worst droughts. Warfare between cities, deforestation and overstretched kings made the drought harder to survive. Northern cities such as Chichen Itza flourished for a time afterwards, and millions of Maya people live in the region today.

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay: 06 A comet in the tree rings?
chunks.text: The Belfast dendrochronologist Mike Baillie, whose oak chronologies helped expose the 536 downturn, made a bolder suggestion. In Exodus to Arthur he argued that cometary debris, not only volcanoes, darkened the sky, and that stories of fiery dragons and wasted lands from this period, including the Arthurian legends, might remember it. Dallas Abbott and colleagues later reported possible cosmic dust in Greenland ice of the time. It is a fair question, and the tree rings are extraordinary. But the ice cores now show volcanic sulphate in both 536 and 540, enough to explain the cooling without an impact, so the comet remains unconfirmed.

chunks.heading: The Dark Year and a Knowledge Relay: 07 What was lost in the relay
chunks.text: The relay was not lossless. The House of Wisdom's library vanished when the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258. Most Maya books were burned by Spanish clergy in the 16th century; four survive. Some Greek works known to Arabic scholars have been lost in both languages. The phrase 'Dark Ages' hides all of this: in this age the light did not go out, it moved. The lamp of learning was never switched off. It was carried from one hand to another, and each hand added something.

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500
chunks.text: 13 c. 1000–1500 CE Rises and Falls to 1500 Cities of a million acres rose on four continents, then a colder climate and the deadliest pandemic in history tested them all. ↕ Rise and fall. Why did so many great cities empty in the same two centuries? The claim on the scales A colder, more erratic climate from about 1300 was a major driver of the collapses of this age, from Angkor to Cahokia and Norse Greenland. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established Climate records do show an abrupt cooling after about 1275–1300, megadroughts and floods in the Asian monsoon, and flooding and drought on the Mississippi, all near the times these places declined. But each case also has strong human causes: shifting trade (walrus ivory for Greenland, maritime commerce for Angkor), war, and the Black Death. And many societies thrived through the same climate. So climate is a plausible major driver, not a demonstrated single cause. Menzies' 1421 voyage, by contrast, has no receipts: Ming records place the fleets in the Indian Ocean, and no Chinese wreck or artefact of that date has been found in the Americas. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks present the Black Death confidently, and with good reason. They are less reliable elsewhere: Great Zimbabwe, Angkor and Cahokia are often squeezed into a sentence, and older colonial accounts even denied that Africans built Great Zimbabwe. On climate they tend to swing between silence and simple determinism. The evidence supports a middle position that few textbooks state: climate shocks mattered most where societies were already rigid or overextended. What is solid The Black Death reached the Black Sea by 1346, Italy and southern France in 1347, and much of Europe by 1351. Benedictow 2004 Ancient genomes place the origin of the Black Death strain in the Tian Shan region around 1338–1339. Spyrou et al. 2022 Angkor's urban complex, mapped from radar and lidar, covered roughly 1,000 km² of houses, canals and reservoirs. Evans et al. 2007; Evans et al. 2013 Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of the Shona-speaking peoples; its Great Enclosure wall is up to about 11 m high. Garlake 1973; Chirikure et al. 2017 About 350,000 Timbuktu manuscripts were evacuated to Bamako in 2012–2013; 4,203 were burned or stolen. UNESCO; Haidara and SAVAMA-DCI What is disputed What share of Europe died in the Black Death: estimates range from about 30% to 60%. Whether Angkor 'collapsed' in the 15th century or declined slowly as elites moved south. How many people lived at Cahokia at its peak: estimates range fr

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500: 01 Cities the textbooks forgot
chunks.text: Around 1100 CE, the largest cities on Earth were not all where you might guess. In Cambodia, radar and lidar surveys have revealed that greater Angkor was a sprawling urban landscape of roughly 1,000 km², stitched together by canals, embankments and vast reservoirs, with Angkor Wat at its heart. On the Mississippi, Cahokia grew almost overnight after about 1050 into a planned city of plazas and earthen pyramids; its Monks Mound still stands about 30 metres high. In southern Africa, the rulers of Great Zimbabwe raised curving dry-stone walls up to about 11 metres high, and traded gold to the Swahili coast for glass beads and Chinese porcelain. Then, within about two centuries, Cahokia was empty, Angkor was fading, the Norse had gone silent in Greenland and the Black Death had killed a large share of everyone from Iceland to Egypt. The question of this age is whether these falls share a cause. Around 1100 the planet held great cities on four continents that most schoolbooks still mention in a single sentence, if at all.

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500: 02 The world turns colder
chunks.text: In 1257 the Samalas volcano on the Indonesian island of Lombok blew itself apart in one of the largest eruptions of the last few thousand years. Its sulphate is in both polar ice caps. Further eruptions followed, and a study of dead plants emerging from Arctic ice caps suggests the cold of the Little Ice Age set in abruptly between 1275 and 1300, then deepened after 1430. Europe suffered the Great Famine of 1315–1317. In the Norse settlements of Greenland, founded around 985, the last written record is a wedding at Hvalsey church in 1408. The Greenland story is often told as a parable of stubborn farmers who refused to adapt. Bones and isotopes tell a subtler tale: the Norse ate a great deal of seal, and their economy leaned on walrus ivory shipped to Europe, whose value fell as hunting pushed further north and African elephant ivory became easier to buy. Climate made life harder; trade removed the reason to stay.

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500: 03 The Great Mortality
chunks.text: The Mongol conquests, begun under Genghis Khan in 1206, created the largest land empire in history and opened routes from China to the Black Sea. Along those routes came plague. In 2022 geneticists sequenced Yersinia pestis from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, where tombstones record deaths from 'pestilence' in 1338–1339, and found the ancestor of the strain that became the Black Death. Step 1 of 5. 1338–39: plague deaths near Lake Issyk-Kul, where the strain's ancestor has been found. 1338–39: plague deaths near Lake Issyk-Kul, where the strain's ancestor has been found. 1346: along Mongol trade routes to the Golden Horde and the Genoese port of Caffa. 1347: by ship to Constantinople, Messina, Marseille and Alexandria. 1348: Florence, Paris, London, Cairo, Damascus. 1349–53: Scandinavia and Russia. Perhaps 30–60% of Europe has died. A map from the Atlantic to Central Asia. Step one marks Lake Issyk-Kul in the Tian Shan, 1338 to 1339. Step two shows the plague moving west along trade routes to the Golden Horde and Caffa in Crimea by 1346. Step three shows it reaching Constantinople, Messina, Marseille and Alexandria in 1347. Step four adds Florence, Paris, London, Cairo and Damascus in 1348. Step five adds Bergen in 1349 and Novgorod and Moscow in the early 1350s, with a note that about 30 to 60 percent of Europe died. Plague reached the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea by 1346, Constantinople, Sicily and Marseille in 1347, and most of Europe by 1351. Estimates of Europe's losses range from about 30% to 60% of the population; Cairo, Damascus and the cities of North Africa were also devastated. The survivors inherited land, wages rose, and some historians see the shock as a turning point toward the modern economy. Three kinds of evidence meet. Chroniclers and ta

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500: 04 Angkor, Cahokia and Great Zimbabwe
chunks.text: Angkor's decline was long, not sudden. Tree rings from Vietnam record decades-long droughts in the mid to late 14th and early 15th centuries, punctuated by violent monsoons that could silt up and break the city's canals and reservoirs. A 2019 study of sediments suggests that the elite core thinned out gradually over a century or more, as the kings shifted their centre south toward the Mekong and sea trade. At Cahokia, lake sediments record a major Mississippi flood around 1200, and chemical traces of human waste in a nearby lake suggest the population fell as summers grew drier. The city was largely empty by about 1350. Great Zimbabwe's people dispersed in the 15th century, probably as trade shifted north and local resources wore thin. One of this age's darkest chapters belongs to modern times. When European colonists reached Great Zimbabwe in the late 19th century, some insisted that Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba must have built it. Archaeologists David Randall-MacIver in 1905 and Gertrude Caton-Thompson in 1929 showed it was African, and the Rhodesian government still pressured guides and museums to blur the point in the 1970s. The Sheba case tells that story.

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500: 05 The manuscripts of Timbuktu
chunks.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, passed through Cairo on pilgrimage with so much gold that, a writer reported about twelve years later, its value there fell. Under Mali and then Songhay, Timbuktu became a city of scholars. Its families collected manuscripts from the late 13th century to the early 20th: law, theology, medicine, astronomy, mathematics, history and poetry. In 2012–2013, when armed groups occupied the city, librarians led by Abdel Kader Haidara smuggled about 350,000 manuscripts to Bamako in footlockers. Militants burned or stole 4,203. It is the knowledge relay of the previous age, still being carried by hand.

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500: 06 Did China discover the world in 1421?
chunks.text: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, with fleets of dozens of large ships and many thousands of men. Then the court stopped them, and many records were later lost. In 2002 Gavin Menzies claimed that his captains had sailed on around the world in 1421, reaching the Americas and Australia. It is a thrilling idea, and the capability and the forgetting are both real. But Ming sources place the fleets in the Indian Ocean in those years, specialists found the book's maps and artefacts misread, and no Chinese wreck, coin or DNA of that date has turned up in the Americas. For now it awaits evidence.

chunks.heading: Rises and Falls to 1500: 07 The long recovery
chunks.text: The end of this age is a rebound. Population recovered, and so did trade. When Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, Greek scholars carried manuscripts to Italy, feeding a Renaissance that also drew on the Arabic science translated in Toledo. Around 1455 Gutenberg printed his Bible with movable metal type, and copying bottlenecks began to fade. For the first time, knowledge could be multiplied faster than it could be lost. Printing broke the old cycle in which every age of darkness burned part of the library.

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols
chunks.text: Signs Across the World The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols Upper Palaeolithic, c. 40,000–10,000 years ago Strong evidence. Were Ice Age Europe's geometric signs a shared code or random doodles? The claim on the scales Ice Age Europe's geometric signs were a shared, meaningful and deliberately transmitted system of conventions, not random doodles. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established A small repertoire, long persistence of individual signs, regional preferences and careful placement are very hard to explain by chance, and specialists broadly agree the signs were intentional and learned. That supports shared, meaningful and transmitted. What remains unknown is what they meant, whether meanings stayed fixed, and whether they formed one continental code or many local ones. The rating covers the system, not any particular reading of it; a claimed decipherment would rate far lower. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Most textbooks and museum labels give the signs a line, calling them 'abstract' or 'enigmatic', and devote the space to the animals. That is underconfident: the signs outnumber the animals and show strong, measurable patterns. On meaning, textbooks are rightly cautious, and popular articles that call the signs 'the first writing' go well beyond the evidence. What is solid Geometric signs outnumber images of animals and people in Ice Age European caves by at least two to one. von Petzinger 2016 Across 367 Upper Palaeolithic rock-art sites in Europe, Genevieve von Petzinger's database records only about 32 sign types recurring over some 30,000 years. von Petzinger 2016; TED 2015 About two-thirds of those sign types were already in use in the earliest phase of the record, the Aurignacian, roughly 40,000–30,000 years ago. von Petzinger 2016; von Petzinger and Nowell 2014 Some signs are tightly restricted: tectiforms appear only about 17,000–13,000 years ago, and at only nine cave sites. von Petzinger, TED Ideas 2016 Europe's oldest dated cave painting is a red disk at El Castillo, older than 40,800 years by uranium-series dating of the calcite that formed over it. Pike et al. 2012 What is disputed Whether the signs carried specific meanings (names, counts, messages) or looser, changing associations. Whether many of the forms began as 'entoptic' images produced by the human visual system in altered states (Lewis-Williams and Dowson 1988), or as purely cultural inventions. How many sign types there really are: categories are defined by modern researchers, so lumping or splitting changes the count (

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols: 01 The shapes nobody looked at
chunks.text: Walk into El Castillo, a cave above the Pas valley in Cantabria, and your guide's torch will find hands first: dozens of them, stencilled in red, fingers spread. Then come the animals. But look between them and you start to see something else: rows of red dots, a disk, lines, ladders, shapes like roofs and feathers. For more than a century, most visitors and many scholars walked straight past them. Genevieve von Petzinger did not. As a graduate student at the University of Victoria in Canada, she set out to count them. She built a database of every geometric sign she could find in the Ice Age art of Europe, then spent 2013 and 2014 crawling through 52 caves in Spain, Portugal, France and Italy, many rarely visited, to check the records against the walls. What she found became a 2015 TED talk and a 2016 book, The First Signs. Across 30,000 years and an entire continent, Ice Age artists drew from a list of about 32 signs.

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols: 02 Thirty-two signs, thirty thousand years
chunks.text: The headline numbers are simple. Her database covers 367 Upper Palaeolithic rock-art sites, from northern Spain to the Urals. In them, geometric signs outnumber animals and people by at least two to one. And yet the variety is tiny: about 32 forms recur, including lines, dots, open angles, circles, zigzags, spirals, crosshatches, ladder shapes (scalariforms), feather shapes (penniforms), roof shapes (tectiforms), negative and positive hands, and finger flutings. The second surprise is timing. About two-thirds of the types were already in use in the Aurignacian, the earliest part of the European record, roughly 40,000–30,000 years ago. Her earlier study of French caves had found a similar share, about 70 percent. In other words, the signs do not slowly accumulate as people settle into Europe. Most arrive early and already formed. A time chart from 42,000 years ago on the left to 10,000 years ago on the right, with the Aurignacian period, 40,000 to 30,000 years ago, shaded. A top bar shows that about two-thirds of the 32 sign types were already in use before 30,000 years ago. Rows show five sign types with small drawings: lines and dots, used in every period across the whole chart; negative hand stencils, most popular from 40,000 to 22,000 years ago with rarer later use dashed; the feather-shaped penniform, first appearing 30,000 to 28,000 years ago; and the roof-shaped tectiform, found only from 17,000 to 13,000 years ago at nine caves. A red dot marks the El Castillo red disk, older than 40,800 years. Few signs can be dated directly. Where calcite has grown over paint, uranium-series dating gives a minimum age: in 2012 Alistair Pike and colleagues showed that a red disk at El Castillo is older than 40,800 years. Where charcoal was used, radiocarbon dates the pigment its

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols: 03 What persists, what spreads
chunks.text: The patterns within the list are the most interesting part. Lines and dots are everywhere and in every period. Negative hands, made by blowing pigment around a hand held to the wall, were most popular between about 40,000 and 22,000 years ago and then faded. The penniform first appears between about 30,000 and 28,000 years ago. The tectiform, a roof-like shape, belongs to a narrow window between about 17,000 and 13,000 years ago and turns up in only nine caves, clustered in one region of France. That combination, a stable core plus signs that come and go in particular places, looks a great deal like how human conventions behave. A few forms are shared by everyone; others work like local dialects or fashions. Some sites show signs grouped deliberately. At La Pasiega, a panel of signs high on a wall was described by the priest and prehistorian Henri Breuil as an 'inscription' carrying a message for initiates, a phrase few would use today but which captures how structured it looks. The signs also leave the caves. A necklace of more than 70 perforated red-deer teeth, buried with a woman at Saint-Germain-la-Rivière in France about 16,000 years ago, carries incised marks that von Petzinger compares to the wall signs. That suggests a portable code, not just a cave decoration.

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols: 04 The mainstream readings
chunks.text: Von Petzinger was not the first to take the signs seriously. In the 1960s André Leroi-Gourhan mapped their positions in dozens of caves and argued that each cave followed a plan, with thin 'male' signs and wide 'female' signs placed in patterned relation to the animals. His sexual reading has largely been abandoned, but his central idea, that the signs are ordered rather than random, has survived. In 1988 David Lewis-Williams and Thomas Dowson offered a different root. Laboratory studies show that in altered states of consciousness, from migraine to trance, the human visual system produces the same geometric forms in everyone: grids, dots, zigzags, nested curves, parallel lines and meanders. The San rock art of southern Africa, made by people whose trance rituals are recorded, contains exactly these forms. They proposed that some Ice Age signs began the same way. Critics answer that such shapes are also simply the easiest to draw, and that the model explains the shapes better than their distribution. The mainstream position today combines these threads. The signs were intentional, learned and culturally patterned. Some may have perceptual roots. Their meaning is lost, and 'code' is a hypothesis about how they worked, not a translation.

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols: 05 The challenger's case: a graphic code
chunks.text: Von Petzinger's argument, at its strongest, is about what the numbers imply. If signs were idle marks, 30,000 years of people should have produced endless variety. Instead they kept to a short list, held some forms for tens of thousands of years, and chose different ones in different regions. That is how shared conventions behave. And because two-thirds of the list was in place by the Aurignacian, she suggests the system may have come with the first modern humans into Europe, with roots in Africa. She is careful: the signs are not writing, because a few dozen signs cannot record the words of a language. She calls it graphic communication. A short list, kept for millennia and chosen by region, is the signature of convention, not chance. Graham Hancock, in Supernatural (2005), drew on Lewis-Williams to push the reading further, treating the geometric signs as traces of visionary experience at the very root of art and religion. That part of the argument concerns what trance experiences mean, which archaeology cannot test. The physical claim underneath it, that the signs were a shared and meaningful system, is the part the evidence can weigh, and it weighs heavily in its favour. The next Open Case, on Ice Age notation, asks whether some of these signs went further and stored information.

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols: 06 What time has erased
chunks.text: Every count here comes from deep caves, where stable air and darkness protected the walls. Most Ice Age life happened outside, and most marks were probably made on wood, bark, hide and skin, all long gone. The coasts where many groups lived are drowned: at the height of the last glaciation sea level stood about 120 metres lower, and the one known painted cave with an entrance now below the sea, Cosquer near Marseille, shows what may be missing. The 32 signs are the survivors, not the whole vocabulary.

chunks.heading: The First Signs: Ice Age Europe's 32 Symbols: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: Three things would move this forward. First, an open database others can test: if the patterns hold under independent statistical analysis, the case for a system becomes very hard to resist. Second, many more direct dates, so that the time patterns do not rest on style. Third, comparable surveys in Africa, Asia and Australia, which could show whether the core signs predate the arrival of people in Europe, as von Petzinger suspects. In February 2026 the linguist Christian Bentz and the archaeologist Ewa Dutkiewicz published in PNAS an analysis of more than 3,000 signs on about 260 objects from the Swabian Jura, roughly 43,000–34,000 years old. They found the sign sequences were structured conventions, statistically comparable in information density to early proto-cuneiform, though not writing. It is the strongest quantitative support yet for the idea that Ice Age signs were a system. The signs have been hiding in plain sight for a century. The honest verdict is that they were not doodles: they were shared, learned and meaningful to the people who made them. What they said is still the open question.

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks
chunks.text: Signs Across the World Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks Middle and Late Pleistocene, c. 540,000–40,000 years ago Plausible. Did humans before our own species make deliberate marks and symbols? The claim on the scales Symbolic marking began before Homo sapiens existed. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established Deliberate abstract marks by other humans are now well supported: the Trinil zigzag is securely dated and accepted as intentional, and Neanderthal finger flutings at La Roche-Cotard are sealed by dated sediment. But 'before Homo sapiens' means older than about 300,000 years, and that rests almost entirely on one shell whose purpose is unknown. Intentional does not automatically mean symbolic. Plausible, and far better supported than twenty years ago, but not yet a pattern. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Older textbooks taught a 'human revolution' in which art and symbols appeared suddenly with modern humans in Europe about 40,000 years ago. That was overconfident and has been overturned by African, Indonesian and Neanderthal evidence. Current textbooks are more open, but many museum labels still credit marking to Homo sapiens alone, which is now too narrow. What is solid A freshwater mussel shell from Trinil, Java, carries a deliberately engraved zigzag, dated to about 540,000–430,000 years ago, when Homo erectus is the only human known on Java. Joordens et al. 2015 At Blombos Cave, South Africa, Homo sapiens engraved crosshatched patterns on pieces of ochre about 100,000–75,000 years ago, and drew a crosshatch with an ochre crayon on a stone flake about 73,000 years ago. Henshilwood et al. 2002, 2009, 2018 Lines traced with fingers on the soft wall of La Roche-Cotard cave in France were sealed by sediment more than 57,000 years ago and are attributed to Neanderthals. Marquet et al. 2023 A hand stencil in Liang Metanduno on Muna island, Sulawesi, lies under calcite at least 67,800 years old, the oldest dated cave art known (2026). Oktaviana et al. 2026 Hand stencils appear on every inhabited continent, from Sulawesi and Spain to Patagonia's Cueva de las Manos and Australia. regional surveys; UNESCO What is disputed Whether the Trinil zigzag was a symbol, a test of a tool, an ownership mark or a moment's play. Whether uranium-thorium ages above 64,000 years for a ladder sign, a hand stencil and painted flowstone in three Spanish caves (Hoffmann et al. 2018) are reliable, and so whether Neanderthals made them. Who made the Muna hand stencil: the team attributes it to Homo sapiens, but Denisovans and other

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks: 01 A zigzag in a museum drawer
chunks.text: In 1891 and 1892 the Dutch anatomist Eugène Dubois dug into the banks of the Solo River at Trinil on Java and found a skullcap and a thigh bone that became famous as Java Man, today classed as Homo erectus. His crews also collected fossil freshwater mussel shells, which went to the Netherlands and sat in the collection now held by Naturalis in Leiden for more than a century. Then a researcher photographing the shells noticed something odd on one of them: a set of sharp, straight grooves forming a zigzag. In December 2014 a team led by Josephine Joordens published the shell in Nature. Microscope work showed the grooves were cut in one session with a hard, pointed tool, on a fresh shell, with care. Dating of the sediment inside the shells, by argon-argon and luminescence methods, gave an age of about 540,000–430,000 years. The oldest known geometric engraving was made by a species that was not ours, and it waited a century in a drawer.

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks: 02 A ladder of marks
chunks.text: Trinil stands alone for a long time. The next securely dated patterns come from Africa and from our own species. At Blombos Cave on the southern Cape of South Africa, people engraved crosshatched designs on pieces of red ochre between about 100,000 and 75,000 years ago. In 2018 Christopher Henshilwood's team reported a small silcrete flake from the 73,000-year-old levels with six roughly parallel red lines crossed by three curved ones, drawn with an ochre crayon: the oldest known drawing. At Diepkloof, about 60,000 years ago, people engraved ostrich-eggshell containers with a small set of repeated designs. A two-part time chart. The top panel runs from 700,000 years ago to today: a bar for the Trinil engraved shell by Homo erectus, 540,000 to 430,000 years ago, and a thin bar showing Homo sapiens existing from about 300,000 years ago. A shaded band from 110,000 to 35,000 years ago is enlarged below. The lower panel has two rows. Homo sapiens: Blombos engraved ochre 100,000 to 75,000; the Blombos drawing at 73,000; the Muna hand stencil, at least 67,800; Diepkloof eggshells, about 60,000; the Sulawesi scene, at least 51,200. Neanderthals: three Spanish caves, at least 64,000 to 66,700, marked disputed; La Roche-Cotard flutings, at least 57,000; Gorham's Cave, at least 39,000. An accent line marks the old creative explosion model at 40,000 years ago. Then come the caves of Indonesia. In 2024 Adhi Agus Oktaviana and colleagues dated a painted scene in Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, showing three human-like figures and a wild pig, to at least 51,200 years ago, the oldest known story told in pictures. Neanderthals appear on the ladder too: finger-traced lines at La Roche-Cotard in the Loire valley were sealed by sediment more than 57,000 years ago, and a crosshatch cut into the

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks: 03 The old story and its collapse
chunks.text: For much of the twentieth century the textbook story was simple. Art, ornament and symbols appeared suddenly around 40,000 years ago, when modern humans reached Europe: the 'creative explosion' or 'human revolution'. Neanderthals, in this story, did not make art. Earlier humans certainly did not. Every part of that story has now been challenged by physical finds. Blombos and Diepkloof put patterned marks by Homo sapiens in Africa tens of thousands of years earlier. Sulawesi put figurative art in Asia earlier than in Europe. And a growing set of Neanderthal ornaments and marks, from eagle talons to cave-wall flutings, showed our closest relatives doing some of the same things. The mainstream has changed its mind, to its credit, but it keeps one careful distinction. A mark can be deliberate without being symbolic. A zigzag may be a design with meaning, or a way of testing a new tool, or a moment's play. We can show intention from the grooves; we cannot yet show meaning.

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks: 04 The challengers' case: Neanderthal painters
chunks.text: In 2018 Dirk Hoffmann, João Zilhão, Alistair Pike and colleagues published in Science uranium-thorium dates for thin calcite crusts over paint in three Spanish caves. A red ladder-shaped sign at La Pasiega, a hand stencil at Maltravieso and red-painted flowstone at Ardales all gave minimum ages above 64,000 years, the Maltravieso stencil about 66,700. Modern humans are not known in Iberia until roughly 42,000 years ago, so the team concluded that Neanderthals were the painters. Step 1 of 5. Pigment goes onto the limestone wall. Pigment goes onto the limestone wall. Over time, seeping water lays down thin layers of calcite over the paint. In a scraped sample, thorium-230 builds up from uranium at a known rate: the ratio dates the crust. The paint lies under the crust, so it is older: the date is a minimum age. The risk: if uranium washes out later, the crust looks too old. Layer-by-layer sampling checks for this. A cross-section of a limestone cave wall. Step 1: a thin band of red pigment on the wall surface. Step 2: water seeping down the wall lays three thin layers of calcite crust over the pigment. Step 3: a sample is taken from the crust; bars show uranium-234 and a growing amount of thorium-230, whose ratio acts as a clock. Step 4: the Muna example, a crust age of 71,600 plus or minus 3,800 years, meaning the paint is at least 67,800 years old. Step 5: arrows show uranium being washed out of the crust later, which would make it look too old, and the check: ages must get younger from the inner layer outwards. The reply was sharp. In 2020 Randall White and a long list of rock-art specialists argued in the Journal of Human Evolution that the crusts may have lost uranium over time, which would make them look too old, and that the sampling did not rule this out. The Hoff

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks: 05 Hands on every continent
chunks.text: One kind of mark links almost all of this story: the hand stencil, made by blowing or spitting pigment around a hand pressed to rock. They appear in Sulawesi and Borneo, in Spain and France, in Australia, in the Sahara and at Cueva de las Manos in Patagonia, where hundreds of hands were stencilled by hunter-gatherers thousands of years ago. The idea may have been invented again and again, because hands are always at hand; or it may be one of the oldest shared human habits. In January 2026 Oktaviana and colleagues reported in Nature a faint hand stencil in Liang Metanduno cave on Muna island, south-east Sulawesi. Calcite over it dates to 71,600 ± 3,800 years, giving a minimum age of 67,800 years, about 1,100 years older than the Maltravieso stencil. Its fingers were deliberately narrowed to look like claws, a style known only from Sulawesi. The team attributes it to Homo sapiens, which would place our species in the region by then, but the identity of the maker is an inference.

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks: 06 What time has erased
chunks.text: The record of early marks is a record of survival, not of practice. Bone, shell, ochre and deep-cave walls last; wood, bark, hide and painted bodies do not. Tropical rock faces erode quickly, and the coasts of Sunda and Sahul, where early seafarers lived, are under the sea. Only a handful of engraved objects older than 100,000 years are known anywhere, and the oldest of them was found by chance, a century after it was dug up. The honest assumption is that the first marks are older than the oldest we have.

chunks.heading: Older Than Us: The First Deliberate Marks: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The strongest test would be more Trinils: engraved objects from securely dated layers older than 300,000 years, which would turn a single case into a pattern. Checking the Spanish dates with a second method, and collecting new samples layer by layer, would settle whether Neanderthals painted there. Ancient DNA and proteins recovered from cave sediments can now show which humans were present in a cave, which could name the makers of marks where no bones survive. The verdict today: deliberate marking by other humans is well supported, and the old creative-explosion story is gone. Whether symbols, in the full sense, began before our species rests on one extraordinary shell. It is plausible, and the evidence has moved in that direction every time a new find has been dated.

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?
chunks.text: Signs Across the World Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing? Upper Palaeolithic and Later Stone Age, c. 45,000–13,000 years ago Plausible. Did Ice Age people record information in signs, long before writing? The claim on the scales Ice Age people used systems of signs to record information, a kind of proto-writing, tens of thousands of years before writing. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established That some Ice Age marks stored information is plausible and increasingly supported: patterned sequences, marks added over time and two quantitative studies point that way. But no study has shown what any sequence records. The calendar reading rests on a statistical fit and on tracings critics dispute, and neither team claims the signs encode language. Information recording is the better-supported description; proto-writing, in the sense of a system that could carry specific messages, remains untested. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks say writing began in Mesopotamia about 5,300 years ago, and for writing that records language they are right. But they usually file everything earlier under 'art', which undersells the evidence for notation. The honest position sits in between: marks that probably stored information for the people who made them, whose content we cannot yet read. What is solid Writing that records language appears around 3300 BCE, with proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk in Mesopotamia, and soon after in Egypt. standard chronology; see Lost Scripts About 260 Aurignacian objects from caves of the Swabian Jura, roughly 43,000–34,000 years old, carry more than 3,000 geometric signs: crosses, dots, notches and lines. Bentz and Dutkiewicz 2026 In French and Spanish caves, rows of dots and lines often sit beside animal images; Bacon and colleagues compiled 862 such sequences, 256 of them including a Y-shaped sign. Bacon et al. 2023 Notched bones are old: a notched baboon fibula from Border Cave, South Africa, is about 43,000 years old, and the Ishango bone from Congo, with 168 marks in three columns, about 20,000. d'Errico et al. 2012; de Heinzelin 1962 Hundreds of engraved ostrich-eggshell fragments from Diepkloof, South Africa, about 60,000 years old, repeat a small set of standardised patterns. Texier et al. 2010 What is disputed Whether dot-and-line rows count lunar months from spring, and whether the Y sign means 'giving birth', as Bacon and colleagues propose. Whether the Swabian sign sequences held specific information or followed decorative traditions. Whether notched bones such as Ishango record count

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?: 01 A lion-man with a message?
chunks.text: In a museum case in Germany sits a small plaque of mammoth ivory, about 38,000 years old, found in Geißenklösterle cave in the Swabian Jura. On one side a figure stands with raised arms, part human, part lion: archaeologists call it the Adorant. Its edges and back carry rows of notches and dots. Nearby caves have given up a lion-headed man carved in ivory, with evenly spaced cuts on one arm, and an ivory figurine from Vogelherd covered in rows of crosses and dots. We are taught that recording began with writing, in Mesopotamia, around 3300 BCE. Before that, the story goes, people remembered, told and drew, but did not record. The dots on the Adorant ask whether that line is in the right place. The question is not whether Ice Age people could write, but whether they could leave a record.

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?: 02 The marks are real, and old
chunks.text: Start with what nobody disputes. Repeated, patterned marks are very old. At Diepkloof in South Africa, people about 60,000 years ago engraved ostrich eggshells, probably water containers, with a small set of standardised designs. At Border Cave, on the border of South Africa and Eswatini, a baboon fibula about 43,000 years old carries a row of cut notches; Francesco d'Errico and colleagues list it among early objects that resemble the material culture of the later San. The Ishango bone, found in 1950 by Jean de Heinzelin beside the Semliki River on today's Congo–Uganda border, is roughly 20,000 years old and carries 168 marks in three columns. In Europe, rows of dots and short lines sit beside painted animals in cave after cave. And in the Swabian Jura, where some of the oldest figurative art in the world was made, about 260 objects carry more than 3,000 geometric signs. The previous Open Case, on the first signs, showed that Ice Age signs formed a shared set of conventions. This case asks a harder question: did any of them store information?

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?: 03 A calendar for hunters
chunks.text: In January 2023 the Cambridge Archaeological Journal published a paper by Bennett Bacon, an independent researcher in London, with academics including the Palaeolithic specialist Paul Pettitt and the psychologist Robert Kentridge of Durham University. Bacon had spent years studying images of cave animals and the marks beside them. The team proposed a simple system. Counting starts at the spring snowmelt. Each dot or line stands for one lunar month. A row of four marks beside an animal means month four, which they link to that species' mating season. A Y-shaped sign in the row means 'giving birth', and its position gives the month. Step 1 of 5. An animal image with a row of marks beside it, a common pairing in Ice Age caves. An animal image with a row of marks beside it, a common pairing in Ice Age caves. The proposal: count lunar months from the spring snowmelt, month 1. Each dot or line is one month; four marks point to month 4, read as the mating season. A Y sign means 'giving birth'; its place in the row, here third, gives the birth month. The test: 862 sequences matched known seasons better than chance; critics dispute the tracings. A schematic painted animal, like an aurochs, with two rows of marks beside it: row A has four red dots; row B has two lines, a Y-shaped sign and another line. Below is a strip of thirteen boxes for lunar months, counted from the spring snowmelt. Step by step, month 1 is marked as spring, where the count starts; an arrow from the four dots points to month 4, labelled mating month; an arrow from the Y in third place points to month 3, labelled birth month. A final panel notes the test on 862 sequences, 606 without a Y and 256 with one, which matched known seasons better than chance, and the critics' objection that some tracings are wrong a

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?: 04 Measuring the information
chunks.text: In February 2026 a different kind of study appeared in PNAS. The linguist Christian Bentz of Saarland University and the archaeologist Ewa Dutkiewicz of the Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte in Berlin digitised the sign sequences on about 260 Aurignacian objects and applied the statistical tools used to study languages and early scripts. They found the sequences were not random, and not like language either: they repeat, in runs such as cross, cross, cross, line, line, line, which spoken language does not do. But their information density was statistically comparable to that of proto-cuneiform, the Mesopotamian accounting tablets from which writing grew. Bentz and Dutkiewicz are careful. Writing in the strict sense encodes spoken language, and these signs do not. What they describe is a system of conventional signs, a way of storing information on objects that seems to have been in place about 40,000 years ago. Not writing, but a system: the Swabian signs repeat like early accounts, not like speech.

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?: 05 The sceptics' reading
chunks.text: This idea has a history, and a cautionary one. From the 1960s Alexander Marshack, a journalist turned researcher at Harvard's Peabody Museum, argued that notched bones and plaques, including a winding row of pits on a plaque from Abri Blanchard in France, were lunar records. His 1972 book The Roots of Civilization was hugely influential. Critics answered that he searched for patterns rather than testing for them, and the historian of mathematics George Gheverghese Joseph warned, about Ishango, that one bone can hardly carry the weight of conjecture piled on it. Bacon's calendar met similar resistance. In 2023 Miguel García-Bustos, Olivia Rivero, Georges Sauvet and Paula García Bustos, writing in the Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology, argued that some of the tracings used do not match the walls, that in several caves the signs counted are not really there, and that 'association' between marks and animals was never defined. The dispute is not settled. Specialists also stress that repeated, regular marks can be decorative, ritual or ownership signs. Structure shows a convention; it does not show a message.

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?: 06 What time has erased
chunks.text: If Ice Age people kept records, most of them are gone. The notched stick, the knotted cord and the painted hide are exactly the kind of objects recent hunter-gatherers used for counting and remembering, and none survives from 40,000 years ago. What survives is carved in ivory and bone or painted in deep caves, which may be the most special, least everyday records. That bias cuts both ways: it may hide a far richer practice of notation, or it may make ritual marks look like bookkeeping. Our case on lost scripts shows how hard even true writing is to read without a key; here there is no key at all.

chunks.heading: Ice Age Notation: Records Before Writing?: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The calendar can be tested. If independent teams re-record the sequences with photographs and the pattern holds, and if sequences recorded since 2023 fit the same counts, it will be hard to dismiss. The Bentz method can be run on other regions, and on marks everyone agrees are decorative, to show what it really distinguishes. And microscope studies of more notched objects can show which were built up over time, the physical signature of a record. Two studies in three years moved this question from speculation to measurement: Bacon and colleagues' calendar in 2023 and Bentz and Dutkiewicz's information analysis in 2026. Neither claims writing. Both claim that some Ice Age signs followed rules that carried information. The next step is independent replication. The fair verdict today: Ice Age people very probably used marks to help them remember, and some sequences look like structured information. What they recorded, and whether any of it amounted to proto-writing, remains open.

chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?
chunks.text: Signs Across the World The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain? Middle Pleistocene to first millennium BCE Awaiting discovery. Why do the same symbols appear in cultures that never met? The claim on the scales The recurring symbols in unconnected cultures point to a single lost source culture that handed them down. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The repeats are real, but their pattern does not fit one source. The oldest zigzag was made by Homo erectus about half a million years ago, and hand stencils were made in Sulawesi and possibly by Neanderthals in Spain before 60,000 years ago. The motifs then appear at scattered dates on different continents, not in a single horizon that later spreads outward. The simplest forms match what the human visual system generates by itself, and the 'handbag' objects are different things on close inspection. No dated trail of intermediate examples has been found. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Museum labels often present the entoptic explanation as if it were settled, when rock-art specialists still debate how far it reaches; there the confidence runs ahead of the evidence. On the lost-source idea the textbooks are right to be sceptical, though they rarely explain why the repeats happen at all, which leaves the field open to bolder stories. What is solid Hand stencils occur on every inhabited continent; the oldest dated one, on Muna island off Sulawesi, is at least 67,800 years old, and Patagonia's Cueva de las Manos stencils begin around 9,300 years ago. chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?: 01 The hand on the wall
chunks.text: Press your palm against a rock, fill your mouth with ground red pigment and blow. When you lift your hand, a ghost of it stays behind. People have done exactly this in Indonesia, Spain, France, Australia, Borneo and Argentina. At the Cueva de las Manos in Patagonia, painted in waves from about 9,300 years ago, hundreds of hands crowd the wall, and 829 of them are left hands against 31 right ones: the painters held the blowpipe in their right hand. Hands are only the start. Spirals curl over the entrance stone at Newgrange in Ireland. Zigzags, grids and dot rows fill Ice Age caves. Hooked crosses appear in Ukraine, Iraq, the Indus Valley, Greece and the American Southwest. And a squat object with a looped handle, nicknamed the 'handbag', is carved at Göbekli Tepe in Türkiye, held by a figure at La Venta in Mexico and carried by winged spirits on Assyrian palace walls. The same shapes recur across oceans and millennia. The question is whether they were inherited, carried or simply rediscovered. To many people that looks like a fingerprint: evidence that one forgotten culture taught the others. Here is what the evidence shows, and three ways to explain it.

chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?: 02 A catalogue of repeats
chunks.text: The oldest repeat is a zigzag. In 2015 Josephine Joordens and colleagues reported a freshwater mussel shell from Trinil on Java, collected in the 1890s, with a zigzag deliberately cut into it about 540,000–430,000 years ago. The maker was Homo erectus. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, a flake of stone carries a red ochre crosshatch drawn about 73,000 years ago. In Europe, Genevieve von Petzinger of the University of Victoria compiled 32 geometric signs, from dots and lines to open angles and 'penniforms', that recur across 367 or more sites between about 40,000 and 10,000 years ago (see the ice-age-signs case). A chart with a logarithmic time axis from one million years ago on the left to one thousand years ago on the right, and seven rows. Lines and zigzags: a bar at 540,000 to 430,000 years for the Trinil shell by Homo erectus and a dot at 73,000 for the Blombos crosshatch. Hand stencils: a dot at 67,800 with an arrow meaning at least that old, for Sulawesi, with a note on Spain at 66,700, and a dot at 9,300 for Patagonia. Ice Age signs: a bar from 40,000 to 10,000 in Europe. Swastika and meander: a bar for the Mezine ivory bird, then dots at 6,000 for Samarra and 5,000 for the Indus. Spirals: a dot at 5,200 for Newgrange. Overlapping circles: a dot for an Assyrian threshold and a dashed bar for Abydos, date unsure. Handbag objects: a dot at 11,500 for Göbekli Tepe and marks around 3,000 for La Venta and Nimrud. A vertical line at 300,000 marks Homo sapiens. The swastika has a long, well-dated story. A meander of joined hooked crosses decorates a mammoth-ivory bird from Mezine in Ukraine, a late Ice Age figurine. The motif sits at the centre of a Samarra bowl of about 4000 BCE and on Indus Valley seals from about 3000 BCE. Its Sanskrit name joins su, 'good', and asti,

chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?: 03 The handbag, the bucket and the pouch
chunks.text: The 'handbag' is the most striking repeat, so it deserves a close look. On Göbekli Tepe's Pillar 43, the Vulture Stone, carved about 11,500 years ago, three box-like shapes with looped tops sit along the upper edge, each with an animal. Klaus Schmidt, who led the excavation, left them unidentified, and the team's publications still treat them as uncertain. Edward Banning suggested in 2011 that similar 'handle' shapes might depict buildings with vaulted roofs. The Assyrian version is not a mystery at all to Assyriologists. On the reliefs of Ashurnasirpal II's palace at Nimrud (883–859 BCE), the winged apkallu sages hold a bucket and a cone. Ritual texts name them: the banduddû, a bucket, and the mullilu, a 'purifier'. As Frans Wiggermann explained in 1992, the bucket held water and the cone sprinkled it, to guard doorways from evil. At La Venta, Monument 19 shows a seated figure framed by a crested rattlesnake, often read as an early feathered serpent, holding a small bag that is usually interpreted as a pouch for copal incense, a common Mesoamerican ritual object. So the three 'handbags' come from cultures thousands of years and kilometres apart, and in context they are a stone-carved object of unknown meaning, a bucket for holy water and an incense pouch. A container with a handle is one of the most useful shapes a human can make. The 'flower of life' tells a similar story: its best-known ancient example, drawn in red ochre on a granite pillar in the Osireion at Abydos, is not listed in Margaret Murray's 1904 survey of the temple's graffiti and is usually dated to the early centuries CE, possibly later.

chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?: 04 Explanation one: the same brain
chunks.text: In the 1920s the psychologist Heinrich Klüver noticed that people who took mescaline reported the same few shapes: lattices and checkerboards, cobwebs, tunnels and funnels, and spirals. Migraine sufferers, people drifting into sleep and people pressing on their closed eyes see them too. In 1988 David Lewis-Williams and Thomas Dowson argued that these entoptic forms, generated inside the visual system, explain much of the geometric art of the Ice Age and of the San painters of southern Africa, whose healers entered trance. The eye's image lands on the cortex stretched: rings in what you see are vertical lines on the cortex, rays are horizontal lines. Stripes of activity across the sheet are seen as concentric rings: the tunnel. Stripes running along the sheet are seen as rays: the funnel or starburst. Slanting stripes are seen as spirals. A grid of spots is seen as a lattice or web. Two panels joined by an arrow labelled log-polar map. On the left, a rectangle standing for the flattened visual cortex, with distance from the centre of gaze running left to right and angle around the gaze running top to bottom. On the right, a circle standing for the visual field. Step 1: vertical lines on the cortex correspond to rings in the visual field and horizontal lines to rays. Step 2: vertical stripes of activity appear as concentric rings, a tunnel. Step 3: horizontal stripes appear as radial rays, a starburst. Step 4: slanting stripes appear as spiral arms. Step 5: a grid of spots appears as a web of dots, larger towards the edge. A note says Klüver sorted such visions into lattices, cobwebs, tunnels and spirals. In 2001 the mathematicians

chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?: 05 Explanation two: symbols travel
chunks.text: Some symbols really did travel, and when they did, they left a trail. The swastika moved with Buddhism from India into China, Korea and Japan, with dated stops along the route. Rosettes of overlapping circles spread through the Roman world on mosaics and silverware. Von Petzinger's own maps show individual Ice Age signs appearing in one region and turning up later in others, which is what cultural transmission looks like. Real diffusion leaves footprints: dated examples, stepping from place to place. Independent invention leaves scattered first appearances. That is the test. A motif carried by people should appear first in one place and then, step by dated step, in neighbouring places. A motif rediscovered by many minds should pop up at unrelated dates in unrelated regions. The simplest repeats (spirals, zigzags, hands) mostly look like the second pattern. Complex, arbitrary combinations, such as a specific script or a particular god with particular attributes, look like the first.

chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?: 06 Explanation three: a lost source
chunks.text: Graham Hancock takes the boldest reading. In Magicians of the Gods he suggests that the civilising sages remembered in several traditions, from the Mesopotamian apkallu to Mesoamerican culture heroes, could be memories of survivors from an advanced culture destroyed at the end of the Ice Age, and that the 'handbag' may be one of their emblems. Michael Button, on Joe Rogan's podcast in August 2026, drew on von Petzinger's work to argue that Ice Age people held a sophisticated symbolic tradition far older than textbooks admit, and that civilisations rose and fell more than once. Button's underlying point has real support: symbolic behaviour is very old, and specialists underrated it for a long time. But a single lost source struggles with the dates. The zigzag was cut by Homo erectus half a million years ago, and hand stencils appear in Sulawesi and possibly among Neanderthals before 60,000 years ago, long before any proposed lost civilisation. The Göbekli carvings sit 8,000 years before the Nimrud reliefs, with no trail of handbags between them, and the objects themselves are different. A lost source would also need to explain why it passed on only the simplest shapes and none of its writing, numbers or tools.

chunks.heading: The Same Signs Everywhere: One Source or One Brain?: 07 What time has hidden, and what would settle it
chunks.text: Honesty cuts both ways. Most human symbols were never carved in stone. Body paint, tattoos, woven patterns, carved wood and drawings in sand vanish within years. The Ice Age coasts, where many people lived, are now deep underwater. The surviving record is a thin, biased sample, so gaps between examples are weak evidence of anything. A dated chain of intermediate examples linking a complex motif across an ocean before 1492. A shared arbitrary detail, not a simple shape, in two unconnected regions at the same date. Direct dates and an agreed reading for the Pillar 43 objects. Pigment or radiocarbon dating of the Abydos circle drawings. Until then, the recurring signs tell us something remarkable, but it is about us: every human mind comes with the same eyes, the same hands and the same urge to leave a mark.

chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species
chunks.text: The Michael Button Files Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species Middle Pleistocene, 476,000 ± 23,000 years ago Strong evidence. Did human relatives build with wood long before our own species appeared? The claim on the scales Human relatives, before our own species existed, shaped and joined logs into a wooden structure nearly half a million years ago. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established The deliberate notch, the shaped ends and the tool marks are well documented, experiments ruled out river damage as the cause, and the age rests on two luminescence methods and 16 samples. No published rebuttal has appeared since 2023. It stops short of established because it is a single join from one excavation, dated by one team, with its builders unidentified and its function still a proposal. Independent replication at Kalambo or another site would lift it further. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks and museum labels still present the Lower Palaeolithic confidently as an age of stone tools and simple spears, because stone is what survives. Kalambo shows that confidence was built on a biased sample. On the capabilities of pre-sapiens humans, the standard account has been overconfident in its modesty; on what Kalambo was used for, the evidence is still thin in both directions. What is solid In 2019 excavators at Kalambo Falls, Zambia, uncovered two logs of bushwillow (Combretum zeyheri) lying across each other at about 75°, the upper one cut with a U-shaped notch 13.2 × 11.4 cm in which the lower trunk sits. Barham et al. 2023 Luminescence dating of the sands around the logs, using two methods on feldspar and quartz, gives an age of 476,000 ± 23,000 years; radiocarbon gives only 'infinite' ages beyond its roughly 50,000-year range. Barham et al. 2023 The upper log carries scraping striations, chopping facets and shaped, tapered ends; experiments exposing wood to the river did not produce similar marks. Barham et al. 2023 Four more worked pieces (a wedge, a digging stick, a cut log and a notched branch) come from the same river deposits, dated between about 476,000 and 324,000 years ago, with Acheulean handaxes and cleavers nearby. Barham et al. 2023 The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old, so the Kalambo join predates our species by well over 150,000 years. Richter et al. 2017 What is disputed What the join was for: the excavators suggest a raised platform, walkway or foundation on a wet floodplain, but only one join has been exposed. Who made it: no human

chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species: 01 A join in the riverbank
chunks.text: Just above Kalambo Falls, where the Kalambo River drops 235 metres on the border of Zambia and Tanzania, a team led by Larry Barham of the University of Liverpool dug into the riverbank in 2019. Below today's river level, in sand that has stayed wet for an almost unimaginable length of time, they found two logs lying across each other. The upper one, a length of bushwillow 141.3 cm long, had a U-shaped notch cut into it. The lower trunk sat in that notch. Someone had made a join. And the sand around it, dated by luminescence, was about 476,000 years old. The oldest known piece of carpentry was made by people who were not us. That is older than the earliest known fossils of our own species by roughly 170,000 years. Whoever cut the notch belonged to an earlier kind of human. The find raises a question that goes to the heart of this site: if wood almost never survives, what else could these people build that we will never see?

chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species: 02 What the logs actually show
chunks.text: The details, published in Nature in 2023, are specific. The upper log crosses the lower trunk at about 75°. Its notch measures 13.2 by 11.4 cm and runs across the log's long axis. Both of its ends were shaped into tapers. Under magnification the surfaces carry V-shaped striations from scraping, small entry facets from chopping, and broad facets from shaping. The lower trunk, left in place where it runs into the cliff, has scraping marks of its own. Step 1 of 5. chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species: 03 Who were the builders?
chunks.text: No human bones have been found at Kalambo Falls. The nearest clue comes from elsewhere in Zambia: the Broken Hill skull from Kabwe, a big-browed archaic human dated in 2020 to about 299,000 years ago. People of that broad kind, often called Homo heidelbergensis, are the usual suspects, but the honest answer is that the builders are known only through their work. Barham put the lesson plainly when the paper came out: "Forget the label 'Stone Age', look at what these people were doing: they made something new, and large, from wood." He also argued that a spot with reliable water and plenty of trees may have let people stay for long periods, which challenges the picture of early humans as constantly on the move.

chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species: 04 The mainstream story, and where it lagged
chunks.text: For more than a century the earliest chapters of the human story were written in stone because stone is what lasts. Wood appears only in rare windows. A broken spear tip from Clacton in England is around 400,000 years old. Ten wooden spears, 1.84 to 2.53 metres long, were excavated at Schöningen in Germany in the 1990s. In France, Neanderthals broke off some 400 pieces of stalagmite deep inside Bruniquel Cave about 176,000 years ago and arranged them into rings, a structure of a different material. A horizontal time chart from 500,000 years ago on the left to today on the right. Kalambo Falls: a bar from about 499,000 to 453,000 years ago for the structure, and dots at 390,000 and 324,000 for other worked wood. Clacton spear tip: a dot at about 400,000. Schöningen spears: a dashed box for the 2015 date of 337,000 to 300,000 and a dot at about 200,000 for the 2025 revision. Gantangqing digging tools: a bar from 350,000 to 250,000. Bruniquel stalagmite rings made by Neanderthals: a dot at about 176,000. Homo sapiens: a bar from 300,000 to today, starting with Jebel Irhoud. An accent line at 300,000 years marks when our species appears. In 2025 two studies reshaped the wooden record around Kalambo.
