A team led by Jian-Hui Liu reported 35 wooden tools, mostly for digging up roots and tubers, from Gantangqing in south-west China, dated to about 350,000–250,000 years ago, the oldest in East Asia. And a new dating study argued that the Schöningen spears are about 200,000 years old rather than 300,000, which would make Neanderthals their likely makers. Specialists accepted Kalambo quickly, which is to their credit. But the find exposes a deeper problem with the conventional picture. Labels like 'Stone Age' and diagrams that show early humans with nothing but a handaxe were built

chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species: 05 Michael Button's case
chunks.text: Michael Button, a British YouTuber who studied ancient history at university, brought Kalambo to a huge audience on The Joe Rogan Experience in August 2025 and again in August 2026. His argument, in his own terms, is that cut, tapered and fitted timber is engineering, and that it pushes signs of a planning, building mind back almost ten times further than the 'cognitive revolution' of about 50,000 years ago that many popular histories still describe. He pairs this with a point about preservation that specialists would recognise. Wood that survives half a million years is a freak of geology. One such survival suggests many structures that rotted away, and he sets this inside his larger picture of a human past in which capability is older than we were taught, and has been gained and lost more than once. If one waterlogged riverbank kept a join this old, the empty record elsewhere says more about rot than about minds. On the first point the evidence is on his side, and so are many archaeologists: the idea of a sudden cognitive revolution was already under attack in the scholarly literature, notably in Sally McBrearty and Alison Brooks's 2000 paper 'The revolution that wasn't'. On the larger thesis, Kalambo is silent. It shows woodworking and a joint, not houses, villages or a lost civilisation. The claim weighed here is the one Kalambo can actually answer.

chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species: 06 What time has erased
chunks.text: Wood decays wherever oxygen and microbes reach it. It survives for hundreds of thousands of years only when it is sealed underwater, frozen or extremely dry. Kalambo's river kept its sediments saturated, which is why Desmond Clark had already found worked wood there in the 1950s and 1960s, including a log 165 cm long with a groove cut across it, though dating it proved hard. Most riverbanks of half a million years ago have long since eroded or dried out. The scarcity of early wooden structures is therefore weak evidence that they were rare: in places nobody could look, or where nothing could survive, absence tells us almost nothing.

chunks.heading: Kalambo Falls: Carpentry Before Our Species: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: Three things would move this case from strong to established. More of the structure: wider excavation around the join to learn whether other logs formed a platform or walkway. The builders: fossils or ancient proteins from deposits of the same age nearby. And replication: independent redating of the sands, and a second joined structure from another waterlogged site. Until then, one notch in one log tells us something remarkable with unusual clarity. Nearly half a million years ago, before there was any Homo sapiens, someone looked at two trees and decided how to make them fit.

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?
chunks.text: The Michael Button Files Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans? Middle to Late Pleistocene, c. 200,000–45,000 years ago Plausible. Were the Denisovans unusually big, and could they be the giants of old stories? The claim on the scales Denisovans were unusually large-bodied people, taller and heavier than most humans of their time. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The big skull, teeth and jaws are securely identified, so robustness is established. Height rests on two dredged leg bones in a 2026 preprint not yet through peer review, estimated at about 180 and 190 cm; Jinniushan, a possible relative, gives about 169 cm for a female. That is a consistent picture of big people, but not yet a population average. The separate idea that Denisovans were the giants of legend has no supporting evidence: no Denisovan remains are known from the Near East, and the latest known ones lived about 40,000 years before the texts were written. Textbook confidence cautious Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks and museum labels have been openly unsure about Denisovan bodies, saying they are known mostly from DNA, teeth and a few bones, and that caution was right. The risk now runs the other way: a single preprint about two dredged bones is already being retold as fact. The evidence supports big and robust well, tall on average only provisionally, and giants not at all. What is solid The Denisovans were discovered through DNA: a finger bone from Denisova Cave yielded their genome in 2010, and their molars are very large, outside the range of Neanderthals and modern humans. Reich et al. 2010; Sawyer et al. 2015 In 2025 proteins and mitochondrial DNA identified the Harbin skull, at least 146,000 years old, as Denisovan. It is about 22 cm long with a brain of about 1,420 cm³, one of the largest archaic human skulls known. Ji et al. 2021; Fu et al. 2025 A heavy jaw dredged from the Penghu Channel off Taiwan was identified by its proteins as a male Denisovan in 2025. Chang et al. 2015; Tsutaya et al. 2025 Many Tibetans carry a version of the EPAS1 gene that helps at high altitude and that entered our species from Denisovans or their close relatives. Huerta-Sánchez et al. 2014 The Jinniushan skeleton from north-east China, about 260,000 years old and sometimes grouped with the same Asian lineage, gives a stature of about 169 cm and a body mass of about 78.6 kg for a female. Rosenberg, Zuné and Ruff 2006 What is disputed Whether the two Penghu leg bones described in a 2026 preprint are correctly identified and dated, and whether two individuals can stand for

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?: 01 Bones from a fishing net
chunks.text: During the colder stretches of the Ice Age, the seabed between Taiwan and the Penghu islands was dry land, grazed by elephants and water buffalo. Today it lies under the sea, and trawlers dragging nets across the Penghu Channel bring up fossil bones, which end up in the hands of collectors. In 2015 one of those bones, a heavy human jaw, was described as the first archaic human from Taiwan. In 2025 the proteins still locked in its teeth marked it as a male Denisovan. Then, in August 2026, a team led by Yousuke Kaifu of the University of Tokyo posted a preprint describing two more human bones from the same waters: a right thigh bone and a right shin bone. Both carried a variant of collagen known only in Denisovans. And both were long. The team estimated that the owner of the femur stood about 180 cm tall and weighed about 83 kg, and the owner of the tibia about 190 cm and 91 kg. For fifteen years the Denisovans were a genome without a body. The first leg bones suggest a tall one. For the British YouTuber and podcaster Michael Button, this is where the story turns. Big-bodied archaic humans who vanished, and ancient texts that speak of giants: are they the same memory? This case weighs both halves separately. First, how big do the bones say Denisovans were? Second, does any of it connect to the giants of legend?

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?: 02 A body built from fragments
chunks.text: The Denisovans were found backwards. In 2010 geneticists read a whole genome from the tip of a girl's little finger found in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, and learned that an unknown human group had lived there. Their DNA survives in living people: many Tibetans carry a Denisovan version of a gene, EPAS1, that helps the body cope with thin air. But for years the people themselves were almost invisible, known from the finger, a few teeth and scraps of bone. Step 1 of 5. 2008–2015: a finger bone gives the genome, and outsize molars hint at a robust people. 2008–2015: a finger bone gives the genome, and outsize molars hint at a robust people. 2019–2024: a jaw and a rib from a Tibetan cave, identified by their proteins. 2025: the Harbin skull and the Penghu jaw give the Denisovans a face. 2026 (preprint): a femur and a tibia from the Taiwan Strait give the first heights. Still missing: a pelvis, a spine and any complete skeleton. A schematic human skeleton outline with parts filled in step by step. Step 1: molars and a finger bone from Denisova Cave, 2008 to 2015, with the note that the molars are far larger than Neanderthal or modern ones. Step 2: the Xiahe jaw from the Tibetan Plateau at 3,280 metres, 2019, and a rib from the same cave, 2024. Step 3: the Harbin skull and Penghu jaw, 2025, the first face, with a brain of about 1,420 cubic centimetres. Step 4: a femur and tibia from the Penghu Channel, 2026 preprint, giving statures of about 1.80 and 1.90 metres. Step 5: a dashed pelvis marks what has never been found: pelvis, spine, a complete limb or skeleton. Proteins, which survive longer than DNA, slowly filled in the outline. A jaw found by a monk on the Tibetan Plateau, at 3,280 metres, was identified in 2019; a rib from the same cave followed in 2

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?: 03 Big teeth, a big head, long legs
chunks.text: The size signal has been there from the start. The Denisova molars are enormous, larger than those of Neanderthals or modern humans and closer in size to much older members of the genus Homo. The Harbin skull, at least 146,000 years old, is about 22 cm long with the longest brow ridge of any human skull measured and a brain of about 1,420 cubic centimetres, well within our own range. Its one surviving molar measures about 13.6 by 16.6 mm, against roughly 10 by 12 mm for a typical modern person. The Penghu jaw is thick and heavy. The best earlier clue to body size came from a possible relative. The Jinniushan skeleton from north-east China, about 260,000 years old, is one of the few archaic Asian skeletons with a pelvis and limbs. In 2006 Karen Rosenberg, Lü Zuné and Christopher Ruff estimated that this woman stood about 169 cm tall and weighed about 78.6 kg, heavy for her height. Some researchers group Jinniushan with Harbin and the Denisovans; others do not. Six human silhouettes standing on one ground line, with a scale bar from 0 to 3 metres. Under the heading Bones: a reference person of 1.70 m; the Jinniushan female, a possible relative, about 1.69 m; Penghu 2, estimated from a femur, about 1.80 m; and Penghu 3, estimated from a tibia, about 1.90 m. A bracket over the two Penghu figures reads Denisovan by proteins, two dredged leg bones, 2026 preprint. Under the heading Texts, two dashed outlines: Goliath in the Septuagint and a Dead Sea Scroll, four cubits and a span, about 2.0 m, and Goliath in the Masoretic Hebrew text, six cubits and a span, about 2.9 m. The August 2026 preprint by Kaifu, Chang, Tsutaya and colleagues recovered 1,856 and 3,283 amino acid residues from the femur and tibia, each with a collagen variant (COL1A2 R996K) specific to Denisovans. It re

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?: 04 The mainstream reading: big, probably
chunks.text: Specialists welcomed the leg bones and urged caution in the same breath. Sally Reynolds of Bournemouth University pointed out that the analysis rests on two incomplete bones, dredged from the seabed with no record of where or in what layer they lay, and that we cannot tell whether the two people lived at the same time. Inferring a trait for a whole people from two individuals is hard, she wrote, and stature estimates have gone wrong before: different assumptions gave very different heights for Nariokotome Boy, the famous Homo erectus youth from Kenya. There is a subtler point. Big teeth and big skulls do not automatically mean big bodies. Tooth size tracks diet, and a massive skull in a cold northern place such as Harbin may reflect climate and muscle as much as height. Radiocarbon ages close to 45,000 years also sit near the limit of the method, where small amounts of modern contamination make bones look younger than they are. None of this makes the Penghu figures wrong. It makes them a first measurement, not an average. What the mainstream does not dispute is the pattern: no adult Denisovan bone identified so far points to a small body. If the preprint holds up, Denisovans join Neanderthals as heavily built people, and the tall end of the Ice Age human range gains a new member.

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?: 05 The challenger's case at its strongest
chunks.text: Michael Button's wider argument, made on The Joe Rogan Experience in August 2025 and again in August 2026, is that human capability and human diversity both run far deeper than the textbook timeline. He points to the 2025 reconstruction of the Yunxian skull from central China, about a million years old, whose authors placed it near the root of the lineage leading to Homo longi and the Denisovans and argued that this lineage separated from ours more than a million years ago. That timing is still debated, but it is a peer-reviewed result, not a fringe one. On size, Button is ahead of the evidence but pointing the right way. For decades, Chinese fossils such as Harbin, Dali and Jinniushan were filed as awkward archaic humans and largely ignored in the West. A skull spent some eighty-five years hidden in a well. Only proteins and ancient DNA forced the rethink, and each new identification has added a large, robust individual. His strongest point is that consistency: in a record of only a dozen or so bones, not one adult bone says small. The challengers ask a fair question: if a whole people stayed hidden until 2010, how sure should we be about their shape?

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?: 06 Giants in the old texts
chunks.text: The link to giants comes mainly from two passages in the Hebrew Bible. The first describes the Nephilim, a word of uncertain meaning that ancient Greek translators rendered as gigantes and the King James Version as giants. The Nephilim were on the earth in those days ... These were the heroes that were of old, warriors of renown. The second is the report of the spies sent into Canaan, who say they saw the Nephilim there: There we saw the Nephilim (the Anakites come from the Nephilim), and to ourselves we seemed like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them. What these passages mean is for readers and their traditions, and this case does not judge it. The physical claim can be tested. Goliath, the best-known giant, is six cubits and a span tall in the Masoretic Hebrew text, about 2.9 m, but four cubits and a span in the Septuagint and a Dead Sea Scroll, about 2.0 m. The tallest Denisovan estimate so far is about 1.9 m. No Denisovan bone or gene has been found in the Near East, and the latest known Denisovans lived around 40,000 years before these texts were written. A tall archaic human is a remarkable thing, but on the evidence it is not the same thing as the giants of legend.

chunks.heading: Denisovan Giants: How Big Were the Lost Humans?: 07 What time has hidden, and what would settle it
chunks.text: Almost every Denisovan fossil arrived by luck: a finger in a Siberian cave, a jaw kept by a monk, a skull hidden in a well, bones in a fishing net. Much of their world, from the tropics of South-East Asia to the drowned plains of the Sunda shelf, destroys bone and DNA or lies under the sea. The first complete Denisovan skeleton, from a dated cave layer, would answer the size question at a stroke. Until then, replication of the Penghu results and protein screening of the many unidentified limb bones in Asian collections are the quickest routes to a real average. The verdict for now: Denisovans were big, robust people, and plausibly tall. As for giants, the bones point to people like the tallest of us, not to the giants of legend.

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us
chunks.text: The Michael Button Files The First Sailors Were Not Us Early and Middle Pleistocene, c. 1.5 million–100,000 years ago Open question. Did humans before our species cross open sea on purpose, or were they swept? The claim on the scales Human relatives before our species crossed open sea on purpose, rather than drifting there by accident on natural rafts. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established The crossings themselves are firmly established: Flores, Sulawesi and Luzon were never joined to the mainland, and hominins were on all three by about 700,000 years ago. Intent is a different matter. No craft survives, island faunas show that animals crossed the same straits without boats, and published models give accidental colonisation real odds. Against that, repeated, lasting colonisation of separate islands is awkward for pure chance. The evidence does not yet favour either reading, so this remains an open question. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Many textbooks still present seafaring as an achievement of Homo sapiens, marked by the settlement of Australia around 50,000–65,000 years ago. On the fact of earlier crossings they are underconfident: the Wallacean evidence is strong and has been for over a decade. On deliberate voyaging, the challengers sometimes sound more certain than the evidence allows. Both sides tend to skip the honest answer: we know they crossed; we do not know how. What is solid Stone tools at Wolo Sege on Flores lie beneath a volcanic deposit dated to 1.02 ± 0.02 million years. Brumm et al. 2010 Seven chert tools at Calio on Sulawesi are at least 1.04 million years old and possibly as old as 1.48 million. Hakim et al. 2025 At Kalinga on Luzon, 57 stone tools and a butchered rhinoceros skeleton date to about 709,000 years ago (777,000–631,000). Ingicco et al. 2018 The Lombok Strait is at least 250 m deep and stayed open when Ice Age sea level fell about 120 m; Flores was always at least 19 km from its neighbours. Dennell et al. 2014 Hominin fossils from Mata Menge on Flores, about 700,000 years old, belong to small-bodied ancestors of Homo floresiensis. van den Bergh et al. 2016; Kaifu et al. 2024 What is disputed Whether the Wallacean crossings were deliberate voyages on built craft or accidental drift on vegetation mats torn loose by storms or tsunamis. Whether the Plakias finds on Crete are Lower Palaeolithic tools at least 130,000 years old, since they were dated through landforms and soils rather than directly. Whether Kefalonia and Zakynthos were islands when Neanderthals reached them about 11

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us: 01 Tools where no one should have been
chunks.text: In the 1850s the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace noticed something odd about the islands of Indonesia. Bali's birds and mammals were Asian. Lombok's, a short sail east, were strikingly different. The line he drew between them follows deep water that stayed open even in the Ice Ages, when sea level fell far enough to join Java, Sumatra and Borneo to Asia. East of it, land animals arrived only by swimming, floating or flying. So did people. On Flores, Sulawesi and Luzon, islands that were never part of the mainland, archaeologists have found stone tools up to a million years old and more, made long before Homo sapiens existed. The crossings are not in doubt. The mystery is whether anyone meant to make them.

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us: 02 Three islands, a million years
chunks.text: The receipts come from careful excavations published in Nature. On Flores, stone tools at Wolo Sege lie beneath volcanic ash dated to 1.02 million years. On Sulawesi, a team led by Budianto Hakim reported in 2025 seven chert flakes at Calio, dated by palaeomagnetism and by uranium-series and electron spin resonance on fossil teeth to at least 1.04 million years, and possibly 1.48 million. On Luzon, at Kalinga, 57 stone tools lay among the bones of a rhinoceros that had been butchered about 709,000 years ago. Step 1 of 5. Java: Homo erectus by about 1.3 million years ago, reached on foot across the dry Sunda Shelf. Java: Homo erectus by about 1.3 million years ago, reached on foot across the dry Sunda Shelf. About a million years ago: tools appear on Sulawesi and Flores, across straits that never dried. About 700,000 years ago: a butchered rhino on Luzon; fossils of hobbit ancestors on Flores. Debated: tools on Crete (at least 130,000 years) and Neanderthal sites on the Ionian Islands. Our species: Australia and New Guinea by about 50,000 years ago, the Ryukyus by about 30,000. A horizontal time chart from 1.6 million years ago on the left to today on the right, with seven rows. Java: Homo erectus by about 1.3 million years ago, with a dashed extension to 1.5 for older estimates, reached on foot. Sulawesi: a solid dot at 1.04 million years for the Calio tools, with a dashed range back to 1.48. Flores: a dot at 1.02 million for Wolo Sege, and a bar from 0.7 million to about 50,000 years ago for fossils and Homo floresiensis. Luzon: a dot at about 709,000 years for the Kalinga butchery site, with its error range. Crete: an open circle at 130,000 years for the debated Plakias tools. Ionian Islands: an open circle at about 110,000 years for Neanderthal tools. Sahul and the R

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us: 03 Why walking was never an option
chunks.text: At the height of an ice age the sea fell by about 120 metres. The Lombok Strait, about 20 km wide at its narrowest, is at least 250 metres deep, so water always remained. Flores stayed at least 19 km from its neighbours even at the lowest sea levels. Sulawesi and Luzon were separated from the Asian shelf by still wider and deeper channels, swept by strong currents. A cross-section with Bali on the left and Lombok on the right. The seabed dips into a channel about 20 km wide at the surface and at least 250 m deep. Pale blue water fills the channel up to today's sea level. A dashed line marks the Ice Age low stand about 120 m lower, and darker blue water still fills the deep part of the channel below it, with a small raft floating on it labelled 'still open sea'. The zone between the two lines is labelled as water lost at the low stand. Bali is labelled as joined to Java and Asia when sea level fell; Lombok as east of the Wallace Line. A 5 km scale bar and a note on 50 times vertical exaggeration sit at the bottom, with a box noting that Flores stayed at least 19 km from its neighbours and that Sulawesi and Luzon were never joined to the mainland. That is why these islands matter so much. On Java, which could be reached on foot across the dry Sunda Shelf, Homo erectus appears by about 1.3 million years ago. To go further, someone had to get wet.

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us: 04 The mainstream reading: a sweepstakes
chunks.text: The most careful sceptical case comes from Robin Dennell and colleagues, who looked at who else made the trip. The early animals of Flores are a strange, thin selection: a dwarf stegodon, a strong swimmer, plus giant rats, a giant tortoise and the Komodo dragon. Biologists call this sweepstakes dispersal, where a few lucky species win a lottery that most never enter. Dennell's team proposed that hominins arrived the same way, clinging to mats of vegetation washed out to sea by tsunamis, perhaps from Sulawesi on the prevailing currents. They offer a vivid modern parallel: after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, a pregnant woman who could not swim was rescued after five days afloat on a sago palm. Their modelling suggested that an accidental colonisation had about half the chance of success of a planned one, which is far from negligible over hundreds of thousands of years. In 2025 the linguist Rudolf Botha argued that inferring boat-building, and from it language, from the crossings involves steps the evidence does not support.

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us: 05 The challengers: when does luck become behaviour?
chunks.text: Michael Button, the British YouTuber and podcaster, puts the other side to a large audience. On The Joe Rogan Experience in August 2026 he described the Wallacean islands as some of his strongest evidence. His argument, in his own terms, is about pattern: one accidental arrival is easy to believe, but Sulawesi, Flores and Luzon lie far apart, and each was reached and settled. At some point, he suggests, repeated accidents start to look like behaviour. He also points to modelling of how many founders a lasting colony needs. He is not alone. Robert Bednarik argued in the 1990s and 2000s that Homo erectus seafaring implies planning and speech, and his First Mariners Project sailed bamboo rafts built with stone-age-type tools in Indonesian waters. Larry Barham, who led the Kalambo Falls excavation described in another case on this site, and the linguist Daniel Everett count early seafaring among their evidence for early symbolic communication. Everett has long argued that Homo erectus had language. The Mediterranean offers tantalising echoes. In 2010 Thomas Strasser and colleagues reported handaxe-like tools near Plakias on Crete, an island for more than five million years, and argued from the marine terraces and soils around them that they were at least 130,000 years old. In 2012 George Ferentinos and colleagues argued that Neanderthals reached Kefalonia and Zakynthos across straits under 12 km wide. Both claims remain debated: the Crete tools were not dated directly, and Nena Galanidou has argued that at low sea levels some Ionian islands were hills on a coastal plain, reachable on foot. One accident is a story. Three islands settled across deep water begin to look like a pattern.

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us: 06 What the sea has taken
chunks.text: The one piece of evidence that would settle the argument, a boat, is the one least likely to survive. Bamboo, logs, bark and fibre rot within years. The oldest known boat in the world, the Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, is about 10,000 years old. The Ice Age beaches where rafts were launched and landed now lie tens of metres underwater, and tropical soils have destroyed most of the bones of the people who made the crossings. In 2025 the Calio dates made Sulawesi the earliest known sea-crossing destination, at least 1.04 million years ago. The same year, Yousuke Kaifu's team published their 2019 voyage: a 7.5 m dugout canoe, hollowed with replica Palaeolithic stone axes, paddled 225 km from Taiwan to Yonaguni in over 45 hours, largely out of sight of land. Reed and bamboo rafts had failed earlier trials in the Kuroshio current. That test concerns our own species 30,000 years ago, but it shows how much simple craft can do.

chunks.heading: The First Sailors Were Not Us: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The case would move with a waterlogged site in Wallacea yielding worked bamboo, cordage or a paddle; fossils or ancient proteins from Calio that identify the crossers; direct dates on the Plakias tools; and seafloor mapping that fixes the Ionian coastline 110,000 years ago. Better drift models, run strait by strait, could test how often natural rafts could deliver enough people to found a population. For now the honest scorecard has two lines. That human relatives crossed the sea a million years ago is well established, and it overturns the old idea that only our species could leave the land behind. Whether they meant to is a genuinely open question, and one of the most interesting in human prehistory.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo
chunks.text: The Michael Button Files The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo Late Pleistocene, c. 31,000 years ago Strong evidence. Could Ice Age foragers perform surgery that a patient survived? The claim on the scales Ice Age foragers performed deliberate surgery that the patient survived, drawing on real medical knowledge. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established TB1 is securely dated, the cut is clean and oblique through both bones, crushing and infection are absent, and healing shows years of survival. Independent specialists accept the surgical reading, and later Ice Age dental work at Villabruna and Riparo Fredian shows deliberate treatment of the living before farming. It falls short of established because it rests on one skeleton for surgery proper, and because planning, anaesthetic plants and infection control are inferred rather than observed. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact General histories of medicine have long opened with Neolithic trepanation and ancient Egyptian papyri, presented with quiet confidence as the beginning of surgery. That confidence was misplaced: it rested on where bones survive and where people looked. The textbooks were underconfident about the skill of Ice Age foragers; the new evidence is a single, strong case rather than a large body of data, so the corrected picture should also stay modest. What is solid A young person known as TB1 was buried in Liang Tebo cave, Borneo, about 31,000 years ago (modelled 31,201–30,714 years ago), and died aged about 19–20. Maloney et al. 2022 The lowest third of TB1's left tibia and fibula is missing, and both bones end in a clean, oblique cut without the crushing or splintering typical of accidents. Maloney et al. 2022 The cut ends had remodelled into a rounded stump, showing survival for 6–9 years after an amputation in childhood, with no sign of bone infection. Maloney et al. 2022 The burial was careful: limestone rocks placed over the head and arms, and a nodule of red ochre near the jaw. Maloney et al. 2022 Later Ice Age and early Holocene people scraped decayed teeth (Villabruna, about 14,000 years ago), drilled living molars (Mehrgarh, 9,000–7,500 years ago) and performed trepanations that healed (Ensisheim, about 7,000 years ago). Oxilia et al. 2015; Coppa et al. 2006; Alt et al. 1997 What is disputed Whether the operation was planned from the start, or was the careful finishing of a traumatic injury such as a crushed foot. How bleeding, pain and infection were controlled: medicinal plants are suggested by the authors but not directly evidenced. Whether TB1

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo: 01 A grave with a missing foot
chunks.text: In 2020, in Liang Tebo, a limestone cave in the rugged forested karst of East Kalimantan on Borneo, Indonesian and Australian archaeologists uncovered a grave. The young person inside, catalogued as TB1, had been laid out with care. Limestone rocks sat over the head and each arm. A lump of red ochre lay near the jaw. And the left foot, with the lowest part of the left leg, was missing. It was not lost after burial. The two bones of the lower leg ended in a clean, angled cut, and the cut ends had healed. The burial was about 31,000 years old, deep in the last Ice Age, when everyone on Earth lived by foraging. A child lost a leg to a deliberate cut, survived, and was cared for until adulthood, 24,000 years before the next known amputation.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo: 02 What the bones say
chunks.text: The study, led by Tim Maloney of Griffith University and published in Nature in 2022, is precise. TB1 died aged about 19–20. The lowest third of the left tibia and fibula is missing. Both bones were severed along a clean oblique plane, and both show new bone growth that rounded off the cut ends into a stump. From the extent of remodelling, the team estimated that TB1 lived for 6–9 years after losing the leg, which means the operation happened in childhood. Step 1 of 5. TB1 was buried in Liang Tebo about 31,000 years ago; the left foot and lowest part of the leg were missing. TB1 was buried in Liang Tebo about 31,000 years ago; the left foot and lowest part of the leg were missing. Both lower-leg bones end in a clean, oblique cut in their lowest third. No crushing or splintering, and no bone infection: signs against an accident or an animal attack. The cut ends had remodelled into a rounded stump: 6–9 years of healing. The operation happened in childhood; TB1 lived to 19–20 with the group's care. On the left, a simple standing human figure with the lower part of the left leg drawn dashed, labelled TB1, died aged 19 to 20. Guide lines lead to an enlarged front view of the left lower leg on the right: the tibia and the thinner fibula run down from the knee and stop about two thirds of the way down, with the missing lowest third and the foot drawn as dashed outlines. Step 2 highlights a clean oblique cut across both bones. Step 3 adds a small inset showing what is not seen: a crushed, splintered fracture, and a note that there is no bone infection. Step 4 draws rounded, remodelled ends labelled 6 to 9 years of healing. Step 5 adds a life bar from age 0 to death at 19 to 20, with the operation in childhood and a note that TB1 lived on with care in steep karst. A 10 cm scale

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo: 03 Why not an accident?
chunks.text: The obvious alternatives are a crushing fall, a rockslide or an animal attack, and the team tested each against the bone. Accidents that sever a limb usually leave crushed and splintered fractures; TB1's bones show a clean section through both. Animal bites carry bacteria deep into wounds, and the resulting bone infection, osteomyelitis, would normally mark the skeleton. None is present. Bone keeps a diary. A fresh cut leaves sharp edges; living bone then lays down new tissue that rounds and seals the end over months and years. Infection leaves pitting and abnormal new bone. By reading how far the healing had gone, and the absence of infection or crushing, bioarchaeologists can tell a healed cut from an injury at death, and estimate how long the person lived afterwards. Outside experts were cautious but supportive. Charlotte Roberts of Durham University, a leading bioarchaeologist, was quoted in Smithsonian magazine calling it 'consistent with an amputation that's been done surgically'. Kate Domett of James Cook University said, 'it certainly could be an amputation'. One alternative remains: an injury that was then finished and treated by cutting. Even that would require the same knowledge of where to cut and how to keep the patient alive.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo: 04 The mainstream catches up
chunks.text: Until 2022 the oldest known amputation was that of an elderly Neolithic farmer at Buthiers-Boulancourt in France, about 7,000 years old, whose left forearm had been removed. Histories of medicine usually opened with trepanation, cutting a hole in the skull, which appears in Mesolithic Ukraine and becomes widespread in Neolithic Europe, where one man at Ensisheim in Alsace survived two operations. The unspoken assumption was that surgery came with farming, villages and specialists. A time chart from 32,000 years ago on the left to today on the right, with the last Ice Age shaded up to 11,700 years ago and a dashed line marking its end. Rows: Liang Tebo, Borneo, leg amputation at about 31,000 years; Villabruna, Italy, scraped cavity at about 14,000; Riparo Fredian, Italy, bitumen filling at about 13,000; Mehrgarh, Pakistan, drilled molars from 9,000 to 7,500; Ensisheim, France, healed trepanations at about 7,000; Buthiers-Boulancourt, France, forearm amputation at about 7,000; Egypt, the Edwin Smith surgical papyrus at about 3,600 years ago. An accent line joins the two amputations, labelled 24,000 years earlier than the next amputation. The dental record had already been hinting otherwise. At Villabruna in northern Italy, a man who died about 14,000 years ago had a cavity scraped out with a pointed stone tool. At Riparo Fredian in Tuscany, about 13,000 years ago, cavities were enlarged and filled with bitumen. At Mehrgarh in Pakistan, living people had molars drilled 9,000–7,500 years ago. Liang Tebo pushes deliberate treatment of the body far deeper, and the mainstream has accepted the revision.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo: 05 Michael Button's case
chunks.text: Michael Button, the British YouTuber and podcaster, raised the Borneo amputation on The Joe Rogan Experience in August 2026 as part of his wider argument that human capability runs much deeper in time than the textbooks allow. In his own terms: cutting through both bones of a child's leg without the patient bleeding to death, going into shock or dying of infection is difficult even with modern medicine, and success on a first attempt is unlikely. The skill must have been learned, practised and passed on. On this point Button stands with the study's own authors, who wrote that the surgeons needed detailed knowledge of limb anatomy and of the muscles and blood vessels to prevent fatal blood loss and infection, and who suggested that local plants with medicinal properties may have been used to clean wounds and ease pain. Borneo's rainforests are famously rich in plants that local healers still use. Here the challenger and the specialists read the bones the same way: someone knew what they were doing. Where the evidence stops is the larger thesis. TB1 shows skilled Ice Age foragers, not a lost medical civilisation. Their knowledge was presumably the practical, oral kind that hunter-gatherer healers hold today, and most of it has vanished because it was never written down.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo: 06 What time has hidden
chunks.text: The Liang Tebo operation left traces only because it cut through bone and the skeleton happened to survive in a tropical cave. Plant remedies, bandages, stitches and the cutting tool itself have all gone. Most Pleistocene burials in Island South-East Asia have dissolved. It would be a mistake to treat TB1 as the first surgery; it is simply the first one we can see. There are hints that plant medicine is very old indeed. DNA preserved in the dental calculus of a Neanderthal from El Sidrón in Spain, who suffered from a dental abscess and a gut parasite, included traces of poplar, a source of the painkiller salicylic acid, and of Penicillium mould. The authors were careful to say this is suggestive rather than conclusive, but it fits the picture of people who noticed what plants did to their bodies and used that knowledge long before anyone wrote it down. Two 2024 studies showed that wound care is older than humanity. In Sumatra, a wild male orangutan named Rakus was filmed chewing leaves of a liana used in traditional medicine and applying the juice to a facial wound, which healed without infection. And Florida carpenter ants were found to amputate the injured legs of nestmates, raising their survival. Deliberate treatment of wounds, it seems, has deep roots in the animal world.

chunks.heading: The Ice Age Surgeons of Borneo: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: More burials from the Sangkulirang–Mangkalihat caves could show whether TB1 was unique or one of many. Residue studies on stone tools from the burial layers might reveal blood or plant compounds. Dental calculus from the region could preserve traces of medicinal plants, as it has for Neanderthals at El Sidrón in Spain. And a fresh look at museum skeletons may reveal healed cuts that were once filed as injuries. The verdict for now is a strong one. Thirty-one thousand years ago, in the forests of Borneo, a community took the life-or-death decision to cut away a child's leg, did it well, and then looked after that child for years.

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?
chunks.text: The Michael Button Files Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish? Archaic period, c. 9,500–3,000 years ago Awaiting discovery. How much copper did ancient miners take from Lake Superior, and where did it go? The claim on the scales Ancient miners removed 0.5–1.5 billion pounds of copper from Lake Superior, which then vanished from the archaeological record. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The mining is established. The tonnage is not: the 0.5–1.5 billion pound range comes from a 1961 calculation that multiplied three assumed numbers, none measured, and the upper figure simply swaps in a richer ore and more pits. Without a measured quantity there is nothing shown to have vanished. What survives, perhaps 20,000 artifacts in Wisconsin alone, fits long local use, and the pulses of lead pollution fit intermittent mining. A real survey could still raise the estimate, which is why this rates as awaiting evidence rather than ruled out. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact General histories of metallurgy often begin in the Near East and leave the Old Copper Complex out, which undersells one of the oldest metal traditions on Earth; there Button has a fair point. On quantity, museums are properly cautious and say the amount is unknown. The weak link is the popular retelling, where a 1961 back-of-envelope sum has hardened into a figure repeated as if it had been measured. What is solid Archaic peoples of the western Great Lakes made tools from native copper beginning at least about 9,500 years ago, with a peak between about 7,000 and 5,000 years ago: among the oldest metalworking anywhere. Pompeani et al. 2021 Lead pollution in Keweenaw lake sediments records copper mining and heating about 8,000 and 7,000 years ago, falling to background levels after about 5,000 years ago. Pompeani et al. 2013 Sediment from McCargoe Cove on Isle Royale records mining 6,500–5,400 years ago, near the Minong Ridge pits, the largest known pre-Columbian copper mine. Pompeani et al. 2015 Thousands of grooved stone hammers survive in and around the pits; miners used fire, water and hammerstones, then shaped the metal by cold hammering and annealing. Milwaukee Public Museum; NPS Wisconsin alone has yielded at least 13,000 and perhaps about 20,000 Archaic copper artifacts. Milwaukee Public Museum Around 3,000 years ago these hunter-gatherers largely gave up copper tools and returned to stone, a reversal that is rare among metal-using societies. Bebber et al. 2019 What is disputed How many ancient pits there were, how large and deep they

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?: 01 Metal that came out of the ground pure
chunks.text: Along the Keweenaw Peninsula and on Isle Royale, in the cold north of Lake Superior, copper lies in the rock as metal. Not ore that must be smelted, but native copper, almost pure, in threads, sheets and lumps, some of them enormous. The Ontonagon Boulder, a single mass of copper weighing about 1.5 tonnes, sat on a riverbank until it was hauled away to Washington in the 1840s. When prospectors arrived in the 1840s, they found they were not the first. Lines of shallow depressions in the forest turned out to be filled-in pits, with grooved stone hammers scattered around them by the thousand. According to accounts gathered by the geologist Charles Whittlesey, miners at one site found an ancient pit holding a copper mass of several tons that the old miners had raised on wooden supports and then, for reasons no one knows, left behind. The first metalworkers of North America were hunter-gatherers, and they started thousands of years before bronze reached Europe. That much is real. The question here is a number that has travelled far beyond the evidence: that these miners took out between half a billion and 1.5 billion pounds of copper, and that almost all of it has vanished.

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The dating has improved sharply in recent years. In 2021 David Pompeani and colleagues gathered 53 radiocarbon dates, including eight new ones, from wood and cordage embedded in copper tools, cremations and mine fills. Their work put the start of copper working at least 9,500 years ago, with a peak between about 7,000 and 5,000 years ago. Dates from the mines themselves came out younger, which they read as the time the pits filled in after abandonment, not when they were worked. Lakes kept their own record. Mining and heating copper-bearing rock releases lead, and cores from Keweenaw lakes show lead rising about 8,000 and 7,000 years ago, then shifting from lake to lake, as if mining moved around, before falling back to background after about 5,000 years ago. On Isle Royale, sediment from McCargoe Cove records mining from about 6,500 to 5,400 years ago, near the Minong Ridge pits. Heating rock with fire and dousing it with water cracks it, the method the ancient miners appear to have used. The same process sends traces of lead into the air and streams. Because lake mud builds up year by year, a core through it is a timeline, and a lead spike that matches radiocarbon-dated layers shows when mining happened nearby, even where the pits themselves have been destroyed. The products survive in quantity. Spear points, knives, axes, awls, fishhooks and beads have been found across the western Great Lakes. P. V. Lawson of Menasha compiled an inventory of at least 13,000 copper artifacts in Wisconsin alone, and the Milwaukee Public Museum suggests the total could be around 20,000.

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?: 03 Where the billion pounds came from
chunks.text: The big number has a traceable origin. In 1961 Roy Drier and Octave Du Temple privately published Prehistoric Copper Mining in the Lake Superior Region, a collection of older articles with their own estimate. The arithmetic went like this. Step 1 of 5. Assume one average pit, 20 ft wide and 30 ft deep: about 1,000–1,200 tons of rock. Assume one average pit, 20 ft wide and 30 ft deep: about 1,000–1,200 tons of rock. Assume the rock was 5% copper: about 100,000 lb per pit. Assume 5,000 pits, all copper-bearing: 500 million lb. Assume 15% copper and more pits: over 1.5 billion lb. None of these inputs was ever measured. A cross-section of a single pit drawn to scale in bedrock, 20 feet or 6.1 metres wide and 30 feet or 9.1 metres deep, beside a 1.7 metre person. To the right, five rows appear step by step. Step 1: assume a pit 20 feet wide and 30 feet deep, giving 1,000 to 1,200 tons of rock. Step 2: assume the rock is 5 percent copper, shown as copper specks in the rock, giving about 100,000 pounds per pit. Step 3: assume 5,000 pits, all copper-bearing, giving 500 million pounds. Step 4: assume 15 percent copper and more pits, giving over 1.5 billion pounds. Step 5: inputs actually measured, none; question marks appear on the width, depth and ore grade. Assume an average pit 20 feet across and 30 feet deep, which works out at 1,000–1,200 tons of rock. Assume the rock was 5 percent copper, about 100 pounds per ton, and each pit yields about 100,000 pounds. Assume 5,000 pits, all copper-bearing, and the total is 500 million pounds. Raise the grade to 15 percent and add more pits, and the total passes 1.5 billion. Later popular books, including Betty Sodders's Michigan Prehistory Mysteries (1990), repeated and enlarged the picture. The researcher David Johnson, who has exami

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?: 04 The challenger's case
chunks.text: Michael Button raised the Old Copper Complex on The Joe Rogan Experience in August 2026 as a case study in lost technology. His framing is striking: a metal industry beginning about 9,500 years ago, peaking 7,000 to 5,000 years ago, extracting something like 1.5 billion pounds, about 680,000 tonnes, and then simply stopping, its know-how forgotten. If that could happen here, he argues, why not elsewhere, with technologies that left even fewer traces? Much of this stands up. The dates he gives match the published radiocarbon work. The pits are real and there are many of them. And the abandonment is genuinely unusual. In 2019 Michelle Bebber and colleagues called it exceptional: most societies that took up metal tools never went back to stone, yet around 3,000 years ago these communities largely did. Button is also right that the tradition is left out of many general histories of metallurgy, which tend to begin in the Near East. Button's deeper point survives the audit: a people can master a material and then choose to put it down.

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?: 05 The mainstream reading: real mining, imaginary tonnage
chunks.text: Where the story breaks is the quantity, and with it the vanishing. A figure of 680,000 tonnes would equal roughly one seventh of everything Michigan's industrial native copper mines produced from the 1840s to the 1960s, about 11 billion pounds, with steam, dynamite and railways. Nothing in the pits, the tools or the lake mud requires anything like that. A horizontal bar chart on a logarithmic scale from 1 tonne to 10 million tonnes. The Ontonagon Boulder, a single native copper mass: about 1.5 tonnes. All Wisconsin Archaic copper artifacts, about 20,000 at a generous 1 kilogram each: about 20 tonnes, drawn faint because it is an upper-end assumption. The 1961 low estimate of 0.5 billion pounds, never measured: about 227,000 tonnes, dashed. The 1961 high estimate of 1.5 billion pounds, the figure Button cites: about 680,000 tonnes, dashed. Michigan's industrial native copper output from the 1840s to the 1960s: about 5 million tonnes. Archaeologists see instead a long, intermittent tradition carried out by small, mobile groups. Some of the copper, especially early on, was float copper picked from glacial gravels rather than mined. Tools were used until worn out, reworked, buried with the dead or lost; copper also travelled as a trade good. Experiments by Bebber and her colleagues found that stone flakes started out sharper and that copper blades showed no clear advantage for many tasks, so the effort of mining may simply not have been worth it once stone did the job. A drier climate after about 5,000 years ago may have added to the cost. In short, no one has shown that a billion pounds was removed, so there is no missing billion pounds to explain.

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?: 06 What time has hidden
chunks.text: The honest gap is large. When industrial mining began, companies deliberately sought out the ancient pits as guides to rich ground and dug straight through many of them. Others were filled by centuries of soil and leaf litter. Collectors took thousands of artifacts from farm fields and never recorded where they came from, and much of what was found in the nineteenth century has been scattered. So the true scale of the ancient mining is not only unknown; parts of it can no longer be known.

chunks.heading: Old Copper: Did a Billion Pounds Vanish?: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The question is answerable, at least in part. Airborne lidar can reveal pits under forest; a survey of every surviving pit, with a sample excavated to measure real volumes, would replace the guessed 5,000 pits and guessed dimensions. Assays of the surrounding rock would replace the guessed ore grade. A census of copper artifacts by weight, and chemical sourcing of copper found far from the lake, would show how much was used locally and how much travelled. Until then, the fair verdict is this: the Old Copper Complex is one of the great early metal traditions of the world, and the billion pounds is a sum that was never measured.

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone
chunks.text: The Michael Button Files The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone Undated: proposals range from the Neolithic to the Roman period Ruled out. How old are the cart ruts, and could they be older than any known civilisation? The claim on the scales The cart ruts were made in the Ice Age or earlier, long before the Bronze Age and before any known society in Malta or Anatolia. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established Several independent lines contradict an Ice Age or older date. No people lived on Malta before about 8,500 years ago, and the first farmers came about 7,900 years ago. Wheeled vehicles appear only around 3500 BCE. The drowned ruts lie in shallow water, which modest sea-level rise since Roman times can explain, whereas Ice Age shorelines lie tens of metres deeper. The Phrygian claim confuses the age of the rock with the age of the grooves cut into it. A Temple Period date, older than the Bronze Age, remains an open question. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Guidebooks and some museum panels still say 'Bronze Age' with more confidence than the evidence carries. Specialists are frank that no rut has a direct date, that the Punic-tomb argument can be read both ways, and that dates from the Neolithic to Roman times are all defended. The textbooks are slightly overconfident about the date, and well founded about how the ruts formed. What is solid Hundreds of paired, parallel grooves are cut into the bedrock of Malta and Gozo, more densely than anywhere else known; Derek Mottershead estimates about 35 km of rut survive as fragments. Groucutt 2022; Mottershead 2011 A measured sample shows fairly standard ruts: mean top width about 26 cm, base about 13 cm, maximum depth about 20 cm, and a centre-to-centre gauge of about 1.39–1.40 m. Groucutt 2022 Geomorphologists showed that two-wheeled carts with a 1.40 m gauge and moderate loads could wear such ruts into Malta's soft limestone when it is wet, until the ruts reach the cart's ground clearance of about 0.675 m. Mottershead, Pearson and Schaefer 2008 Some ruts are interrupted by the shafts of Punic rock-cut tombs, the usual basis for saying the ruts existed by about 700 BCE, though the reading of that evidence is itself disputed. Bugeja 2001; Sagona 2004 At several coastal sites, such as St George's Bay at Birżebbuġa, ruts run down to the shore and continue a short way under the water. Trump 2002 Hunter-gatherers first reached Malta by sea about 8,500 years ago, and farmers followed about 7,900 years ago; there is no evidence of people on the islands before that. Scer

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone: 01 Clapham Junction in the limestone
chunks.text: On a bare, wind-scoured plateau above the cliffs near Siġġiewi in southern Malta, the rock is scored with lines. They come in pairs, about a metre and a half apart, and they curve, cross, split and merge like the tracks outside a busy station. The archaeologist David Trump nicknamed the place Clapham Junction, after the tangle of lines at the London railway interchange, and the name stuck. The local name is Misraħ Għar il-Kbir. Some of these grooves are a few centimetres deep. Others, here and at San Ġwann, sink half a metre or more into the limestone. Some run to the edge of a cliff and stop in the air. Others slide down the shore at St George's Bay in Birżebbuġa and continue under the sea. Nobody has found the vehicles that made them, and nobody has a direct date for a single rut. They look like the rails of a lost railway, and they are one of the few ancient puzzles you can stand inside. That combination, precise engineering-like lines with no date and no maker, has made the ruts a favourite of anyone arguing that history is older than we were taught. It is worth taking them slowly.

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone: 02 What the measurements show
chunks.text: The ruts were described in print as early as 1647 by the Maltese historian Giovanni Francesco Abela, and Sir Temi Zammit gave them their modern vocabulary in a 1928 paper in Antiquity. The first large statistical study came in 2022, when Huw Groucutt measured the shapes. Across 159 ruts, the mean top width was about 26 cm and the mean base width about 13 cm, a V or U shape that narrows downwards. Mean maximum depth was about 20 cm. The distance between the centres of a pair averaged about 1.39 m, and between the inner edges about 1.11 m. A cross-section drawn to scale, looking along the ruts. A flat limestone surface has two V-shaped grooves 1.40 metres apart, centre to centre. Each typical groove is about 26 centimetres wide at the top, 13 centimetres at the base and 20 centimetres deep. A dashed outline shows the deepest ruts, about 60 centimetres. A schematic two-wheeled cart stands with its wheels in the grooves; its axle is 0.675 metres above the rut bottom, the ground clearance. When ruts get deeper than that, the cart's underside hits the rock between them and drivers move to a new line. A 50 centimetre scale bar is shown. That consistency matters. Groucutt concluded that the ruts are fairly standardised, 'perhaps suggesting that they are of a consistent age and function', while noting that the popular comparison with railway gauge is misleading because the two are measured differently. In 2008 the geomorphologists Derek Mottershead, Alastair Pearson and Martin Schaefer tested the rock itself. Malta's Globigerina limestone is weak, and when soaked it loses most of its strength. Their calculations showed that a two-wheeled cart with a 1.40 m gauge carrying moderate loads would gradually cut into wet rock. Once the ruts reached the cart's ground clearance, about 0.

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone: 03 The dating problem
chunks.text: Here is the honest difficulty. Bare limestone carries no charcoal, seeds or pottery to radiocarbon date, and the soil that might once have filled the ruts has long since washed away. So every date comes from context. The most quoted clue is the Punic tombs. At places such as Mtarfa, Għar il-Kbir and Ras il-Ġebel, the square shafts of rock-cut tombs of the Phoenician and Punic period interrupt the ruts, which suggests the ruts were already there by about 700 BCE. But as Anton Bugeja showed in a 2001 review, identical evidence has been read in opposite ways: Anthony Bonanno pointed out that Punic tombs could have been dug into ruts made by Punic quarry traffic, so the tombs would not be later at all. Step 1 of 5. About 13,000 years ago the land bridge to Sicily drowns. No people are known on Malta. About 13,000 years ago the land bridge to Sicily drowns. No people are known on Malta. People arrive by sea: hunter-gatherers about 6500 BCE, farmers about 5900 BCE. No wheels yet. The Temple Period, 3600–2500 BCE: Sagona's proposed date for the ruts. Wheels appear about 3500 BCE; the Bronze Age, 2500–700 BCE, is Trump's favoured date. Punic tombs cut some ruts from about 700 BCE; Roman sea level was 1.36 m lower. A time line from 12,000 BCE on the left to the start of the Common Era on the right. Step 1: the land bridge from Malta to Sicily drowns about 13,000 years ago; no people are known on Malta. Step 2: hunter-gatherers arrive by sea about 6500 BCE and farmers about 5900 BCE, without wheels. Step 3: the Temple Period, 3600 to 2500 BCE, Sagona's proposed date for the ruts. Step 4: wheeled vehicles appear about 3500 BCE and the Bronze Age runs 2500 to 700 BCE, Trump's proposed date. Step 5: Punic tombs cut some ruts from about 700 BCE, and Roman sea level stood 1.36 metres

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone: 04 Tracks into the sea
chunks.text: The ruts that disappear under the water are the most striking argument for great age. If the sea has risen over them, surely they must be very old? The answer depends on how far the sea has risen, and when. At the end of the last Ice Age, global sea level was far lower, and a low land bridge between Malta and Sicily, now about 95 m deep, was drowned around 13,000 years ago. But the Maltese ruts go under the water by metres, not by tens of metres. A 2013 study of submerged Roman remains around Malta found that relative sea level in Roman times stood about 1.36 m below today's. So even a Roman-era cart track that ended at the old shore could now be in the water. A Bronze Age track would be deeper still, but only modestly. In 2025 Eleanor Scerri and colleagues published evidence from Latnija cave that hunter-gatherers reached Malta by boat about 8,500 years ago, crossing roughly 100 km of open sea from Sicily, about a thousand years before the first farmers. It is a reminder that Malta's human story is older than we thought. It also sets a hard floor: before about 8,500 years ago, nobody is known to have been on the islands to make any ruts.

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone: 05 The challengers: Ice Age roads and 14-million-year tracks
chunks.text: The boldest claim comes from central Turkey. In the Phrygian highlands, around the rock-cut monuments of Midas City, long tracks with paired grooves cross the volcanic tuff, some cut deep into the rock. In the mid-2010s the Russian geologist Alexander Koltypin argued that these were made 12–14 million years ago by huge, heavy vehicles, pressed into soft ground that later hardened into stone. His reasoning, published on his own website rather than in a journal, was that the tuff is of that age. Graham Hancock, in Underworld (2002), took Malta's drowned ruts seriously as a clue to lost coastlines, and Michael Button has discussed the 'fossil' ruts on The Joe Rogan Experience, in a wider conversation about whether a far older civilisation could have been almost erased from the record. That question is fair, and the challengers' strongest point is real: not one rut has a direct date. The age of a rock is not the age of a groove cut into it. A 14-million-year-old rock can carry a two-thousand-year-old road. But the specific claim of Ice Age or older ruts runs into several walls at once. Nobody lived on Malta before about 8,500 years ago. The wheel appears around 3500 BCE. The drowned Maltese ruts sit in shallow water that Roman-era sea level can explain. And the Phrygian tracks lie in a landscape that Phrygians, Romans and Byzantines used intensively, with Midas City's monuments dating mainly to the 8th–6th centuries BCE. Tracks cut into old rock are exactly what we would expect from ancient roads.

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone: 06 What time has erased
chunks.text: Much of what would answer the question is gone. Soil loss on the Maltese plateaus has removed the deposits that once filled or covered the ruts. Centuries of quarrying for Malta's building stone have cut through whole stretches of the network; Mottershead argued that the 35 km or so that survive are fragments of a much larger system. The wooden carts, sledges or baskets that moved along them have rotted away. Even the drowned sections are poorly surveyed, which leaves room for speculation that a careful dive with a depth gauge could close.

chunks.heading: The Cart Ruts: Railway Lines Cut in Stone: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The ruts are dateable in principle. Optically stimulated luminescence can tell when a grain of sand last saw daylight, so sediment sealed at the bottom of a rut under an undisturbed wall or soil layer could give a real age. Excavating where ruts pass under Bronze Age or Punic floors, and recording the layers properly, would replace nearness with stratigraphy. A measured underwater survey at Birżebbuġa would show exactly how deep the tracks go. If sealed sediments give ages in the last 4,000 years, the Bronze Age or later readings win. If they give ages around 5,000 years, Sagona's Temple Period reading gains ground. An Ice Age age would need people on Malta before 8,500 years ago, and no such evidence exists. Until then, the cart ruts remain what they have been since 1647: a genuine puzzle about when, with a fairly clear answer about how.

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?
chunks.text: The Michael Button Files The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down? Pyramid c. 2570 BCE; the claimed structures undated Awaiting discovery. Is there a vast structure hundreds of metres beneath the pyramid of Khafre? The claim on the scales A large built structure, including shafts about 648 m deep, lies hundreds of metres beneath the pyramid of Khafre. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Nothing independent supports it. The Khafre results were announced at a press conference, not in a paper, and the data and code have not been released. The team's peer-reviewed paper on the Khufu pyramid, the basis for the method, was retracted in 2026. Radar specialists doubt the vibrations exist at a level satellites could measure. Yet no other survey has looked hundreds of metres down, so the rock beneath Giza has not been shown to be empty. It is a claim still waiting for evidence, not one that evidence has tested and refuted. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks describe Khafre's pyramid, its passages and its burial chamber with confidence, and that confidence is earned: the chambers were entered in 1818 and the pyramid was muon-scanned in the 1960s. They say nothing about what lies hundreds of metres down, because no one has looked. The confidence is justified for the monument; silence, not certainty, is the right stance on the deep rock. What is solid The pyramid of Khafre was built around 2570 BCE; it stood about 143.5 m high on a base about 215 m square, and its known passages and burial chamber lie near or just below its base. Lehner 1997 In the late 1960s Luis Alvarez's team placed a cosmic-ray muon detector in Khafre's burial chamber and found no unknown chambers in the part of the pyramid it could see. Alvarez et al. 1970 Muon imaging does find real hidden spaces at Giza: the 'Big Void', at least 30 m long, in Khufu's pyramid in 2017, and a corridor about 9 m long and 2 m by 2 m in 2023, later seen with an endoscope. Morishima et al. 2017; Procureur et al. 2023 In March 2025 Corrado Malanga, Filippo Biondi and Armando Mei announced at a press conference in Italy eight vertical shafts about 648 m deep, spiral paths and two cube-shaped structures beneath Khafre, from satellite radar data. Moss 2025 (National Geographic); Jerusalem Post 2025 No peer-reviewed paper setting out the Khafre results had appeared by mid-2025, and the team's earlier Remote Sensing paper on Khufu's pyramid was retracted on 10 August 2026 for 'serious methodological flaws and statistical errors'. Pilicy 2025; Remote Sensing retractio

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?: 01 Eight pillars in the dark
chunks.text: In March 2025, at a press conference in Italy, a small team made one of the most startling claims ever attached to the Giza pyramids. Using radar data from Italian satellites, Corrado Malanga, Filippo Biondi and the Giza researcher Armando Mei said they had found, beneath the pyramid of Khafre, eight vertical cylinders plunging about 648 m into the bedrock, wrapped in spiral paths, ending in two cube-shaped chambers reported as about 80 m on a side. Above them, they said, lay five multi-level structures joined by passages. Some reports spoke of features reaching 2 km down. The images spread worldwide within days, and the claims came up again that August when Joe Rogan raised them with Michael Button on The Joe Rogan Experience. If true, it would be the most important archaeological discovery ever made, a buried complex several times deeper than the pyramid is tall. A 648-metre shaft beneath Khafre would reach about four and a half times deeper than the pyramid once stood tall.

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?: 02 What we know about Khafre
chunks.text: Khafre's pyramid, the second largest at Giza, was built around 2570 BCE for the son of Khufu. It stood about 143.5 m high on a base about 215 m on each side, and it still keeps a cap of its original casing. Its interior is modest: two descending passages, a small subsidiary chamber, and a burial chamber cut into the bedrock and roofed with gabled limestone slabs. Giovanni Belzoni forced his way in on 2 March 1818 and painted his name on the wall. A vertical cross-section drawn to a single scale. At the top, the pyramid of Khafre, 143.5 metres high and 215 metres wide, sits on the ground line. The known burial chamber sits near its base, with a cone showing the region Alvarez's 1960s muon detector could see, where no hidden chambers were found. A thin band at the surface shows that satellite radar reaches at most about 2 metres into dry sand. Below the pyramid, eight dashed vertical lines marked 'claimed, not verified' descend to 648 metres, ending in two dashed squares about 80 metres across. A depth scale runs from 0 to 700 metres. A dashed arrow at the bottom notes reports of features to about 2 kilometres, off the chart. In the late 1960s the Nobel laureate physicist Luis Alvarez placed a detector for cosmic-ray muons in Khafre's burial chamber. Muons rain down constantly and are absorbed by stone, so a hidden room shows up as an excess of muons from one direction. His team found no unknown chambers in the part of the pyramid the detector could see. It was the first use of the technique that later found the Big Void in Khufu's pyramid.

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?: 03 How the scan was meant to work
chunks.text: Synthetic aperture radar, or SAR, sends microwave pulses from a moving satellite and builds a sharp image from the echoes. It is superb for mapping ground movement of millimetres over a city. What it normally cannot do is see deep underground: the pulses are absorbed or scattered within the top metres of the ground, and in dry sand the reach is up to about two metres. Biondi and Malanga argue that their method sidesteps this. In a 2022 paper in the journal Remote Sensing, they described 'SAR Doppler tomography' of Khufu's pyramid, using data from the COSMO-SkyMed satellites. The idea is that constant, tiny seismic vibrations make the ground and the monument shiver, that these shivers subtly change the radar echoes, and that the pattern of shivering reveals the solid and hollow parts inside. The paper reported many internal features and was cited a handful of times. Notice what that requires. The satellites orbit hundreds of kilometres up and revisit a scene only every so often, while seismic noise at Giza shakes the ground by tiny amounts. To turn those echoes into a picture of a shaft 600 m down, the method has to pull a faint, deep signal out of noise, and then show that the signal is not the processing talking to itself. That is exactly the step outside experts have asked to see, and it is where the retraction later focused its criticism: on method and statistics.

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?: 04 The challengers' case
chunks.text: At their strongest, the Khafre researchers make three points. First, critics who say radar cannot pass through rock may be answering a claim the team never made, since the signal they use is the vibration, not the penetrating radar pulse. Second, their earlier paper passed peer review. Third, and most important, nobody has ever imaged the bedrock hundreds of metres beneath Giza by any other means, so there is no survey that shows the space is empty. Writing on Graham Hancock's website in June 2025, Dakota Pilicy argued that most critics responded to press images rather than the method, and lacked remote-sensing expertise. Michael Button, for his part, was cautious on Rogan's show: he said he is wary of sensational claims made with new technology, while allowing that this does not make them wrong. That is a fair position, and it is the right question to ask of any new instrument: has it been tested where we already know the answer? A new instrument earns trust by finding what we already know is there, before it is believed about what we do not.

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?: 05 The critics, and a retraction
chunks.text: Specialists were blunt. Lawrence Conyers of the University of Denver, a leading authority on ground-penetrating radar, called the claims 'a huge exaggeration' and argued that the vibrations would be far too small for a satellite to measure. The Egyptologist Zahi Hawass called them baseless and noted that no permits had been granted for the work. The archaeologist Sarah Parcak, a pioneer of satellite archaeology, put it memorably: 'I could get any satellite imagery to look almost any way I wanted with enough manipulation.' On 10 August 2026 Remote Sensing retracted Biondi and Malanga's 2022 paper on Khufu's pyramid. After an investigation prompted by a reader's concerns, the editorial board found 'serious methodological flaws and statistical errors that were deemed to undermine the scientific conclusions of the article.' The authors disagreed with the retraction. The Khafre results, based on a related approach, have still not been set out in a peer-reviewed paper. The retraction does not by itself show that nothing lies under Khafre. It does remove the one peer-reviewed foundation the method had, which means the Khafre images now stand on press statements alone.

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?: 06 What real scanning has found
chunks.text: It would be wrong to conclude that Giza has no secrets left. Muon imaging by the ScanPyramids project found the Big Void in Khufu's pyramid in 2017, a space at least 30 m long above the Grand Gallery. In 2023 two independent muon teams measured a corridor behind the north face, about 9 m long and about 2 m by 2 m in section, and a camera pushed through a joint in the stones confirmed it. These finds came from independent teams, published data and a physical check. They also show the scale of what careful work has found: rooms and corridors of metres to tens of metres, inside the monument. A complex reaching hundreds of metres into the rock would be a discovery of a wholly different kind, and would need evidence of a wholly different weight. There is a deeper point too. Giza's limestone, like most limestone, can hold natural cavities, and the plateau has been quarried, tunnelled and built on for more than 4,500 years. Any honest survey of the deep rock would have to tell natural voids, faults and old workings apart from anything built, which is one more reason the raw data matter.

chunks.heading: The Khafre Scans: Pillars 600 Metres Down?: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The path is simple, if not quick. The team could release the full data and code, so that other radar groups can reprocess the same COSMO-SkyMed scenes. The vibration method could be tested blind over something known and deep, such as a mine shaft or a metro line, with the answer withheld until the images are produced. And conventional geophysics, such as a seismic reflection survey or a borehole near the plateau, could sample the rock hundreds of metres down, with Egypt's permission. Until then, the pillars under Khafre remain a striking picture without a measurement behind it. The deep rock under Giza is unexplored, and that is a real gap in knowledge. It is not the same as evidence that something is there.

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?
chunks.text: Lost Ice Age World Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation? Proposed: before c. 12,900 years ago (Late Pleistocene) Awaiting discovery. Did an advanced civilisation flourish in the Ice Age, then vanish almost without trace? The claim on the scales An advanced civilisation, with knowledge beyond any known Ice Age culture, existed before 12,900 years ago and was destroyed by the Younger Dryas catastrophe. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Every ingredient Hancock uses is real: drowned coasts, an abrupt climate upheaval, sophisticated foragers, early monuments. But the civilisation itself has left no physical trace: no domesticated crops or animals, no inland quarries or mines, no tools or pottery of an unknown culture, no sudden newcomers in ancient DNA. Some of those traces could drown; genetic ones could not. The key supporting claims, the Younger Dryas impact and Gunung Padang's great age, have not survived testing. This does not rule the idea out forever, but the claim is still waiting for its evidence. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks confidently present civilisation as starting with farming and cities about 11,000–5,500 years ago, preceded by simple foragers. The first half holds up well: no Ice Age civilisation has been found. The second half has been too dismissive: Göbekli Tepe, mammoth-bone architecture and early seafaring show Ice Age societies were more capable than the old ladder of progress allowed. What is solid Ice Age people were fully modern and highly capable: they painted caves, built mammoth-bone houses, made ceramic figurines and crossed open sea to reach Australia more than 50,000 years ago. Clarkson et al. 2017; standard Palaeolithic record Sea level stood about 120 m lower until about 20,000 years ago, and rising seas drowned vast coastal plains between about 16,000 and 7,000 years ago. Lambeck et al. 2014 The Younger Dryas, c. 12,900–11,700 years ago, was an abrupt global climate upheaval, with a near-glacial cold snap and a sudden warming at its end. Greenland ice cores; Walker et al. 2009 Göbekli Tepe's monumental carved enclosures were begun about 11,500 years ago by people who were still largely hunter-gatherers. Schmidt 2010; DAI Göbekli Tepe project Genetic and archaeological evidence places the domestication of the major crops after about 11,500 years ago, with fully domesticated cereals from about 10,500 years ago. Larson et al. 2014, PNAS What is disputed Whether the drowned shelves could hide the remains of a civilisation more advanced than any known Ice Age cultu

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?: 01 The most seductive idea in prehistory
chunks.text: Imagine that everything we were taught about the beginning of civilisation is missing its first chapter. That before Sumer and Egypt, before the first farmers, there was a people who mapped the stars, sailed the oceans and raised great monuments, until a catastrophe at the end of the Ice Age drowned their coasts and scattered their survivors. This is Graham Hancock's thesis, set out in Fingerprints of the Gods (1995), refined in Magicians of the Gods (2015) and America Before (2019), and seen by millions in Netflix's Ancient Apocalypse (2022 and 2024). It deserves a fair hearing, because it is built from real pieces. The last Ice Age did end in upheaval. The sea did rise about 120 metres. Monumental building did begin earlier than anyone expected. The question is not whether these things happened. It is whether they add up to a lost civilisation. Every ingredient of Hancock's story is real. The disputed part is the civilisation itself.

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?: 02 The teachers from the sea
chunks.text: Hancock's case begins with myth. Many peoples remember a culture hero who arrived after a catastrophe and taught the arts of civilisation. The Babylonian priest Berossus, writing about 280 BCE, described Oannes, a fish-bodied being who emerged from the sea. He taught them to construct cities, to found temples, to compile laws, and explained to them the principles of geometrical knowledge. In the Andes, Spanish chroniclers of the 16th century recorded stories of Viracocha, who rose from Lake Titicaca after a flood and walked the land teaching. In Mesoamerica, Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, was remembered as a bringer of learning who departed over the sea. For Hancock these are echoes of real survivors.
