Scholars answer that culture heroes are one of humanity's most universal story types, that these accounts were written down thousands of years after the proposed events, and that details such as Quetzalcoatl's pale beard appear mostly in sources written after the Spanish conquest. The myths are real witnesses to human imagination and memory; what they remember is the open question.

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?: 03 What is solid about the Ice Age world
chunks.text: The people of 20,000 years ago were us: same brains, same hands. They painted Lascaux and Chauvet, built houses from mammoth bones on the Ukrainian plains, fired clay figurines at Dolní Věstonice more than 25,000 years ago, and had crossed open sea to reach Australia by at least 50,000 years ago. They tracked the Moon and the seasons. Then, around 11,500 years ago, just after the Younger Dryas ended, people who still hunted gazelle and gathered wild cereals began carving the great T-shaped pillars of Göbekli Tepe in south-east Türkiye. A timeline from 16,000 to 4,000 years ago. At the top a line shows sea level rising from about minus 110 metres to today's level by about 7,000 years ago. A pale band marks the Younger Dryas from 12,900 to 11,700 years ago. A dashed box before 12,900 years ago marks Hancock's proposed lost civilisation, with no remains found. An orange marker shows Plato's date for Atlantis at about 11,600 years ago. Below the axis, markers show Göbekli Tepe begun about 11,500 years ago, first domesticated crops about 11,000 to 10,000 years ago, the town of Çatalhöyük about 9,100 years ago, the first cities at Uruk about 5,500 years ago, and the Great Pyramid about 4,560 years ago. Göbekli Tepe genuinely shocked archaeology. It showed that monuments came before farming, not after, and it overturned the tidy ladder of hunters, then farmers, then temples. Hancock reads its sudden sophistication as a sign of inherited knowledge. Most archaeologists read it as what capable foragers could achieve once climate stabilised and they gathered in large numbers.

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?: 04 Hancock's strongest card: the drowned coasts
chunks.text: The most serious part of the case is geographical. Ice Age people, like people today, probably favoured coasts, deltas and river mouths, rich in fish, shellfish and fresh water. Those landscapes now lie tens of metres underwater. The world's continental shelves cover roughly 30 million square kilometres, and much of that, outside the ice sheets, was dry land at the glacial maximum. Only a tiny fraction has been examined by archaeologists. Hancock argues that the evidence for his civilisation, if it exists, would be precisely where nobody has looked. On this point he is on firm ground. Recent finds, such as the 971-metre Blinkerwall hunting structure under the Baltic and Homo erectus fossils dredged from drowned Sundaland, show that the seabed hides real surprises. Our Drowned Coasts case explores this in depth. There is a limit, though, to what the drowned-coast argument can do. Coastal people did not live in isolation. They traded shells, stone and ideas inland, as the shell beads found hundreds of kilometres from the sea in Ice Age Europe show. A culture far more advanced than its neighbours should have left some echo on the land that stayed dry, even if its heartland drowned.

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?: 05 The Rogan debate: what should survive?
chunks.text: In April 2024 the archaeologist Flint Dibble, of Cardiff University, debated Hancock for more than four hours on the Joe Rogan Experience (episode 2136). Dibble chose not to argue about individual sites. Instead he asked what any advanced society leaves behind, drowned or not, and whether we find it. Step 1 of 5. What Ice Age people did leave: caves, mammoth-bone houses, hearths and tools, found by the thousand. What Ice Age people did leave: caves, mammoth-bone houses, hearths and tools, found by the thousand. What a civilisation would add: quarries and mines, crop fields, towns, ports and ships. The sea rises about 120 m and drowns the coastal plain, with its towns, fields and ports. What drowning cannot erase: inland quarries and mines, crop genes in living plants, pollution in ice cores. What we find: domestication only from about 11,000 years ago, and metal pollution only in the metal ages. A schematic cross-section of land sloping from inland hills on the left, across a coastal plain, to the sea of 20,000 years ago on the right, with today's sea level marked by a dashed line partway down the slope and a Greenland ice core drawn at top right. Step 1 shows a painted cave, mammoth-bone houses, a hearth and tools on the inland slopes. Step 2 adds a quarry and mines on the hills, crop fields, a coastal town and a port with a ship. Step 3 fills the coastal plain with water up to today's sea level, drowning the town, fields and port, with an arrow showing the 120 metre rise. Step 4 circles the inland quarry and the fields and adds symbols for domestication genes in living crops and for metal pollution in the ice core. Step 5 adds the findings: no domesticated crop genes older than about 11,000 years and no metal pollution before the metal ages. His sharpest point was abo

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?: 06 What time could erase, and what it could not
chunks.text: Honesty cuts both ways. Rising seas could erase ports, towns and ships. Twelve thousand years of rot could erase wood, cloth and rope. What they could not easily erase are inland quarries and mines, the genetic legacy of domesticated plants and animals, and chemical traces in ice cores: lead pollution from Greek and Roman mining shows up clearly in Greenland ice, but nothing comparable appears in the Ice Age layers. A lost civilisation small and knowledge-based enough to leave none of these traces is possible in principle, but it would also be hard to tell apart from the capable foragers we already know. So what would a lost civilisation have to look like to fit the evidence we have? It would need to be small enough, or coastal enough, that almost all its settlements drowned. It would need to live without farming, or with farming that never spread and left no feral crops. It would need to work stone without inland quarries anyone has found, and to teach survivors things that left no new tools, pots or genes in their camps. Hancock has moved towards exactly this picture: a civilisation of knowledge, astronomy and ritual rather than of industry. That version is harder to rule out. It is also harder to test, and the harder an idea is to test, the less weight it can carry as history. Two pillars of the case have weakened recently. In October 2023 Danny Hilman Natawidjaja and colleagues claimed that Gunung Padang in Java was a buried pyramid whose first stages dated back to around 25,000 BCE. In March 2024 the journal retracted the paper because the radiocarbon dates came from soil that showed no reliable sign of human work; the authors disagreed. And the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis has suffered retractions of key papers in 2025 and 2026 (see our case on the Younger Drya

chunks.heading: Was There a Lost Ice Age Civilisation?: 07 An honest weighing
chunks.text: Hancock deserves credit for asking questions that archaeology was slow to ask. He was early to stress the importance of drowned landscapes, of the Younger Dryas as a human catastrophe, and of how old and ambitious Göbekli Tepe really is. In the Americas, the experts he criticised really did hold on to Clovis-first for too long. A field that dismissed him with sneers rather than evidence did itself no favours. But on the central claim, the evidence points the other way. Every line that should carry a civilisation's signature through a flood, from genes to quarries to ice, is silent before the Holocene. The fair verdict is awaiting discovery. What would change it is clear and testable: a drowned site with unmistakable architecture or metal, domesticated crops older than 12,900 years, or ancient DNA revealing a population of teachers. Until one of those turns up, the lost civilisation remains a question, and a good one, rather than a chapter of history.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago?
chunks.text: Lost Ice Age World The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago? c. 12,900–11,700 years ago (the Younger Dryas) Awaiting discovery. Did a cosmic impact trigger the Younger Dryas cold and end the Clovis world? The claim on the scales A comet impact or airburst swarm around 12,800 years ago triggered the Younger Dryas cooling and the end of the Clovis world. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The Younger Dryas, the megafaunal losses and the end of Clovis are real. The link to an impact is not established. Core markers have not been reproduced by independent teams, many boundary ages are insecure, the platinum spike now has a strong volcanic explanation, and several flagship papers have been retracted for problems with data or dating. The proposers dispute these judgments, and a cosmic event cannot be excluded in principle, but at present the physical evidence does not carry the claim. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks usually say that meltwater weakened the Atlantic circulation and the Younger Dryas followed. That is the best-supported explanation, but its details (which route the water took, and when) are still argued over, so the textbook tone is a little too settled. On the impact itself, textbooks either skip it or dismiss it, and there they are close to the evidence. What is solid The Younger Dryas was real and abrupt: about 12,900 years ago the North Atlantic region plunged back towards glacial cold for some 1,200 years, ending about 11,700 years ago. Greenland ice cores; Walker et al. 2009 Across North America the Clovis style of stone tools disappears around the same time, and many large mammals, including mammoths, mastodons and native horses, vanish within a few centuries of it. Waters et al. 2020; Meltzer 2009 At many western US sites a dark organic 'black mat' layer lies directly on top of the last Clovis and mammoth remains. Haynes 2008, PNAS A platinum anomaly appears in the GISP2 Greenland ice core close to the onset of the Younger Dryas. Petaev et al. 2013, PNAS Several key impact papers have been retracted: the Tall el-Hammam 'Sodom' airburst paper (April 2025) and two PLOS ONE papers, including the 2025 shocked-quartz study (February 2026). Scientific Reports 2025; PLOS ONE 2026 What is disputed Whether spherules, nanodiamonds, melt glass and metal spikes really peak in one thin layer of the same age on several continents. Whether the Greenland platinum anomaly came from space or, as Green and colleagues argued in 2025, from Icelandic volcanic eruptions starting abo

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago?: 01 The world slips back into the cold
chunks.text: Around 14,700 years ago the Ice Age was finally letting go. Greenland warmed by several degrees in a few decades, forests marched north and people spread across newly open land. Then, about 12,900 years ago, the warmth broke. Across the North Atlantic region temperatures plunged back towards glacial levels and stayed there for some 1,200 years. Geologists call this the Younger Dryas, after a little alpine flower, Dryas octopetala, whose pollen returns to European lake muds in the cold. In North America, the same centuries saw the end of the Clovis culture, famous for its beautifully fluted spear points, and the disappearance of mammoths, mastodons, native horses and giant ground sloths. Three dramatic changes, close together. In 2007 a team of scientists offered one explosive explanation: the sky fell. Three dramatic changes close together invite a single sudden cause. The question is whether the ground agrees.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago?: 02 The comet hypothesis at its strongest
chunks.text: Richard Firestone, Allen West, James Kennett and colleagues, later known as the Comet Research Group, argued in PNAS that a fragmenting comet exploded over the Northern Hemisphere about 12,900 years ago. At Clovis sites from Arizona to the Great Lakes they reported a thin layer, just beneath the black mat, rich in magnetic grains and microspherules, carbon spherules, nanodiamonds, iridium and soot. Their reading: debris and fire from airbursts, powerful enough to shift climate and devastate animals and people. Step 1 of 5. The section: layers laid down over the last 15,000 years, oldest at the bottom. The section: layers laid down over the last 15,000 years, oldest at the bottom. The Clovis surface: mammoth bones and a Clovis point, about 12,900 years old. The black mat drapes the Clovis surface: wet, spring-fed ground as the cold began. The impact team's reading: a thin boundary layer rich in spherules, nanodiamonds, metals and soot. The critics' reading: similar particles occur at other levels, and many boundary ages do not match. A schematic vertical section through sediments. At the top, grass over thick pale Holocene deposits. Below them a dark band labelled black mat, then pale older sands and gravels. Step 1 introduces the section. Step 2 shows mammoth bones and a Clovis point on the surface directly beneath the black mat. Step 3 highlights the black mat, which formed in wet ground at the start of the Younger Dryas. Step 4 highlights a thin orange layer at the base of the mat dotted with particles, labelled as the claimed impact layer with spherules, nanodiamonds, iridium, soot and melt glass. Step 5 scatters similar particles through the other layers, representing the critics' finding that such particles are not confined to one level. The team kept adding lines

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago?: 03 What independent tests found
chunks.text: Extraordinary claims draw testers, and the testers mostly came back empty-handed. Todd Surovell's team (2009) looked for the spherule peak at boundary sites and did not find it. Tyrone Daulton's group (2010) looked for the nanodiamonds and found none; other researchers identified some 'carbon spherules' as fungal bodies or insect droppings. Nicholas Pinter and colleagues (2011) titled their review 'The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis: a requiem'. David Meltzer and colleagues (2014) examined the dating of 29 claimed boundary sites and argued that only a handful had reliable ages at the right moment. The glass at Abu Hureyra has a rival explanation too. Peter Thy and colleagues (2015) found similar glassy droplets at northern Syrian sites of several different ages and argued that they form when mud-brick and reed buildings burn, melting silica-rich plant material. Black mats, meanwhile, formed at many times in the past, as Jeffrey Pigati's team showed in 2012, because they record wet, spring-fed ground, not fire from the sky. A vertical timeline from 2007 at the top to 2026 at the bottom. On the left, papers offering evidence for an impact: Firestone 2007, Petaev 2013, Kennett 2015, Wolbach 2018, Pino 2019, Moore 2020, Sweatman 2021, Sweatman, Powell and West 2024, and Kennett 2025 on shocked quartz. On the right, challenges: Surovell 2009, Daulton 2010, Pinter 2011, Meltzer 2014, Thy 2015, Kenny 2022 dating the Hiawatha crater to 58 million years, Holliday 2023, the 2025 retraction of the Tall el-Hammam paper with Green's volcanic reading of the platinum, and the February 2026 retraction of two PLOS ONE papers. In 2023 Vance Holliday and a large team of archaeologists, geologists and impact scientists published a 'comprehensive refutation' in Earth-Science Reviews. In 20

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago?: 04 Fresh from the field: a hard two years for the comet
chunks.text: Recent events have gone badly for the hypothesis. In April 2025 Scientific Reports retracted the 2021 paper claiming that an airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam in Jordan, proposed as biblical Sodom, after concerns about images, methods and data. In September 2025 Charlotte Green and colleagues re-examined the Greenland platinum and concluded that it begins some 45 to 50 years after the cooling started, lasts about 14 years, and most likely came from a volcanic fissure eruption in Iceland rather than from a meteorite. Then, on 11 February 2026, PLOS ONE retracted two Comet Research Group papers published only months earlier: a study reporting shocked quartz at Murray Springs, Blackwater Draw and Arlington Canyon, and a study of a Baffin Bay core. The editors cited problems with the age models, incomplete sampling and data reporting. Most of the authors who responded disagreed with the retractions. A retraction does not falsify an idea. But when the flagship evidence keeps failing checks, the burden of proof grows heavier.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago?: 05 What time has hidden
chunks.text: The fair-minded reader should notice what is genuinely hard here. The boundary layers are thin, often a few centimetres, and easily mixed by roots, burrowing animals and water. Many were sampled once, by one team, years ago. Abu Hureyra is underwater. Any airburst debris landing on open ground would have been reworked by 12,000 years of rain and wind. Impact specialists note that an airburst leaves no crater, which removes the most decisive kind of evidence. So absence of a crater does not settle the matter on its own. The standard explanation has its own open questions. A flood of glacial meltwater, from Lake Agassiz or elsewhere, is thought to have weakened the Atlantic overturning circulation, but where the water went and exactly when it arrived are still argued over. Megafaunal extinction in the Americas probably involved both a changing climate and skilled human hunters, in proportions nobody can yet fix.

chunks.heading: The Younger Dryas Comet: Did the Sky Fall 12,900 Years Ago?: 06 The verdict, and how to change it
chunks.text: The Younger Dryas, the losses of large animals and the end of Clovis are real, and they happened close together. The comet is the part that has not survived testing. Its core markers have not been independently reproduced, its dates are often insecure, its best physical signal now has a volcanic rival, and several of its flagship papers have been withdrawn. We rate the impact claim as awaiting discovery, not ruled out, because a cosmic event could in principle leave the kind of subtle traces that are hard to find. What would change that verdict is simple to state: blind, multi-lab re-sampling of the same boundary sections; shocked minerals or an impact signature confirmed by specialists outside the proposing group; and ice and ocean cores that separate a cosmic signal from a volcanic one. If those tests come back positive, the story of the end of the Ice Age will need rewriting. So far, they have not.

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land
chunks.text: Lost Ice Age World The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land c. 21,000–7,000 years ago (Last Glacial Maximum to mid-Holocene) Plausible. What human history lies on the seabed of the drowned Ice Age coasts? The claim on the scales Some of the most important human settlements of the late Ice Age lie undiscovered on the drowned continental shelves. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established That people lived on the shelves is established: fossils, walls, villages and tools keep coming up from the seabed. That the most important settlements are down there is a reasonable inference, because coasts are rich places and they are almost entirely unsearched, but it remains an inference. Every drowned site found so far matches the technology known inland, so 'important' here most likely means populous and inventive rather than industrial. The evidence supports the idea of a large missing chapter, not yet its contents. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks state the land bridges and sea-level fall confidently, and rightly so. What they underplay is the consequence: prehistory is told from the uplands because the coasts are gone. Maps of early human sites look inland-heavy partly because the coastal half of the record is underwater. Here the textbooks are overconfident by omission, presenting a partial sample as if it were the whole picture. What is solid At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000–20,000 years ago, global sea level stood roughly 120–130 m below today's. Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS The rise was uneven: during Meltwater Pulse 1A, about 14,650–14,310 years ago, the sea climbed some 14–18 m in about 350 years. Deschamps et al. 2012, Nature The Bering land bridge was cut by the sea about 11,000 years ago; Britain became an island around 6500 BCE as Doggerland drowned. Jakobsson et al. 2017; Gaffney et al. 2007 Real human structures lie on the seabed: the Atlit Yam village (8–12 m down, c. 8,700–8,300 years old) and the 971 m Blinkerwall stone line in the Baltic (21 m down, over 10,000 years old). Galili et al. 1993; Geersen et al. 2024, PNAS In 2025 the first hominin fossils from submerged Sundaland were published: two Homo erectus skull fragments dredged from c. 32 m below sea level in the Madura Strait, dated c. 146,000–131,000 years ago. Berghuis et al. 2025, Quaternary Environments and Humans What is disputed How many people lived on the shelves, and whether coastal populations were larger and more settled than the inland record implies. Whether the Persian Gulf basin was a major refuge whose people reapp

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land: 01 The biggest missing chapter in prehistory
chunks.text: Stand on a beach in Java, Norfolk or the Gulf coast of Qatar and look out to sea. Twenty thousand years ago you would have been looking at dry land: river valleys, lagoons, forests and grasslands stretching to a shoreline tens or even hundreds of kilometres away. So much water was locked up in ice sheets that the world's oceans stood roughly 120 metres lower than today. Then the ice melted, and over some fourteen thousand years the sea came back and took the coasts. This is not a fringe idea. It is one of the most secure facts in Earth science. What remains open, and genuinely exciting, is what the sea took with it. Coasts are where foragers find shellfish, fish, birds, fresh springs and easy travel. If you were an Ice Age human choosing where to live, the coastal plain was often the best address on the map. And almost none of it has been searched. Prehistory is told from the uplands because the coasts are underwater.

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land: 02 What is solid: a sea that rose in bursts
chunks.text: Sea-level curves are built from drowned coral reefs, dated peat and shells, and computer models of how the Earth's crust responds to the weight of ice. The synthesis by Kurt Lambeck and colleagues (2014) puts the low point at about 120 to 130 metres below present, around 26,000 to 20,000 years ago. The rise that followed was not smooth. During Meltwater Pulse 1A, dated at Tahiti to about 14,650 to 14,310 years ago, the sea climbed some 14 to 18 metres in roughly 350 years: several centimetres a year, enough for a grandparent to remember beaches their grandchildren could not walk on. A line chart with time on the horizontal axis from 22,000 years ago to today and sea level on the vertical axis from 0 to minus 135 metres. The curve starts near minus 130 metres at the Last Glacial Maximum, rises slowly, jumps steeply around 14,500 years ago during Meltwater Pulse 1A, keeps rising through and after the Younger Dryas band, and flattens near zero about 7,000 years ago. Area above the curve is shaded as dry land then, seabed now. Four dashed depth lines mark Bouldnor Cliff at 11 metres, reached about 7,800 years ago; the Blinkerwall at 21 metres, about 8,600 years ago; the Cosquer Cave entrance at 37 metres, about 9,900 years ago; and the Bering Strait sill at about 53 metres, about 11,200 years ago. By the end of the Younger Dryas, about 11,700 years ago, the sea was still some 60 metres below today. The Bering land bridge between Siberia and Alaska was cut about 11,000 years ago (Jakobsson and colleagues, 2017). Doggerland, the lowland joining Britain to the continent, shrank to islands and was gone by around 6500 to 6000 BCE, battered on the way by the tsunami of the Storegga submarine landslide off Norway, about 8,150 years ago. By about 7,000 years ago most coasts were cl

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land: 03 Five lost landscapes
chunks.text: Step 1 of 4. Today: the coastlines we know, with the sea at its present level. Today: the coastlines we know, with the sea at its present level. About 21,000 years ago: with the sea some 120 m lower, broad shelves become dry land (simplified outlines). The great lost landscapes: Sundaland, the Sahul shelf, Beringia, Doggerland, the Gulf basin and more. Where drowned sites and fossils have been found so far: a handful of points on millions of square kilometres. A world map in the Equal Earth projection. Step 1 shows present coastlines. Step 2 adds shaded areas of continental shelf that were dry at about minus 120 metres: the Sunda Shelf joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to Asia; the East China Sea shelf; the Sahul shelf joining Australia and New Guinea; Bass Strait; Beringia between Siberia and Alaska; the Siberian Arctic shelf; the southern North Sea and English Channel; the Persian Gulf; the Patagonian shelf; and smaller areas off Florida, Yucatan and in the northern Adriatic. Step 3 labels the main regions. Step 4 adds numbered markers for Bouldnor Cliff, the Blinkerwall, Cosquer Cave, Atlit Yam, the Madura Strait and the Gulf of Carpentaria. Sundaland: the Sunda Shelf joined Sumatra, Java, Borneo and mainland Southeast Asia into one great lowland crossed by rivers. Hanebuth and colleagues (2000) recorded its rapid flooding during Meltwater Pulse 1A. Doggerland: rolling country of rivers, marshes and hills between Britain, the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. Trawlers have dragged up mammoth bones, a Neanderthal skull fragment and, in 1931, a barbed antler point from a lump of peat. Beringia: the land bridge over which the ancestors of Native Americans crossed, and where they may have lived for millennia before moving south. The Gulf basin: the floor of today's Persia

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land: 04 What the seabed has already given back
chunks.text: Where people have looked, they have found. Off Atlit in Israel, Ehud Galili's team excavated a whole Neolithic village 8 to 12 metres down: houses, a stone-lined well 5.5 m deep, burials and a semicircle of seven standing stones of about 600 kg each around a spring, dated roughly 8,700 to 8,300 years ago. In the Solent off the Isle of Wight, Bouldnor Cliff (11 m down, about 8,000 years old) was found in 1999 when divers watched a lobster kicking worked flints out of its burrow. It has yielded worked timber and a burnt-clay floor. In 2024 Jörn Geersen and colleagues published the Blinkerwall: 1,673 stones in a line 971 m long, 21 m under the Bay of Mecklenburg, most plausibly a drive lane for hunting reindeer, built more than 10,000 years ago and drowned between about 8,570 and 8,000 years ago. It is a Stone Age megastructure nobody had suspected. In 2025 Harold Berghuis, Yousuke Kaifu and colleagues described two Homo erectus skull fragments from the Madura Strait, off Java. They came from some five million cubic metres of sand dredged from about 32 m below sea level for a land-reclamation project, together with 6,732 other fossils. The sand filled an ancient valley of the Solo River, and the fossils date to about 146,000 to 131,000 years ago. They are the first hominin fossils from drowned Sundaland, and they were found by accident.

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land: 05 The challengers: we have been searching the wrong half of the world
chunks.text: Graham Hancock put the argument most forcefully in Underworld (2002). If archaeologists want to know what Ice Age people were capable of, he argued, they are sampling the harsh uplands and ignoring the warm, rich lowlands where most people probably lived. He paired that with flood myths from India to the Pacific, reading them as memories of drowned homelands. Stephen Oppenheimer's Eden in the East (1998) argued that the flooding of Sundaland pushed people and ideas across Asia and the Pacific. The Indonesian geologist Danny Hilman Natawidjaja has gone further, arguing that Sundaland was home to an advanced culture. The strongest version of this case has good archaeology behind it. Jeffrey Rose's Gulf Oasis model (2010) notes that more than 60 new settlements appear along the Gulf shoreline around 7,500 years ago, well built and with no obvious local ancestors, just as the basin finished flooding. His reading: a population that had sheltered in the fertile basin for millennia was pushed onto the new coast. That is a testable, sober hypothesis, and it has not been ruled out. Every time divers and dredgers look carefully, the drowned coasts give something back.

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land: 06 Why the sea keeps its secrets
chunks.text: Underwater archaeology is slow, expensive and often blind. Visibility in the North Sea can be a metre or less. Sites may lie under metres of later sediment, or may have been scoured away as the surf zone swept across them. Organic finds survive only when buried quickly in mud or peat, and trawlers have been ploughing parts of the seabed for more than a century. A single dive team can excavate a few square metres a season, while the drowned shelves cover millions of square kilometres. Oil, gas and wind-farm surveys record seismic images of the seabed and the layers beneath it. From these, the Birmingham team led by Vince Gaffney mapped about 23,000 km² of drowned North Sea landscape, tracing rivers, lakes and coastlines. The Europe's Lost Frontiers project then cored old river channels and read their sediment DNA to rebuild the plants and animals. Archaeologists can now target the likeliest places, such as river mouths, springs and sheltered bays, instead of searching at random. The important caution runs both ways. Absence of evidence on the shelves means little, because so little has been searched. But the finds so far also match the technology of their time on land: flint, antler, timber, stone walls. None of them hints at metal, writing or cities. The drowned coasts are a vast unread library, and its first pages read like the rest of the Stone Age, only richer.

chunks.heading: The Drowned Coasts: A Continent's Worth of Lost Land: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: Three things would transform this debate. First, North Sea style mapping of the Sunda Shelf and the Gulf basin, where the stakes are highest and the surveys thinnest. Second, the excavation of a well-preserved coastal settlement from the Last Glacial Maximum or just after, below 40 metres, to show what the richest Ice Age homes were really like. Third, ancient DNA from the first Gulf-coast villages to test whether their people came from the drowned basin. Until then, the fair summary is this: the drowned coasts almost certainly hold a large part of the human story from 20,000 to 7,000 years ago, and it is a scandal of attention, not of evidence, that we know so little about it.

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell
chunks.text: Lost Ice Age World The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell c. 23,000–13,000 years ago (contested claims far older) Strong evidence. When did people first reach the Americas, and why did it take so long to admit? The claim on the scales People were living in the Americas more than 20,000 years ago, thousands of years before Clovis. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established White Sands is the key. The footprints are unmistakably human, and their age has been measured four ways: aquatic plant seeds (2021), terrestrial conifer pollen and quartz luminescence (2023), and the mud of the ancient lake (2025), all pointing to about 23,000–21,000 years ago. Genetics allows a split from Siberians in that window. What remains thin is everything around the footprints: tools, camps and skeletons from that age. The claim is strong; the fuller picture is still being assembled. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact For most of the 20th century textbooks presented Clovis-first as settled, a clear case of overconfidence. Many now say 'about 15,000–16,000 years ago', which is safe but lags behind White Sands. Meanwhile, much older claims like Cerutti are sometimes repeated in popular media as if established. The honest line is: more than 20,000 years is strong, much older is open. What is solid The Clovis culture, known for fluted spear points, is dated to about 13,050–12,750 years ago. Waters et al. 2020, Science Advances Monte Verde II in southern Chile was occupied about 14,500 years ago; a panel of sceptics accepted it after a site visit in 1997. Dillehay 1997; Meltzer et al. 1997 Several other sites predate Clovis: Paisley Caves, Oregon (c. 14,300 years), Page-Ladson, Florida (c. 14,550) and Cooper's Ferry, Idaho (c. 16,000). Gilbert et al. 2008; Halligan et al. 2016; Davis et al. 2019 Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago using seeds, conifer pollen, quartz grains and ancient lake mud. Bennett et al. 2021; Pigati et al. 2023; Holliday et al. 2025 Genetic studies place the separation of Native American ancestors from Siberian populations at roughly 25,000–20,000 years ago. Raghavan et al. 2015, Science What is disputed Which route the first people took: down the Pacific coast by boat, through an ice-free corridor, or both at different times. Whether sites claimed at 24,000 to 33,000 years old (Bluefish Caves, Chiquihuite Cave, Pedra Furada) show human work or natural breakage. Whether the Cerutti Mastodon site in California records humans breaking bones about 130,000 years ago

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell: 01 Footprints that rewrote a continent
chunks.text: Some 23,000 years ago, on the soft shore of a lake in what is now New Mexico, a group of people walked through the mud. Children ran and splashed. Adults strode past the tracks of mammoths and giant ground sloths. The mud dried, was buried, and waited. When archaeologists published the footprints in 2021, the tracks landed like a small earthquake, because according to the story most of us were taught, nobody should have been there for another 10,000 years. The peopling of the Americas is one of the great stories of prehistory, and one of the best examples of a scientific consensus that held too tightly for too long. It is also a live lesson in how evidence finally wins. For sixty years, the oldest Americans had a fixed birthday. Then the ground kept offering older ones.

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell: 02 The age of Clovis first
chunks.text: In 1927 at Folsom, New Mexico, a spear point was found lodged among the ribs of an extinct bison, finally showing that people had lived in America during the Ice Age. In the early 1930s, at Blackwater Draw near Clovis, New Mexico, larger fluted points turned up with mammoth bones. The Clovis style was soon found across North America. By 1964, C. Vance Haynes had set out an elegant model in Science: big-game hunters crossed Beringia, walked south through a gap between the ice sheets and spread across the continents within a few centuries. The model was tidy, testable and, for decades, treated as the rule. Clovis is now dated to about 13,050 to 12,750 years ago. Claims of anything older were examined with a severity rarely applied to Clovis itself, and almost all were rejected. Careers suffered. The phrase 'Clovis police' entered the field's vocabulary. Step 1 of 5. About 20,000 years ago: Beringia is dry land and ice sheets cover most of Canada. About 20,000 years ago: Beringia is dry land and ice sheets cover most of Canada. Clovis first: hunters walk south through an ice-free corridor about 13,000 years ago. Monte Verde (accepted 1997) and Paisley Caves: people were here before Clovis, perhaps via the coast. White Sands: footprints dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, during the glacial maximum. Still contested: claims from 24,000 to 130,000 years that have not won broad acceptance. A map of North and South America at the end of the Ice Age. Step 1 shows ice sheets covering most of Canada and the dry Beringia land bridge joining Alaska and Siberia. Step 2 adds a dashed arrow for the ice-free corridor between the ice sheets and a marker for Clovis sites in New Mexico, dated about 13,050 to 12,750 years ago. Step 3 adds a moving dashed line down the Pacific coast and

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell: 03 The wall breaks at Monte Verde
chunks.text: The site that broke the wall was a boggy creek bank in southern Chile. From 1977 Tom Dillehay excavated Monte Verde, where a peat layer had preserved wooden foundations of huts, reeds knotted around stakes, seaweed carried from the coast and bones of gomphotheres, elephant relatives. Its radiocarbon dates came out at about 14,500 years ago, a thousand years before Clovis and some 16,000 km from Beringia. For twenty years many colleagues refused to accept it. In 1997 a group of leading sceptics visited the site, examined the finds and, remarkably, agreed: Monte Verde was real and pre-Clovis. Other sites followed. Human DNA in dried faeces from Paisley Caves in Oregon dated to about 14,300 years ago. Cut-marked mastodon bones and tools at Page-Ladson in Florida came in at about 14,550 years. At Cooper's Ferry in Idaho, Loren Davis's team reported occupation about 16,000 years ago. The ice-free corridor may not have been open or livable until about 13,500 years ago, so attention turned to the coast: people may have followed a 'kelp highway' of rich shorelines down the Pacific edge, now drowned by the rising sea. In March 2026 a team led by Todd Surovell argued in Science that the Monte Verde layers are only about 4,200 to 8,200 years old, reopening the site's age. The original excavators, including Tom Dillehay, replied that the new work sampled the wrong deposits, and the argument is still running. The case for people in the Americas before Clovis no longer rests on Monte Verde alone: White Sands carries most of the weight.

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell: 04 White Sands: tested four ways
chunks.text: Matthew Bennett, David Bustos and colleagues dated the White Sands footprints in 2021 using seeds of the aquatic plant Ruppia from layers above and below the tracks: 23,000 to 21,000 years ago. Critics raised a fair objection. Water plants can absorb old carbon dissolved in lake water, which makes them look older than they are. In 2023 Jeffrey Pigati and colleagues answered the critics with two independent methods: radiocarbon dates on pollen from land-growing conifers, which take carbon from the air, and optically stimulated luminescence on quartz grains, which measures when sediment was last exposed to light. Both agreed with the seed dates. In June 2025 a team led by the geoarchaeologist Vance Holliday dated the mud of ancient Lake Otero and found 20,700 to 22,400 years. Four materials, one answer. A horizontal bar chart of site ages from 0 to 36,000 years ago. Solid bars: Clovis culture about 13,000 years, Paisley Caves about 14,300, Monte Verde II about 14,500, and White Sands 21,000 to 23,000, falling inside a shaded band for the glacial maximum from 26,000 to 20,000 years ago. Dashed bars for contested claims: Bluefish Caves about 24,000 years, Chiquihuite Cave 31,000 to 33,000, Pedra Furada 32,000 to over 50,000, and the Cerutti Mastodon at 130,000 years, shown running off the chart. The implication is profound. People were south of the ice sheets during the Last Glacial Maximum, when Beringia was dry land and the northern route was frozen shut. They must have arrived even earlier, or come along the coast. Genetic estimates, which place the split between Native American ancestors and Siberians at roughly 25,000 to 20,000 years ago, allow exactly that.

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell: 05 Why the resistance lasted so long
chunks.text: It is tempting to cast the Clovis-first era as simple stubbornness, but the story is more instructive than that. Many early pre-Clovis claims really were weak: charcoal that could have come from natural fires, 'tools' that were stones cracked by frost or rockfall, and dates run on contaminated samples. Sceptics were right to reject those. The trouble was that the scepticism hardened into a filter. A site that did not fit was assumed to be wrong before it was examined, and a single ambiguous detail was enough to dismiss years of careful work. The cost was real. Jacques Cinq-Mars, who excavated Bluefish Caves in the Yukon from the late 1970s and argued for an Ice Age human presence there, later described the hostility he met; in 2017 Lauriane Bourgeon's re-analysis of cut-marked bones from the caves pushed their age to about 24,000 years. Dillehay's Monte Verde volumes sat under suspicion for two decades. The lesson for this site is the one the challengers draw: consensus can lag behind evidence. The lesson the mainstream draws is also fair: the claims that finally won did so with excavation, dating and replication, not with argument alone. Scepticism is a tool. Clovis-first turned it into a wall.

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell: 06 The challengers: older, and stranger?
chunks.text: If Clovis-first was wrong, how much else might be? Niède Guidon argued from the 1980s that Pedra Furada, a painted rock shelter in north-east Brazil, held hearths more than 30,000 years old; sceptics answered that its 'tools' could be quartzite broken by falling rocks. At Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico, Ciprian Ardelean's team (2020) reported stone tools as early as 33,000 to 31,000 years ago; others doubt they are artefacts. Most startling, Steven Holen and colleagues (2017) argued that mastodon bones at the Cerutti site near San Diego were broken by people using stone hammers about 130,000 years ago. Critics, including prominent pre-Clovis researchers, doubt the bones were broken by hand. Graham Hancock's America Before (2019) and season two of Ancient Apocalypse (2024) use this history to argue that the Americas have a much deeper past than archaeology admits. He highlights the 'Population Y' signal, a faint Australasian genetic trace identified by Pontus Skoglund and colleagues in 2015 among some Amazonian peoples, and asks what else the orthodoxy has missed. On the central point, that the experts held a too-young date far too long, history is on his side. The challengers were right about the direction. The open question is how far back the evidence can really carry us.

chunks.heading: The First Americans: How Clovis-First Fell: 07 What time has hidden, and what would settle it
chunks.text: The earliest Americans were probably few and mobile, and the likeliest route, the Ice Age Pacific shore, now lies 50 to 120 metres underwater. Their camps would leave scattered hearths and flakes, not monuments. Human skeletons older than about 13,000 years are almost unknown. So absence of older evidence is weak evidence. But it cuts both ways: a broken bone is not a person, and extraordinary ages need unmistakable tools, hearths or human remains. What would settle it: a human skeleton or unambiguous stone tools at a securely dated site older than 25,000 years; ancient DNA from a pre-Clovis individual; and survey of drowned coastal landscapes off Alaska and British Columbia. For now the verdict is clear on one point: people were in the Americas more than 20,000 years ago, and the textbooks have some catching up to do.

chunks.heading: The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre?
chunks.text: Lost Ice Age World The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre? c. 2500 BCE (conventional); 7000–5000 BCE or earlier (Schoch) Awaiting discovery. Does the weathering of the Sphinx enclosure show it is thousands of years older than Khafre? The claim on the scales The core body of the Great Sphinx was carved thousands of years before Khafre, around 7000–5000 BCE or earlier. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Schoch's observation is real and his argument is geological, not mystical. But weathering rates in soft, salt-laden limestone are too uncertain to date a monument, and credible alternatives (salt crystallisation, dew, flash floods, wet sand) exist. Against the early date stands concrete archaeology: temples built of blocks from the ditch, a building sequence tied to Khafre's complex, and no trace of an earlier carving culture at Giza. Reader's modest version (a few centuries earlier) remains plausible; the far older date awaits evidence. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks usually state flatly that Khafre built the Sphinx. The evidence for that is strong but circumstantial: no Old Kingdom text says so, and Colin Reader's case for a slightly earlier start is respectable. A more honest label would read 'probably carved for Khafre, c. 2500 BCE'. On the far older date, the textbooks' silence is closer to the evidence. What is solid The Sphinx was carved from the living rock of the Giza plateau: it is about 73 m long, 20 m high and 19 m wide. Lehner & Hawass 2017 Its body lies in layered limestone of alternating hard and soft beds (Member II of the Mokattam Formation); the head is in harder rock above and the base in a hard lower bed. Gauri et al. 1995 The walls of the Sphinx enclosure are deeply weathered, with a rolling, recessed profile and vertical fissures. Schoch 1992; Gauri et al. 1995 No inscription of Khafre's time names the Sphinx; the attribution to Khafre rests on its position, architecture and building sequence. Lehner 1992; Hawass & Lehner 1994 Seismic surveys found weathered rock beneath the enclosure floor, about 1.8–2.4 m deep in front and along the sides and roughly half as deep behind the Sphinx. Dobecki & Schoch 1992 What is disputed Whether the enclosure's weathering profile requires long periods of heavy rainfall or can be produced by salt crystallisation, dew and occasional storms. How fast weathering proceeds, and whether the depth of subsurface weathering can be turned into an age at all. Whether the Sphinx and its temples predate Khufu's quarrying, as Colin Reader argued, placi

chunks.heading: The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre?: 01 A geologist looks at the walls
chunks.text: In 1990 a geologist from Boston University stood in the trench around the Great Sphinx and ran his hand along the rock. Robert Schoch had come at the invitation of John Anthony West, a writer who believed the Sphinx was far older than Egyptologists said. Schoch expected to find nothing surprising. Instead he saw walls that looked, to his eye, as if they had been worn by rain: a rolling, rounded profile and deep vertical fissures, the kind of weathering produced when water runs down a rock face for a very long time. The problem was obvious. Giza has been desert for about five thousand years. If rain carved these walls, the Sphinx might date from a time when Egypt was green, long before the pyramids. In 1991 Schoch presented the idea to the Geological Society of America, and the fight that followed has never quite ended. Egyptologists read the Sphinx through its temples. Schoch read it through its rock. They reached very different ages.

chunks.heading: The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre?: 02 What is solid: a statue carved from a quarry
chunks.text: The Sphinx was not built; it was carved. Quarrymen cut a U-shaped trench into the plateau, leaving a block of rock about 73 metres long that they shaped into a lion with a human head, about 20 metres high. The body lies in layered limestone of alternating hard and soft beds, which weather at very different rates. That is why the Sphinx's flanks look ribbed and why its body has been patched with masonry again and again, in the New Kingdom, in Roman times and in the 20th century. Its date is inferred, not written. No text of Khafre's reign names the Sphinx. Mark Lehner, who spent years mapping every stone of it with Zahi Hawass from 1979, built the conventional case from the ground up. Even the best-known 'inscription' does not help much. Around 1400 BCE, Thutmose IV set up a granite stela between the paws recording a dream in which the Sphinx asked to be freed from the sand. Early copyists read part of a royal name, 'Khaf', in a damaged line, but the text is now largely lost and the reading cannot carry any weight. By Thutmose's day the Sphinx was already more than a thousand years old on anyone's reckoning, half-buried and in need of repair. Step 1 of 4. Khafre's Valley Temple and causeway are laid out on the plateau. Khafre's Valley Temple and causeway are laid out on the plateau. Quarrymen cut a ditch into the rock, leaving a core that is carved into the Sphinx. Blocks from the ditch are used for the Sphinx Temple's core walls. The Sphinx Temple is fitted against the Valley Temple's north wall: Khafre's complex came first. A plan view with north at the top. At the lower right is Khafre's Valley Temple, a square about 45 metres across, with Khafre's causeway leading west-north-west from its corner. Step 2 adds a rectangular quarried enclosure north of the causeway with

chunks.heading: The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre?: 03 The mainstream story: Khafre's guardian
chunks.text: Lehner's argument is architectural. The south side of the Sphinx enclosure runs along the line of Khafre's causeway, which leads up from his Valley Temple to his pyramid. The Sphinx Temple, directly in front of the statue, was built of enormous limestone blocks, and those blocks carry the same fossil-rich layers as the beds exposed in the Sphinx ditch: they are the stone removed to free the Sphinx. The Sphinx Temple was also fitted against the north wall of Khafre's Valley Temple, so Khafre's complex already stood. Quarry, statue and temple, on this reading, are one project, around 2500 BCE. The geologists who disagree with Schoch offer mechanisms too. K. Lal Gauri and colleagues (1995) argued that the soft beds of the enclosure are destroyed chiefly by salt: moisture from dew and groundwater carries dissolved salts into the rock, which crystallise and burst its surface. James Harrell proposed that wet sand, which filled the enclosure for much of its history, did the damage. Egyptologists add that the Old Kingdom was not entirely dry. Flash floods still struck: the Sadd el-Kafara dam, built in the Old Kingdom in a wadi near Helwan, appears to have been breached by one.

chunks.heading: The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre?: 04 The challengers at their strongest
chunks.text: Schoch's case has three parts. First, the shape of the weathering: the enclosure walls have a rolling, undulating profile with vertical fissures that open at the top, which he regards as a textbook signature of precipitation running down a rock face. Nearby tombs cut into the same beds in the Old Kingdom, he says, show a sharper, wind-scoured profile instead. Second, the ground: seismic surveys he carried out with the geophysicist Thomas Dobecki found weathered rock beneath the enclosure floor about 1.8 to 2.4 metres deep in front and along the sides, but only about half as deep at the back. Schoch reads that as the rear being excavated much later, perhaps under Khafre, while the front and sides are far older. Three schematic vertical cross-sections through limestone walls with alternating hard and soft beds. The first, the Sphinx enclosure wall, has deep rounded coves in the soft beds and is cut back most near the top, with a dashed line of rain running down it; the label gives Schoch's reading of rain runoff over thousands of wet years. The second, an Old Kingdom tomb face, has sharp rectangular notches where soft beds are cut back, which Schoch reads as wind and sand erosion. The third shows the salt-weathering model, with rising moisture and salt crystals flaking the soft beds into rounded recesses, which Gauri and Harrell argue can happen without rain. Third, the climate. Egypt was much wetter before about 3000 BCE, during what is now called the African Humid Period. Assuming weathering proceeded at a steady rate, Schoch in 1992 dated the core body to about 7000 to 5000 BCE, noting that if weathering slowed with depth, the Sphinx could be older still. In later books he has linked it to the end of the Ice Age, around 9700 BCE. John Anthony West's 1993 NBC documentar

chunks.heading: The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre?: 05 Where the argument breaks down
chunks.text: The difficulty for any very early date is rates. Weathering speed depends on rock chemistry, salt load, humidity, burial by sand and exposure, all of which changed repeatedly over 4,500 years. Soft Member II beds can lose centimetres in decades under the wrong conditions, and the Sphinx spent long periods buried to the neck in sand, which alters both moisture and wear. Turning a depth of weathering into an age is therefore very uncertain, as Schoch himself acknowledges when he describes his date as a minimum. The second difficulty is people. A monument carved in 7000 BCE implies a society in Egypt capable of organised, large-scale stone working and long-term planning. Göbekli Tepe shows that Stone Age foragers could build megaliths, so the idea is not absurd in principle. But in the Nile Valley the archaeology of that period shows small groups of hunters and herders, and nothing on the Giza plateau is securely older than the Early Dynastic period. There is also a problem of comparison. The tombs Schoch contrasts with the enclosure were cut at different heights, in slightly different beds, and some were buried or roofed for long stretches, so they have not faced identical conditions. Critics argue that like is not being compared with like. Supporters reply that the contrast between the enclosure and its neighbours is too systematic to be an accident. Neither side has yet published the kind of measured, bed-by-bed survey that would decide it. The rock may be telling us something real. So far it has not told us a date.

chunks.heading: The Sphinx and the Rain: Older Than Khafre?: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The best hope is a physical clock. Cosmogenic-nuclide exposure dating measures how long a rock surface has faced the sky, and has dated rock-cut features elsewhere. Applied carefully to the enclosure floor and walls, it could test whether the trench is 4,500 years old or 9,000. Controlled monitoring of how Giza limestone weathers today would test the salt and rain models against each other. And any datable material sealed at the very bottom of the ditch fill would anchor the quarrying directly. Until then the fair verdict is this. Khafre remains the best-supported builder, with a respectable case for a slightly earlier start. Schoch deserves credit for asking a geological question that Egyptology had not, and for publishing his data. But a Sphinx from the age of the rains is still waiting for its evidence.

chunks.heading: Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence
chunks.text: Lost Ice Age World Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence c. 9600 BCE (Plato's setting); written c. 360 BCE Ruled out. Was Atlantis a real drowned civilisation, a memory, or Plato's invention? The claim on the scales A large island empire, as Plato describes it, existed beyond Gibraltar and sank into the Atlantic around 9600 BCE. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established The ocean floor itself contradicts a sunken island 'larger than Libya and Asia': it is young volcanic crust with no drowned continent. Nowhere in the world does archaeology show a bronze-using naval empire around 9600 BCE. The candidate sites fail on scale or date: Thera is 8,000 years too late, Spartel Bank was a small islet, and Richat is a natural landform 40 km across, far larger than Plato's city. The date coincidence with the Younger Dryas is real and interesting, but it cannot rescue the empire. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks call Atlantis a Platonic myth, and on the empire they are right. They are more confident than the evidence about Plato's intentions, which nobody can read. He may have woven real Egyptian lore or folk memories of drowned lands into his fable. The fair statement: the empire is ruled out; whether any memory lies beneath the story remains open. What is solid Atlantis appears first in Plato's Timaeus and Critias, written about 360 BCE; no earlier Greek or Egyptian text that mentions it has been found. Plato, Timaeus 20d–25d; Critias Plato says the story came from Egyptian priests at Saïs via the Athenian lawgiver Solon, and that the war happened 9,000 years before Solon, which works out to about 9600 BCE. Timaeus 23e; Critias 108e The Younger Dryas cold interval ended, and sea level rose steeply, about 11,700 years ago, around 9700 BCE. Walker et al. 2009 The Atlantic floor beyond Gibraltar is oceanic crust formed at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; there is no foundered continent-sized island. Standard plate-tectonic mapping The eruption of Thera (Santorini) devastated the Bronze Age Aegean in the 16th century BCE, and the Greek city of Helike sank in an earthquake and tsunami in 373 BCE, in Plato's lifetime. Pearson et al. 2023; Strabo, Geography 8.7.2 What is disputed Whether Plato invented the story outright to illustrate his ideal state, or built it on real Egyptian traditions or Greek memories of catastrophe. Whether the 9600 BCE date is a genuine memory of the end of the Ice Age or a round, symbolic number. Whether any real place (Thera and Crete, Spartel Bank, the Richat Structure, the drowned shelves) su

chunks.heading: Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence: 01 A story from the priests of Saïs
chunks.text: Around 360 BCE Plato wrote a dialogue in which the Athenian politician Critias tells a story passed down from his great-grandfather's friend Solon, the famous lawgiver. Solon, the story goes, had visited the Egyptian city of Saïs, where the priests laughed at the Greeks' short memory. Greece had forgotten its own past, they said, because fire and flood had destroyed it again and again. Solon, Solon, you Hellenes are never anything but children, and there is not an old man among you. Then they told him of Atlantis: a great island beyond the Pillars of Heracles, the Strait of Gibraltar, whose kings ruled much of the Mediterranean world and attacked Athens and Egypt. A heroic ancient Athens beat them back. Then catastrophe struck both sides. But afterwards there occurred violent earthquakes and floods; and in a single day and night of misfortune all your warlike men in a body sank into the earth, and the island of Atlantis in like manner disappeared in the depths of the sea.

chunks.heading: Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence: 02 What Plato actually describes
chunks.text: In the unfinished Critias, Plato adds astonishing detail. Poseidon's island city was built in rings: a central island five stadia across, surrounded by alternating rings of water and land, one, two, two, three and three stadia wide, all bridged and tunnelled for ships. A canal 50 stadia long led to the sea, and a great wall ran round the whole city 50 stadia out from the largest ring. Beyond lay a vast, level plain of 3,000 by 2,000 stadia, ringed by a ditch 10,000 stadia long. With a stadion of about 185 metres, the ring city is some 5 km across and the plain about 555 by 370 km. Step 1 of 4. Plato's ring city, enlarged: island of 5 stadia, rings of 1, 2, 2, 3 and 3 stadia. Plato's ring city, enlarged: island of 5 stadia, rings of 1, 2, 2, 3 and 3 stadia. At true scale the city is about 5 km across; its canal runs about 9 km and its outer wall about 23 km across. The Richat Structure at the same scale: about 40 km across, rings of natural rock ridges. Plato's plain, about 555 × 370 km, dwarfs both. Left: an enlarged diagram of concentric circles, a central island five stadia across surrounded by rings of water and land of one, two, two, three and three stadia, with a canal leading south to the sea; total about 27 stadia or 5 kilometres. Right, at true scale: step 2 shows the same city as a small ringed disc about 5 kilometres wide with a 9 kilometre canal and a dashed outer wall circle about 23 kilometres across. Step 3 adds the Richat Structure, a circle about 40 kilometres across with concentric ridges, around it. Step 4 adds an inset rectangle for Plato's plain of 555 by 370 kilometres, with Richat as a small dot at the same scale. Plato also gives a date. The Egyptian priests told Solon that their own records went back 8,000 years and that Athens and the war were 9

chunks.heading: Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence: 03 The mainstream reading: a philosopher's fable
chunks.text: Most classicists think Plato invented Atlantis. The story does exactly the job he needed: the Republic had sketched an ideal city, and Timaeus and Critias set that city in motion against a rich, arrogant sea power that the gods punish. Plato invents myths elsewhere too, from the Ring of Gyges to the Myth of Er, and he often gives them solemn chains of witnesses. No earlier author mentions Atlantis. According to the late commentator Proclus, Plato's early follower Crantor took the story as history, but even in antiquity readers disagreed. Science adds hard limits. The Atlantic floor beyond Gibraltar is young crust spreading from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; there is no sunken continent. Around 9600 BCE people everywhere lived as foragers or very early cultivators. Göbekli Tepe, being built in Anatolia at about that time, shows remarkable skill in stone, but there is no bronze, no orichalcum, no fleets of triremes, no kings of ten nations anywhere in the record.

chunks.heading: Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence: 04 The challengers: Thera, Spartel, Richat and the date
chunks.text: The modern Atlantis industry began with Ignatius Donnelly, a Minnesota congressman whose Atlantis: The Antediluvian World (1882) argued that Atlantis was a real mid-Atlantic continent and the mother of Egypt, Mexico and much else, pointing to shared flood myths, pyramids and alphabets. Donnelly wrote before plate tectonics and before radiocarbon, and his parallels have not survived scrutiny, but his instinct, that similar myths on both sides of the ocean call for an explanation, still drives the debate. The most scholarly alternative came from Greece. In 1939 Spyridon Marinatos proposed that the Bronze Age eruption of Thera (Santorini) helped bring down Minoan Crete, a real island sea power. Angelos Galanopoulos later suggested that Plato's numbers had slipped by a factor of ten: 900 years before Solon puts the catastrophe near 1500 BCE, close to Thera. Radiocarbon now dates the eruption to the 16th or late 17th century BCE. The fit in spirit is good; the fit in place and size is poor, because Crete lies inside the Mediterranean, not beyond Gibraltar. In 2001 the geologist Jacques Collina-Girard pointed to Spartel Bank, west of the Strait of Gibraltar, which was a small island when the sea was low and drowned as it rose. Marc-André Gutscher tested the idea in 2005 and found evidence for great earthquakes and tsunamis in the region, but concluded that the islet was small and drowned gradually, not in a day and a night. More recently, online researchers have championed the Richat Structure in Mauritania, a spectacular set of rings 40 km across visible from space. Geologists mapped Richat in detail in the 2000s. It is an eroded dome: molten rock pushed up the layers about 100 million years ago, hot fluids dissolved and collapsed the centre, and erosion then carved the tilt

chunks.heading: Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence: 05 Weighing the coincidence
chunks.text: It is worth taking the date seriously and testing it. Plato did not know about ice ages, so the match is not a trick of hindsight. But the end of the Ice Age was not one day and night of disaster; sea level rose over thousands of years, and the fastest pulses came before 9600 BCE. The number 9,000 is also a round figure in a story full of round figures, and Plato's Egyptian priests needed their records to be far older than Greek memory to make his point. A coincidence within a century or two, among many possible dates, is suggestive but weak evidence. There is also a much closer candidate for the ending. In the winter of 373 BCE, when Plato was in his fifties, an earthquake struck the Gulf of Corinth and the sea swept over the prosperous city of Helike in a single night, drowning it so completely that later visitors said they could see its ruins under the water. Plato's audience would have known the story well. A city swallowed by the sea overnight was not a far-off legend to them; it was recent news. What survives the test is smaller but still interesting. Real islands and coastal plains did drown in the millennia around Plato's date. Real catastrophes, Thera and Helike among them, struck the Greek world. Plato's story may be a fable built from these materials, and his priests' warning, that fire and water had repeatedly wiped out human memory, reads today like a fair summary of the drowned coasts. The empire is ruled out. The drowning of the Ice Age world is not a myth at all.

chunks.heading: Atlantis: Plato's Island and the 9600 BCE Coincidence: 06 What would change the verdict
chunks.text: An Egyptian source, independent of Plato, that tells the story would transform the debate. So would a drowned site of about 10,000 BCE showing monumental building or metalwork, or human traces on Spartel Bank. None has appeared. For now, Atlantis as Plato describes it, a vast Atlantic empire of 9600 BCE, is ruled out by the seafloor and the archaeological record. Atlantis as a question, whether ancient stories can carry faint memories of real drowned lands, remains open, and the rest of this site returns to it often.

chunks.heading: Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts
chunks.text: Lost Ice Age World Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts c. 13,070–7,250 years ago (proposed age of the events remembered) Plausible. Can a spoken story accurately remember a coastline that drowned 10,000 years ago? The claim on the scales Some Aboriginal Australian stories preserve accurate memories of coastal drowning that happened more than 7,000 years ago. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The pattern is striking: 21 locations, many different language groups, and every calculated age inside the known window of postglacial sea-level rise. Strict, cross-checked transmission is documented in Aboriginal societies. But each individual story could also be a later inference from landscape clues, and the recorded versions passed through colonial hands. Long memory is the most economical explanation for the whole set, and a serious possibility, but it is hard to test any one story independently. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact History textbooks rarely address this at all, and when they discuss oral tradition they usually assume it fades within a few centuries. For Aboriginal Australia that assumption now looks too pessimistic. Here the conventional view is underconfident about oral memory rather than overconfident, while the sea-level science behind the dates is secure. What is solid Sea level around Australia stood roughly 120 m lower at the Last Glacial Maximum and reached close to its present level about 7,000 years ago, drowning wide coastal plains. Lambeck et al. 2014 Aboriginal groups recorded from the 19th century onward tell stories, at 21 coastal locations studied by Nunn and Reid, of land that is now under the sea. Nunn & Reid 2016, Australian Geographer Matching each story's claim to the depth of water that now covers the land, and then to the sea-level curve, gives ages of about 7,250–13,070 years. Nunn & Reid 2016 Kangaroo Island was cut off from the mainland about 10,000 years ago; Ngarrindjeri tradition tells of the ancestral being Ngurunderi making the waters rise between them. Ngarrindjeri tradition; regional sea-level data Elsewhere, oral traditions demonstrably preserve real events: Pacific Northwest stories of the great Cascadia earthquake of January 1700 match the Japanese record of its tsunami. Ludwin et al. 2005 What is disputed Whether the stories are memories handed down for some 300 generations, or later inferences from clues in the landscape such as drowned trees, submerged shell middens and reefs. How much 19th- and 20th-century recording, translation and editing resh

chunks.heading: Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts: 01 When the gulf was a plain
chunks.text: On the Yorke Peninsula of South Australia, the Narrangga people tell of a time when Spencer Gulf was not sea at all. It was marshy country with freshwater lagoons where animals came to drink, until the sea broke through a barrier at its mouth and flooded in. The gulf is now up to several tens of metres deep. For its floor to be dry land, the sea would have to fall far below today's level, something that last happened roughly 9,000 to 12,000 years ago. Stories like this are found all around Australia's coast. Islands that people once walked to. Reefs that were hills. Bays that were hunting grounds. The possibility they raise is thrilling: that people have been passing on an accurate description of a vanished landscape for some 400 generations, far longer than any written record. If these stories are memories, they are among the oldest accurate histories anywhere on Earth.

chunks.heading: Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts: 02 What is solid: the sea really did come in
chunks.text: The geology is not in doubt. At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 21,000 years ago, sea level stood roughly 120 metres lower than today. Tasmania and New Guinea were joined to mainland Australia in one landmass, Sahul, and the Gulf of Carpentaria was a great lake. As the ice sheets melted, the sea climbed, sometimes several centimetres a year, and reached close to its present level around 7,000 years ago. Aboriginal people had lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years by then. Their coastal homelands were drowned while they watched. In 2016 the geographer Patrick Nunn and the linguist Nicholas Reid published a study of stories from 21 coastal locations that describe this kind of change. Their method was simple and testable. Step 1 of 4. Today an island is separated from the mainland by a channel; its deepest point is, say, 30 m. Today an island is separated from the mainland by a channel; its deepest point is, say, 30 m. The story says people once walked across, so the sea must then have been at least 30 m lower. The sea-level curve shows when the sea was last that low: here about 9,300 years ago, a minimum age. Applied to 21 Australian stories, the method gives ages between about 7,250 and 13,070 years. Left: a cross-section through a channel between a mainland and an island, with today's sea level and the channel's deepest point marked at 30 metres as an example. Right: a curve of sea level rising from about minus 95 metres 14,000 years ago to zero about 6,000 years ago. Step 1 shows the channel and its depth. Step 2 adds a dashed arrow of people walking across and a dashed line for a sea at least 30 metres lower. Step 3 draws a line from minus 30 metres across to the curve and down to the time axis, giving a minimum age of about 9,300 years. Step 4 adds a band

chunks.heading: Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts: 03 Three stories and a warning
chunks.text: Near Cairns in Queensland, the Yidindji remember a time when the shoreline lay out near the Great Barrier Reef, Fitzroy Island was part of the mainland and Green Island was much larger, with named places that are now underwater. Nunn and Reid estimate this landscape at about 10,000 to 13,000 years ago. In the Gulf of Carpentaria, a Wellesley Islands story tells how the peninsula was cut through and flooded, a change dated to about 6,000 to 7,000 years ago. Off South Australia, Kangaroo Island was separated from the mainland about 10,000 years ago. Ngarrindjeri tradition tells how the ancestral being Ngurunderi, pursuing his wives as they waded across to the island, made the waters rise and drown them. The Kaurna name for the island, Karta Pintingga, is usually translated 'island of the dead'. The island's own Aboriginal population disappears from the archaeological record some time after it became an island. Stories from around Melbourne describe Port Phillip Bay as a dry plain where people hunted kangaroo before the sea rushed in. These have often been cited as memories of postglacial flooding. But in 2011 Guy Holdgate and colleagues proposed, from seismic surveys and cores, that the bay was partly dry as recently as about 1,000 years ago, when its narrow entrance was blocked. If so, the stories may remember a much later flood. It is a reminder that every story needs its own local geology.

chunks.heading: Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts: 04 How could a story last 10,000 years?
chunks.text: Historians of oral tradition have usually assumed that stories drift and blur within a few centuries. Nunn and Reid argue that some Aboriginal societies worked differently. Knowledge was law, tied to land, ceremony and kin. In many groups, the owners of a story were checked by people from a complementary kin group whose duty was to see that it was told and performed correctly. A mistake was not just embarrassing; it was a breach of law. Such cross-checking can, in principle, keep a story's key facts stable for a very long time. A chart with a logarithmic time axis from 100 to 50,000 years ago. A shaded band from 100 to 1,000 years is labelled often assumed limit of oral memory. Dots and bars show the Cascadia earthquake of 1700 at about 325 years, the Mount Mazama eruption remembered in Klamath accounts at about 7,700 years, the 21 Australian drowning stories spanning 7,250 to 13,070 years, Kangaroo Island's separation at about 10,000 years, and a dashed outline for the Budj Bim eruption at 33,600 to 40,200 years, whose link to Gunditjmara tradition is proposed but debated. There are hints from elsewhere that long memory is possible. The Klamath people of Oregon tell of a battle between spirits of the mountain and the sky that ended with a great mountain collapsing; Crater Lake formed when Mount Mazama erupted about 7,700 years ago. In Victoria, the Gunditjmara tell of an ancestral being who became the volcano Budj Bim, which geologists have dated to about 37,000 years ago; whether the story truly remembers the eruption is debated. On firmer ground, Pacific Northwest stories of a great earthquake and flood match the Cascadia earthquake of January 1700, which is fixed to the day by the tsunami it sent to Japan. This matters far beyond Australia. Writers such as Graham Ha

chunks.heading: Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts: 05 The case for caution
chunks.text: The strongest objection is inference. A person standing on a beach can see drowned tree stumps at low tide, shell middens eroding from the shoreline, or an island covered in the same animals as the mainland. It would be natural to conclude that the land was once joined, and to tell a story about how it was lost. Such a story would be accurate, but it would not be a memory. The second objection is the record itself. Most versions were written down by colonists, missionaries and anthropologists from the 1800s onward, often in paraphrase and without noting who told them or how. By then European ideas of changing sea levels were in circulation. And the people who held these stories were being displaced from their land, which broke the chains of transmission the argument relies on. None of this makes long memory impossible. It does mean each story must be judged on its own evidence. Accurate is not the same as remembered. The hard part is telling them apart.

chunks.heading: Stories Older Than the Sea: Australia's Drowned Coasts: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The most convincing test would be a story that names a specific drowned feature nobody could see today, a hill, a spring, a stone arrangement, which is then found on the seabed at the depth and in the place the story implies. Underwater surveys off Western Australia have already found submerged Aboriginal stone artefacts, so such a match is not fanciful. Careful work in the archives, finding the earliest recorded version of each story, would also help separate old tradition from later influence. Any such research depends on the communities who hold these stories and decide what may be shared. For now the verdict is plausible, and leaning hopeful. The sea-level science is secure, the pattern across 21 places is hard to dismiss, and Aboriginal Australians may be the keepers of the oldest accurate histories anywhere.

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone Middle and Late Pleistocene, c. 350,000–40,000 years ago Strong evidence. How many kinds of humans shared the Earth with our ancestors, and until when? The claim on the scales Within roughly the last 60,000 years, Homo sapiens shared the planet with at least four other human groups. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established For Neanderthals and Denisovans the case rests on fossils plus DNA that entered our own genomes after about 60,000 years ago, which is very hard to dispute. For Homo floresiensis, skeletons reach about 60,000 years and tools about 50,000. For Homo luzonensis, the dates are minimum ages of about 50,000 and 67,000 years. Those last two sit close to the line, which is why the rating is strong rather than established. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact University textbooks now teach a crowded, interbreeding human past, and they are right to. But many school books and museum murals still show a single march from ape to human, and they rarely mention that several groups were found only in the last twenty years. On diversity, popular accounts are still overconfident in a simple story. What is solid DNA from a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in 2008 revealed a previously unknown human group, the Denisovans, whose genome was published in 2010. Krause et al. 2010; Reich et al. 2010 Neanderthals survived in Europe until about 40,000 years ago, and people outside Africa today carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA. Higham et al. 2014; Green et al. 2010 Homo floresiensis, about 1.1 m tall, lived on Flores; its skeletons date to about 100,000–60,000 years ago and its tools to about 50,000. Brown et al. 2004; Sutikna et al. 2016 Homo luzonensis, described in 2019 from Callao Cave in the Philippines, has minimum ages of about 50,000 and 67,000 years.
