Détroit et al. 2019 In 2025, ancient proteins identified a jaw from the Taiwan Strait and the near-complete Harbin skull as Denisovan. Tsutaya et al. 2025; Fu et al. 2025 What is disputed Whether small-brained Homo naledi deliberately buried its dead and engraved cave walls, about 300,000–240,000 years ago. Whether the Harbin skull should be called Homo longi, a species of its own, or simply the Denisovans with a face. When the last Denisovans, hobbits and Luzon people died out, and whether they met modern humans. What time has hidden Tropical heat and acid soils destroy bone and DNA, so the islands of South-East Asia, where several groups lived, preserve very little. The Sunda and Sahul shelves, dry la

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone: 01 A finger bone with a secret
chunks.text: In 2008, digging in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, Russian archaeologists found a scrap of bone smaller than a fingernail: the tip of a child's little finger. It looked like nothing. Then geneticists at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig extracted its DNA, expecting a Neanderthal or a modern human, and found neither. The girl belonged to a group of people no one had ever seen, known from no skull, no skeleton and no tool that could be tied to them. They were named after the cave: the Denisovans. When their genome was published in 2010 it revealed something even stranger. Their DNA is still walking around. People in New Guinea carry about 4–6 percent of it, and many Tibetans owe their tolerance of thin air to a gene variant they inherited from these vanished people. For a decade, a whole branch of humanity was known mainly as a genome in search of a face. We were taught a simple picture: a single line of ancestors climbing from ape to human, with us at the top, alone. The last twenty years have replaced that picture with something far stranger.

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone: 02 A crowded planet
chunks.text: Set the clock to 60,000 years ago, when our own species was beginning to spread out of Africa in numbers. Neanderthals still lived across Europe and western Asia, and they would last until about 40,000 years ago. Denisovans lived somewhere across Asia, from Siberia to the tropics. On the island of Flores in Indonesia lived Homo floresiensis, the 'hobbit', about 1.1 metres tall with a brain about a third the size of ours, found in Liang Bua cave in 2003. To the north, on Luzon in the Philippines, lived Homo luzonensis, known from a handful of teeth and small bones in Callao Cave and described in 2019. A horizontal time chart from 350,000 years ago on the left to today on the right, with six rows. Homo sapiens: a bar from about 300,000 years ago to today. Neanderthals: a bar from before 350,000 to about 40,000 years ago. Denisovans: a bar from about 200,000 to 50,000 years ago, with open dots for the Xiahe jaw at 160,000 and the Harbin skull at 146,000, and two dashed boxes for the two possible age ranges of the Penghu jaw, 190,000 to 130,000 or 70,000 to 10,000. Homo floresiensis: dashed stone-tool range from 190,000 to 50,000 and skeletons from 100,000 to 60,000, with an arrow noting ancestors on Flores by 700,000. Homo luzonensis: two dots at minimum ages of 67,000 and 50,000 with a dashed arrow meaning they may be older. Homo naledi: a bar from 335,000 to 236,000. A vertical accent line at 60,000 years ago crosses five rows. Further back, the crowd grows. In South Africa, cavers squeezing into the Rising Star cave system in 2013 found more than 1,550 pieces of bone from at least fifteen individuals of Homo naledi, a small-brained species that lived between about 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, when early Homo sapiens was already walking the continent. And in north-east

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone: 03 New tools, new faces
chunks.text: DNA breaks down in heat and time, so for years the Denisovans could only be studied in cold Siberia. The breakthrough came from proteins, which last longer. In 2019 proteins from a jaw found in 1980 by a Buddhist monk in Baishiya Karst Cave, at 3,280 metres on the Tibetan Plateau, showed it was Denisovan and at least 160,000 years old. Sediment DNA from the same cave showed Denisovans had lived there for a long time. Step 1 of 5. 2008–2010: a finger bone from Denisova Cave yields a new human genome, still found in people of New Guinea today. 2008–2010: a finger bone from Denisova Cave yields a new human genome, still found in people of New Guinea today. 2019: proteins identify a Denisovan jaw from 3,280 m up on the Tibetan Plateau. 2022: a child's molar from a cave in Laos extends the range south. 2025: a jaw dredged from the Taiwan Strait is identified as a male Denisovan. 2025: the Harbin skull is identified as Denisovan: the first face. A latitude and longitude grid from 60 to 150 degrees east and 60 degrees north to 10 degrees south, without coastlines. Step 1: Denisova Cave in the Altai, with the 2008 finger bone and 2010 genome, and a dashed arrow to New Guinea, where people today carry about 4 to 6 percent Denisovan DNA. Step 2: the Xiahe jaw on the Tibetan Plateau at 3,280 metres, over 160,000 years old, identified by proteins in 2019. Step 3: a child's molar from Tam Ngu Hao 2 in Laos, 164,000 to 131,000 years old, probably Denisovan. Step 4: the Penghu jaw dredged from the Taiwan Strait, identified by proteins in 2025. Step 5: the Harbin skull in north-east China, over 146,000 years old, with a 1,420 cubic centimetre brain, identified in 2025 by proteins and mitochondrial DNA: the first Denisovan face. In 2025 two finds gave the Denisovans a body. Proteins fro

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone: 04 The mainstream story, rewritten
chunks.text: To its credit, mainstream palaeoanthropology has changed its mind quickly. The older 'Out of Africa' model, in which our species replaced every other human without mixing, has given way to replacement with interbreeding. Our ancestors met Neanderthals and Denisovans and had children with them, and those children's genes are in most people alive. A bone fragment from Denisova Cave even came from a girl, nicknamed Denny, whose mother was a Neanderthal and whose father was a Denisovan. The islands of South-East Asia add a different lesson. The ancestors of the Flores hobbits were already small 700,000 years ago, according to a tiny arm bone published in 2024, and they survived in isolation for hundreds of thousands of years. The ladder picture never had room for such a long, parallel human story.

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone: 05 The challengers' case
chunks.text: Lee Berger and John Hawks argue that Homo naledi carried its dead into the deepest chambers of Rising Star, buried them in dug pits, and scratched cross-hatched patterns into the walls. If true, a creature with a brain the size of an orange behaved in ways once reserved for big-brained humans. Critics, including María Martinón-Torres and colleagues in 2024, reply that the sediment work cannot yet rule out natural accumulation, and that the engravings are neither dated nor clearly made by naledi. The papers were finally published by eLife in 2025, with reviewers still divided. Ji Qiang and Ni Xijun named the Harbin skull Homo longi and argue it represents a lineage close to our own; a reconstruction of the million-year-old Yunxian skull, published in 2025, pushed the split of these lineages further back, a result still debated. And the anthropologist Gregory Forth has spent years recording stories among the Lio people of Flores about small, hairy wild people, which he suggests may preserve a memory of Homo floresiensis, or even a late survival. The challengers ask the right question: if we missed whole kinds of humans until yesterday, what else have we missed? The verdicts differ. The naledi burials are a genuine open question with serious work on both sides. The Homo longi name is a dispute about labels more than facts. The hobbit-survival idea has no fossil, tool or DNA younger than about 50,000 years to support it, so it remains a hypothesis awaiting discovery, though the stories themselves deserve respect as a record of how people saw their world.

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone: 06 What time has erased
chunks.text: Almost every one of these groups was found by luck. Bone and DNA survive best in cold, dry caves; the tropics, where much of human history happened, destroy them. During the Ice Age the Sunda shelf joined Java, Sumatra and Borneo to Asia, a landmass now under the sea. Wallacea, the island world between Asia and Australia, has barely been excavated. When the evidence comes from a finger bone, a jaw from a fishing net and a skull from a well, the honest conclusion is that the family tree is still incomplete.

chunks.heading: The Other Humans: We Were Never Alone: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: Nuclear DNA from Harbin or Penghu would fix the Denisovans' place on the tree. Direct dates on the naledi remains inside the proposed graves, with independent studies of how the sediment formed, would test the burial claim. And sediment DNA surveys in the caves of Wallacea could reveal when the island humans disappeared, and whether they met us. The idea that we 'started at the bottom and climbed alone' does not survive the evidence. Humanity was a crowd of cousins, some tall, some tiny, some big-brained, some not, and for most of our history we were not the only people on Earth.

chunks.heading: The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe Late Younger Dryas to earliest Holocene, c. 10,000 cal BCE Strong evidence. Who carved a five-metre wooden figure in the Urals at the end of the Ice Age? The claim on the scales The Shigir Idol was carved around 12,000 years ago, making it the oldest known monumental wooden sculpture. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Seven AMS dates were run in two laboratories, and the pattern makes sense: the outer wood, soaked in conservation resin, gave young ages, while the untouched core gave the oldest. Tool marks show carving in green wood, so the felling date is close to the carving date. The earlier 9,500-year result used older methods on contaminated samples. Only one object has been dated this way, and the exact century remains uncertain, which keeps the rating short of established. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Museum labels now give the early date with confidence, and that is fair. The larger gap lies in general histories, which still present monumental art as a product of farming villages. Shigir, like Göbekli Tepe, shows that account was overconfident: foragers built monuments, and the archaeological record is biased toward stone because wood almost never survives. What is solid The sculpture was recovered in ten pieces on 24 January 1890 from about 4 m down in the Shigir peat bog, a gold-mining area east of the Middle Urals. Zhilin et al. 2018 It is carved from a single larch trunk; the tree was about 159 years old when it was felled. Zhilin et al. 2018 Tool marks from a polished stone adze and two or three kinds of stone chisel show it was carved in fresh, green wood, soon after felling. Zhilin et al. 2018 AMS radiocarbon dates on the innermost, uncontaminated wood place the carving close to the end of the Younger Dryas, about 12,000 years ago (c. 10,000 cal BCE). Terberger et al. 2021 In 1914 Vladimir Tolmachev reconstructed the complete figure at about 5.3 m, using fragments that were later lost. Zhilin et al. 2018 What is disputed What the faces and zigzag bands mean: a creation story, a map, guardian spirits, or a warning about dangerous places. Whether the idol stood upright as a pole, leaned against a rock, or lay in a sanctuary. Whether monumental art in the Urals and at Göbekli Tepe share any connection, or arose independently at the same climatic moment. What time has hidden The lower fragments used in the 1914 reconstruction are lost; only Tolmachev's drawings remain. The find was made by gold miners, not archaeol

chunks.heading: The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe: 01 A face in the peat
chunks.text: On 24 January 1890, gold miners digging through the Shigir peat bog, on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals, hit wood about four metres down. It came out in ten pieces. When the pieces were laid side by side, a face looked up at them: a long head with straight brows, a narrow nose and an open mouth, sitting on top of a flat plank covered in zigzags and more faces. Nobody knew what to make of it. There were no written records from the region before the Russians arrived, no known local tradition of giant carvings, and no way to date wood. It went to the museum in Yekaterinburg, where in 1914 the archaeologist Vladimir Tolmachev pieced together the fragments into a figure some 5.3 metres tall, about the height of a giraffe. Then the fragments he had used for the lower part went missing, and the idol, now shorter, stood in its case as a curiosity: very old, probably, but how old? For a century the Shigir Idol was a carved question mark: a monument without a date, a culture or a name. The answer, when it came, rearranged a textbook chapter. The wood turned out to be about 12,000 years old. The people who carved it did not farm, keep animals or live in towns. They probably hunted elk, fished and gathered in the forests at the very end of the Ice Age.

chunks.heading: The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe: 02 What the wood can tell us
chunks.text: The idol is cut from a single larch trunk. Counting the growth rings gives 159, so the tree was about a century and a half old when it came down. Under the microscope, the cut marks are sharp and flat, with no crushed fibres: the carvers worked the wood green, soon after felling, with a polished stone adze and two or three kinds of stone chisel. That detail matters, because it ties the date of the tree to the date of the carving. An elevation drawing on a height grid from 0 to 5 metres. On the left, a 1.7 metre person. In the middle, a narrow carved plank: the upper part, about 2.8 metres, is drawn solid with a carved head at the top, horizontal rib lines, zigzag bands and two smaller faces; the lower part is a dashed outline labelled as Tolmachev's 1914 reconstruction, whose fragments were later lost. A dimension line gives 5.3 metres for the reconstructed figure. On the right, a dashed T-shaped Göbekli Tepe central pillar from Enclosure D, about 5.5 metres tall, for comparison. Radiocarbon first reached the idol in 1997, and gave about 9,500 years. That was already startling. Then, in 2014, a Russian and German team led by Mikhail Zhilin, Svetlana Savchenko and Thomas Terberger took seven fresh samples for accelerator dating in two laboratories. The results fanned out, and the pattern explained itself. After the first dating, the sampling holes had been filled with wood powder mixed with butyl acrylate, and the whole sculpture had been soaked in the same resin to stop it cracking. Modern carbon in the resin makes wood look younger. The outer samples, most affected, gave the youngest ages; the innermost wood gave the oldest. The team published the early date in Antiquity in 2018 and refined it in Quaternary International in 2021, to about 12,000 years ago. Step 1 of 5.

chunks.heading: The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe: 03 The story it broke
chunks.text: For most of the twentieth century the story of civilisation ran in a neat order. First came farming, in the Fertile Crescent, around 11,000 years ago. Farming produced surplus, surplus produced villages and priests, and priests produced temples and monumental art. Hunter-gatherers, in this picture, were small bands with little time for anything grand. Göbekli Tepe, in south-eastern Turkey, began to crack that order in the 1990s: massive carved stone pillars raised by people who had not yet domesticated crops. Shigir cracks it from the other side of the map. If the new dates are right, a monumental carved figure stood in the Urals at, or a few centuries before, the first enclosures at Göbekli Tepe, about 11,500 years ago. The carvers lived nearly 3,000 kilometres to the north, in a forest, with no connection to the Near Eastern farming world. The mainstream has absorbed this without much fuss, and to its credit. Terberger and his colleagues present Shigir as evidence that Late Glacial foragers in Eurasia had complex ritual lives and a developed visual language. The zigzags and lines on the idol are common in Late Palaeolithic and early Mesolithic art, so the idol belongs to a long tradition rather than appearing from nowhere.

chunks.heading: The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe: 04 The challengers' reading
chunks.text: Readings of what the figure means are many, and most are honest guesses. Svetlana Savchenko, who has studied the idol for decades at the Sverdlovsk Regional Museum, has suggested it records a creation story in coded form. Others have read it as a map of the landscape. The Danish archaeologist Peter Vang Petersen has suggested it may have served as a warning to keep away from dangerous places. Stanislav Koksharov sees an 'X-ray' style of skeletal ancestral figures that echoes through later Ural art, and Vladimir Bobrov argues that the whole tradition grew in the taiga and lasted for thousands of years. Writers interested in lost Ice Age cultures push the pattern further. Two traditions of monumental human figures appear within a few centuries of each other, one in stone in Anatolia and one in wood in Siberia's western gateway. Both were made by foragers. Both appear as the Younger Dryas cold snap ends and the climate lurches warmer. Is that a coincidence, or a shared response to a world-changing event, or a sign of a wider, older symbolic world that we see only in the two places where it happened to survive? Stone lasts and wood rots. The real surprise of Shigir may be how much of the Ice Age world we have simply never seen. The evidence supports part of this. The timing is real, and so is the point about preservation. What is missing is any sign of contact: the materials, styles and motifs differ, and nothing links the Urals to Anatolia at that date. A shared climatic trigger is a testable idea; a single lost source remains a speculation.

chunks.heading: The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe: 05 What the bog has kept, and what it has eaten
chunks.text: The idol survived because it fell, or was placed, in water. In the airless peat of a bog, bacteria and fungi cannot break wood down, so a larch trunk can last twelve millennia. On dry ground it would have been gone in a century or two. That means the Shigir Idol is not evidence that such monuments were rare; it is evidence that they almost never survive. The lower third of the figure is known only from drawings, because the fragments were lost after 1914. The miners who found it recorded no layers, no associated objects and no exact position. Other wooden figures are known from the nearby Gorbunovo bog, but they are thousands of years younger, and the older landscape around Shigir has barely been explored. It is a reminder that absence of evidence in forests and wetlands says very little. How many carved poles stood on riverbanks across Ice Age Eurasia? We cannot count them, because the ground has kept almost none.

chunks.heading: The Shigir Idol: A Wooden Giant Older Than Göbekli Tepe: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The date itself can be tightened. The idol's 159 rings are a gift: by radiocarbon-dating several rings at known intervals and matching the series to the calibration curve, a method called wiggle-matching, the felling date could be fixed to within a few decades. More dates from independent laboratories, on the innermost wood, would test the 2021 result. The bigger questions need new finds. Cores and radar surveys of the Shigir and Gorbunovo bogs could reveal other structures, platforms or figures. Careful study of the idol's base could show whether it stood upright. And a systematic comparison of tools and motifs across early Holocene Eurasia would test the most intriguing idea of all: that the end of the Ice Age drove people in very different places to build their first monuments at the same time. For now, the verdict is simple. The evidence strongly supports a carving date around 12,000 years ago. What it meant to the people who raised it is still, in the best sense, open.

chunks.heading: Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors c. 2 billion years ago (Palaeoproterozoic) Established. Who, or what, ran nuclear reactors in Gabon two billion years ago? The claim on the scales The Oklo reactors were entirely natural, formed and run by geology and groundwater without any intelligent design. Weight of evidence Established Ruled out Established Several independent lines agree: the uranium-235 shortfall, fission-product isotopes, the xenon record of a water-driven cycle, the ore geometry and the known decay of uranium-235 through time, which made natural enrichment high enough only in the deep past. The mechanism was predicted in 1956 before anyone knew Oklo existed. No manufactured material has ever been found. The rarity of natural reactors is real, but it is explained by the narrow window of time and chemistry, not by design. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Where Oklo appears in textbooks and museum displays it is presented as a settled natural phenomenon, and here the confidence matches the evidence. If anything, textbooks undersell how strange and informative it is: it is one of the best natural tests we have of whether physics has changed over billions of years, and a real-world experiment in storing radioactive waste. What is solid In 1972 uranium ore from Oklo, Gabon, was found to be short of the fissile isotope uranium-235: 0.717% instead of the 0.720% found in ore everywhere else, and as low as about 0.44% in some samples. Meshik 2005; Gauthier-Lafaye et al. 1996 The ore also holds fission products such as neodymium, ruthenium and xenon isotopes in the proportions produced by splitting uranium, not in their natural proportions. Gauthier-Lafaye et al. 1996 At least 16 reactor zones are known in the Oklo, Okélobondo and Bangombé deposits of the Franceville basin, the only natural reactors yet found. Gauthier-Lafaye et al. 1996; Meshik 2005 Xenon trapped in phosphate grains records a cycle of about 30 minutes of fission followed by about 2.5 hours of shutdown, consistent with water acting as the moderator. Meshik, Hohenberg and Pravdivtseva 2004 Paul Kuroda had calculated in 1956 that a uranium deposit could go critical on its own under the right conditions, sixteen years before Oklo was found. Kuroda 1956 What is disputed Exactly how long each zone operated and at what power: recent isotope work suggests durations from about a quarter of a million to about two million years depending on the zone. How far some fission products, such as caesium and strontium, migrated after the reactors

chunks.heading: Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors: 01 The uranium that came up short
chunks.text: In May 1972, at the French uranium enrichment plant at Pierrelatte, a routine measurement did not add up. Natural uranium is almost entirely uranium-238, with a small, famously constant share of the fissile isotope uranium-235: about 0.720 percent, in ore from around the world and even in meteorites and Moon rock. A sample traced to the Oklo mine in Gabon held 0.717 percent. The difference sounds tiny. Across the shipments it meant that roughly 200 kilograms of uranium-235 appeared to be missing. For a nuclear agency, missing fissile uranium is an alarm bell. Had someone diverted it? Had the ore been contaminated with spent fuel? The French Atomic Energy Commission traced the anomaly back to the mine, and there it found something far stranger. Some ore was even more depleted, down to about 0.44 percent. And mixed in with it were the telltale products of nuclear fission. The uranium had not been stolen. It had already been burned, about 2 billion years before anyone was there to burn it. The uranium had not been stolen. It had already been burned, about 2 billion years before anyone was there to burn it.

chunks.heading: Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors: 02 A prediction nobody had tested
chunks.text: The idea was not entirely new. In 1956 the chemist Paul Kuroda, at the University of Arkansas, published a two-page note in the Journal of Chemical Physics asking whether a uranium deposit could ever sustain a chain reaction on its own. His answer was yes, if several conditions came together: a thick, rich ore body; enough uranium-235 in the mix; water to slow neutrons down so they split nuclei efficiently. Later work added a further condition: few neutron-absorbing elements, such as boron or some rare earths, to poison the reaction. The key was time. Uranium-235 decays faster than uranium-238, so the further back you go, the richer natural uranium becomes. Today it holds 0.72 percent uranium-235, too little for a natural reactor moderated by ordinary water. Two billion years ago it held about 3.7 percent, close to the 3 to 5 percent enrichment of fuel in many modern power reactors. Nature did not need to enrich anything. The clock had done it. A line chart. The horizontal axis runs from 2.5 billion years ago on the left to today on the right; the vertical axis shows the percentage of uranium-235 in natural uranium, from 0 to 6 percent. A curve falls from about 5.5 percent 2.5 billion years ago to 0.72 percent today. A shaded band between 3 and 5 percent marks typical modern reactor fuel. A marker at 2 billion years ago, at about 3.7 percent, is labelled Oklo reactors. A marker at today, 0.72 percent, is labelled too little for a water-moderated natural reactor.

chunks.heading: Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors: 03 How a rock became a reactor
chunks.text: The second ingredient was oxygen. Before about 2.4 billion years ago the air held almost none, and uranium stayed locked in insoluble minerals. Once photosynthesising microbes filled the atmosphere with oxygen, uranium could dissolve in water, travel, and then precipitate again where conditions changed, building rich seams in the sandstones of the Franceville basin. The reactors are, in a sense, a side effect of the planet learning to breathe. Where a seam was rich and thick enough, groundwater filling its pores acted as a moderator, exactly the role water plays in most power reactors today. The seam went critical. The reaction heated the rock, the water boiled away, the neutrons stayed too fast to split much uranium-235, and the reaction stopped. When the rock cooled and water seeped back, it started again. Step 1 of 4. Groundwater soaks a rich uranium seam and slows neutrons down. Groundwater soaks a rich uranium seam and slows neutrons down. The seam goes critical: a chain reaction runs for about 30 minutes, heating the rock. The heat boils the water away; without a moderator the reaction stops itself. After about 2.5 hours the rock cools, water returns and the cycle restarts. A schematic cross-section with pale sandstone on top, a dark uranium ore seam in the middle and older basement rock below. Step 1 shows groundwater flowing down into the ore seam. Step 2 shows a glowing orange lens in the seam, the reaction zone, with arrows for heat. Step 3 shows wavy dashed lines of steam rising as the water boils away and the reaction stops. Step 4 shows water seeping back in. A bar along the bottom shows one three-hour cycle: 30 minutes on in orange and about 2.5 hours off in blue, with a pointer showing where each step falls. In 2004 Alex Meshik and colleagues at Washingto

chunks.heading: Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors: 04 The case for something stranger
chunks.text: It is not surprising that Oklo became a favourite of ancient-astronaut websites and videos. A working nuclear reactor, two billion years old, sounds like the ultimate out-of-place artefact. The strongest version of the argument is not silly. A self-sustaining chain reaction is a narrow target: too little uranium-235 or too much neutron poison and nothing happens, too much and the system could run away. Humans reached it only in 1942, with Enrico Fermi's graphite pile in Chicago, after years of work. Oklo also regulated itself, which looks like engineering. And it is unique: no other natural reactor has been found anywhere. Those are fair observations, and they are exactly what the natural model has to explain. It does so well. The narrow target was hit because the uranium-235 fraction was high enough only in a limited window of Earth history, and rich uranium seams could only form after oxygen appeared, so the window was short and the places few. The self-regulation is simple physics: water moderates, heat removes water. Nothing in the reactor zones looks manufactured. The ore lies in its natural sedimentary layers, the reaction zones follow the shape of the seams, and the fuel was never processed. A designed reactor would leave more than a pattern of isotopes in ordinary rock. The self-regulation that looks like engineering is simple physics: water slows neutrons, and heat drives the water away. There is also the question of who. Two billion years ago life on Earth was microbial. Complex cells were only beginning to appear. An outside visitor cannot be excluded by any experiment, but nothing at Oklo requires one, and nothing points to one.

chunks.heading: Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors: 05 What a dead reactor teaches physics
chunks.text: Oklo's real surprise is how useful it has become. One isotope, samarium-149, swallows slow neutrons only at a very precise energy set by the strength of the electromagnetic force. In 1976 the Soviet physicist Alexander Shlyakhter realised that the amount of samarium-149 left at Oklo tests whether that force was the same two billion years ago. In 1996 Thibault Damour and Freeman Dyson reworked the analysis and found that the fine-structure constant, the number that measures the electromagnetic force, cannot have changed by more than about one part in ten million since the reactors ran. Oklo is one of the tightest natural checks that the laws of physics have held steady over billions of years. It is also a two-billion-year experiment in nuclear waste storage. Much of the plutonium and many fission products stayed within metres of where they formed, held by the surrounding clays and minerals, while more mobile elements escaped. A European research programme in the 1990s studied the site as a natural analogue for deep geological repositories. The lesson is encouraging but not a guarantee: Oklo's rocks, water and history are not those of any modern waste store.

chunks.heading: Oklo: The Two-Billion-Year-Old Nuclear Reactors: 06 Fresh work, lost rock and open questions
chunks.text: In February 2026 Hiroshi Hidaka, Alex Meshik and colleagues reviewed new isotope work on the reactors using modern mass spectrometry. They report that reactor zone 13 behaved differently from the others: uranium-235 supplied only about 75 percent of its fissions, against roughly 88 to 95 percent elsewhere, and it ran for about 240,000 years, while other zones operated for roughly 0.6 to 2.2 million years. The reactors were not identical machines, and each has its own history still being read. Time and industry have both taken their toll. Oklo was a working mine, and several reactor zones were dug out for their uranium before and after the discovery. Mining ended in the late 1990s. Other natural reactors may have existed in similar ore elsewhere, only to be eroded or reworked long ago. What remains open is mostly detail: how long each zone ran, how hot it became, and how the fission products moved afterwards. The central question, whether nature built these reactors, has a clear answer. What would change that answer? A manufactured object, a processed fuel or an engineered structure in the reactor zones would. Fifty years of drilling, sampling and isotope work have not found one. What they have found is arguably more wonderful: a planet that, for a brief window in its youth, could run its own nuclear reactors, and left the ashes where we could read them.

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library Library buried 79 CE; reading since 2023 Established. Can we read ancient books that would crumble if anyone tried to open them? The claim on the scales Machine learning applied to X-ray scans can recover readable text from unopened carbonised scrolls. Weight of evidence Established Ruled out Established Several independent lines agree. Different teams, working from the same scans with different models, reached the same letters and words. The recovered text reads as coherent Greek on subjects and in a style that fit Philodemus. The method was validated on fragments where ink can be seen directly. And results have grown steadily from a word in 2023 to a title in 2025 and a whole scroll in 2026. The open questions are about how much, how fast and how accurately, not whether. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Older reference works described the unopened Herculaneum rolls as practically unreadable, and many museum labels still do; on that, the textbooks are now behind the evidence. The opposite risk comes from headlines implying a lost ancient library has been read. So far a handful of scrolls have yielded text, much of it Epicurean philosophy, and every reading still needs human papyrologists. The reality is extraordinary, and narrower than the hype. What is solid About 1,800 papyrus rolls and fragments were recovered from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum from 1752, carbonised by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE. Sider 2005 Attempts to open the scrolls, including Antonio Piaggio's silk-thread unrolling machine from the 1750s, read many texts but damaged or destroyed many rolls. Sider 2005 In 2016 Brent Seales's team virtually unwrapped the charred En-Gedi scroll from CT scans and read a passage of Leviticus. Seales et al. 2016 In February 2024 the Vesuvius Challenge awarded its $700,000 Grand Prize for more than 2,000 characters read inside an unopened scroll, a previously unknown work attributed to Philodemus. Vesuvius Challenge 2024 In May 2025 the title of the unopened scroll PHerc. 172 was read: a work of Philodemus, On Vices, confirmed by papyrologists. Vesuvius Challenge 2025 In 2026 PHerc. 1667 became the first Herculaneum scroll virtually unwrapped and read end to end. Vesuvius Challenge 2026 What is disputed How far machine-learning ink detection can be trusted letter by letter, and how best to guard against a model producing letter-like shapes that are not there. Whether the Villa belonged to Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, Julius Caesar

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library: 01 A library of charcoal
chunks.text: In 1752 workmen tunnelling through hardened volcanic rock under the town of Ercolano broke into the rooms of a great Roman villa. Among the statues and bronzes they found blackened cylinders, some of which they took for lumps of charcoal and burned. Then someone noticed traces of writing. They had found a library, the only one to survive intact from the classical world, carbonised by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE. The Villa of the Papyri gave up about 1,800 rolls and fragments. The problem was obvious at once. The scrolls were fused, fragile lumps of carbon, and every attempt to open them destroyed part of what they held. The mystery was not who wrote them or where they came from. It was simpler and more painful: what is inside, and can anyone ever read it? The only surviving library of the ancient world was a shelf of books nobody could open.

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library: 02 Two centuries of opening and losing
chunks.text: The earliest efforts were brutal: rolls were sliced in half and the layers scraped away one by one, each copied before it was destroyed. In the 1750s the priest Antonio Piaggio built a machine that unrolled scrolls by gluing silk threads to the outer edge and turning a winch, a few millimetres at a time. It worked, slowly, and it read many texts. It also tore away the beginnings and often the ends of scrolls, where titles were written. What did come out was surprising. Most readable texts belong to Philodemus of Gadara, an Epicurean philosopher of the first century BCE who wrote on ethics, music, poetry and death; more than 40 of his works have been identified. There are books of Epicurus's own On Nature and fragments of the Stoic Chrysippus. The Villa's owner may have been Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, Julius Caesar's father-in-law and a patron of Philodemus, though that attribution remains a proposal. From 1999, multispectral imaging by Brigham Young University made opened fragments far more legible, because infrared light shows dark carbon ink against charred papyrus better than the eye can. But hundreds of rolls stayed closed, judged too fragile to risk.

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library: 03 Unwrapping without touching
chunks.text: The idea of reading a scroll without opening it came from Brent Seales, a computer scientist at the University of Kentucky, who spent two decades on it. The plan: scan the roll with X-ray computed tomography, like a medical CT but at far higher resolution, trace the papyrus surface as it spirals through the 3D volume, flatten it into an image, and find the ink. Step 1 of 5. Scan: X-ray computed tomography turns the roll into thousands of 3D slices. Scan: X-ray computed tomography turns the roll into thousands of 3D slices. Trace: software follows one sheet of papyrus round the spiral (segmentation). Flatten: the traced surface is unrolled into a flat image. Detect ink: a model trained on ink's 'crackle' texture shows letters. Read and check: papyrologists read the Greek and compare teams' results. Four panels in a row joined by arrows. Step 1: a dark scroll lies in an X-ray beam, drawn as moving dashed lines, labelled X-ray CT turns the roll into 3D slices. Step 2: a cross-section shows a tight spiral with one turn highlighted, labelled follow one sheet of papyrus round the spiral. Step 3: a flat rectangular sheet, labelled unroll the surface into a flat image. Step 4: the flat sheet with faint crack marks and the Greek word porphyras appearing in white, labelled machine learning spots the texture of dried ink. Step 5: a box below explains that papyrologists read and check the letters; the first word, found in October 2023, was porphyras, purple. In 2016 the method worked on a charred scroll from En-Gedi on the Dead Sea shore, revealing the opening verses of Leviticus. Herculaneum was harder. The En-Gedi ink contained metal, which shows up brightly in X-rays. Herculaneum's ink is mostly carbon, written on papyrus that is now also carbon, so the two look almost identical

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library: 04 The crowd cracks it
chunks.text: In March 2023 Seales teamed up with the investors Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross to launch the Vesuvius Challenge. They released high-resolution scans of scrolls from the Institut de France, made at the Diamond Light Source synchrotron in England, and offered prizes. Thousands joined. One of them, Casey Handmer, noticed a faint 'crackle' texture on the scanned papyrus that matched where ink should be: a physical signal a model could learn. In October 2023 Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old student at the University of Nebraska, trained a model on that texture and saw a word emerge: ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑϹ, porphyras, 'purple'. In February 2024 Farritor, Youssef Nader and Julian Schilliger won the $700,000 Grand Prize for more than 2,000 characters, about 5% of one scroll. Papyrologists found a previously unknown text, apparently by Philodemus, on pleasure, music and food. In May 2025 Marcel Roth and Micha Nowak of the University of Würzburg read the title of PHerc. 172, a still-rolled scroll in Oxford's Bodleian Library: Philodemus, On Vices. Sean Johnson of the Vesuvius Challenge found it independently, and papyrologists led by Federica Nicolardi confirmed it. It was the first title ever recovered noninvasively from a rolled Herculaneum scroll. In 2026 the team announced that PHerc. 1667, held in Naples, had been virtually unwrapped and read end to end. A word nobody had seen for almost two thousand years was 'purple'. The colour of kings, read by a student's software.

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library: 05 Can we trust a machine's letters?
chunks.text: The fair worry is obvious. Machine-learning models find patterns, and a model trained to see letters might see letters that are not there. The challenge answered this in three ways. Winning entries had to be reproducible from the public data. Independent teams, using different models, had to converge on the same readings, as happened with the title of PHerc. 172. And papyrologists judged whether the result made sense as Greek, in grammar, spelling and content. No model invents a coherent sentence of Epicurean philosophy in first-century Greek hand by accident. That is the strongest check of all, and it is why scholars who study these texts have accepted the readings, while still arguing, as they always have, over individual letters. It also matters what is being read. So far the recovered texts are philosophy, mostly Epicurean, which is what the opened scrolls led scholars to expect from this collection. That is not a disappointment. Each new passage fills gaps in how Greek thinkers argued about pleasure, virtue and the good life, and each confirmed reading makes the next one faster, because models improve with every letter that experts verify.

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library: 06 What is still buried
chunks.text: The Villa itself was never fully excavated. The eighteenth-century tunnellers followed walls underground and then left; excavations in the 1990s and 2000s exposed part of the building and showed it had lower levels, but much remains buried beneath volcanic deposits and the modern town. Some scholars hope more of the library lies there, perhaps including Latin literature. That hope is reasonable but untested: nobody knows what the unexplored rooms contain. The scrolls already found are a race against time and money. Each must be moved, scanned at a synchrotron and processed, and the carbonised rolls are fragile. By 2026 some 45 scrolls and fragments had been scanned for the challenge, a small share of those that remain unopened.

chunks.heading: The Herculaneum Scrolls: Reading a Burned Library: 07 What would settle the rest
chunks.text: The core claim is already settled: text can be read inside unopened scrolls. What remains is scale and accuracy. Scanning the remaining rolls, publishing images for independent checking, and blind tests on fragments whose text is known would measure the method's error rate. Reading a work that also survives in another copy would give a direct letter-by-letter check. And careful excavation of the Villa's unexplored levels could show whether the library of Herculaneum was larger than the shelves found in 1752. It is a rare thing for a mystery to end with the evidence itself speaking. Here, new tools are letting a burned library tell us what it held.

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain? Late Intermediate Period and Inca (c. 1000–1532 CE) Plausible. Who dug thousands of holes in rows on a Peruvian ridge, and why? The claim on the scales The holes of Monte Sierpe were laid out as a pre-Inca and Inca system for exchange and tribute accounting. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The reading is the first one based on systematic evidence: a full drone map with repeating counts, pollen of maize and basket plants inside the holes, a date in the fourteenth century, and a location between two Inca centres on trade routes. Rival uses find little support in the ground. But the accounting idea is an interpretation of patterns, supported by one date and a set of sediment samples, and the khipu parallel is suggestive rather than direct. It is the best current explanation, not yet a demonstrated one. Textbook confidence cautious Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks and museum labels have mostly said nothing, and popular guides called the band unexplained, which was fair. The risk now runs the other way: headlines in 2025 said the mystery was solved. The evidence supports a strong hypothesis with one date and a first set of pollen samples. A little more caution than the headlines, and more confidence than the old silence, would match the evidence. What is solid Monte Sierpe is a band of about 5,200 holes running some 1.5 km along a ridge in the Pisco Valley, 14–22 m wide; the holes are 1–2 m across and 0.5–1 m deep, many rimmed with stone. Bongers et al. 2025 The band was brought to wide attention by aerial photographs taken by the Shippee-Johnson expedition and published in 1933. Shippee 1933 Drone mapping divides the band into at least 60 sections, several with repeating counts, such as nine rows of eight holes. Bongers et al. 2025 Charcoal from one hole gave a radiocarbon date of 635 ± 15 BP, calibrated to about 1320–1405 CE. Bongers et al. 2025 Pollen from sediments in the holes includes maize and reed or bulrush types used for baskets. Bongers et al. 2025 The site lies between two Inca administrative centres, Tambo Colorado and Lima La Vieja, on routes linking coast and highlands. Bongers et al. 2025; Hyslop 1984 What is disputed Whether the numerical regularities in some sections reflect a counting design or are partly a product of which sections were picked out. Whether the band began as a marketplace and only later became an Inca tribute-counting device, or served one purpose throughout. How closely the layout really mirrors khipu structure, since no one

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?: 01 A serpent of holes
chunks.text: Fly over the dry foothills of the Pisco Valley, about 35 km inland from the Pacific, and a strange stripe crosses the ridges below. It looks like a line of pockmarks, or the track of some enormous creature, winding up and down the slopes for about a kilometre and a half. Up close it is a band of holes, each wide enough for a person to stand in, thousands upon thousands of them, set in rows as neatly as seats in a stadium. Local people call the place Monte Sierpe, serpent mountain, and it has also been known as Cerro Viruela, smallpox hill. The outside world noticed it in 1933, when aerial photographs from the Shippee-Johnson expedition were published. Then the questions began. Who dug some 5,200 holes in a desert with no water to spare? Why in rows? Why here? Nobody left an account. No Spanish chronicler described the site. The pits were empty. For ninety years the band was a message written in holes, with nobody left who could read it.

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The measured facts are now good. The band runs roughly north to south for about 1.5 km and is 14–22 m wide, averaging around 19 m. The holes are 1–2 m across and 0.5–1 m deep, and many have raised rims lined with stones. There are about 5,200 of them, a figure from a full drone survey, replacing older estimates of 5,000 to 6,000. What the drone survey revealed was structure. The band is not one continuous field of pits but at least 60 distinct sections, separated by gaps or changes in pattern. Some sections repeat numbers with striking regularity. One has nine consecutive rows of eight holes. Another has six rows of seven and a final row of eight, 50 holes in all. A third alternates rows of seven and eight for at least twelve rows. Top: a schematic ridge with a winding band of small dots running across it, labelled about 1.5 km long, about 5,200 holes and at least 60 sections; notes give the band as 14 to 22 metres wide and the holes as 1 to 2 metres across and half a metre to a metre deep. A small box on the band leads to two grids below. Section A shows nine rows of eight holes, 72 in all. Section B shows six rows of seven and one row of eight, 50 in all. On the right, a khipu is drawn as a main cord with four groups of hanging cords of 10, 11, 12 and 11 strings with knots, labelled 80 groups, most of 10, 11 or 12 cords. The location matters too. Monte Sierpe sits in the chaupiyunga, the transitional zone between coast and highlands, where routes carrying goods between the two met. It lies between two Inca administrative centres, Tambo Colorado and Lima La Vieja, and close to the heartland of the Chincha, one of the richest trading societies of the late pre-Hispanic Andes.

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?: 03 Every guess on the table
chunks.text: Before any systematic study, almost every idea was possible, and most were tried. Graves, perhaps looted long ago. Storage pits for crops. Defensive positions for slingers. Little gardens that trapped moisture. Devices for collecting water or fog. Mines. On television the band joined the catalogue of sites said to be beyond ordinary explanation. The challengers deserve credit for one thing: they refused to let a thin explanation pass. The early visitors, including Victor von Hagen on his 1953 survey of Inca roads and Dwight Wallace and Frederic Engel in the early 1970s, recorded the site but never settled it. Without dates, maps or tests of the soil, every interpretation was a guess, and calling the band a mystery was the honest position. The 2025 study tested these ideas against the ground. There are no fortifications or sling stones, which counts against defence. Very few human remains have turned up, which counts against a cemetery. There is no ore, which counts against mining. And in one of the driest places on Earth, rain and fog are too scarce for the holes to have made sense as water traps.

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?: 04 What the drones and the pollen found
chunks.text: In November 2025 Jacob Bongers and eleven colleagues published the first detailed study of Monte Sierpe in the journal Antiquity. They mapped the whole band with a drone, took 21 sediment samples from holes and identified at least 27 types of pollen, including maize in at least six samples, two of them from the centre of the site, and reeds or bulrushes of the kind woven into baskets. Charcoal from one hole gave a radiocarbon date of about 1320–1405 CE. The pollen is the quiet star of the study. Maize does not grow on a bare desert ridge, and neither do marsh reeds. Their pollen in the holes suggests that people brought plants there, most simply as goods: cobs of maize, and baskets or bundles woven from reeds. It is the first physical hint of what once filled the pits. The date places use of at least one hole in the fourteenth century, before the Inca took the region in the fifteenth. That fits the idea of a pre-Inca origin in the Late Intermediate Period, roughly 1000–1400 CE, followed by continued use under the Inca. One date, though, is a single point on what may be a long history.

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?: 05 A spreadsheet dug into the ground
chunks.text: Here is the reading the team proposes. In the Late Intermediate Period, the Chincha world was a hub of exchange. A Spanish document of the sixteenth century, studied by the historian María Rostworowski, describes Chincha as home to thousands of merchants. Perhaps, Bongers suggests, Monte Sierpe began as a kind of periodic market, a place where traders and farmers set out goods such as maize and cotton, each community in its own section, with the holes acting as standard measures. Step 1 of 5. Goods arrive: maize, cotton and other produce, carried in reed baskets (proposed). Goods arrive: maize, cotton and other produce, carried in reed baskets (proposed). Each group sets its goods in its own section, one hole per unit (proposed). Rows of 7 or 8 let officials or traders read totals at a glance (proposed). Under the Inca, totals could be knotted onto a khipu (proposed). What survives: maize and reed pollen in the soil of the holes, found in 2025. A cross-section through the ground shows a row of seven shallow holes with stone rims. Step 1: two people arrive carrying baskets. Step 2: baskets holding yellow cobs sit in five of the holes. Step 3: a bracket over the row reads five of seven holes filled in this row. Step 4: a knotted khipu cord appears at top right, labelled knot the totals. Step 5: small green dots in the soil of every hole represent pollen, labelled maize and basket-reed pollen found in 2025. After the Inca conquest, the same grid could have been turned to the empire's great concern: tribute. Inca administrators recorded quantities on khipu, bundles of knotted cords. A complex khipu found near Pisco, now in Berlin, has 80 groups of cords, most containing 10, 11 or 12 strings. That grouped structure resembles the band's sections of repeating rows. A section o

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?: 06 What time has taken
chunks.text: Whatever the holes held is gone. Goods were collected, baskets rotted, wind filled and emptied the pits for five centuries. The Spanish conquest broke the administrative system that might have used the band, and with it went the people who could have explained it. Most khipu were lost, and even the ones that survive can be read for numbers but only partly for meaning. That loss cuts both ways. It means the accounting reading will probably never be confirmed as directly as a written label would allow. It also means that the absence of other evidence, such as residues of specific goods, may reflect decay more than a different purpose.

chunks.heading: The Band of Holes: A Spreadsheet Dug Into a Mountain?: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The next steps are clear. Many more radiocarbon dates, from sections along the whole band, would show whether it was dug at once or grew over time. Full excavation of a sample of holes, with fine sieving for seeds, fibres and fragments, could show what was set down in them. A statistical test of all the sections, not only the tidiest, would show whether the counts are more regular than chance. And a close comparison of the Pisco khipu with the band could reveal whether their numbers match. For now, the band has moved from a riddle with no evidence to a hypothesis with some. That is real progress, and a good example of how drones and microscopes can make an old puzzle testable. It is not yet the last word.

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read Proto-Elamite c. 3100–2900 BCE to Rongorongo, before the 1860s Plausible. Do the Indus signs write a language, and could we ever read them? The claim on the scales The Indus signs encode a spoken language rather than a non-linguistic symbol system. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The signs behave like writing in several ways: consistent direction, positional rules, recurring sequences and use on seals and tags as in Mesopotamia. But the texts are very short, statistical tests have not separated writing from other symbol systems convincingly, and no decipherment has survived testing. The balance leans toward some kind of writing tied to language, which is why most specialists accept it, but the challengers' case is serious and the question remains open. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks and museum labels usually say simply that the Indus people had a writing system that has not been deciphered. That is probably right, but it hides a real debate: whether the signs spell out a language at all. Labels are somewhat overconfident here, and quieter than they should be about how little evidence there is to test any reading. What is solid About 4,000–5,000 Indus inscriptions are known, mostly on seals, dating mainly to c. 2600–1900 BCE; they average about five signs. Parpola 1994; Rao et al. 2009 Linear A, used on Crete c. 1800–1450 BCE, survives in about 1,400 inscriptions; sound values borrowed from Linear B can be read aloud, but the language is unknown. Salgarella 2020 About 26 Rongorongo objects survive; in 2024 the wood of one tablet was dated to c. 1493–1509 CE, before Europeans reached Rapa Nui in 1722. Ferrara et al. 2024 Linear Elamite, used in Iran c. 2300–1850 BCE, was largely deciphered in 2022 using royal names on silver beakers and a bilingual inscription. Desset et al. 2022 The Phaistos disc, found on Crete in 1908, carries 242 stamped signs of 45 types, and is the only object of its kind. Robinson 2002 What is disputed Whether the Indus signs record spoken language at all, or a non-linguistic system of emblems and administrative codes. What language family lay behind the Indus script: Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, Munda or a lost language. Whether Rongorongo was invented before European contact, and whether the 2024 wood date reflects the date of carving. How complete and secure the 2022 Linear Elamite decipherment is, given that key beakers lack recorded findspots. What time has hidden No bilingual text pairs the Indus script with a know

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read: 01 A unicorn and five silent signs
chunks.text: Pick up an Indus seal, a square of fired steatite a few centimetres across, and you meet a beautifully carved animal, often a one-horned bull the excavators nicknamed the unicorn. Above it runs a short line of signs: fish shapes, jars, strokes, a man with raised arms. Someone carved it more than 4,000 years ago in one of the great cities of the Indus Valley, Harappa or Mohenjo-daro, in a civilisation as large as Egypt or Mesopotamia. Its message is perfectly preserved. Nobody can read it. The Indus script is the most famous of a small club: writing systems whose signs we can see but whose words we cannot hear. Egypt and Mesopotamia speak to us in tens of thousands of documents. The Indus people, with their planned streets and drains, remain silent after a century of study. A civilisation that built cities for a thousand years left us thousands of messages and not a single sentence we can understand.

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read: 02 The unread shelf
chunks.text: The Indus script is not alone. Each member of the club is stuck for a different reason. Indus script (c. 2600–1900 BCE): about 4,000–5,000 inscriptions, averaging about five signs, with estimates of 400 to nearly 700 distinct signs. Linear A (Crete, c. 1800–1450 BCE): about 1,400 inscriptions. We can pronounce most of it, thanks to its descendant Linear B, and a few words such as ku-ro, 'total', are understood, but the Minoan language itself is unknown. Proto-Elamite (Iran, c. 3100–2900 BCE): more than a thousand clay accounts, mostly from Susa. The numbers are understood; the words are not. Rongorongo (Rapa Nui): about 26 wooden objects carrying more than 15,000 glyphs, first reported by a missionary in 1864. The Phaistos disc (Crete): a single clay disc 16 cm across, stamped with 242 signs of 45 types, found in 1908. A chart with a logarithmic horizontal axis of distinct signs from 10 to 1,000, shaded into three bands: alphabets at 20 to 40 signs, syllabaries at 40 to 100, and systems of word-signs plus sounds at hundreds of signs. Scripts we can read: the English alphabet at 26, the Cherokee syllabary at about 85, and Linear B at about 87 sound signs. Scripts unread or newly read: the Phaistos disc at 45 signs on one object; Linear Elamite at 80 to 110 in the 2022 decipherment; Linear A from about 90 core signs to over 300 with variants; and the Indus script from about 420 to 690 depending on who counts. The number of distinct signs is the first clue decipherers look for. An alphabet needs 20 to 40 letters, a syllabary 40 to 100, while systems mixing word signs and sound signs need hundreds. Linear A and the Phaistos disc look like syllabaries. The Indus count points to a mixed system, like cuneiform or Egyptian hieroglyphs, which is far harder to crack.

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read: 03 How a script falls
chunks.text: Every successful decipherment has needed some combination of three things: enough text, a known language, and an anchor, usually names or a bilingual. Egyptian hieroglyphs fell with the Rosetta Stone. Linear B fell in 1952 when Michael Ventris found that place names on the tablets read as Greek. Step 1 of 5. Collect every text and list the distinct signs. Collect every text and list the distinct signs. Spot repeated sign groups, often names or titles. Anchor sound values with names known from another script, ideally a bilingual. Test the values on other texts: they should produce words in a known language. The Indus script lacks a bilingual, known names, a known language and long texts. A silver beaker with a short inscription on the left. Step 1: three lines of schematic signs are listed, standing for collected texts. Step 2: the same three-sign group is boxed at the start of each line, suggesting a recurring name or title. Step 3: a card below says royal names known from cuneiform and a bilingual, with a note naming kings Shilhaha, Ebarat and Puzur-Sushinak; each sign in a name gets a sound value. Step 4: a new line of signs gets a tick, meaning the values yield Elamite words already known from cuneiform. Step 5: a panel shows five Indus-style signs with a large question mark: no bilingual, no known names, no known language, and texts averaging about five signs. In 2022 François Desset and colleagues published a decipherment of Linear Elamite, using royal names on silver beakers and a bilingual with Akkadian; many specialists welcomed it, though some beakers lack recorded findspots. In 2024 a radiocarbon study dated the wood of a Rongorongo tablet to about 1493–1509 CE, before European contact. In 2025 the longest Linear A text yet, about 119 signs on an ivory ring fr

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read: 04 Is the Indus script even writing?
chunks.text: In 2004 three scholars, Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel, published a paper with a deliberately provocative title, 'The collapse of the Indus-script thesis'. They argued that the signs were never writing in the linguistic sense but emblems: marks of clans, gods, offices and ritual. Their strongest point is hard to wave away. After excavations at hundreds of sites, there is still no long Indus text, no sentence-length inscription, nothing like the archives of Mesopotamia. The reply came with statistics. In 2009 Rajesh Rao and colleagues showed in Science that the way Indus signs follow one another resembles known languages more than random or rigidly ordered sequences. Sproat answered that some non-linguistic systems, such as Mesopotamian deity symbols, pass the same test. The statistical round ended roughly in a draw. A newer voice, the independent researcher Bahata Ansumali Mukhopadhyay, reads the seals as mostly logographic records of taxation, trade licences, commodity control and access control. On her view the signs carried meaning without spelling out spoken words, which would explain both their regularity and their brevity. Meanwhile, many claimed full decipherments into Sanskrit, Tamil or other languages have come and gone without surviving independent testing. The honest position is uncomfortable: the Indus signs probably relate to language, but nobody has shown how.

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read: 05 Can AI read the unreadable?
chunks.text: Machine learning is already changing epigraphy. DeepMind's Ithaca, published in Nature in 2022, restores missing letters in ancient Greek inscriptions and suggests their date and place of origin; historians working with it did markedly better than either the historians or the machine alone. Algorithms developed at MIT by Jiaming Luo, Regina Barzilay and colleagues have re-deciphered Ugaritic and Linear B automatically, by matching them to a known related language, and have since been tried on harder cases such as Iberian. That last condition is the catch. These methods work when the underlying language, or a close relative, is known and when there is enough text. For Linear A and the Indus script neither is true. AI can sort signs, spot patterns, and test thousands of hypotheses a scholar could never check by hand, and open databases such as SigLA for Linear A make that possible. But no algorithm can invent a bilingual. The bottleneck is not computing power; it is evidence in the ground.

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read: 06 What time erased
chunks.text: Writing survives by accident. Linear A and Linear B tablets were unbaked clay, preserved because the palaces that stored them burned. If the Indus people also wrote on palm leaves, cloth, bark or wood, as later South Asian scribes did, all of it has rotted, and the seals may be just the durable tip of a literate world. On Rapa Nui, the loss was human: Peruvian slave raids in 1862 and the epidemics that followed killed much of the population, probably including the people who could read the tablets. By the time scholars asked, the knowledge was gone or garbled.

chunks.heading: Lost Scripts: The Writing Nobody Can Read: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: One lucky find could change everything. Indus seals travelled to Mesopotamia and the Gulf, where scribes wrote in cuneiform, so a bilingual tag or seal is not impossible. A single long text, or an archive of tablets from one building, would give decipherers the volume they need. Open, complete corpora would let both human and machine test every proposal honestly. Until then the verdict is plausible, not established: the Indus signs probably encode language in some form, but the case is unproven and the challengers deserve a hearing. The strangeness is part of the story. Five thousand years after these people wrote, their words are in our museums and still out of reach.

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense? Early 15th century (vellum radiocarbon dated 1404–1438) Open question. Does the Voynich script hide a real language, or nothing at all? The claim on the scales The Voynich text encodes a real language rather than meaningless writing. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established There is real evidence on both sides. The text follows Zipf's law, its keywords cluster by section and match the pictures, and Bowern and Lindemann found no argument for gibberish persuasive. But its character entropy is far below any known language, words repeat in odd runs, and experiments show that people writing deliberate nonsense also produce structured, language-like text. After more than a century, no reading has survived independent testing. The question is genuinely open. Textbook confidence cautious Openly unsure Settled fact The Beinecke Library and scholarly surveys describe the text honestly as undeciphered and of unknown meaning, and that caution matches the evidence. The overconfidence lives elsewhere: headlines announcing that the manuscript has been 'solved' appear every few years, and none of those solutions has survived review by specialists. What is solid Four samples of the vellum, cut from four pages, were radiocarbon dated at the University of Arizona in 2009 to 1404–1438. Hodgins, University of Arizona 2011 release The book has about 240 surviving pages and roughly 38,000 words written in a script known from no other document, with about 20–25 common characters. Beinecke MS 408; Bowern and Lindemann 2021 It was in Prague by the early 1600s: the name of Rudolf II's chemist Jacobus Hořčický de Tepenec appears on the first page, and letters of 1639 and 1665/66 send it towards Athanasius Kircher in Rome. Beinecke; Davis 2024 Inks and paints are iron-gall ink and inexpensive mineral pigments consistent with a medieval or Renaissance workshop. McCrone Associates analysis, 2009 The text follows strong rules: words built from ordered slots, two statistical 'dialects' (Currier A and B) and at least five scribal hands. Currier 1976; Davis 2020 What is disputed Whether the text records a natural language, a cipher of one, an invented language, or meaningless but structured writing. Whether the very low character entropy rules out an ordinary alphabet for a known language. Where and by whom it was made; the zodiac month names in Latin letters, in a Romance dialect, may be a later addition. Whether the text was written soon after the vellum was prepared, or decades later on old sto

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?: 01 A book nobody can read
chunks.text: Open it anywhere and the strangeness starts. Plants that match no species a botanist can name, with roots like bulbs and leaves like fans. Wheels of stars and tiny naked women holding them. Women bathing in green pools joined by tubes that look like plumbing, or intestines. Rosettes, jars and short paragraphs marked with stars. And on every page, neat, flowing lines in an alphabet found in no other document on Earth. This is Beinecke MS 408 at Yale, named after Wilfrid Voynich, the book dealer who bought it in 1912 from the Jesuits at the Villa Mondragone near Rome. About 240 pages survive, carrying roughly 38,000 words. The greatest codebreakers of the 20th century, including William and Elizebeth Friedman's circle and the British cryptanalyst John Tiltman, tried and failed to read it. The oldest question about the Voynich is not what it says. It is whether it says anything at all.

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?: 02 What is solid: an old book with a real history
chunks.text: Whatever the text is, the object is genuine. In 2009 Greg Hodgins of the University of Arizona cut four slivers, each about 1 by 6 millimetres, from four pages and radiocarbon dated them. The calfskin was prepared between 1404 and 1438, about a century earlier than many had assumed. McCrone Associates analysed the inks and paints and found iron-gall ink and cheap mineral pigments, nothing a medieval workshop could not supply. Step 1 of 5. The calfskin for the pages is prepared between 1404 and 1438; then 160 years without a record. The calfskin for the pages is prepared between 1404 and 1438; then 160 years without a record. By about 1600 the book is in Prague, at the court of Rudolf II. 1639 and 1665/66: Prague scholars ask Athanasius Kircher in Rome to read it, then send it to him. 1912: Voynich buys it from the Jesuits; 1969: it reaches Yale. 2009–2025: radiocarbon dating, multispectral images, scribe studies and new cipher experiments. A horizontal timeline from 1400 to 2030. Step 1: a band at 1404 to 1438 marks when the calfskin was prepared, by radiocarbon dating of four samples in 2009, followed by a dashed line labelled owners unknown until about 1600. Step 2: Prague around 1600, where Rudolf II reportedly paid 600 ducats, and the name of his chemist Hořčický on the first page. Step 3: 1639, Georg Baresch writes to Athanasius Kircher, and 1665 or 1666, Marci sends the book to Kircher. Step 4: 1912, Wilfrid Voynich buys it from the Jesuits, and 1969, it is given to Yale's Beinecke Library. Step 5: 2009 to 2025, scientific study: radiocarbon dating, multispectral imaging, scribe analysis and cipher experiments. The book's paper trail begins in Prague around 1600. A later letter from the physician Johannes Marcus Marci reports hearsay that Emperor Rudolf II paid 60

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?: 03 Writing that behaves like language
chunks.text: Counted by computer, the text shows several habits of real language. Its word frequencies follow Zipf's law: the commonest word appears about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third. In 1976 the cryptologist Prescott Currier showed that it comes in two statistical 'dialects', A and B, and in 2020 Davis identified at least five scribes whose hands change between sections, never within them. A horizontal strip divided in proportion to page counts. Herbal, 126 pages, languages A and B; Astronomical, 17 pages, mostly labels; Balneological, 20 pages, language B; Cosmological, 14 pages, mostly labels; Pharmaceutical, 16 pages, language A; Recipes, 25 pages, language B. A note explains that Currier A and B are two statistical dialects identified in 1976 and that about 8 text-only pages and about 28 missing pages are not shown. In 2013 the physicists Marcelo Montemurro and Damián Zanette went further. They measured which words cluster in particular parts of the book and found keyword networks that line up with the pictures: the herbal and pharmaceutical sections, both about plants, share vocabulary more than either shares with the bathing pages. 'The accumulated evidence about organization at different levels', they wrote, 'limits severely the scope of the hoax hypothesis and suggests the presence of a genuine linguistic structure.'

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?: 04 And not like any language we know
chunks.text: Yet the same statistics are deeply odd. Voynich words are assembled from a small kit of parts in a fixed order, like beads on a string, and nearly all are between 2 and 10 characters long. Some characters appear only at the start of a paragraph or the end of a line. The same word can appear two, three or more times in a row, and neighbouring words often differ by a single letter. A bar chart with an axis from 0 to 4 bits. A shaded band from 3 to 4 bits is labelled natural languages. Voynich A has a bar reaching 2.17 and Voynich B a bar reaching 2.01, both well to the left of the band, meaning each Voynich character is much more predictable from the one before it. The most striking number is entropy, a measure of how predictable the next character is. In Claire Bowern and Luke Lindemann's 2021 review, Voynich A scores 2.17 bits and Voynich B 2.01, well below the roughly 3–4 bits of every natural language in their sample. That rules out a simple letter-for-letter code of Latin, German or Italian. It leaves room for a syllable-based script, a heavily abbreviated one, a verbose cipher that turns each letter into several symbols, or no language at all.

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?: 05 The case for beautiful nonsense
chunks.text: In 2004 the psychologist Gordon Rugg showed that a Renaissance forger could have generated Voynich-like words by sliding a card with holes (a Cardan grille) over a table of syllables. In 2020 Torsten Timm and Andreas Schinner went further with a 'self-citation' method: a scribe copies earlier words with small changes, and the result reproduces the repeats, the near-duplicate neighbours and the Zipf curve. In 2022 Daniel Gaskell and Claire Bowern asked volunteers to write pages of meaningless text by hand. Their gibberish was far from random, with its own repeated units and structure. The hoax idea has problems of its own. A forger would need 15th-century vellum, a consistent invented script, five cooperating scribes and hundreds of detailed paintings, all to deceive a buyer, and Rugg's grille does not explain why vocabulary tracks the pictures. Bowern and Lindemann concluded that they were 'not persuaded by any of the arguments in favor of the Voynich text being gibberish'. The hoax has not been ruled out; it has not been shown either.

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?: 06 A graveyard of solutions
chunks.text: Few objects have attracted so many announced decipherments. In 1921 William Newbold claimed to find microscopic Greek shorthand in the pen strokes, crediting Roger Bacon; the 'shorthand' turned out to be cracks in the ink. Since then readers have proposed Ukrainian, Old Turkic, Hebrew, Latin abbreviations and more. In 2019 Gerard Cheshire announced in Romance Studies that the book was written in a lost 'proto-Romance' language; specialists found his readings circular, and the University of Bristol distanced itself from the claim. Some attempts were more cautious. The linguist Stephen Bax proposed in 2014 that a few plant labels could be read as names such as 'centaury', offering them as a starting point rather than a solution. The pattern repeats: a hypothesis picks a language, the letters are matched until words appear, and the matching is too flexible to fail. (Scripts that really were cracked, like Linear B, are discussed in the lost-scripts case.) A true decipherment does not just find words. It reads the next page correctly before anyone has looked. The most interesting recent work is not a solution at all. In 2025 the science journalist Michael Greshko published the Naibbe cipher in Cryptologia: a scheme using dice and a deck of playing cards, both available in 15th-century Italy, that turns Latin or Italian into Voynich-like text following the manuscript's word grammar. Greshko does not claim this is how the book was made. He shows that a meaningful cipher could have produced text this strange.

chunks.heading: The Voynich Manuscript: Language or Beautiful Nonsense?: 07 What time has hidden, and what would settle it
chunks.text: Time has taken a lot. About 28 pages are missing, possibly including any title page or opening that named the author. The book's first 160 years are blank. And no other document in the script has turned up, although countless archives in Central Europe and Italy have never been fully catalogued. A decipherment that makes testable predictions on unread pages and matches the pictures. A key, a draft or a second text in the script, found in an archive. A date for the ink itself, to tie the writing to the vellum. Tests that reliably separate structured gibberish from ciphered language in texts this size. Until then the Voynich Manuscript is one of the rare mysteries where the object is firmly dated and fully visible, yet its central question remains as open as it was when Baresch first wrote for help in 1639.

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age Late Bronze Age collapse, c. 1200–1150 BCE Mixed record. Did the invading Sea Peoples bring down the Bronze Age world? The claim on the scales Invading Sea Peoples were the main cause of the collapse of the Late Bronze Age world around 1200–1150 BCE. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established Parts of the claim are well supported: named sea-borne groups attacked Egypt twice, some cities show violent destruction at the right time, and ancient DNA shows newcomers settling at Ashkelon.
