But drought is independently dated to the same decades, several centres were abandoned rather than stormed, some destructions have no sign of outside attackers, and Carchemish survived despite Egypt's claim. The Sea Peoples were a real force within the collapse; the evidence does not support them as its main cause. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact For much of the twentieth century, textbooks and documentaries told the collapse as an invasion, taking Ramesses III's inscription largely at face value. Specialists have since moved to a many-causes, systems-collapse account, and popular books such as Eric Cline's 1177 B.C. brought that to the public. The newer story is better supported, but it too can sound neater than the scattered, loosely dated evidence allows. What is solid Between about 1225 and 1150 BCE, many palace centres of the eastern Mediterranean were destroyed or abandoned, including Pylos and Mycenae in Greece, the Hittite capital Hattusa and the port-city of Ugarit in Syria. Cline 2014; Knapp and Manning 2016 Egyptian texts name groups from the sea: Merneptah fought Sherden, Shekelesh, Ekwesh, Lukka and Teresh alongside Libyans in his Year 5 (c. 1208 BCE); Ramesses III lists Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh in his Year 8. Wilson in Pritchard 1969; Cline 2014 Radiocarbon dates from the destruction layer at Tell Tweini, a harbour town of the kingdom of Ugarit, place its fall at about 1192–1190 BCE. Kaniewski et al. 2011 Tree rings from Gordion in central Anatolia record an unusually severe three-year drought around 1198–1196 BCE (±3 years), coinciding with the end of the Hittite empire. Manning et al. 2023 Pollen from the Sea of Galilee and from Cyprus shows a marked dry period around the end of the Late Bronze Age, driest roughly 1250–1100 BCE in the southern Levant. Langgut et al. 2013; Kaniewski et al. 2013 Early Iron Age burials at Ashkelon, a Philistine city, show a new European-related genetic component that is absent in the Bronze Age people b

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age: 01 The year the lights went out
chunks.text: Carved on the walls of Ramesses III's mortuary temple at Medinet Habu, across the Nile from Luxor, is one of the most dramatic war reports of the ancient world. It tells of enemies who came from the sea and the islands, who overran one kingdom after another, and who were finally beaten on Egypt's own borders. The foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands. All at once the lands were removed and scattered in the fray. No land could stand before their arms, from Hatti, Qode, Carchemish, Arzawa and Alashiya on, being cut off at one time. Around 1200 BCE, something very like that did happen. Within a few decades, the Mycenaean palaces of Greece, the Hittite empire of Anatolia and rich port-cities such as Ugarit on the Syrian coast were destroyed or abandoned. Writing disappeared from Greece for centuries. When Michael Button sat down with Joe Rogan in August 2025, he used this moment as his prime example of how fast a sophisticated, connected world can fall. Egypt gave the collapse a villain. The harder question is whether the villain was the cause.

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The Egyptian records are specific. In his Year 5, about 1208 BCE, the pharaoh Merneptah defeated a Libyan invasion that included Sherden, Shekelesh, Ekwesh, Lukka and Teresh, people 'of the sea'. About thirty years later, in his Year 8, about 1177 BCE on Eric Cline's dating, Ramesses III fought a coalition of Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh in battles on land and in the Nile mouths. The reliefs at Medinet Habu show warriors with horned helmets and with tall headdresses, ships with bird-headed prows, and ox-carts carrying women and children. The archives of Ugarit add a view from the victims' side. In one surviving letter, the last king, Ammurapi, wrote to the king of Alashiya, on Cyprus, that enemy ships had come, that his towns had been burned, and that his own troops and ships were away. At Tell Tweini, a harbour town of the same kingdom, radiocarbon dates from the destruction layer point to about 1192–1190 BCE, and the layer held bronze arrowheads. The name 'Sea Peoples' is modern. The French Egyptologist Gaston Maspero coined it in 1881. Of the groups, only one is securely identified: the Peleset are the Philistines, who settled on the southern coast of Canaan in cities such as Ashkelon and Ashdod.

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age: 03 The case for the invaders
chunks.text: The invasion story has real strengths. It is what the people who lived through the crisis said happened, under two pharaohs and in the letters of a Syrian king. Destruction layers at several sites show fire and fighting. And in 2019, ancient DNA from Ashkelon added hard evidence: people buried there in the early Iron Age carried a European-related genetic component absent in the Bronze Age population before them, and it faded within a few centuries as the newcomers mixed with locals. Robert Drews argued in 1993 that a military revolution explains the speed of the collapse: the palace kingdoms relied on expensive chariot armies, and swarms of infantry with javelins and long swords learned to beat them. Eberhard Zangger argues that the Luwian-speaking states of western Anatolia formed the backbone of the Sea Peoples in a region-wide war. Both take the Egyptian texts seriously as history, not just propaganda. Step 1 of 5. c. 1250 BCE: palace states from Greece to Egypt are tied together by trade. c. 1250 BCE: palace states from Greece to Egypt are tied together by trade. Drought: tree rings, lake pollen and salt-lake cores all record a dry crisis around 1200 BCE. Destruction and abandonment: Greek palaces, Hattusa and Ugarit fall; Carchemish survives. The Sea Peoples reach Egypt: c. 1208 BCE under Merneptah, c. 1177 BCE under Ramesses III. Aftermath: the Peleset become the Philistines of Ashkelon, with new DNA to match. A latitude and longitude grid of the eastern Mediterranean from 19 to 41 degrees east and 42 to 25 degrees north, without coastlines. Step 1: palace centres at Mycenae, Pylos, Hattusa, Ugarit, Carchemish, Cyprus and Egypt, linked by moving trade lines. Step 2: drought markers at Gordion (tree rings, 1198 to 1196 BCE), Larnaca on Cyprus (a long dry spell fro

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age: 04 Drought, earthquakes and a brittle system
chunks.text: The strongest challenge to the invasion story comes from the environment. A sediment core from the Sea of Galilee, studied by Dafna Langgut, Israel Finkelstein and Thomas Litt, shows the driest phase of the Bronze and Iron Ages at roughly 1250–1100 BCE. Pollen from Larnaca Salt Lake on Cyprus shows a long dry spell beginning around 1200 BCE. Then, in 2023, Sturt Manning and colleagues dated juniper timbers from Gordion in central Anatolia ring by ring and found an unusually severe three-year drought around 1198–1196 BCE, just when the Hittite empire fell. Manning's team measured both ring widths and carbon isotopes in the Gordion timbers. Between 1270 and 1135 BCE, only one interval had three consecutive years in the driest 6.25 percent of values, pointing to serious harvest failure. The team did not argue that drought alone ended the empire. They argued that it was the kind of shock a grain-dependent state could not absorb, especially if other things were going wrong at the same time. Other stresses pile on. The geophysicist Amos Nur and Eric Cline proposed in 2000 that an 'earthquake storm', a run of large quakes over several decades, damaged many centres. Excavations at Hattusa suggest the capital was largely emptied before it burned. Carchemish, which Ramesses III lists among the lands cut off, survived as a kingdom. In this reading, which Cline set out for a general audience in 1177 B.C. (2014), the palace world was a web of mutual dependence, and once drought, quakes, revolts and raids arrived together, the web tore.

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age: 05 Who were they?
chunks.text: Beyond the Philistines, identifications rest mostly on similar-sounding names. The Sherden are often linked with Sardinia, the Shekelesh with Sicily, the Denyen with Homer's Danaans or with Adana in Cilicia, and the Lukka with Lycia in south-west Anatolia. Some of them were not strangers at all: Sherden warriors had served as bodyguards and mercenaries of Ramesses II generations earlier. That points to a picture more human than a tidal wave. Some Sea Peoples were probably raiders, some refugees fleeing famine, some soldiers of fortune already part of the system, and some settlers looking for land. When the palaces that employed and fed them failed, they moved. The Sea Peoples may have been as much the shipwrecked survivors of the collapse as its authors.

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age: 06 What time has hidden
chunks.text: Almost everything we know about the Sea Peoples comes from their enemies. Egyptian royal texts turn every war into a triumph over chaos. The newcomers left no texts of their own. Their ships, probably built of wood and pegged together, have not been found. Many destruction layers were dug decades ago, before modern radiocarbon methods, so we cannot always tell whether two cities burned in the same year or fifty years apart. That uncertainty makes 'one great invasion' and 'a slow, spreading failure' hard to separate. The 2023 Gordion tree-ring study gave the Hittite collapse a dated climatic shock for the first time, and in 2024 Eric Cline's After 1177 B.C. turned attention to how different societies survived, from Cyprus and Phoenicia, which adapted and thrived, to Greece, which lost writing. The research question is shifting from 'who destroyed the Bronze Age?' to 'why did some places recover and others not?'

chunks.heading: The Sea Peoples and the End of the Bronze Age: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The test is timing and origin. Tight radiocarbon series for each destruction would show whether the fires came in one wave or over decades, and whether they followed the drought or preceded it. Ancient DNA from Sardinia, Sicily, Cyprus and western Anatolia could show where the newcomers at Ashkelon came from. A Sea Peoples shipwreck would tell us more about them in a season than a century of reading Egyptian inscriptions. For now, the fairest verdict is the one many specialists have reached: the Sea Peoples were real, they fought, and some of them settled and founded new cities. But they sailed into a world that was already failing, and they were one of its many causes, not the single hand that brought it down.

chunks.heading: The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven?
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven? Early Bronze Age (Únětice culture), buried c. 1600 BCE Strong evidence. Is the Nebra sky disc really 3,600 years old, and what did it know? The claim on the scales The Nebra sky disc is an Early Bronze Age object, buried around 1600 BCE. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Several independent lines agree: the soil at the find spot matches the disc, the metal sources fit the Early Bronze Age, the tin and lead isotopes match other objects of that time, and the hoard's organic material dates to about 1600 BCE. The weak point is real: nobody recorded the disc in place, and its date is borrowed from the hoard. Gebhard and Krause raised fair questions, but the answers published since leave the Iron Age date much less likely. Textbook confidence presented as settled fact Openly unsure Settled fact Museum labels and guidebooks state '3,600 years old' as a plain fact. The evidence strongly supports that date, so the label is almost right. What it leaves out is the looting: the date depends on association with the hoard and on scientific matching, not on excavation. A small 'probably' would make the label honest without making it less astonishing. What is solid The disc is bronze, about 32 cm across and about 2 kg, inlaid with gold: a sun or full Moon, a crescent, 32 stars, two horizon arcs (one now lost) and a curved 'boat'. Meller 2004; Pernicka et al. 2020 It was dug up illegally in 1999 on the Mittelberg near Nebra and recovered in a police sting in Basel in February 2002. Meller & Michel 2018 Excavation at the looters' hole found their pickaxe marks and raised gold and copper levels in the soil, and the soil matched sediment stuck to the objects. Pernicka et al. 2020 The copper comes from the Mitterberg area of the Austrian Alps and the gold from Cornwall, sources worked in the Early Bronze Age. Ehser et al. 2011; Pernicka et al. 2020 Birch bark on a sword found with it gives a radiocarbon date of about 1600–1560 BCE. Pernicka et al. 2020 What is disputed Whether the disc really belongs with the swords and axes that date it, or was added to the hoard from elsewhere. Whether the seven-star cluster and the crescent encode a calendar rule for adding a leap month. How long the disc was in use before burial, and who owned it. What time has hidden The disc was ripped out of the ground by looters, so its exact position and layer were never recorded by archaeologists. The left horizon arc was removed or lost in antiquity. The disc itself contains no organic material, so it can

chunks.heading: The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven?: 01 A night dig and a hotel sting
chunks.text: In July 1999, two men with metal detectors climbed the Mittelberg, a wooded hill near the small town of Nebra in eastern Germany. They were digging illegally. Their detectors sang, and with a pickaxe they pulled out a hoard: two bronze swords, two axes, a chisel, spiral arm rings, and a crusty green disc the size of a dinner plate, spangled with gold. The pickaxe gouged the disc. They soon sold the lot for 31,000 Deutsche Marks. For almost three years the disc moved through the black market. Then, in February 2002, Harald Meller, the state archaeologist of Saxony-Anhalt, posed as a buyer in a hotel in Basel, Switzerland, with a price of 700,000 marks on the table. Swiss police burst in. The disc was saved, and the looters later led investigators to the hole they had dug. It is often called the oldest concrete picture of the sky ever found, and it spent its first years back in daylight as stolen goods. Cleaned, the disc was astonishing: a blue-green bronze sky with a golden sun or full Moon, a crescent Moon, a scatter of stars, and a tight cluster of seven that looked like the Pleiades. Along the rim ran golden arcs. Below, a curved band like a boat. Nothing like it had ever been found from prehistoric Europe.

chunks.heading: The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven?: 02 A sky built in stages
chunks.text: The disc was not made in one go. It was changed several times, and each change tells a story. First came the sun or full Moon, the crescent and 32 stars. Later, someone added two golden arcs on opposite sides of the rim, covering or moving two stars to make room. Later still came the boat. Then the rim was pierced with 38–40 small holes, perhaps to fix it to something. By the time it went into the ground, one of the arcs had been torn away. Step 1 of 5. The first sky: sun or full Moon, crescent and 32 stars, including a cluster of seven. The first sky: sun or full Moon, crescent and 32 stars, including a cluster of seven. Two gold horizon arcs are added; two stars are covered or moved. A curved gold 'boat' is added at the bottom. The rim is pierced with 38–40 small holes. One arc is lost; the disc is buried c. 1600 BCE with swords, axes, a chisel and arm rings. A round green bronze disc about 32 centimetres across with a 10 centimetre scale bar. Step 1: gold sun or full Moon, crescent and 32 stars, including a tight cluster of seven usually read as the Pleiades. Step 2: two gold horizon arcs are added on the left and right edges, each spanning about 82 degrees of the rim. Step 3: a curved gold boat with feathered lines is added at the bottom. Step 4: the rim is pierced with a ring of small holes, 38 to 40 in the original. Step 5: the left arc is shown dashed, lost before the disc was buried around 1600 BCE with two swords, two axes, a chisel and spiral arm rings. The gold of the later additions differs chemically from the gold of the first stars, so the pieces were not added at the same time. The metal of the disc points to copper from the Mitterberg in the Austrian Alps and gold from the River Carnon in Cornwall, sources worked in the Early Bronze Age. The bronze was o

chunks.heading: The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven?: 03 What the arcs knew
chunks.text: The most remarkable thing about the disc is not the stars but the arcs. Each spans about 82 degrees. At the latitude of the Mittelberg, the sun rises in the north-east at midsummer and in the south-east at midwinter; the angle between those two points on the horizon is roughly 81–82 degrees. The same angle separates the midsummer and midwinter sunsets. The arcs seem to encode the sun's yearly swing along the horizon, measured at this place. Left: the disc with its surviving right arc; two accent lines from the centre to the ends of the arc mark an angle of 82 degrees, with a 10 centimetre scale bar. Right: a plan of the horizon seen from the Mittelberg, north at the top. On the eastern side, gold dots mark the summer solstice sunrise in the north-east and the winter solstice sunrise in the south-east, joined by an accent arc labelled about 81 degrees. On the western side, the winter solstice sunset in the south-west and summer solstice sunset in the north-west are joined by a matching arc. A small mountain symbol in the north-west marks the Brocken, about 85 kilometres away, behind which the midsummer sun sets. The hill itself adds to the effect. Seen from the Mittelberg, the midsummer sun sets behind the Brocken, the highest peak of the Harz mountains, some 85 kilometres to the north-west. The astronomer Wolfhard Schlosser, who studied the disc early on, argued that the hilltop could have served as a natural observatory. A bolder reading comes from the astronomer Rahlf Hansen. He noticed that the crescent beside the Pleiades is thick, a Moon several days old. In a rule later written down in Babylonian astronomy, when a thick crescent appears beside the Pleiades in spring, a leap month should be added to keep the lunar year in step with the sun. If Hansen is right, some

chunks.heading: The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven?: 04 The challengers: a disc a thousand years younger?
chunks.text: In September 2020, two respected archaeologists, Rupert Gebhard of the Bavarian State Archaeological Collection in Munich and Rüdiger Krause of Goethe University Frankfurt, published a sharp critique. The find circumstances, they argued, had not been described accurately. The disc could not be shown to belong with the swords and axes that date it. And its style and symbols, they suggested, fit the Iron Age better, perhaps a thousand years later. If they were right, the Bronze Age astronomer would vanish. Their strongest point is simple and fair. No archaeologist saw the disc in the ground. The only eyewitnesses were looters, and the date rests on the objects buried with it, not on the disc itself. Earlier, at the looters' appeal in 2005, a defence expert had even argued the disc was a modern forgery; the court was not persuaded. The reply came fast. A thirteen-member team led by Ernst Pernicka set out the case in Archaeologia Austriaca. The looters' pickaxe marks, a discarded water bottle and raised gold and copper concentrations were found at the spot they described. Soil stuck to the disc matched the soil from the hole. The tin and lead isotopes of the whole hoard match other Early Bronze Age objects, and the boat motif belongs to the Bronze Age, not the Iron Age. Gebhard and Krause replied again in 2021, but most specialists have sided with the Early Bronze Age date.

chunks.heading: The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven?: 05 What the looters destroyed
chunks.text: The worst damage was not the pickaxe gouge. By digging at night, the looters destroyed the context: the exact layer, the arrangement of the objects, any organic remains that might have dated the disc directly, and any traces of how it was placed. Much of the debate since 2020 exists because that information is gone for ever. A single hour of careful excavation in 1999 would have answered questions that experts still argue over. The disc also stands alone. No other Bronze Age object like it has been found, which makes comparison hard. That does not make it suspicious, since unique objects exist in every period, but it does mean each interpretation rests on one piece.

chunks.heading: The Nebra Sky Disc: A Bronze Age Map of Heaven?: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The date is already strongly supported. Full publication of the raw soil, corrosion and isotope data would let independent laboratories check the matches. Any organic material trapped in the corrosion of the disc itself could give a direct radiocarbon date. And a comparable object from a recorded Bronze Age excavation would do more than any argument. What the disc meant is more open. It may have been a calendar, a ritual object, a record of observations made on one hilltop, or all of these at different times in its long life. What it shows beyond reasonable argument is that people in Bronze Age central Europe watched the sky carefully, measured the sun's path, and wanted to hold that knowledge in their hands.

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead? Jars placed possibly from c. 1240–660 BCE; burials dated 9th–13th century CE Strong evidence. Were the giant stone jars of Laos made to hold the dead? The claim on the scales The stone jars of the Xieng Khouang plateau were funerary vessels. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Every excavation that has found anything datable in or around the jars has found the dead: Colani's burnt bone and beads, the pits, pots and marked graves at Site 1, and at Site 75 a jar packed with the bones of at least 37 people. That is a strong, consistent pattern. It falls short of established because the bodies are dated to the 9th to 13th centuries CE, while the jars may have been set up far earlier, and most jars are empty. Funerary use is well supported; original purpose remains partly open. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Guidebooks and the UNESCO listing now describe the jars as funerary, usually with a 'probably'. That is broadly fair. What the labels rarely say is that the dates for burials and the dates for the jars sit up to two thousand years apart, so the funerary reading is firmest for the medieval period. On origins, the confident tone runs slightly ahead of the evidence. What is solid More than 2,100 hollowed stone jars are recorded at over 120 sites on the Xieng Khouang plateau, from single jars to groups of about 400; the largest stand up to about 3 m tall. Shewan et al. 2021; UNESCO 2019 Madeleine Colani's 1930s excavations at Site 1 found burnt human bone and teeth, glass beads and bronze and iron objects in and around the jars. Colani 1935 Detrital zircon ages match the sandstone of a Site 1 jar to the Phoukeng quarry (Site 21), about 8 km away, where unfinished jars still lie in the rock. Shewan et al. 2021 Radiocarbon dates on human bone and charcoal place burial activity around the jars at Site 1 between roughly the late 9th and 13th centuries CE. Shewan et al. 2021 Jar 1 at Site 75 held the disarticulated bones of at least 37 people, from toddlers to adults, dated cal 890–1160 CE, with glass beads, an iron knife and a copper-alloy bell. Skopal et al. 2024; 2026 What is disputed When the jars were first made and set up: the OSL ages of 1240–660 BCE at Site 2 are maximum ages from sediment under the jars, not a date for the carving itself. Whether the jars were built as burial vessels from the start, or were ancient monuments that later people reused for their dead. Whether most jars ever held bodies at all, since the great majority now con

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?: 01 A field of stone cups
chunks.text: On a grassy upland in northern Laos, hollow stone jars lie scattered across the hills like cups left after a party of giants. Some are knee high. The largest stand up to about 3 m tall and weigh several tonnes. More than 2,100 have been recorded at over 120 sites, sometimes one jar alone on a ridge, sometimes hundreds in a group. Nobody in living memory made them, and no written record says who did. The people who live here have an answer. Long ago, the story goes, the giant king Khun Cheung defeated his enemy and ordered jars carved to brew and store rice wine for the victory feast; the biggest jar was his. The jars themselves are silent. They are cut from sandstone, granite, conglomerate and limestone, and many have a carved rim, as if shaped for a lid that has long since vanished. The jars kept their secret for a simple reason: for half a century, it was dangerous to dig beside them.

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The first serious excavator was the French archaeologist Madeleine Colani, who worked on the plateau in the early 1930s and published two volumes in 1935. At the largest group, now called Site 1, she found burnt human bone and teeth, sometimes from more than one person, along with coloured glass beads, bronze and iron objects, spindle whorls and ear ornaments. A natural limestone cave on the site had two holes cut through its roof, and she proposed it had been used as a crematorium, a chimney for the dead. The modern picture comes from the Plain of Jars Archaeological Project, a Lao and Australian team led by Dougald O'Reilly, Louise Shewan and Thonglith Luangkhoth, which returned to Site 1 in 2016. They found a burial ground, not a village: bones in pits, bones in buried ceramic pots, and graves marked by limestone boulders and flat sandstone discs. The discs carry human figures and animals, and lie over graves rather than on top of the jars. Sandstone is made of grains eroded from older rocks, and each grain of the mineral zircon carries its own uranium-lead age. The 2021 study compared the zircon age pattern in a Site 1 jar with rock from Site 21, a quarry at Phoukeng about 8 km away where unfinished jars still sit in the bedrock. The patterns match, so that outcrop is the likely source. How the finished jars crossed 8 km of hills is still unknown.

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?: 03 The mainstream story: a landscape for the dead
chunks.text: Most archaeologists now read the plateau as a mortuary landscape. The model is a two-stage funeral, common across Southeast Asia: a body is left to decompose in one place, then the bones are gathered and placed in a final resting place, often with ceremony and gifts. On this reading, some jars were the first stage and others the second, and the ground around them filled with graves over generations. Step 1 of 5. A jar is carved and set up. At Site 2, sediment beneath jars gives OSL ages of 1240–660 BCE, a maximum age for placement. A jar is carved and set up. At Site 2, sediment beneath jars gives OSL ages of 1240–660 BCE, a maximum age for placement. Proposed first stage: a body is laid in a smaller jar or grave to decompose. The bones are gathered and carried to a large jar: a secondary burial. Generation after generation, Jar 1 fills: at least 37 people, cal 890–1160 CE, with glass beads, an iron knife and a bell. Around the jars, stone discs and limestone boulders mark buried pots and graves, as at Site 1. Cross-section of a large stone jar 2.05 m across and 1.3 m high, drawn beside a 1.7 m person, with a smaller jar to its left. Step 1: the jar is carved and set in place, possibly as early as 1240 to 660 BCE. Step 2: a body is laid to decompose in a smaller jar or grave, a proposed first stage. Step 3: bones are gathered and carried to the large jar. Step 4: the large jar fills with the disarticulated bones of at least 37 people between about 890 and 1160 CE, with beads, a knife and a bell. Step 5: stone discs and boulders mark graves on the ground around the jars. Until recently that story had a hole in the middle: very few bones had been found inside a jar. That changed at Site 75, about 70 km northeast of Phonsavan. In 2024 a team led by Nicholas Skopal reported

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?: 04 The case for a longer, stranger story
chunks.text: The strongest challenge does not come from the giants of legend. It comes from the calendar. In 2021 Louise Shewan and colleagues dated sediment beneath jars at Site 2 by optically stimulated luminescence, which measures when mineral grains last saw daylight. The result: the jars were set in place possibly as early as 1240–660 BCE, in the late Bronze and early Iron Age. Every dated burial, though, is far younger. Human bone at Site 1 gave radiocarbon ages of roughly 772–950 and 1046–1219 CE, and the Site 75 bones date to about 890–1160 CE. A horizontal time chart from 1500 BCE to 1500 CE, with a scale bar of 500 years. The top bar, far left, marks optically stimulated luminescence ages for jar placement at Site 2, 1240 to 660 BCE, noted as a maximum age. Two bars far to the right mark radiocarbon ages for burials: Site 1, about 772 to 1219 CE, and Jar 1 at Site 75, cal 890 to 1160 CE, with at least 37 people. A bracket between them marks about 1,400 years with no dated activity yet. That leaves a gap of well over a thousand years with no dated activity at all. Maybe early burials exist and simply have not been found, since so little has been dug. Or maybe the medieval people who packed Jar 1 with their ancestors were reusing monuments that were already ancient to them, just as later peoples in Europe placed their dead in Neolithic tombs. The legend of rice wine, the idea of rain-water cisterns, and the lids that seem to fit storage all remain possible readings of what the jars were first cut to do. The bones tell us what the jars became. They do not yet tell us what the jars were born to be. The dating team says as much. Its OSL ages are maximum values, and it notes that whether all the sites are of the same age still needs work. Treating the burials and the jars as one

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?: 05 How new tools changed the picture
chunks.text: Almost everything we know with numbers is new. Zircon geochronology tied a jar to its quarry. Luminescence gave the first estimate of when the jars were set up. Radiocarbon on bone and teeth dated the funerals. At Site 75, the chemistry of the glass beads added a surprise: most were of a South Asian mineral soda, high alumina type, two were Mesopotamian soda plant-ash glass, and one probably came from southern China or northern Vietnam. The people who used the jars were tied into trade routes that reached the Indian Ocean and beyond. In 2024 Skopal and colleagues reported the first substantial evidence of uncremated bodies inside a Lao stone jar, at Site 75. In 2026, in Antiquity, they published Jar 1 at the same site: at least 37 people, eight radiocarbon dates spanning cal 890–1160 CE, twenty glass beads, an iron knife and a copper-alloy bell. They propose that smaller jars were where bodies first decomposed, and the big jar was a multigenerational ossuary.

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?: 06 What the bombs are hiding
chunks.text: The plateau sits on one of the most heavily bombed landscapes on Earth. During the Secret War of the 1960s and early 1970s, the United States dropped an estimated 270 million cluster bomblets on Laos, and tens of millions failed to explode. Craters still pock the jar sites, and some jars were shattered. Since 2004 the Mines Advisory Group, working with UNESCO and the Lao government, has cleared the main visitor sites, but many of the more than 120 sites remain unsafe to excavate. So the sample is tiny. A handful of sites, a few trenches, and a few jars with contents intact. Absence of early burials in that sample is weak evidence against them. Colani's finds, dug before radiocarbon dating existed, cannot now be tied to exact layers. And the villages where the jar makers lived, ate and carved have not been found.

chunks.heading: The Plain of Jars: Stone Vessels of the Dead?: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: The question has become sharp enough to test. If the jars were funerary from the start, then sealed deposits under and inside early-placed jars should contain first-millennium BCE bone, beads or ash. If they were made for something else, residues on the inner walls might show it. OSL dates from under many more jars, across many sites, to see whether placement was early everywhere. Excavation of intact jars at sites with early OSL ages, looking for burial material of the same age. Residue analysis on the inner walls of empty jars. Ancient DNA and isotopes from the Site 1 and Site 75 skeletons, to learn who these people were and where they grew up. More bomb clearance, so the other sites can be read at all. For now the verdict is clear on one point and open on another. These were places of the dead for centuries. Whether they were made that way, in the second millennium BCE, is the part of the mystery still waiting under the grass.

chunks.heading: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose c. 600–1500 CE (chiefdom settlements of the Diquís Delta) Awaiting discovery. Were the Diquís spheres lined up to point at the sky or the sea? The claim on the scales Lines of Diquís spheres were laid out to mark astronomical or navigational directions. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The rows exist, but almost every sphere was moved before it could be mapped, and the surviving in-place groups are few. With two or three points, any line points somewhere. We found no published archaeoastronomical survey showing solar or lunar orientation, and the navigation idea has no supporting evidence of ocean voyaging from the delta. The spheres date to c. 600–1500 CE and sit in local settlements. The idea is testable at Finca 6; it has simply not been shown. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Museum labels and UNESCO say the spheres were made by Diquís chiefdoms and that their purpose is uncertain, which matches the evidence well. Popular accounts go wrong in the other direction, calling them perfect spheres or linking them to Atlantis. The one soft spot in the official story is dating: spheres are dated by the layers and pottery around them, not directly, and most were moved from those layers long ago. What is solid More than 300 stone spheres are known from the Diquís Delta and Isla del Caño, from a few centimetres to about 2.57 m across. UNESCO 2014; Hoopes 2010 Most are of hard igneous rock (gabbro or granodiorite); about a dozen are of shell-rich limestone and about a dozen of sandstone. Lothrop 1963; Museo Nacional de Costa Rica They belong to chiefdom settlements with mounds, paved areas and cemeteries dated c. 500–1500 CE; the earliest spheres are placed around 600 CE and most after 1000 CE. UNESCO 2014; Hoopes 2010 They were first reported when the United Fruit Company cleared land for banana plantations in the 1930s; Doris Stone published the first study in 1943 and Samuel Lothrop a major survey in 1963. Stone 1943; Lothrop 1963 At Finca 6 some spheres still stand in their original linear arrangements, and in 2007 a sphere was excavated in place beside a mound. UNESCO 2014; Corrales and Badilla 2005 What is disputed What the spheres meant: symbols of rank and authority, markers of territory, images of the Sun and Moon, or something else. Whether their lines and groupings were oriented to astronomical events, to landmarks, or simply to the plazas and houses around them. Exactly how they were shaped and checked for roundness, and how t

chunks.heading: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose: 01 Balls in the banana fields
chunks.text: In the 1930s, crews of the United Fruit Company were clearing forest on the delta of the Río Grande de Térraba, in southern Costa Rica, to plant bananas. Their machines kept hitting stone. Not rubble, but balls: smooth, heavy, astonishingly round, some the size of an orange and some taller than the men who found them. Nobody in the region remembered who had made them. Many lay in rows. More than 300 are now known, from the delta and from Isla del Caño off the coast. The largest, at El Silencio, is about 2.57 m across. Weights of 15–16 tonnes are widely quoted for the giants, although simple geometry for a solid ball of this dense rock that size gives more like 24–27 tonnes, so the true figure is uncertain. They were carved from gabbro and granodiorite, tough igneous rocks, far harder than the limestone of most ancient sculpture. They have since rolled into popular culture. According to the University of Kansas archaeologist John Hoopes, the spheres helped inspire the giant rolling boulder in the opening of Raiders of the Lost Ark. They also attracted a flood of speculation, from Atlantis to visitors from space, which Hoopes has spent years answering with evidence. A perfect-looking sphere is one of the hardest shapes to make by hand. Someone thought it was worth doing, hundreds of times.

chunks.heading: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: Doris Stone published the first study in 1943, and Samuel Lothrop of Harvard's Peabody Museum surveyed the delta and published a major report in 1963. Later work by the National Museum of Costa Rica, led in the field by Francisco Corrales and Adrián Badilla from 2002, tied the spheres to villages with house mounds, paved areas and cemeteries. Layers and pottery around them place the first spheres around 600 CE, with most made after 1000 CE and the tradition ending before the Spanish conquest. Side view at a scale of 110 pixels per metre. On the left, the largest known sphere, about 2.57 m across, from El Silencio, labelled with quoted weights of 15 to 16 tonnes and a geometric estimate of 24 to 27 tonnes. Next to it a 1.7 m person reaches about two thirds of its height. Then a sphere 0.7 m across, the smallest size at the UNESCO sites, and a tiny dot for spheres only a few centimetres across. An inset on the right compares a true circle with an oval exaggerated ten times, showing a diameter difference of over 5 cm, about 2 percent on a 2.5 m sphere. A scale bar shows 1 m. Their roundness is impressive but not magical. Lothrop's often-quoted precision figures were averages, and some spheres vary by more than 5 cm in diameter. On a ball 2 m across that is about 2.5%, invisible to the eye and entirely within reach of patient hand work. Partly from the spheres and partly from the hills. Some carry the marks of hammerstones. Unfinished spheres lie in the hills near the gabbro sources, several kilometres from the finished ones. The method archaeologists reconstruct is simple and slow: rough out a boulder, peck it into shape with harder stones, then grind and polish it with sand. No sphere-making workshop has been fully excavated, and the exact way roundness was checked is sti

chunks.heading: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose: 03 The mainstream story: symbols of power
chunks.text: In the archaeological reading, the spheres belong to the chiefdoms that ruled the delta for about a thousand years. They stood in public plazas and along approaches to the houses of important families, sometimes on low mounds, sometimes in lines. Making and moving a multi-tonne ball required skilled carvers and many hands, and a chief who could command that labour had something to show for it. The spheres were, on this view, monuments to rank and community, the way a cathedral or a courthouse is today. Step 1 of 5. Choose a boulder of gabbro or granodiorite in the hills, several kilometres from the delta villages. Choose a boulder of gabbro or granodiorite in the hills, several kilometres from the delta villages. Rough it out by hammering off high points; heating and cooling to crack off the surface is a proposed extra. Peck the surface with harder hammerstones, thousands of blows, until the stone is nearly round. Check the curve against a gauge or cords and correct the high spots (proposed; no gauges found). Grind and polish with sand and water, then move the sphere to a plaza or mound; how is unknown. Five panels in a row show one stone changing shape. Step 1: an irregular boulder of gabbro in the hills. Step 2: the boulder is roughed out by hammering, with a dashed circle showing the target sphere and flakes flying off; heat and water to crack the surface is marked as proposed. Step 3: a near-round stone covered in small pecking marks, with a hammerstone. Step 4: a curved gauge held against the sphere to check roundness, marked as proposed. Step 5: a smooth polished sphere, with an arrow toward the delta settlement and a question mark over how it was moved. The spheres were not the only prestige objects of the delta. The same societies worked gold and carved stone st

chunks.heading: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose: 04 Lines that point somewhere?
chunks.text: The strongest unconventional case starts with the rows. Early investigators found spheres set in straight lines, and some of those lines still stand at Finca 6. In their 1998 book Atlantis in America, Ivar Zapp and George Erikson argued that such lines encoded bearings used by an advanced seafaring culture, a lost science of navigation. A more modest reading, common in popular accounts, is that some rows marked sunrise or sunset at the solstices and equinoxes. Both ideas are worth taking seriously, because they are testable. The Diquís people certainly watched the sky; farmers everywhere do. And a society that spent so much effort on the shape of a stone may well have cared where it stood. The question is whether any surviving line points to something that chance would not explain. The test is harder than it sounds. At the delta's latitude, about 9° north, the Sun on the June solstice rises roughly 24° north of due east, and on the December solstice roughly 24° south of it; equinox sunrise is due east (our calculation for a flat horizon). A straight line points two ways, so it can hit one of just three directions. Allow 2° of error either side and a line placed at random would still match one about one time in fifteen. A handful of hits among a handful of lines means little. Many lines, measured on the real horizon, could mean a lot. The rows are real. What they point at, if anything, has never been measured and published.

chunks.heading: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose: 05 What bulldozers and dynamite erased
chunks.text: Here time and greed did their worst. Plantation workers pushed spheres aside with heavy machines. Rumours spread that they held gold, and treasure hunters drilled holes in them and blew them apart with dynamite; the National Museum reassembled six of the broken ones. Others were hauled away as garden ornaments and status symbols for homes across the country. By the time archaeologists arrived, most had been moved from the spots where their makers set them. That matters above all for the alignment question. A line needs its points. Stone's and Lothrop's notes and maps are now the main record of many original groupings, and they were made before modern survey tools. Recent work has been about rescue more than revelation. In 2022 conservators from Mexico's INAH and the National Museum of Costa Rica cleaned, stabilised and reburied six spheres at Finca 6 to protect them. In 2024 a 65 cm gabbro sphere was among 395 artefacts returned to Costa Rica from the United States. In 2025 the museum restored three limestone spheres from Finca 4. We found no published lidar or archaeoastronomical survey of the delta yet.

chunks.heading: The Stone Spheres of the Diquís: Round on Purpose: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Measure every in-place line at Finca 6 and other sites and compare the bearings with solstice, equinox and lunar events on the real horizon, with a test for chance. Georeference the old maps to rebuild lost arrangements before the last witnesses fade. Excavate beneath in-place spheres for charcoal or pottery that dates when each was set. Fingerprint the rock of each sphere to find its quarry, and so its route to the plaza. Until then the verdict splits in two. That the Diquís chiefdoms made the spheres, by hand, over many centuries, is strongly supported. That their lines were aimed at the stars or across the oceans is an idea still waiting for its first measurement.

chunks.heading: The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence Probably dug by the Han period or earlier; no record of their making Open question. Who dug the Longyou caverns, and what were they for? The claim on the scales The Longyou caverns were dug mainly as quarries for building stone. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established Quarrying explains the location beside a river and the sheer volume removed, and it needs no lost knowledge. But the evidence that would confirm it is missing: nobody has traced Longyou stone into a dated building, and the caverns' careful finishing, stairs, pillars and drainage suggest the space itself mattered. The purpose-built readings have no direct evidence either, such as burials or stored goods. Both sides argue from the architecture alone, so this is a genuinely open question. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Guides and news stories state confidently that the caverns are 'more than 2,000 years old' and then say the purpose is a mystery. The honesty about purpose is right. The age is stated more firmly than the evidence allows: the Han pots show the caverns existed when the pots came to rest in the silt, which could be long after the pots were made, and the only firm minimum date comes from a text written before 1626. What is solid At least 24 artificial caverns have been identified near Shiyan Beicun on the Qu River; ten are complete and stable, the rest failed or partly collapsed. Yang, Yue and Li 2011 The caverns were cut by hand into Cretaceous argillaceous siltstone; floor areas range from about 367 to 1,352 m² and heights from about 8 to 18 m. Cavern No. 2 covers about 1,057 m². Yang, Yue and Li 2011 The walls carry regular bands of chisel marks, the bands 500–600 mm apart and the troughs about 6–14 mm deep. Yang, Yue and Li 2011 Glazed pots of Western Han type (206 BCE–23 CE) were found in Cavern No. 2, and a written reference shows the caverns were known before 1626. Li et al. 2009; Yang, Yue and Li 2011 The complete caverns were full of water when found, and engineering studies conclude that the water helped keep their thin roofs standing. Yang, Yue and Li 2011 What is disputed What the caverns were for: quarries, tombs, storage, a military base, a palace or a place of offering. How old they are: the Han pottery gives a date for when the pots came to rest, not for the digging itself. Who organised the work, and whether all 24 caverns belong to one project or several periods. What time has hidden No text records the digging, the workers or the purpose, although the scal

chunks.heading: The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence: 01 The pond that was a doorway
chunks.text: In June 1992, villagers in Shiyan Beicun, in the hills of western Zhejiang, began pumping out a pond. As the water dropped, walls appeared. Then steps. Then a vast chamber, its sloping ceiling held up by pillars of rock, every surface covered in neat parallel grooves. The pond had been the flooded mouth of a hand-cut hall. Nearby ponds turned out to be the same. Engineers now count 24 artificial caverns along the north bank of the Qu River. The biggest, Cavern No. 2, has a floor of about 1,057 m², bigger than four tennis courts, and a ceiling up to 15 m high. Some caverns reach about 18 m. They are cut into soft red siltstone, and no chronicle, inscription or local legend records who made them or why. A project on this scale must have needed a large, organised workforce. It left behind no name, no date and no reason.

chunks.heading: The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The caverns were measured in detail by engineering geologists led by Yang Zhifa, Yue Zhongqi and Li Lihui. They found ten complete, stable caverns and fourteen that have failed or partly collapsed. The rock is a Cretaceous argillaceous siltstone, fairly strong when dry but much weaker when wet. Floor areas range from about 367 to 1,352 m². Fifteen rock pillars between 4.6 and 12 m tall were left in place to hold the roofs. Cross-section through a hillside of layered red siltstone whose beds dip at about 24 degrees. A large hall is cut into it: a tall side wall leaning inward at about 78 degrees, a roof sloping down at about 21.6 degrees parallel to the rock layers, a rock pillar about 10 m tall, and a stair from the portal down to the floor. The hall is shaded as full of water, as found in 1992. A person 1.7 m tall stands on the floor for scale, and a scale bar shows 10 m. The span is about 34 m and the tallest wall about 15 m. The design is subtle. The ceilings slope at an average of about 21.6°, close to the 24° dip of the rock beds, so the roof follows a natural layer instead of cutting across it. The side walls lean inward at about 78°. Each cavern has a stair from its entrance to the floor and a drainage system for rainwater. And between Caverns No. 1 and No. 2 the dividing wall is only 0.55–1.3 m thick over 16.5 m, yet the two halls never break into each other. Not very precisely. Two glazed clay pots of a type typical of the Western Han dynasty (206 BCE–23 CE) were found in Cavern No. 2, a relief sculpture has been placed stylistically between 206 BCE and 589 CE, and a written reference shows the caverns were known before 1626. The pots show the cavern existed when they came to rest, which may have been long after they were made. So 'over 2,000 years old' is a re

chunks.heading: The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence: 03 The ordinary answer: a quarry
chunks.text: The simplest explanation is that Longyou was a stone quarry. The siltstone is even, fine and easy to cut with iron tools, and the caverns open onto a river that could carry heavy blocks downstream. The chisel marks show cutting from the top down, layer by layer, which is how underground quarries are commonly worked. And the rock had to go somewhere: on the published dimensions, each large cavern represents thousands of cubic metres of stone removed, and the whole complex probably tens of thousands. A rough sum shows the scale. Cavern No. 2 has a floor of about 1,057 m² and a ceiling that slopes from about 15 m down to a few metres. If its average height is around 8 m, some 8,000 m³ of rock came out of that one hall, perhaps 20,000 tonnes of siltstone (our estimate, from the published dimensions). Cutting that with hammers and chisels is a big job, but not an impossible one: it is the kind of volume that organised quarry crews moved across the ancient world. Step 1 of 5. Open a portal and cut the first lift just below the roof line. Open a portal and cut the first lift just below the roof line. Work downward in horizontal lifts, layer by layer, from the top to the floor. Leave rock pillars and a stair in place as the hall deepens. Dress each band of wall, 500–600 mm tall, with parallel strokes at 60–75°, about 10 mm deep. Thousands of cubic metres per cavern were removed. Where the stone went is still unknown. Left: a small section of a cavern growing downward in horizontal lifts from a portal, with a pillar left in place. Right: an enlarged wall panel showing horizontal bands 50 to 60 cm tall, each filled with parallel chisel grooves at 60 to 75 degrees, 6 to 14 mm deep. Step 1: a portal and first lift. Step 2: more lifts taken from the top down. Step 3: a pillar and st

chunks.heading: The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence: 04 The case for design
chunks.text: Stand in Cavern No. 2 and the quarry idea feels thin. Quarrymen want blocks; they rarely spend time finishing the walls they leave behind. Yet the Longyou walls and ceilings are covered in bands of parallel chisel strokes, each band 500–600 mm wide, the grooves set at 60–75° to the band and about 10 mm deep on average. The pattern runs unbroken over huge surfaces, like the texture of a finished room. Then there are the features a quarry does not need: stairs, drainage, pillars placed at intervals, roofs tuned to the bedding, a single portal to each hall, and partitions so thin that the diggers must have known exactly where their neighbours were. Popular writers go further and ask how such precision was achieved in near darkness, and why no one wrote it down. Those questions are fair, even if the answer is probably organised hand labour rather than lost technology. Some of the design argument cuts both ways, and fairness means saying so. A roof that follows the rock beds is exactly what a practical quarryman would choose, because stone splits most easily along its layers and a roof in one layer is less likely to fall. Leaving pillars is standard practice in underground quarries too, because it saves the workers' lives. The finished chisel bands and the stairs are harder to explain as pure extraction, and those are where the case for a purpose-built space is strongest. A quarry takes stone and leaves scars. Longyou left patterned walls, stairs and pillars in 24 halls that never touch.

chunks.heading: The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence: 05 What water saved and air is destroying
chunks.text: The strangest twist is that the caverns may have survived because they were forgotten underwater. Yang and colleagues concluded that the complete caverns stayed stable for two thousand years largely because they were full of water, which supported the roofs and kept the rock damp and uniform. Once pumped dry for visitors, the rock began to change. In 2010 the roof of Cavern No. 24 collapsed, bringing down about 250 m³ of rock. The newest work is about survival rather than origins. A 2023 study in Tunnelling and Underground Space Technology by Zhang Huihui and colleagues, and a 2024 paper in Engineering Failure Analysis by Wang Tie and Yan Chengzeng, used monitoring and numerical models to show how swings in humidity drive cracking in the caverns' siltstone. Earlier, a Japanese and Chinese team used ground electrical resistivity to map moisture in the hill. Draining also disturbed whatever lay on the cavern floors. Much of the evidence that might have answered the purpose question, from tools to offerings to spilled grain, was either never there or went out with the mud.

chunks.heading: The Longyou Caves: Halls Carved in Silence: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Trace the stone: match Longyou siltstone to dated walls, bridges, tombs or buildings along the Qu River. Date the digging more directly, for example luminescence dating of the earliest sediment sealed on cavern floors. Survey the hillside and riverbank for spoil heaps, loading areas, split blocks or abandoned half-cut stones. Search regional gazetteers and archives for any record of works at this place before 1626. If Longyou stone turns up in a dated Han or earlier building, the quarry reading will be hard to beat. If the floors yield burials, stored goods or ritual objects, the caverns were built to be used. Until then, Longyou remains one of the few ancient places on Earth where we can measure almost everything except the one thing we most want to know: why.

chunks.heading: Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia Origins undated (Phrygian start proposed); greatly enlarged in the Byzantine period Awaiting discovery. How old are the deepest levels of Cappadocia's underground cities? The claim on the scales The deepest levels of Derinkuyu were dug in the Iron Age or earlier. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established No find from the lowest floors has been dated to the Iron Age or earlier, and nothing physical ties them to the Younger Dryas. The Phrygian start is a reasonable guess for the first small rooms near the surface, not for the depths. The challengers are right that the digging is undated and that carving erases evidence, which is why the question stays open. But the evidence we do have, chapels, doors, wells and written accounts of raids, all points to Byzantine communities as the builders of the deep city. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Guidebooks often say Derinkuyu dates back to the Phrygians of the 8th century BCE and could hold 20,000 people, stated as facts. Both are estimates. The Phrygian start rests on analogy, not a dated find, and the capacity is a calculation. Textbooks are right that the city we can walk through is mostly Byzantine, and overconfident about how and when it began. What is solid Derinkuyu is carved into volcanic tuff and reaches a depth of about 85 m, with up to 18 floors reported and more than 50 ventilation shafts. Nývlt et al. 2016 Passages could be sealed from inside with large rolling stone doors, and each level could be closed off separately. Nývlt et al. 2016; site descriptions The complex was rediscovered in 1963 when a resident broke through a basement wall, and it opened to visitors in 1969. Nývlt et al. 2016 It was greatly enlarged in the Byzantine period, when Christian communities sheltered from raids during the Arab–Byzantine wars (c. 780–1180), and it was used by local Christians until the population exchange of 1923. Ousterhout 2017; site histories Cappadocia holds hundreds of underground settlements; researchers have geolocated more than 360. HISTORY 2026; Yamaç and Tok 2026 What is disputed Who dug the first rooms: Phrygians of the 8th–7th centuries BCE, earlier Anatolian peoples, or Roman-era and Byzantine communities. How many people Derinkuyu could hold: the widely quoted 20,000 is an estimate, not a count. Whether tunnels really link Derinkuyu to Kaymaklı, about 8–9 km away; the connection is often stated but has not been demonstrated. What time has hidden Nobody has directly dated the cutting of any le

chunks.heading: Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia: 01 A door in the basement
chunks.text: In 1963 a man in the town of Derinkuyu, on the high plateau of Cappadocia in central Türkiye, was renovating his house. He knocked through a wall in the basement and found a room that should not have been there. Behind it was a passage. Behind the passage, another room, and a stair going down. It kept going down. Derinkuyu, whose name means deep well, turned out to be a city carved entirely into volcanic rock, reaching about 85 m below the surface, with up to 18 floors reported and more than 50 ventilation shafts. There are stables, halls, wells, chapels and storage rooms, and passages that could be sealed from inside with round stone doors that roll across the corridor like giant coins. Estimates of how many people it could shelter run to 20,000, though that is a calculation, not a count. It is not a cave. Every cubic metre of it was cut by hand, and nobody wrote down when the cutting began.

chunks.heading: Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The rock explains a lot. Cappadocia's volcanoes blanketed the region in ash that hardened into tuff, soft enough to carve with hand tools but strong enough to stand without supports. People here have cut homes, churches, dovecotes and storerooms into it for thousands of years. Roberto Bixio, founder of the Centro Studi Sotterranei in Genoa, who has spent decades mapping these sites, calls a typical village 'a stone iceberg', with far more of it below ground than above. A vertical section through the ground, 85 m deep, with a small town and church on the surface. A long ventilation shaft about 55 m deep, also used as a well, drops through the centre. Stairs and sloping passages zigzag down to chambers at many levels: stables and storage near the top, a chapel lower down, and the deepest level at about 85 m. Round rolling stone doors are marked on several passages. Depth ticks mark every 20 m, and a note reads that no level has been directly dated. A scale bar shows 10 m, and a 1.7 m person stands at the surface for comparison. Derinkuyu is not alone. Researchers have geolocated more than 360 underground settlements across Cappadocia. Kaymaklı, about 8–9 km away, is another; a tunnel between the two is often described, but a 2016 engineering study notes the connection is assumed rather than demonstrated. The later history is clearer. The city was greatly enlarged when Byzantine Christians hid from Arab raiders between roughly 780 and 1180, and local Christians still used it until they left Cappadocia in the Greek–Turkish population exchange of 1923.

chunks.heading: Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia: 03 The mainstream story: a refuge that grew for centuries
chunks.text: In the standard account, the underground cities are a slow accumulation. Iron Age people, possibly the Phrygians of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, may have cut the first cellars. Around 400 BCE the Greek soldier Xenophon described villages further east, in Armenia, where houses were dug underground and entered by a shaft like a well, with animals kept below (Anabasis 4.5.25). In Roman and Byzantine times the cellars were joined, deepened and fitted with chapels, wells and doors, and the Arab raids made them refuges for whole communities. Step 1 of 5. Soft tuff under a village. The first small cellars may be Iron Age, perhaps Phrygian (proposed, undated). Soft tuff under a village. The first small cellars may be Iron Age, perhaps Phrygian (proposed, undated). Roman and early Byzantine communities join the rooms into levels and cut chapels. c. 780–1180 CE: raids drive the city deeper; rolling stone doors seal each level from inside. Every enlargement shaves away older walls, so tool marks record only the last cut. The start is erased. Used until 1923, forgotten, and rediscovered in 1963 through a basement wall. A simple section through soft tuff. Step 1: a surface village with a few small cellars just below it, drawn dashed as a proposed Iron Age start. Step 2: rooms are joined into levels with a chapel, in the Roman and early Byzantine period. Step 3: the complex is deepened as a refuge with rolling stone doors between about 780 and 1180 CE. Step 4: a close-up of one room enlarged, with its older, smaller outline dashed inside, showing that the new cut removes the old surface. Step 5: the city is left in 1923 and rediscovered in 1963 through a basement wall. This account is sensible, but its first chapter is soft. The Phrygian attribution rests on the region's wider trad

chunks.heading: Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia: 04 The case for a much older shelter
chunks.text: Graham Hancock makes the challenge in Magicians of the Gods (2015) and in the episode 'A Fatal Winter' of his Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse (2022). In a 2015 essay he asked: 'Could this cold episode have been the Younger Dryas (from 12,800 years ago to 11,600 years ago) and if so might the underground "cities" be much older than archaeologists imagine?' His frame comes from the Younger Dryas impact idea championed by the Comet Research Group and, for Anatolia, by Andrew Collins: a comet-driven catastrophe at the end of the Ice Age, remembered in myth. His key text is Zoroastrian. In the Vendidad, part of the Avesta, the god Ahura Mazda warns the righteous king Yima of a coming winter and tells him to build a Vara, a square enclosure, and bring into it the seeds of people, animals and plants. Upon the material world the evil winters are about to fall, that shall bring the fierce, deadly frost ... Therefore make thee a Vara, long as a riding-ground on every side of the square, to be an abode for man. It is a haunting parallel: a shelter built against a killing cold, with life carried inside to survive it. The text does not say the Vara was underground, and it names no place, but the image of a sealed refuge fits Derinkuyu well. Hancock's sharpest point is fair: archaeologists have no direct date for the cutting of the city, so the conventional start is an inference too. Carving erases its own history. Each new chisel stroke removes the surface that recorded the last one.

chunks.heading: Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia: 05 What time has hidden, and what new tools see
chunks.text: Dating a hole is hard. Radiocarbon needs organic material, and cutting rock leaves none behind. Floor deposits that might hold charcoal or pottery have been cleared by centuries of reuse, by inhabitants cleaning their rooms, and by modern work to open the site to visitors. Critics of Hancock, such as the writer Jason Colavito, note that he offers no dated evidence for an Ice Age start either. That is the honest state of play: an undated excavation, with a Byzantine city on top and an unknown beginning. The mainstream has a reasonable answer to the question of why anyone would dig so deep. The Arab–Byzantine frontier ran through this region for about four centuries, and raids came again and again. A refuge that each generation deepened a little, in rock soft enough to cut with iron picks, needs no single heroic project and no Ice Age. The same logic cuts against the conventional story, though: a city that grew by small additions over centuries could just as easily have started earlier than anyone has shown. Growth by accretion explains the size; it does not date the seed. In 2020, restoration work in Midyat, in southeastern Türkiye, uncovered Matiate, an underground city its excavators date to the 2nd or 3rd century CE. By 2022, 49 rooms had been exposed, with a church, silos, wells, coins and lamps; the excavation's director, Gani Tarkan, suggested it could once have held 60,000–70,000 people, an estimate from a small explored fraction. At Derinkuyu, a 2023 study used satellite radar interferometry to track ground movement above the tunnels, and 2024–2026 studies mapped its layout and soundscape.

chunks.heading: Derinkuyu: The City Beneath Cappadocia: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Excavate sealed floor layers in unopened chambers at the lowest levels, and date anything organic in them. Date the fill at the bottom of the deepest shafts and wells by luminescence, which gives a minimum age for the cutting. Build a chronology of tool marks from dated Cappadocian tombs and churches, then read the deep levels against it. Map Derinkuyu, Kaymaklı and Matiate in 3D to see which spaces cut through older ones. If the deepest chambers yield Iron Age pottery sealed beneath their floors, the Phrygian start will firm up; if they yield anything older, the story changes dramatically. For now, the deep city belongs to the Byzantine world on the evidence we have, and its first shovel of tuff belongs to no one we can name.

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef Saudeleur era, megalithic building from c. 1180 CE Strong evidence. Who stacked a city of basalt logs on a Pacific reef, and when? The claim on the scales The megalithic city of Nan Madol was built by Pohnpeians under the Saudeleur dynasty, beginning in the late twelfth century CE. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Several independent lines agree: uranium-thorium dates on coral put the royal tomb at about 1180–1200 CE; geochemistry ties the basalt to Pohnpei's own quarries; oral history describes Saudeleur rule from Nan Madol; and excavations show earlier settlement on the reef from the first centuries CE, not a vanished older city. What keeps this short of fully established is how few islets have been dated, so the start of construction elsewhere on the site may differ. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Guidebooks and heritage listings present Nan Madol as a Saudeleur capital with confidence, and on the main point they are right. They sometimes state a single building date as if the whole site were dated, when only a few structures are, and they rarely mention that the transport methods are reasoned proposals. The mainstream account is well founded but a little more precise than its evidence. What is solid Nan Madol consists of about 92 to 100 artificial islets, depending on how they are counted, built of basalt and coral fill on the reef flat off Temwen Island and separated by tidal canals. McCoy & Athens 2011; UNESCO 2016 Uranium-thorium dates on coral used in the construction of Nandauwas, the royal mortuary, place its building at about 1180–1200 CE. McCoy et al. 2016 Geochemical (XRF) sourcing shows the builders used basalt from several sources on Pohnpei, favouring columnar basalt from an older volcanic phase. McCoy & Athens 2011 Pohnpeian oral history describes the Saudeleur dynasty ruling from Nan Madol until it was overthrown by the hero Isokelekel, an event traditionally placed around 1628. Hanlon 1988 Nandauwas measures roughly 80 by 60 m, with walls 5.5–7.5 m high built of columns laid in alternating crosswise and lengthwise courses. Morgan 1988; McCoy et al. 2016 What is disputed When the first islets were built, since most structures have not been directly dated and the earliest platforms may be centuries older than the megalithic walls. Exactly how the heaviest columns were moved and lifted, since no contemporary account or tool kit for transport survives. How large a workforce was needed and over how many generations, which depends

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef: 01 A city of stone logs
chunks.text: Paddle through the mangroves off Pohnpei's southeast coast at high tide and walls rise out of the green water: black stone laid like a log cabin, prism crossed over prism, some courses higher than a two-storey house. The stones are natural basalt columns, five- and six-sided, some several metres long and weighing tonnes. Around them lie nearly a hundred artificial islets separated by canals, on a coral reef, in one of the most remote places humans ever settled. Nan Madol baffled the Europeans who reached it in the nineteenth century. Pohnpei is a small island, about 334 square kilometres, with no draught animals and no metal. Who had moved so much stone, and why build a city on the reef rather than on land? Pohnpeians had their own answer. Two sorcerer brothers, Olisihpa and Olosohpa, came from over the sea looking for a place to build an altar, and with a spell they made the stones fly through the air and settle into place. A city built on the sea, from stone logs that nature had already cut: it looks impossible until you see how the island made it possible.

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The site covers roughly 80 hectares of reef flat off Temwen Island. It divides into two parts: Madol Pah in the southwest, linked to the ruler and his court, and Madol Powe in the northeast, a precinct of priests and tombs. The grandest structure is Nandauwas, the royal mortuary, an enclosure about 80 by 60 metres with walls 5.5 to 7.5 metres high, an inner enclosure and a central tomb. Left: a wall face drawn to scale, 1 metre to 34 pixels, rising 7.5 metres from the ground. Alternating courses show long basalt columns laid lengthwise and rows of hexagons, the ends of columns laid crosswise. A 1.7 metre human figure stands at its foot, reaching less than a quarter of the height. A dimension line reads 5.5 to 7.5 metres high and a scale bar shows 2 metres. Right: a simplified plan of Nandauwas, about 80 by 60 metres, with an outer wall, an approximate inner enclosure drawn dashed and a small central tomb labelled built about 1180 to 1200 CE by uranium-thorium coral dating. A tidal canal runs below, and a scale bar shows 20 metres. The building technique is distinctive. Columns were laid in alternating courses, a layer end-on across the wall, then a layer lengthwise, the pattern archaeologists call header and stretcher. The crossing layers lock each other in place without mortar, and the core is packed with coral rubble. Tradition and archaeology agree on the purpose: this was the capital of the Saudeleur, lords who ruled all of Pohnpei, until the hero Isokelekel overthrew them, an event traditionally dated around 1628.

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef: 03 Dating a city with coral
chunks.text: Living coral takes up a little uranium from seawater but almost no thorium. Once it dies, the uranium decays to thorium at a known rate, so the ratio acts as a clock. In a 2016 study, Mark McCoy and colleagues dated coral used in building Nandauwas and got about 1180–1200 CE, a precise date for the start of the megalithic tomb, and an earlier date than many had assumed. The same team matched the chemistry of the stones to outcrops on Pohnpei. An earlier XRF study by McCoy and Steven Athens found that the builders drew on several sources: most boulders came from Temwen Island and nearby, while the columns were chosen from basalt of an older volcanic phase, roughly 7 to 8 million years old, on the main island. Different structures used different quarries, perhaps as sources ran out or as political alliances changed. Radiocarbon dates show people living on the reef edge from the first centuries CE, and islets were built up over the following centuries. The megalithic walls came late in a long story, not at its beginning.

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef: 04 The case for something older
chunks.text: The challengers begin with the numbers. A popular estimate, repeated in the Smithsonian's coverage, puts the stone and fill at about 750,000 tonnes, and single stones at Nandauwas are often estimated at up to around 50 tonnes. That is a heavy burden for an island population with only wood, fibre and muscle. James Churchward made Nan Madol a relic of Mu, his sunken Pacific continent; David Hatcher Childress set it among the lost cities of Lemuria and the Pacific. Graham Hancock's version is more careful. In Underworld he took Pohnpeian traditions seriously: stories speak of Kahnihmweiso, a city now under the sea beyond the reef, and divers have reported columns standing in deep water. If sea level or land had shifted, might Nan Madol be the last visible part of an older complex? It is a fair question, and one that tradition raises, not only modern writers. The evidence so far points the other way. Dives to check the reports have not documented a human-made structure at depth, and the features investigated have been read as natural. Pohnpei was settled only around 2,000 years ago, and the settlement layers under the islets show an ordinary village on the reef, not the ruins of an older city.

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef: 05 How to move a basalt log
chunks.text: The first trick was done by nature. When thick lava cools slowly, it shrinks and cracks into long prisms, the same process that made the Giant's Causeway. Pohnpei has cliffs of these ready-made columns, so the builders did not need to cut stone; they needed to pry it loose and move it. Step 1 of 5. Nature makes the columns: cooling lava cracks into long prisms. Nature makes the columns: cooling lava cracks into long prisms. Levers pry columns loose along natural joints (proposed). Rafts float them across the lagoon inside the reef at high tide (proposed). Ropes haul them up inclined logs onto the islet (proposed). Crossed courses of columns, with coral rubble behind, make the wall. A cross-section from a rocky shore on the left, across a lagoon, to a coral-fill islet on the right. Step 1: vertical basalt prisms stand in the cliff, labelled cooling lava cracks into prisms. Step 2: a lever pries a column loose. Step 3: a column rides on a raft floating on the lagoon at high tide. Step 4: a column is hauled up two inclined logs onto the islet. Step 5: a wall of alternating lengthwise columns and end-on hexagonal columns stands on the islet. Most archaeologists think columns were levered from outcrops, floated on rafts across the calm lagoon inside the reef at high tide, and hauled up onto the walls along inclined logs with ropes, as tradition in some versions also suggests. No ancient raft has been found, which is no surprise in a wet tropical climate, and the method is a reasoned proposal rather than a documented one. Spread over generations, the work looks demanding but within reach of a chiefdom that could command the labour of the whole island. Perhaps the stones did fly, in a sense: carried by a society organised enough to lift them.

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef: 06 What time is taking now
chunks.text: The Saudeleur left no writing. Their history was held in oral tradition, much of it sacred and restricted, and recorded only after European contact. The wooden tools and ropes are gone. And the city itself is under threat: silt is choking the canals and mangrove roots are prying walls apart, which is why UNESCO listed Nan Madol as a World Heritage Site in Danger in the same year, 2016, that it was inscribed. What we have lost is not only stone but the life inside it. Tradition and excavation give glimpses: on the islet of Idehd, priests kept a sacred eel in a well and fed it turtle offal; other islets held canoe houses, places for preparing food, and tombs of rulers. Excavations have turned up shell ornaments, drilled animal teeth, quartz crystals and pounders for kava. The ceremonies, the songs and the full political story that tied them together survive only in fragments, held by Pohnpeian families and chiefly titles that still exist today. It is worth pausing on how remarkable that continuity is. The Nahnmwarki, the traditional paramount chiefs whose office tradition traces back to Isokelekel's victory over the last Saudeleur, still exercise customary authority over the site. Few megalithic cities anywhere keep a living link to the people who say their ancestors built them.

chunks.heading: Nan Madol: The Basalt City on the Reef: 07 What would settle it
chunks.text: Direct dates from many more islets, especially their lowest fill, would map the full building sequence. A systematic sonar and diving survey of the reef edge, with samples from any columnar features, would test the sunken-city tradition head on. More stone sourcing would show how the quarries were organised, and experimental trials with columns of known weight would put numbers on the labour. On current evidence, Nan Madol is a Pacific achievement of the twelfth century onward, built by Pohnpeians, and no less astonishing for that.

chunks.heading: The Carolina Bays: Half a Million Ovals Pointing One Way
chunks.text: Mysteries of the Earth The Carolina Bays: Half a Million Ovals Pointing One Way Luminescence ages c. 109,000–2,000 years ago Ruled out. Did a single cosmic impact punch half a million aligned ovals into the Atlantic coast?
