chunks.heading: Egypt's Stone Vases: Too Perfect for Human Hands?: 01 A jar that went viral
chunks.text: Hold a Predynastic Egyptian vase and the first surprise is the weight: dense grey-green stone, turned into something with a narrow neck, a swelling belly and walls in places only a few millimetres thick. The second surprise is the date. Many were made before writing, before the pyramids, more than 5,000 years ago. The third, for a growing online audience, arrived in 2023, when a privately owned rose granite vase was scanned with a structured-light scanner and presented as symmetrical to about a thousandth of an inch. Videos followed, then a movement. Engineers and collectors began scanning more vessels, and claims grew bolder: surfaces round and centred to a few hundredths of a millimetre, better than modern industrial pottery, too good for copper and sand. For some, these jars became the clearest physical trace of a lost advanced civilisation, hidden in plain sight in museum cases. The vases are real, the skill is real, and the question is fair. Everything turns on which vases were measured.

chunks.heading: Egypt's Stone Vases: Too Perfect for Human Hands?: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: Stone vessels are one of the great crafts of early Egypt. They appear in Predynastic graves of the fourth millennium BCE and reach a peak in the First and Second Dynasties, in hard stones such as basalt, granite, diorite and gneiss as well as softer travertine and serpentine. When Djoser built his Step Pyramid at Saqqara around 2670–2650 BCE, he sealed more than 40,000 of them in galleries under its east side. Many were already antiques, inscribed with names of earlier kings such as Den, Semerkhet and Nynetjer. The tool that made them is also known. The hieroglyph used to write 'craft' shows a drill with a forked top and two weights, and tomb paintings, including the New Kingdom tomb of the vizier Rekhmire at Thebes, show craftsmen hollowing vessels with it. Excavations have produced drill cores, crescent and figure-of-eight stone borers, and unfinished vessels at every stage. Why so many? Stone vessels held oils, perfumes, ointments and food offerings, and in the early dynasties they were status objects in their own right, buried by the hundred in royal and elite tombs at Abydos and Saqqara. A hard-stone jar was a statement of wealth because everyone knew how long it took. Djoser's hoard reads like a royal attempt to gather and protect the treasures of earlier kings, perhaps rescued from their plundered or restored tombs, within his own monument. Step 1 of 5. Shape the outside: the blank is pounded with hammerstones and ground with sandstone. Shape the outside: the blank is pounded with hammerstones and ground with sandstone. Tube drill: a bow spins a copper tube; dry quartz sand under it does the cutting. Core out: the central core is snapped out, leaving a hole through the neck. Undercut: a crescent stone borer on a forked, weighted shaft grinds the belly wider than

chunks.heading: Egypt's Stone Vases: Too Perfect for Human Hands?: 03 How the hand method works
chunks.text: The engineer and experimental archaeologist Denys Stocks spent years reproducing Egyptian stoneworking. His sequence begins with shaping the outside by pounding and grinding. A copper tube, spun by a bow, then drills down through the neck; the copper does not cut the stone, the dry quartz sand under it does, and the tube wears away steadily as it goes. The central core is snapped out, leaving a clean hole. The hard part is the belly, which is wider than the neck. For this the craftsman used a borer: a crescent-shaped stone bit fixed to a forked shaft, pressed down by two heavy stones tied to the top and swung back and forth. Changing bits widened the cavity step by step until the walls were thin. Finally everything was ground and polished with finer abrasives. Stocks estimated that one vessel in the Manchester Museum would have taken about 800 hours, roughly three months of one specialist's work. Three kinds of evidence meet. Art shows the weighted drill in use, from the Old Kingdom to the New Kingdom. Archaeology supplies the borers, the cores and unfinished pieces. Experiments show that copper tubes with sand, and stone borers, cut granite and softer stones and leave the same kinds of marks.

chunks.heading: Egypt's Stone Vases: Too Perfect for Human Hands?: 04 The challengers and their scanners
chunks.text: The precision case is new because the measurements are new. Adam Young of the Artifact Foundation argued that the vessels had never been measured properly and set out to scan them. Max Fomitchev-Zamilov of the research company Maximus Energy reported shape errors as small as 15 microns on some vases, and the collector Matt Beall, presenting a collection of 85 vessels in 2025, called the copper-and-stone explanation absurd and suggested lathes, perhaps with diamond tools. Their strongest point deserves credit. Nobody in mainstream Egyptology had put these objects through modern metrology, and some hard-stone pieces do look astonishingly regular. The argument echoes the engineer Christopher Dunn, whose books have long claimed signs of machining in Egyptian stonework. And the logic is sound as far as it goes: if such numbers held for authentic ancient pieces, the story of early Egyptian technology would need rewriting. Left: two cross-sections with exaggerated errors. Circularity shows a lumpy outline against a perfect dashed circle, labelled how round one slice is. Concentricity shows an inner circle whose centre is offset from the outer one, labelled do inner and outer share one centre. Right: a logarithmic scale from 10 micrometres to 1 millimetre, marking the claimed best error of 15 micrometres, one thousandth of an inch at 25.4 micrometres, a human hair at about 70 micrometres, paper at about 100 micrometres, and 1 millimetre. Below, a box summarises the 2025 study: 19 Petrie Museum vessels compared with 25 machine-made and 24 handmade modern vases; the ancient outer surfaces match the handmade group, and their insides are rounder but poorly centred.

chunks.heading: Egypt's Stone Vases: Too Perfect for Human Hands?: 05 The provenance problem, and a surprising result
chunks.text: Here the case runs into the oldest rule in archaeology: an object without a findspot cannot date itself. Most of the star vessels in the precision debate came from private collections and the antiquities market. Egypt has banned the sale and export of antiquities since its 1983 law, so pieces in circulation have uncertain histories, and modern Egyptian workshops make stone vessels, some of them on lathes. A perfect machine-made vase would be exactly what a modern workshop produces. There is a second trap. Precision numbers depend on how a scan is processed: which surface points are kept, how a best-fit shape is chosen, and whether a chipped or weathered area is excluded. Two teams can scan the same vase and report different figures in good faith. That is why measurement protocols, control objects and raw data matter as much as the headline number. Fresh from the field: in December 2025 Fomitchev-Zamilov himself published a peer-reviewed study in npj Heritage Science. He scanned 19 Predynastic vessels from the Petrie Museum in London, which have documented histories, alongside 25 modern machine-made and 24 modern handmade vases, and measured roundness and centring. The machine-made vases formed their own tight cluster. The ancient vessels' outer surfaces matched the modern handmade group; their insides were rounder but poorly centred, a pattern unlike either modern group. He also used the method to flag some private pieces as probably modern. When the vessels with known histories were measured, they looked handmade. That is what good science looks like: the test was proposed by a challenger and he published the answer.

chunks.heading: Egypt's Stone Vases: Too Perfect for Human Hands?: 06 What an independent test needs
chunks.text: The question is not closed, because the most precise claims concern vessels outside the study. A decisive test would scan a large set of vessels from recorded excavations, such as the Step Pyramid galleries and the early royal tombs at Abydos, in independent laboratories, blind to origin, with the raw scans released. Microscopes inside the vessels could separate the spiral marks a lathe leaves from the concentric grooves of a hand borer. Replication should be scanned too: hard-stone vases made with copper tubes, sand and stone borers, timed and measured with the same equipment. Until an ultra-precise vessel turns up in a sealed, dated context, the lost-machine idea remains unsupported. Meanwhile the real achievement is plain to see: thousands of hours of patient, skilled work, repeated tens of thousands of times, in the first great age of Egyptian craft.

chunks.heading: The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older?
chunks.text: Impossible Megaliths The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older? Greater Vaults c. 612–30 BCE; Apis burials from Amenhotep III Awaiting discovery. Who made the Serapeum's giant boxes, when, and how precisely? The claim on the scales The Serapeum boxes were machined to modern precision by a lost technology and are older than the Apis burials. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Several boxes carry the names of Late Period kings, and the galleries, stelae and burial records form a dated sequence from the seventh century BCE onwards. The precision claim rests on spot checks with a 6-inch straightedge at a few places inside one or two boxes, never published as full measurements. Flat faces can be produced by hand lapping, and Late Period workshops made other superbly finished hard-stone sarcophagi. No box has been shown to be older than its gallery. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Guidebooks say simply that the boxes held bulls. That is well supported, but the confident tone hides real unknowns: we have no record of how boxes and lids were installed, no complete metrology survey, and little direct evidence of what each uninscribed box contained. The textbooks are right on who and when, and vague on how. What is solid The Serapeum was the burial place of the Apis bulls of Memphis for about 1,400 years, from Amenhotep III (14th century BCE) to the end of the Ptolemaic period. Mariette 1857; Dodson 2005 The Greater Vaults were begun under Psamtik I (664–610 BCE) and extended under the Ptolemies; 24 stone boxes remain in them. Mariette 1857 One box measured by Linant de Bellefonds is about 3.85 m long and 2.3 m wide, with a body of about 38 t and a lid of about 24 t. as reported from Linant de Bellefonds Some boxes carry royal inscriptions: Amasis II (red granite), Cambyses II (inscribed lid) and Khababash (year 2, c. 336 BCE). Mariette 1857 Hundreds of stelae from the site record Apis burials and visits, many dated to regnal years. Malinine, Posener & Vercoutter 1968 What is disputed How flat and square the inner surfaces really are, since no full independent survey of all boxes has been published. Exactly how the boxes were hollowed and how the lids were set on them underground. Whether any uninscribed box is older than the gallery it stands in. What time has hidden The Greater Vault boxes were robbed in antiquity; their original contents are largely lost. No written account of how the boxes were made or installed survives. Early excavation in the 1850s was poorly recorded by modern standards, and m

chunks.heading: The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older?: 01 Boxes in the dark
chunks.text: In 1850 the young French archaeologist Auguste Mariette saw the head of a sphinx sticking out of the sand at Saqqara. He followed an avenue of sphinxes to a buried temple, and in November 1851 he broke into a vast tunnel cut into the rock. Along it, in side chambers to left and right, stood enormous polished boxes of granite and basalt, each big enough to park a small car in, their lids pushed aside by robbers long before. The Serapeum is one of the most atmospheric places in Egypt, and one of the most argued about online. Visitors walk a lit gallery past boxes weighing sixty tonnes and more, set into chambers barely wider than they are, and ask two questions. How did anyone get them in there? And were they really made to hold the bodies of bulls? Top: a schematic plan of a long gallery entered from the left, with side chambers on both sides, each holding a small rectangle for a stone box, and later side galleries at the right end. Labels: main gallery begun under Psamtik I, extended under the Ptolemies, tunnels about 350 m in total, 24 boxes remain. Bottom: one box at 40 pixels per metre in side view, about 3.85 m long, and end view, about 2.3 m wide, with an approximate cavity, and a lid on each. A 1.7 m person stands beside them, reaching below the top of the box. Labels: lid about 24 tonnes and about 1 m thick; box about 38 tonnes, granite or basalt; total about 60–70 tonnes.

chunks.heading: The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older?: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The Apis was a living sacred bull kept at Memphis, the herald of the god Ptah. When it died it was mummified and buried with state ceremony, and a new Apis was sought. Bulls were buried at Saqqara from the reign of Amenhotep III in the fourteenth century BCE, first in separate tombs. Prince Khaemwaset, a son of Ramesses II, opened a shared gallery, the Lesser Vaults. The Greater Vaults, with the giant boxes, were begun under Psamtik I (664–610 BCE) and extended under the Ptolemies until the tunnels ran to about 350 m. Twenty-four boxes remain there, of red and grey granite, basalt and similar hard stones. One measured by the engineer Linant de Bellefonds is about 3.85 m long and 2.3 m wide, with a body of about 38 tonnes and a lid of about 24. Some carry royal names: a red granite box of Amasis II, a grey granite box of the Persian king Cambyses with an inscribed lid, and one of the short-lived ruler Khababash, dated to his second year, about 336 BCE. Hundreds of stelae left by priests and visitors record burials of individual bulls by year and reign. The site was also a place of pilgrimage. Above ground an avenue of sphinxes, probably laid out under Nectanebo I in the fourth century BCE, led to the temple, and Greek and Egyptian visitors left dedications for centuries. Under the Ptolemies the cult of Apis merged with Osiris into the god Serapis, whose name the whole complex still carries. A bull burial was a national event, attended by priests from across Egypt, and its date was worth recording in stone. The dating does not rest on one clue. Royal inscriptions on boxes, stelae dated to regnal years, the growth of the galleries from the older Lesser Vaults outward, and burial goods in the earlier tombs, including canopic jars and bovine bones, fit together into one sequ

chunks.heading: The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older?: 03 The challenge: surface-plate flatness
chunks.text: In 1995 the American engineer Christopher Dunn, a machinist by training, climbed into a box with a broken corner carrying a 6-inch precision straightedge rated to 0.0002 inch, about 5 microns. Laid against the inner wall, he reported, it showed no light, whichever way he turned it. A precision square seemed to sit true between lid and wall. He compared the surfaces to the surface plates used to calibrate machine-shop tools, and in Lost Technologies of Ancient Egypt (2010) argued that only machining could explain them. Others have gone further. Because the Greater Vault boxes were found without intact bull mummies, some suggest they were never bull coffins at all, that they are older than the tunnels and were reused, or that the rough royal cartouches on a few were later additions to much finer stonework. The strongest part of this case is simple: the logistics are staggering, and nobody wrote down how it was done. A 6-inch straightedge can tell you a patch is flat. It cannot tell you a box is.

chunks.heading: The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older?: 04 Testing the claims
chunks.text: Dunn's check was real but small: a few placements of a short straightedge inside one or two boxes, never published as a full survey. A surface can be locally flat in many places and still wander over its whole area, and other boxes show visibly uneven faces and rounded interior corners. Flatness itself is not a machine signature. Engineering surface plates were traditionally made by lapping, rubbing surfaces together with abrasive until the high spots wear away, which is a hand method that Egyptians used on hard stone with quartz sand. The dating evidence also runs one way. Boxes with the names of Amasis, Cambyses and Khababash sit in the same gallery system as the uninscribed ones, and the gallery itself was cut in the Late Period. Late Period workshops made other superbly finished hard-stone sarcophagi for kings and officials. The absence of intact bulls in the Greater Vaults is what ancient robbery predicts: the lids were pushed aside precisely so robbers could reach the valuables inside. There is a fair point buried in the challenge, though. Mainstream accounts rarely discuss the boxes as engineering at all, and the only published measurements of their surfaces come from a challenger with a straightedge. That is a gap Egyptology created, and one it could close with a week of modern scanning.

chunks.heading: The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older?: 05 How to move a sixty-tonne box
chunks.text: The engineering is still impressive. Granite boxes came from Aswan, probably roughed out at the quarry to save weight, then floated some 900 km downstream on barges. Egyptians routinely moved heavier loads: Hatshepsut's standing obelisk at Karnak weighs roughly 300 tonnes. At Saqqara a box would be dragged on a sledge over a timber track, down into the gallery and along it, hauled with ropes by teams of workers. Step 1 of 5. Quarry and hollow: at Aswan the box is cut and hollowed with dolerite pounders, copper saws and tube drills fed with sand. Quarry and hollow: at Aswan the box is cut and hollowed with dolerite pounders, copper saws and tube drills fed with sand. By barge: the box floats about 900 km down the Nile to Memphis. Down the gallery: on a sledge over a timber track, hauled with ropes. Turn and push: levers and rollers swing it sideways into its chamber. Burial: the mummified Apis is placed inside, the lid slid on and the chamber walled up. Left: a schematic strip of the Nile with Aswan at the bottom and Saqqara at the top, about 900 km downstream. Step 1: at Aswan a granite block is quarried and hollowed with pounders, copper saws, tube drills and sand. Step 2: the box travels downstream on a barge. Right: a plan of a gallery with a side chamber. Step 3: the box on a sledge is hauled down the gallery over a timber track. Step 4: levers swing the box into the side chamber. Step 5: the box sits in the chamber with its lid on, the Apis inside, and the chamber mouth sealed. The tight part is the turn into a side chamber. Levers, rollers and patient work can swing a box sideways a few centimetres at a time. How the lids were placed is less clear: they may have been set on props or sand and lowered after the burial. No ancient text describes the method, and the a

chunks.heading: The Serapeum Boxes: Tombs for Bulls, or Something Older?: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The Serapeum reopened in 2012 after a decade of conservation, and since 2020 a mission has worked to stabilise the older galleries. That creates an opportunity. A full, independent 3D scan of all 24 boxes, inside and out, with raw data released, would replace a quarter century of anecdotes with numbers. Tool marks inside the boxes, compared under magnification with dated Late Period sarcophagi, would show how the surfaces were finished. Dating mortar and debris in the chamber sealing walls, and the fill beneath the boxes, would test the idea of reuse. Until then, the evidence strongly supports the Late Period and Ptolemaic date and the Apis burials. The boxes deserve their fame as one of the heaviest and most precise stone projects of ancient Egypt, carried out by people whose working notes are lost.

chunks.heading: Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted
chunks.text: Impossible Megaliths Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted terraces c. last centuries BCE–1st millennium CE; 27,000-year claim retracted 2024 Awaiting discovery. Is there a human-made structure tens of thousands of years old inside Gunung Padang? The claim on the scales Gunung Padang contains a human-built pyramid whose construction began around 27,000 years ago. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The claim rests on radiocarbon dates from soil between rocks, with no tools, hearths, bones or unambiguous construction features in the dated layers. That is why the journal retracted the paper. Columnar andesite forms naturally, so arranged-looking columns are not in themselves evidence of building. The interior has not been excavated, so an older human phase cannot be ruled out, but nothing yet shows one. The evidence for the visible terraces supports a date within the last 2,500 years or so. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Mainstream statements that the hill is natural and the terraces are late are reasonable, but they rest on cores and surface work rather than a deep excavation, and the terrace dates themselves vary by centuries. The confident dismissal is a little ahead of the digging. Still, the burden lies with the extraordinary claim, and it has not met it. What is solid Gunung Padang is a megalithic site of five stone terraces at about 885 m above sea level, reached by a stairway of some 370 andesite steps. national heritage site records The terraces are built of natural columnar andesite, stone that forms long prisms as lava cools, taken from the hill and its surroundings. site surveys; Yondri Archaeologists date the surface terraces to roughly the last centuries BCE to the first millennium CE; published estimates range from the 2nd to the 8th century CE for main use. Yondri; Simanjuntak A 2023 paper in Archaeological Prospection claimed construction began 27,000–16,000 years ago; the journal retracted it in March 2024. Natawidjaja et al. 2023; retraction notice 2024 The retraction stated that the dated soil samples were not associated with any artefacts or features reliably interpreted as man-made. Archaeological Prospection 2024 What is disputed Whether any layer below the visible terraces is artificial, as Natawidjaja's team maintains. What the geophysical anomalies read as 'chambers' really are: cavities, loose rubble or natural features. How old the terraces themselves are, since estimates span most of a millennium. What time has hidden No deep, fully published archaeological excavation

chunks.heading: Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted: 01 A pyramid in the rainforest?
chunks.text: The first episode of Graham Hancock's Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse, released in November 2022, opens on a green hill in West Java. At the top, five terraces are paved and walled with long, angular stones, stacked like firewood, reached by a stairway of some 370 steps. Beside Hancock stands the Indonesian geologist Danny Hilman Natawidjaja, who believes the hill is not a hill at all but a pyramid, and that its oldest parts were built during the last Ice Age. A year later, in October 2023, Natawidjaja and eleven colleagues published that claim in a peer-reviewed journal, Archaeological Prospection. Headlines around the world announced the oldest pyramid on Earth, perhaps 27,000 years old. Five months after that, the journal retracted the paper. Gunung Padang is now a case study in how a real site, real data and a very big claim can come apart. The terraces are real and ancient. The question is what lies beneath them, and how to date it.

chunks.heading: Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: Gunung Padang, a name often translated as 'mountain of light', sits at about 885 m above sea level in Cianjur Regency. It was first recorded by a Dutch visitor in 1890 and listed by the geologist Rogier Verbeek the following year; the archaeologist N. J. Krom described it in 1914. Local farmers drew fresh attention to it in 1979, and it became a national site in 2014. The terraces are built from prisms of andesite, 1 to 3 m long with three to six sides. Such columns form naturally when lava cools and cracks, and the hill itself is made of this rock, so the builders had an abundant supply of ready-shaped stone. Indonesian archaeologists place the megalithic sanctuary in roughly the last centuries BCE to the first millennium CE: Lutfi Yondri has argued for the 2nd to 5th centuries CE, while Harry Truman Simanjuntak suggested the 6th to 8th centuries. Either way it is a major prehistoric monument of Southeast Asia. Walk the terraces and the site's purpose feels clear even without a written record. The stones mark out enclosures, paths and small platforms, oriented roughly towards the volcano Gede-Pangrango to the north. Megalithic terraced sanctuaries like this, built for gatherings and ancestor rites, are known elsewhere in the Sundanese and wider Austronesian world. Some of the columns are said to ring when struck, and local tradition treats the hill as a sacred place to this day.

chunks.heading: Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted: 03 The 27,000-year claim
chunks.text: Natawidjaja's team spent years drilling cores and imaging the hill with seismic waves, radar and electrical resistivity. They reported layers under the terraces that looked organised: columns set in rows, fine material between them that they read as mortar, and zones that behaved like cavities. In one borehole, about 32,000 litres of drilling water vanished into the hill. They then radiocarbon-dated soil from between the rocks at different depths and built a sequence. A natural lava hill, they proposed, was first sculpted between about 25,000 and 14,000 BCE; new layers were added around 7900–6100 BCE and 6000–5500 BCE; and the terraces visible today were built around 2000–1100 BCE. If right, it would be older than Göbekli Tepe by more than ten thousand years, and would place skilled builders in Java at the height of the Ice Age. Two cross-sections of the same hill side by side. Left, labelled claimed in 2023, paper retracted: bands from top to bottom marked terraces 2000–1100 BCE, 6000–5500 BCE, 7900–6100 BCE, and a large sculpted lava core 25,000–14,000 BCE, with dashed boxes labelled chambers and a dimension line for cores to about 30 m. Right, labelled mainstream reading: a small row of terrace stones on top of a grey natural andesite body filled with near-vertical columns, with small pockets of soil and clay in cracks. A box below explains that the dates came from soil between rocks, not tied to any reliably man-made artefact or feature, so they date the soil, not a building. The team's geophysical work is extensive, and the questions they raise are legitimate: why are there voids, why is soil deep in the hill so old, and why do some columns lie in orderly rows? Natawidjaja also points to what he reads as tool marks and a carved stone. He and his co-authors disagree

chunks.heading: Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted: 04 Why the paper was retracted
chunks.text: Soon after publication, archaeologists including Bill Farley of Southern Connecticut State University and Flint Dibble of Cardiff University raised concerns, and the publisher Wiley and the journal's editors investigated. On 18 March 2024 the paper was retracted. The notice was blunt. The radiocarbon dating was applied to soil samples that were not associated with any artifacts or features that could be reliably interpreted as anthropogenic or ‘man-made.’ Therefore, the interpretation that the site is an ancient pyramid built 9000 or more years ago is incorrect. The logic is easy to see with an everyday example, one the blog Southeast Asian Archaeology used: dating the soil under the Eiffel Tower would not tell you when the tower was built. Soil accumulates, and carbon gets into it from roots, rotting plants and water seeping down cracks, long before or long after anything is built on top. To date construction, you need something people made or used, sealed in a construction layer: charcoal from a hearth, a tool, a posthole. Step 1 of 5. Drill: cores are taken through the terraces into the hill. Drill: cores are taken through the terraces into the hill. Date: soil from between rocks at depth is radiocarbon-dated, giving ages up to about 27,000 years. Leap: the paper treats the soil's age as the age of a built layer, and so of a pyramid. Objection: the dated soil had no artefact or feature reliably made by people; carbon in soil can accumulate before or after any building. Better test: excavate and date charcoal, tools or hearths sealed inside a construction layer. A schematic drill core on the left: terrace stones and topsoil at the top, rubble with soil, andesite columns with clay in the cracks, and massive andesite at the bottom. Step 1: the core is drilled. Step 2: s

chunks.heading: Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted: 05 What the hill may still hide
chunks.text: None of this shows the interior is empty of human work; it means the evidence offered does not show it. The deep layers have been sampled only by narrow cores, never opened in a trench, and the 2014 excavations drew criticism from other archaeologists for how they were run. In a hot, wet climate, bone, wood and charcoal decay fast, so the traces that would settle the question may be scarce even if they exist. That is a real limit, and it cuts both ways: it weakens any confident claim that nothing is there. Fresh from the field: in August 2025 Indonesia's Ministry of Culture launched a new programme of excavation and restoration, led by the archaeologist Ali Akbar, one of the co-authors of the retracted paper, with a multidisciplinary team and more than a hundred local workers. By October 2025 the team reported collecting carbon samples from several terraces for dating. As of this writing we could not find peer-reviewed results from that work.

chunks.heading: Gunung Padang: The Pyramid That Was Retracted: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The test is straightforward to describe and hard to do well. Open a deep, stepped trench from the terraces into the hill, record every layer, invite independent specialists, and publish everything. If there is a built layer thousands of years old, it should contain things that people leave behind, such as charcoal from fires, flakes from stone tools, postholes, or surfaces that were walked on, and these can be dated directly. Luminescence dating can tell when a buried surface last saw sunlight. Until then, Gunung Padang is a genuine megalithic site of early Southeast Asia, perched on a natural volcanic hill whose depths are only partly known. The 27,000-year pyramid is not ruled out by a trench that nobody has dug, but it is not supported by the evidence published so far, and the journal that printed it has said so.

chunks.heading: Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan
chunks.text: Impossible Megaliths Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan Rock c. 20 million years old; last dry land c. 9,500–7,000 years ago Awaiting discovery. Is the Yonaguni formation a drowned monument, or a natural sandstone outcrop? The claim on the scales The Yonaguni formation was cut or shaped by people while it stood on dry land. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The rock is natural bedrock, and its flat terraces and square corners follow bedding planes and joints that also shape the dry coast nearby. The best-published analysis finds erosion enough to explain the forms. Kimura's worked stones and marks have not been independently studied in print. But the site has never been excavated, and people lived in the Ryukyus while it was dry, so human use cannot be ruled out. What is missing is evidence, not a reason to look. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Official bodies and most reference works state flatly that Yonaguni is natural. For the rock itself that confidence is earned. It is overconfident on the wider point: no one has excavated the terraces, the local sea-level history is only roughly known, and the drowned Ryukyu shelf, where Ice Age islanders surely camped, is almost untouched. 'Natural outcrop' is well supported; 'nothing human was ever here' is untested. What is solid The formation lies off Arakawabana on the south coast of Yonaguni, Japan's westernmost inhabited island, about 110 km east of Taiwan. Its top is roughly 5 m below the surface and its base about 25 m. Schoch 1999; Kimura's surveys It is cut into medium to very fine sandstones and mudstones of the Early Miocene Yaeyama Group, deposited about 20 million years ago, and it is joined to the bedrock rather than built from separate blocks. Geological mapping of the Yaeyama Group; Ogata et al. 2020 Global sea level was about 120 m lower at the height of the last Ice Age and rose fastest between about 15,000 and 7,000 years ago; on the global curve the base of the formation was last dry roughly 9,000–10,000 years ago and the top roughly 7,000 years ago. Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS People were living in the Ryukyu islands by about 30,000 years ago, and in 2019 a team paddled a replica dugout canoe 225 km from Taiwan to Yonaguni in over 45 hours. Kaifu et al. 2025, Science Advances Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs and Okinawa Prefecture do not list the formation as a cultural property. Official heritage listings What is disputed Whether the right angles, flat terraces, 'steps' and trench-like channels need human tools, or follow natural bedd

chunks.heading: Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan: 01 A staircase in the Kuroshio
chunks.text: In 1986 Kihachiro Aratake, a diving instructor on Yonaguni, went looking for hammerhead sharks off the island's southern cape. What he found instead was stone: broad flat terraces dropping in giant steps into blue water, walls that met at crisp corners, and a narrow trench running between cliff-like faces. Yonaguni is the last island in the Japanese chain before Taiwan, swept by the warm, fast Kuroshio current. On a clear day the whole formation is visible from the surface, a pale stepped mass sinking from about 5 m to about 25 m. Within a few years it had a name, the Yonaguni Monument, and a champion. Masaaki Kimura, a marine geologist at the University of the Ryukyus, began diving and mapping it and became convinced that he was looking at a building: a terraced platform, perhaps a castle or a ceremonial site, carved by people when the sea was lower and later drowned. The question it raises is exactly the one this site cares about. If Ice Age coastlines held cultures that we have never seen because the sea took them, where better to look than a place like this? If the sea swallowed the Ice Age coast, a drowned staircase at the edge of Japan is exactly where you would hope to find its builders.

chunks.heading: Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan: 02 What the rock and the sea tell us
chunks.text: Some things are not in dispute. The formation is not built of separate blocks hauled into place; it is part of the bedrock, cut into sandstones and mudstones of the Yaeyama Group, laid down on an ancient seabed about 20 million years ago. Those layers are flat and thin, and they are crossed by sets of vertical cracks, called joints, that run in straight lines across the area. That combination matters, because it is how nature makes shapes that look designed. The other certainty is the sea. At the peak of the last Ice Age, about 20,000 years ago, so much water was locked in ice sheets that global sea level stood roughly 120 m lower than today. As the ice melted the sea rose, fastest between about 15,000 and 7,000 years ago. Read against the global curve, the base of the formation at about 25 m was last dry land roughly 9,000 to 10,000 years ago, and the top terrace at about 5 m went under roughly 7,000 years ago. The drawing below steps through that drowning. Step 1 of 5. 20,000 years ago, at the height of the last Ice Age, the sea is about 120 m lower. The sandstone outcrop is a dry hillside above a coastal plain. 20,000 years ago, at the height of the last Ice Age, the sea is about 120 m lower. The sandstone outcrop is a dry hillside above a coastal plain. About 10,500 years ago the sea is still roughly 35 to 45 m lower. The whole formation stands on dry land. Kimura's first estimate put its builders about here. About 9,500 years ago the rising sea reaches the base platform, now 25 m deep, and waves begin working on the lowest ledges. About 7,000 years ago the top terrace, now 5 m deep, goes under. From here on the formation is entirely submarine. Today the top lies about 5 m down and the base about 25 m. Kimura's later date of 2,000 to 3,000 years ago would require ab

chunks.heading: Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan: 03 The case for a monument
chunks.text: Kimura's case, built over hundreds of dives, rests on the whole ensemble. He describes a main terrace with steps leading up to it, a straight channel he reads as a drainage ditch or road, two tall parallel slabs standing side by side, a 'triangle pool', and a rock he compares to a carved face. He has reported stones that look worked and incised marks that he compares with signs used later in the Ryukyus. In his view nature might make one of these features, but not all of them together in one place. His first estimate for the builders was about 10,000 years ago. At the Pacific Science Congress in Okinawa in 2007 he proposed instead that the site was shaped 2,000 to 3,000 years ago and later sank through earthquakes and subsidence. Graham Hancock dived Yonaguni repeatedly while writing Underworld (2002), his survey of coastlines drowned at the end of the Ice Age. His position is more cautious than the popular image of it. He accepted that the core of the formation is natural rock and argued that people may have cut it back, levelled it and added to it, turning an outcrop into a place of ceremony. That reading, a natural feature improved by human hands, is how many undisputed sacred sites began. The strongest part of the challengers' case is not a single right angle. It is context. People reached the Ryukyu islands at least 30,000 years ago, crossing open sea to do it. For most of the time they lived here, the coastline lay far below today's. The site has been photographed and filmed, but it has never been excavated.

chunks.heading: Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan: 04 The case for nature
chunks.text: Here the story takes a turn that surprises many readers. The most influential sceptic is himself a challenger of the mainstream. Robert Schoch, the Boston University geologist famous for arguing that the Great Sphinx is far older than Egyptologists allow, dived Yonaguni in 1997 and 1998. He came up convinced that it was most likely natural. The rocks, he wrote, contain numerous well-defined parallel bedding planes crossed by parallel joints, and it is along those natural fractures that the rectangular forms break away. Waves pounding the jointed sandstone as the sea rose would strip blocks off layer by layer, leaving steps and terraces behind. Others agree. The German geologist Wolf Wichmann studied the site in 1999 and 2001 and found natural processes enough. Patrick Nunn, a geographer of Pacific coasts, notes the same step-and-terrace forms in the sandstone along Yonaguni's dry shore. In 2020 a Japanese team led by Takayuki Ogata analysed the submarine topography and concluded that weathering and erosion acting on bedding and linear joints can explain the landform. The Japanese government does not list it as a heritage site. The most influential sceptic of the Yonaguni monument is Robert Schoch, the geologist who argues the Sphinx is thousands of years older than Egyptologists allow. The sceptics also point to what is missing. There are no coursed walls of separate blocks, no quarry debris laid out in a pattern, no dated charcoal, no tools found in place. The loose blocks lie where gravity dropped them. Kimura's worked stones and marks have not been published in a way that other specialists can test.

chunks.heading: Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan: 05 What the sea has hidden
chunks.text: Even if the formation is natural, the bigger question behind it is a good one. The people who crossed to the Ryukyus 30,000 years ago were skilled mariners, and their beaches, camps and landing places now lie under tens of metres of water. On land, archaeologists have found their traces in caves on Okinawa and Ishigaki. Offshore, almost no one has looked, and a coast drowned by 100 m of rising sea is hard to search. Wood rots, hearths wash out, and currents like the Kuroshio scour the seabed clean. In 2019 a Japanese and Taiwanese team led by Yousuke Kaifu carved a 7.5 m dugout canoe from a single cedar trunk with replica stone-age tools and paddled it from eastern Taiwan across the Kuroshio to Yonaguni, 225 km in over 45 hours, navigating by sun, stars and swell. Published in Science Advances in 2025, the voyage shows that Ice Age people could have made exactly this crossing on purpose. So the Yonaguni debate has two layers. On the first, whether this particular rock was carved, the evidence leans heavily towards nature. On the second, whether drowned Ice Age coasts in this region held human settlements we have never seen, the answer is almost certainly yes, and the search has barely begun.

chunks.heading: Yonaguni: A Drowned Staircase Off Japan: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Arguments from photographs will not end this. Digging will. The channels and lower terraces hold sediment that has sat there since the sea arrived. If people worked the rock while it was dry, their debris, flakes, charcoal and broken tools, should lie at the base of that sediment, and radiocarbon could date it. A complete 3D model of the formation, compared feature by feature with the same sandstone exposed on the island, would show whether anything underwater is truly unlike what waves make on land. Alleged tool marks can be sampled and examined under the microscope beside marks made by waves, boring shellfish and known tools. If dated tools or hearths turn up in the sediment: a human site, at least in part. If the underwater forms match the dry-land outcrops in every respect and the sediments are sterile: a beautiful natural monument, and a clue to where not to look. Either way: a measured local sea-level history for Yonaguni, which would pin down when each terrace was last dry. Until then, Yonaguni is best described as what it certainly is: one of the most striking underwater landscapes on Earth, on a coast that Ice Age sailors knew, still waiting for the excavation that could change its story.

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?
chunks.text: Impossible Megaliths Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea? Setting: end of the Dvapara Yuga; finds: late 2nd millennium BCE to medieval Awaiting discovery. Does a city from the age of the Mahabharata lie under the sea off Gujarat? The claim on the scales A city of great antiquity, from the age of the Mahabharata or earlier, lies submerged off Dwarka or in the Gulf of Khambhat. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Off Dwarka, the dated evidence points to a historic harbour: anchors of early historic to medieval types and blocks consistent with jetties, in water that was already sea by 1500 BCE. In the Gulf of Khambhat, the sonar images have not been tested by excavation, the finds were dredged without context, and the wood date shows only that the drowned land surface is old. A drowned ancient settlement there is geologically plausible, but it has not been demonstrated. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Standard accounts rightly reject the headline claims: no Mahabharata-era city has been dated under the sea. But they tend to say little about how poorly explored this coast is. The Gulf of Khambhat was dry land when early villages were spreading across the region, and no one has excavated its drowned surface. Dismissing Khambhat's methods is fair; treating the whole drowned coast as empty is not. What is solid Underwater surveys off Dwarka by the National Institute of Oceanography found dressed stone blocks, semicircular structures and well over a hundred stone anchors, at depths of roughly 3–16 m. Gaur, Sundaresh and Tripati 2004, Current Science The anchor types span from the early historic period to medieval times, the kinds used by Indian Ocean traders; the same authors read the site as a long-lived harbour. Gaur, Sundaresh and Tripati 2004 Onshore excavations beneath and beside modern Dwarka found occupation going back about two thousand years; the nearby island of Bet Dwarka has a Late Harappan settlement with a thermoluminescence date of about 1570 BCE. Deccan College 1963; ASI; Rao 1999 In 2001 the National Institute of Ocean Technology reported geometric features on sonar 30–40 m deep in the Gulf of Khambhat; a piece of dredged wood was later radiocarbon dated to roughly 7500–7200 BCE. NIOT reports; announcement of 19 May 2001 Global sea level was roughly 30–40 m lower around 9,500 years ago and close to today's level by about 1500 BCE. Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS What is disputed Whether S. R. Rao's offshore 'fort walls' at Dwarka date to the 2nd millennium BCE, as he argued, or belong to a later

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. After Krishna's departure the ocean flooded Dvaraka (Mahabharata, Mausala Parva 7). Awaiting discovery Sea level and coastline change along Gujarat are real, and underwater stone structures off Dwarka are reported; none is securely dated to the Mahabharata age.

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?: 01 The city the ocean took back
chunks.text: On the western tip of the Saurashtra peninsula, where the Gomti creek meets the Arabian Sea, the tall spire of the Dwarkadhish temple rises over one of the holiest towns in India. Pilgrims come here because of Krishna. In the Mahabharata and the later Harivamsa and Bhagavata Purana, Krishna leads his Yadava people to the western sea and founds Dvaraka, the city of gates, splendid with gold and jewels. After his death, the tradition says, the sea took it back. After all the people had set out, the ocean, that home of sharks and alligators, flooded Dvaraka, which still teemed with wealth of every kind, with its waters. In the epic, the drowning happens as Arjuna leads the survivors away, the waves following behind them. It is one of the most vivid flood images in any sacred text, and it raises an obvious question. The coast of Gujarat really has changed. The sea around India stood far lower in the Ice Age and has eaten into this shore within recorded history. Could divers find Krishna's city?

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?: 02 What the divers found off Dwarka
chunks.text: From the 1980s the archaeologist S. R. Rao, famous for excavating the Harappan port of Lothal, led marine surveys off Dwarka for the National Institute of Oceanography in Goa. His teams mapped lines of stone blocks and rounded structures in the shallow sea, which Rao read as the walls and bastions of a fortified city of around the 15th century BCE. His book The Lost City of Dvaraka (1999) made the case to the public, and the finds caused a sensation. Later work by the same institute, led by A. S. Gaur, kept surveying and came to a more cautious view. The finds lie mostly between about 3 and 16 m deep. Among them are well over a hundred stone anchors, of types used by ships over a long span, from the early historic period into medieval times, including grapnel-style anchors known from Indian Ocean trade. Dressed blocks look more like the parts of jetties and landing stages than city walls. In 2004 the team summarised the site in Current Science as an ancient harbour, submerged largely through coastal erosion. Anchors are dropped from ships. Finding them on the seabed shows a busy harbour, not a drowned city. On land, excavations beside the temple in 1963 and later found occupation going back about two thousand years. On Bet Dwarka, an island in the bay, excavators found a Late Harappan settlement with a thermoluminescence date of about 1570 BCE. So people were living on this coast in the 2nd millennium BCE. What has not been found is a dated city of that age under the water.

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?: 03 Reading the depth
chunks.text: The simplest test of a drowned-city claim is the depth of the finds and the sea-level history. Step through the drawing to see how that works for both of Gujarat's underwater claims. Step 1 of 5. Where the finds lie: blocks and stone anchors off Dwarka at about 3–16 m; sonar features and dredged finds in the Gulf of Khambhat at 30–40 m. Where the finds lie: blocks and stone anchors off Dwarka at about 3–16 m; sonar features and dredged finds in the Gulf of Khambhat at 30–40 m. Around 1500 BCE, the age often proposed for Krishna's Dvaraka, the sea stood within a few metres of today, so the deeper Dwarka finds were already under water unless the land sank. Anchors belong under water. Off Dwarka their types range from the early historic period to medieval times: the signature of a long-used harbour. Around 9,500 years ago the sea was 30–40 m lower, so the Khambhat seabed was dry land. Wood dated to about 7500 BCE fits that drowned surface. But the Khambhat finds were dredged, not excavated: without layers and context, a date on wood cannot show a city. Two side-by-side seabed profiles under a shared depth ruler from 0 to 40 m. Left, off Dwarka: the town and a temple on land, and a seabed sloping down to about 20 m, with small triangular stone anchors and blocks scattered between about 3 and 16 m deep. Right, the Gulf of Khambhat: a flat seabed at 33 to 38 m, with a dashed zigzag marking the sonar 'grid'. Step 2 adds a thin band near the surface on the left: around 1500 BCE the sea was within a few metres of today. Step 3 notes that anchors belong under water, with types from early historic to medieval times. Step 4 draws a line at about 35 m on the right: 9,500 years ago the sea was 30 to 40 m lower, and a piece of wood dated about 7500 BCE lies on the old surface. Step 5

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?: 04 The Gulf of Khambhat: a lost city at 40 m?
chunks.text: The bigger claim came from the other side of the peninsula. On 19 May 2001 India's education minister, Murli Manohar Joshi, announced that the National Institute of Ocean Technology, surveying pollution in the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay), had found regular, geometric structures on sonar about 20 km off the coast, at depths of 30–40 m. Dredging brought up pottery fragments, stones that looked worked, bone, and a piece of wood. The wood was radiocarbon dated to roughly 7500–7200 BCE, some 9,500 years ago. The implications were enormous: a settlement thousands of years older than the Indus cities, drowned by the rising sea. NIOT geologist S. Badrinarayan became its leading advocate, and Graham Hancock featured it prominently in his book Underworld (2002) as potential evidence of the flooded kingdoms of the Ice Age. The geology behind the idea is sound. At 30–40 m depth, the Khambhat seabed was dry land until roughly 9,000–10,000 years ago, a broad plain crossed by rivers. The critics' objections are about method, not imagination. Dredging scoops material from the seabed without recording where or in what layer it lay, so a potsherd and a piece of wood from the same bucket need not be the same age. The archaeologist D. P. Agrawal and others pointed out that a date on wood dates the tree, not any building. Some 'artefacts' may be natural stones shaped by currents, and regular patterns on sonar can be produced by sediment waves and processing.

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?: 05 What the sea hides
chunks.text: Here the challengers' strongest point deserves full weight. When the Ice Age ended, the sea rose by about 120 m worldwide. Along western India that drowned a wide coastal shelf, including the whole Gulf of Khambhat, just as farming and settled life were spreading through the wider region. People must have lived on those plains, along those rivers. Their camps and villages are now under tens of metres of turbid water, swept by some of the strongest tides in the Indian Ocean. No one has yet carried out a controlled excavation of a single drowned site there. That is a real gap in our picture of South Asian prehistory, and the Khambhat announcement, whatever its flaws, pointed at it. The fair conclusion is double. The specific claim of a planned city at 40 m remains untested and, as presented, is weakly supported. The broader idea that drowned settlements lie under the Gulf is geologically reasonable and archaeologically unexplored. In February 2025 the Archaeological Survey of India's revived Underwater Archaeology Wing began new exploration off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka, led by Alok Tripathi, with a team of five that included three women archaeologists, following earlier ASI work there in 2005–2007. Its results have not yet been published.

chunks.heading: Dwarka: Krishna's City Under the Sea?: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Dwarka's offshore puzzle could be moved forward by dating material sealed inside the structures themselves, such as mortar, wood or charcoal, rather than objects lying on them. For Khambhat, the need is simpler and harder: dive, or core, and excavate. Sediment cores across the drowned plain would map its old land surface and show whether any occupation layers lie within it. A single excavated trench on one of the sonar features, with finds recorded in place and dated, would do more than two decades of argument. For believers, Dvaraka's sanctity does not depend on sonar. For history, the question is still open in an interesting way: not whether the Mahabharata's golden city has been found, which it has not, but what the drowned coasts of Gujarat really hold.

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?
chunks.text: Impossible Megaliths Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea? Setting: Treta Yuga; geology: dry land in the Ice Age, drowned c. 8,500–7,000 years ago Awaiting discovery. Is Adam's Bridge a human-made causeway, or a ridge built by the sea? The claim on the scales Adam's Bridge is, in whole or in part, a human-built causeway. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established All published mapping and geophysics describe a natural ridge: a continuation of the land tips, built of sand, beachrock and coral, drowned by the post-glacial sea and partly re-exposed as sea level settled. No placed stones, construction layers or artefacts have been reported in peer-reviewed work. The ridge has never been systematically cored or excavated, so a human addition on a natural core has not been tested, but there is no positive evidence for one. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Scientific summaries say confidently that the ridge is natural, and the geology strongly supports that for its core. Where they go too far is in implying the question is fully closed: there is still no published, systematic dating of the ridge's surface layers, and no excavation. 'Natural ridge, no evidence of construction' is the honest wording, not 'natural in every part, case closed'. What is solid A chain of limestone and sand shoals, sandbanks and small islands runs about 48 km from Pamban Island to Mannar Island; the core ridge between Dhanushkodi and Talaimannar is about 30 km long, mostly 1–3 m under water. Survey of India charts; Dandabathula et al. 2024 Laser bathymetry from NASA's ICESat-2 satellite mapped the ridge in detail in 2024 and found almost all of it submerged, interpreting it as a submarine continuation of the two land tips. Dandabathula et al. 2024, Scientific Reports Seismic profiling shows the Palk Strait was largely land, with freshwater lakes, during the last Ice Age; the sea began to flood it around 8,500 years ago, and from about 7,000 years ago it could not be crossed on foot. Dubey et al. 2023, Quaternary Research Records of the Ramanathaswamy temple at Rameswaram say storms broke a walkable link in 1480 CE. Temple records, as cited in Adam's Bridge literature In 2007 the Archaeological Survey of India told the Supreme Court there was no historical proof that the bridge had been built; the government withdrew the affidavit within days after political protest. Supreme Court proceedings, September 2007 What is disputed Whether any part of the ridge carries placed stones or other signs of human building, on top of its natural

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. An army built a bridge of rocks across the sea to Lanka (Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda). Awaiting discovery Adam's Bridge is a chain of shoals and sandbanks; studies so far read it as natural. A causeway laid on top of a natural ridge has not been tested by excavation.

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?: 01 A line across the sea
chunks.text: Look at a satellite image of the narrow sea between India and Sri Lanka and you see something that looks drawn with a ruler: a pale, broken line of shoals running from the tip of Pamban Island to Mannar. Pilgrims at Rameswaram call it Rama Setu, Rama's Bridge. Many maps call it Adam's Bridge, after a tradition that Adam crossed here from Sri Lanka, whose Adam's Peak bears a footprint revered by several faiths. Either way, the line invites the question: did someone build this? In the Ramayana, the demon king Ravana carries Sita off to Lanka. Rama and his allies, the vanaras, reach the shore and face the sea. The ocean god advises that Nala, son of the divine craftsman Vishvakarma, can bridge it. The army hurls trees and rocks into the water and in five days the causeway is complete. Then the great bridge of wondrous strength / Was built, a hundred leagues in length. / Rocks huge as autumn clouds bound fast / With cordage from the shore were cast The epic's geography is poetic and its hundred leagues are far longer than the real strait. Scholars also note that the identification of Ravana's Lanka with the island of Sri Lanka is not explicit in the earliest text and appears in inscriptions from later centuries. But the belief that this ridge is Rama's bridge is centuries old, and in 2007 it became the centre of a national argument.

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?: 02 What the seabed shows
chunks.text: The ridge is not a single wall but a chain of sandbanks, shoals and low sand islands, about 48 km from Pamban to Mannar, with a core ridge of about 30 km between Dhanushkodi and Talaimannar. Most of it lies 1–3 m under water. Beneath the loose sand are layers of beachrock and calcareous sandstone, sand cemented by carbonate close to sea level, and coral. India's space agency has mapped more than a hundred small patch reefs along it. In 2024 a team from India's National Remote Sensing Centre used laser pulses from NASA's ICESat-2 satellite, which can see a few metres into clear water, to build a detailed elevation model of the whole ridge. They found almost all of it submerged and interpreted it as the underwater continuation of the land at Dhanushkodi and Talaimannar, shaped by currents and sea-level change. A year earlier, a seismic study led by K. M. Dubey of the National Institute of Oceanography looked beneath the seabed and traced buried river channels and old land surfaces. Step 1 of 5. 20,000 years ago, at the height of the last Ice Age, the sea is about 120 m lower. The Palk Strait is land, with rivers and freshwater lakes. 20,000 years ago, at the height of the last Ice Age, the sea is about 120 m lower. The Palk Strait is land, with rivers and freshwater lakes. About 8,500 years ago the rising sea starts to flood the strait, first through the lowest gaps. By about 7,000 years ago the ridge is drowned. From now on the strait cannot be crossed on foot. From about 5,000 years ago the sea settles slightly lower. Sand builds up on the cemented beachrock and small cays re-emerge. Temple records say storms broke the last walkable link in 1480 CE. In 2024 ICESat-2's laser mapped the ridge: almost all of it now lies under shallow water. A long side profile of Adam's Br

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?: 03 2007: when a shoal became a political storm
chunks.text: Ships sailing between India's west and east coasts must go right round Sri Lanka, because the Palk Strait and Adam's Bridge are too shallow. In 2005 the Indian government approved the Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project to dredge a channel through, cutting voyages by hundreds of kilometres. One proposed route cut across the ridge. Protests followed. Political parties and religious groups said the canal would destroy a sacred structure built by Rama. In September 2007 the Archaeological Survey of India filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court saying there was no historical evidence that the bridge had been built by Rama. The reaction was so fierce that the government withdrew the affidavit within days. The project stalled and the route has never been dug. In later years the government told the court it would explore alternatives that avoided the ridge. The question of who built the ridge was never really about geology alone. It was about who has the authority to say what a sacred landscape is. Satellite images, including some from NASA, were widely shared as evidence of a man-made bridge. NASA itself responded that its images might be real, but the interpretation was not its own: remote sensing shows the shape of a feature, not whether humans made it.

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?: 04 The case for a causeway
chunks.text: Advocates of Rama Setu, among them the politician Subramanian Swamy, who went to the Supreme Court to have the ridge protected, make a case in several parts. The ridge runs in a remarkably straight, narrow line between the two closest points of land. It lies exactly where the epic places the crossing. Temple records at Rameswaram say it could be walked until storms broke it in 1480. Some writers argue that boulders on the shoals sit on younger sand, which would suggest they were carried in rather than formed there, and in 2017 an American television promotion aired that argument to a large audience. The most reasonable version of the idea does not require an army to have built 30 km of seabed. It proposes that people piled stones along an existing natural shoal to make a crossing easier, turning a line of fords into a causeway. That kind of improvement to a natural feature is common in human history, and it would be hard to detect from satellites alone. The claim that stones float also has a real basis: pumice and porous coral do float, and floating stones are displayed at temples in Rameswaram.

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?: 05 What time and the sea have hidden
chunks.text: The ridge is a restless place. Monsoon storms from both sides move sand constantly, cays appear and vanish, and cyclones reshape the shallows. Any small stone setting or trackway would be buried, scattered or rebuilt by nature within decades. At the same time, the most useful evidence, the internal structure and age of the ridge, lies below the surface and has never been cored along its length. No systematic radiometric dating of the ridge's sand, beachrock and coral has yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal, and claims about rocks being older than the sand beneath them have not been published in a form others can check. There is also a deeper human history here. People lived in Sri Lanka and southern India through the Ice Age, when the two were joined by land. Dubey and colleagues suggest that from the early Holocene, as the strait flooded, crossing would have needed boats or other aids. The ridge may well have been a landmark, a fishing ground and a fording route for thousands of years, sacred long before anyone wrote it down.

chunks.heading: Rama Setu: A Bridge Built by an Army or by the Sea?: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The tests are straightforward, though costly and politically delicate. A line of drilled cores along and across the ridge, dated by radiocarbon on shells and coral and by luminescence on sand, would show how and when the ridge built up. A diving survey could map any boulders and test whether they are embedded in the natural beachrock, as natural blocks would be, or rest loose on sand as placed stones might. Petrographic analysis could show whether any stone came from far away. India's authorities approved underwater study of the ridge in 2021; full publication of dated results would help everyone. For now the evidence points one way: a natural ridge, drowned by the rising sea and partly returned by it. That does not diminish its meaning. For millions of people, Rama Setu is sacred because of what it represents, and that has never depended on who laid the stones.

chunks.heading: Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due
chunks.text: Impossible Megaliths Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due Great Pyramid c. 2560 BCE; Nazca lines c. 400 BCE–600 CE; Pakal buried 683 CE Ruled out. Did ancient monuments need help from visitors from space? The claim on the scales Monuments such as the Giza pyramids, the Nazca lines and Pakal's tomb lid required, or depict, help from extraterrestrial visitors. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established For each of the classic examples the evidence points directly to the human builders: Merer's logbook, the Giza workers' town and harbour, the stone-clearing technique and pottery motifs of Nazca, and the named king and standard iconography of the Pakal lid. The alien readings require ignoring or misreading that evidence. Some construction methods are still debated, but those debates are between human techniques, and no physical trace of visitors has ever been found. Textbook confidence presented as settled fact Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks are right, and confident, about who built these monuments. They are sometimes overconfident about how: the lifting of the Great Pyramid's upper courses and the purpose of the Nazca lines are still argued among specialists, and diagrams of a single ramp can look more certain than they are. Saying so openly would take the wind out of alien claims, not feed them. What is solid Papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea include the logbook of an official named Merer, recording his crew's boat trips carrying limestone from the Tura quarries to Giza for Khufu's pyramid. Tallet 2017; Tallet and Lehner 2021 Excavations at Giza found a workers' town with bakeries and breweries and a cemetery of pyramid builders, and a now-buried Nile branch, the Ahramat, ran along the pyramid fields. Lehner 1997; Ghoneim et al. 2024 The Nazca lines were made by clearing dark, weathered stones to expose paler ground; the designs match motifs on Nazca pottery, and an AI-assisted survey in 2024 added 303 new figurative geoglyphs, many small ones beside footpaths. Aveni 1990; Sakai et al. 2024, PNAS The Palenque sarcophagus lid names K'inich Janaab' Pakal, who died in 683 CE, and shows him at the entrance to the underworld beneath the World Tree, in standard Maya religious imagery. Schele and Freidel 1990 Erich von Däniken's Erinnerungen an die Zukunft (1968), published in English as Chariots of the Gods?, launched the modern ancient-astronaut idea; he died in January 2026 at the age of 90. Publisher records; obituaries 2026 What is disputed Exactly how the upper courses of the Great Pyramid were raised: straight, spi

chunks.heading: Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due: 01 The book that sent the gods into orbit
chunks.text: In 1968 a Swiss hotel manager named Erich von Däniken published a book called Erinnerungen an die Zukunft, 'Memories of the Future'. In English it became Chariots of the Gods?, question mark included. Its argument was simple and exciting. Ancient peoples, he said, could not have built the pyramids, drawn giant figures in the Peruvian desert or carved certain images on their own. The gods who descended from the sky in their myths were real visitors from other worlds, and their technology left traces that archaeologists refused to see. The book and its sequels sold in the tens of millions across dozens of languages, and its ideas spread through documentaries and, from 2009, the long-running television series Ancient Aliens. Von Däniken died in January 2026, aged 90, still convinced. His challenge deserves a fair answer, because the big question behind it is one this site cares about: have we underestimated the past? The answer, in his three most famous cases, is yes. But not in the way he meant. Von Däniken asked whether we had underestimated the ancients. We had. The mistake was to hand their achievements to someone else.

chunks.heading: Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due: 02 The builders' own receipts
chunks.text: Start at Giza. The ancient-astronaut case said the Egyptians lacked the tools, organisation and know-how to raise the Great Pyramid. Since then, archaeology has filled in the human story in remarkable detail. Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass excavated a whole town beside the pyramids, with bakeries, breweries, storerooms and houses, and a cemetery where pyramid builders were buried with honour, some with healed injuries showing they received medical care. In 2013 Pierre Tallet's team, digging at the ancient harbour of Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea, found the oldest inscribed papyri known. Among them is the logbook of an inspector named Merer. For months, day by day, he recorded his crew of about forty men sailing blocks of fine limestone from the quarries at Tura, across the Nile valley, to Giza for the casing of Khufu's pyramid. In 2024 Eman Ghoneim and colleagues mapped a buried branch of the Nile, which they called the Ahramat branch, running along the edge of the desert beside dozens of pyramids, the waterway that made such deliveries possible. Merer's diary is written in hieratic, the cursive form of Egyptian script, and dated to the later years of Khufu's reign. It names the harbour at Giza, the quarry at Tura and the official in charge, Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother. It is not a description of the pyramid; it is the paperwork of the project, which is exactly why it is so convincing.

chunks.heading: Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due: 03 Lines in the desert
chunks.text: On the high desert plain between the Nazca and Ingenio rivers in southern Peru, hundreds of straight lines, trapezoids and spirals, and dozens of large animal and plant figures, have survived for up to two thousand years. Von Däniken suggested the long straight lines looked like runways for alien craft. The Nazca ground tells a simpler story. Its surface is a desert pavement of dark, weathered stones over paler silt and sand. Rake the stones aside and a pale line appears. Rain almost never falls, so the marks survive. Step 1 of 5. The Nazca pampa is covered with dark, weathered stones lying on paler silt and sand. It almost never rains, so marks made here can last for centuries. The Nazca pampa is covered with dark, weathered stones lying on paler silt and sand. It almost never rains, so marks made here can last for centuries. Draw the design small, on a grid. The same motifs appear on Nazca pottery and textiles. Scale it up on the ground with stakes and cord, copying the grid square by square. Remains of wooden stakes have been found at Nazca. Rake the dark stones aside along the cord and pile them at the edges. The pale ground underneath forms the line. Many figures are a single continuous line, a path that can be walked. Small figures found in 2024 sit beside footpaths, meant to be seen from the ground. Three panels. Bottom left, a cross-section of the Nazca desert: a layer of dark pebbles lying on pale silt and sand. Top left, a small bird-shaped design drawn on a six-by-six grid. Right, a larger dark desert patch with the same six-by-six grid scaled up. Step 1 shows the desert section. Step 2 shows the small sketch on its grid. Step 3 adds an arrow from the sketch to the large grid, where stakes mark each corner of the bird and a dashed cord joins them. Step 4 turn

chunks.heading: Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due: 04 The king who fell into the underworld
chunks.text: In 1952 the Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier, clearing a rubble-filled stairway inside the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque, reached a vaulted tomb. Inside lay a carved stone sarcophagus. Its lid shows a man reclining over a great open maw, with a cross-shaped tree rising above him topped by a bird. Von Däniken, viewing the lid sideways, saw an astronaut leaning forward at the controls of a rocket, with exhaust flames beneath. Maya scholars, who from the 1970s onward learned to read Maya inscriptions, see something quite different and clearly labelled. The text around the lid names K'inich Janaab' Pakal, king of Palenque, born in 603 CE and died in 683 CE, and lists his ancestors. The 'rocket' is the World Tree, the axis linking heavens, earth and underworld, a motif carved across the Maya world. The 'flames' are the jaws of the underworld into which the dead king descends, to be reborn like the maize god. Read in its own language, the lid is a statement of royal death and resurrection, and one of the finest carvings of the ancient Americas.

chunks.heading: Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due: 05 What is genuinely still unexplained
chunks.text: Dismissing aliens does not mean that every question is answered, and it is worth being honest about the real open problems, because they are more interesting than the myths. The Great Pyramid's upper courses: no one knows for certain how the top third was built. Straight, spiral and internal ramp models all have supporters. In 2018 a steep ramp with post holes and stairs was found at the Hatnub alabaster quarries, showing one sophisticated Old Kingdom hauling system. Hidden spaces: in 2017 muon imaging revealed a large void above the Grand Gallery, and in 2023 a corridor behind the north face was confirmed. Their purpose is unknown. Precision in hard stone: some Egyptian stone vessels and Andean polygonal walls are finished with remarkable accuracy. Experimental work shows human methods (abrasives, pounding, repeated fitting), but full-scale time and labour costs are still argued. Puma Punku's standardised andesite blocks in Bolivia look machine-made to many visitors. Alexei Vranich's 2018 3D-printed reconstruction suggests modular design with templates, a clever human solution. Other famous 'anomalies' are simple misreadings. The 'helicopter' at the temple of Seti I in Abydos is a palimpsest: hieroglyphs of one royal title were plastered and recarved with another, and the overlap looks like a machine. The Nazca 'astronaut' is a figure with an owl-like face on a hillside, one of several human figures there.

chunks.heading: Ancient Astronauts: Credit Where Credit Is Due: 06 Why the credit matters
chunks.text: Many archaeologists point out an uncomfortable pattern in ancient-astronaut writing: the monuments said to need outside help are overwhelmingly those built by Egyptians, Maya, Andean and other non-European peoples. The effect, whatever the intention, is to take their greatest achievements away from them. The evidence gives those achievements back: to Merer and his crew, to the Nazca families sweeping lines across the pampa, to the sculptors who carved Pakal's lid. Graham Hancock, often lumped together with von Däniken, explicitly rejects aliens and argues instead for a lost human civilisation, which is at least a claim about human ability. The question of what ancient people knew, and how much was lost, remains open and worth asking. The tests are the same as for any claim: an artefact of non-human manufacture in a sealed ancient layer would change everything. None has ever been found. Until one is, the credit belongs where the evidence puts it.

chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts The Flood: One Story, Many Waters Deglaciation (c. 15,000–7,000 years ago) to the first flood texts (c. 1700 BCE) Open question. Do the world's flood stories remember real floods, and which ones? The claim on the scales The world's flood stories preserve a shared memory of the rising seas and outburst floods at the end of the last Ice Age. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established Two things are clear. A single flood covering all land in human times is contradicted by every continuous natural archive, and the post-glacial floods were real and enormous. The open question is the bridge between them. Nunn and Reid show that oral memory of drowned coasts can last 7,000 years in Australia, which makes the Ice Age reading possible. But the best-documented flood family, the Near Eastern one, is tied to Mesopotamian river floods, and most other traditions cannot be dated. Plausible in places, unproved as a shared origin. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks confidently file flood stories under local floods and literary borrowing, and for the Genesis and Mesopotamian family that is well supported. They have been too quick to assume that oral memory fades within a few centuries. Research on Aboriginal Australian traditions suggests otherwise, so the Ice Age reading deserves more than a footnote, even though it remains unproved. What is solid The oldest written flood stories are Mesopotamian: Ziusudra in Sumerian, Atrahasis (tablets copied c. 1646–1626 BCE) and Utnapishtim in Tablet XI of Gilgamesh. They share a warned hero, a boat, released birds and a sacrifice with Genesis 6–9. Lambert and Millard 1969; George 2003 As the last Ice Age ended, global sea level rose by about 120 m. During Meltwater Pulse 1A, around 14,600 years ago, it rose roughly 14–25 m (estimates vary by study) in a few centuries. Lambeck et al. 2014; Deschamps et al. 2012 Glacial Lake Missoula burst through its ice dam 40 or more times between about 15,000 and 13,000 years ago, scouring the Channeled Scablands of Washington State. Bretz 1923; Waitt 1980 A flood deposit at Shuruppak, the city the Mesopotamian texts name as the flood hero's home, dates to about 2900 BCE; flood layers at Ur and Kish fall at different dates. Schmidt 1931; Mallowan 1964 No continuous natural archive (Greenland ice layers counted back some 60,000 years, tree rings, lake sediments) shows a single flood covering all land within human times. Svensson et al. 2008 Oral traditions can carry landscape memories for thousands of years: Aboriginal Australi
