chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. A flood of rain from the sky and water bursting from the ground destroyed Noah's people (Quran 54:11–12; 11:44; Genesis 7:11). Plausible The Quran names a people, not the whole world, and gives no date. Catastrophic floods that wiped out whole communities are well recorded: flood layers at Ur, Kish and Shuruppak, meltwater outbursts and rising seas at the end of the Ice Age. The waters rose above all the high mountains under the whole heaven (Genesis 7:19–20). Ruled out Read as one worldwide flood a few thousand years ago, the geological record does not allow it. Many Jewish and Christian readers take 'the earth' here as the known land, which returns the question to the regional reading above.

chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters: 01 A tablet that made a man undress
chunks.text: London, 1872. George Smith, a self-taught assistant at the British Museum, is reading a clay tablet from the ruins of Nineveh when he finds a ship stranded on a mountain and a dove sent out to look for land. A colleague later recalled that Smith was so excited he began to take off his clothes. He had found a Babylonian flood story, older than any written copy of Genesis, and it told almost the same tale. That shock has never quite worn off. A god or gods decide to end the world with water. One righteous man is warned. He builds a vessel, loads his family and living creatures, rides out the deluge, sends out birds, lands on a mountain and offers thanks. The Babylonians called him Utnapishtim or Atrahasis, the Sumerians Ziusudra. The Hebrew Bible calls him Noah, and the Quran Nuh. In India, Manu is warned by a fish. In Greece, Deucalion and Pyrrha survive in a chest. In China the story turns: Yu the Great does not escape the flood, he tames it. on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened. So the question at the heart of this case is simple and enormous. Are these stories memories? And if so, of what?

chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters: 02 How each tradition tells it
chunks.text: The Mesopotamian versions are the oldest on clay. Atrahasis survives on tablets copied around 1646–1626 BCE. The gods send the flood because noisy humanity disturbs their rest, and the wise god Ea warns his favourite to tear down his house and build a boat. In a tablet published by Irving Finkel of the British Museum in 2014, the boat is a giant round coracle of rope and bitumen, a very Mesopotamian vessel. Genesis gives the flood a moral cause, human violence, and describes it as universal: the waters covered all the high mountains under the whole heaven. The Quran tells the story in several places, and its emphasis is different again. Nuh is sent to his own people and preaches to them for a very long time. They mock him as he builds, and the flood comes when the command arrives. Surah Hud (11:25–49) gives the most detailed account, from the building of the Ark to its landing on al-Judi, and Surah Nuh (71) is devoted to his preaching. So We opened the gates of the sky with torrential water, burst the earth with gushing springs: the waters met for a preordained purpose. Because the Quran frames Nuh's mission as being to his people (71:1), Muslim scholars have long discussed whether the flood covered the whole earth or the land of those people. Many classical commentators took it as universal; others, especially in modern times, read it as regional. The text itself can carry either reading, which matters, because a regional flood is exactly what geology can test. Beyond the Near East, the Shatapatha Brahmana tells how Manu raised a small fish that grew huge and towed his ship to a northern mountain. Greek writers told of Deucalion. The Chinese Classic of Documents describes waters that overtop the hills, which Yu drains over thirteen years by cutting channels. The skelet

chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters: 03 What the rocks remember
chunks.text: Geology gives a firm answer to one version of the question. There is no sign of a single flood that covered every continent within human times. Greenland's ice holds annual layers counted back some 60,000 years without a break, and trees, lakes and cave deposits tell the same story. But the rocks record something almost as dramatic: an age of floods. A chart of global sea level from 20,000 years ago to today. The line starts about 125 metres below today's level, rises slowly, then jumps steeply around 14,600 years ago during Meltwater Pulse 1A, then climbs more steadily to near today's level by about 6,000 years ago. Shaded bands mark the Missoula outburst floods between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago and the Younger Dryas cold snap. Markers show the drainage of Lake Agassiz 8,200 years ago and the debated dates for the Black Sea refill. A lower zoom lane covering the last 6,000 years marks the Shuruppak flood silt about 2900 BCE, the Jishi Gorge outburst about 1920 BCE, the Atrahasis tablets about 1640 BCE, Yu on a Zhou bronze about 900 BCE, Genesis and the Shatapatha Brahmana in the first millennium BCE, and the Quran in 610 to 632 CE. Twenty thousand years ago, so much water was locked in ice that the sea stood about 120 m lower than today. As the ice melted, the sea rose, sometimes in lurches. During Meltwater Pulse 1A, around 14,600 years ago, it climbed something like 14–25 m in a few centuries (the estimates vary), several centimetres a year, enough to move a shoreline by kilometres within a lifetime on a flat coast. The Persian Gulf, a broad river valley during the Ice Age, filled with sea over the following millennia. On land, ice dams failed. In what is now Montana, Glacial Lake Missoula, holding up to about 2,184 cubic kilometres of water, burst out 40 or more t

chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters: 04 The case for an Ice Age memory
chunks.text: Here the challengers make their move, and it is not a weak one. Graham Hancock and Randall Carlson argue that the flood stories are too vivid, too universal and too specific about waters bursting from below and pouring from above to be only the memory of ordinary river floods. The end of the Ice Age, they point out, was the biggest environmental catastrophe people have ever lived through. Coasts, the richest places to live, were swallowed. Ice lakes emptied in torrents. The abrupt Younger Dryas cold snap, beginning about 12,900 years ago, threw the climate into reverse. Geologists once laughed at a man who said the Scablands were cut by a flood. They were wrong. They also have history on their side. When J Harlen Bretz argued in 1923 that Washington's Channeled Scablands were carved by a colossal flood, the geological establishment resisted for decades. He was right. Catastrophe is not unscientific when the evidence is there. The strongest support comes from an unexpected direction. In 2016 the geographer Patrick Nunn and the linguist Nicholas Reid matched Aboriginal Australian stories from 21 coastal places to shorelines that drowned as the sea rose after the Ice Age, some more than 7,000 years ago. If Australians could keep such memories for hundreds of generations, others might have too. William Ryan and Walter Pitman proposed one candidate: a sudden refill of the Black Sea from the Mediterranean, which they first dated to about 7,600 years ago.

chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters: 05 Where the argument gets harder
chunks.text: The difficulty is the bridge. The Near Eastern flood family, the one that includes Genesis and the Quran, is written in the language of Mesopotamian river floods, and its hero comes from Shuruppak, a city with a real flood layer from around 2900 BCE. That is thousands of years after the great Ice Age pulses. The Black Sea catastrophe has itself been challenged: cores studied by Aksu, Hiscott, Görür and others suggest a gentler rise, and even Ryan and Pitman's team moved their date. Elsewhere, many flood stories were written down only after missionaries arrived, so a Noah-like detail may be borrowed rather than remembered. And floods are everywhere. A motif that any river valley can produce is weak evidence of a single shared source. Time has also destroyed most of what could decide the matter. The people who watched the Ice Age coasts drown lived on land that now lies tens of metres under the sea, largely unexplored. Their stories, if they told them, passed from mouth to mouth for thousands of years before anyone could write. Absence of evidence on a seabed nobody has searched is very weak evidence of absence.

chunks.heading: The Flood: One Story, Many Waters: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The most decisive evidence would come from the drowned shelves themselves. Settlements found under the Persian Gulf or the Sunda Shelf, overwhelmed by rapid sea rise, would show what people saw. Well-dated sediment cores from the Gulf floor could show how fast its valley flooded. A careful catalogue of flood stories recorded before missionary contact, each tested against its own region's flood history, could show whether the motifs track local geology or something older and shared. For now the fairest verdict holds two truths together. The texts' water was real: the people of the ancient Near East lived through floods that swept away cities, and their ancestors lived through the rise of a whole ocean. Whether the stories remember one, the other, or both remains open. The stories may be wrong about one sea covering the world, and still right that the world once drowned.

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar Landing traditions from the 1st millennium BCE; the formation noticed 1948–1959 Durupınar site: Ruled out. Is the Durupınar formation the Ark, and where do the texts place the landing? The claim on the scales The Durupınar formation is the fossilised remains of Noah's Ark. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established Geological mapping shows the boat shape is made of folded, iron-stained layers of local rock, and the features read as rivets, beams and anchors are natural minerals and local andesite. Excavation found soil and rock, and no wood or joinery has been published. Soil ages cannot date a vessel and remain unpublished in peer-reviewed form. This verdict concerns one hillside only. It says nothing about the flood accounts themselves, and the Quran's al-Judi points to a different mountain altogether. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Geology references state firmly that Durupınar is natural, and the evidence supports that confidence. Where popular treatments fall short is on the texts: they often assume the Ark tradition always meant the high peak of Ararat. The older witnesses, including Berossus, the Syriac and Aramaic traditions and the Quran, point to the Cudi range, a point textbooks rarely mention. What is solid Genesis 8:4 places the landing on 'the mountains of Ararat', a region rather than one peak: Ararat is the Hebrew form of Urartu, the kingdom around Lake Van in the 9th–6th centuries BCE. Genesis 8:4; Bailey 1989 The Quran (11:44) names al-Judi. An older regional tradition put the landing in the Gordyaean or Qardu mountains south of Lake Van: Berossus (as quoted by Josephus), Syriac Christian writers and the Aramaic Targum all point there, to the range now called Cudi Dağı near Cizre. Josephus, Antiquities 1.93; Bailey 1989 The peak called Mount Ararat (Ağrı Dağı, 5,137 m) became the favoured landing place later, in medieval Armenian and European tradition. Bailey 1989 The Durupınar formation is about 164 m long, lies 29 km south of Ararat's summit at roughly 2,000 m, was exposed after heavy rain and earthquakes in May 1948 and was photographed in 1959 on a Turkish mapping flight. Collins and Fasold 1996 Geologists describe it as iron-rich (limonite and magnetite) layers in the steep limbs of a doubly plunging syncline; the nearby 'anchor stones' are local andesite. Collins and Fasold 1996 A 1960 expedition dug into the formation and found only soil and rock. Collins and Fasold 1996 What is disputed Soil samples announced from 2

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The Ark came to rest on al-Judi (Quran 11:44); 'on the mountains of Ararat' (Genesis 8:4). Awaiting discovery An old Mesopotamian and Syriac tradition places Judi at Cudi Dağı in southeast Turkey, the 'mountain of the Cordyaeans' where Berossus said pieces of the ship were still carried off. Neither Cudi nor Ararat has been searched systematically for ancient timber. The Durupınar formation is a natural rock fold and is not on either mountain.

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar: 01 A ship in the hills
chunks.text: In May 1948, after heavy rains and a run of earthquakes, a Kurdish shepherd on the slopes south of Mount Ararat saw something new: a long, pointed oval standing out from the hillside like the hull of a ship. Eleven years later, in 1959, a Turkish Air Force photograph taken on a mapping mission caught the same shape from above, and a Turkish army captain, İlhan Durupınar, drew attention to it. The name stuck. The oval is about 164 m long. Genesis 6:15 gives the Ark as 300 cubits long, and with a cubit of about 52 cm that comes to about 157 m. Stand on the ridge above it today, where Turkey has built a small visitor centre, and it is easy to see why people have wondered. The mountains of Ararat, the land where Genesis says the Ark came to rest, are all around you. But there is more than one sacred text in this story, and more than one mountain. Before weighing the hillside, it helps to ask where the traditions themselves put the landing.

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar: 02 Two texts, two mountains
chunks.text: and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Genesis does not name a peak. It says the mountains of Ararat, and Ararat is the Hebrew form of Urartu, a kingdom centred on Lake Van that rivalled Assyria in the 9th to 6th centuries BCE. Its mountains covered a large part of what is now eastern Turkey, Armenia and north-western Iran. Urartu is not a legend. Its kings left inscriptions in cuneiform, its capital Tushpa stood on the rock of Van, and Assyrian annals record wars against it. Anyone in the ancient Near East hearing 'the mountains of Ararat' would have pictured the high, cold country beyond the Tigris headwaters, a natural place for a story's ship to meet the first dry land. The Ark settled on Mount Judi, and it was said, 'Gone are those evildoing people!' The Quran names al-Judi, and here the evidence for an old, specific tradition is warm and consistent. The Babylonian priest Berossus, writing around 280 BCE and quoted by Josephus, said remains of the ship could still be seen in the mountains of the Cordyaeans, where people scraped off its bitumen for amulets. Corduene, known in Syriac as Qardu, is the rugged country south of Lake Van. The Aramaic Targum and Syriac Christian writers placed the landing there too. A monastery stood on the mountain until lightning destroyed it in 776 CE, and the range still carries the name Cudi Dağı, the mountain of Judi, above the Tigris near Cizre. Map of eastern Turkey and northern Iraq. A dashed shaded oval around Lake Van marks the old kingdom of Urartu, the Ararat of Genesis. In the north-east, a peak symbol marks Mount Ararat, 5,137 metres, with the Durupinar formation marked 29 kilometres to its south. The Aras river runs north of Ararat. In the south, a hig

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar: 03 What the hillside is made of
chunks.text: In 1996 the geologist Lorence Collins published a study of Durupınar with an unexpected co-author: David Fasold, a former merchant mariner who had been one of the site's most energetic promoters and had surveyed it with ground-penetrating radar in 1985. Their conclusion was that the ship is geology. Step 1 of 5. Layers of sediment and volcanic debris lie flat on the slope. Layers of sediment and volcanic debris lie flat on the slope. Earth movements fold them into a trough that closes at both ends: a doubly plunging syncline. Erosion planes off the fold. Seen from above, its tilted layers crop out as nested, pointed ovals. Mud and debris flow downslope around the hard core, sharpening a boat-like outline about 164 m long. Iron-rich layers produce the regular stripes and points that were read as ribs and rivets. Two panels, a cross-section above and a plan view below. Step 1: flat layers of sediment and volcanic debris. Step 2: the layers are folded into a trough, and the upper parts of the fold are shown dashed as eroded away. Step 3: seen from above, the tilted layers crop out as nested pointed ovals, with arrows showing the fold plunging at both ends. Step 4: mud and debris flow around the hard core, and a dimension line compares the 164 metre formation with 300 cubits of 52.4 centimetres, about 157 metres. Step 5: iron-rich bands and spots, limonite and magnetite, are shown as the stripes and points that radar and metal detectors read as ribs and rivets, and nearby anchor stones are labelled as local andesite. The layers of rock there were folded into a trough that closes at both ends, which geologists call a doubly plunging syncline. When erosion planes off such a fold, its tilted layers crop out as nested, pointed ovals, a shape that can look remarkably like a hull

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar: 04 The case for the Ark
chunks.text: The site's champion was Ron Wyatt, an American nurse anaesthetist and amateur archaeologist who visited from 1977. He argued that the size matched, that radar showed internal walls like bulkheads, that iron points marked rivets, and that the stones nearby were the drogues that steadied the drifting Ark. Turkey's government took enough interest to designate the site and build a visitor centre in the late 1980s. The size argument deserves a closer look, because it is the heart of the case. Cubits varied. With the common cubit of roughly 45 cm, Genesis's 300 cubits come to about 135 m, well short of the formation. The match to about 157 m works only with the longer Egyptian royal cubit of about 52.4 cm, and Wyatt chose that cubit because Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, was raised in Egypt. That is a reasonable guess, but it is a choice made to fit. Natural folds come in every length, so a length that falls within about 5 per cent of one chosen value is a weak signature on its own. The newest chapter began in 2021, when researchers from Ağrı İbrahim Çeçen University, Istanbul Technical University and Andrews University in the United States began sampling. In 2023 they reported rock and soil ages between roughly 5500 and 3000 BCE. Supporters saw a match with the age of Noah. The team's results, however, have not yet appeared in a peer-reviewed paper, and the method has a basic limit: an age for soil tells you when that sediment formed or was last exposed, not whether a vessel ever lay there. The test for a wooden ship is simple in principle: wood, or its carbonised remains, and the shaped joints that hold planks together. Organic remains can be radiocarbon dated directly, and joinery is unmistakable. Neither has been published from Durupınar. Iron-rich layers, in c

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar: 05 What time has hidden
chunks.text: Honesty cuts both ways here. An ancient wooden vessel left on a mountainside would not be expected to survive for thousands of years, so the failure to find an Ark, at Durupınar or anywhere else, says very little about the flood accounts themselves. What the evidence does say is that this particular hillside is natural. The mountain the Quran names has had far less attention than the one the Ark hunters chose. Cudi Dağı's summit shrines, the ruins of its monastery and the pilgrim routes described by medieval writers have hardly been surveyed, partly because the border region has been a conflict zone for decades. Gertrude Bell and other travellers described a shrine on the summit early in the 20th century, and local people long made pilgrimage there. Whatever archaeology can say about the landing tradition is waiting on that mountain, not in the fold near Doğubayazıt.

chunks.heading: Where the Ark Came to Rest: Ararat, Judi, Durupınar: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: For Durupınar, the tests are straightforward: publish the sample data in full, drill cores through the formation's centre and its supposed hull lines, and look for wood or worked material. An independent survey comparing Durupınar with the natural folds around it would show whether it is unusual at all. The evidence so far, from mapping, digging and mineralogy, all points one way. For the landing tradition, the most promising work is historical and archaeological: a careful survey of Cudi Dağı, where Berossus, the Syriac Christians and the Quran all seem to be looking, and of the texts that record pilgrimages there. That would not test a miracle. It would tell us how old and how continuous the memory of that mountain is.

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty Proposed flood c. 1920 BCE; Xia dynasty traditionally c. 2070–1600 BCE Open question. Did a real megaflood around 1920 BCE lie behind Yu's flood and the Xia? The claim on the scales An outburst flood from Jishi Gorge around 1920 BCE lies behind the tradition of Yu's flood and marks the beginning of the Xia dynasty. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established The flood itself is real geology, but its date and its link to Lajia are both under challenge. Zhang and colleagues place the Jishi lakes thousands of years earlier, and other teams read the Lajia deaths as an earthquake and mudflow event. Even if the date holds, a flood of the upper river is a long way, in space and in centuries, from the first texts about Yu and from Erlitou. A striking hypothesis with real evidence behind it, still genuinely open. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Chinese textbooks traditionally present the Xia as China's first dynasty, often with the Chronology Project's dates of about 2070–1600 BCE, which is more certain than the archaeology allows. Many Western surveys swing the other way and treat Yu as pure myth. The evidence sits in between: a genuine early state at Erlitou, a genuine megaflood, and no secure bridge between them yet. What is solid At Jishi Gorge on the upper Yellow River, a landslide once dammed the river and the lake behind it later burst; Wu and colleagues estimated a peak outburst of about 400,000 cubic metres per second. Wu et al. 2016 At Lajia, downstream of the gorge, people died suddenly inside their houses, including an adult cradling a child; the site also preserved a bowl of millet noodles about 4,000 years old. Wu et al. 2016; Lu et al. 2005 Yu's flood work is an old tradition: a Western Zhou bronze vessel, the Sui Gong xu (c. 9th century BCE), already credits Yu with channelling the waters, centuries before the classic written accounts. Sui Gong xu inscription Erlitou in Henan, the leading archaeological candidate for a Xia capital, is radiocarbon dated to roughly 1750–1530 BCE, and no writing from that period names a Xia state. Liu and Xu 2007 What is disputed The flood's date, 1922 ± 28 BCE, comes from the Lajia skeletons and assumes the flood killed them. Zhang and colleagues (2019) found two Jishi landslide lakes that drained about 6,300 and 5,600 years ago, far earlier. Whether the Lajia disaster was caused by the outburst at all, or by an earthquake followed by local mudflows and flash floods, as several teams argue. Whether an upp

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. In Yao's time vast waters overtopped the hills, and Yu tamed them over years of labour (Shujing; Mencius). Open question A huge landslide-dam outburst on the Yellow River around 1920 BCE is well documented; linking it to Yu depends on dating and on reading the texts as history.

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty: 01 The man who passed his door three times
chunks.text: Every Chinese schoolchild knows the story. In the age of the sage-king Yao, the waters rose until they covered the hills. Yao appointed a minister, Gun, to stop them, and Gun built dykes and walls. For nine years they failed. His son Yu took over and did the opposite: instead of blocking the water, he gave it somewhere to go, cutting channels, dredging rivers and leading the floods to the sea. During that time, Yu was eight years away from his home, and though he thrice passed the door of it, he did not enter. Later tellings make it thirteen years. Either way the reward was the kingdom. Yu became ruler, and when he died the throne passed to his son Qi, which tradition counts as the start of the Xia, China's first hereditary dynasty. For more than two thousand years, Chinese historians treated all this as history. In 2016 a team of geologists said they could put a date on it.

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty: 02 The legend in its own terms
chunks.text: The fullest classical accounts are in the Shujing, the Classic of Documents, and in Sima Qian's Shiji, written around 94 BCE. The Canon of Yao describes waters that embrace the hills and overtop the great heights. The Tribute of Yu then reads almost like an engineer's survey: Yu divides the land into nine provinces, surveys mountains and rivers, and sets the tribute each region owes. In their vast extent they embrace the hills and overtop the great heights, threatening the heavens with their floods This is a different kind of flood story from Noah's. There is no ark and no divine wrath: the hero is a worker who tames nature through patient labour and good government. The story is also old. A bronze vessel of the Western Zhou period, the Sui Gong xu, made around the 9th century BCE, opens by crediting Yu with dredging the rivers. So by about 900 BCE, Yu the flood-tamer was already a figure worth casting in bronze. No ark, no drowned world: in China the hero does not escape the flood, he engineers it away.

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty: 03 The gorge that held a lake
chunks.text: Wu Qinglong and colleagues, including the historian David Cohen, published their case in Science in August 2016. In Jishi Gorge, where the upper Yellow River cuts through mountains in Qinghai Province, they found the remains of a huge landslide that had blocked the river, sediments of the lake that filled behind it, and thick flood silts downstream. Picture the scene they proposed, with the caution it deserves. Perhaps a spring earthquake shakes the gorge. A mountainside slides into the river and the water stops. Downstream, the familiar roar of the Yellow River falls silent while, upstream, a lake creeps back towards the Xunhua basin for months. Step 1 of 5. The Yellow River flows east through Jishi Gorge, between the Xunhua and Guanting basins. The Yellow River flows east through Jishi Gorge, between the Xunhua and Guanting basins. A landslide, perhaps set off by an earthquake, blocks the gorge with a dam roughly 200 m high. A lake backs up behind the dam, perhaps within 6–9 months according to Wu et al. The dam fails: an outburst of about 400,000 m³/s scours the gorge and spreads silts downstream to Lajia. The dating debate: one flood in 1920 BCE (Wu et al. 2016) or two lakes gone thousands of years earlier (Zhang et al. 2019)? A long profile of the upper Yellow River running left to right from the Xunhua basin through Jishi Gorge to the Guanting basin, where the Lajia village ruins are marked. Step 1: the river flows east through the gorge. Step 2: a landslide from the gorge wall, perhaps triggered by an earthquake, forms a dam about 200 metres high. Step 3: a lake fills behind the dam, perhaps within six to nine months. Step 4: the dam breaches and an outburst of about 400,000 cubic metres per second pours downstream, leaving silts near Lajia. Step 5: two labels co

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty: 04 The pushback
chunks.text: The reply came quickly. In 2017 Science published comments from Han Jianfeng and from Huang Chunchang and colleagues, questioning both the dating and the link between the outburst and Lajia. Dong Guanghui's team and others argued that the Lajia disaster was caused by an earthquake followed by local mudflows and flash floods, not by a lake bursting upstream. Wu's team answered, and the debate went on. The most direct challenge arrived in 2019. Zhang Yuzhu, Huang Chunchang and colleagues studied seven sediment profiles in the gorges using luminescence and radiocarbon dating. They found not one landslide lake but two: the first formed about 8,300 years ago and was gone by about 6,300 years ago; the second formed about 6,100 years ago and drained by about 5,600 years ago. Their title was blunt: no relation to China's Great Flood and the Xia dynasty. None of this means Wu's team imagined the flood. Everyone agrees that landslides have dammed Jishi Gorge and that dammed lakes there have burst. The argument is about when, and about whether one particular flood touched one particular village. That matters, because the whole chain from rocks to legend to dynasty hangs on the Lajia dates. Remove that link and the Jishi outburst becomes a spectacular event from the deep Neolithic, thousands of years before anyone could have written about Yu. A flood date needs something the flood itself touched. Wu's team dated bones of people they believed the flood killed, which ties the date to the Lajia disaster rather than directly to the dam. Zhang's team dated the lake and dam sediments themselves, by luminescence (when grains last saw sunlight) and radiocarbon. When the two methods disagree by thousands of years, the key question becomes whether the Lajia deaths and the outburst belong tog

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty: 05 Dynasty, memory or both?
chunks.text: Even a perfectly dated flood would leave the second half of the claim open. Erlitou, near Luoyang in Henan, is the best archaeological candidate for a Xia capital: a planned centre with palaces, bronze workshops and the earliest known bronze ritual vessels in China. But radiocarbon places its main phases at roughly 1750–1530 BCE, and nothing written at Erlitou names it. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project gave the Xia dates of about 2070–1600 BCE, which many archaeologists outside China regard as too precise. Time has hidden much of the answer. The earliest readable Chinese writing, on Shang oracle bones, begins around 1250 BCE, centuries after the proposed flood. If earlier records existed on bamboo or silk, they have rotted. Any flood deposits on the lower plain lie under metres of later Yellow River silt, a river that has changed course again and again. What survives is a strong memory, a real early state and a real megaflood, without a secure thread tying them together.

chunks.heading: Yu the Great and the Flood That Made a Dynasty: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Three findings would move the needle. First, direct dates on the Jishi dam debris and the outburst silts themselves, from several laboratories, would show whether the flood happened around 1920 BCE or thousands of years earlier. Second, a detailed stratigraphy at Lajia would show whether its people died in an outburst flood or a quake-triggered mudflow. Third, cores from the lower Yellow River plain could reveal an outburst layer or a sudden channel change at the right time. Until then the fairest reading honours both the story and the rocks. The Yellow River has always been dangerous, and a people who lived beside it remembered, above all, the ruler who made it safe. Whether one specific catastrophe in 1920 BCE started that memory is one of the most interesting open questions in early Chinese history.

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands ʿĀd: before Thamud in the Quran's sequence; Shisr fort mainly 1st millennium CE, used into the Islamic period Awaiting discovery. Was the fort at Shisr in Oman the lost Iram of the people of ʿĀd? The claim on the scales The fort at Shisr in Oman is Iram of the pillars, the city of the people of ʿĀd. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Shisr is real, and the collapse into its sinkhole is real, but nothing ties it to Iram or ʿĀd. There is no inscription, the fort's main phases are far younger than a people placed before Thamud, and the man who excavated it concluded that Ubar was a region, not this town. The identification rests on legend, tracks and a striking coincidence of ruin. It remains possible that ʿĀd's remains lie elsewhere under the sands, but at Shisr the claim awaits evidence. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Scholarly works are cautious, but tourist signage and much of the 1992 press coverage announced 'the lost city of Ubar' with a confidence the evidence never had. At the same time, dismissing ʿĀd as pure legend goes too far: Arabia's greener past, its lost incense towns and its unsurveyed dunes leave real room for peoples that archaeology has simply not yet found. What is solid Radar from the Space Shuttle (SIR-B, 1984) and Landsat and SPOT satellite images, processed at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, showed old caravan tracks in southern Oman that helped guide ground expeditions in 1990–1992. JPL 1992; Blom et al. 2007 Excavations directed by Juris Zarins at Shisr uncovered a fortified settlement with walls and towers around a well above a limestone cavern; part of the fort had collapsed into the resulting sinkhole. Zarins 2001 Dhofar was a heartland of the frankincense trade; Shisr, the port of Khor Rori (Sumhuram), al-Baleed and the frankincense trees of Wadi Dawkah form UNESCO's 'Land of Frankincense' (inscribed 2000). UNESCO World Heritage listing 1010 Arabia's deserts were far greener in humid phases: lakes formed in the Rub' al-Khali during the early Holocene and in earlier interglacials. McClure 1976; Rosenberg et al. 2011 What is disputed Whether Shisr was 'Ubar' or 'Iram' at all. Its excavator, Juris Zarins, concluded that Ubar was a region and a people, not a single town; the geologist H. Stewart Edgell called Shisr a small caravanserai. The site's age: early announcements spoke of roots around 3000 BCE, while later summaries place the fort mainly in the first millennium CE, with use continui

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The people of ʿĀd lived among the sand dunes, al-Ahqaf, and Iram was a place of lofty pillars unlike any other (Quran 46:21; 89:6–8). Awaiting discovery No inscription yet names ʿĀd with certainty, and Iram has not been identified. Southern Arabia has drowned sites under moving dunes; the Shisr fort is one candidate among several. ʿĀd were destroyed by a furious wind over seven nights and eight days (Quran 69:6–7). Awaiting discovery Climate records show the Arabian interior drying sharply after the Holocene wet phase, and dust storms that bury settlements are real, but no single dated catastrophe has been linked to ʿĀd.

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands: 01 The city the wind erased
chunks.text: In a short, thundering chapter of the Quran called al-Fajr, the Dawn, the listener is asked to remember what happened to three proud peoples. The first is ʿĀd. Have you [Prophet] considered how your Lord dealt with [the people] of 'Ad, of Iram, [the city] of lofty pillars, whose like has never been made in any land, Iram of the pillars became one of the great lost cities of the Arab imagination. Medieval storytellers turned it into a city of gold and gems hidden in the deep desert. In 1930 the British explorer Bertram Thomas, crossing towards the Empty Quarter, was shown old tracks by his Bedouin guides and told they led to a city destroyed long ago for its wickedness. He seems to have coined the phrase later popularised as the Atlantis of the Sands, often wrongly credited to T. E. Lawrence. Sixty years later, a filmmaker from Los Angeles would chase those tracks with the help of the Space Shuttle.

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands: 02 ʿĀd in the Quran's own words
chunks.text: The Quran tells the story of ʿĀd in several places, and it is worth hearing on its own terms before any spade goes in. ʿĀd were a strong, prosperous people who came before Thamud. God sent them a prophet from among themselves, Hud, who warned them to worship God alone. Surah al-Ahqaf, named after the sand dunes, says he warned them 'among the sand dunes'. They mocked him and asked him to bring on the punishment he promised. When they saw a cloud approaching their valley, they said, 'This cloud will give us rain!' 'No indeed! It is what you wanted to hasten: a storm-wind bearing a painful punishment which will destroy everything by its Lord's command.' In the morning there was nothing to see except their [ruined] dwellings Surah al-Haqqa adds that the wind blew for seven nights and eight days, and ends with a question that is also an archaeologist's question: can you see any trace of them now? Muslim tradition generally located ʿĀd in southern Arabia, in the dune belt between Hadramawt and Oman, and a much-visited shrine in Wadi Hadramawt, Qabr Hud, is honoured as the prophet's tomb. The text itself names a people and Iram, but not a map reference. The Quran ends ʿĀd's story with an archaeologist's question: can you see any trace of them now?

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands: 03 Radar over the Empty Quarter
chunks.text: Nicholas Clapp became fascinated by the legend of Ubar, the incense city that later tradition linked to Iram. In 1981 he first approached NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory about searching from space. In 1984 the Shuttle Challenger carried an imaging radar that could see through thin, dry sand, and JPL scientists including Ronald Blom and Charles Elachi helped read the results. Combined with Landsat and French SPOT satellite images, the data showed faint old tracks, the paths worn by centuries of camels, running across southern Oman. The team was an adventure novelist's cast: Clapp, the lawyer George Hedges, the explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes and the archaeologist Juris Zarins. After expeditions in 1990 and 1991, attention settled on Shisr, a village with a well at the edge of the sands, where Wilfred Thesiger had noted a crude ruined fort in 1946. In February 1992 the New York Times carried the news: Ubar found.

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands: 04 A fort that fell into the earth
chunks.text: What Zarins's team uncovered was a genuine desert stronghold: walls and towers enclosing a well, with pottery and goods that spoke of long-distance trade. Frankincense, the resin of Boswellia sacra, grows in Dhofar's hills and was carried by caravan and ship to Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Mediterranean. A fortified water point on the desert edge made sense on that trade. Step 1 of 5. A limestone plateau at the edge of the sands: groundwater has dissolved a cavern, and a well reaches water. A limestone plateau at the edge of the sands: groundwater has dissolved a cavern, and a well reaches water. A walled fort with towers is built around the well; incense caravans gather here. Water drawn for people, animals and fields lowers the water table; the cavern roof weakens and cracks. The roof gives way and part of the fort falls into the new sinkhole (the expedition suggested c. 300–500 CE). Sand drifts in. The site stays in reduced use for centuries; in 1991–92 excavators find walls and a tower lying in the pit. A cross-section through a limestone plateau at the edge of the sand. Step 1: underground water has dissolved a cavern beneath the surface, and a well shaft reaches a pool at the water table. Step 2: a walled fort with towers is built around the well, and incense caravans approach from the dunes. Step 3: the water table falls as water is drawn, and cracks spread through the thinning cavern roof. Step 4: the roof gives way and part of the fort, including a tower, drops into the pit as tumbled blocks. Step 5: sand drifts into the sinkhole, and a label notes that in 1991 and 1992 excavators found walls and a tower lying in it after long, reduced use of the site. Then came the detail that made headlines. The fort had been built over a limestone cavern, the very cavity that

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands: 05 Is it Iram?
chunks.text: Here the story turns, and it is the excavator who turns it. Juris Zarins came to the view that Ubar was not a single town but a region and a people. The geologist H. Stewart Edgell argued that Shisr was a small caravanserai and that the Ubar legend was essentially mythical. Nigel Groom questioned the link to Ptolemy's 'Omanum Emporium', which Fiennes had proposed. The biggest problem is time. In the Quran's sequence, ʿĀd came before Thamud, and Thamud appear in the annals of the Assyrian king Sargon II around 715 BCE. Shisr's fort, in most later summaries, belongs mainly to the first millennium CE and was used into the Islamic period. Early press releases spoke of a settlement going back to about 3000 BCE, but the fortified town that fell into the sinkhole is far younger than any plausible date for ʿĀd. Iram itself remains uncertain. Some commentators read it as the name of ʿĀd's tribe or ancestor, with the 'pillars' as tent poles or tall stature; others as a place. At Wadi Rum in southern Jordan, inscriptions at a Nabataean-era temple of the goddess al-Lat mention Iram, and some scholars think that a better candidate. None of these identifications is secure.

chunks.heading: ʿĀd and Iram of the Pillars: The City Under the Sands: 06 A greener Arabia, and what the sands still hide
chunks.text: There is a deeper background that makes the story of a lost desert people more plausible than it first sounds. Arabia has not always been desert. Lake beds in the Rub' al-Khali record wet phases in the early Holocene, and older lakes date to earlier interglacials. When the monsoon reached further north, grassland, lakes and animals followed, and so did people. When it retreated, communities had to move, shrink or vanish. Time and sand have hidden most of that story. Dunes migrate and bury; wind erases mudbrick; the dune country of al-Ahqaf, where the Quran places Hud's warning, has hardly been surveyed. The absence of ʿĀd from the archaeological record is the absence of evidence in a place almost nobody has looked. What would settle it? An inscription naming Iram or ʿĀd would change everything. So would systematic survey and dating in the dunes between Hadramawt and Dhofar, and further work at Wadi Rum. Shisr remains a remarkable place, a real incense fort that really did fall into the ground. It is simply not, on present evidence, the city of lofty pillars.

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains Thamud attested c. 715 BCE–5th century CE; Hegra's tombs dated c. 1 BCE–75 CE Established. What does archaeology show about Thamud, and are Hegra's rock-cut facades theirs? The claim on the scales Thamud were a real people of northwest Arabia, the region where the Quran places al-Hijr. Weight of evidence Established Ruled out Established Few ancient Arabian peoples are better documented. Sargon II names them around 715 BCE, Greek and Roman geographers locate them in northwest Arabia, they built a temple for Roman emperors at Ruwafa in the 160s CE, and their horsemen served Rome around 400 CE. That places them in exactly the region the Quran implies. The narrower question, whether Hegra's carved facades are Thamud's houses, is different: those facades are Nabataean tombs, and a Thamudic phase at Hegra itself is still to be shown. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Where textbooks mention Thamud they treat them as a real tribe, and the evidence supports that confidence. The weaker link is in popular presentations, which often call Hegra's tombs Thamud's houses; they are Nabataean tombs. Conversely, some sceptical accounts treat the Quranic Thamud as legend, which ignores how well the people are attested outside the Quran. What is solid The annals of the Assyrian king Sargon II list the Tamudi among Arab groups he claims to have subdued around 715 BCE, describing desert dwellers who knew neither overseers nor officials. Eph'al 1982 Greek and Roman writers from Agatharchides (2nd century BCE) and Diodorus to Pliny and Ptolemy place the Thamudeni in northwest Arabia, near the Red Sea coast and inland. Retsö 2003 At Ruwafa, in the 160s CE, a Greek and Nabataean bilingual inscription records a temple built by the Thamud of Robathu, dedicated to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Bowersock 1975 The Notitia Dignitatum, a Roman list of offices and units from about 400 CE, includes cavalry units of Thamudeni, one in Egypt and one in Palestine. Notitia Dignitatum Hegra has 111 monumental tombs, 94 of them decorated, cut into sandstone outcrops by the Nabataeans, with dated inscriptions from about 1 BCE to 75 CE and some 50 earlier, pre-Nabataean inscriptions. UNESCO World Heritage listing 1293 What is disputed Whether Thamud lived at Hegra before the Nabataeans. The monumental tombs are Nabataean, but earlier inscriptions show people were there before them. 'Thamudic' is a modern label for some 15,000 Ancient North Arabian inscriptions; the name does not sh

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. A people called Thamud lived in northwest Arabia and carved homes from the mountains at al-Hijr (Quran 7:74; 15:80–82; 26:149). Established Thamud appear in an inscription of the Assyrian king Sargon II (715 BCE), in Classical geographers and in a 2nd-century CE temple at Ruwafa. Rock-cut façades crowd the cliffs of al-Hijr (Hegra). The tombs we see today are Nabataean, but the text does not say which carvings it means. They were destroyed suddenly, by an earthquake and a blast, early one morning (Quran 7:78; 15:83). Awaiting discovery No destruction layer at al-Hijr has yet been tied to Thamud, and most of the pre-Nabataean town remains unexcavated. The region is seismically active.

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains: 01 Cliffs like ships in a sea of sand
chunks.text: Drive north from AlUla at sunrise and the sandstone outcrops of Hegra rise from the plain like beached ships. Carved into their flanks are facades: doorways framed by pilasters, heavy cornices, and above them the stepped crowns that look like staircases to nowhere. The largest, Qasr al-Farid, the Lonely Castle, stands alone in a single boulder, its lower part never finished. For Muslims, this place has another name. It is al-Hijr, remembered in the Quran as the home of the people of Thamud, and it has long been called Mada'in Salih, the cities of Salih, after the prophet sent to them. The Quran speaks of them in many places, among the 'people of old' whose ruins still stood. and the Thamud, who hewed into the rocks in the valley, So who were Thamud, and did they carve these rocks? Unusually for a people in a sacred story, we can follow them through other records for more than a thousand years.

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains: 02 Salih and the she-camel
chunks.text: The Quran tells the story from several angles. Thamud were heirs to the power of ʿĀd, settled in a land of gardens, springs and palms, building castles on the plains and carving houses from the mountains. God sent them Salih, one of their own, with a sign: a she-camel that must be left to graze and drink in peace. The powerful mocked him. The most wicked among them hamstrung the camel, and they dared Salih to bring on the punishment. and then they hamstrung the camel. They defied their Lord's commandment and said, 'Salih, bring down the punishment you threaten, if you really are a messenger!' An earthquake seized them: by the next morning they were lying dead in their homes. Other passages speak of a blast that overwhelmed them early in the morning (15:83). The account is a moral one, about security that breeds arrogance and a community that turns on a sign of mercy. But it is also rooted in a particular landscape of rock-cut dwellings, oases and a named place, al-Hijr. That is where history can listen in. Few peoples in any sacred story can be followed through outside records for more than a thousand years. Thamud can.

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains: 03 A people in the Assyrian annals
chunks.text: The first outside witness is an enemy. Around 715 BCE the Assyrian king Sargon II boasted in his annals of defeating distant Arab groups, among them the Tamudi, whom he described as desert people who knew neither overseers nor officials. Six centuries later, the Greek geographer Agatharchides described the Thamud along the Red Sea coast south of the Gulf of Aqaba, and Diodorus, Pliny and Ptolemy all place Thamudeni in northwest Arabia. The most remarkable witness is a building. At Ruwafa, in the desert north-west of Hegra, a small temple carries a bilingual inscription in Greek and Nabataean Aramaic from the 160s CE. It records that the Thamud of Robathu built the shrine in honour of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, with the support of the Roman governor. Two centuries later, the Notitia Dignitatum lists cavalry units of Thamudeni serving the empire in Egypt and Palestine. Here the Quran's account fits the evidence warmly and specifically. It places Thamud after ʿĀd, in northwest Arabia, as a settled people of oases and rock. The outside sources agree on the people, the region and their long presence. Whatever one believes about their end, Thamud were not a legend.

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains: 04 Who carved Hegra's facades?
chunks.text: Hegra's great facades were carved by the Nabataeans, the Arab kingdom whose capital was Petra, about 450 km to the north-north-west. Hegra was their southern city on the incense road. UNESCO counts 111 monumental tombs, 94 of them decorated, and many carry an inscribed panel above the door naming the owner, the year of the reigning king, and curses on anyone who reuses the tomb without permission. The dates run from about 1 BCE to 75 CE. On the left, the front of a rock-cut tomb carved into a sandstone outcrop: a smooth facade about 11 metres tall crowned by two stepped merlons, the crow-step motif, above two cornices, with corner pilasters, a doorway topped by a triangular pediment, and an inscription panel above it. An arrow down the left edge notes that the facade was carved from the top down. A person 1.7 metres tall stands beside it. On the right, a cut-through of the same tomb shows the thin carved facade on the cliff face and a burial chamber cut into the rock behind the door, with niches cut into the back wall and graves cut into the floor. A 5 metre scale bar is shown. The unfinished facades show how they were made: the masons started at the top and worked down, cutting the stepped crown first and the doorway last. Behind the door is a chamber cut into the rock, with niches in the walls and graves in the floor. These are houses for the dead, not the living. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE, and a Latin inscription of 175–177 CE calls the place civitas Hegrenorum, the city of the Hegrans. The tombs date themselves. Nabataean inscriptions over many doorways give the year of the reigning king, such as Aretas IV, which can be converted to our calendar. Some 50 older inscriptions, in scripts such as Lihyanite (Dadanitic) and so-called Thamudic, show that

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains: 05 Tombs, houses and memory
chunks.text: So are Hegra's facades Thamud's houses? Not in the strict sense: they are Nabataean tombs. But the question is subtler than a simple no. The Quran speaks of Thamud carving homes in the mountains of al-Hijr, and people were living and writing at Hegra before the Nabataeans. Most of the site's settlement area, and its earlier layers, remain unexcavated. A Thamudic phase at Hegra has not been demonstrated; it has not been ruled out either. A related caution applies to the word Thamudic. Scholars use it for about 15,000 short inscriptions in Ancient North Arabian scripts scattered across the peninsula. It is a convenient label, not evidence that the Thamud tribe wrote them. Muslim tradition, for its part, kept the site's identity with Salih vivid: it records that when the Prophet's army passed al-Hijr on the way to Tabuk around 630 CE, he told his companions to pass quickly, as by a place of warning. What of the earthquake and the blast? The Hijaz sits beside the Red Sea rift, with vast lava fields called harrats. In 2009 a swarm of tens of thousands of earthquakes at Harrat Lunayyir, less than 200 km south of Hegra, forced the evacuation of some 40,000 people. A seismic end to a settlement in this region is physically plausible. No dated destruction layer has yet been tied to Thamud.

chunks.heading: Thamud, Salih and the Houses Carved in Mountains: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The best hope lies in the excavations now underway across the AlUla valley and at Hegra itself, where French and Saudi teams have been working since the early 2000s. An inscription from an early layer naming Thamud, or a dated destruction horizon at a pre-Nabataean settlement, would bring the Quranic account and the archaeology into direct contact. So would a careful study of the 'Thamudic' texts around Hegra to see whether any writer calls himself a man of Thamud. Until then, the verdict can be warm without claiming too much. The people of the story are real and well attested, in the right land and over the right centuries. The famous facades belong to their Nabataean neighbours and successors. And the rocks of al-Hijr still keep some of their secrets.

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell Bab edh-Dhra c. 3000–2350 BCE; Tall el-Hammam's destruction c. 1650 BCE (proposed) Awaiting discovery. Did an earthquake, a fire from the sky or something else destroy a real Sodom? The claim on the scales A cosmic airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam around 1650 BCE, and that event lies behind the story of Sodom. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The city and its destruction are real. The airburst is not supported by the evidence as published: independent analysis found no mineralogical or geochemical signs of impact, image problems were flagged, and the journal retracted the paper in 2025, citing errors in method and interpretation and an overstated Tunguska comparison. Its authors disagree and continue to defend the idea, so it is not strictly ruled out. The identification of Tall el-Hammam as Sodom is a separate, open question. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Standard works present Sodom confidently as legend with no identified site, and on the site question that caution is justified. They are sometimes too quick to treat the story as pure invention: the region really did have destroyed Bronze Age towns, earthquakes and burning bitumen. On the airburst, the retraction shows the peer-review system catching an overconfident claim. What is solid Tall el-Hammam is a large Bronze Age mound of about 36 ha in the Jordan Valley, 12.6 km north-east of the Dead Sea, excavated from 2005 by Steven Collins's team; it has a Middle Bronze Age destruction layer. Bunch et al. 2021 (retracted); Collins and Scott 2013 Bunch and colleagues (2021) proposed that a Tunguska-sized airburst destroyed the city around 1650 BCE. Jaret and Harris (2022) found no mineralogical or geochemical evidence of impact, and Scientific Reports retracted the paper on 24 April 2025. Jaret and Harris 2022; Retraction Note 2025 Bab edh-Dhra, a walled Early Bronze Age town beside the Lisan peninsula, was occupied from about 3000 BCE and abandoned about 2350 BCE; its cemeteries hold an estimated 20,000 shaft tombs. Nearby Numeira ended in fire earlier. Rast and Schaub 2003 The Dead Sea lies in an active rift: its surface is about 430 m below sea level, its faults produce damaging earthquakes, and its rocks and waters yield bitumen, sulphur and salt, including the salt ridge of Mount Sodom. Neev and Emery 1995 What is disputed Where Sodom stood: in the north, in the 'plain of the Jordan' where Tall el-Hammam lies, or in the south near the Lisan and Mount Sodom, where

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The towns of Lot's people were overturned and rained on with stones of baked clay, at sunrise (Quran 11:82; 15:73–74; Genesis 19:24–25). Awaiting discovery Several Bronze Age sites near the Dead Sea were destroyed, including Bab edh-Dhra, Numeira and Tall el-Hammam. The airburst paper on Tall el-Hammam was retracted in 2025, and none of the sites is yet securely identified with the story. Their ruins lie on a road still travelled (Quran 15:76). Open question The candidate sites lie on or near the ancient routes around the Dead Sea, but until one is identified this remains open.

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell: 01 Smoke like a furnace
chunks.text: On the south-western shore of the Dead Sea, a ridge of almost pure rock salt about 11 km long rises from the lowest land on Earth. Rain carves its flanks into columns and fins, and one of them has long been pointed out to travellers as Lot's wife. The air smells faintly of sulphur. Lumps of black bitumen once floated up from the lake, which the Greeks and Romans called Asphaltites. No landscape on Earth seems more made for a story of divine fire. And the story is one of the most famous ever told. Then the Lord rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven; and he overthrew those cities, and all the Plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground. But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt. Where were those cities, and what happened to them? Archaeology has three serious candidates, a retracted comet paper, and a rift valley that still shakes.

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell: 02 The story in both texts
chunks.text: In Genesis, Abraham bargains with God to spare the city if ten righteous people can be found. Two angels come to Lot's house in Sodom, the men of the town surround it, and at dawn Lot's family is led out. Fire and sulphur fall, the cities of the Plain are overthrown, and Abraham, looking down the next morning, sees smoke rising like the smoke of a furnace. The Quran tells the story of Lut, as it names him, in several surahs, and its account shares the core while framing it as the fate of a people who rejected their prophet. The messengers come to Lut after visiting Ibrahim. They tell him to leave with his household in the dead of night, without turning back, and that his wife will share the fate of the others. At the appointed morning the town is turned upside down and stones of baked clay rain upon it. and the blast overtook them at sunrise: We turned their city upside down and rained on them a shower of clay stones. There truly is a sign in this for those who can learn- it is still there on the highway- That last line is striking. The Quran speaks to listeners who travelled the caravan roads between Arabia and Syria, and it tells them the ruins lie on their route. The great north-south trade roads did pass close to the Dead Sea, whose shores are dotted with ruined Bronze Age towns. It is a detail that fits the geography well. The Quran tells its first listeners that the ruins are still there, on the road they travel.

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell: 03 A landscape made for the story
chunks.text: The Dead Sea fills a gash in the Earth's crust where the Arabian plate slides past the African plate. Its surface lies about 430 m below sea level, and its faults have produced destructive earthquakes throughout history. The rocks hold bitumen and natural sulphur, and beneath Mount Sodom a body of salt pushes slowly upwards. On the left, a map of the Dead Sea area with north at the top. The Jordan river flows into the northern end of the Dead Sea. Two dashed red lines mark the rift faults on either side. Tall el-Hammam is marked north-east of the sea as the northern candidate, near Jericho on the west side. The Lisan peninsula divides the northern basin from the former southern basin, now evaporation ponds. Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira are marked on the east shore beside the Lisan as southern candidates, and Mount Sodom, a salt ridge, on the south-west. Masada is marked on the west shore. A 10 kilometre scale bar and a line A to B across the sea are shown. On the right, section A to B shows the Judean hills on the west and the Moab plateau on the east, both cut by faults that drop steeply to the Dead Sea, whose surface is about 430 metres below sea level and whose deepest point is about 730 metres below, above a deep fill of salt and mud. A box lists what the landscape offers a storyteller: earthquakes, bitumen and sulphur, salt pillars, a lifeless sea, and burned Bronze Age towns. Geologists have long noticed how many elements of the story this setting can supply. In 1995 the engineers Graham Harris and Anthony Beardow argued that an earthquake could have liquefied waterlogged ground near the southern shore, letting buildings slide and sink, a physical version of a town turned upside down. The geologists David Neev and Kenneth Emery linked the region's earthquakes, bitumen

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell: 04 The southern towns
chunks.text: For much of the 20th century, attention focused on the south, where later tradition placed Sodom and where Zoar, the town Lot fled to, was identified with the area of Safi. On a plateau beside the Lisan peninsula stands Bab edh-Dhra, a walled town of the Early Bronze Age, occupied from about 3000 BCE and abandoned around 2350 BCE. Its cemeteries are vast: excavators estimate some 20,000 shaft tombs. Paul Lapp dug there in the 1960s, and Walter Rast and Thomas Schaub excavated the town from 1975. A few kilometres south lies Numeira, a smaller town that ended in fire earlier. Some scholars, notably the archaeologist Bryant Wood, argued that Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira were Sodom and Gomorrah. The difficulty is chronology: these towns ended many centuries before the dates usually proposed for Abraham, and Bab edh-Dhra's final phase shows abandonment rather than a single catastrophe.

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell: 05 The airburst, and its fall
chunks.text: Steven Collins of Trinity Southwest University argued instead for the north. Genesis says Lot looked out from the hills near Bethel over the well-watered plain of the Jordan and chose it, which fits the northern end of the Dead Sea better than the south. There, Tall el-Hammam is the largest Bronze Age city in the southern Jordan Valley, about 36 ha, and Collins's team began excavating it in 2005. It ended in a violent destruction around 1650 BCE. In 2021 a team led by Ted Bunch, with Allen West, James Kennett and others associated with the Comet Research Group, published a paper in Scientific Reports proposing that a Tunguska-sized cosmic airburst had destroyed the city. They reported melted pottery surfaces and mudbrick, tiny spherules, shocked quartz and unusual salt, and connected the event to the Sodom story. It made headlines around the world. The criticism was swift. Image specialists, including Elisabeth Bik, flagged altered figures. In 2022 Steven Jaret and Scott Harris reported no mineralogical or geochemical evidence of impact in the paper's own data. Mark Boslough and a colleague argued that the Tunguska comparison greatly overstated that blast's temperatures and winds. On 24 April 2025 the journal retracted the paper, citing errors in methodology, analyses and interpretation. Eleven authors disagreed with the retraction, and the team continues to defend the idea. Shocked quartz is one of the classic impact markers: grains crossed by sets of microscopic parallel planes that form only under enormous, sudden pressure. The challenge is telling them from ordinary fractures and features formed in other ways. Jaret and Harris argued that the fractures shown in the 2021 paper did not have the diagnostic properties of shock, which is one reason the claim did not hold

chunks.heading: Sodom, the People of Lut, and a Comet Paper That Fell: 06 What time hides, and what would settle it
chunks.text: The Dead Sea keeps changing. Its level has fallen by tens of metres in the last century, the southern basin is now a grid of industrial evaporation ponds, and sinkholes open along its shores. Ancient sites on the old shoreline may be submerged, buried or destroyed. No inscription naming Sodom or Gomorrah has been found anywhere. Three things would move this case. A full publication of Tall el-Hammam's stratigraphy with independently dated destruction layers; independent laboratories testing the claimed melt and quartz against ordinary burned buildings; and regional surveys showing whether other sites of the same date share the same damage, as an airburst would require. For the southern candidates, better dating of Numeira's fire and Bab edh-Dhra's end would help. Meanwhile the texts' setting fits the landscape remarkably well: a sunken plain of towns, fire and sulphur in the ground, salt pillars, and ruins beside the road. What remains unproved is which ruins, and which fire.

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog Quran 7th century CE; Syriac Alexander Legend 6th–7th century; Derbent and Gorgan walls 5th–6th century CE Open question. Who was Dhul-Qarnayn, and can archaeology find his barrier? The claim on the scales The barrier of Dhul-Qarnayn was a real fortification in a Caucasus or Caspian pass, such as Derbent or the Darial Pass. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established Walls closing the passes between steppe and south were very real, and both Christian and Muslim tradition located the barrier there. But every surviving wall is a Sasanian work of the 5th–6th century CE, far later than Cyrus or Alexander, and none is built of iron fused with molten metal. Earlier phases may be hidden beneath them, and the builder's identity remains a matter of textual, not archaeological, argument. The historical core is plausible; a specific match is still open. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Western reference works usually state flatly that Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander and that the story derives from the Syriac legend. The Alexander link is strongly supported, but the direction and date of influence are more debated than that confidence suggests, and the long tradition of Muslim scholarship identifying a different, monotheist ruler is rarely given a fair hearing. What is solid Late antique empires walled the gaps between the steppe and the south. At Derbent the Sasanians built two parallel walls about 3.6 km long and 300–400 m apart from the citadel to the Caspian, running 500 m into the sea, with a mountain wall continuing about 40 km west. UNESCO World Heritage listing 1070 The Great Wall of Gorgan, east of the Caspian, runs 195 km with more than 30 forts and was dated by luminescence and radiocarbon to the late 5th or 6th century CE; in Persian it is called Sadd-i Iskandar, Alexander's Barrier. Sauer et al. 2013 Josephus, in the 1st century CE, gives the first surviving reference to gates built by Alexander as a barrier against the Scythians. Josephus, Jewish War 7.244–251; Antiquities 18.97 The Syriac Alexander Legend (the Neshana), dated to the 6th or early 7th century, tells how Alexander built a gate of iron and bronze between two mountains to shut in the Huns, whose kings include Gog and Magog, and how he saw the sun set into foul waters. Budge 1889; Reinink 1983; van Bladel 2008 What is disputed Who Dhul-Qarnayn was: Alexander, as many classical commentators held; an earlier righteous king, as Ibn Kathir and others argued; a South Arabian king; or Cyrus th

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. A ruler reached a people between two mountain barriers and built a barrier of iron blocks filled with molten copper against Gog and Magog (Quran 18:93–97). Awaiting discovery The walls of the Caspian passes (Derbent, Darial, Gorgan) are stone, mud brick and fired brick, built mostly in Sasanian times. A barrier of iron and copper between two mountains has not been identified. The text itself says it will be levelled when the promise comes (18:98).

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog: 01 The ruler of the two horns
chunks.text: Surah al-Kahf, the Cave, is one of the most beloved chapters of the Quran, recited by many Muslims every Friday. Near its end come sixteen verses about a ruler called Dhul-Qarnayn, the One of the Two Horns. He is given power and means, and he travels: to where the sun sets, to where it rises, and finally to a gap between two mountains where a frightened people ask for protection from Gog and Magog. bring me lumps of iron!' and then, when he had filled the gap between the two mountainsides [he said], 'Work your bellows!' and then, when he had made it glow like fire, he said, 'Bring me molten metal to pour over it!' Their enemies could not scale the barrier, nor could they pierce it, It is an engineer's verse: iron blocks packed into a gap, bellows roaring, metal poured to bind it. And it has sent travellers, caliphs and scholars searching for a real wall for more than a thousand years.

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog: 02 The journey in its own terms
chunks.text: The Quran introduces the story as an answer to a question: they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. It then tells three journeys. In the west he finds the sun, as it seemed to him, setting into a muddy spring, and a people over whom he is given the choice to punish or to show kindness; he chooses justice, punishing wrongdoers and rewarding those who believe and do good. In the east he finds a people with no shelter from the sun. Then comes the gap between the mountains. What stands out is his character. He refuses the tribute offered, saying that what God has given him is better. He asks only for labour. When the barrier is finished he takes no credit: this is a mercy from my Lord, and when my Lord's promise comes, He will level it. The story is less about conquest than about power used humbly, and about the limits of any human wall. and he said, 'This is a mercy from my Lord. But when my Lord's promise is fulfilled, He will raze this barrier to the ground: my Lord's promise always comes true.' Gog and Magog, Yajuj and Majuj in Arabic, also appear in the Hebrew Bible, where Ezekiel speaks of Gog of the land of Magog, and in the New Testament's Revelation, as nations of the last days. The barrier's final breaking belongs to the end of time. That part of the story is a matter of faith, not of archaeology. The barrier's building, in a real place, is where evidence can speak.

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog: 03 Who was he? The great Muslim views
chunks.text: Muslim scholars have discussed Dhul-Qarnayn's identity for fourteen centuries, with real care and disagreement. Many classical commentators identified him with al-Iskandar, Alexander. Others objected. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Taymiyyah, among others, argued that Alexander of Macedon, a pagan who was hailed as a god, could not be the God-fearing ruler of the Quran, and that Dhul-Qarnayn must be an earlier, righteous king. The exegete al-Tabari recorded explanations of the name, including that he reached the two 'horns', the extremities, of the world. A South Arabian tradition, preserved by Wahb ibn Munabbih and in Ibn Hisham's book on the kings of Himyar, made him a Himyarite king, al-Saʿb Dhu Marathid. In the 19th and 20th centuries a different candidate gained ground. Sayyid Ahmad Khan, and then the Indian scholar and statesman Abul Kalam Azad, proposed Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian empire, and Abul A'la Maududi also considered him the most likely candidate. As for the ram that you saw with the two horns, these are the kings of Media and Persia. The Cyrus case is thoughtful. Cyrus is remembered in the Hebrew Bible as God's anointed, the liberator who let the exiles return. He was famous for justice and tolerance. His campaigns reached west to the Aegean coast, east into Central Asia and north towards the steppe, where he died around 530 BCE fighting the Massagetae. Daniel's two-horned ram stands for the kings of Media and Persia. Supporters also point to a relief at Pasargadae, Cyrus's capital, showing a winged figure wearing a crown set on long horns.

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog: 04 Alexander's gates in late antique legend
chunks.text: Western scholarship has mostly followed a different trail. By the 1st century CE, Josephus already mentions gates built by Alexander as a barrier against the Scythians. Over the following centuries the gates grew into legend. The Syriac Alexander Legend, known as the Neshana, tells how Alexander went to the place where the sun sets into fetid waters, then built a gate of iron and bronze between two mountains to shut in the Huns, among whose kings are Gog and Magog, and prophesied their breakout at the end of time. The parallels with Quran 18 are close, and scholars from Theodor Nöldeke to Kevin van Bladel and Tommaso Tesei have argued that the Quranic passage engages with this Christian legend. The dating is part of the argument. The Syriac text was long placed around 629–630 CE, after the emperor Heraclius defeated Persia; recent work suggests an earlier 6th-century core with later additions. The direction of influence, and whether both drew on a wider body of Alexander lore, is still debated. The earliest surviving writer to put Alexander's gates in the Caucasus wrote in the first century, six centuries before the Quran.

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog: 05 Walls between the steppe and the south
chunks.text: Whatever the texts' relationship, the landscape behind them is real. For a thousand years, horse peoples of the steppe raided south through a few narrow gaps: the Darial Pass through the high Caucasus, the coastal strip at Derbent where the mountains nearly meet the Caspian, and the plain east of the Caspian. Empires closed those gaps with walls. A map with the Black Sea at far left and the Caspian Sea in the centre-right. The Greater Caucasus range runs diagonally from the Black Sea to the Caspian coast. A highlighted point in the middle of the range marks the Darial Pass, the Caucasian Gates. On the Caspian coast where the mountains nearly meet the sea, a red line marks the Derbent walls, called Bab al-Abwab, Gate of Gates, 5th to 6th century CE. South-east of the Caspian, below the Alborz mountains, a red line running east from the coast marks the Great Wall of Gorgan, 195 kilometres long, called Sadd-i Iskandar in Persian. Labels mark the steppe peoples to the north, Armenia, Caucasian Albania and Sasanian Persia, plus Tbilisi and Baku. A 200 kilometre scale bar and north arrow are shown. At Derbent, the Sasanian Persians first built mudbrick defences in the 5th century and then, under Khosrow I in the 6th, massive stone walls. Two parallel walls run about 3.6 km from the citadel of Naryn-Kala down to the sea, 300–400 m apart, and continued 500 m into the water to protect the harbour. A mountain wall ran some 40 km west. Arab geographers called the city Bab al-Abwab, the Gate of Gates. Plan view with the Caspian Sea on the right and foothills on the left. The Naryn-Kala citadel sits on the high ground at the west end. From it two nearly parallel walls run east for about 3.6 kilometres to the shore, 300 to 400 metres apart, with towers marked along the north wall; th

chunks.heading: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Wall Against Gog and Magog: 06 What archaeology can and cannot test
chunks.text: Archaeology cannot test who was granted power by God, or what will happen at the end of time. It can test whether a barrier of the kind described once closed a real pass, when, and by whom. So far the answer is mixed. Such barriers existed, and tradition put Dhul-Qarnayn's in exactly those places. But the walls we can date are Sasanian, built nine centuries after Cyrus and eight after Alexander, and of stone and brick rather than iron bound with molten metal. Time may hide the rest. Pass fortifications were rebuilt again and again on the same lines, so any earlier barrier would lie beneath later ones. The Achaemenid northern frontier is almost unknown on the ground. Excavation beneath Derbent's walls and at the Darial fortress, and any trace of early metal-reinforced masonry, would give the question new evidence. Until then the barrier stands where it has always stood: firmly in the text, plausibly in the passes, and not yet in a trench.

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back Setting c. 16th–13th century BCE (debated); texts written down later Awaiting discovery. Did an exodus from Egypt happen, and which pharaoh faced Moses? The claim on the scales A mass departure of the whole people of Israel from Egypt, some 600,000 men plus families, took place in the Late Bronze Age.
