Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established On its full scale the Exodus should have left traces: two million people crossing Sinai, an army lost, a labour force gone. None has been found, and Israel's first villages look local. But the evidence is uneven. The Delta has lost its archives, Sinai nomads leave little behind, and Semitic workers in Egypt are well attested. A smaller exodus remains plausible and cannot be ruled out, while the mass departure awaits evidence. The divine events at the heart of the story are matters of faith, not archaeology. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks often say flatly that the Exodus 'did not happen'. That is fair for the scale described, where the silence of Sinai is telling. It is overconfident for a smaller movement, because the Delta, the one place Egyptian paperwork could have mentioned escaped workers, preserves almost none. The honest summary is narrower: no evidence yet for a mass exodus, a real but faint Egyptian thread in early Israel. What is solid The Merneptah Stele, carved about 1208 BCE, names 'Israel' as a people in Canaan, written with the sign for a group of people rather than a city. Cairo Museum JE 31408; Pritchard (ed.) 1969 West Semitic people lived and worked in the eastern Nile Delta throughout the 2nd millennium BCE; the Hyksos, rulers of Levantine origin, governed from Avaris until they were driven out around 1550 BCE. Bietak 1996 Ramesses II built a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, at Qantir in the eastern Delta; Exodus 1:11 names the store city 'Rameses'. Shaw (ed.) 2000 No known Egyptian text mentions Israelites in Egypt, the plagues, or the loss of a pharaoh's army in the sea. Finkelstein and Silberman 2001; Hoffmeier 1997 Ocean modelling shows that a steady 28 m/s east wind for 12 hours can expose a mud-flat land bridge 3–4 km long and 5 km wide in a Delta lagoon for about 4 hours. Drews and Han 2010 What is disputed Which pharaoh, if any: Ahmose I (the Hyksos expulsion), Thutmose III or Amenhotep II (the biblical 1446 BCE date), Ramesses II or Merneptah. Whether a smaller group, perhaps the ancestors of the Levites, carried a real memory of Egypt into early Israel. Where the Yam

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Moses led the Children of Israel out of Egypt, and the sea parted before them (Quran 26:63; Exodus 14:21–22). Awaiting discovery No Egyptian record describes the event, which is expected: Egyptian monuments rarely recorded defeats. Semitic-speaking people in the eastern Delta are well documented, and 'Israel' is in Canaan by about 1208 BCE (Merneptah Stele). Pharaoh called them 'a small band' (Quran 26:54). Plausible A small group leaves almost no trace in the desert, which fits the silence of the ground far better than the 600,000 men of Exodus 12:37, a number archaeology has not supported. Pharaoh's body would be preserved as a sign for later generations (Quran 10:92). Open question Many New Kingdom royal mummies survive, including Ramesses II and Merneptah, but the text does not name the Pharaoh, so no mummy can be matched to it on present evidence.

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: 01 A king at the water's edge
chunks.text: Two scriptures tell the same night from different sides. In the book of Exodus, an east wind blows until dawn, the sea divides, and the Israelites walk through with water standing like walls on either side. When Pharaoh's chariots follow, the sea returns. In the Quran, Moses is told to strike the sea with his staff, and each side rises 'like a great towering mountain'. Then the camera, as it were, turns to Pharaoh himself. But as he was drowning he cried, 'I believe there is no God except the one the Children of Israel believe in. I submit to Him.' The reply comes two verses later: 'Today We shall save only your corpse as a sign to all posterity.' It is one of the most arresting lines in either tradition, a promise that the tyrant's body would outlast him as a warning. It also raises questions a historian can actually chase. Which pharaoh? When? And what, if anything, did Egypt itself record? Egypt is the best-documented civilisation of the Bronze Age. Its kings carved their victories on temple walls and buried their dead with their names. That makes the silence around the Exodus loud, and it makes every scrap of evidence around its edges precious.

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: 02 What the stones do say
chunks.text: In 1896 Flinders Petrie found a black granite slab, over 3 m tall, in a funerary temple at Thebes. It celebrates the victories of Merneptah, son of Ramesses II, in about 1208 BCE. Near the end comes a roll call of the defeated in Canaan: Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam, and then Israel. The first three are written with the sign for a city or land. Israel carries the sign for a people. By the late 13th century BCE, a group called Israel was living in Canaan and was worth boasting about. A horizontal timeline from 1650 to 1150 BCE. At the top left a dashed band marks the Thera eruption, radiocarbon dated around 1600 BCE and debated. Below it a short bar marks Ahmose I, 1550 to 1525 BCE, who expelled the Hyksos. Next come bars for Thutmose III and Amenhotep II with an accent marker at 1446 BCE, the date implied by 1 Kings 6:1. Near the right, a long bar for Ramesses II, 1279 to 1213 BCE, is followed by a short red bar for Merneptah. A thick vertical line marks the Merneptah Stele at about 1208 BCE, after which a shaded band shows Israel already in Canaan. The stele sets a latest date, and the chart above shows how the candidate pharaohs line up against it. Egypt also shows that Semitic people were a normal part of Delta life. A tomb at Beni Hasan paints a caravan of Asiatics arriving around 1890 BCE. A papyrus now in Brooklyn lists household servants with Semitic names. At Tell el-Dab'a, Manfred Bietak excavated Avaris, capital of the Hyksos, Levantine rulers who governed the north until Ahmose I expelled them around 1550 BCE. Later, under the Ramessides, Papyrus Leiden 348 records rations for 'Apiru dragging stone for a great pylon. The 'people' sign on the Merneptah Stele is a throw stick plus a seated man and woman over three plural strokes. Scribes used it for groups without a

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: 03 Why most scholars doubt a mass exodus
chunks.text: The text itself sets the bar high. Exodus 12:37 counts 'about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides little ones', which implies some two million people. A population that size, wandering for forty years, should leave something: hearths, pottery, burials. Surveys across Sinai have found camps of herders from other periods, including the 3rd millennium BCE and the Byzantine era, but nothing that fits a Late Bronze Age multitude. At Kadesh Barnea, where Israel is said to have stayed for decades, excavation found forts no older than about the 10th century BCE. Meanwhile the first Israelite villages in the hills of Canaan, founded around 1200 BCE, look local. Their pots and houses continue Canaanite traditions. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman argued in 2001 that Israel emerged mainly from within Canaan and that the Exodus took its classic shape in the 7th century BCE, when Judah had its own reasons to tell a story of freedom from Egypt. Egypt kept its stones, but almost none of the paperwork where escaped workers would appear.

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: 04 Four pharaohs and their champions
chunks.text: Each candidate has serious defenders. Readers of 1 Kings 6:1, which places the Exodus 480 years before Solomon built the Temple, arrive at about 1446 BCE and the reigns of Thutmose III or Amenhotep II. Others look to Ahmose I and the expulsion of the Hyksos: a real mass departure of Semitic people from the Delta. Josephus, quoting the Egyptian priest Manetho, already linked the two in the 1st century CE. Some add the eruption of Thera, which radiocarbon places around 1600 BCE or somewhat later, and the Ahmose 'Tempest Stela', which describes a storm and darkness over Egypt. The best-known candidate is Ramesses II, because Exodus names the city 'Rameses'. The French physician Maurice Bucaille, who examined royal mummies in the 1970s, argued instead for his son Merneptah, a view many Muslim readers adopted. David Rohl goes further and rebuilds the whole Egyptian chronology, placing the Exodus centuries earlier among the Semitic population of Avaris. Most Egyptologists reject his redating. James Hoffmeier, digging at Tell el-Borg in north Sinai, argues that the route and geography in Exodus fit a Late Bronze Age frontier of forts and lakes. Richard Elliott Friedman offers a smaller, testable-sounding idea: the people who came out of Egypt were the Levites. Egyptian names are concentrated among them, from Moses to Phinehas, and the laws about welcoming strangers are strongest in texts linked to them. It would explain how a real memory could be carried into a people most of whom had never left Canaan.

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: 05 Could wind really part a sea?
chunks.text: The Hebrew name of the sea is Yam Suph, most likely 'Sea of Reeds'. Reeds grow in fresh or brackish marshes, not the deep Red Sea, which is one reason modellers look at the shallow lagoons of the Delta. Exodus names the mechanism plainly: 'a strong east wind all night'. Step 1 of 4. Calm: a shallow coastal lagoon about 2 m deep, where the Pelusiac branch of the Nile met the Lake of Tanis. Calm: a shallow coastal lagoon about 2 m deep, where the Pelusiac branch of the Nile met the Lake of Tanis. A steady east wind of 28 m/s (about 100 km/h) pushes the water west. It piles up downwind and drops upwind. After about 9.5 hours the mud flats break the surface: a land bridge 3–4 km long and 5 km wide that stays dry for about 4 hours. When the wind stops, the water flows back as a shallow-water wave at about 4.4 m/s, far faster than people walk. A cross-section of a shallow lagoon with west on the left and east on the right. Step 1: calm water about 2 metres deep over a gently rising bed. Step 2: arrows show an east wind of 28 metres per second; the water surface tilts, piling up on the west and dropping in the east. Step 3: after about twelve hours the eastern bed is exposed as mud flats, a land bridge 3 to 4 kilometres long and 5 kilometres wide that stays dry for about 4 hours. Step 4: the wind stops and an arrow shows the water flowing back at about 4.4 metres per second. Carl Drews and Weiqing Han modelled the ancient Lake of Tanis, where the Pelusiac branch of the Nile once met a coastal lagoon. With a steady east wind of 28 m/s for 12 hours, mud flats rose above the water after about nine and a half hours: a land bridge 3–4 km long and 5 km wide, dry for about 4 hours. When the wind dropped, the water came back fast. Doron Nof and Nathan Paldor had shown in 1992 that a s

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: 06 The body kept as a sign
chunks.text: Quran 10:92 promises that Pharaoh's body would be saved 'as a sign to all posterity'. Classical commentators such as al-Tabari reported that the sea cast the drowned king up on dry ground, so that the Israelites, who doubted that he was truly dead, could see him. In the 20th century many readers connected the verse to the royal mummies of Egypt. The mummy of Ramesses II was found in 1881 in a hidden cache at Deir el-Bahari and flown to Paris in 1976 for conservation. Merneptah's was found in 1898 in the tomb of Amenhotep II. Here the testable part is narrow. Dozens of New Kingdom royal mummies survive, embalmed in the usual way, and published studies have not identified any one of them as a drowned king. Claims circulating online that a mummy shows sea salt or drowning are not supported by peer-reviewed work. For believers, the sign of the verse does not depend on which body it was, and the classical reading is complete without a museum at all.

chunks.heading: Moses, Pharaoh and the Sea That Stepped Back: 07 What time hid, and what would settle it
chunks.text: Time has been unkind to exactly the right places. The Delta is wet, and its papyri have rotted, so the kind of document that might mention runaway workers survives mainly from the dry south. The Pelusiac branch of the Nile has vanished under silt and farmland. Pi-Ramesses was dismantled to build Tanis. Nomads in Sinai left a few stones in a circle. The case is open because the evidence was fragile to begin with. A Delta text naming Israelite or Hebrew labourers, or a flight of workers, from the right centuries. Late Bronze Age camps in Sinai that match early Israel's material culture. Cores from the ancient Lake of Tanis with chariot fittings or weapons in a single layer. A firm date tying Thera, the Tempest Stela and the Hyksos expulsion together.

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon Tower rebuilt c. 620–560 BCE on older foundations; story set in the primeval age Strong evidence. Was the Tower of Babel a real building, and did language begin as one? The claim on the scales The Tower of Babel story in Genesis 11 was modelled on Babylon's real ziggurat, Etemenanki. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Several independent lines agree: the city's name, the pun on it, the stepped tower, the fired brick and bitumen, the royal boast of workers from many lands, and the presence of Judean exiles in Babylon while the rebuilt tower rose. What keeps this from 'Established' is dating. If the story is older than the exile, its model may be the tower in ruins after 689 BCE, another ziggurat, or the idea of ziggurats in general. The scattering of languages in one day is a theological point that linguistics does not test. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Museum labels usually say plainly that Etemenanki inspired the Tower of Babel, and the evidence largely earns that confidence. The gap is in the details: the tablet's 90 m height is often repeated as fact though some reconstructions are much lower, and the timing of the Genesis text, which decides which phase of the tower its authors knew, remains uncertain. What is solid Etemenanki, the stepped temple tower of the god Marduk in Babylon, had a square base about 91 m on each side; its foundations were identified by Robert Koldewey's German excavation. Koldewey 1914; George 2005/2006 The tower was wrecked when Sennacherib sacked Babylon in 689 BCE and rebuilt by Esarhaddon, Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II (604–562 BCE). George 2005/2006 The Tower of Babel stele in the Schøyen Collection, from Nebuchadnezzar's reign, shows the king beside the stepped tower and is the oldest known image of it. George 2011 Judeans were deported to Babylon in 597 and 586 BCE and lived there while the rebuilt tower dominated the city. 2 Kings 24–25; Babylonian Chronicles Genesis 11:3 describes fired brick with bitumen for mortar, the characteristic building method of southern Mesopotamia rather than of stone-built Judah. Genesis 11:3; Finkel and Seymour 2008 What is disputed When the Babel story was written: before the exile (so modelled on an earlier or ruined tower) or during and after it. How tall Etemenanki really stood: about 90 m by the Esagila tablet, or nearer 66 m in some modern reconstructions. Whether all human languages descend from a single ancestral language, and whether that could ever be detected. W

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. People built a city and a tower of fired brick, with bitumen for mortar (Genesis 11:3–4). Established This is exactly how Mesopotamian ziggurats were built, including Etemenanki at Babylon. The diversity of human languages is a sign (Quran 30:22); languages were confused at Babel (Genesis 11:7–9). Matter of faith Linguists trace language families far back in time, but where human speech first came from is still unknown.

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon: 01 A city, a tower and a pun
chunks.text: Genesis 11 is only nine verses long. 'Now the whole earth had one language and the same words.' People move east, settle on a plain in the land of Shinar, bake bricks and decide to build 'a city and a tower with its top in the heavens'. God comes down to see it, confuses their language, and scatters them. The city is named Babel, 'because there the Lord confused the language of all the earth'. In Hebrew the joke is sharp. Babel is simply the Hebrew name for Babylon. The Babylonians understood their city's name as Bab-ili, 'gate of the god'. Genesis hears it as balal, 'to mix up'. The gate of heaven becomes the capital of confusion. The gate of the god becomes the capital of confusion, and the building behind the joke was real.

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon: 02 The real tower
chunks.text: Babylon's great ziggurat was called Etemenanki, Sumerian for 'house, foundation platform of heaven and earth'. It stood beside Esagila, the temple of the god Marduk. When the German archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated Babylon from 1899, he found its footprint: a square about 91 m on each side, with a massive stair on its south face. Very little else survived. Side elevation of a seven-stage stepped tower drawn to scale. The lowest stage is 90 metres wide and 33 metres high, the second 78 metres wide and 18 metres high, then four stages each 6 metres high and narrowing from 60 to 33 metres wide, topped by a temple 24 metres wide and 15 metres high, for a total of about 90 metres. A central staircase climbs the front of the first two stages. A dimension line marks the square base of about 91 metres. A dashed line at 66 metres marks a lower modern estimate. A tiny 1.7 metre person stands at ground level next to a 20 metre scale bar. The height comes from a clay tablet. The so-called Esagila tablet, copied at Uruk in 229 BCE from an older text and translated by George Smith in 1876, gives the dimensions of each stage. Converted at about 6 m per Babylonian nindan, it describes seven stages rising to roughly 90 m, as tall as the base was wide. Some modern reconstructions come out lower, around 66 m including the temple. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BCE, described a tower of eight stages with a stair winding around the outside and a shrine on top. The tower had a violent history. Sennacherib of Assyria sacked Babylon in 689 BCE and wrecked it. Esarhaddon began repairs. Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt it on a grand scale. Nabopolassar's foundation cylinder boasts that he had his own sons carry earth and building materials. A b

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon: 03 Exiles in the tower's shadow
chunks.text: In 597 BCE and again in 586 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar's armies deported thousands of Judeans to Babylonia. Among them were priests and scribes, the people who would shape much of the Hebrew Bible. They lived in a city dominated by a mountain of brick that the king described as reaching to heaven, built with labour drawn from across his empire. The details of Genesis fit that world closely. 'They had brick for stone and bitumen for mortar,' the text explains, as if to readers who knew stone buildings. Judah built in stone. Babylonia, a land of river mud with no quarries, built in baked brick set in bitumen. The story sounds like a hill people's description of a lowland empire. Babylonian ration tablets found in Nebuchadnezzar's palace list oil issued to 'Jehoiachin, king of Judah' and his sons. They confirm what 2 Kings says: the Judean royal family lived in Babylon, in the city of the tower. There is a complication. Many scholars assign the Babel story to an older strand of Genesis, which may have been written before the exile. If so, its authors may have known Etemenanki as a ruin after 689 BCE, a half-finished tower abandoned by its builders, which is exactly how the story ends.

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon: 04 A Sumerian Babel, and a Quranic sign
chunks.text: The idea that languages were once one is older than Genesis. The Sumerian epic Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, known from copies of the early 2nd millennium BCE, includes a spell of the god Nudimmud (Enki). It imagines a time when many peoples 'address Enlil together in a single language', and says that Enki 'shall change the speech in their mouths'. In 1968 Samuel Noah Kramer read it as a Sumerian 'Babel of tongues'. Other Sumerologists read the same lines as a hope that languages would be made one again. The text is ambiguous, but the theme is there. The Quran does not tell the Babel story. It does treat the variety of human speech as something to reflect on: 'Another of His signs is the creation of the heavens and earth, and the diversity of your languages and colours.' And it gives a different tyrant a tower. In Quran 28:38, Pharaoh tells Haman to 'light me a fire to bake clay bricks, then build me a tall building' so that he may climb up to the God of Moses. The motif of baked brick raised against heaven appears in both scriptures, and in both it ends in failure.

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon: 05 Did everyone once speak one language?
chunks.text: Here the challengers have a real point. More than 7,000 languages are spoken today, grouped into a few hundred families. Linguists can reconstruct parent languages by comparing regular sound changes. Proto-Indo-European, ancestor of English, Hindi and Persian, is dated to somewhere between about 6,000 and 8,000 years ago, and a 2023 study by Paul Heggarty and colleagues favoured the older end. Beyond roughly 10,000 years, most linguists think the signal fades into noise. Merritt Ruhlen and John Bengtson argue that it does not fade completely. They list word roots, such as a form like 'tik' for finger or one, that they claim to find across many families, and they read them as fossils of a single mother tongue. Most linguists doubt these matches, because chance resemblances are common. Quentin Atkinson took a different route in 2011, showing that languages far from Africa tend to use fewer distinct sounds, as if speech had lost variety as humans spread out. That result is also debated. What linguistics does not see is a sudden break. Latin became French, Spanish and Romanian over some 1,500 years, gradually, speaker by speaker. A deep single origin is possible. A single afternoon of confusion is outside what the discipline can test.

chunks.heading: The Tower of Babel Stood in Babylon: 06 Other candidates, and what time erased
chunks.text: Babylon's tower was not the only candidate. Travellers for centuries pointed to the tall ruin at Borsippa, Birs Nimrud, a few kilometres south, because it still stood high when Etemenanki had vanished. David Rohl proposes Eridu, the ancient city of Enki, whose temple mound was rebuilt again and again from the 6th millennium BCE. Later Islamic storytellers, in collections of prophets' tales, gave the tower to the tyrant Nimrod. The real Etemenanki had a sad ending. Alexander the Great ordered it cleared for rebuilding around 323 BCE and died before work began. Its bricks became a quarry for later builders. Today its base is a square outline, often flooded. Whatever inscriptions once lined its faces went with the bricks. A text from the exile that names Etemenanki in a Judean setting. A secure date for Genesis 11 from manuscripts or the history of its Hebrew. Excavation of the tower's earliest phases below the water table. A tested method that can reach beyond 10,000 years of language history.

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam Visit set in the 10th century BCE; kingdom of Saba c. 8th century BCE–6th century CE Awaiting discovery. Did a queen of Saba visit Solomon, and does the dam story fit Marib? The claim on the scales A ruling queen from Saba in South Arabia made a state visit to Solomon in Jerusalem in the 10th century BCE. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Saba's existence, wealth and incense trade are well established, and the Quran's account of its two irrigated oases and the flood of the dam fits the archaeology of Marib remarkably well. The visit itself has no independent witness. No inscription names a Sabaean queen, the kingdom's records begin about two centuries after Solomon, and the one possible 10th-century link, the Ophel jar, is disputed. Because early Saba is so poorly explored, this is an absence in unexcavated ground, not evidence against. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks tend to file the queen under legend with some confidence, and on present evidence that is fair. But they sometimes imply that 10th-century Saba did not exist, which goes further than the evidence: the kingdom's earliest phase is simply unexcavated and war now blocks fieldwork. Meanwhile the dam story, often treated as pious folklore, is one of the best-documented engineering disasters of antiquity. What is solid Saba (Sheba) was a real kingdom centred on Marib in Yemen, with monumental inscriptions from about the 8th century BCE and a history lasting until the 6th century CE. Simpson (ed.) 2002; UNESCO 2023 Assyrian records mention Saba: Sargon II received tribute from It'amra the Sabaean around 715 BCE, and Sennacherib gifts from Karib-il of Saba around 685 BCE. Eph'al 1982 The Great Dam of Marib, about 580 m long and eventually about 14 m high, diverted flash floods into irrigated oases north and south of the wadi, around 100 km² of fields. Brunner 1983; UNESCO 2023 The dam was breached and repaired in 449–450 and 548 CE (the second repair recorded in an inscription of Abraha) and finally failed around 570–575 CE. Vogt 2004; Simpson (ed.) 2002 No South Arabian inscription found so far names a queen of Saba or a mission to Jerusalem; the early rulers named in inscriptions are men. Simpson (ed.) 2002 What is disputed Whether Sabaean kingship and long-distance trade already existed in the 10th century BCE, when the visit is set. Whether a 10th-century jar inscription from Jerusalem's Ophel is written in Sabaic and mentions an incense ingredient. Whether the q

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. A woman ruled Saba, a land that had been given of all things (Quran 27:23; 1 Kings 10:1–2). Awaiting discovery The Sabaean kingdom is real and was rich by the early 1st millennium BCE. No inscription yet found names a ruling queen, and many early Sabaean texts are still unpublished or unexcavated. Saba had two gardens, one on the right and one on the left, and lost them to 'the flood of the dam' (Quran 34:15–16). Established The great dam of Marib watered two oases, north and south of the wadi. Sabaean inscriptions record its breaches and repairs into the 6th century CE, and it failed for the last time around 570–575 CE; the oases were then abandoned.

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam: 01 A letter carried by a bird
chunks.text: In the Quran the story begins with a missing bird. Solomon, who has been taught 'the speech of birds', reviews his assembly and notices that the hoopoe is absent. It returns with news from a land he does not know: a kingdom called Sheba, ruled by a woman who 'has been given a share of everything' and sits on a magnificent throne, whose people bow to the sun. Solomon sends a letter. The queen consults her counsellors, tests him with a gift, and finally comes herself. Her own throne has been brought ahead of her. She walks into a hall, takes its glass floor for a pool of water, lifts her skirts, and understands. 'My Lord, I have wronged myself: I devote myself, with Solomon, to God, the Lord of the Worlds.' The Hebrew Bible's version is shorter and more worldly. The queen hears of Solomon's fame, arrives in Jerusalem 'with camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones', tests him with riddles, and goes home impressed. Ethiopia's Kebra Nagast, written down in the 14th century CE, adds a son, Menelik, founder of a royal line. Arab tradition calls her Bilqis. Ethiopia calls her Makeda. Three civilisations claim her.

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam: 02 The kingdom was real
chunks.text: Saba lay on the edge of the Yemeni desert, at Marib, where the highlands give way to the sands of the Ramlat as-Sab'atayn. It grew rich on frankincense and myrrh, resins that grow only in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa and that every temple in the Mediterranean wanted. UNESCO, which inscribed the 'Landmarks of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba' in 2023, describes it as controlling much of the incense route from about the 8th century BCE. Outsiders noticed. Sargon II of Assyria recorded tribute from It'amra the Sabaean around 715 BCE. Sennacherib received gifts from Karib-il, king of Saba, around 685 BCE. At Marib itself, the great oval temple of the god Almaqah, called Awam, still bears the local name Mahram Bilqis, 'sanctuary of Bilqis'. A second temple nearby, Bar'an, is known as 'Arsh Bilqis', her throne. The Sabaean pantheon included a sun goddess, and some scholars now read Almaqah himself as a solar god rather than a moon god, which sits well with the Quran's people who bowed to the sun. The Quran's 'two gardens, one on the right, one on the left' describes Marib's two oases with a surveyor's accuracy.

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam: 03 Two gardens and the flood of the dam
chunks.text: The Quran tells a second Sheba story, and this one archaeology can follow closely. Saba had 'two gardens, one on the right, one on the left'. When its people turned away, God 'let loose on them a flood from the dam', and the gardens became scrub of bitter fruit, tamarisk and a few lote trees. The Arabic phrase, sayl al-'arim, became proverbial for a catastrophe that scatters a people. Step 1 of 5. Flash floods: a few times a year, rain in the highlands sends a torrent down the Wadi Dhana. Flash floods: a few times a year, rain in the highlands sends a torrent down the Wadi Dhana. The dam, about 580 m long, holds the flood briefly and lifts it to stone sluices at each end. Canals carry the silty water to two oases, north and south of the wadi: about 100 km² of fields, 'two gardens'. Silt raises the fields, so the dam is raised: about 4 m at first, about 7 m by c. 500 BCE, about 14 m in its last phase. After breaches in 449–450 and 548 CE, a flood around 570–575 CE overtops the dam. It is not rebuilt, and the gardens revert to scrub. A schematic plan with north at the top. Wadi Dhana runs from west to east through a gap between two hill masses. Step 1: blue dashes show a flash flood coming down the wadi toward a dam that spans the gap, with a stone sluice at each end. Step 2: water ponds behind the dam, about 580 metres long, rising to the sluices. Step 3: canals carry water from the northern sluice to a large green north oasis with Marib city, and from the southern sluice to a south oasis with the Awam temple; a caption quotes Quran 34:15 on two gardens. Step 4: an inset section shows the dam raised from about 4 metres to about 7 and finally about 14 metres. Step 5: the middle of the dam is breached around 570 to 575 CE, water runs through the gap, and both oases fade to

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam: 04 Where is the queen?
chunks.text: The difficulty is the calendar. Solomon's reign is traditionally placed in the 10th century BCE. Saba's monumental inscriptions start in the 8th. The earliest rulers they name, the mukarribs, are all men. Assyria did record powerful Arabian queens, Zabibe in 738 BCE and Samsi a few years later, but they led tribes of northern Arabia, not Saba. Other clues cut both ways. Camel caravans were the engine of the incense trade, and camel bones from the copper mines of the Arabah show domestic camels arriving in the southern Levant only in the last decades of the 10th century BCE. Frankincense residue on an altar at Arad in Judah dates to the 8th century. That fits a trade that boomed after Solomon. Yet in 2021 the epigrapher Daniel Vainstub reread a short inscription on a 10th-century jar from Jerusalem's Ophel as South Arabian Sabaic, naming an incense ingredient. If he is right, Sabaean traders were in Jerusalem in Solomon's century. Other specialists read the same letters as a local script. In 2023 UNESCO placed seven Sabaean sites at Marib, including the dam, the Awam and Bar'an temples and the city of Sirwah, on both the World Heritage List and the List of World Heritage in Danger, citing damage and risk from Yemen's war.

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam: 05 The case for the queen
chunks.text: Challengers point out that Saba did not stay on its own shore. Sabaean inscriptions and a Sabaean-style temple at Yeha in the Ethiopian highlands, built around the 8th–7th century BCE, show settlers or elites from South Arabia across the Red Sea. The Ethiopian claim to the queen, written down late, stands on real contact. The Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen argued that early Sabaean chronology may run longer than the inscriptions show, leaving room for a 10th-century kingdom. In 2012 the archaeologist Louise Schofield announced an ancient gold mine and temple in northern Ethiopia that she linked to the queen's wealth; the link has not been independently confirmed. The strongest argument is about what has not been dug. Marib is one of the least excavated great capitals of the ancient world. Wendell Phillips' expedition to the Awam temple in 1951–52 ended in a hurried escape, and work resumed only decades later. A 10th-century queen could be waiting in an unexcavated layer, or could have left nothing that survives.

chunks.heading: The Queen of Sheba and the Flood of the Dam: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Since 2015 war has closed Marib to archaeologists, and an airstrike damaged the ancient dam. Looted inscriptions appear on the antiquities market without context. The evidence that could answer this case is still in the ground, and some of it is being lost. A Sabaean inscription naming a ruling queen, or contact with Israel or Judah. Securely dated 10th-century BCE monuments at Marib or Sirwah. Agreement on the script and reading of the Ophel jar. Incense residues from 10th-century Jerusalem. Until then the verdict is split in an interesting way. The queen's journey awaits evidence. The Quran's portrait of Saba's two gardens and the flood of the dam stands on solid ground.

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom? Copper boom c. 11th–9th century BCE, peaking in the 10th Established. Were the Arabah copper mines booming in Solomon's day, and whose were they? The claim on the scales Industrial-scale copper production flourished in the Arabah (Faynan and Timna) during the 10th century BCE, the century tradition gives to Solomon. Weight of evidence Established Ruled out Established Independent teams on both sides of the modern border, using hundreds of radiocarbon dates, slag chemistry, stratigraphy and organic finds, agree that the Arabah copper industry peaked in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE. That is as firm as Iron Age dating gets. What is not established is the link to Solomon: nothing ties the mines to Jerusalem, and most researchers credit a local, largely nomadic polity. The century is right. The owner remains an open question. Textbook confidence fairly sure Openly unsure Settled fact From the 1970s many guidebooks and textbooks said flatly that 'Solomon's mines' were a myth, because Rothenberg had found an Egyptian shrine at Timna. That was overconfident about the date: radiocarbon moved the peak back into the 10th century. It remains fair about the owner. Some popular accounts now swing too far the other way, treating the dates as confirmation of Solomon's empire. What is solid High-precision radiocarbon dating at Khirbat en-Nahas in Faynan shows large-scale copper smelting in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE, with slag layers more than 6 m deep. Levy et al. 2008 At Timna, about 100 km to the south, smelting camps such as Site 30 and 'Slaves' Hill' date mainly from the 11th to 9th centuries BCE. Ben-Yosef et al. 2012 An Egyptian shrine to Hathor at Timna shows an earlier phase of mining under New Kingdom Egypt in the 13th–12th centuries BCE. Rothenberg 1972 Slag chemistry shows a sudden jump in efficiency and standardisation in the late 10th century BCE, which its authors link to the campaign of Pharaoh Sheshonq I around 925 BCE. Ben-Yosef et al. 2019 PLOS ONE Textiles dyed with true royal purple were found at Timna in layers of about 1000 BCE, a sign of a wealthy, well-connected elite. Sukenik et al. 2021 What is disputed Who controlled the mines: an early Edomite kingdom of largely nomadic people, a chiefdom based at Tel Masos in the Beersheba Valley, or Jerusalem. How large and powerful Jerusalem was in the 10th century BCE: the 'Low Chronology' of Israel Finkelstein versus the modified conventional chronology of Amihai Mazar. Whether monumental buildings in Jerusalem excavate

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Copper flowed for Solomon, and craftsmen made great basins and fixed cauldrons (Quran 34:12–13; 1 Kings 7:45–46). Established Industrial copper smelting at Faynan and Timna peaked in exactly the 10th century BCE, and Iron Age bronze casting in the Jordan valley is attested. That this industry worked for Solomon's kingdom. Open question The smelters may have been run by an Edomite or local polity that traded with Jerusalem. The texts and the slag heaps agree on the century; who controlled the mines is still argued.

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: 01 A fountain of molten copper
chunks.text: Both scriptures surround Solomon with metal. The Hebrew Bible describes the bronze pillars, basins and a vast 'sea' cast for his Temple 'in the plain of the Jordan', and calls the promised land a place 'from whose hills you may mine copper'. The Quran, speaking of Solomon, or Sulayman, as a prophet-king granted extraordinary gifts, says: 'We made a fountain of molten brass flow for him', and lists what was made for him: palaces, statues, basins like troughs, great fixed cauldrons. In 1885 H. Rider Haggard gave the world a novel called King Solomon's Mines, set in southern Africa. Fifty years later the American archaeologist Nelson Glueck walked the Wadi Arabah, the long desert valley between the Dead Sea and the Red Sea, and found hills of black slag, the glassy waste of copper smelting. He borrowed Haggard's title. The name stuck, then fell, then came back.

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: 02 A name that flipped three times
chunks.text: Glueck dated the smelting sites to the 10th century BCE by their pottery and credited them to Solomon. In 1969 the Israeli archaeologist Beno Rothenberg uncovered a small shrine to the Egyptian goddess Hathor at Timna, beneath the striking sandstone cliffs now called Solomon's Pillars. It was full of Egyptian objects of the 13th and 12th centuries BCE. Rothenberg concluded that the mines were Egyptian and older than Solomon. For thirty years guidebooks said 'Solomon's mines' were a myth. Then came radiocarbon. From 2002 Thomas Levy and Mohammad Najjar excavated Khirbat en-Nahas, 'ruins of copper' in Arabic, in the Faynan district of Jordan. They cut through more than 6 m of slag and dated charcoal and seeds layer by layer. The biggest phase of production fell in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE. At Timna, Erez Ben-Yosef's team found the same: most smelting camps were active from the 11th to the 9th centuries. The mines were booming in exactly the century the Bible gives Solomon. The mines were booming in exactly the century the Bible gives Solomon. The question is who owned them.

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: 03 An industrial landscape in the desert
chunks.text: Khirbat en-Nahas covers about 10 hectares, with around 100 buildings, a fortress with a four-chambered gate, and slag heaps over 6 m deep. Miners followed veins and nodules of green copper ore in the sandstone. Smelters mixed crushed ore with charcoal and flux and fired it in small clay furnaces driven by bellows. Step 1 of 5. Mine: shafts and galleries cut into the sandstone reach nodules of green copper ore. Mine: shafts and galleries cut into the sandstone reach nodules of green copper ore. Prepare the charge: crush the ore and mix it with charcoal and a flux of iron and manganese oxides. Smelt: bellows drive air through a clay tuyère; at around 1,200 °C the ore gives up its copper. Tap: liquid slag runs off and the copper collects below. Waste slag builds mounds metres deep. The leap: in the late 10th century BCE, larger tuyères and standard recipes left about 55% less copper in the slag. A side-view strip. On the left, a sandstone cliff with a mine shaft and gallery where a miner reaches green ore nodules. Step 2: a stone anvil and hammer stone beside three small heaps of green ore, black charcoal and red flux. Step 3: a clay shaft furnace glowing inside, fed by leather bellows through a clay tuyère, labelled about 1,200 degrees Celsius. Step 4: dark slag runs from the furnace, copper collects at its base, and black slag mounds build up on the right. Step 5: an inset bar chart compares copper left in slag before and after the late 10th-century leap, showing about 55 per cent less after larger tuyères were introduced. The chemistry of the slag tells a story of its own. In 2019 Ben-Yosef, Levy and colleagues showed that the Arabah industry improved gradually for three centuries and then leapt forward in the late 10th century BCE: larger tuyères and furnaces, standard

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: 04 Edom, Judah or a desert chiefdom?
chunks.text: The mines lie in the land the Bible calls Edom, south of the Dead Sea. The camps show desert pottery, donkeys and goats, and very few stone houses. Most excavators credit a largely nomadic Edomite polity. Genesis 36:31 even lists 'the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites'. Israel Finkelstein argues instead that the copper trade was run from Tel Masos, a hub in the Beersheba Valley, and moved west to the coast and to Egypt. Nothing found so far ties the Arabah to Jerusalem. There is no Judahite inscription, seal or administrative building in the mines. The Bible itself never says Solomon mined in the Arabah; it places his bronze casting in the Jordan Valley, far to the north. Where Arabah copper went is partly traceable: lead-isotope studies have matched some bronze tripods offered at Olympia in Greece, from about 950–750 BCE, to Faynan ore.

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: 05 Finkelstein versus Mazar
chunks.text: The mines matter because they sit inside a long argument about how big Solomon's kingdom was. Finkelstein's 'Low Chronology' moves many buildings once called Solomonic into the 9th century and sees 10th-century Jerusalem as a modest highland town. Amihai Mazar defends a 'modified conventional chronology' in which a real, if smaller, kingdom existed in the 10th century. His cousin Eilat Mazar, excavating in the City of David from 2005, claimed a massive building as David's palace; many colleagues doubted her dating. Ben-Yosef turned the Arabah into an argument about method. If a society with barely any stone architecture could run one of the largest copper industries of its age, then an absence of palaces is weak evidence that a kingdom was weak. In 2024 Johanna Regev and colleagues published 103 radiocarbon dates from Jerusalem, showing occupation and building across the 12th to 10th centuries BCE; Finkelstein responded with reservations. The argument is live, and the Arabah is now evidence on both sides.

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: 06 Solomon in two scriptures
chunks.text: The Hebrew Bible's Solomon is a builder, a trader and a sage. Beyond the Temple bronzes, 1 Kings 9:26 says he built ships 'at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea', at the southern tip of the very valley where the mines lie. Glueck thought he had found Ezion-geber at Tell el-Kheleifeh near Aqaba; later study of the pottery moved that site's main phases to the 8th–6th centuries BCE, so the port of Solomon's fleet remains unlocated. The Quran's Sulayman is a prophet-king, son of David, and the gifts of metal run in the family. Of David it says 'We softened iron for him' and told him to make coats of mail. Of Solomon it says a fountain of molten brass was made to flow for him, and it closes with a charge: 'Work thankfully, family of David, for few of my servants are truly thankful.' Classical commentators mostly understood the fountain as a miraculous spring of molten metal; some modern readers see in it a mastery of casting on a grand scale. Either way the verse is about gifts and gratitude, not mining logistics, and archaeology cannot test a miracle. What it can say is warm and specific: the generation the tradition remembers lived in the one century when copper was flowing out of the southern Levant on an industrial scale. The Quran's Solomon is surrounded by flowing copper, and so, archaeology now shows, was his century.

chunks.heading: King Solomon's Mines: Right Century, Whose Kingdom?: 07 What time hid, and what would settle it
chunks.text: Nomads leave hearths and dung, not archives. Jerusalem's 10th-century layers lie under a living city. No inscription from the Arabah names a king. The Quran's image of copper flowing for Solomon, and the Bible's bronze Temple, are set in an age when, archaeology now shows, copper really was pouring out of the southern desert. Who held the ladle is still unknown. An inscription or seal from Faynan or Timna naming a ruler or buyer. Lead-isotope matches between Arabah copper and dated 10th-century bronzes from Jerusalem or the Jordan Valley. Published radiocarbon sequences for 10th-century public buildings in Jerusalem. Excavation of the workers' own camps to learn who they were.

chunks.heading: The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us Traditionally c. 617 CE, some years before the migration to Medina Rille theory: Ruled out. What can science test about the splitting of the Moon, and what can't it? The claim on the scales Lunar rilles such as Rima Ariadaeus are physical scars left by a splitting of the Moon in the 7th century CE. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established This rating covers only the modern 'lunar scar' claim, not the Quranic account or the miracle it describes. Rilles are explained by crustal stretching and ancient volcanism; craters that overprint even the youngest grabens give ages of tens of millions of years; rock samples show no recent Moon-wide remelting; and a single 300 km trough is not the shape a whole-Moon fracture would leave. The claim also asks more of the text than the text asks. Neither the Quran nor the hadith reports speak of marks left behind. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Planetary geology textbooks present rilles as grabens and lava channels with confidence, and that confidence is earned by crater counts, orbital imaging and samples. Where they are less certain is the precise age of individual rilles, which can carry error bars of tens of millions of years. None of that uncertainty stretches to 1,400 years. What is solid Quran 54:1–2 links the nearing of the Hour with the Moon being split and describes people who see a sign and dismiss it as magic. Quran 54:1–2 Reports in the hadith collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim, attributed to several Companions, describe the Moon seen split in two at Mina, with the Prophet saying 'Be witnesses'. Sahih al-Bukhari 3869, 3637; Sahih Muslim 2800a Rima Ariadaeus, the lunar feature most often shared as a 'scar', is a graben about 300 km long: a strip of crust that dropped between parallel faults as the crust was stretched. Wilhelms 1987; Watters et al. 2012 The youngest lunar grabens are estimated at less than about 50 million years old from the craters that overprint them; most rilles are far older. Watters et al. 2012 NASA has stated that no current scientific evidence shows the Moon was split into parts and reassembled. Bailey, NASA Lunar Science Institute, 2010 What is disputed Whether 54:1 describes a past event witnessed in Mecca, as most classical commentators held, or a sign still to come at the Hour, a reading several commentators recorded. Whether a brief sign seen in Arabia at night would be expected to appear in chronicles elsewhere. Whether the Kerala tradition of a king who saw the Mo

chunks.heading: The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The Hour draws near and the Moon is split (Quran 54:1). Matter of faith Believers read it as a miracle witnessed at Mecca, or as a sign of the Hour still to come; both readings are old. Lunar samples show no physical trace of a recent split, and a miracle is by its nature beyond what instruments can test. The site rates only the modern claim that rilles are its scars.

chunks.heading: The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us: 01 The Hour draws near
chunks.text: Surah 54 of the Quran is named al-Qamar, the Moon. It opens with two short verses that pair the end of time with a sign in the sky and a very human reaction to it. The Hour draws near; the moon is split in two. Whenever the disbelievers see a sign, they turn away and say, 'Same old sorcery!' The hadith collections fill in a scene. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recalls being with the Prophet at Mina, near Mecca, when the Moon was seen in two pieces, one going towards the mountain, and the Prophet said, 'Be witnesses.' Anas ibn Malik reports that the people of Mecca had asked for a miracle, and this was what they were shown. Tradition places the night some years before the migration to Medina in 622, often around 617 CE. Picture Mina on a clear desert night: a valley a few kilometres east of Mecca, ringed by bare granite hills, perhaps under a Moon bright enough to read by. Perhaps a small group stands talking with the Prophet when someone looks up. That is the scene the reports describe, brief and local, witnessed by a handful of people who later told others what they had seen. Fourteen centuries later the story acquired a second life online, attached to photographs of a long, straight crack on the Moon's face. That modern claim can be tested. The older account, as its tellers understood it, is of another kind.

chunks.heading: The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us: 02 How Muslim scholars read the verse
chunks.text: Most classical commentators, including Ibn Kathir, understood the verses as describing a real event witnessed in Mecca, one of the signs granted to the Prophet. They leaned on the number of Companions who reported it, among them Ibn Mas'ud, Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar. The later hadith scholar al-Kattani listed it among the mass-transmitted reports, those carried by so many independent chains that forgery was thought implausible. Other commentators recorded a second reading. Al-Raghib al-Isfahani, al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari noted that the Arabic verb can be understood as 'the moon will be split', one of the signs of the end of time, and a minority held that this is the verse's only meaning. The wording that follows, about people who see signs and dismiss them, is read by the majority as pointing to something the first audience had witnessed. The setting matters for how the verse was heard. Other Meccan passages record the Prophet's opponents demanding proofs on their own terms, such as a spring gushing from the ground or a ladder into the sky (Quran 17:90–93). Surah 54 answers in a different register: it reminds its listeners of peoples before them, Noah's, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot's and Pharaoh's, who were warned and turned away. The split Moon is presented as one more sign, and after each story its refrain asks whether anyone will take heed. In Islamic theology a miracle (mu'jiza) is by definition an act of God outside the ordinary course of nature, granted as a sign to particular people. It is not a claim that the laws of physics were quietly obeyed. That is why many Muslim scholars have been as unimpressed by the 'lunar scar' posts as astronomers are.

chunks.heading: The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us: 03 The crack that went viral
chunks.text: The photograph usually shared shows Rima Ariadaeus, a straight trench about 300 km long near the centre of the Moon's near side. Posts claim that NASA found it to be the seam where two halves rejoined. NASA has said otherwise. In 2010 Brad Bailey of the NASA Lunar Science Institute wrote that 'No current scientific evidence reports that the Moon was split into two (or more) parts and then reassembled at any point in the past.' The Egyptian geologist Zaghloul El-Naggar, among others, nonetheless helped spread the idea in popular lectures. Three panels. Top left: a disc representing the Moon, 3,474 kilometres across, with a short orange line near the centre marking Rima Ariadaeus, about 300 kilometres long, less than a tenth of the Moon's width. Top right: a schematic cross-section of the crust with arrows pulling outward and two inward-dipping faults; the block between them has dropped to form a flat-floored trough, with small craters on its floor and rim. Bottom: a logarithmic time axis from 100 years to 10 billion years, with a marker at about 1,400 years for the reported event, a blue bar for the youngest lunar grabens at under about 50 million years, and an orange bar for Apollo rock ages of 3.1 to 4.5 billion years. Rima Ariadaeus is a graben. When a planet's crust is stretched, it breaks along two parallel faults and the strip between them drops, leaving a flat-floored trough. Grabens are common on the Moon, on Mars and on Earth, where the Rhine valley and parts of the East African Rift are giant examples. Some lunar rilles are different, winding channels cut by lava flowing billions of years ago. Neither kind requires the Moon to have come apart.

chunks.heading: The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us: 04 Why rilles are not evidence either way
chunks.text: Geologists date lunar surfaces by counting the craters that land on them after they form. In 2012 Thomas Watters and colleagues, using images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, found small grabens so fresh that few craters cross them, and estimated them at less than about 50 million years old. Those are among the youngest tectonic features on the Moon. Rima Ariadaeus, pocked by craters of its own, is generally considered far older. The 'scar' has been collecting craters for far longer than 1,400 years. Shape tells the same story. At about 300 km, the rille spans less than a tenth of the Moon's 3,474 km width. A fracture right through the Moon would not leave one tidy trench on one face. Gravity maps from the GRAIL mission in 2013 revealed ancient dikes of cooled magma deep in the crust, but no Moon-wide break. The rille is real and fascinating. It simply belongs to a different story, one measured in millions of years. The reverse also holds. The absence of a scar says nothing against the account as the tradition tells it, because neither the Quran nor the hadith reports claim that the Moon kept a mark. Using a rille as evidence, for or against, asks a trench in the lunar crust to answer a question it was never part of.

chunks.heading: The Splitting of the Moon: What a Rille Can't Tell Us: 05 What a physical test could and could not show
chunks.text: Physics can say something about one specific version of the event: a Moon that physically broke into pieces that drifted apart and then fell back together. Pulling the Moon's mass apart and letting it reassemble would release energy on the order of 10²⁹ joules by our rough estimate, comparable to the energy needed to melt much of the Moon. Rocks returned by Apollo and the Soviet Luna probes have crystallisation ages of about 3.1 to 4.5 billion years. A Moon-wide remelting 1,400 years ago would have reset those clocks. That natural, physical version is excluded by the evidence. What physics cannot reach is a sign given to witnesses by an act outside nature, which is how classical scholars described it. History can ask different questions. The event was reported at night; if the Moon was near full, as is often assumed, it would have been above the horizon across much of Asia and Europe too. No record of it has been identified in Chinese, Byzantine, Persian or Indian sources, though 7th-century observational records are patchy outside China. A Kerala tradition tells of a king, Cheraman Perumal, who saw the Moon split and travelled to Arabia, but historians such as Sebastian Prange date the story to the 12th–14th centuries and treat it as legend. A dated 7th-century record from outside Arabia describing a strange Moon on a known night. Evidence of a young, Moon-wide resurfacing in samples or crater counts; none exists. For the miracle itself, no instrument applies: it rests on the Quran and the reports of those present. So the verdict on this page is narrow on purpose. The internet claim that a lunar trench is the seam of a 7th-century split is ruled out by the Moon's own geology. The account in the Quran and the hadith, of a sign seen by a few people on one night, lies out

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record? Proposed date 30 October 1207 BCE; text compiled c. 7th–6th century BCE Open question. Did Joshua's poet see an annular eclipse, or something else entirely? The claim on the scales Joshua 10:12–14 preserves a record of the annular solar eclipse visible from Canaan on 30 October 1207 BCE. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established The astronomy is solid: the eclipse happened, and it was visible from the right place in the right era. The link to the text is where the case divides. It rests on a disputed reading of two Hebrew verbs, it has to set aside the narrator's clear comment about a day that 'did not hurry to set', and the poem's date is unknown. Yet the fit of date and place is unusual, and the reading is argued in a peer-reviewed journal. Neither side can close the case, so it stays open. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Introductions to the Bible usually treat the passage briefly as poetry or omen language, and rarely mention the eclipse proposal. That caution is reasonable, but the brevity undersells a genuine, calculable coincidence. Popular retellings go the other way and present the 1207 BCE eclipse as solved. The astronomy deserves more confidence than it gets; the textual link deserves less. What is solid An annular solar eclipse was visible from Canaan on the afternoon of 30 October 1207 BCE; it was the only annular eclipse visible from Gibeon between 1500 and 1050 BCE. Humphreys and Waddington 2017 At Azekah the partial phase would have begun about 15:27 local sundial time, with annularity between about 16:48 and 16:53. Humphreys and Waddington 2017 The Merneptah Stele shows a people called Israel in Canaan by about 1208 BCE, so a date near 1207 BCE is historically possible. Cairo JE 31408 Joshua 10:12–13 quotes its lines from an older lost book, the Book of Jashar, and they are written as poetry, with 'sun' and 'moon' in parallel. Joshua 10:13; 2 Samuel 1:18 Excavations at el-Jib found jar handles inscribed with the name Gibeon, but little trace of a Late Bronze Age town. Pritchard 1962 What is disputed Whether the Hebrew verbs dom and 'amad can mean 'stop shining' rather than 'stand still'. Whether the text describes a lengthened day ('did not hurry to set for about a whole day'), which an eclipse does not produce. Whether the conquest stories in Joshua reflect events of the late 13th century at all. Whether other readings (celestial omen, hailstorm, poetic exaggeration) fit the text better. What time has hidden The Book

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The sun stood still at Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Aijalon (Joshua 10:12–13). Open question Read as an eclipse, it fits a real annular eclipse over Canaan in 1207 BCE; read as a halted sky, it is a matter of faith. The text is poetry quoted from an older lost book, the Book of Jashar.

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?: 01 Sun, stand still
chunks.text: The story in Joshua 10 is a war story. The people of Gibeon, a town in the hills north of Jerusalem, have made peace with the Israelites. Five Amorite kings march against Gibeon to punish them. Joshua's army marches all night from Gilgal in the Jordan Valley, falls on the besiegers and chases them west down the pass of Beth-horon towards the valley of Aijalon and the lowlands around Azekah. Great hailstones fall on the fleeing army. Then the narrator stops, and quotes a poem. 'Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and Moon, in the valley of Aijalon.' And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. The narrator adds: 'Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in midheaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day. There has been no day like it before or since.' Few verses have caused more argument. Martin Luther is reported to have cited them against Copernicus. Immanuel Velikovsky built a cosmic catastrophe on them. And in 2017 two British scientists proposed that they record something that really did happen in the sky over Canaan.

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?: 02 Poem, prayer or report?
chunks.text: The lines are poetry. They pair 'sun' with 'moon' and 'Gibeon' with 'Aijalon' in the parallel style of Hebrew verse, and they come from the Book of Jashar, a lost collection also quoted for David's lament over Saul in 2 Samuel 1:18. Many scholars think a later narrator took a poetic image literally and supplied the comment about a whole day. Others hear the language of omens. In Mesopotamian astronomy, whether the sun and moon were seen together on a given day of the month, and where, was read as a sign of victory or defeat. John Holladay in 1968 and John Walton in 1994 argued that Joshua was praying for a favourable sign, and that 'stand still' may mean to hold a position rather than to stop moving. The medieval Jewish philosopher Gersonides had his own solution: the sun did not stop at all; the miracle was that so complete a victory was won before it set. An annular eclipse turns the Sun into a ring of fire, and the Moon, directly in front of it, cannot be seen at all.

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?: 03 A ring of fire over Canaan
chunks.text: Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington started from the words. The verb translated 'stand still', dom, is related to a Babylonian word meaning 'to be dark', a connection suggested by Robert Dick Wilson in 1918. The second verb, 'amad, 'to stop', could mean that the moon stopped doing what it normally does. Put together, they argue, the poem says the sun and moon stopped shining. That is a description of an eclipse. Step 1 of 4. 15:27: the Moon's edge first bites into the Sun, about 25° above the west-southwest horizon. 15:27: the Moon's edge first bites into the Sun, about 25° above the west-southwest horizon. About 16:15: more than half the Sun is covered and the light dims and cools. 16:48–16:53: annularity. A ring of Sun surrounds the dark, invisible Moon for about five minutes. About 17:30: the Sun reaches the hills, still partly eclipsed on our rough estimate. A view of the western sky above a line of low hills, with the compass points south-west, west-south-west and west along the horizon and markers towards Azekah and the valley of Aijalon. A dashed line shows the Sun's path descending from upper left to the horizon at lower right. Step 1: at 15:27 the Sun, about 25 degrees up, has a small dark bite at its lower edge. Step 2: around 16:15 more than half the Sun is covered. Step 3: from 16:48 to 16:53 the dark Moon sits inside the Sun, leaving a bright ring, about 9 degrees above the horizon. Step 4: around 17:30 the Sun reaches the hills still partly eclipsed. They then searched the sky. Calculating eclipses three thousand years back requires correcting for the slow, irregular braking of the Earth's spin by the tides. With that correction, they found that the only annular eclipse visible from Gibeon between 1500 and 1050 BCE happened on the afternoon of 30 October

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?: 04 What the eclipse would mean
chunks.text: If the reading is right, the consequences reach Egypt. Merneptah's stele, which places Israel in Canaan, is dated to his fifth year. Combining the eclipse with Egyptian lunar dates, Humphreys and Waddington proposed that Ramesses II ruled from 1276 to 1210 BCE and Merneptah from 1210 BCE, each give or take a year. It would also make Joshua 10 the oldest datable report of a solar eclipse anywhere. The rival claim, a clay tablet from Ugarit on the Syrian coast once dated to 1223 BCE by Teije de Jong and Wilfred van Soldt, is itself disputed. One detail fits oddly well, and one does not. Seen from Gibeon, the eclipsed Sun hung low in the west-southwest, above the lowlands between the valley of Aijalon and Azekah, the very ground over which the chase ran. Perhaps soldiers on the descent of Beth-horon looked up into a dimming afternoon and saw the ring. But the poem puts the sun 'at Gibeon' and the moon 'in the valley of Aijalon', two places, not one, and in an eclipse sun and moon stand together. Supporters answer that poetic parallelism splits one image across two lines; critics reply that this is exactly the kind of flexibility that lets a reading fit almost anything.

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?: 05 The case against
chunks.text: Critics answer on several fronts. William Osborn questioned the reading in a reply in the same journal, and other Hebraists note that dom elsewhere usually means to be silent or still. The narrator's remark about a day that 'did not hurry to set' describes lengthened daylight, which an eclipse does not produce. The comparative mythologist Marinus Anton van der Sluijs argued in the journal Culture and Cosmos that Joshua's celestial miracle was not an eclipse at all. And Sawyer's 1972 case for a partial eclipse in 1131 BCE shows that eclipse readings can be fitted to more than one date. Archaeology adds its own doubt. James Pritchard's excavations at el-Jib from 1956 found jar handles stamped with the name Gibeon, a great rock-cut pool and Iron Age wine cellars, but only scraps of Late Bronze Age occupation, mostly tombs. The walled city of the story is hard to find in the 13th century. Many of the conquest stories in Joshua sit uneasily with the ground. At the far end of the spectrum, Velikovsky's claim that a passing Venus stopped the Earth's spin finds no support: ice cores and tree rings run unbroken through the period, and the orbits of the planets show no such encounter. A tale that NASA computers found a 'missing day' in astronomical calculations has circulated since the 1970s; NASA has described it as false.

chunks.heading: Joshua's Long Day: The Oldest Eclipse on Record?: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: For believers, Joshua 10 records a day on which 'the Lord fought for Israel', whatever the mechanism, and nothing in the eclipse debate touches that confession. For historians, the question is narrow and testable: did a poet in Canaan describe the eclipse of 1207 BCE? Other ancient texts using dom or 'amad for a darkened sun or moon. An early translation or manuscript that reads the verse as darkness. A Late Bronze Age town at Gibeon, with signs of conflict around 1200 BCE. An independent record of the 1207 BCE eclipse from Canaan or Egypt.

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading
chunks.text: Peoples of the Sacred Texts The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading c. 7–4 BCE (setting); Gospel of Matthew written c. 80–90 CE Plausible. Was Matthew's star a real event in the sky, and which one? The claim on the scales A real astronomical event of 7–5 BCE lies behind the star in Matthew's Gospel. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The candidates are real and datable: the 7 BCE conjunctions can be computed and were predicted by Babylonian astronomers, and the 5 BCE comet is recorded in China. The Magi, as sky-readers, would have watched such events. That makes a real sign behind the story plausible. It stops short of 'strong' because the account comes from one Gospel written decades later, fits a known scriptural motif, and no candidate matches every detail without special pleading. Which event, if any, remains open. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact New Testament introductions tend to treat the star as symbolic, while planetarium shows often present the 7 BCE conjunction as the answer. Both are more confident than the evidence. The symbolic reading ignores that the Magi were real astrologers in a year full of real signs; the planetarium answer ignores that a conjunction 1° apart would not look like one star, and that other events compete. What is solid Only the Gospel of Matthew, written around 80–90 CE, tells of the star and the Magi. Brown 1977 Jupiter and Saturn met three times in the constellation Pisces in 7 BCE, in late May, around the start of October and in early December, each time about 1° apart. Computed ephemeris; Hughes 1976 A Babylonian astronomical almanac for 7/6 BCE predicted the positions of the planets for that year, including Jupiter and Saturn in Pisces. Sachs and Walker 1984 Chinese records in the Han shu describe a 'broom star' (a comet) in spring 5 BCE that was visible for over 70 days. Humphreys 1991 Herod the Great, who appears in the story, died around 4 BCE by the usual reckoning, which bounds the window; a minority argue for 1 BCE. Josephus, Antiquities 17; Filmer 1966 What is disputed Which event, if any: the 7 BCE conjunctions, a lunar occultation of Jupiter in Aries in 6 BCE, or the comet of 5 BCE. Whether Matthew's phrase usually translated 'in the east' means 'at its rising', an astrological technical term. Whether any natural object could 'go ahead' of travellers and 'stop' over one place. Whether the star is a literary symbol built from Numbers 24:17 rather than a remembered observation. What time has hidden No Parthian or Babylonian astrological report interpreting a

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Magi saw a star rise and followed it to Bethlehem (Matthew 2:1–2, 9–10). Plausible Real sky events of 7–5 BCE include a triple conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn and a Chinese record of a 'broom star' in 5 BCE. A star that stops over one house is best read as a matter of faith or of storytelling.

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading: 01 Travellers asking about a star
chunks.text: Matthew's Gospel tells it in a dozen verses. In the last years of King Herod, 'magi from the east' arrive in Jerusalem with an unsettling question: where is the child born king of the Jews? They have seen his star. Herod's scholars point them to Bethlehem, a few kilometres south. The star goes ahead of them 'until it stopped over the place where the child was', and they are 'overwhelmed with joy'. They offer gold, frankincense and myrrh, and go home another way. No other Gospel mentions the star. Luke's birth story has shepherds and a manger instead. Matthew was written around 80–90 CE, some eighty years after the events it describes. Yet since at least the 3rd century, when the scholar Origen suggested the star was a kind of comet, people have searched the sky of those years for it. In Padua around 1305, Giotto painted it as a blazing comet, very likely inspired by Halley's Comet of 1301.

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading: 02 Who were the Magi?
chunks.text: The Greek word magoi first named a priestly tribe of the Medes, according to Herodotus, known for interpreting dreams. By Roman times it meant experts in Persian and Babylonian lore, and above all in reading the heavens. Babylonian astronomer-scribes were still at work: the latest datable cuneiform tablets, from the 1st century CE, are astronomical. Magi 'from the east' would most naturally be astrologers from Parthian Mesopotamia or Persia. That changes what we should look for. The NRSV Updated Edition notes that 'in the east' can also be read 'at its rising', a technical phrase for a star's first appearance in the dawn sky. Professional astrologers did not need a dazzling light. They needed a meaningful configuration: which planet, in which sign, doing what. An event could have meant everything to them and nothing to a shepherd. An event could have meant everything to an astrologer and nothing to a shepherd looking at the same sky. The gifts point east too. Frankincense and myrrh are resins of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, the same incense trade that had made the kingdom of Saba rich centuries before. Gold, incense and myrrh were the classic tribute of eastern peoples to a king, and Matthew's readers would have heard the list that way.

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading: 03 Kepler's conjunction
chunks.text: In December 1603 Johannes Kepler watched Jupiter and Saturn meet in the sky. The following October a brilliant new star, a supernova, appeared near them. In his book De Stella Nova (1606) Kepler wondered whether a similar conjunction around the time of Christ's birth had been joined by a similar new star. Working back, he found that Jupiter and Saturn had met in Pisces in 7 BCE. A sky chart with ecliptic longitude from 356 to 344 degrees running left to right, east on the left. An orange track shows Jupiter moving left, looping back to the right around September, then moving left again. A blue track below shows Saturn doing the same in a smaller loop. Dashed vertical lines mark three conjunctions where the planets share the same longitude, about 1 degree apart: around 29 to 30 May, around 30 September to 2 October, and around 4 to 6 December 7 BCE. Dots mark every ten days, and a scale bar shows 1 degree, the width of two full Moons. It was not one meeting but three. Jupiter, moving faster, overtook Saturn in late May 7 BCE. Around opposition in mid-September both planets reversed direction for a few weeks, as outer planets do when Earth passes them, and Jupiter slipped back past Saturn around the start of October. When they turned forward again, Jupiter passed a third time in early December. Each time they were about 1° apart, two full-Moon widths, close but still clearly two points of light. A cuneiform almanac for that year, published by Abraham Sachs and Christopher Walker in 1984, shows that Babylonian astronomers had calculated the planets' positions in advance. Planetary positions can be computed backwards with great accuracy; the drawing here uses a standard ephemeris. The dates of the three conjunctions differ by a day or two depending on whether they are measu

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading: 04 A royal occultation and a Chinese comet
chunks.text: Other candidates compete. Michael Molnar, an astronomer who studied the coins of Antioch, noticed that some show a ram looking back at a star, and argued that Aries was the sign of Judea for Roman-era astrologers. On 17 April 6 BCE the Moon passed in front of Jupiter in Aries, and by Molnar's calculation Jupiter was then rising in the east before dawn. For an astrologer, Molnar argued, that was a royal birth announced for Judea. Colin Humphreys favoured something that anyone could see. The Han shu, the official history of China's Former Han dynasty, records a 'broom star', a comet with a tail, appearing in spring 5 BCE and visible for over 70 days. It was logged by court astronomers with no interest in Judea, which makes it the strongest independent witness to something new in the sky in that window. In 2025 the NASA planetary scientist Mark Matney published an orbit for the 5 BCE comet in the Journal of the British Astronomical Association. In his best fit the comet passed close to Earth in June 5 BCE and, for several hours, moved almost in step with the sky's rotation, appearing to stand still overhead. It is the first natural model for a star that seems to 'stop'. It depends on an orbit inferred from sparse records.

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading: 05 A star in the story
chunks.text: Many scholars, following Raymond Brown's classic study of the birth narratives, think the star belongs to Matthew's storytelling. Centuries earlier, the Book of Numbers had given an oracle of Balaam, himself a seer from the east: 'a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel'. Jewish readers took it as messianic. Romans, for their part, expected stars to herald rulers. After Julius Caesar's death in 44 BCE a comet appeared, and Augustus presented it as Caesar's soul rising among the gods. The sceptical case has been put most fully by Aaron Adair, who argues that no candidate fits the text's movements and that the story is shaped to fulfil scripture. The believer's reading need not depend on any of this. For many Christians the star is a sign given for a purpose, and whether God used a comet, a conjunction or neither is secondary to what it pointed to. The two readings are not as far apart as they sound. A writer steeped in Numbers 24:17 could still have drawn on a memory that astrologers from the east had seen something in the sky around the time of Herod's death. The historian's job is to weigh how likely that is.

chunks.heading: The Star of Bethlehem: A Sky Worth Reading: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: The calendar keeps every candidate in play only if the usual date for Herod's death holds.
