chunks.heading: The Oracle of Delphi: Did the Earth Speak Through Her?: 05 The pushback: which gas, and how much?
chunks.text: The chemistry has been harder. In 2006 a team led by Giuseppe Etiope measured gas coming out of the soil and groundwater around Delphi. They confirmed that gas is escaping, but it is mostly methane, ethane and carbon dioxide from deep, thermally altered hydrocarbons. They concluded that this environment is not prone to producing ethylene in the hundreds or thousands of parts per million needed for neurotoxic effects. If gas affected the Pythia, they suggested, it might have been through lack of oxygen in a closed room, or through sweet-smelling aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzene dissolved in the spring. Foster and Lehoux went further, arguing in 2007 that the ethylene hypothesis does not match the clinical picture or the measured concentrations. Defenders reply that today's seepage is a weak echo, that earthquakes periodically reopen fractures, and that Plutarch himself noticed the vapour fading. Both sides agree the ancient spring has been diverted and its gas cannot now be measured. Parallel sites help. At the Plutonium of Hierapolis in Turkey, a 'gate to the underworld' where ancient writers said birds dropped dead, researchers have measured carbon dioxide from a fault building up to lethal levels near the ground at night, killing small animals just as described. Ancient sanctuaries really were built on gas vents, and ancient reports of their effects can be accurate.

chunks.heading: The Oracle of Delphi: Did the Earth Speak Through Her?: 06 What time has hidden, and what would settle it
chunks.text: The crucial evidence was disturbed long ago. The adyton's floor was dug out before anyone thought to sample gas, the spring was rerouted, and a vapour that waxed and waned with earthquakes left no ancient measurements. Absence of a chasm tells us little: the 'mouth' may have been a small fissure or a spring outlet, easily lost in a rebuilt floor. There is also a deeper layer of memory. Delphi's founding myth tells how Apollo killed the serpent Python, a child of Earth, whose rotting body gave the sanctuary its old name, Pytho. Luigi Piccardi and colleagues have read this as geomythology: an old story shaped by a landscape of earthquakes, rockfalls, springs and smelly gas. It cannot be tested directly, but it fits the site's restless geology surprisingly well. Continuous gas monitoring at the temple, especially after local earthquakes. Chemical analysis of dated travertine and spring deposits for trapped hydrocarbons. A physical model of the adyton testing whether carbon dioxide and methane could lower oxygen enough to alter a sitting woman's state. A fresh study of the old excavation records for the adyton's openings and drains. Until then Delphi remains a satisfying half-victory for the ancient witnesses: the earth under the god really did breathe, even if we cannot yet say what it breathed.

chunks.heading: The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth
chunks.text: Legends and Relics The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth 1st century CE (claimed); documented from c. 1355 CE Ruled out. Is the Shroud's linen ancient, and how did its image form? The claim on the scales The linen of the Shroud of Turin dates to the 1st century CE. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established The most direct test available, radiocarbon dating in three independent laboratories, contradicts a 1st-century date by more than a thousand years, and it agrees with the first documentation in the 1350s. The critiques are real but narrow: heterogeneity widens the range, it does not move it to antiquity, and the 2026 textile study undercuts the reweave and contamination explanations. The X-ray result rests on one thread and an uncalibrated storage assumption. The image's formation remains open, and the cloth's religious meaning is not a scientific question. Textbook confidence confident Openly unsure Settled fact Encyclopedias and museum texts present the medieval date as settled, and on the age of the linen that confidence is largely earned. They are slightly overconfident in two ways: the 1988 sample came from one small corner, so the result is strictly a date for that strip, and the image's making has not been convincingly reproduced. Treating the Shroud as a simple painting undersells a genuinely unusual object. What is solid The Shroud is a linen cloth about 4.4 by 1.1 m in a 3/1 herringbone twill, bearing faint front and back images of a man with wounds consistent with crucifixion. Freer-Waters and Jull 2026 It first appears in the historical record at Lirey in France in the 1350s; in 1389 Bishop Pierre d'Arcis wrote that an earlier inquiry had found the artist who painted it. d'Arcis memorandum 1389 In 1988 laboratories in Arizona, Oxford and Zurich independently radiocarbon-dated samples from one strip to 1260–1390 CE with at least 95 per cent confidence. Damon et al. 1989 A 2026 study of retained fragments of the 1988 sample found pure flax linen matching the main cloth, with no cotton, no repairs and no significant surface contamination. Freer-Waters and Jull 2026 The image is extremely superficial, confined to the outermost fibres of the threads, and behaves like a photographic negative, which is why its method of formation is still debated. STURP reports; Fanti et al. What is disputed Whether one sample strip from one corner represents the whole cloth, given statistical signs of heterogeneity in the 1988 raw data. Whether new methods such as wide-angle X-ray scattering can date linen reliably at all. How the image was

chunks.heading: The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth: 01 The photograph that changed everything
chunks.text: On 28 May 1898 an Italian lawyer and amateur photographer, Secondo Pia, developed a glass plate he had just exposed in Turin Cathedral. On the negative, the faint brownish stains on an old linen sheet turned into something startling: a positive image of a bearded man, with realistic light and shade, marked with wounds on his wrists, feet, side and scalp. The cloth itself behaves like a negative. Nobody in the Middle Ages knew what a photographic negative was. That moment turned a relic into a scientific mystery. The Shroud of Turin is venerated by many Christians as the burial cloth of Jesus, and it is also probably the most tested single object in history. Two questions have to be kept apart: how old is the linen, and how did the image get there? Science can say a lot about the first and rather less about the second.

chunks.heading: The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The cloth is a single piece of linen about 4.4 by 1.1 metres, woven in a fine 3/1 herringbone twill, with the image of a man laid out front and back as if the cloth had been folded over a body from head to feet. It enters written history in the 1350s at Lirey in France, in a church founded by the knight Geoffroi de Charny; a pilgrim's badge from Lirey, now in the Musée de Cluny, shows it on display. In 1389 Bishop Pierre d'Arcis of Troyes wrote to the Pope that a predecessor had investigated and found the artist who painted it. The cloth passed to the House of Savoy in 1453, was scorched in a fire at Chambéry in 1532, and has been in Turin since 1578. Then Joseph bought a linen cloth, and taking down the body, wrapped it in the linen cloth, and laid it in a tomb that had been hewn out of the rock.

chunks.heading: The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth: 03 Three labs, one answer
chunks.text: On 21 April 1988, in the cathedral sacristy, a strip was cut from one corner of the cloth and divided among laboratories in Arizona, Oxford and Zurich. Each also received control samples of known age, among them linen from a Nubian tomb and fibres from a medieval cope, without being told which was which. The labs used accelerator mass spectrometry, which can count carbon-14 atoms directly in samples of a few tens of milligrams. Step 1 of 6. Growing flax takes in carbon dioxide from the air, including about one carbon-14 atom in every trillion carbon atoms. Growing flax takes in carbon dioxide from the air, including about one carbon-14 atom in every trillion carbon atoms. Once harvested and woven, the fibres take in no new carbon. Carbon-14 decays, halving every 5,730 years. 21 April 1988: one strip is cut from a corner of the Shroud and shared between Arizona, Oxford and Zurich, with control samples. Each lab cleans its piece with acid and alkali washes, burns it to carbon dioxide and turns that into graphite. An accelerator mass spectrometer counts carbon-14 atoms against carbon-12. Combined result: 689 ± 16 radiocarbon years. A calibration curve built from tree rings converts this into calendar years: 1260–1390 CE at 95 per cent confidence. Six panels. Step 1: flax plants grow in the sun, taking in carbon dioxide, with one highlighted carbon-14 atom among many ordinary ones. Step 2: a woven cloth and a decay curve showing half the carbon-14 left after 5,730 years; after 700 years about 92 per cent remains. Step 3: the 4.4 metre Shroud with a small strip at one corner sampled and sent to Arizona, Oxford and Zurich. Step 4: the sample washed, burned to carbon dioxide and turned into graphite. Step 5: an accelerator mass spectrometer bends ions in a magnet so carbon-14

chunks.heading: The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth: 04 The challengers: one corner, many questions
chunks.text: Critics of the test do not have to argue that three labs all blundered. Their case is subtler. The strip came from a single spot at the edge of the cloth, a place handled for centuries during displays and close to repairs made after the 1532 fire. In 2005 the chemist Raymond Rogers, a veteran of the 1978 STURP investigation, argued that threads from the sample area were chemically different from the main cloth and might include later, rewoven material. In 2019 Tristan Casabianca and colleagues obtained the labs' raw data through a freedom-of-information request. Their statistical analysis found that the individual measurements were not homogeneous: the dates appear to vary across the strip in a way that should not happen in a uniform sample. That does not produce an ancient date, but it means the famous 1260–1390 range was reported with more confidence than the data strictly support. The critics' best point is not that the labs failed, but that they were only ever allowed to test one small corner. In 2022 Liberato De Caro's team in Italy tried a different clock. Wide-angle X-ray scattering measures how far the cellulose in linen has naturally broken down, which depends on time, temperature and humidity. Testing one thread, they reported a structure like that of linen from the siege of Masada, 55–74 CE, if the cloth had been stored at typical room conditions for 13 centuries.

chunks.heading: The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth: 05 The replies, and what is still unexplained
chunks.text: The strongest reply came from the fragments themselves. In 2010 Rachel Freer-Waters and Timothy Jull examined a retained piece of the Arizona sample and found no evidence that it came from a medieval repair. In April 2026 they published a fuller study of two dated fragments: pure flax, with the same herringbone weave and yarn twist as the main cloth, no repairs and no significant surface contamination. The 2026 npj Heritage Science study removes the most popular explanation for a wrong date, the invisible medieval patch. Meanwhile a 2025 digital study by Cicero Moraes argued that the image matches a low relief better than a wrapped human body, which suits a medieval craft technique; Casabianca and colleagues published a rebuttal in 2026. The image debate is very much alive. The X-ray claim has not persuaded most specialists. It rests on one thread, the method has not been calibrated on a series of linens of known age and history, and its answer depends heavily on the assumed storage temperature, which for this cloth included a fire hot enough to melt silver. As for the image, it is real and odd: the colour lies only in the outermost fibres, a layer a small fraction of a thousandth of a millimetre deep, with no paint soaking into the threads. Researchers have produced images with some of its properties by rubbing, dusting and scorching, but none that match all of them together.

chunks.heading: The Shroud of Turin: The Most Tested Cloth on Earth: 06 What would settle it
chunks.text: Blind radiocarbon dating of several distant areas of the cloth, in several laboratories, with the raw data published from the start. Calibration of X-ray and other structural dating methods on dozens of linens of known age and storage history. A reproduction of all the image's physical properties, by any technique, on real linen. An archival reference that securely identifies this particular cloth before the 1350s. The date of the linen is as well established as a single sampling can make it, and it is medieval. The image is a separate and genuinely open puzzle. And for millions of people the Shroud's meaning has never depended on a laboratory, which is exactly as it should be: science can weigh the cloth, not the faith of those who pray before it.

chunks.heading: The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded?
chunks.text: Legends and Relics The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded? c. 10th–6th century BCE (Temple setting) Awaiting discovery. What happened to the Ark, and could the Aksum tradition ever be tested? The claim on the scales The original Ark of the Covenant survives today in the Chapel of the Tablet at Aksum. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The Aksum tradition is sincere, ancient in Ethiopian terms, and central to a living church, but there is currently no physical or early textual evidence linking the object in the chapel to Solomon's Temple. The written account is about 1,900 years later than the events, and the object has never been examined. Hancock's route uses real places, such as the Elephantine temple, but no source says the Ark passed through them. This is a case of missing evidence rather than contrary evidence: it cannot be tested while the chapel stays closed, and respecting that is the custodians' right. Textbook confidence leaning one way Openly unsure Settled fact Textbooks usually say the Ark 'was probably destroyed or taken by the Babylonians in 586 BCE'. That is the most economical reading, but it is an inference from silence, not a recorded event, and the Bible's own list of Babylonian loot omits it. A little more humility would be honest: we know when the Ark stops being mentioned, not what happened to it. On Aksum, textbooks are appropriately cautious. What is solid Exodus describes a chest of acacia wood overlaid with gold, 2.5 by 1.5 by 1.5 cubits (about 1.1 by 0.7 by 0.7 m), carried on poles, with two cherubim on its cover. Exodus 25:10–22 Gilded wooden chests and shrines carried on poles are well attested in New Kingdom Egypt, such as the Anubis shrine from Tutankhamun's tomb, so the described object fits its world. Tomb KV62, Egyptian Museum The biblical list of what the Babylonians took from the Temple in 586 BCE does not mention the Ark, and Roman writers say Pompey found the inner sanctuary empty in 63 BCE. 2 Kings 25:13–17; Tacitus, Histories 5.9 Excavations at Kiriath-jearim, where the Bible says the Ark rested for twenty years, revealed a monumental Iron Age platform on the hilltop. Finkelstein et al. 2021 The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that the Ark is kept in the Chapel of the Tablet at Aksum, guarded by a single monk; the tradition is set out in the Kebra Nagast, compiled in the early 14th century. Kebra Nagast; Munro-Hay 2005 What is disputed Whether the Ark was taken by Egypt around 925 BCE, destroyed or carried off by Babylon in 586 BCE, or hidden before the fall of Jerusalem. Whether

chunks.heading: The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded?: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. A chest held the tablets and relics left by the families of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 25:10; 1 Kings 8:9; Quran 2:248). Awaiting discovery Portable sacred chests carried on poles are well known from Egypt. The Ark's fate after the Babylonian conquest of 586 BCE is unknown, and no object has been found.

chunks.heading: The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded?: 01 The object that vanished
chunks.text: Few objects have been described so exactly and then lost so completely. The book of Exodus gives the Ark's measurements to the half-cubit, its wood, its gold, its carrying rings and the two winged cherubim facing each other over its lid. It led Israel across the Jordan, was captured in battle by the Philistines, brought plague on their cities, and was finally carried into Jerusalem by a dancing King David. Solomon set it in the innermost room of his Temple. They shall make an ark of acacia wood; it shall be two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. Then the record falls silent. When the Babylonians sacked Jerusalem in 586 BCE, the Bible lists the bronze pillars, stands and basins they carried away, but not the Ark. Five centuries later, when the Roman general Pompey pushed into the Holy of Holies in 63 BCE, Tacitus says he found the room empty. Where did it go?

chunks.heading: The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded?: 02 What is solid
chunks.text: The Ark fits its ancient world remarkably well. Egypt's New Kingdom produced gilded wooden chests and shrines carried on poles, the best known being the Anubis shrine found in Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, with a jackal crouching on a gilded chest mounted on sledge runners and poles. Winged guardian figures flanking a sacred object are common in the art of the Levant. A cubit of about 44.5 cm makes the Ark about 1.1 m long and 0.7 m wide and high: small enough for a few bearers to carry on poles, as the scale drawing in the map shows. Step 1 of 5. The biblical story: from Sinai to Jerusalem, where Solomon places the Ark in the Temple. Inset: its size from Exodus 25, beside a person. The biblical story: from Sinai to Jerusalem, where Solomon places the Ark in the Temple. Inset: its size from Exodus 25, beside a person. c. 925 BCE: Shishak of Egypt (Shoshenq I) takes the Temple treasures. Did the Ark go too? The Bible later mentions it again. 586 BCE: Babylon destroys the Temple. The Bible lists the loot, and the Ark is not on it. Hancock's proposal: removed in the 7th century BCE to the Jewish temple at Elephantine, then south to Lake Tana. Aksum: the Chapel of the Tablet, where Ethiopian tradition holds the Ark is kept, unseen by outsiders. A map from the Mediterranean to Ethiopia, with the Nile, Red Sea, Euphrates and Tigris. Step 1: the biblical route from Sinai to Jerusalem, and an inset drawing of the Ark to scale, about 1.1 m long and 0.7 m high, beside a 1.7 m person. Step 2: an arrow from Jerusalem to Tanis in Egypt for Shishak's raid around 925 BCE. Step 3: an arrow from Jerusalem to Babylon for 586 BCE. Step 4: Graham Hancock's proposed dashed route from Jerusalem to Elephantine on the Nile and on to Tana Kirkos in Lake Tana. Step 5: the route ends at Aksum, high

chunks.heading: The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded?: 03 The mainstream story: lost in the fall of Jerusalem
chunks.text: The simplest reading is that the Ark was lost when Jerusalem fell, or before. The last clear mention is in Chronicles, where King Josiah, around 622 BCE, tells the Levites to put the holy ark in the house that Solomon built. The prophet Jeremiah, active in those same decades, looks ahead to a time when people will no longer say 'The ark of the covenant of the Lord', which reads like a community coming to terms with its absence. Two other departures are possible. Around 925 BCE Pharaoh Shoshenq I, the biblical Shishak, raided the region; 1 Kings says he took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king's house, and took everything. Yet the Ark reappears later in Chronicles, and Shoshenq's own victory list at Karnak does not name Jerusalem. Later Jewish traditions offered hopeful alternatives: 2 Maccabees says Jeremiah hid it in a cave on Mount Nebo, and rabbinic sources debated whether it lay hidden beneath the Temple itself. Mostly from what the texts do not say. Biblical scholars date the relevant books, compare their lists and note where the Ark disappears. It is a case built on silence, which is why the Babylonian ending, though most likely, remains an inference. An inscribed Babylonian booty list from 586 BCE would be the kind of document that could close the question.

chunks.heading: The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded?: 04 The challengers: the road to Aksum
chunks.text: In the ancient city of Aksum in northern Ethiopia, a small green-domed chapel beside the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion is said to hold the Ark itself. One monk, chosen for life, guards it and may see it; no one else may. The story is told in the Kebra Nagast, the 'Glory of the Kings': Menelik, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, visits his father in Jerusalem and returns to Ethiopia with the Ark. Every Ethiopian Orthodox church keeps a tabot, a consecrated replica of the tablets, and at the festival of Timkat these are carried in procession under brocade, much as the Ark was carried in the Bible. No text records the Ark's destruction. Only one tradition says where it went, and only one people has built its worship around guarding it. Graham Hancock's The Sign and the Seal (1992) gave the tradition a historical route. He argued that loyal priests removed the Ark from the Temple during the reign of Manasseh in the 7th century BCE and took it to Egypt, to the Jewish temple on Elephantine island at Aswan, which Aramaic papyri show was flourishing in the 5th century BCE until its destruction in 410 BCE. From there, he suggested, it went up the Nile into Ethiopia, rested for centuries on Tana Kirkos island in Lake Tana, where monks still point to ancient stone pillars, and reached Aksum after the kingdom converted to Christianity in the 4th century CE. The route uses real places, and Ethiopian Christianity does have deep Israelite roots. But no ancient source places the Ark at Elephantine, whose papyri describe its temple in some detail, or on Lake Tana. The Kebra Nagast was compiled around 1314–1322 CE from older materials, and Stuart Munro-Hay argued that the object at Aksum is most likely a revered tabot whose identification with Solomon's Ark grew up in medieval time

chunks.heading: The Ark of the Covenant: Lost, Hidden or Guarded?: 05 What could be tested, and what cannot
chunks.text: The Ark is one of the rare legends with a testable physical claim. If the object in Aksum is a wooden chest overlaid with gold, a few milligrams of wood could be radiocarbon-dated and the gold analysed for its source and working. A date around 1000 BCE would transform the case; a date around 1300 CE would settle it the other way. Other claimed Arks have met this fate: Tudor Parfitt traced a sacred drum of the Lemba people of southern Africa, identified by them with the Ark, and radiocarbon dating placed it around 1350 CE. But testing requires permission, and the Ethiopian Church has consistently refused, as is its right. The Temple Mount cannot be excavated. Mount Nebo has been searched by enthusiasts without result. Wood burns and gold melts, so an Ark destroyed in 586 BCE would leave no recognisable trace. This is a case where time and reverence together keep the evidence out of reach. And their prophet said to them, 'Indeed, a sign of his kingship is that the chest will come to you in which is assurance from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron had left, carried by the angels.' The Quran, too, remembers the Ark, the tabut, as a sign of divine favour in the time of Saul, holding relics of Moses and Aaron. Across three traditions the object is remembered with awe. None of them, in its own texts, tells us where it is now.

chunks.heading: The Laetoli footprint makers
chunks.text: Laetoli, Tanzania The Laetoli footprint makers A few upright walkers crossed a field of wet volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago, and their stride is still there. 3.66M yrs ago. Laetoli, Tanzania The Laetoli footprint makers A few upright walkers crossed a field of wet volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago, and their stride is still there. 3.66M yrs ago The first walkers whose actual steps we can follow about 3.66 million years ago In 1976, at Laetoli in northern Tanzania, a playful fight with dried elephant dung sent the researcher Andrew Hill diving to the ground, where he noticed animal tracks pressed into hardened ash. The search that followed, led by Mary Leakey, uncovered in 1978 what she had hoped for: a trail of about 70 hominin footprints stretching some 24 metres at Site G. They were made about 3.66 million years ago, after ash from a nearby eruption was dampened by light rain and then set almost like cement. At least two walkers left the trail, and a third probably stepped into the prints of one of them. Heel strikes, raised arches and big toes in line with the other toes show upright striding. The story keeps growing. In 2015 a new trail at Site S revealed an individual nicknamed S1 who may have stood about 165 cm, much taller than Lucy, hinting at large size differences within the species. In 2019 a team re-excavated odd tracks at Site A, first uncovered in 1976 and once blamed on a bear. They concluded a hominin made them, walking with a cross-over step, which suggests more than one kind of biped shared this landscape. What we actually have Hominin trackways in the Footprint Tuff at Laetoli Sites G, S and A, plus casts, photographs and 3D scans. How we know Radiometric dating of the volcanic tuffs; footprint shape compared with humans, other primates and bear

chunks.heading: Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh
chunks.text: Hadar, Ethiopia Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh She is the most famous skeleton on Earth, and much of what people think they know about her is wrong. 3.2M yrs ago. Hadar, Ethiopia Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh She is the most famous skeleton on Earth, and much of what people think they know about her is wrong. 3.2M yrs ago Celebrity fossil who never asked to be the 'missing link' about 3.2 million years ago On 24 November 1974, Donald Johanson and Tom Gray spotted a piece of arm bone in a gully at Hadar, Ethiopia. Over the following weeks the team recovered several hundred bone fragments from one individual, about 40 percent of a skeleton. That night the camp played the Beatles' 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' over and over, and the name stuck. In Ethiopia she is Dinkinesh, 'you are marvelous'. She stood about 1.1 metres tall, weighed perhaps 29 kg, and walked upright, while keeping long, strong arms useful for climbing. Now, what she was not. She was not the 'missing link': human evolution is a branching bush, not a chain. She was not the oldest hominin; older ones, such as Ardipithecus, are known. She was probably not alone: other hominin species likely shared the region at around the same time. And her death is an open case. A 2016 CT study argued that her unhealed fractures fit a fall from a tall tree; critics answer that many breaks could have formed long after death, as the bones fossilized and eroded. In 2025 she left Ethiopia for her first European exhibition, in Prague. What we actually have Several hundred fragments of a single skeleton (about 40 percent complete), held at the National Museum of Ethiopia, Addis Ababa. How we know Radiometric dating of volcanic layers bracketing the find; comparative anatomy of pelvis, knee and ankle for upright

chunks.heading: The Nariokotome boy (KNM-WT 15000, 'Turkana Boy')
chunks.text: Nariokotome, Kenya The Nariokotome boy (KNM-WT 15000, 'Turkana Boy') The icon of early human long-distance walking was a child, probably with a toothache. 1.5M yrs ago. Nariokotome, Kenya The Nariokotome boy (KNM-WT 15000, 'Turkana Boy') The icon of early human long-distance walking was a child, probably with a toothache. 1.5M yrs ago Homo erectus kid with a sore back and a bad tooth about 1.5 million years ago In August 1984 Kamoya Kimeu, the celebrated fossil finder of the National Museums of Kenya, spotted a small piece of skull on a slope near the Nariokotome River, west of Lake Turkana. Excavations led by Richard Leakey and Alan Walker grew it into the most complete early human skeleton then known: about 1.5 million years old and assigned to Homo erectus (some call it Homo ergaster). He was young. His teeth were still coming in, and studies of tooth growth lines suggest he was probably around 8 years old, although estimates have ranged from about 7 to 12, because his species likely grew up faster than we do. He was already tall for his age, long-legged and narrow-hipped, a body plan suited to walking in heat. Early estimates had him becoming a 180 cm giant; later work suggests a more modest adult height. His lower jaw shows signs of infection, and a 2013 re-study argued that his spine reflects a herniated disc rather than a growth disorder, as had once been proposed. So one of the best-known fossils of our lineage is probably best imagined as a lanky, sore-backed kid with a bad tooth. What we actually have A nearly complete skeleton, including skull, jaw, spine, ribs, pelvis and limb bones. How we know Dental development and tooth microstructure for age; skeletal proportions for body size; comparative anatomy and pathology studies of the spine and jaw. A fossil pri

chunks.heading: Denny (Denisova 11)
chunks.text: Denisova Cave, Russia Denny (Denisova 11) A bone splinter the size of a thumbnail revealed a girl whose parents came from two different human groups. 90,000 yrs ago. Denisova Cave, Russia Denny (Denisova 11) A bone splinter the size of a thumbnail revealed a girl whose parents came from two different human groups. 90,000 yrs ago Daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father about 90,000 years ago Denisova Cave in Siberia has produced thousands of bone scraps too broken to identify by eye. Researchers screened them with ZooMS, a method that fingerprints the collagen protein in bone, and in 2016 reported that one splinter, among roughly 2,000 fragments, came from a hominin rather than a mammoth or a bear. It was only about 2.5 cm long. Its genome, published in 2018, told one of the most surprising family stories in science. This individual, a girl at least 13 years old, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father: not distant mixed ancestry, but first-generation parents from two different groups. Her father's own genome carried traces of an earlier Neanderthal ancestor, so meetings like this had happened before. Her mother was genetically closer to Neanderthals who lived later in Croatia than to an earlier Neanderthal from the same Siberian cave, which hints that Neanderthal populations moved across Eurasia. Denny lived roughly 90,000 years ago. We have no face, no grave and no tools linked to her; just a sliver of long bone that changed estimates of how often these groups met and had children. What we actually have A single fragment of long bone (specimen DC1227), about 2.5 cm long. How we know ZooMS collagen fingerprinting to spot the fragment; ancient DNA sequencing, including patterns of heterozygosity showing one Neanderthal and one Denisovan parent; bo

chunks.heading: Shanidar Z
chunks.text: Shanidar Cave, Iraq Shanidar Z Her skull had been flattened to about 2 cm thick; scientists put her face back together piece by piece. 75,000 yrs ago. Shanidar Cave, Iraq Shanidar Z Her skull had been flattened to about 2 cm thick; scientists put her face back together piece by piece. 75,000 yrs ago Neanderthal woman rebuilt from 200 fragments about 75,000 years ago In 2018, working at Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan for the first time in about half a century, a team led by Cambridge researchers found the upper body of a Neanderthal. Her skull had been crushed in the ground to roughly 2 cm thick. Conservator Lucia Lopez-Polin strengthened the fragile pieces on site, and in the lab more than 200 fragments were reassembled, a high-stakes 3D jigsaw. Proteins in her tooth enamel point to a female; heavy wear, with front teeth ground down to the roots, suggests she died in her mid-40s, about 75,000 years ago. She stood roughly 150 cm tall and had some of the smallest adult arm bones in the Neanderthal record. She lay on her side with her left hand under her head, with a rock behind the head, within a cluster of burials beside a tall vertical rock. She lies close to Shanidar 4, the famous 'flower burial' reported in the 1960s. A 2023 study argues that the pollen there was most likely carried in by burrowing bees rather than left by mourners. The flowers may be gone, but the pattern of repeated burial at one spot still suggests these Neanderthals returned to, and remembered, their dead. What we actually have A crushed skull and upper skeleton excavated in 2018, reconstructed from more than 200 fragments. How we know Enamel peptide analysis for sex; dental wear for age; stratigraphy and luminescence dating of the cave deposits; palynology and bee-burrow analysis for the pollen

chunks.heading: Mungo Lady (Lake Mungo 1)
chunks.text: Lake Mungo, Australia Mungo Lady (Lake Mungo 1) Forty thousand years ago, on the shore of a lake that no longer exists, people cremated a young woman with care. 40,000 yrs ago. Lake Mungo, Australia Mungo Lady (Lake Mungo 1) Forty thousand years ago, on the shore of a lake that no longer exists, people cremated a young woman with care. 40,000 yrs ago Woman at the centre of one of the oldest known cremations about 40,000 years ago In July 1968 the geologist Jim Bowler was mapping ancient shorelines in the dry Willandra Lakes of New South Wales when he noticed burnt bone weathering out of a sand dune at Lake Mungo. The remains were of a young woman. Her body had been burned, the bones broken, and then burned again before being placed in a small pit: one of the oldest known cremations anywhere. In 1974, nearby, Bowler found a man buried on his back with his hands clasped, his body sprinkled with red ochre. Dating arguments ran for decades, with estimates from under 30,000 to over 60,000 years. A 2003 multi-method study placed both burials at about 40,000 years old, which makes these among the oldest funeral rituals known for modern humans. Her story also belongs to the present. Mungo Lady was returned to her Traditional Owners, the Paakantyi, Mutthi Mutthi and Ngiyampaa peoples, in 1992; Mungo Man was returned in 2015 and brought home to Lake Mungo in 2017. For these communities she is an ancestor, not a specimen, and her return reshaped how Australian science works with Aboriginal people and their dead. What we actually have Burnt and fragmented skeletal remains from a small pit in the Mungo lunette, plus the nearby ochre burial of Mungo Man. How we know Optically stimulated luminescence and other dating of the dune layers; osteology of burnt bone; burial context. Lake Mu

chunks.heading: The children of the Ice Age caves
chunks.text: Rouffignac, France The children of the Ice Age caves Some of the marks in France's painted caves were made by toddlers, probably held up by an adult to reach the ceiling. 17,000–13,000 yrs ago. Rouffignac, France The children of the Ice Age caves Some of the marks in France's painted caves were made by toddlers, probably held up by an adult to reach the ceiling. 17,000–13,000 yrs ago Toddlers who drew on ceilings and teenagers who fetched clay about 17,000 to 13,000 years ago In Rouffignac Cave in the Dordogne, probably around 13,000 years ago, people dragged soft fingers through the clay of a chamber ceiling, leaving looping lines called flutings. Kevin Sharpe and Leslie Van Gelder measured the width of three-finger marks and compared them with flutings made by modern volunteers. They concluded that some ceiling marks were made by children about 2 to 5 years old. Given the height of the ceiling, the smallest artists were probably lifted by adults. Picture an Ice Age grown-up holding a toddler up so the child could add their own lines. Footprints tell related stories. In 2013 three expert San trackers from Namibia, invited by the Tracking in Caves project, read Ice Age prints in caves of the French Pyrenees. At Tuc d'Audoubert they identified a man of about 38 and a boy of about 14 walking on their heels near a clay pit, probably gathering clay for the famous modelled bison about 15 metres away. At Niaux they read one set of prints as those of a girl of about 12, although those prints are not securely dated. Children were not just tagging along; they were probably taking part. What we actually have Finger flutings in Chamber A1 of Rouffignac; human footprints preserved in cave clay at Tuc d'Audoubert and Niaux. How we know Metric comparison of finger-mark widths with ex

chunks.heading: Naia (Hoyo Negro 5/48)
chunks.text: Hoyo Negro, Mexico Naia (Hoyo Negro 5/48) A teenage girl fell into a pitch-black pit at the end of the Ice Age; divers found her lying among saber-toothed cats. 13,000–12,000 yrs ago. Hoyo Negro, Mexico Naia (Hoyo Negro 5/48) A teenage girl fell into a pitch-black pit at the end of the Ice Age; divers found her lying among saber-toothed cats. 13,000–12,000 yrs ago Teenager who helped link the first Americans to living Native peoples about 13,000 to 12,000 years ago Around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, on the Yucatan Peninsula, a teenage girl walked through a dry cave system in the dark, probably searching for water. She fell into a deep pit now called Hoyo Negro, 'black hole'. Later, as the Ice Age ended and sea levels rose, the caves flooded. In 2007 cave divers exploring the drowned passages found her skeleton on the pit floor alongside the bones of saber-toothed cats, giant ground sloths and other animals that had made the same fatal mistake. Researchers named her Naia, after water nymphs. She was about 15 or 16. Her mitochondrial DNA belongs to a lineage (D1) found among living Native Americans, while her skull has the long, narrow shape typical of early Paleoamericans. Together these support the idea that the first Americans and today's Indigenous peoples share ancestry despite differences in appearance. Later analyses, presented at a 2017 conference, suggest she was small and slender, went through repeated periods of hunger, and may have given birth before she died. Hers was likely a hard and mobile life, cut short by a single misstep in the dark. What we actually have A nearly complete skeleton recovered from an underwater pit, with associated Ice Age animal bones. How we know Radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dating of tooth enamel and cave mineral deposits; mitocho

chunks.heading: Otzi the Iceman
chunks.text: Tisenjoch, Italy Otzi the Iceman Hikers thought they had found a recent climber; he had been lying in the ice for 5,300 years, with an arrowhead in his shoulder. 5,300 yrs ago. Tisenjoch, Italy Otzi the Iceman Hikers thought they had found a recent climber; he had been lying in the ice for 5,300 years, with an arrowhead in his shoulder. 5,300 yrs ago Copper Age traveller, murder victim and the most studied body on Earth about 5,300 years ago (c. 3350 to 3100 BCE) On 19 September 1991, hikers Erika and Helmut Simon saw a brown body emerging from melting ice high in the Otztal Alps and assumed he was an unlucky modern climber. He had died about 5,300 years ago. Surveyors later placed the spot 92.56 metres inside Italy, which is why he now rests in a museum in Bolzano. For a decade he seemed to have died of exposure; then, in 2001, X-rays revealed a stone arrowhead in his left shoulder. He also had a head injury. His stomach, analysed in 2018, held a last meal eaten between half an hour and two hours before death: very fatty ibex meat, red deer, einkorn wheat and traces of bracken. The copper of his axe came from southern Tuscany. His 61 tattoos, a 2024 experimental study argues, were most likely hand-poked rather than cut. And a 2023 genome re-analysis changed his look: he probably had dark skin, dark eyes and male-pattern baldness, and more than 90 percent of his ancestry came from early farmers with roots in Anatolia. The pale, shaggy Iceman of older museum reconstructions reflected modern assumptions more than his DNA. What we actually have A naturally mummified body with clothing, a copper axe, a bow, arrows, a dagger and other gear. How we know Radiocarbon dating; X-ray and CT imaging; stomach-content analysis (proteomics, lipids, DNA, microscopy); lead-isotope sourc

chunks.heading: Kushim
chunks.text: Uruk, southern Iraq Kushim The first individual whose name we may be able to read left no poem, no battle and no face; just a receipt. 3200–3000 BCE. Uruk, southern Iraq Kushim The first individual whose name we may be able to read left no poem, no battle and no face; just a receipt. 3200–3000 BCE Possibly the first named person in history, and possibly an accountant about 3200 to 3000 BCE Around 3200 to 3000 BCE, in the city of Uruk in what is now southern Iraq, administrators pressed signs into small clay tablets. The earliest writing, called proto-cuneiform, was not yet used for letters or poems; it was bookkeeping. One tablet, now in the Schoyen Collection, records a large total of barley over 37 months and ends with two signs read KU and SHIM. The same combination appears on about 18 tablets. Yuval Noah Harari's bestseller Sapiens made the reading famous, rendering it as 29,086 measures of barley, signed Kushim. Specialists are more cautious. The signs could be a personal name, but they could also be a job title or the name of an office, because the earliest script rarely made the difference clear. The texts linked to Kushim deal with barley and grain products, probably connected with the malting and brewing work of a large institution. If Kushim was a person, then the first name we can read belongs not to a king but to someone checking that the numbers added up. That is a rather reassuring start for written history. What we actually have Proto-cuneiform clay tablets from Uruk (for example MS 1717 in the Schoyen Collection) bearing the sign sequence KU.SHIM. How we know Decipherment of proto-cuneiform numerical systems and administrative formats, comparing sign use across hundreds of archaic tablets. A rival for the 'oldest known name', Gal-Sal, appears on a tablet

chunks.heading: Merer, inspector of boatmen
chunks.text: Tura quarries and Giza, Egypt Merer, inspector of boatmen The oldest inscribed papyri ever found are not royal decrees; they are the work diary of a mid-level boss hauling stone for the Great Pyramid. 2560 BCE. Tura quarries and Giza, Egypt Merer, inspector of boatmen The oldest inscribed papyri ever found are not royal decrees; they are the work diary of a mid-level boss hauling stone for the Great Pyramid. 2560 BCE Middle manager whose logbook tracks work on the Great Pyramid about 2560 BCE (reign of Khufu, year 27) In 2013, at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbour on Egypt's Red Sea coast, a team led by Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard found papyrus rolls left at the entrance of storage galleries cut into the rock. They are the oldest inscribed papyri known, from late in the reign of King Khufu, around 2560 BCE. Among them is the logbook of an inspector named Merer, who led a crew of about 40 boatmen. His entries are laid out day by day in neat columns, recording a steady rhythm: loading limestone at the Tura quarries across the Nile, sailing to Akhet-Khufu, 'Horizon of Khufu', the ancient name for the Great Pyramid site at Giza, stopping overnight at places such as the She-Khufu basin, and heading back for more. The fine Tura limestone was probably destined for the pyramid's outer casing. Merer also mentions Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother, as the official in charge of a harbour at Giza. No pharaoh speaks in these pages, and there are no secret machines; just a supervisor counting trips and days. It is the closest thing we have to a worker's view of the Great Pyramid in its final years of construction. What we actually have Fragments of papyrus logbooks (the 'Diary of Merer') found at Wadi al-Jarf, now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo. How we know Hieratic palaeography and

chunks.heading: Puabi of Ur
chunks.text: Royal Cemetery, southern Iraq Puabi of Ur Her headdress of gold leaves is one of the most dazzling objects of the ancient world; the people buried around her tell a darker story. 2600–2500 BCE. Royal Cemetery, southern Iraq Puabi of Ur Her headdress of gold leaves is one of the most dazzling objects of the ancient world; the people buried around her tell a darker story. 2600–2500 BCE Queen or high lady buried in gold, and not alone about 2600 to 2500 BCE In the late 1920s, Leonard Woolley's excavators at Ur opened a tomb numbered PG 800 and found a woman on a wooden bier, her upper body covered in beads of gold, silver, lapis lazuli and carnelian, with a spectacular headdress of gold leaves, ribbons and flowers. A lapis cylinder seal nearby named her Puabi, with the title nin, meaning 'queen' or 'lady'. Unusually, the seal names no husband, which likely signals that her rank stood on its own. She died around 2600 to 2500 BCE, probably at about 40 years old. She was not buried alone. Woolley recorded dozens of attendants in her burial complex, about 52 by one count, and imagined them calmly drinking poison. In 2011, CT scans of two skulls from other graves in the Royal Cemetery suggested a harsher end: blunt-force wounds, probably from a pointed, weighted weapon, plus signs of heating and traces of mercury sulphide, possibly used to slow decay while the bodies were laid out. Behind the glitter of the headdress sits a sobering question: what did royal display cost the people around it? What we actually have Tomb PG 800 with Puabi's skeleton, jewellery, headdress and inscribed cylinder seals, now largely at the Penn Museum, Philadelphia. How we know Excavation records; reading of the cuneiform seal inscription; later CT scanning and forensic analysis of skulls from the Roy

chunks.heading: Enheduanna
chunks.text: Ur, southern Iraq Enheduanna The first author known by name in world literature may have been a princess-priestess writing about her own exile. 2300–2250 BCE. Ur, southern Iraq Enheduanna The first author known by name in world literature may have been a princess-priestess writing about her own exile. 2300–2250 BCE Princess, high priestess and the first named author about 2300 to 2250 BCE Around 2300 BCE, Sargon of Akkad built the first great empire of Mesopotamia and installed his daughter as en-priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. She took, or was given, the name Enheduanna. In the 1920s Leonard Woolley's team at Ur found a calcite disk showing her at a ritual in a flounced robe, with an inscription naming her as Sargon's daughter. Her fame rests on poetry. Several Sumerian hymns, copied by scribes centuries later, name her as their author, which would make her the first named author in world literature. In the poem known as 'The Exaltation of Inana' she speaks in the first person: pushed out of her office during a revolt, she describes her exile with raw emotion and pleads with the goddess Inana to restore her. It is vivid, personal and startlingly angry. Scholars debate how much she composed herself, because the surviving copies are around 500 years younger than she is, and the attribution may partly reflect later tradition. Either way, Mesopotamian scribes chose to remember a woman as the voice behind some of their greatest hymns. I, En-hedu-ana the en priestess, entered my holy jipar in your service. The Exaltation of Inana (Inana B), ETCSL translation, University of Oxford What we actually have An inscribed calcite (alabaster) disk from Ur (Penn Museum) naming her; Old Babylonian clay-tablet copies of hymns attributed to her; seals of her servants. How we know

chunks.heading: Hammurabi of Babylon
chunks.text: Babylon, central Iraq Hammurabi of Babylon His famous law code was carried off as war loot, lost for three thousand years, and dug up in a different country. 1792–1750 BCE. Babylon, central Iraq Hammurabi of Babylon His famous law code was carried off as war loot, lost for three thousand years, and dug up in a different country. 1792–1750 BCE King who carved his idea of justice into stone reigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE Hammurabi ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE and turned a mid-sized city-state into the leading power of Mesopotamia. Late in his reign he set up a tall black stone stele, over 2 metres high, topped by a carving of the king standing before a god usually identified as Shamash, the sun god and guardian of justice. Below it: a prologue, about 282 laws, and an epilogue inviting anyone wronged to come and have the inscription read to them. The laws are not an even-handed modern code. Penalties depend on social status: destroying the eye of a free man could cost an eye, while injuring a commoner or an enslaved person meant a payment. A builder whose badly built house collapsed and killed the owner could be put to death. Many scholars now read the collection less as a rulebook judges followed and more as a royal showcase of wise judgments. The stele had its own adventures: an Elamite king carried it to Susa as war booty in the 12th century BCE, and French excavators found it there in 1901 and 1902. Today it stands in the Louvre, still making its case to visitors. to bring about the rule of righteousness in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil-doers; so that the strong should not harm the weak Prologue to the Laws of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King (1910) What we actually have The basalt stele in the Louvre, fragments of other copies, and later clay-t

chunks.heading: Ea-nasir and Nanni
chunks.text: Ur, southern Iraq Ea-nasir and Nanni The oldest known customer complaint was found in the house of the merchant it was aimed at. 1750 BCE. Ur, southern Iraq Ea-nasir and Nanni The oldest known customer complaint was found in the house of the merchant it was aimed at. 1750 BCE Copper merchant with a bad reputation, and his furious customer about 1750 BCE Around 1750 BCE, a man named Nanni in the city of Ur was fed up. He had dealt with Ea-nasir, a merchant who brought copper up the Gulf through Dilmun (modern Bahrain), and received ingots he considered below the agreed quality. Worse, he said his servant had been treated rudely and his money had not come back. So he had a clay tablet written, and it survives: a small letter about 11.6 cm tall, now in the British Museum. He complains that messengers he sent to collect his money came back empty-handed, several times, even through dangerous territory, and he demands to be treated with respect. The best twist: the tablet was found in Ea-nasir's own house at Ur during Leonard Woolley's excavations, alongside other letters grumbling about copper deliveries. Either Ea-nasir kept his complaints on file, or complaints were simply a large share of his business correspondence. Nearly 4,000 years later he has become an internet legend, a sort of patron saint of bad suppliers. The tablet is also a serious window onto long-distance metal trade, credit and business etiquette in the Old Babylonian world. What do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt? Nanni to Ea-nasir, UET V 81, trans. A. Leo Oppenheim, Letters from Mesopotamia (1967) What we actually have Clay tablet BM 131236 (UET V 81), written in Akkadian cuneiform, plus other letters from the same house at Ur. How we know Excavation context at Ur; deci

chunks.heading: Hatshepsut
chunks.text: Thebes, Egypt Hatshepsut She ruled Egypt as king for about twenty years; the smashing of her statues afterwards may not have been the revenge story we were told. 1479–1458 BCE. Thebes, Egypt Hatshepsut She ruled Egypt as king for about twenty years; the smashing of her statues afterwards may not have been the revenge story we were told. 1479–1458 BCE Queen who made herself king reigned about 1479 to 1458 BCE Hatshepsut was the daughter of one pharaoh, the wife of another, and regent for a third, the young Thutmose III. Then she did something unusual: she had herself crowned king. For about two decades she ruled with full royal titles and was often shown with a king's kilt and false beard. Her projects include the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri, whose reliefs celebrate an expedition to the distant land of Punt that returned with incense trees and exotic animals. After her death her images were broken and her name cut from monuments, long read as Thutmose III's revenge. A 2025 study of 1920s excavation archives suggests a cooler motive. Many statues were broken at weak points such as the neck, waist and knees in ways consistent with ritual 'deactivation', some faces were left intact, and the pieces were reused as building material. The erasure also came years into Thutmose's sole reign, which fits succession politics better than personal hatred. Even her body is debated: a mummy from tomb KV60 was identified as hers in 2007 on the basis of a tooth, but that match has not been confirmed by DNA and some scholars remain unconvinced. What we actually have Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, obelisks at Karnak, hundreds of statue fragments, inscriptions, and a debated mummy (KV60-A). How we know Hieroglyphic inscriptions; archaeology of statue deposits and archival excavat

chunks.heading: Tutankhamun
chunks.text: Valley of the Kings, Egypt Tutankhamun Behind the golden mask was a young man who probably walked with a cane. 1323 BCE. Valley of the Kings, Egypt Tutankhamun Behind the golden mask was a young man who probably walked with a cane. 1323 BCE Teenage king whose body tells a story of illness died about 1323 BCE Howard Carter's 1922 discovery of a nearly intact royal tomb made Tutankhamun the world's most famous pharaoh, although he was a minor king who died young, around 1323 BCE. What does his body tell us? A 2010 study combining CT scans and DNA from royal mummies concluded that he died at about 19 and that his parents were probably brother and sister: the mummy from tomb KV55, most likely Akhenaten, and an unnamed woman known as the 'Younger Lady' from tomb KV35. The study reported a clubfoot, bone death in part of his left foot (Kohler disease II), a cleft palate, and DNA from the most dangerous malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. It proposed malaria combined with the bone disease as the most likely cause of death. His tomb held about 130 walking sticks and staves, some with signs of use, which fits a king who probably walked with pain. Treat the details with care: other researchers have questioned the ancient DNA methods and some diagnoses, and a broken leg remains debated as either injury or damage from embalming or excavation. The golden mask covered a young man who was probably often unwell. What we actually have His mummy, CT data, DNA samples, and the contents of tomb KV62, including about 130 sticks and staves. How we know CT scanning, ancient DNA (Y-chromosome and autosomal markers) for kinship, pathogen DNA testing, and study of the tomb objects. Two mummified foetuses buried in his tomb may have been his daughters, according to the same 2010 DNA study.

chunks.heading: The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht)
chunks.text: Deir el-Medina, Egypt The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht) When the grain rations were late, the pharaoh's tomb builders put down their tools and walked out. 1157 BCE. Deir el-Medina, Egypt The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht) When the grain rations were late, the pharaoh's tomb builders put down their tools and walked out. 1157 BCE Royal tomb workers who staged the first recorded strike about 1157 BCE (year 29 of Ramesses III) The craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings lived in their own walled village, Deir el-Medina, and were paid in rations of grain. In year 29 of Ramesses III, around 1157 BCE, those rations were badly overdue. So the crew did something no earlier record shows: they stopped work and walked out. The scribe Amennakht kept notes, which survive on a papyrus now in Turin. The workers marched past the guard posts of the necropolis, sat down behind temples on the west bank, and refused to go back, insisting their grievance be reported to Pharaoh. Officials delivered rations; the crew returned; supplies slipped again; they struck again. The dispute stretched over several months. For the officials it was an embarrassment. For historians it is priceless: a record of ordinary workers in a powerful state organizing, negotiating and getting at least part of what they were owed. The village was unusually literate, and its rubbish heaps have yielded thousands of inscribed potsherds and limestone flakes, including a register of work absences whose excuses range from illness to brewing beer. On this day the crew passed the five guard-posts of the tomb saying: 'We are hungry.' Turin Strike Papyrus, trans. P. J. Frandsen, 'Editing Reality: The Turin Strike Papyrus' (1990) What we actuall

chunks.heading: Tollund Man
chunks.text: Bjaeldskovdal bog, Denmark Tollund Man His face looked so fresh that the peat cutters who found him called the police. 405–380 BCE. Bjaeldskovdal bog, Denmark Tollund Man His face looked so fresh that the peat cutters who found him called the police. 405–380 BCE Iron Age man with a peaceful face and a noose around his neck about 405 to 380 BCE On 8 May 1950, peat cutters near Silkeborg in Denmark uncovered a face so well preserved that they called the police, fearing a recent death. He had died around 405 to 380 BCE. The acidic, oxygen-poor bog had tanned his skin and preserved his head in extraordinary detail: closed eyes, short-cropped hair and a faint stubble. He wore a pointed skin cap and a belt, and around his neck was a plaited leather noose. He was about 40 and had been hanged, then laid in an old peat cutting in a curled, sleeping position. Many archaeologists interpret him as a sacrifice, although the reasons remain uncertain. A 2021 re-examination of his gut found that his last meal, eaten roughly 12 to 24 hours before death, was a porridge made mainly of barley, pale persicaria seeds and flax, with some fish. He also carried whipworm, roundworm and tapeworm. The researchers found nothing obviously festive or special about the meal. A ritual death, then, but perhaps preceded by an ordinary day's food, which makes him feel even closer to us. What we actually have A bog body whose head is exceptionally well preserved, with the noose, cap and belt; gut contents. How we know Radiocarbon dating; autopsy, X-ray and CT scanning; macrofossil, pollen, protein and parasite analysis of gut contents. At Silkeborg Museum his head is original, but most of the body on display is a replica, because only parts of it were conserved in 1950.

chunks.heading: Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai)
chunks.text: Mawangdui, China Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai) Her body was so well preserved that doctors could perform an autopsy 2,100 years after she died, and they found melon seeds in her stomach. 168 BCE. Mawangdui, China Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai) Her body was so well preserved that doctors could perform an autopsy 2,100 years after she died, and they found melon seeds in her stomach. 168 BCE Han dynasty noblewoman with a modern-looking medical file died about 168 BCE In 1972, at Mawangdui near Changsha, archaeologists excavated Tomb 1, a deep Han dynasty grave sealed with thick layers of charcoal and white clay. Inside four nested coffins, in a mysterious liquid, lay Xin Zhui, wife of Li Cang, Marquis of Dai and chancellor of the Changsha kingdom. She had died around 168 BCE, at about 50, and her body was astonishingly preserved: soft skin, joints that could still bend, hair still in place. The autopsy reads like a modern medical file. She had hardened coronary arteries, gallstones, spinal problems that probably caused back pain, and schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection. In her digestive tract were more than a hundred melon seeds, suggesting she ate melon a few hours before a heart attack killed her, probably in summer. She was buried with over a thousand objects, including silk garments, lacquerware, food and a painted T-shaped silk banner that depicts a journey from the underworld to the heavens. Her body suggests the privileged life of a Han noblewoman also brought diseases we still link to rich diets and little exercise. What we actually have A remarkably preserved body, her tomb furnishings and a painted silk banner, now in the Hunan Museum, Changsha. How we know Modern medical autopsy and pathology (1972); study of tomb inscriptions and seals naming he

chunks.heading: The graffiti writers of Pompeii
chunks.text: Pompeii, Italy The graffiti writers of Pompeii Pompeii's walls were its social media, and one ancient writer complained that there was too much of it. up–79 CE. Pompeii, Italy The graffiti writers of Pompeii Pompeii's walls were its social media, and one ancient writer complained that there was too much of it. up–79 CE A whole town of scribblers, gossips and election campaigners up to 79 CE When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE it froze a town whose walls were covered in writing. Archaeologists have recorded thousands of painted notices and scratched graffiti: election endorsements, gladiator fan messages, greetings to friends, love notes, insults, sums and occasional crude boasts. One line, found in the Basilica, the Theatre and the Amphitheatre, is a joke about the whole scene: the wall deserves praise for not collapsing under so much boring writing. Graffiti were not mainly vandalism; studies of houses show messages answering one another, like comment threads. And the walls still make news. In 2018 a charcoal note in a house under renovation at the time of the eruption recorded a date equal to 17 October. The year is not written, but it supports other evidence, such as autumn fruits and lit braziers, that the eruption came later than the traditional 24 August. In January 2026, a Sorbonne-led team using reflectance transformation imaging, which lights a surface from many angles, announced 79 previously unknown graffiti in the corridor leading to the theatres, including a declaration of love and a drawing of two gladiators. Admiror, paries, te non cecidisse ruinis, qui tot scriptorum taedia sustineas. (I wonder, wall, that you have not fallen in ruins, bearing the tedious scribbles of so many writers.) chunks.heading: Claudia Severa
chunks.text: Vindolanda, UK Claudia Severa The earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman is the end of a birthday invitation. 97–105 CE. Vindolanda, UK Claudia Severa The earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman is the end of a birthday invitation. 97–105 CE Officer's wife who sent a birthday invitation on the Roman frontier about 97 to 105 CE Around 100 CE, at the Roman fort of Vindolanda in northern Britain (Hadrian's Wall came a couple of decades later), Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the commander Flavius Cerialis, received a thin wooden leaf tablet written in ink. It came from her friend Claudia Severa, wife of Aelius Brocchus, who commanded a fort nearby. The message: please come to my birthday celebration on 11 September; it will make the day more enjoyable. Most of the letter was written by a scribe. At the end, a different hand adds a personal farewell. Scholars identify this as Claudia herself, which makes these lines among the earliest known examples of Latin written by a woman. The tablet was excavated in 1985, one of hundreds of documents preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free layers at Vindolanda, alongside requests for beer, lists that mention socks, and a report sneering at the 'Brittunculi', the 'wretched little Britons'. What survives here is not grand history but friendship on a cold frontier: two women arranging a party, and one of them adding her own words. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul, as I hope to prosper, and hail. Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, Tab. Vindol. 291, trans. A. K. Bowman and J. D. Thomas What we actually have Vindolanda tablet 291, a wooden leaf tablet written in ink, now in the British Museum (1986,1001.64).
