chunks.heading: Greek fire: 01 Fire that walked on water
chunks.text: Imagine rowing towards Constantinople in the 670s. The city's sea walls are ahead, and a line of long, low warships slides out to meet you. At the bow of each, under a raised platform, a crew member aims a bronze tube. There is a roar, a gout of thick black smoke, and a jet of liquid fire arcs across the water, sticks to your hull and keeps burning on the sea around you. Throwing water on it only seems to spread it. That is roughly what Byzantine and Arab sources describe, and it is why this weapon became a legend. Western crusaders later called it Greek fire. The Byzantines, who thought of themselves as Romans, had plainer names: sea fire, liquid fire, prepared fire, Roman fire. For five centuries, the most feared weapon at sea was a liquid, a pump and a crew trained to keep a secret. The mystery is not whether it existed. Dozens of passages across five centuries show that it did. The mystery is what exactly was in the tank, how it was pushed through the tube, and how a state could guard the answer so well that the answer died with it.

chunks.heading: Greek fire: 02 The refugee with a recipe
chunks.text: The story begins with a single line in the Chronographia of Theophanes the Confessor, written in the early 9th century from older sources. Under the year corresponding to about 672 CE, he records the arrival of a refugee from the eastern provinces then under Arab rule. At that time Kallinikos, an artificer from Heliopolis, fled to the Romans. He had devised a sea fire which ignited the Arab ships and burned them with all hands. Context explains why a single engineer mattered so much. In the 630s and 640s the eastern Roman Empire had lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt, its richest provinces, to the new Arab state. By the 650s Arab fleets built in Syrian and Egyptian shipyards were raiding Cyprus, Rhodes and the Aegean coasts, and in 655 they defeated the imperial navy off the coast of Lycia. For the first time in centuries, Constantinople faced a serious enemy at sea. A weapon that could burn ships before they came alongside was worth a fortune. Heliopolis here is the Syrian city now called Baalbek, not the one in Egypt. Theophanes calls Kallinikos an architect or artificer, a technical man, and the timing was perfect. The Umayyad Caliphate had been pushing into the Aegean and was preparing to attack the imperial capital itself. It is worth being cautious about the inventor story. Incendiary weapons were old news: Assyrians, Greeks and Romans had all thrown burning pitch, sulphur and oil. Petroleum seeps were known around the Black Sea and in Mesopotamia. What seems to have been new was the combination of a particular fuel with a way of projecting it as a pressurised jet from a ship. Kallinikos may have brought the key idea, or later tradition may have pinned a gradual development on one memorable name.

chunks.heading: Greek fire: 03 Saving Constantinople, twice
chunks.text: According to Theophanes, the emperor Constantine IV had large 'cauldron-bearing' warships equipped with siphons, and fire played a decisive part in repelling Arab fleets that blockaded the city from a base at Cyzicus in the 670s. The traditional account describes a siege lasting from 674 to 678. Some historians, notably Marek Jankowiak, now argue that the 'first siege' is a later reshaping of a shorter blockade in the late 660s. Either way, the fire entered the record as a city-saving weapon. The second great test came in 717–718, when a huge Arab army and fleet besieged Constantinople by land and sea. Theophanes describes Byzantine ships attacking the enemy fleet with fire siphons and burning many vessels. Combined with a harsh winter, disease, supply failures and Bulgar attacks on the besiegers, the defence held, a turning point in the history of the eastern Mediterranean. Later uses are scattered through the chronicles: against the rebel Thomas the Slav in the early 820s, against a Rus' fleet led by Prince Igor that attacked the Bosporus in 941, and against a Pisan fleet around 1099, described by the princess and historian Anna Komnene. By then the weapon had acquired theatre as well as power. And the fire which was to be directed against the enemy through tubes he made to pass through the mouths of the beasts, so that it seemed as if the lions and the other similar monsters were vomiting the fire.

chunks.heading: Greek fire: 04 How the siphon may have worked
chunks.text: The Byzantine word siphōn simply means a tube, and the sources never draw the machine. What they do give are clues. Emperor Leo VI's military handbook, the Taktika, written around 900, instructs that a dromon should carry a siphon in its prow, sheathed in bronze, to shoot the prepared fire at the enemy, and it mentions a newer hand-held version. Other passages mention cauldrons, heat and the roar and smoke of discharge. Step 1 of 6. Load: crude oil, perhaps thickened with resin, fills a sealed bronze tank. Load: crude oil, perhaps thickened with resin, fills a sealed bronze tank. Heat: a small brazier warms the tank, thinning the oil and raising its vapour pressure. Pump: two crewmen work a double-cylinder bronze force pump to build pressure. Release: a valve opens and the oil surges along the pipe to the swivelling nozzle. Ignite: a burning match at the nozzle lights the stream as it leaves. Fire: a burning jet reaches about 15 m (in the 2002 test), spreading flame across the water. A side view of a reconstructed fire siphon. On the left, a sealed bronze tank sits over a small brazier. A two-cylinder force pump with a rocking handle feeds air or oil pressure into the tank. A pipe leads from the tank through a valve to a long bronze tube and a swivelling nozzle, where a small burning match ignites the liquid. In the final step a jet of burning oil arcs to the right, about 15 metres long in the reconstruction, drawn shortened. Labels mark each part as a reconstruction. The ship mattered as much as the pump. The standard 10th-century warship was the dromon, a long, narrow galley that John Pryor and Elizabeth Jeffreys reconstruct at about 31–32 m, with two banks of oars, 25 oars per bank on each side. A heavy dromon carried around 230 rowers and 70 marines. The main siphon

chunks.heading: Greek fire: 05 Testing the idea with real fire
chunks.text: In 2002, for a television documentary, Haldon worked with engineers Andrew Lacey and Colin Hewes to build a full working model. It had a cast bronze double-cylinder force pump worked by two people, an oil reservoir, bronze piping, simple one-way flap valves and a swivelling nozzle. Wooden pistons were wrapped in hemp and flax and sealed with tallow. For fuel they used light crude oil from Azerbaijan, geologically similar to sources the Byzantines could have reached around the Black Sea and Caucasus. It worked. The apparatus threw a jet of burning oil about 15 m, with flame temperatures reported above 1,000 °C, far enough to reach a neighbouring ship without the two hulls touching. Smoke billowed and the burning liquid spread across water, just as the sources describe. The team also learned what could go wrong: the connecting pipes had to be protected, for instance by packing them in sand, so that flames could not creep back towards the tank. Side profile of a long, low Byzantine war galley about 31 metres long, with two banks of oars, two masts with lateen yards, a raised forecastle at the bow and a steering oar at the stern. A bronze siphon projects from the bow beneath the forecastle. From it an arcing jet of fire reaches about 15 metres towards the bow of an enemy ship on the right. A 10 metre scale bar and a 1.7 metre human figure on deck give scale. Labels mark the siphon, the forecastle, the two oar banks and the jet range, with a note that the profile is a reconstruction. A successful reconstruction is not the same as recovering the original, and Haldon is careful to say so. It shows that the texts can be satisfied by technology the Byzantines had. It does not tell us their exact recipe, pressures or nozzle design. Other arrangements, such as a pump system with n

chunks.heading: Greek fire: 06 What was in the tank?
chunks.text: Over the centuries, writers have proposed almost every flammable substance known to the medieval world. The main hypotheses fall into a few families. Petroleum-based: light crude oil or naphtha, possibly distilled or 'prepared', often with pine resin added to make it sticky and longer-burning. This is the majority view today. Quicklime: calcium oxide heats up violently when wet, which once seemed a neat explanation for fire that water could not quench. Most scholars now reject it as the main ingredient, because quicklime alone cannot produce a projected jet of flame. Saltpetre and gunpowder: popular in older books, but saltpetre-based mixtures are not documented in the Mediterranean until the 13th century, centuries after Greek fire appeared. Sulphur and other additives: possible minor ingredients, mentioned in later medieval incendiary recipes, but no Byzantine text confirms them. The petroleum case rests on several converging clues. Constantine VII's handbook on foreign peoples, the De administrando imperio, names oil-bearing places around the Black Sea and Caucasus, such as Tamatarcha and Zichia. Descriptions of fire floating and spreading on water fit a light oil. Thick smoke fits incomplete combustion of crude petroleum. And the sources' list of extinguishers, sand, strong vinegar and old urine, fits a burning oil that water scatters but a smothering or wetting agent might suppress. Resin is the best candidate for the 'prepared' part. Adding pine resin to oil raises its viscosity, helping it cling to a hull and burn longer. It is chemistry any Byzantine workshop could manage. But no text states it outright, and we should say so plainly. There is one more practical clue. Greek fire needed a steady, reliable supply. Crude oil seeps around the Black Sea and Caucasus w

chunks.heading: Greek fire: 07 A secret too well kept
chunks.text: The Byzantines treated the fire as a state secret, perhaps the most successful one in medieval history. In the mid-10th century Emperor Constantine VII told his son that the preparation of the liquid fire must never be handed to any foreign people, whatever they asked. He wrapped the rule in a sacred origin story: the recipe, he wrote, had been revealed from heaven to Constantine the Great, the empire's founder, and anyone who betrayed it would be struck down. He even told of an official who had been bribed into giving some away and was consumed by fire from the sky as he entered a church. Historians such as Alex Roland have argued that the Byzantines protected the secret by splitting it. One group of specialists knew how to prepare the fuel, another built and serviced the siphons, and ships' crews learned only to operate them. Nobody outside the inner circle held the whole system. The secrecy seems to have been strategic as well as practical. Enemies did capture Byzantine equipment from time to time. According to Theophanes, the Bulgar khan Krum seized a stock of the fire and its siphons in 812 but could not use them. If true, it suggests that the hardware alone was useless without the prepared fuel and the knowledge of how to handle it. That strategy worked for centuries, and then it failed from the inside. After the late 11th century, references to ship-mounted siphons become rare. When crusaders stormed Constantinople in 1204, the defenders used improvised fire ships, but no chronicle describes the famous siphons. Haldon suggests that loss of access to Caucasus oil, as Byzantine influence around the Black Sea shrank, may have undermined the whole supply chain. Other explanations include the collapse of the navy itself and the death of the few specialists who knew th

chunks.heading: Greek fire: 08 What is still unknown
chunks.text: Greek fire earns a high mystery rating because the core questions remain open. We do not have the recipe. We do not know whether the oil was distilled, whether resin, sulphur or other substances were added, or in what proportions. We do not know the siphon's exact layout, the operating pressure, or how often it was actually decisive rather than simply terrifying. And some of its most famous victories, like the first siege, are themselves under historical review. Other powers eventually built their own incendiary weapons. Arab armies fielded specialist naphtha troops, and fire pots and burning arrows became common across the medieval Mediterranean. But none of them seems to have matched the Byzantine combination of a pumped liquid jet mounted on a fast warship. Archaeology might still help. Small ceramic containers, often called 'grenades', are found across the medieval Mediterranean and Near East, and some may have carried incendiary liquids. Chemical analysis of residues inside such vessels, and of any bronze fittings from Byzantine wrecks such as those excavated at Yenikapı in Istanbul, is the kind of evidence that could one day move the debate from texts to tangible remains. It was less a miracle substance than a system: oil, bronze, a pump, a ship and a guarded body of know-how. The strongest evidence points to a petroleum-based liquid projected by a heated, pressurised siphon, a hypothesis that has now been built and fired. The rest remains uncertain, and perhaps it always will, unless a wreck on the floor of the Sea of Marmara one day gives up a corroded bronze tube.

chunks.heading: Greek fire: debate
chunks.text: Was Greek fire based on petroleum? Yes, crude oil with additives Fire floating on water, heavy smoke, named oil sources around the Black Sea in De administrando imperio, and a successful 2002 reconstruction using light crude oil. Other key ingredients Earlier writers proposed quicklime or saltpetre; later medieval recipes add sulphur and resins, and no Byzantine recipe confirms petroleum explicitly. The bold claim: Greek fire was a petroleum-based liquid, probably light crude oil perhaps thickened with resins. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Several independent lines of evidence point the same way: descriptions of the fire's behaviour, Byzantine interest in specific oil-bearing regions, the known chemistry of alternatives, and an experiment that reproduces the described effects. The exact recipe is still missing, so this is strong support for the base fuel, not a full solution.

chunks.heading: Greek fire: debate
chunks.text: Did the siphon heat and pressurise the liquid? Heated pressure siphon References to cauldrons, braziers and bronze tubes; Roman force-pump technology; the working 2002 model. Other designs possible No siphon has been excavated; the texts are brief and could fit a simpler pump without heating, or different arrangements of tank and nozzle. The bold claim: Byzantine ships used a heated, pump-pressurised bronze siphon with a lit nozzle. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The design fits the texts and has been shown to work with technology the Byzantines possessed. But it is reconstructed from a handful of short passages, and other layouts could also satisfy them. Until a siphon or a detailed technical text is found, it remains a well-tested hypothesis.

chunks.heading: Greek fire: debate
chunks.text: Was Greek fire an early form of gunpowder? Yes Some 19th and 20th-century writers linked 'fire that roars' to saltpetre mixtures. No Saltpetre-based mixtures are not documented in the Mediterranean before the 13th century, and the sources describe a projected burning liquid, not explosions. The bold claim: Greek fire contained saltpetre and was a precursor of gunpowder. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established The chronology does not work: Greek fire appears in the 670s, centuries before saltpetre mixtures are attested in the region, and its described behaviour is that of a burning liquid jet. Partington's classic study and later work by Haldon both reject the gunpowder identification.

chunks.text: Khujut Rabu, near Baghdad, Iraq The 'Baghdad battery' 10 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read c. 14 cm height of the clay jar König 1938, as summarised in later literature c. 9 cm length of the rolled copper cylinder König 1938 c. 0.78 V ideal voltage of a copper–iron cell from standard electrode potentials standard electrochemistry tables c. 4.3 V from ten replica jars wired in series on MythBusters MythBusters, 2005 up to 1.4 V best result from Alexander Bazes's 2026 reconstruction Bazes 2026 0 wires wires, conductors or electrical devices found with any such jar Keyser 1993; Hafford, quoted by History.com 2026 c. 14 cm (reports range from 13 to 15 cm) Jar height c. 8 cm at its widest Jar width c. 9 cm long, c. 2.6 cm across Copper cylinder heavily corroded, projecting c. 1 cm above an asphalt (bitumen) stopper Iron rod 1936, Khujut Rabu; described by Wilhelm König in 1938 Found roughly 0.5–2 V per jar, depending on the electrolyte Replica voltage none Wires or electrical devices found with it unknown; missing after the looting of the Iraq Museum Whereabouts since 2003 The object is a small unglazed clay jar. Inside stood a sheet of copper rolled into a tube about 9 cm long, closed at the bottom with a copper disc and held in place with bitumen. An iron rod hung inside the tube, fixed by a bitumen stopper, with its top poking out. Filled with an acid such as vinegar, the same arrangement makes a weak galvanic cell, which is why Wilhelm König suggested in 1938 that it was a battery, perhaps for gilding. Very similar jars from nearby Seleucia and Ctesiphon contained bronze tubes with remains of rolled organic material, such as papyrus, which points many archaeologists towards a container for written scrolls or a ritual deposit. The myth The ancient Mesopotamians had electricity: they used batteries like this to electroplate jewellery, light temples or even run lost machines inherited from an advanced civilisation. The reality Any two different metals in an acid make a small voltage, so replicas do work as feeble cells. But no wires, conductors, electrodes, plated objects or texts about electricity have been found anywhere in the ancient Near East, and gilding of the period was done with mercury and heat, not current. Close parallels contained rolled organic material, which fits a container for scrolls or a sealed ritual object. The function remains uncertain; the battery reading lacks supporting evidence. Flip it Wow The world's most famous 'ancient battery' has been missing since the Iraq Museum was looted in 2003, so every modern experime

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 01 A jar that launched a thousand theories
chunks.text: It would fit in your hand. A pale, unglazed clay jar about 14 cm tall, a little bulbous, with a narrow neck. Inside it, a sheet of copper rolled into a tube. Inside the tube, a corroded iron rod, held in place by a plug of black asphalt. That is all. And yet since 1938 this modest object has been called the 'Baghdad battery', and it has turned up in school textbooks, museum exhibitions, science television and countless books about lost ancient technologies. The reason is simple and genuinely intriguing. Copper and iron in an acid really do make electricity. Pour vinegar into a replica and a voltmeter twitches. So the question is not whether this arrangement can make a current. It can. The question is whether anyone, two thousand years ago, ever used it to do so. Part of the jar's fame comes from timing. König described it in the late 1930s, when electrification was still transforming daily life and radio was new. The idea that ancient people might have beaten Volta, who built the first battery in 1800, by some two thousand years was irresistible. Over the following decades the jar became a staple of books arguing that ancient people possessed lost high technology, and replicas became a favourite science fair project. It is easy to see why: it is simple, cheap and it really does make a spark of current. This article gives the battery idea a fair hearing. It tests the idea against what archaeologists found in the ground, what the object is made of, what ancient craftspeople already knew, and what the jar's closest relatives contained. Any two metals in an acid make a battery. The real question is whether anyone ever plugged anything into this one.

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 02 From a hill near Baghdad to the Iraq Museum
chunks.text: The jar came from Khujut Rabu, a low mound near Baghdad not far from Ctesiphon, the great capital of the Parthian and then the Sasanian empires. It was found in 1936 during work at the site and entered the Iraq Museum. There it caught the eye of Wilhelm König, an Austrian working at the museum in the 1930s (sources describe him variously as an assistant and as head of its laboratory), who had a painter's training and a keen interest in ancient crafts. Picture the setting. Ctesiphon and its twin city Seleucia, on opposite banks of the Tigris, were among the largest cities of the ancient world, crowded with merchants, officials, artisans and scholars speaking Aramaic, Greek and Persian. Workshops produced glazed pottery, glass, textiles and silver vessels. Several religious communities lived side by side, and many households used written charms and inscribed objects for protection. A small sealed jar with a metal tube inside would not have been out of place in that world, whatever it was for. In 1938 König published a short article in the German journal Forschungen und Fortschritte with a cautious question for a title: Ein galvanisches Element aus der Partherzeit?, 'A galvanic cell from the Parthian period?'. He described the jar, the copper cylinder and the rod, and noticed that the iron was badly corroded, as if by an acid. He had seen silver objects from ancient Iraq with extremely thin gold layers, and he wondered whether jars like this, filled with an acidic liquid, had supplied current to gild them. On the left, a cutaway of a bulbous clay jar about 14 centimetres tall and 8 centimetres wide, with a copper cylinder standing inside it. On the right, the parts are shown pulled apart in a vertical column: an asphalt stopper, a corroded iron rod, the rolled copper cylin

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 03 Cousins from Seleucia and Ctesiphon
chunks.text: The Khujut Rabu jar is not alone, and its relatives matter more than it does. In 1930, excavators from the University of Michigan working under Leroy Waterman at Seleucia on the Tigris found several clay vessels sealed with bitumen that contained bronze or copper cylinders. Inside some of those cylinders were traces of rolled organic material, described as papyrus. At Ctesiphon, a German expedition in 1931–1932 found further vessels. According to reports of these finds, one contained a number of bronze tubes, each holding decayed rolled material, and others held iron nails, bronze pieces and lead sheets. The excavator Ernst Kühnel interpreted similar objects as containers for written charms or blessings. This is a crucial clue. If jars built the same way sometimes contained rolled scrolls, the simplest reading is that the Khujut Rabu jar belonged to the same family: a small sealed container for something written, whose contents rotted away, leaving acids and corrosion that look, to a modern eye, like the residue of an electrolyte. Rolling a text and sealing it in a metal tube was a widespread habit in the ancient world. Across the Roman Empire and the Near East, people wore thin sheets of gold, silver or lead inscribed with protective words, rolled tight and slipped into small metal capsules. Archaeologists find these amulet cases in graves and houses from Britain to Syria. Seen against that background, a copper tube holding a rolled text inside a sealed jar looks far less mysterious. Mostly from old excavation reports, a few photographs and König's description and drawing. The original jar cannot currently be examined, the Seleucia and Ctesiphon parallels are scattered across collections, and no modern chemical analysis of residues inside the Khujut Rabu cylinder has b

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 04 Turning it on: the experiments
chunks.text: The battery idea is testable, and people tested it. Around 1940, Willard Gray, an engineer at General Electric in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, built a replica from König's description, filled it with a copper sulphate solution and reported that it worked, briefly, as a cell. Later the German Egyptologist Arne Eggebrecht reported using several replicas with grape juice to deposit a thin layer of gold onto a small silver figure, though no written documentation of that experiment was published. In 2005 the television programme MythBusters built ten replica jars, filled them with lemon juice and wired them in series. Together they produced a little over 4 V, around half a volt per jar. Most recently, in January 2026, independent researcher Alexander Bazes published a reconstruction in the journal Sino-Platonic Papers arguing that the jar may have worked as two cells at once, reaching about 1.4 V, comparable to an AA battery. Step 1 of 4. One object: a clay jar with a copper tube and an iron rod, sealed with bitumen. One object: a clay jar with a copper tube and an iron rod, sealed with bitumen. Battery reading: pour in an acid such as vinegar. Container reading: roll a written scroll and slide it into the copper tube. Battery: a meter would read about 0.5–2 V. Container: the tube is sealed with bitumen and the jar closed. Battery: but connect it to what? No wires, plated objects or devices have been found. Container: the scroll decays, acids corrode the iron, as seen in the parallels. Two columns share one jar drawing. Left column, battery hypothesis: acid such as vinegar is poured in; a voltmeter reads about 0.5 to 2 volts; but there is nothing to connect it to, shown by an empty dashed box labelled no wires, no device found. Right column, container hypothesis: a written scr

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 05 The problem of the missing wires
chunks.text: Here the battery case runs into trouble. A battery is only useful if you connect it to something. The Khujut Rabu jar has no terminal on the copper cylinder, which was sealed inside the jar with bitumen, an excellent electrical insulator. To draw current you would have to attach a wire to the copper, and nothing on the object shows how that was done. No wires or conductors have been found with any of these jars. No electroplated objects from ancient Mesopotamia have been identified; thin gold layers of the period match known non-electrical methods. No text in Aramaic, Middle Persian, Greek or any other language of the region describes electricity, currents or plating by current. Related jars held multiple bronze tubes or organic scrolls, which do not fit a single working cell. The iron rod's top sits inside a bitumen plug, again awkward for making a connection. It is worth being fair here. Ancient smiths could certainly draw copper wire, so the absence of wires is not because they were impossible to make. The point is that none has been found with these jars, in any report, and nothing about the jar's construction provides a place to attach one. For a device whose whole purpose would be to deliver current somewhere else, that silence is significant. William Hafford, an archaeologist at the Penn Museum, points out that modern replicas tend to follow König's drawing, which reconstructed the object as a battery in the first place, so it is no surprise that they behave like batteries. Elizabeth Stone, a specialist in Mesopotamian archaeology, put the field's view bluntly to a History.com reporter in 2026: she knew of nobody working in the area who thought it was a real battery.

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 06 Gold without electricity
chunks.text: König's gilding hypothesis was a sensible idea in 1938, because he had seen very thin gold layers on silver objects. But ancient craftspeople had excellent ways to gild without current. The most important was fire-gilding, also called mercury gilding. Gold is dissolved in mercury to make a paste, the paste is brushed onto a metal surface, and the object is heated so that the mercury evaporates, leaving a thin, firmly bonded layer of gold. According to conservation scientist Katharina Anheuser, fire-gilding was used in China from about 300 BCE and in Europe from about 200 CE, and it remained the main gilding method until electroplating arrived in the 19th century. Sasanian silversmiths were masters of it: many of their famous silver plates carry scenes picked out with mercury gilding. Thin gold leaf, applied with adhesives or by burnishing, was even older. None of this needs a battery, and the physical traces left by fire-gilding, such as residual mercury, are recognisable in laboratory analysis. Other techniques were available too. Craftspeople in several regions practised depletion gilding, treating a gold alloy so that the base metals at the surface were removed, leaving a gold-rich skin. Gold leaf could be beaten thinner than a micrometre and burnished onto a surface. Laboratory study of ancient gilded objects routinely identifies which method was used, and electroplating is not among the methods found on objects from antiquity. In other words, the problem König was trying to solve already had a well-documented solution. That does not make his question foolish. It makes the battery answer unnecessary.

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 07 Other explanations: medicine, scrolls and ritual
chunks.text: If not for gilding, could a small current have had some other use? In 1993 the classicist Paul Keyser suggested, in the Journal of Near Eastern Studies, that such cells might have been used for mild electrical pain relief, much as Greek and Roman doctors applied electric fish to patients with headaches or gout. It is a creative idea, and the electric-fish practice is well documented in ancient medical writers, but there is no evidence that anyone used jars this way. The explanation favoured by many archaeologists is more modest. The jar was a small container, perhaps for a written scroll, sealed with bitumen, whose organic contents decayed into acids that corroded the iron. Hafford goes further, reading jars of this type as ritual deposits: the iron rod as a nail, the copper tube as a sealed case for a protective text, the whole object buried for its symbolic power rather than any practical function. Protective inscriptions were common in the region in this period, most famously on clay incantation bowls buried under houses. Bazes, interestingly, bridges the two camps. His 2026 paper takes the electrochemistry seriously but proposes that any current was a side effect with a ritual meaning, visibly corroding the metal and perhaps the written prayer sealed inside, rather than a power supply for a device. Each explanation makes predictions that could be checked. If the jar held an electrolyte, residues of acetic acid or wine and a particular pattern of copper and iron corrosion products should survive. If it held a scroll, fibres, ink traces or impressions of a rolled sheet might remain inside the cylinder. If it was a ritual deposit, its findspot should resemble those of other buried protective objects, such as under a floor or at a threshold. Frustratingly, the published

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': 08 Lost again, and what remains unknown
chunks.text: In April 2003, during the invasion of Iraq, the Iraq Museum in Baghdad was looted and thousands of objects were taken. The Khujut Rabu jar is reported to have disappeared at that time, and its current whereabouts are unknown. Many objects have since been recovered and returned, but we could find no verified report that this one has been among them. That loss is painful for science as well as for Iraq's heritage. Modern techniques could analyse residues in the copper cylinder, identify whether the corrosion products came from vinegar, wine, organic decay or something else, and look for traces of written material. Until the jar is found, or a parallel from Seleucia or Ctesiphon is analysed with the same care, key questions stay open. When exactly was it made, Parthian or Sasanian? What liquid, if any, did it hold? Were the parallel jars' tubes all scroll holders, or did they vary? Is the iron rod a structural pin, a ritual nail or an electrode? The honest verdict is that the jar's function is uncertain, the scroll or ritual container reading fits the evidence best, and the battery hypothesis, however fun, has no supporting archaeological evidence. It remains a wonderful classroom demonstration and a reminder to ask not only whether something could work, but whether anyone ever used it that way.

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': debate
chunks.text: Was the jar a working battery? Yes Replicas produce roughly 0.5–2 V; the iron shows acid corrosion; Bazes (2026) argues for an efficient two-cell design. No evidence it was used as one No wires, terminals, electrical devices or texts; the copper is sealed in insulating bitumen; similar jars held scrolls and multiple tubes. The bold claim: The Khujut Rabu jar was built and used as an electric battery. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established That the arrangement can make a voltage is not in dispute. But there is no archaeological evidence that anyone drew current from it: no conductors, no powered devices, no electroplated objects and no texts. The closest parallels point to containers. Unless the jar or a parallel yields new evidence, the battery reading has no receipts.

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': debate
chunks.text: Was it used for electroplating gold or silver? Yes König saw very thin gold layers on ancient silver; Eggebrecht reported plating a figure with replicas. No Fire-gilding with mercury was well established and explains thin gold layers; no electroplated ancient object has been identified; Eggebrecht's experiment was not documented in print. The bold claim: Ancient Mesopotamian smiths used jars like this to electroplate metal objects. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established The gilding König observed has a documented non-electrical explanation, mercury fire-gilding, whose traces are detectable in analysis, and no object from the region has been shown to be electroplated. The one experiment claiming success was never properly published. The claim rests only on possibility.

chunks.heading: The 'Baghdad battery': debate
chunks.text: Was it a container for a scroll or a ritual deposit? Yes Similar jars from Seleucia and Ctesiphon held bronze tubes with rolled organic material; protective texts were common in the period. Not yet shown for this jar No scroll remains have been reported from the Khujut Rabu cylinder itself, and the original cannot now be analysed. The bold claim: The jar was a sealed container for a written scroll, probably with a protective or ritual purpose. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established This reading fits the construction, the bitumen seals and the contents of close parallels without requiring any unknown technology. But direct evidence from the Khujut Rabu jar is missing, its context is poorly published and the object is lost, so the case rests on analogy.

chunks.text: Late Roman glass The Lycurgus Cup 10 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read c. 16.5 cm height with its later metal mounts Freestone et al. 2007; British Museum c. 70 nm typical size of the silver-gold particles (range c. 50–100 nm) Barber and Freestone 1990 c. 300 ppm silver silver in the glass Barber and Freestone 1990; Freestone et al. 2007 c. 40 ppm gold gold in the glass Barber and Freestone 1990; Freestone et al. 2007 c. 700 g weight of the cup British Museum collection record c. 100 × more sensitive Illinois 'nano Lycurgus cup' sensor vs commercial sensors, for salt-level changes Gartia, Liu et al. 2013 (as reported) c. 16.5 cm with its later metal mounts (museum catalogue: 15.9 cm) Height c. 13.2 cm Diameter c. 700 g Weight opaque jade green in reflected light; translucent red in transmitted light Colour c. 300 ppm silver and c. 40 ppm gold in the glass Silver and gold silver-gold alloy nanoparticles, c. 50–100 nm across Colour-making particles cage cup: cut and ground from a thick glass blank Technique 1958, from Lord Rothschild, for £20,000 Bought by the British Museum The cup is a cage cup, or diatretum. A glassworker first made a thick-walled blank of a special glass that contained tiny amounts of silver and gold. Cutters then spent a very long time grinding most of that wall away with rotating wheels and abrasives, leaving the figures of the myth standing proud of the inner cup and linked to it by small hidden bridges of glass. The colour comes from the metal: during heating, the dissolved silver and gold came together as alloy particles about 50–100 nanometres across. Those particles scatter green light back towards the viewer and let red light pass through, so the glass changes colour depending on where the light comes from. The myth The Romans understood nanotechnology and deliberately engineered nanoparticles with modern precision, or the cup was made with a lost chemical secret no one can reproduce. The reality Roman glassmakers clearly knew that adding tiny amounts of precious metal and controlling the heat produced this remarkable glass, and their control of trace amounts was impressive. But they had no concept of particles, electrons or plasmonics; the effect was reached by experiment, recipe and skill. Very few dichroic glasses survive, so how reliably they could repeat it is uncertain. Modern scientists explain the colour with plasmon physics and have borrowed it for sensors and reproductions. chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 01 A cup that changes its mind
chunks.text: In a gallery of the British Museum stands a glass cup about the size of a large coffee mug. Lit from the front, as most museum objects are, it looks like polished jade: an opaque, slightly milky green, carved with writhing figures. Then someone places a light inside it, and the whole cup turns a deep, glowing red, like wine held up to a candle. Same glass, same cup, two completely different colours. This is the Lycurgus Cup, made in the Late Roman Empire in the 4th century CE. It is famous for two separate reasons. The first is craftsmanship: it is one of the finest surviving cage cups, vessels whose decoration was cut free from the body so that it stands away from the surface like a net. The second is physics. Its colour change comes from metal particles only tens of nanometres across, which is why materials scientists sometimes call it the oldest known piece of nanotechnology. Picture it, perhaps, on the table of a wealthy household in the 4th century, in a dining room lit by oil lamps. By daylight the cup would have looked like carved green stone. As evening fell and a lamp was set behind it, or wine was poured and the vessel lifted towards the flame, the green would have warmed to amber and then to red. We do not know how its owners used it, or even whether it was meant for drinking at all, since the delicate cage makes it awkward to hold. But it is easy to imagine the gasp around the table. Two colours from one glass: green where light bounces back, red where light passes through. Both claims deserve a careful look, because the story of how the cup was made is at least as remarkable as the story of what it does.

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 02 A king trapped by a vine
chunks.text: The figures on the cup tell a savage myth. Lycurgus, a king of the Edonians in Thrace, attacked the god Dionysus and his followers. The earliest version appears in Homer's Iliad, where the hero Diomedes cites Lycurgus as a warning about fighting gods. He it was that drove the nursing women who were in charge of frenzied Bacchus through the land of Nysa, and they flung their thyrsi on the ground as murderous Lycurgus beat them with his oxgoad. Later versions of the story add the episode shown on the cup. One of Dionysus's followers, the nymph Ambrosia, is attacked by Lycurgus and calls for help. She is transformed into a vine, which wraps around the king and holds him fast. On the cup, Lycurgus is caught mid-struggle, almost naked, tangled in the vine's branches. Around him the god's companions close in: Dionysus himself with his thyrsus, the staff tipped with a pine cone, and his panther; Pan; and a satyr preparing to hurl a rock. Why this scene? Wine and Dionysus suit a drinking cup, and the colour change, from green to wine red, may have seemed a delightful echo of the vine and its grapes. Some scholars have also suggested a political meaning, linking the punished king to a defeated ruler of the early 4th century, perhaps the emperor Licinius, defeated by Constantine in 324 CE. That reading is possible but cannot be confirmed.

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 03 How to carve a cage from glass
chunks.text: Cage cups, known in Latin as diatreta, are among the most difficult objects ancient craftspeople ever made. Only a few dozen are known, most of them fragmentary, and they date mainly to the 3rd and 4th centuries CE. Nearly all have an openwork net of glass rings standing away from an inner bowl. The Lycurgus Cup is unusual because, instead of a net, its 'cage' is a crowd of figures. On the left, an outline of the Lycurgus Cup about 16.5 centimetres tall including its later metal rim and foot, and 13.2 centimetres wide, with figures in openwork relief and a dimension line for each. In the centre, three small cross-sections of the cup wall: first a thick plain blank, then the outer glass cut away to leave a raised figure, then the figure undercut so it stands free, linked to the inner wall by small glass bridges. On the right, a circular inset shows several round particles in glass with a 100 nanometre scale bar, labelled silver-gold alloy particles about 70 nanometres across. The method that most specialists accept is subtractive. A glassworker first blew or cast a thick-walled blank, a plain cup with walls far thicker than the finished object. Cutters then removed glass with rotating wheels fed with abrasives, and with drills and files, working from the outside in. They cut the figures in high relief, then carefully undercut behind them, leaving the figures linked to the inner wall only by small bridges of glass hidden behind limbs and drapery. One slip could crack the blank and waste weeks of work. The tools were simple, and that is what makes the result so astonishing. Roman glass cutters used wheels of stone or metal, turned by a bow or a treadle-driven lathe, fed with a slurry of abrasive sand or emery in water. Drills and small files did the finer work. Every curve

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 04 Green by day, red by lamplight
chunks.text: What causes the colour change? For centuries nobody could say. Harden and Toynbee's classic 1959 study described the glass in detail but could not see what was inside it. The answer came in 1990, when David Barber and Ian Freestone examined tiny fragments of the cup under an analytical transmission electron microscope, an instrument that can image and analyse particles far too small for any optical microscope. They found scattered particles of a silver-gold alloy, typically about 70 nm across and ranging from roughly 50 to 100 nm, with a little copper. Chemical analysis showed the glass contains only about 300 parts per million of silver and about 40 parts per million of gold. The rest is ordinary Roman soda-lime-silica glass, about 73.5% silica, 13% soda and 6% lime. Step 1 of 4. Lamp outside: light bounces back from the glass towards you, and the cup looks green. Lamp outside: light bounces back from the glass towards you, and the cup looks green. Lamp inside: light passes through the glass wall to you, and the cup glows red. Zoom into the glass: tiny silver-gold particles absorb and scatter green and blue light, and let red light through. The particles are only c. 50–100 nm across, made from c. 300 ppm silver and c. 40 ppm gold in the glass. Step 1 shows the cup lit by a lamp in front: rays bounce back from the glass to an eye and are drawn green, and the cup appears green. Step 2 shows a lamp inside the cup: rays pass through the glass wall to the eye and are drawn red, and the cup appears red. Step 3 zooms into the glass wall, where white light meets small round silver-gold particles: green and blue light are scattered or absorbed, red continues through. chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 05 Did the Romans do nanotechnology?
chunks.text: It is tempting to say yes, and headlines often do. The honest answer is more interesting. The Romans did make nanoparticles, and they did it on purpose in the sense that someone deliberately added silver and gold to the glass batch and controlled the heating to get this effect. Such low concentrations suggest that the precious metal was added in a finely divided form, perhaps as dust, filings or a dilute solution, and thoroughly mixed. But they had no idea that particles were involved, let alone how light interacts with electrons. Their knowledge was practical: a recipe, a sequence of heating and a skilled eye that could judge when the glass had 'struck' its colour. We might call it nanotechnology by craft rather than by design. How do such particles form? In a hot glass melt, small amounts of gold and silver can dissolve as individual atoms or ions, and the glass then looks nearly colourless. When the glass is held at a suitable temperature, or reheated after cooling, the metal atoms drift together and cluster into particles, which grow until they are large enough to colour the glass. Glassmakers call this 'striking' the colour. It is highly sensitive to temperature and time, which may be one reason why so few ancient dichroic glasses survive. The effect was also hard to control. Only a handful of dichroic glasses of this kind survive, and they vary: a fragment of a cage cup in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, showing a satyr, shifts from olive green to reddish amber rather than jade to ruby. A letter attributed to the emperor Hadrian, preserved in the unreliable Historia Augusta, mentions 'cups of changing colours' among precious gifts, which hints that such glass was known and prized, though the passage cannot be tied to this cup. Deliberate: adding precious metals to

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 06 A 1,600-year-old idea in modern labs
chunks.text: The physics behind the Lycurgus Cup is now central to a branch of modern science called plasmonics. Gold and silver nanoparticles are used in pregnancy tests, where they give the familiar red line, and in sensors that detect tiny changes in their surroundings, because the colour a particle scatters shifts when the material around it changes. In 2013 a team at the University of Illinois led by engineer Gang Logan Liu took direct inspiration from the cup. They imprinted billions of tiny cup-shaped wells onto a plastic plate and coated them with metal nanoparticles, creating what they called nano Lycurgus cup arrays. When liquids were placed on the plate, its colour changed: light green for water, red for oil. The researchers reported that the prototype was about 100 times more sensitive to changes in salt levels than comparable commercial sensors. The same principle turns up in everyday medicine. The coloured line in many rapid diagnostic tests is made by gold nanoparticles a few tens of nanometres across, which appear red for exactly the kind of reason the Lycurgus Cup glows red: their electrons resonate with green light and remove it from what reaches your eye. The Romans knew how to make and use nanoparticles for beautiful art. We wanted to see if this could have scientific applications. Other groups have used silver and gold nanoparticles in polymers, including 3D-printable materials, to recreate the cup's green-to-red switch. The old glassmakers would have recognised the effect at once, even if the explanation would have baffled them.

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 07 From a dealer's shop to Room 41
chunks.text: Where the cup was found is unknown. It first appears in print in 1845, in the possession of a collector recorded as M. Dubois. By 1857 it belonged to the banker Lionel de Rothschild, and it was lent to a major exhibition in London in 1862. Not every viewer was impressed: the German art historian Gustav Waagen dismissed it as barbaric and debased, a reminder that taste changes as much as science does. In 1958 Victor, Lord Rothschild sold the cup to the British Museum for £20,000, with £2,000 contributed by the Art Fund. Its metal mounts were removed for study that year and later reunited with the glass. Today it is on display in Room 41, among objects of the Late Roman and early Byzantine world. Where was it made? The quality of the cutting points to one of the great glass centres of the Late Roman world. Rome and Alexandria have both been proposed, but there is no inscription or workshop evidence to settle it.

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: 08 What remains uncertain
chunks.text: Compared with many ancient wonders, the Lycurgus Cup holds few deep mysteries. We know what it is made of, why it changes colour and, broadly, how it was cut. Its mystery level is low. The open questions are about people and places. Which workshop made it, and where? In what form was the silver and gold added, and how did the glassmakers control the heat? Was the glass made for this cup, or was a dichroic blank bought from a specialist glassmaker and then cut elsewhere? Does the myth carry a political message about Constantine and Licinius, or is it simply a good wine story? How many cutting hours did it take? Estimates range widely, and no ancient source records it. Perhaps the best way to think of it is as a meeting point. A myth about wine and the punishment of pride, a feat of cold-working that pushed glass to its limits, and a trace of precious metal that happened to put physics on display. Roman craftspeople did not need to understand plasmons to make something that still stops visitors in their tracks. They needed patience, experience and an eye for light. The science is modern. The wonder was always there, waiting for someone to put a lamp inside.

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: debate
chunks.text: Did Roman glassmakers deliberately create nanoparticles? Yes, in effect The silver and gold were clearly added on purpose in tiny, controlled amounts, and the colour requires suitable heat treatment. Not knowingly They had no concept of particles or plasmons; few similar glasses survive and colours vary, suggesting a hard-won, partly unpredictable recipe. The bold claim: The Romans practised nanotechnology deliberately. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established The ingredients and probably the heating were deliberate, so the Romans did intentionally make a material whose properties depend on nanoparticles. But they did not know that particles existed or controlled their size by design. Calling it nanotechnology is fair as a description of the material, misleading as a description of Roman knowledge.

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: debate
chunks.text: Was the cage cut from a solid blank, or partly moulded? Cut and ground Tool and polishing marks, the undercut figures and the hidden bridges fit subtractive cold-working, the view of most specialists. Partly moulded Lierke argued that hot-shaping in moulds could have produced the basic cage before finishing. The bold claim: The Lycurgus Cup was made by cutting and grinding away a thick glass blank. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established The surfaces and structure of the cup match cold-cutting, and the moulding alternative has found little acceptance among glass specialists. Experimental reproductions of cage cups by cutting also succeed. Some details of the tools and time involved remain uncertain.

chunks.heading: The Lycurgus Cup: debate
chunks.text: Does the cup celebrate Constantine's victory over Licinius? Possibly Some scholars link the punished king to Licinius, defeated in 324 CE, and date the cup to around that time. Not necessarily Dionysiac scenes and wine myths were popular decorations for drinking vessels without any political meaning. The bold claim: The Lycurgus scene was a coded reference to Licinius's defeat by Constantine. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established The dating allows it and the idea is attractive, but there is no inscription, documented commission or other direct evidence. The myth suits a wine cup on its own terms. This remains an interpretation, not a demonstrated fact.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan
chunks.text: Basin of Mexico Teotihuacan 10 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read c. 100,000 people a common estimate of the peak population Millon 1973; Cowgill 2015 c. 2,000 compounds walled apartment compounds mapped across the city Millon 1973 15.5 ° tilt of the street grid east of true north Šprajc 2000 260 days between the two sunsets the Sun Pyramid faces Šprajc 2000 103 m length of the tunnel under the Feathered Serpent Pyramid Gómez Chávez, in La Jornada 2014 over 50,000 objects offerings recovered from the tunnel by 2014 La Jornada 2014; INAH c. 20 km² City area at its height c. 75,000–125,000 (estimates vary) Population c. 222–225 m a side, c. 63–65 m high today Pyramid of the Sun c. 43 m high, seven building phases Pyramid of the Moon c. 15°28′ east of true north Grid orientation c. 2,000 Apartment compounds 103 m long, c. 18 m deep Tunnel under the Feathered Serpent Pyramid Teotihuacan grew from scattered villages after about 100 BCE into a city planned on one tilted grid, about 15°28′ east of true north. Its great pyramids are mostly fill: earth, rubble and adobe held in place by stone retaining walls, then faced with stone and thick lime plaster that was often painted. The Pyramid of the Sun rose in a few big episodes, with radiocarbon dates from inside it clustering in about 170–310 CE; the Pyramid of the Moon was enlarged at least six times over its first earlier structure. Builders quarried local volcanic stone, including red tezontle and basalt, and carried fill in baskets, with no draft animals and no wheeled carts. Around 150–200 CE the Feathered Serpent Pyramid went up over more than 200 sacrificial burials, and beneath it a 103 m tunnel was cut, filled with offerings and sealed around 250 CE. The myth The Aztecs built Teotihuacan, or giants did; or its pyramids are a scale model of the solar system, laid out with a lost unit of measurement or knowledge from somewhere far away. The reality The city was already centuries in ruins when Nahuatl speakers named it Teotihuacan, 'the place where the gods were made'. Excavation shows a home-grown, multi-ethnic city with neighbourhoods of migrants from Oaxaca and elsewhere, built on a calendar-linked grid. Solar-system readings do not survive careful survey. Real open questions remain: the city's own name and language, who ruled it, and why its centre burned around 550 CE. chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 01 The place where the gods were made
chunks.text: Stand at the foot of the Pyramid of the Moon just after sunrise and look south. A dead-straight avenue, about 40 m wide, runs away from you for more than two kilometres, lined with the stumps of temples. On your left the Pyramid of the Sun sits like a man-made mountain. Behind you rises Cerro Gordo, a real one. It is hard to shake the feeling that the whole view was composed, and it was. By the time the Aztecs came here in the 1400s, the city had been a ruin for roughly nine centuries. They did not know who had built it, so they gave it a name that fitted its grandeur: Teotihuacan, usually translated as 'the place where the gods were made' or 'where the gods were born'. They also gave its main street the name we still use, the Avenue of the Dead, because they took the rubble mounds along it for tombs. They were wrong about that, but their awe was well placed. It is told that when yet [all] was in darkness, when yet no sun had shone and no dawn had broken, it is said, the gods gathered themselves together and took counsel among themselves there at Teotihuacan. In that Aztec story, two gods throw themselves into a bonfire at Teotihuacan to become the Sun and the Moon. It is a myth about the city, not from it. The people who actually lived here left no readable history of their own, and we still do not know what they called their home, which language they spoke, or who governed them. What they did leave is an astonishing amount of physical evidence, and some of the best of it has turned up in the last twenty years.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 02 A city drawn with one ruler
chunks.text: Teotihuacan began as a cluster of farming villages in a side valley of the Basin of Mexico around 100 BCE. Within three centuries it had become a city of roughly 20 km² and, by the most common estimates, somewhere between 75,000 and 125,000 people. René Millon's Teotihuacan Mapping Project, which began in 1962 and walked and recorded the whole urban area, showed something unusual: almost everything was built on one grid. That grid is not aligned to true north. Streets, walls and buildings run about 15°28′ east of north, and the cross-streets at right angles to them. When the archaeoastronomer Ivan Šprajc measured the major buildings, he found the east–west axis of the Pyramid of the Sun points to where the Sun sets on about 29–30 April and 12–13 August. The interval between those two sunsets, counted through the winter, is 260 days, exactly the length of the sacred calendar used across Mesoamerica. The north–south axis, meanwhile, lines up with the summit of Cerro Gordo. Schematic plan of Teotihuacan's ceremonial core drawn with true north at the top. The Avenue of the Dead runs from the Pyramid of the Moon at the north end down toward the lower left, tilted 15.5 degrees east of north, shown by an arc between a true-north line and the avenue axis pointing toward Cerro Gordo. The square Pyramid of the Sun sits east of the avenue; further south the Ciudadela enclosure holds the Feathered Serpent Pyramid, with the 103 metre tunnel marked in accent colour. The Great Compound lies opposite, and the canalised Río San Juan crosses the avenue. A 500 metre scale bar is included. The builders bent a river to fit their plan. That tells you how seriously they took the grid. The commitment was total. The Río San Juan, which crosses the city, was straightened into a channel that foll

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 03 Mountains made by hand
chunks.text: The Pyramid of the Sun is about 222–225 m a side, almost as broad as Khufu's pyramid at Giza, though at roughly 63–65 m it is less than half as tall. It is not a solid stone mountain. Inside, tunnels dug by archaeologists show layers of earth, rubble and adobe held in by stone retaining walls, with an outer skin of stone and lime plaster that was once painted. How tall it originally stood is uncertain, partly because Leopoldo Batres, who rebuilt it between 1905 and 1910 for Mexico's independence centenary, stripped away some of the outer fabric, a decision archaeologists still lament. In 1971 a cave was found under the pyramid, reached by a stairway near its front. It had been dug or reshaped by people and was sealed long ago. When exactly the pyramid itself rose is a lively argument. Excavations from 2008 to 2011 produced radiocarbon and pottery dates that place its main construction at about 170–310 CE. Rebecca Sload re-analysed the dates in 2015 and argued that the cave's use began in the first century CE, with the later dates marking a ritual closing rather than the first building. The debate below sets out both sides. At the north end of the avenue the Pyramid of the Moon, about 43 m high, grew in at least seven stages between roughly 100 and 400 CE, each one wrapping the last. Saburo Sugiyama and Rubén Cabrera's tunnels through it, begun in 1998, found five dedicatory burial complexes inside the layers. They held sacrificed people, some of them apparently foreigners, along with pumas, wolves, eagles and serpents, animals linked with warfare. Sacred mountains, in other words, were also stages for political theatre.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 04 The serpent's secret tunnel
chunks.text: The third great monument sits inside the Ciudadela, a walled enclosure about 400 m square at the southern end of the avenue. The Feathered Serpent Pyramid, built around 150–200 CE, is famous for its facade of stone serpent heads. Excavations in the 1980s found that it had also been dedicated with more than 200 sacrificial burials, many of them young men buried with weapons and ornaments, laid out in patterns that suggest careful planning. On 2 October 2003, after a heavy rainstorm, a hole about a metre wide opened in the plaza at the pyramid's foot. The archaeologist Sergio Gómez Chávez of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) looked down it and saw a shaft. It took years of radar survey, fundraising and permits before digging started in earnest. The team sank a shaft 14 m deep and about 5 m wide, found a deliberately sealed entrance, and began to clear a passage that runs 103 m east to a point under the centre of the pyramid, about 18 m below the surface. Step 1 of 6. October 2003: after heavy rain, a hole about 1 m wide opens in the plaza at the foot of the temple. October 2003: after heavy rain, a hole about 1 m wide opens in the plaza at the foot of the temple. 2004–2005: ground-penetrating radar traces a passage running about 100 m east, under the pyramid. 2009–2010: the team digs a shaft 14 m deep and about 5 m wide and meets the ancient, sealed entrance. Nearly 1,000 tonnes of fill packed in by the builders is cleared by hand; small robots scout ahead. Tens of thousands of offerings line the way; walls and ceiling carry powdered magnetite, pyrite and hematite. At the far end, about 18 m down under the pyramid's centre: chambers, greenstone figures and liquid mercury. Sealed c. 250 CE. True-scale cross-section. On the right stands the step

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 05 Life in the apartment blocks
chunks.text: Most Teotihuacanos did not live in temples. They lived in walled apartment compounds, of which the mapping project recorded about 2,000. A typical compound was a single-storey block of rooms, patios and small shrines, housing perhaps 60–100 people, often several related families sharing a trade. Some compounds made obsidian tools, others pottery, figurines or lapidary work. The better-off ones had painted murals of gods, priests, jaguars and flowering trees. Tetitla, Atetelco and Zacuala: compounds known for their fine murals. Teopancazco: a neighbourhood centre with evidence of foreign cooks, tailors and craftworkers. La Ventilla: a district with a large plaza and a rare set of painted glyphs on its floor. Life expectancy was not high, and skeletons show hard work and seasonal hunger. But the compounds were solid, drained and plastered, and for centuries they kept a very large population housed in one place, something few ancient cities managed so well.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 06 A city of migrants
chunks.text: On Teotihuacan's western edge lies a neighbourhood archaeologists call the Oaxaca Barrio, Tlailotlacan. Its houses used pottery in the style of the Zapotec valley of Oaxaca, roughly 400 km to the southeast, and at least one tomb was built in the Oaxacan way. People there appear to have kept their homeland's customs for centuries. Chemistry backs this up. Oxygen isotopes in teeth and bones record the water a person drank while those tissues formed, and water differs from place to place. Christine White, Michael Spence and colleagues found that the enclave's residents kept moving between Teotihuacan, the Oaxaca homeland and other diaspora communities, with some children apparently spending years away before returning. It looks strikingly like a modern migrant community, with ties that stretch across hundreds of kilometres. Other districts held people with Gulf Coast and Maya-lowland connections. Teotihuacan was not a monoculture but a magnet, and its planners found room for all of them inside the same tilted grid.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 07 Strangers at Tikal, 378 CE
chunks.text: Some 1,000 km away, in the Maya city of Tikal in Guatemala, carved inscriptions record that on a day in January 378 CE a man called Siyaj K'ahk' 'arrived'. According to the epigrapher David Stuart's reading, Tikal's king Chak Tok Ich'aak 'entered the water', a phrase for dying, on that same day. Soon a new king, Yax Nuun Ahiin, took the throne; he was the son of a figure the texts call Spearthrower Owl, and on a later Tikal monument, Stela 31, he is shown dressed as a Teotihuacan-style warrior. Whether this was conquest, a coup backed by Teotihuacan, or a political alliance dressed up in foreign prestige is still argued. In 2021 a team led by Stephen Houston reported, using lidar and excavation, a compound at Tikal that copies the layout of Teotihuacan's Ciudadela at a smaller scale, with Teotihuacan-style incense burners and green obsidian points from central Mexico. Whatever happened in 378, Teotihuacan's influence reached deep into the Maya world.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 08 Fire in the centre
chunks.text: Around 550 CE, the temples and elite buildings along the Avenue of the Dead were burned. Sculptures were broken and some buildings were dismantled. A Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates from the neighbourhood of Teopancazco, published in 2009, places the end of the city's main Classic phase at about 550 CE, roughly a century earlier than once thought. The fire picked its targets. Temples and palaces burned; many ordinary homes did not. That selectivity is why many archaeologists favour an internal revolt, perhaps against an elite that had grown rich while the rest of the city struggled. Others keep outside attackers in the frame. Either way, people did not vanish. The population fell sharply but some lived on among the ruins for centuries, and later groups farmed and built in the valley.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: 09 Legends, measurements and what is still unknown
chunks.text: Teotihuacan attracts big theories. In the 1970s an engineer, Hugh Harleston Jr., proposed that the city's monuments were laid out as a scale model of the solar system, using a unit of about 1.059 m. The idea still circulates online. It does not hold up: the matches depend on choosing convenient points, and they include planets nobody could see before telescopes. The alignments that do show up clearly are to sunsets, a sacred calendar and a mountain, which is what we would expect from what we know about Mesoamerican religion. The genuinely unsolved questions are more interesting. Who ruled? Why no royal portraits? What did the Teotihuacanos call themselves? In 2025 the linguists Magnus Pharao Hansen and Christophe Helmke argued in Current Anthropology that some signs in Teotihuacan writing can be read as an early Uto-Aztecan language, ancestral to Nahuatl, Cora and Huichol. If they are right, the Aztecs who named the ruins may have been distant linguistic relatives of the builders. The proposal is bold and is being debated; the corpus of signs is small, and many readings remain uncertain. So the city keeps its secrets, but it no longer keeps them silently. A sinkhole, a radar scan and a lot of patient digging have given us a glittering underworld, sealed for 1,750 years. The next surprise may already be waiting under a patch of grass.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: debate
chunks.text: When was the Pyramid of the Sun built? Later: mostly in the late second to early fourth century CE. Tunnelling into the pyramid in 2008–2011 produced radiocarbon and ceramic evidence placing its main construction at about 170–310 CE (Sugiyama, Sugiyama and Sarabia 2013). Earlier: begun in the first century CE, with the late dates marking a remodelling. Sload (2015) modelled new dates from the cave below with Bayesian statistics and argued its use began in the mid first century, reading the third-century dates as a ritual closing of the cave and a redefinition of the pyramid. The bold claim: The Sun Pyramid we see was essentially built in the third century CE, not the first. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established Both camps use real radiocarbon dates; they disagree about which events those dates record. Samples from fill can be older than the construction they end up in, and ritual activity can add later dates, so the choice of model drives the answer. More dated samples from sealed contexts inside the pyramid are needed before either reading can be called settled.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: debate
chunks.text: Is the city a scale model of the solar system? Yes: distances between monuments encode planetary orbits in a special unit. In the 1970s Hugh Harleston Jr. proposed a unit of about 1.059 m and argued that spacings along the Avenue matched the orbits of the planets. No: the layout follows the calendar, the landscape and ordinary units. Surveys show the grid follows sunset dates and the peak of Cerro Gordo (Šprajc 2000). Sugiyama (1993) found a unit of about 83 cm that fits many buildings without any astronomy of orbits. The bold claim: Teotihuacan's builders laid out the planets' orbits to scale. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established The planetary matches depend on choosing which points to measure and on including planets unknown before telescopes, which the builders could not have seen. The same measurements are better explained by a calendar-linked grid and a human-scale unit of length. Nothing in the city's art or writing refers to such a model.

chunks.heading: Teotihuacan: debate
chunks.text: Who set fire to the city's centre around 550 CE? Insiders: a revolt against the ruling elite. Burning concentrates on temples and elite buildings along the Avenue of the Dead, and statues were smashed, which looks targeted rather than random (Millon 1988). Outsiders: raiders or rival groups from beyond the valley. The city was already declining, and new groups with different pottery traditions appear in the valley in the following century. The bold claim: The fire of about 550 CE was an internal uprising, not an invasion. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established The selective pattern of destruction fits an internal upheaval well, and the revised radiocarbon chronology places it around 550 CE (Beramendi-Orosco et al. 2009). But archaeology rarely records who held the torch, and the two explanations are not exclusive: a weakened city could suffer both.

chunks.heading: Great Zimbabwe
chunks.text: Near Masvingo, Zimbabwe Great Zimbabwe 10 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read c. 250 m length of the Great Enclosure's outer wall Britannica; Zimbabwe Field Guide up to c. 11 m maximum height of the outer wall Britannica nearly 1,000,000 blocks granite blocks in the outer wall (estimate) Zimbabwe Field Guide (2025) 8 birds carved soapstone birds known from the site Bent 1891, via Wikipedia 'Zimbabwe Bird' c. 722 ha total area of the site Chirikure et al. 2017; Wikipedia nearly 80 m length of the chevron band atop the outer wall Zimbabwe Field Guide (2025) c. 7.2 km² (Hill Complex, Great Enclosure, valley ruins) Site area c. 250 m long, up to c. 11 m high Great Enclosure wall up to c. 5 m at the base, tapering upward Wall thickness nearly 1 million blocks, c. 5,000 m³ (estimate) Stones in the outer wall c. 9–10 m tall, c. 5.5 m across, solid Conical tower none Mortar used 8 known, c. 40 cm tall on columns Soapstone birds older estimates up to c. 18,000; recent work suggests far fewer Population The builders used the local granite, which naturally peels off its domed outcrops in flat sheets. By heating a rock surface with fire and letting it cool quickly, perhaps helped by water, they could make sheets split away on purpose. The slabs broke at right angles into brick-like blocks, which were trimmed with hammerstones and laid in level courses without any mortar. The best walls have two carefully fitted faces and a core of rubble, and both faces lean inward as they rise, a slope called batter that makes a tall dry-stone wall stable. Near the top of the Great Enclosure, blocks set on edge form a decorative chevron band. A Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates (Chirikure et al. 2013) suggests walling began in the late 12th or early 13th century and peaked in the 14th and 15th. The myth Great Zimbabwe was built by Phoenicians, Arabs or the Queen of Sheba, because, colonial writers claimed, Africans could not have built it. The reality Excavations by David Randall-MacIver (1905) and Gertrude Caton-Thompson (1929), and all later research, show that it was built by the ancestors of the Shona-speaking people of the region. Pottery, house remains, architecture and radiocarbon dates all fit local development. The foreign-builder claims served colonial politics, and Rhodesian authorities pressured archaeologists into keeping them alive into the 1970s. chunks.heading: Great Zimbabwe: 01 Into the passage
chunks.text: Step through the north entrance of the Great Enclosure and the world narrows. On your left and right, two walls of grey granite rise far above your head, their faces made of thousands of neat, flat blocks, each about the size of a large book. The corridor between them, the Parallel Passage, is so tight in places that two people can barely pass. It curves, and curves, and then opens onto a small court where a solid cone of stone, taller than a three-storey house, stands in silence. This is Great Zimbabwe, in the south-east of the modern country that took its name from it. Between about 1200 and 1450 CE it was the capital of a wealthy state on the Zimbabwe plateau, whose rulers controlled cattle, farmland and gold, and traded, through coastal towns, with the Indian Ocean world. Its builders used no mortar at all. The name itself is usually explained as coming from Shona words meaning 'houses of stone'. For more than half a century, the most remarkable thing about Great Zimbabwe was not how it was built, but how hard outsiders tried to deny who built it. Today the answer is settled. What remains open is more interesting: how many people lived here, how its society was organised, and why its rulers eventually moved on.

chunks.heading: Great Zimbabwe: 02 A city in three parts
chunks.text: Great Zimbabwe covers roughly 7.2 km² of hills and valleys. Archaeologists usually describe three main areas. The Hill Complex crowns a steep granite ridge above the valley, its walls woven between huge natural boulders; it was the earliest area to be occupied, from around 1000 CE, and is often interpreted as a royal and ritual centre. Below it lies the Great Enclosure, the largest and most famous structure. Around and between them sprawl the valley ruins, smaller walled compounds and the remains of many houses. The houses themselves were not stone. People lived in round buildings of daga, a hard mix of clay and gravel, many of them finely finished with moulded steps and platforms. The stone walls did not hold up roofs. They defined space: who could go where, what could be seen, and by whom. In that sense the walls are architecture of power, a language of entrances, screens and passages. When was it all built? The site was dug over so carelessly in the colonial period that the chronology was muddled for decades. In 2013 Shadreck Chirikure and colleagues combined radiocarbon dates with dated imported objects in a Bayesian model. Their result: stone walling probably began in the late 12th or early 13th century and peaked in the 14th and 15th, overlapping with the older centre of Mapungubwe to the south rather than simply following it.

chunks.heading: Great Zimbabwe: 03 Walls without mortar
chunks.text: Great Zimbabwe's builders had an unusual gift from geology. The region's granite forms great bare domes, sometimes called whalebacks, and as the rock is heated by day and cooled by night over thousands of years, it peels off in curved sheets, a process called exfoliation. Those sheets split naturally into slabs of fairly even thickness. Accounts of the builders' method describe them speeding this up by lighting fires on the rock surface for hours and then cooling it quickly, perhaps with water, so that sheets cracked away where they wanted them. Step 1 of 5. A fire is built on a bare granite outcrop to heat the rock surface. A fire is built on a bare granite outcrop to heat the rock surface. As the rock cools, a sheet splits away along the granite's natural exfoliation layers. Hammerstones split the slabs at right angles into brick-like blocks. Blocks are laid in level courses without mortar: two faces with a rubble core, both leaning inward as the wall rises. Blocks set on edge form a chevron band near the top, nearly 80 m long on the Great Enclosure. Left: a domed granite outcrop with a fire on its surface, then a curved sheet of rock splitting away, then rectangular blocks stacked on the ground beside a hammerstone. Right: a cross-section of a dry-stone wall up to about 10 to 11 metres high and about 5 metres thick at the base, with two faces of coursed blocks leaning inward and a rubble core, beside a 1.7 metre person; and an elevation of the wall face with level courses and a zigzag chevron band near the top. Because the granite also tends to break at right angles to those layers, the slabs could be split with hammerstones into brick-like blocks. The masons laid them in courses, each row resting on the one below. In the best walls, such as the outer wall of the Gre

chunks.heading: Great Zimbabwe: 04 The Great Enclosure and its tower
chunks.text: The Great Enclosure is a vast, roughly elliptical ring. Its outer wall is about 250 m long and rises to about 11 m at its highest (some surveys give about 9.6 m for the tallest surviving stretch), with an average nearer 7 m. It contains around 5,000 m³ of stone, by one estimate nearly a million blocks. Along the top of part of the wall runs a band of chevrons nearly 80 m long, made by setting blocks at angles, about 9 m above the ground. Simplified plan of the Great Enclosure: a thick, roughly elliptical outer wall about 90 metres across and about 250 metres long, with three entrances. Along the eastern side an inner wall runs parallel to the outer wall, forming the narrow Parallel Passage, which leads to the solid Conical Tower, about 5.5 metres across, and a smaller tower. A dashed circle marks Enclosure 1, about 21 metres across, and dashed lines mark inner walls and hut platforms. A dotted line outside the eastern wall marks the approximate position of the chevron band, about 80 metres long. An inset shows the outer wall up to about 11 metres high and 5 metres thick at the base, the conical tower about 9 to 10 metres tall, and a 1.7 metre person. Inside, walls divide the space into smaller enclosures, including an older circular one about 21 m across, and platforms where daga houses stood. The Parallel Passage runs between the outer wall and an inner wall along the eastern side and leads to the Conical Tower: about 9 to 10 m tall and about 5.5 m across at the base, solid all the way through. Colonial treasure hunters dug under and into it looking for a hidden chamber. There is none. Look closely at the base of the outer wall and you find another sign of careful engineering: drains.
