In 2012 Norbert Mercier and colleagues tried a different trick: they used optically stimulated luminescence to date sediments at the foot of painted walls, layers that could be linked to the paintings. Their result was that the paintings are younger than about 9,000 to 10,000 years, but they could not narrow the window further. For decades, two camps argued. The Italian researcher Fabrizio Mori favoured a long 'high' chronology, with the oldest art reaching back well over 10,000 years. The French researcher Alfred Muzzolini argued for a much shorter 'low' chronology that brought many styles thousands of years closer to the present. Today most specialists sit between the two, but single dates for single paintings remain rare.

chunks.heading: Sefar, the Painted Rock City: 08 Lhote's copies and the fake Egyptians
chunks.text: The Tassili paintings had been noticed by French officers and travellers from the early 20th century; Lieutenant Charles Brenans drew attention to them in the 1930s. They became world-famous thanks to one man. In 1956 the French explorer and ethnographer Henri Lhote led a large team of painters onto the plateau. Over some 16 months they traced and copied hundreds of paintings, about 800 by his own account. The copies went on show in Paris in 1957 and 1958, and Lhote's book, translated into English as The Search for the Tassili Frescoes, was widely read. The expedition also did lasting harm. To make faded paintings stand out for tracing and photography, team members wetted and sponged the rock surfaces, a practice now known to accelerate fading and damage pigments. Some copies added or improved details. Worst of all, a few images appear to have been painted by expedition members themselves. The best-known case is a group of 'bird-headed goddesses' in an Egyptian style at Jabbaren, another painted site on the plateau. They supported Lhote's idea that Egyptian influence had reached the Tassili. The anthropologist Jeremy Keenan, in a 2002 paper, argued that several such images were fakes and that the expedition's methods had been damaging and misleading; researchers including Jean-Loïc Le Quellec have discussed the fakes too. The pseudo-Egyptian scene nonetheless became famous enough to be reproduced in a mosaic at Djanet airport. The most famous 'Egyptian' figures on the Tassili were probably painted in the 1950s, by the people who came to copy the ancient ones.

chunks.heading: Sefar, the Painted Rock City: 09 Martians on the wall?
chunks.text: Lhote's team gave nicknames to striking figures. One huge Round Head at Jabbaren, with a round head and odd projections, became the 'Great Martian God'. The name stuck. In the 1960s ancient-astronaut writers, including Erich von Däniken, cited Tassili figures as astronauts in pressurised suits and helmets. It is worth testing the claim properly. If the round heads show helmets, we might expect consistent technical details, equipment, craft or scenes unlike ordinary life. Instead we find figures with bows, figures dancing and swimming, figures with horns, feathers and masks, and figures in groups with women and children. Round heads appear on small figures as well as giants. Across the central Sahara the style belongs with hunting and ritual scenes painted by Holocene hunter-gatherers. The 'helmets' are best read as a stylistic convention, masks or hairstyles. The honest mystery is richer than the alien one. We still cannot say exactly what the Round Heads meant to their painters, or why a small, mobile population invested so much effort in giant figures on the walls of a sandstone maze.

chunks.heading: Sefar, the Painted Rock City: 10 A fragile gallery
chunks.text: Rock art that survived ten thousand years of sun and wind can be ruined in an afternoon. The threats at Sefar are mostly human. Visitors and guides have long been tempted to splash water on faded paintings so they photograph better, the same method Lhote's team used, and every wetting helps dissolve and detach pigment. Touching leaves oils and dirt. Across the Sahara, some sites have been looted, with painted or engraved panels cut out and sold; Keenan documented the problem in the 2000s. The Tassili is protected as a national park as well as a World Heritage Site, and visits to the painted sites are made with local guides, usually Tuareg, who know the routes and the rules. The remoteness that makes Sefar so hard to reach is also part of its defence. The best way to see it, for most of us, is through careful photography and recording, which is why modern digital documentation projects matter so much: they preserve the images without touching them.

chunks.heading: Sefar, the Painted Rock City: 11 What we still don't know
chunks.text: Almost every big question about Sefar is still open. How old, exactly, are the Round Heads? Were the giant figures gods, spirits, ancestors or people in costume? How did the painters relate to the herders who followed them: did they meet, trade, or replace one another? How many paintings have already faded, been damaged by wetting and handling, or been lost to looting? What is certain is that these walls are one of the best records we have of how people lived through a dramatic climate change, from a green, wet Sahara to the desert we know. Sefar's painters were witnesses. The work of dating and protecting their testimony is far from finished.

chunks.heading: Sefar, the Painted Rock City: debate
chunks.text: Do the Round Head figures show visitors in space helmets? Yes: helmets and suits. Round, featureless heads and odd projections look like helmets; Lhote's team nicknamed one figure the 'Great Martian God'; ancient-astronaut writers took this up in the 1960s. No: a human artistic tradition. The same convention appears on figures that hunt with bows, dance, swim and appear with women and children; masks, horns and headdresses are common; the style spans the central Sahara among Holocene hunter-gatherers (Soukopova 2011, 2012). The bold claim: The Round Head paintings depict extraterrestrial visitors. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established The 'Martian' label began as an expedition nickname, not a finding. When the whole corpus is examined, round heads appear in ordinary human scenes and at every size, alongside clear masks and costumes. Nothing in the art or the archaeology requires outside visitors, and a well-understood human tradition explains the images.

chunks.heading: Sefar, the Painted Rock City: debate
chunks.text: How old are the Round Head paintings? Early: c. 9,500–7,500 years ago. Soukopova's synthesis of superimpositions, fauna and associated archaeology places the Round Heads among early Holocene hunter-gatherers; OSL dating shows the paintings are younger than c. 9,000–10,000 years (Mercier et al. 2012). Later, or longer-lived. Proponents of a shorter chronology (after Muzzolini) place many styles later, and the lack of direct dates means some Round Head figures may be younger than the core range. The bold claim: Round Head paintings date mainly to c. 9,500–7,500 years ago. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The OSL result sets an upper limit and the artistic sequence places the Round Heads before the herding scenes, which fits the early Holocene. But without direct dates on paint, the range rests on indirect evidence, and individual paintings could fall outside it.

chunks.heading: Sefar, the Painted Rock City: debate
chunks.text: Did the Green Sahara end suddenly? Yes: within decades to centuries. Dust records off West Africa show a sharp shift around 5,500 years ago (deMenocal et al. 2000). No: it moved south over millennia. Leaf-wax records show a time-transgressive end, earlier in the north and later in the south (Shanahan et al. 2015). The bold claim: The African Humid Period ended abruptly everywhere around 5,500 years ago. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established Some records show rapid change, others a gradual, region-by-region retreat. Both can be true: local tipping points may have occurred at different times as the rain belt slowly moved south. A single date for the whole Sahara oversimplifies.

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars
chunks.text: Barabar Hills, Bihar and Halebidu, Karnataka India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars 10 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read 10.2 m length of Karan Chaupar, a single polished granite room 4.27 m wide published plans of the Barabar Caves c. 2,280 years since Ashoka gave the first Barabar caves to the Ajivikas Ashokan inscriptions; Falk 2006 up to 64 points on the most elaborate star-shaped Hoysala pillars (others have 16 or 32) Foekema 1996 c. 0.1 mm roughly the smallest step the eye can see at reading distance standard visual acuity 0 surveys published precision measurements of the pillars or caves that we could find our literature search, 2026 c. 1,800 gems inside the stone boxes from the Piprahwa stupa, returned to India in 2025 Peppé 1898; Ministry of Culture 2025 one polished granite room, 10.2 × 4.27 m Karan Chaupar cave, Barabar Ashoka's years 12 and 19 (c. 257 and 250 BCE); Dasharatha c. 230 BCE Barabar dedications granite, with a mirror-like 'Mauryan polish' Barabar rock begun c. 1121 CE, work into the 1160s Hoysaleswara temple, Halebidu chloritic schist ('soapstone'), soft when fresh Hoysala stone none found for either site Published precision surveys At Barabar, Mauryan masons cut rooms straight into a granite hill: they split and chipped out the rock with iron tools, dressed walls and vaults to shape, then ground and burnished the surfaces with progressively finer abrasives until they shone. The unfinished Lomas Rishi cave still shows lumps of rock left on its floor and an uncompleted vault, freezing the process. At the Hoysala temples, pillar shafts of soft chloritic schist were most likely turned on large horizontal lathes: a roughed-out shaft hung between pivots was spun back and forth by a rope while a turner held an iron tool against it, then polished with fine sand and water. Architects worked to proportional systems of the kind described in Sanskrit architectural manuals such as the Mayamata and Manasara. The myth India has perfectly symmetrical stone boxes, granite rooms and pillars cut to machine tolerances, with mirror-smooth faces and flawless circles, so they must have been made with lost high technology, lasers or power tools. The reality The objects are real and superb, but no one has published measurements showing machine-level precision. Inscriptions date the Barabar caves to the reigns of Ashoka and his grandson, unfinished work shows hand methods, and the Hoysala pillars fit what a hand-powered lathe produces in soft stone. 'Perfect' in the viral claims usually means 'looks perfect to the eye'. Flip it Wow

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 01 Which 'stone box'?
chunks.text: Scroll long enough through ancient-mystery videos and you will meet 'the symmetrical stone box of India'. It is usually a granite room with walls like glass, or a flawless pillar that looks as if it came off a factory lathe, set to dramatic music and a caption asking how anyone could have made it 2,000 years ago. What the posts rarely tell you is where the object actually is. The phrase gets attached to different places, and sometimes to no place at all. So we did some detective work. The claims that best match a 'perfectly symmetrical stone box' point to two real sets of monuments, and we cover both. The first is the Barabar Caves in Bihar, where rooms were cut into solid granite in the 3rd century BCE and polished to a mirror shine; the smallest, Karan Chaupar, is literally a single rectangular stone box, 10.2 m long and 4.27 m wide. The second is the Hoysala temples of Karnataka, at Belur and Halebidu, whose round pillars are often called 'machined'. Along the way we look at real stone boxes, the relic caskets of early Buddhism, which were sometimes turned on lathes too. The objects are real and superb. The question is not whether they are impressive, but whether they needed anything more than skilled hands.

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 02 Rooms cut into a granite hill
chunks.text: About 24 km north of Gaya, a ridge of bare granite boulders rises out of the Bihar plain. Walk up to one of them and you find a plain doorway cut into the rock. Step inside and the temperature drops. The walls, ceiling and floor are smooth, the corners crisp, and the surface throws back light from the entrance like dark glass. Hum a note and the room hums it back to you for a long, ringing moment. These are the Barabar Caves, among the oldest rock-cut rooms in India. Inscriptions carved at their doorways tell us who paid for them. The emperor Ashoka, famous for spreading his edicts across the subcontinent, gave caves here to the Ajivikas, an ascetic sect that rivalled early Buddhists and Jains, in the twelfth year of his reign, around 257 BCE. A further inscription at Karan Chaupar dates to his nineteenth year, around 250 BCE. The German epigraphist Harry Falk has read it as naming the cave Supriyekṣā and recording that it was given to the Ajivikas. His grandson Dasharatha dedicated three more caves in the nearby Nagarjuni hills around 230 BCE. The rooms are modest in size but not in ambition. Sudama cave has a rectangular hall about 9.98 by 5.94 m leading to a round inner chamber about 6 m across. Lomas Rishi has a similar hall of 9.86 by 5.18 m and a doorway carved to imitate a timber building, with curved eaves and a frieze of elephants. Karan Chaupar is the simplest: one long room. It is also the one that most looks like a polished stone box. Who were the people meant to sit in these boxes? The Ajivikas were followers of Makkhali Gosala, a teacher contemporary with the Buddha and Mahavira. Their central idea, as reported mostly by their rivals, was niyati: that the course of every life is fixed by destiny, and that no action can change it. Their own scriptures are l

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 03 The mirror finish, explained
chunks.text: The shine has a name: Mauryan polish. It is not unique to the Barabar Caves. The same glassy finish appears on Ashoka's great sandstone pillars, on the lion capital from Sarnath that is now India's national emblem, and on other sculpture of the period. Scholars have long suggested a link with the polished stonework of Achaemenid Persia, whose empire fell in 330 BCE, scattering its craftsmen. Polishing grains and stones have been reported from the ruins of Persepolis. How is granite polished by hand? The principle is the same one used by any modern stonemason, only slower. First the surface is ground flat with a coarse abrasive, such as sand or crushed harder stone, rubbed under a heavy block with water. Then the grit is changed for finer and finer powders, each step removing the scratches left by the last. Finally the surface is burnished, perhaps with a very fine powder on leather or with a hard polishing stone, until it reflects. Some sources say agate burnishers were used; the exact recipe is not documented. What is certain is that it is labour, not magic: many weeks of rubbing for each wall. Lomas Rishi was never finished. Its walls are polished, but the vault of its inner chamber was left incomplete, apparently after problems with a rock slide, and lumps of unworked rock still sit on its floor. That frozen moment shows the order of work: rough out the room, dress it to shape, then polish, one surface at a time. A machine cutting the room in one pass would leave nothing of the kind. The acoustic effect is real and delightful. Hard, smooth, parallel walls reflect sound with little loss, so a voice rings for a long time. E. M. Forster, who visited, turned the caves into the 'Marabar Caves' of his 1924 novel A Passage to India, where the echo turns every sound into a h

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 04 Pillars that look machined
chunks.text: Jump forward almost fourteen centuries and about 1,600 km southwest, to the Hoysala kingdom of southern Karnataka. In 1117 CE King Vishnuvardhana's court began the Chennakeshava temple at Belur; from about 1121 his officer Ketamalla sponsored the Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu, the royal capital, where work continued for decades. In 2023 UNESCO listed these temples and a third at Somanathapura as the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. Inside the halls stand rows of round pillars that stop people in their tracks. Their shafts swell into bells and cushions, pinch into rings, and gleam as if lacquered. Some have star-shaped cross-sections with 16, 32 or even 64 points, according to the Dutch scholar Gerard Foekema. No two are quite alike. Online, a popular video from the channel of Praveen Mohan asked whether the Hoysaleswara temple was 'built with ancient machining technology', and similar claims circulate widely: the pillars are said to be too circular, too smooth and too repetitive for hand work. Here is the twist: the historians agree they were turned. K. A. Nilakanta Sastri in 1955, Foekema in 1996 and Suryanath Kamath in 2001 all describe the Hoysala pillars as 'lathe-turned'. The disagreement is not about whether a machine was involved but about what kind. A lathe is simply a device that spins a workpiece while a cutting tool is held against it. It needs no electricity.

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 05 How to turn a stone pillar
chunks.text: The Hoysala builders chose their stone cleverly. Their temples are carved from chloritic schist, a fine-grained greenish-grey rock often called soapstone. It is much softer than granite when fresh, which is why Hoysala sculpture can be so deeply undercut, with jewellery and fingers standing free of the background. Guides often add that the stone hardens on exposure to air; that is repeated widely but we found little testing of it. Step 1 of 6. Rough out: quarry a block of soft chloritic schist and chip it roughly round with chisels. Rough out: quarry a block of soft chloritic schist and chip it roughly round with chisels. Mount: fix iron pivots in the ends and hang the blank horizontally in a strong timber frame. Spin: a rope wrapped round the shaft is pulled in turn, so the stone turns one way, then back. Cut: a hard iron tool on a rest shaves rings and bells; a cut-out template checks the profile. Polish: fine sand, water and cloth applied while it turns give the glassy, light-catching finish. Erect: stand the shaft on its square base and crown it with brackets and carved figures. Six-step reconstruction. A worker chips a block of schist into a rough shaft. The shaft is hung horizontally between iron pivots in a timber frame. Two workers pull a rope wrapped around it so it spins one way then the other. A turner rests an iron tool on a wooden rest and cuts rings and bell shapes, checking them against a profile template. The shaft is polished with sand, water and cloth. Finally the finished pillar stands upright on a square base with a bracket on top. Picture, then, a strong timber frame with two iron pivots. A roughly rounded shaft of schist is hung between them. Hand-powered lathes of this general kind, where a rope or strap wrapped around the work is pulled one way a

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 06 Manuals, masters and signatures
chunks.text: Precision in Indian temple building did not depend on machines. It depended on systems. Sanskrit treatises on architecture and sculpture, such as the Mayamata and the Manasara, set out proportional rules: a building or an image is laid out in units, and every part is a fixed multiple of those units. Master builders, called sthapatis and sutradharas, carried these rules in memory and in practice, together with measuring cords, rods and templates. A pillar made to such a scheme will match its neighbours because they were drawn from the same rule, not because a computer controlled the cutter. The Hoysala craftsmen were proud of their work and often signed it. Names such as Mallitamma and Dasoja appear on sculptures at Belur and elsewhere, a small reminder that these 'impossible' objects were made by particular people with reputations to protect. Like Kailasa at Ellora or the rock-cut temples of Mamallapuram, the Hoysala temples belong to a long Indian tradition of astonishing stonework made by known methods.

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 07 How precise is 'precise'?
chunks.text: The heart of the viral claim is precision: the boxes and pillars are said to be accurate to the fraction of a millimetre, like modern machined parts. That is a testable claim, so we went looking for the test. We could not find a published laser scan, a metrology survey or even a set of careful hand measurements of the flatness of the Barabar walls or the roundness of the Hoysala pillars. Without numbers, 'perfect' means 'looks perfect in a photograph'. A horizontal logarithmic scale from 0.001 to 100 millimetres. Rows show a laboratory granite surface plate at a few micrometres, precision CNC machining at about 0.005 mm, the limit of the naked eye at about 0.1 mm, the ISO 2768 fine workshop tolerance of 0.2 mm, the Great Pyramid casing straightness of 0.25 mm and joints of 0.5 mm measured by Petrie, and Khufu's granite coffer about 7.6 mm out of square. A final dashed band for the Hoysala pillars and Barabar walls spans a wide range and is labelled unmeasured. For comparison, the best-measured ancient precision stonework is at Giza. In the 1880s Flinders Petrie measured the Great Pyramid's casing blocks and found their faces departed from a straight line by an average of about 0.25 mm over 1.9 m, with joints about 0.5 mm wide. He also found Khufu's granite coffer 'not finely wrought', its corners out of square by 13 minutes of arc, about 7.6 mm across 2 m. Those are superb results for hand work, and they are still hundreds of times coarser than a modern precision machine, which works to around 0.005 mm. The naked eye is a poor judge of this. At reading distance it can resolve about 0.1 mm; across a room, far less. So a pillar that is round to within a millimetre will look flawless, and a polished wall that bows by a few millimetres over several metres will look perfectl

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: 08 Verdicts, and what is still unknown
chunks.text: Put the claims side by side with the evidence and a clear picture emerges. The Barabar Caves are dated by the donors' own inscriptions, one of them was abandoned half-finished, and their famous polish appears on other hand-carved Mauryan works. The Hoysala pillars are almost certainly the product of hand-powered lathes turning a soft, cooperative stone. None of it needs lasers or lost machinery, and the idea that it does is best treated as busted. Unknown: the exact abrasives and burnishers used for Mauryan polish, and how long each wall took. Unknown: the design of the Hoysala lathes, and whether every round pillar was turned or some were carved by hand. Unknown: how precise any of these surfaces really are, because nobody has published measurements. Known: who paid for Barabar, roughly when, and that the work was done in stages by people with iron tools. That third unknown is an invitation. A few hours with a modern 3D scanner in Karan Chaupar or in the hall at Halebidu would settle the precision question for good, one way or the other. Whatever the numbers show, they will tell the story of craftspeople who knew their stone intimately and had the patience to make it sing.

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: debate
chunks.text: Were the Barabar caves made with lost machine technology? Yes: the geometry and polish are too perfect for hand tools. Viral posts describe the rooms as perfectly symmetrical, 'machined' boxes with mirror walls cut into some of the hardest rock there is. No: they show a hand process, dated by inscriptions. Ashoka's and Dasharatha's inscriptions date the caves; the unfinished Lomas Rishi cave has an uncompleted vault and lumps of rock left on its floor; the same Mauryan polish appears on hand-worked sandstone pillars and sculpture. The bold claim: The Barabar caves required machine tools or lost high technology. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established Nothing at Barabar requires more than iron tools, abrasives and a great deal of labour, and the unfinished cave shows the work stopped mid-process, which is exactly what hand work looks like. No measurement shows machine tolerances. The details of the polishing recipe are not documented, but 'we do not know the recipe' is very different from 'humans could not do it'.

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: debate
chunks.text: Were Hoysala pillars really turned on a lathe? Yes: they are circular, ringed and repeated in a way only turning produces. Historians from Sastri (1955) to Foekema (1996) and Kamath (2001) describe them as lathe-turned; their concentric rings and bell shapes suit a rotating workpiece in soft stone. Not established: they may have been carved by hand with templates. No Hoysala lathe or written description of one survives, and skilled carvers can produce round forms by hand with guides and templates. The bold claim: The shafts of the round Hoysala pillars were turned on large lathes. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The shapes and surface patterns fit turning well, hand-powered lathes were familiar in India, and chloritic schist is soft enough to turn with iron tools. But the argument rests on the look of the pillars, not on a surviving machine, text or tool-mark study, so it stays plausible rather than strong.

chunks.heading: India's 'impossible' stone boxes and pillars: debate
chunks.text: Are the pillars and boxes made to machine-shop tolerances? Yes: they look flawless, so they must be precise to a fraction of a millimetre. Videos compare pillar circles and cave corners to modern machined parts and describe them as perfect. Unknown: nobody has measured them. We found no published laser scan or metrology of the pillars or the Barabar walls. The eye can only judge to about 0.1 mm at close range and much less across a room. The bold claim: Indian 'stone boxes' and pillars match modern machining tolerances. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established A tolerance is a number, and no number has been published. Until someone scans the objects, claims of machine-level precision rest on photographs and impressions. The best-measured ancient comparison, Petrie's survey of Giza, found fine but clearly hand-made accuracy, which is what we should expect here too.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves
chunks.text: Gornaya Shoria, Siberia and Sablino, near St Petersburg Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves 9 min deep dive · 2 drawings Mystery. The quick read 1,570 m height of Mount Mustag, a granite peak in Gornaya Shoria Russian Wikipedia, Gornaya Shoria over 25 km length of the Mustag granite massif Russian Wikipedia, Gornaya Shoria often 3 sets of joints at roughly right angles, typical in granite Pollard and Aydin 1988 c. 6,500 m of hand-dug passages in Sablino's longest sand-mine cave Kovalyov 2017 c. 0.1 mm thickness of the polished slip zone on a fault Siman-Tov et al. 2013 down to 0.01 µm size of the smallest grains that make a fault mirror Siman-Tov et al. 2013 1,570 m, part of a granite massif over 25 km long Mount Mustag, Gornaya Shoria from expeditions in 2013, worldwide in 2014 Viral 'megalith' photos sand mines dug from the early 1800s to the mid 1900s Sablino caves c. 6,500 m (Levoberezhnaya) Longest Sablino cave c. 0.1 mm thick Slip zone on a polished fault c. 0.01–1 µm Grain size on a fault mirror Nobody built the Shoria blocks: they were split by nature. Granite crystallises from magma kilometres underground. As it cools and is squeezed by tectonic forces, it cracks in sets of nearly flat, parallel fractures called joints, often in three directions at roughly right angles. When uplift and erosion bring the granite to the surface, the release of weight opens more cracks parallel to the ground. Frost, water and roots then widen the joints until the rock stands as stacks of straight-sided blocks, known as tors, with rubble fields below. Flat, shiny cave and mine walls have two usual origins: people digging along easy layers, as in the Sablino sand mines near St Petersburg, or natural fault surfaces, called slickensides, polished when blocks of rock ground past each other. The myth A Siberian mountain hides a colossal wall of cut granite blocks, some said to weigh thousands of tonnes, built by a lost civilisation; smooth, flat-walled Russian caves were cut by advanced machines. The reality The Shoria 'megaliths' match natural granite jointing and weathering seen on mountains worldwide, and no tool marks, quarries or archaeology accompany them. The best-known flat-walled caves near St Petersburg are documented 19th and 20th century sand mines. Mirror-smooth natural rock faces are slickensides, polished by fault movement; geologists have measured how they form down to the scale of nanometres. Flip it Wow A fault surface can be polished to a mirror by an earthquake: grinding crushes grains to less than a thousandth of a millimetre, finer than a wavel

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 01 The mountain that looks built
chunks.text: The photographs are genuinely startling. On a forested ridge in southern Siberia, huge grey blocks of granite stand in rows, their faces flat, their edges straight, their corners close to right angles. Some sit on top of others like courses of a wall. A person standing beside them comes up to the knee of the lowest block. It is very easy to look at these pictures and think: someone cut and stacked these. That is exactly what happened in 2013 and 2014, when images from the mountains of Gornaya Shoria, also called Mount Shoria, in Kemerovo Oblast began to spread across the internet as 'the Siberian megaliths'. Around the same time, a second family of images took off: long, flat-roofed passages and glassy, smooth rock walls inside Russian caves and hills, offered as proof of ancient tunnelling machines. The site owner's shorthand for all this, 'Russian mountain geological anomalies: seemingly smooth-cut rocks inside deep caves', captures both. Nature is a surprisingly good stonemason. The trick is knowing what her tool marks look like. This deep dive takes both sets of claims seriously, tests them against geology and history, and gives a verdict on each. Spoiler: the rocks are real and remarkable, and the most likely explanations are natural or industrial rather than ancient. But the way they got that way is a better story than any lost civilisation.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 02 What the claims actually say
chunks.text: It helps to be precise about what we are testing, because the viral versions are often vague about places. After searching, we matched the phrase to three things. The Gornaya Shoria 'megaliths': photographs from expeditions in 2013 associated with the Russian writer Georgy Sidorov, showing giant blocks on granite peaks, especially around Mount Mustag near the ski village of Sheregesh. Posts described blocks with flat surfaces, straight corners and sharp edges, some claimed to weigh thousands of tonnes, and some compared the stacks to the polygonal stone walls of Peru. Flat-walled 'ancient tunnels': images of long, square-edged passages with level ceilings, many of which trace to the Sablino caves and similar workings south of St Petersburg. Mirror-smooth walls inside caves and mines: glossy, flat rock faces, sometimes finely scratched, presented as evidence of cutting and polishing. We could not trace every image to a single site, and some circulate with no location at all. We also could not verify the tonnages quoted for the Shoria blocks; they appear to be estimates from photographs. Where a claim is specific enough to test, we test it. Where it is not, we say so.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 03 A granite mountain in Siberia
chunks.text: Gornaya Shoria is a mountainous, heavily forested region in the south of Kemerovo Oblast, where the ranges of the Altai, the Kuznetsk Alatau and the Salair ridge meet. Its peaks rise to about 1,630 m. Mount Mustag, at 1,570 m, is the heart of a large granite massif that runs for more than 25 km from southwest to northeast. Russian reference works describe how weathering has shaped its summits into forms that look like camel humps and the towers of medieval castles. That description matters. Long before anyone called them megaliths, the blocky crags of Mustag were known as a natural landscape of weathered granite. Mountains like this exist across Siberia and around the world, and geologists have been explaining them for well over a century. The explanation starts deep underground. Gornaya Shoria is also a place of long, snowy winters, taiga forest and steep, rocky summits above the tree line, which is exactly the setting in which frost shatters exposed rock most effectively. The same summits are visited by hikers and skiers, which is partly why the photographs exist at all.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 04 How granite breaks into bricks
chunks.text: Granite forms when a large body of molten rock, a magma, cools and crystallises slowly, kilometres below the surface. As it cools, it contracts. Later it is squeezed and stretched by the movements of the Earth's crust. Rock is strong in compression but weak in tension, so it cracks. The cracks are not random: they form in families of roughly parallel, roughly flat fractures called joints, and in granite there are often three families at close to right angles to one another. Step 1 of 5. Deep and hot: a body of granite magma cools slowly under kilometres of older rock. Deep and hot: a body of granite magma cools slowly under kilometres of older rock. Cracking: shrinking as it cools and squeezed by tectonic forces, the granite cracks in sets of joints, often at roughly right angles. Unloading: uplift and erosion strip away the cover; relieved of weight, sheet joints open parallel to the surface. Weathering: water freezes and thaws in the joints, roots pry, and the cracks slowly widen. Blocks: loose rock is carried off, leaving straight-sided blocks stacked like masonry, a tor, with fallen blocks below. Five-step schematic cross-section. Step 1: a body of granite magma cools under kilometres of older rock. Step 2: vertical joints crack the granite, and an inset cube shows three joint sets at roughly right angles. Step 3: uplift and erosion remove the cover, and curved sheet joints open parallel to the surface. Step 4: frost, water and roots widen the cracks near the surface. Step 5: loose rock has been removed, leaving a tor of straight-sided blocks stacked like masonry, with fallen blocks on the slopes and a tiny person for scale. When uplift and erosion eventually strip away the kilometres of rock above, the granite is relieved of an enormous weight. It expands slightly

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 05 Testing the 'megalith' idea
chunks.text: How could we tell a natural tor from a ruined wall? Archaeologists and geologists would ask a few simple questions. Are the blocks still attached to bedrock, or were they moved? Are there tool marks, drill holes or wedge sockets? Is there mortar, or blocks deliberately shaped to fit their neighbours? Is there a quarry nearby, with waste flakes and abandoned pieces? Are there artefacts, hearths or burials that can be dated? For the Shoria blocks, the answers available in the public record are all negative or unknown. We found no published report of tool marks, quarries, fitted joints, mortar or datable artefacts, and no peer-reviewed study of the outcrops at all. Meanwhile, everything that is visible in the photographs, the flat faces, square corners, stacked 'courses' and toppled blocks, is exactly what jointed granite produces. In jointed granite anywhere, it is common to find blocks that have split but not yet moved apart, the natural process caught halfway. The weight claims deserve a quick sanity check too. Granite weighs about 2.6–2.7 tonnes per cubic metre. A block 20 m long, 6 m high and 6 m deep would weigh around 1,900 tonnes. That sounds like an argument for giant machines until you remember that the block did not need to be lifted: jointed blocks are usually where they formed, and gravity alone moves the ones that fall. A natural block does not need to be lifted into place. It was always there; the rock around it left.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 06 Why our eyes see walls
chunks.text: There is a reason these photos fool so many people, and it is not gullibility. Human brains are tuned to spot straight lines and right angles, because in everyday life those features almost always mean people made something. Buildings, furniture and roads are rectangular; trees, clouds and hills are not. So when nature produces a right angle, we notice, and we reach for a builder. Photographs make it harder. Without a familiar object in the frame, scale collapses: a two-metre block and a twenty-metre block can look identical. Moss and lichen soften the rough fracture textures that would give the game away, and a wide-angle lens exaggerates the straightness of nearby edges. Choosing the most wall-like angle, and leaving out the chaotic jumble a few metres to the side, finishes the illusion. The same thing has happened elsewhere. In Rockwall, Texas, buried sandstone dikes, sheets of sand that filled ancient cracks and hardened, were long claimed to be a buried man-made wall; geologists explain them as natural. The basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland are so regular that legend credited them to a giant. Off Yonaguni in Japan, stepped underwater sandstone terraces are still argued over, although most geologists read them as natural jointing. Russia's Shoria blocks belong to a large, worldwide family of rocks that look built.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 07 Caves with flat ceilings
chunks.text: The second set of images shows passages with level ceilings and square-cut walls, sometimes stretching into the dark for hundreds of metres. Many of the most photogenic come from the Sablino caves, on the Tosna and Sablinka rivers south of St Petersburg, now a popular nature park. They are not ancient. They were dug by miners. From the early 1800s to the middle of the 20th century, the region's pale, soft quartz sandstone was mined for glass-making. A 2017 survey of bat roosts in the Leningrad region's artificial caves lists the Sablino group among them and gives the longest, Levoberezhnaya, a length of about 6,500 m. Miners dug the soft sand with hand tools and left the firmer layer above as a natural roof, which is why the ceilings are so often flat. Elsewhere in the region, similar galleries were cut to quarry good building limestone. Russia also has spectacular natural caves, such as the Kungur Ice Cave in the Urals, surveyed by the cartographer Semyon Remezov in 1703 and open to visitors since 1914. Caves dissolved in layered, soluble rock often have flat ceilings too, because the water follows bedding planes, the natural boundaries between layers. Flatness in a cave, in other words, has at least two ordinary causes: miners following a layer, or water following one.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 08 Mirror walls: rock polished by earthquakes
chunks.text: The most beautiful 'impossible' surfaces are the glossy ones: rock faces so smooth they reflect a torch beam, marked with fine parallel scratches. These are slickensides, and they are one of the classic sights of structural geology. A slickenside forms on a fault, where two blocks of rock grind past each other, either in sudden earthquake slips or in slow creep. The scratches, called slickenlines, run parallel to the direction of movement. Panel 1 shows a large tilted rock face with a glossy band and many parallel grooves, called slickenlines, running in the direction of slip marked by an arrow; a 1.7 metre person stands beside it. Panel 2 is a section in which two blocks of rock move past each other along an inclined fault plane, one up and one down. Panel 3 magnifies the contact: coarse rock grains on both sides and between them a thin slip zone about 0.1 millimetres thick filled with tiny grains, with a 0.2 millimetre scale bar. Why do they shine? In 2013 Shalev Siman-Tov and colleagues examined naturally polished 'fault mirrors' under electron microscopes. They found that the shiny layer is only about a tenth of a millimetre thick and made of grains crushed down to nanometre sizes, from about 0.01 to 1 micrometre. Grains that small are finer than the wavelength of visible light, so the surface behaves optically like a polished one. The same year, James Kirkpatrick and colleagues showed that some fault mirrors formed from a silica gel produced during slip, which later hardened into a glassy film. Fault surfaces are often exposed in mines, quarries and caves, because water and miners both tend to follow weaknesses in the rock, and a fault is a ready-made weakness. When a cave passage runs along a fault plane, one wall may be a slickenside: dead flat, glossy and stripe

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 09 A field guide: nature, miners or masons?
chunks.text: Next time a 'cut stone' photo crosses your screen, a few questions will usually sort it out. Do the flat faces continue into the solid rock around them? Then they are probably joints, not cut blocks. Are the scratches parallel, long and all in one direction on a glossy face? That points to a slickenside, not a tool. Do the cuts show short, repeated strokes, drill holes or wedge sockets? That points to human work, and usually a date can be found. Is there a record of mining or quarrying nearby? In Russia, many 'ancient tunnels' have well-documented industrial histories. Are there artefacts, foundations or quarry waste? Their absence does not rule out people, but their presence would be the real evidence. None of this takes away from the wonder. A granite mountain that splits itself into giant bricks, and an earthquake that polishes a cave wall to a mirror, are marvels in their own right, and they have far more to teach than a story about builders who left no trace.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: 10 Verdicts, and what is still open
chunks.text: The Sablino tunnels are documented sand mines: that claim is busted. Mirror-smooth rock faces have a well-measured natural explanation in fault slip: also busted as evidence of machines. The Shoria 'megaliths' are the most interesting case. Everything we can see fits natural jointing and weathering of a known granite massif, and nothing specific to human building has been reported, so the man-made idea has no receipts. But we should be honest that no geologist appears to have published a detailed study of these particular outcrops. That is a gap worth filling, and it would not be hard. A field survey measuring the orientations of the block faces, looking for fracture markings and tool marks, and dating the exposure of the surfaces could settle the question and would make a fine student project. Until then, the most reasonable reading is the one the mountain itself suggests: these are granite blocks made by cooling, cracking and cold, on a timescale that makes any human wall look very young indeed.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: debate
chunks.text: Are the Gornaya Shoria 'megaliths' man-made? Yes: the blocks are too large, flat and square to be natural. Photos from 2013 expeditions associated with the Russian writer Georgy Sidorov show huge granite blocks with straight edges and flat faces stacked in wall-like rows; posts claimed some weighed thousands of tonnes. No: they are jointed granite outcrops, like tors on mountains worldwide. Mount Mustag is part of a large granite massif known for castle-like weathering forms. Granite commonly splits along three sets of joints at near right angles, producing exactly such blocks; no tool marks, quarries, ramps or datable artefacts have been reported. The bold claim: The Shoria blocks are the remains of a giant wall built by a lost civilisation. Weight of evidence Awaiting discovery Ruled out Established Everything visible in the photos has a well-understood natural explanation, and nothing specific to human building, such as tool marks, mortar, quarries or settlements, has been documented. We found no peer-reviewed study of these particular outcrops, so the natural explanation rests on general geology rather than a site survey, but the burden of evidence lies with the extraordinary c

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: debate
chunks.text: Were Russia's smooth-walled 'ancient tunnels' cut by lost technology? Yes: the flat ceilings and straight walls look machined. Photos of long, square-edged passages with flat roofs circulate as evidence of ancient tunnelling machines. No: the best-known examples are recent mines. Caves in the Leningrad region, including the Sablino group, were dug for quartz sand for glass-making from the early 1800s to the mid 1900s (Kovalyov 2017); flat roofs follow the firmer rock above the sand. The bold claim: Flat-walled caves near St Petersburg are ancient high-tech tunnels. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established These passages are documented industrial workings, well within living memory of the region's history, and are now even studied as bat roosts. Their shapes are exactly what miners create when they dig soft sand beneath a firmer layer. Unless a specific image can be traced to somewhere else, this claim fails.

chunks.heading: Russia's 'cut stone' mountains and caves: debate
chunks.text: Can nature make a mirror-smooth rock face? No: only cutting and polishing make a rock shine. Glossy, flat faces inside caves and mines are presented as proof of tools or machines. Yes: fault movement polishes rock. Slickensides form when rocks grind past each other; laboratory and field studies show slip zones about 0.1 mm thick made of nanometre-sized grains that reflect light like a mirror (Siman-Tov et al. 2013; Kirkpatrick et al. 2013). The bold claim: A mirror-smooth rock face in a cave must have been cut and polished by people. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established Natural fault mirrors are well documented and their physics has been measured, including the grain sizes that cause the shine. Their scratches, called slickenlines, run parallel to the direction of slip, a tell-tale sign that distinguishes them from tool marks. Some shiny surfaces in mines are human-made, but shine alone says nothing about who, or what, made it.

chunks.heading: Hinduism
chunks.text: South Asia Hinduism A family of traditions with no single founder, carrying hymns memorised syllable by syllable for over three thousand years, beside epics and Puranas that kept growing. from the 2nd millennium BCE. How the tradition sees its text The Vedas are eternal and authorless, 'heard' by the rishis. Their power lies in exact sound, so every syllable and pitch accent must be kept. Teacher-to-pupil recitation, checked through several patterns, is the true text; a manuscript is at best an aid to memory. On this view the Rigveda heard today is the Rigveda of the seers. What manuscript scholarship shows Scholars agree that the oral safeguards worked remarkably well: the surviving recension is internally consistent and regional lineages agree closely. The text was fixed in the 1st millennium BCE with a few pronunciation updates. There are no written witnesses from antiquity, so fidelity before the padapatha stage is inferred from metre and comparison with Avestan, not checked against copies.

chunks.heading: Hinduism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The Vedas are shruti: eternal truths 'heard' by the rishis rather than composed by people. Matter of faith Central to Vedic orthodoxy; the Mimamsa school argued that the Vedas have no author at all. This is a matter of faith. Historians ask a different question: when, where and by whom the hymns were first recited. Mimamsa Sutra; Flood 1996 Brahman, the one reality, is known by many names. Matter of faith Already voiced in the Rigveda ('To what is One, sages give many a title') and developed in the Upanishads. A theological claim, not rated. Rigveda 1.164.46, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896) The self is reborn through many lives according to karma until liberation. Matter of faith First set out clearly in the oldest Upanishads and shared, in different forms, with Buddhism and Jainism. A matter of faith. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4; Chandogya Upanishad 5.10 (trans. Olivelle 1998) Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, taught the Bhagavad Gita to Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Matter of faith The divine identity of Krishna is a matter of faith. The Gita as a text is historical: it forms chapters 23–40 of the Bhishma Parvan of the Mahabharata and is usually dated to the last centuries BCE or the first centuries CE. Mahabharata 6.23–40; BORI UNESCO nomination 2024 The Rigveda was composed in north-western South Asia in the second half of the 2nd millennium BCE. Strong evidence Its rivers are those of the Punjab and its language is closely related to the Avestan of Iran. A treaty between the Hittites and the Mitanni kingdom (c. 1380 BCE) invokes Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas, a close Vedic parallel. Most scholars place the core at c. 1500–1200 BCE. Witzel 1995; Jamison and Brereton 2014 The Vedic hymns have been handed down orally with extraordinary accuracy. Strong evidence Several recitation modes check each other word by word, and lineages far apart in India recite essentially the same text, including its pitch accents. UNESCO proclaimed Vedic chanting a masterpiece of intangible heritage in 2003 and inscribed it in 2008. UNESCO ICH 00062; Staal 1986 The Mahabharata remembers a real war among the Kuru clans at Kurukshetra. Open question The Kuru realm of the late Vedic period is well attested, and its region matches Painted Grey Ware sites. A specific great battle has left no identified archaeological trace, and the epic's scale reflects centuries of retelling. Witzel 1995; Lal 1954–55 The Kurukshetra war took place in 3102 BCE, at the start o

chunks.heading: Hinduism: 01 A library kept in the voice
chunks.text: Picture a boy of eight in a Kerala courtyard or a Maharashtra pathashala, sitting cross-legged before his teacher, repeating a line until every syllable and every rise and fall of pitch is exact. He will spend years doing this. What he is learning was composed, by the best estimates of historians, well over three thousand years ago, before iron was common in India and long before anyone wrote it down. The Rigveda is one of the oldest religious texts still in daily use anywhere, and for most of its life it was never a book at all. Hinduism is not a single religion with a founder, a founding date and one scripture. It is a vast family of traditions, schools and devotional paths that share a sacred history and recognise the Vedas as a source of authority, even when they rarely read them. That breadth makes its textual record unusually varied. Some of its texts were guarded with a precision that has impressed every scholar who studied them. Others were meant to grow, and did. For most of its life the Rigveda was never a book at all. It lived in trained memory, checked syllable by syllable.

chunks.heading: Hinduism: 02 How the tradition understands its own texts
chunks.text: Hindu tradition divides its scriptures into two kinds. Shruti, 'what was heard', means the Vedas: the four Samhitas of hymns and formulas, with their Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads. They are held to be eternal, perceived by the rishis rather than invented, and for the Mimamsa school they have no author at all, human or divine. Smriti, 'what is remembered', covers the epics, the Puranas, the law books and much else. Smriti texts are revered and often more widely loved, above all the Bhagavad Gita, but they are understood as human compositions in the service of eternal truth. This distinction shapes how each kind of text was kept. Because the power of a Vedic hymn lies in its exact sound, changing a syllable was a serious fault. The epics and Puranas, by contrast, were stories to be told to new audiences, and the tradition accepted that tellers would expand and adapt them. Both attitudes are visible in the manuscripts historians study today. They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, and he is heavenly nobly-winged Garutman. To what is One, sages give many a title they call it Agni, Yama, Matarisvan.

chunks.heading: Hinduism: 03 How the hymns survived
chunks.text: The Vedic reciters built an error-checking system long before anyone thought of the phrase. The continuous text, the samhitapatha, runs words together according to the sound rules of Sanskrit. The padapatha separates every word in its basic form. The kramapatha recites overlapping pairs: word one and two, two and three, three and four. The jata and ghana patterns weave the words forwards and backwards in longer knots. A pupil who has mastered all of them cannot easily slip a word, because each pattern exposes errors in the others. UNESCO proclaimed this tradition of Vedic chanting a masterpiece of humanity's intangible heritage in 2003 and inscribed it in 2008, noting that only a small number of the old recitation branches still survive. Did it work? The strongest evidence is internal. Only one recension of the Rigveda, the Shakala, survives complete, and lineages separated by a thousand miles recite it with remarkable agreement, including accents that had stopped mattering in ordinary speech many centuries earlier. Metrical study shows a few small modernisations of pronunciation crept in before the text was frozen, which is itself a sign that later reciters did not rewrite the hymns wholesale. Writing came very late. The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune holds 30 Rigveda manuscripts, one on birch bark in Sharada script; the oldest dated one was copied in 1464 CE, and the collection joined UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2007. The oldest known Vedic manuscripts of any kind, copies of the White Yajurveda from Nepal and western Tibet, date to about 1150 CE. So for the Rigveda the gap between composition and the oldest written copy is well over two thousand years, and the case for its accuracy rests on the oral system, not on old parchment.

chunks.heading: Hinduism: 04 Epics and Puranas: texts that kept growing
chunks.text: The Mahabharata is a different kind of survivor. It calls itself the story of the Bharatas, and it also tells us it once existed in a shorter form of 24,000 verses; the version most Indians know runs to about four times that. Between 1919 and 1966 scholars at the same Pune institute compared manuscripts from Kashmir to Kerala in order to separate what almost every tradition shares from what only some regions added. The result, the critical edition, is one of the great achievements of textual scholarship. It is also, as its critics note, a reconstruction of a text that may never have existed in a single fixed form. The physical record is thin for the early centuries. A Central Asian manuscript in Berlin, the Spitzer manuscript from the early centuries CE, lists the epic's books, and land grants on copper plates from the 5th and early 6th centuries quote its verses. The oldest actual copy used for the critical edition is from the mid-16th century, and a Kashmiri manuscript of the Bhagavad Gita in Pune is dated to about 1376 CE. As a recent study of India's oldest manuscripts put it, on Indian soil outside the Himalayas nothing survives before the 11th century: heat, damp and insects destroyed palm leaf and birch bark, and texts survived by being recopied. The Puranas show the same pattern more sharply. A palm-leaf Skandapurana copied in Nepal around 810 CE is one of the oldest dated Sanskrit religious manuscripts anywhere. When scholars edited it, they found it was largely a different work from the enormous 'Skanda Purana' printed in modern India, which grew by adding whole sections over the centuries. Nothing in the tradition hides this: the Puranas were meant to be retold.

chunks.heading: Hinduism: 05 History inside the stories
chunks.text: Taken as witnesses to the past, these texts preserve a surprising amount. The Rigveda's rivers are those of the Punjab, and its gods Mitra, Varuna and Indra appear in a treaty between the Hittites and the kingdom of Mitanni in northern Syria around 1380 BCE, the kind of external anchor ancient texts rarely get. The later Vedic texts describe a Kuru kingdom around Kurukshetra, the stage of the Mahabharata, and archaeology finds a matching spread of Painted Grey Ware villages in that region in the early 1st millennium BCE. At Hastinapur, B. B. Lal found that the Painted Grey Ware town ended with a severe Ganges flood, which fits the Puranic report that the Kuru capital was moved to Kaushambi after the river swept Hastinapura away. Other memories are harder to test. Many Harappan sites cluster along the dry Ghaggar-Hakra valley, which many identify with the Sarasvati, 'best of rivers' in the Rigveda. Sediment dating has complicated the picture: the Sutlej, the glacier-fed river that once filled this valley, moved away about 8,000 years ago, so the Harappan towns grew beside a former channel fed by monsoon streams. The river may still be the Sarasvati of memory, perhaps remembered as greater than it was when the hymns were composed. Whether the Indus civilisation contributed yogic postures, a proto-Shiva or ritual bathing to later Hinduism is debated, and it cannot be settled until its script is read. Where the texts can be tested against the ground, they often point in the right direction, even when the scale has grown in the telling.

chunks.heading: Hinduism: 06 What is still open
chunks.text: The dating of the Kurukshetra war is the best-known open question. Tradition, following the astronomer Aryabhata, puts it at 3102 BCE, and an inscription of Pulakeshin II in 634 CE implies a similar date. No archaeological layer of that age has yet been tied to the epic, and the kingdoms it describes fit the Iron Age. That is not a verdict on the story's heart, which may preserve memories of real rivalries among Kuru clans. The drowned Dwarka off Gujarat is a similar case: divers have found anchors and stone blocks, and a Late Harappan settlement on Bet Dwarka, but not yet a city of Krishna's age. Ancient DNA has reopened an old argument about where the Vedic language came from. Most geneticists read the data as showing steppe-related migrants entering South Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE, a time that fits the Rigveda's age; others in India argue for a homeland within the subcontinent. The strongest point of the tradition's own account is not in doubt: whatever its ultimate origins, the Rigveda has been carried across more than three millennia with a care that few human records can match. He, the first origin of this creation, whether he formed it all or did not form it, Whose eye controls this world in highest heaven, he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not.

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism
chunks.text: Eastern Iran Zoroastrianism One of the oldest living faiths, whose hymns were carried by memory for perhaps two thousand years before anyone wrote them down. c. 1500–500 BCE (date debated). How the tradition sees its text Zoroastrians hold that the Gathas are Zarathustra's own words, received from Ahura Mazda and guarded without change by a hereditary priesthood that recited them daily. Much of the wider Avesta was lost through the invasions of Alexander and the Arabs, but the core liturgy, and above all the Gathas, survived because it was always in the priests' mouths. What manuscript scholarship shows Philologists largely agree that the Gathas are remarkably well preserved in sound and wording: their metre and archaic grammar survive, which would be unlikely after heavy editing. But the written record begins very late, the Sasanian archetype is lost, and the earliest complete copies are 14th century. Interpretation of the Gathas themselves is difficult and translations differ widely.

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Ahura Mazda is the one uncreated, wise creator of all good things. Matter of faith The central teaching of the Gathas and of all later Zoroastrian theology. It is a statement about God, so it is not rated here. Gathas, e.g. Yasna 44; Boyce 1979 Zarathustra received revelation from Ahura Mazda and composed the Gathas. Matter of faith The revelation itself is a matter of faith. That the Gathas come from a single early poet is a separate historical question: most philologists accept a single composer, while a minority (notably Jean Kellens) treats Zarathustra as a figure the texts construct. Yasna 28–34, 43–51, 53; Skjærvø 2011 Zarathustra was a real person who lived in eastern Iran long before the Persian Empire. Plausible No inscription or object names him. The case rests on the Gathas' archaic language and their picture of a small pastoral society. Dates range from c. 1500 to c. 500 BCE; the traditional '258 years before Alexander' is widely judged too late. Boyce 1979; Stausberg and Vevaina 2015 The world is a battlefield between good and evil, and each person chooses a side. Matter of faith A moral and theological teaching. Yasna 30 describes two primal spirits and the choice between them, and later texts build a whole cosmic history on it. As a claim about the spiritual order of the world, it is not rated. Yasna 30.3–5 At death the soul crosses the Chinvat Bridge and is judged by its deeds. Matter of faith A teaching about the afterlife, first hinted at in the Gathas and developed in Young Avestan and Pahlavi texts, where the soul meets its own conscience at the bridge. It concerns the unseen world, so it is not rated. Yasna 46.10–11; Arda Viraz Namag The Persian kings of the Achaemenid dynasty worshipped Ahura Mazda. Established Darius I names Auramazda repeatedly at Behistun (c. 520 BCE) and later kings continue to do so. Whether these kings were Zoroastrian in the full sense is a separate, debated question, because Zarathustra is never named in royal inscriptions. Schmitt 1991; Kent 1953 The Avesta was once far larger, and much of it was lost through conquest. Strong evidence The 9th–10th century Denkard summarises a 21-part Sasanian Avesta; only about a quarter of the passages it cites survive. Loss after the 7th-century Arab conquest is well supported; blaming Alexander for the loss is a later Persian tradition. Denkard 8; Kellens, Encyclopaedia Iranica Parsi Zoroastrians descend from refugees who sailed from Iran to Gujarat. Strong evidence T

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism: 01 A faith older than its books
chunks.text: Imagine a hymn that is sung every day for two thousand years before anyone writes it down. That is the story Zoroastrian priests tell about the Gathas, seventeen short poems attributed to the prophet Zarathustra (Zoroaster to the Greeks). They were composed in Old Avestan, a language so archaic that it sits beside the Sanskrit of the Rigveda like a sibling. They were memorised, recited in ritual, and passed from priest to priest across empires, conquests and migrations. Zoroastrianism is today one of the smallest world religions, with about 110,000 to 125,000 followers according to a 2012 FEZANA survey, most of them Parsis in India and Zoroastrians in Iran and the diaspora. Yet it once shaped the court religion of three Persian empires, and its ideas about a final judgement, a bridge the soul must cross and the renewal of the world have echoes far beyond Iran. Whether those echoes are inheritance or coincidence is one of the great open questions of religious history. This page follows the site's rule for every tradition: first the faith in its own words, then the historical record. Claims about Ahura Mazda, revelation and the afterlife are matters of faith and are not rated. Claims about people, places, dates and manuscripts are rated on the evidence, and the texts are scored only on how much of them survives and how close the surviving copies stand to the original, never on whether they are true. The Gathas are the rare case where memory, not parchment, carried a text across two thousand years.

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism: 02 When did Zarathustra live?
chunks.text: No inscription, seal or grave names Zarathustra. Everything we know comes from the Gathas themselves and from much later tradition. That leaves a remarkable spread of dates. Greek writers such as Xanthus and Eudoxus placed him 6,000 years before Xerxes, which most scholars now read as a misunderstanding of Zoroastrian world-ages. Medieval Zoroastrian tradition put him '258 years before Alexander', around the 6th century BCE, which fits the Persian kings but not the language of the hymns. The philologists' argument runs the other way. Old Avestan is so close to Vedic Sanskrit that the two cannot have separated long before the Gathas were composed. The hymns speak of cattle, pastures and raiding, with no cities, no kings of the Persian kind and no iron. Mary Boyce argued for a date between about 1700 and 1000 BCE; most scholars today place the Gathas between about 1500 and 900 BCE, with a minority holding out for later. The honest summary is a range of several centuries, and the place is just as uncertain: Bactria, Chorasmia, Sistan and the Central Asian steppe all have supporters. Dating by language works like dating by accent. Old Avestan and Vedic Sanskrit share sounds, grammar and even whole poetic phrases. Since the Rigveda is usually dated c. 1500–1100 BCE, and the Gathas are at a similar stage of development, most linguists place them in the same broad era. The method gives a window of centuries, never a year, and it is open to challenge if the Rigveda's own dates move.

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism: 03 The Wise Lord on a Persian cliff
chunks.text: The first time the Wise Lord appears in a text we can date to the year is on a cliff at Behistun in western Iran. Around 520 BCE Darius I had his victory over rivals carved in three languages beside a relief of himself and a winged figure. Again and again the text credits Ahuramazda for his throne. Saith Darius the King: By the favor of Ahuramazda I am King; Ahuramazda bestowed the kingdom upon me. So the Wise Lord was worshipped at the Persian court by the late 6th century BCE. But here the record turns puzzling. Darius never names Zarathustra, and later kings also honour Mithra and Anahita. Herodotus describes Persian Magi and fire rites but not a prophet. Some historians see Achaemenid religion as an early, royal form of Zoroastrianism; others see a related Iranian religion that shared the Wise Lord without the prophet's reform. Both readings fit the surviving evidence.

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism: 04 How the Avesta was written, and how it was lost
chunks.text: For most of its history, the Avesta existed only in memory. Priests learned the sounds precisely because a mispronounced prayer was thought to lose its power. When the Sasanian dynasty (224–651 CE) organised a state priesthood, someone designed a new alphabet, adapted from the Pahlavi script but with many extra vowel signs, to capture that exact pronunciation. The date is not recorded; scholars usually place it in the 5th or 6th century CE. The German scholars Karl Hoffmann and Johanna Narten showed that every surviving manuscript descends from one written Sasanian master copy, now lost. That master Avesta was huge. The Denkard, a 9th–10th century encyclopedia in Middle Persian, describes it in 21 books (nasks) covering liturgy, law, cosmology and legend. Only a fraction survives: roughly a quarter of the Avestan passages quoted by those medieval commentators can be found in the texts we have. The rest disappeared after the Arab conquest of Iran in the 7th century, as the community shrank, priests fled, and only texts in daily ritual use kept being copied. Zoroastrian tradition also blames Alexander, who burned Persepolis in 330 BCE. The burning is well attested. The idea that an Avesta written in gold on prepared ox hides perished there comes from books written over a thousand years later, and most historians doubt that a full written Avesta existed so early. Here the tradition may remember a real trauma, the fall of the Persian Empire, while placing the loss of the book too early. What survives is not the whole Avesta but the part the priests could never stop saying aloud.

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism: 05 The manuscripts that survive
chunks.text: The oldest dated Avestan manuscripts were copied in 1323 and 1324 CE by a single priest, Mihrabān Kay-Khosrow, working at Cambay in Gujarat. Two are copies of the Yasna with a Pahlavi translation, now in Oxford (J2) and Copenhagen (K5); two are copies of the Vendidad, in London (L4) and Copenhagen (K1). Their colophons give the dates and the scribe's name. An older fragment, from Dunhuang in western China around 800 CE or later, preserves a single Avestan prayer written in the Sogdian script, a reminder of how far Iranian religion travelled along the Silk Road. More than 300 Avestan manuscripts are now known, divided into an Indian branch, copied by Parsi priests, and an Iranian branch. Karl Friedrich Geldner used about 133 of them for his edition (1886–96), still the standard text. New projects, such as the Avestan Digital Archive and the Corpus Avesticum, are photographing hundreds of manuscripts and rethinking Geldner's choices, especially by paying attention to how the texts were actually used in ritual. Strength of the record: the Gathas keep their metre and archaic grammar, which heavy editing would have destroyed. Weakness of the record: the written tradition begins about two thousand years after composition, and its archetype is lost. Loss: most of the Sasanian Avesta survives only as summaries in Pahlavi books.

chunks.heading: Zoroastrianism: 06 What remains open
chunks.text: Three questions remain genuinely unsettled. First, Zarathustra's date and homeland: a securely dated find naming him, or new linguistic anchors, would narrow a window that currently spans centuries. Second, the religion of the Achaemenid kings: more of the Persepolis Fortification Tablets, the Elamite administrative archive that records offerings to many gods including Ahura Mazda, are still being published. Third, the question of influence on the Abrahamic faiths, which depends on dating Zoroastrian ideas more precisely than the late manuscripts allow. What is not in doubt is the tenacity of the tradition. A small priesthood carried a hymn book in memory through the rise and fall of empires, then copied it by hand in exile. The Gathas may be the finest example on Earth of oral preservation checked, much later, by writing. For a site that treats religions as the oldest way of keeping account of history, the Avesta is a humbling witness: fragile on parchment, astonishingly durable in the mouth.

chunks.heading: Judaism
chunks.text: Land of Israel Judaism One of the oldest living scriptural traditions, whose Hebrew texts can be checked against scrolls copied more than two thousand years ago. from c. 1200 BCE. How the tradition sees its text In Jewish tradition the Torah was given by God to Moses letter by letter, and scribes have guarded it with strict rules: a Torah scroll with a single wrong letter may not be read in public until corrected. The Prophets and Writings were written by prophets and sages under divine inspiration. Maimonides relied on the Aleppo Codex as the model for Torah scrolls. What manuscript scholarship shows Scholars read the Hebrew Bible as a library written, edited and collected over many centuries, from the Iron Age kingdoms to the 2nd century BCE. The Dead Sea Scrolls show that before the 1st century CE several text forms circulated together; one, the proto-Masoretic, became the standard. From then on the consonants were copied with striking care, as the agreement between Qumran, Masada and the medieval codices shows.

chunks.heading: Judaism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. God made an everlasting covenant with Abraham and his descendants. Matter of faith The founding promise of Jewish scripture: land, descendants and a relationship with God. It is a matter of faith; whether Abraham himself can be traced in the historical record is weighed separately below. Genesis 12:1–3; 15; 17 (NRSV) God gave the Torah to Moses at Mount Sinai. Matter of faith The heart of Jewish belief and practice. Rabbinic chronology places the giving of the Torah about 1313 BCE. Revelation is a matter of faith and is not rated here. Exodus 19–20; Seder Olam Rabbah An Oral Torah was given alongside the written Torah and handed down teacher to student. Matter of faith Historians can follow the written record of this teaching from the Mishnah (c. 200 CE) onward; the belief that it reaches back to Sinai is held in faith. Mishnah Avot 1:1 Moses wrote down the whole Torah in the late 2nd millennium BCE. Awaiting discovery No inscription, manuscript or linguistic layer of the Torah has been traced that early; the oldest Hebrew writing is about 10th century BCE. Most critical scholars see a composite text finalised by c. 400 BCE. Traditional scholars reply that later scribes may have updated spelling and language. Schmid 2012; Baden 2012; Talmud Bava Batra 14b–15a A people called Israel lived in Canaan by about 1200 BCE. Established The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) names Israel as a people in Canaan, and hundreds of small highland villages appear in the same age. Merneptah Stele, Egyptian Museum, Cairo; Dever 2003 Kings of the house of David ruled Judah from Jerusalem. Strong evidence The Tel Dan Stele (9th century BCE) names a "House of David" beside a king of Israel; Assyrian records name later Judean kings such as Hezekiah. How large David's own kingdom was remains debated. Biran and Naveh 1993, 1995 Babylon destroyed the First Temple and exiled Judah's leaders in the early 6th century BCE. Established Babylonian chronicles, ration tablets naming King Jehoiachin, burn layers in Jerusalem and tablets from the Judean exile community agree with the biblical account in outline. Weidner 1939; Pearce and Wunsch 2014 Rome destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE. Established Described by the eyewitness historian Josephus, commemorated on the Arch of Titus in Rome, and visible in the burnt houses and toppled stones of 1st-century Jerusalem. Josephus, Jewish War 6 A Messiah descended from David will come and bring an age of peace. Matter of faith Listed by Maimonid

chunks.heading: Judaism: 01 A people who kept their records
chunks.text: Few peoples have carried their memory as far as the Jews. The same Hebrew words are read aloud in a synagogue in Buenos Aires this week and were copied onto leather in a desert cave more than two thousand years ago. Judaism is not only a faith in one God; it is a people's long conversation with a text, and with the history that text describes. That makes it a natural place to ask the questions this section asks of every tradition. What does the tradition say about its own scriptures? What survives, and how close is it to the first writing? And which of the historical events the texts describe can be checked in the ground, in foreign archives or in the scrolls themselves? Hear, O Israel: The LORD is our God, the LORD alone. The answers are unusually rich, and in places unusually warm. Stones name Israel's kings, Babylonian clerks record rations for an exiled king of Judah, and the scrolls from the Judean Desert let us watch the Bible's text while it was still being copied by hand in the age of the Maccabees.

chunks.heading: Judaism: 02 The tradition's own account
chunks.text: In Jewish teaching the Torah, the five books of Moses, was given by God at Sinai. Rabbinic chronology places the moment about 1313 BCE. Alongside the written Torah came an oral one: the explanations, laws and methods that tell a reader how to live the text. The Mishnah opens its tractate on the fathers with a chain of transmission. Moses received the Law from Sinai and committed it to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, and the elders to the Prophets; and the Prophets committed it to the men of the Great Synagogue. The Prophets and the Writings, the other two parts of the Tanakh, were written by prophets and sages, and the tradition credits the sages with deciding which books belonged. Scribal law is strict: a Torah scroll with a single wrong or missing letter may not be read in public until it is corrected. The medieval scholar Maimonides named one manuscript, the codex later known as the Aleppo Codex, as the model for copyists. The Talmud itself is candid about details. It records a view that Joshua wrote the last eight verses of Deuteronomy, which describe Moses's death, and it lists places where the written consonants and the traditional reading differ. The tradition, in other words, has long paid close attention to its own text.

chunks.heading: Judaism: 03 Scrolls from the caves
chunks.text: In 1947 Bedouin shepherds entered a cave near Qumran, above the Dead Sea, and found jars holding leather scrolls. Over the next decade eleven caves gave up the remains of roughly 800 to 900 manuscripts. About 220 of them are copies of biblical books, covering every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. They were copied between about 250 BCE and 68 CE, a thousand years before the oldest complete Hebrew Bibles then known. The star is the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a): seventeen sheets of parchment, about 7.3 metres long, holding all 66 chapters of Isaiah in 54 columns. Palaeography places it around 150–100 BCE, and two radiocarbon tests gave calibrated ranges between 356 and 103 BCE. Set beside the Leningrad Codex of 1008 CE, it differs in more than 2,600 places, but most are spelling, grammar or single words. A reader of one can follow the other line by line. Dates for the scrolls come from three independent methods: the evolving shapes of Hebrew letters (palaeography), radiocarbon tests on the parchment, and the archaeology of Qumran, which was destroyed by Roman troops around 68 CE. In 2025 a team led by Mladen Popović combined radiocarbon dates with an AI model of handwriting called Enoch; it placed a Daniel fragment (4Q114) at about 230–160 BCE, possibly within the lifetime of the book's author. Handwriting dates remain estimates, not certainties. Older still are two tiny silver amulets from a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, found in 1979 by Gabriel Barkay's team. Unrolled and re-read with modern imaging in 2004, they carry a version of the Priestly Blessing that Jewish congregations still hear today.
