The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you, and give you p

chunks.heading: Judaism: 04 From many texts to one
chunks.text: The scrolls held a surprise. Before the 1st century CE, the Bible's text was not yet single. Beside copies close to the later Masoretic text, Qumran had copies resembling the Hebrew behind the Greek Septuagint, and copies close to the Samaritan Pentateuch. Jeremiah existed in a long edition and in a short one about one-seventh shorter. Scholars such as Emanuel Tov and Eugene Ulrich describe a period of textual plurality. The Septuagint, begun in Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE when Greek-speaking Jews translated the Torah, is therefore a witness to Hebrew texts that differed in places from the later standard. The Samaritan Pentateuch, kept by the Samaritan community to this day, differs from the Masoretic text in about 6,000 places, mostly spelling, and adds a command to build an altar on Mount Gerizim. The Dead Sea Scrolls show both things at once: a text still in motion, and a line of copying so careful that the motion almost stops. After about 100 CE the picture changes. Biblical scrolls from Masada, sealed before the fortress fell in 73 or 74 CE, and from the Bar Kokhba caves are almost all proto-Masoretic. A charred scroll from En-Gedi, read without unrolling by virtual imaging in 2016, gave the opening of Leviticus in consonants identical to the medieval text. Between about the 7th and 10th centuries CE the Masoretes of Tiberias added vowels, accents and notes. Their finest work, the Aleppo Codex (c. 920–930), lost about 40 percent of its leaves after the synagogue holding it was burned in 1947. The Leningrad Codex, copied in Cairo in 1008 or 1009, is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible and the base of modern scholarly editions.

chunks.heading: Judaism: 05 Who wrote the Torah?
chunks.text: Here tradition and critical scholarship part ways, and both deserve a fair hearing. Tradition holds that Moses wrote the Torah at God's word. Since the 19th century, and especially Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena (1883), many scholars have read it as woven from sources: the documentary hypothesis named four, known as J, E, D and P. Today the field is more varied. Neo-documentarians such as Joel Baden still defend four continuous sources. Many European scholars prefer a supplementary or fragmentary model, in which smaller blocks of tradition were joined and expanded by Priestly and non-Priestly editors. Most agree that the Torah reached something close to its present form in the Persian period, around the 5th century BCE, while containing older material. Arguments scholars give for a composite text: doublets (two creation accounts, two versions of the flood), different names for God, different legal codes, and Hebrew that fits the 1st millennium BCE. Arguments traditional scholars give: the doublets may be deliberate literary design, language can be updated by later scribes without new composition, and a single revealed source explains the Torah's unity. What the evidence can settle: dates of copies and language. What it cannot settle: whether the text is revealed. That remains a matter of faith.

chunks.heading: Judaism: 06 Stones that name the kings
chunks.text: When the biblical story reaches the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the outside record begins to answer back. Pharaoh Merneptah's victory stele, around 1208 BCE, lists Israel as a people in Canaan. In the 9th century BCE the Mesha Stele of Moab names Omri, king of Israel, and the Aramaic Tel Dan Stele mentions a "House of David". Assyrian scribes name Ahab, Jehu and Hezekiah, and Sennacherib boasts of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage". The exile is especially well lit. Tablets excavated near Babylon's Ishtar Gate, published by Ernst Weidner in 1939 and now in Berlin, list oil rations for "Ya'ukinu, king of the land of Yahudu" and his sons around 592/591 BCE, the same Jehoiachin whom the Book of Kings says was taken to Babylon and later given a daily allowance. Tablets from Al-Yahudu, "Judah-town", published by Laurie Pearce and Cornelia Wunsch in 2014, record exiled families buying, renting and naming children with the divine name from 572 BCE onward. From about the 9th century BCE onward, the Books of Kings and the foreign records agree on names, order and rough dates to a degree that surprised early 20th-century sceptics. The closer the biblical account comes to the time it was written down, the more often archaeology finds its people.

chunks.heading: Judaism: 07 Where the record falls silent
chunks.text: Further back, the evidence thins. No inscription names Abraham, Isaac or Jacob, which is unsurprising for pastoral families. No Egyptian record describes an exodus of 600,000 men with their families, and no campsite of that scale has been found in Sinai, although Semitic-speaking people certainly lived in the Nile Delta. Many scholars think a smaller group's memory may lie behind the story. Of the conquest, Hazor was burned in the 13th century BCE, but Jericho and Ai were largely empty then. Time has worked against the evidence. Papyrus and leather rot in most of the Levant, Jerusalem has been rebuilt and fought over dozens of times, and the Temple Mount cannot be excavated. Much that could settle these questions may never be found; some may still lie in unexcavated mounds or in Egyptian archives not yet read. What the record does show is striking enough. The Jewish scriptures are among the best-documented ancient texts on earth, with copies reaching back to within centuries, sometimes decades, of their last editing. The tradition's claim that it guarded its text with great care is, for the last two thousand years at least, strongly supported by the manuscripts themselves.

chunks.heading: Jainism
chunks.text: Ganges plain, India Jainism A path of radical non-violence taught by twenty-four 'ford-makers', whose scriptures were remembered, partly lost, and finally written down at Valabhi. 6th–5th century BCE (Mahavira). How the tradition sees its text The truths the Tirthankaras teach are eternal. Mahavira's words were arranged by his disciples into the Angas. Svetambaras hold that most of this survived through careful councils and was faithfully written at Valabhi, with honest admission of what was lost. Digambaras hold that the original Angas and Purvas were lost entirely, and that only partial knowledge passed through Dharasena to Puspadanta and Bhutabali. What manuscript scholarship shows The canon has layers spanning perhaps eight centuries. Its oldest parts, such as the first book of the Acaranga and Sutrakrtanga, are archaic in language and metre and among the oldest Indian texts after the Vedic corpus. No manuscript earlier than the 11th century survives, and the pre-Valabhi text is reconstructed from internal evidence and Mathura inscriptions.

chunks.heading: Jainism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The universe is eternal, has no creator, and turns through endless cycles of time. Matter of faith A foundational Jain teaching about the nature of the cosmos. It concerns metaphysics rather than a datable event, so it is a matter of faith and is not rated. Tattvartha Sutra; Jaini 1979 Twenty-four Tirthankaras teach in each half-cycle; Rishabha, the first of our age, lived an immensely long time ago. Matter of faith The earlier Tirthankaras are given lifespans and heights beyond any historical measure, placing them in sacred rather than historical time. A matter of faith; only the last two can be studied as historical figures. Kalpasutra; Dundas 2002 Mahavira (Vardhamana) was a real teacher and a contemporary of the Buddha. Strong evidence Jain texts describe his life, and early Buddhist discourses independently name a rival teacher, Nigantha Nataputta, with Jain doctrines. Two separate traditions agreeing is strong evidence, though no contemporary inscription names him. Acaranga Sutra; Samannaphala Sutta (Digha Nikaya 2) Parshva, the 23rd Tirthankara, was a historical teacher who lived about 250 years before Mahavira. Plausible Jain texts describe followers of Parshva meeting Mahavira's disciples, and Buddhist texts attribute a 'fourfold restraint' to the Niganthas, which Jains associate with Parshva. Historians often accept him as real, of the 8th or 7th century BCE. Uttaradhyayana 23; Dundas 2002 Mahavira attained nirvana in 527 BCE. Open question This is the traditional Svetambara date; Digambaras differ. Because Mahavira and the Buddha were contemporaries, many scholars move him about a century later, c. 480–425 BCE, in line with the short chronology for the Buddha. Dundas 2002; Wikipedia 'Mahavira' (accessed 2026) Souls that reach omniscience (kevala jnana) are liberated and never return to rebirth. Matter of faith The goal of Jain practice. It describes the fate of the soul beyond death, a matter of faith that the site does not rate. Tattvartha Sutra 10 The canon was gathered from monks' memories at Pataliputra after a famine and written down at Valabhi in 453 or 466 CE. Plausible This Svetambara account is detailed and self-critical, admitting losses and variants, which scholars find credible in outline. Its sources were written long after the events, so the dates are traditional rather than independently confirmed. Dundas 2002; Jaini 1979 The deepest part of the teaching, the Purvas in the twelfth Anga, has been lost. Plausible Both main sect

chunks.heading: Jainism: 01 A religion that admits its losses
chunks.text: Most scriptural traditions insist that nothing essential has been lost. Jainism is unusual. Both of its great branches openly say that the deepest part of Mahavira's teaching, the fourteen Purvas, vanished long ago, and they disagree about how much of the rest survived. For a historian that candour is precious. It means the tradition has kept a record of its own gaps, and it invites us to compare that record with inscriptions, manuscripts and the witness of neighbouring religions. Jainism is small in numbers, about 4.5 million people in the 2011 Census of India, but its influence on Indian thought, art and commerce is large, and its ethic of ahimsa, non-violence toward every living being, is among the most demanding moral codes any religion has asked of its followers. Both branches openly say the deepest part of Mahavira's teaching vanished long ago. For a historian, that candour is precious.

chunks.heading: Jainism: 02 The ford-makers
chunks.text: In the Jain view time turns like a wheel, rising and declining through vast ages without beginning or end. In each half-turn twenty-four Tirthankaras appear, 'makers of the ford' across the river of rebirth. They are not gods and did not create anything; they are human beings who conquered their own passions, reached omniscience and taught the way. The first of our age, Rishabha, lived an unimaginably long time ago. The last two, Parshva and Mahavira, stand at the edge of recorded history. Mahavira, born Vardhamana into a warrior clan near Vaishali, left home at about thirty, practised severe austerities for twelve years, reached omniscience and taught for three decades. Jain tradition dates his death to 527 BCE; many historians place it about a century later. Either way, he was active in the same towns and at the same time as the Buddha, and the Buddhist discourses describe a rival teacher, Nigantha Nataputta, whose doctrines are recognisably Jain. That independent notice from a competing tradition is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for any founder in ancient India. The Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future, all say thus, speak thus, declare thus, explain thus: all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away.

chunks.heading: Jainism: 03 A world the texts remember
chunks.text: Jain scriptures set Mahavira's life in a real political landscape. They name King Shrenika of Magadha and his son Kunika, the rulers known to Buddhist texts as Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, and they describe the Licchavi confederacy of Vaishali, a clan republic that Buddhist sources also portray. The two traditions were rivals and did not copy each other's stories, so when both describe the same kings, cities and tensions between Magadha and Vaishali, historians gain an independent check on the world of the 5th century BCE. The texts also preserve memories of an older Jain community. The Uttaradhyayana describes a meeting between Keshi, a monk in the line of Parshva who wore clothes and kept four vows, and Gautama, Mahavira's disciple, who kept five; the two reconcile their practice. Such a story reads less like invention than like a community remembering how two groups of followers came together. The branches differ on details of Mahavira's own life too: Svetambaras say he married and had a daughter, and that his embryo was transferred from a Brahmin mother to Queen Trishala, while Digambaras reject both accounts.

chunks.heading: Jainism: 04 Memory, famine and three councils
chunks.text: According to Svetambara tradition, Mahavira's words were arranged by his chief disciples into twelve Angas and learned by heart. Then came famine. Around the time of the Maurya empire a twelve-year famine scattered the monks, and when they reassembled at Pataliputra they could piece together eleven Angas but not the twelfth, the Drstivada, because the only monk who knew it, Bhadrabahu, was away. Centuries later two more recitations, at Mathura and at Valabhi, tried again. Finally, at a second council at Valabhi in Gujarat, 980 or 993 years after Mahavira by the traditional count (453 or 466 CE), the teacher Devarddhigani Ksamasramana had the surviving canon written down, noting where recitation lineages disagreed. Digambara Jains tell the story differently. For them the original Angas and Purvas were lost completely by about the 2nd century CE. What survived was partial knowledge, which the teacher Dharasena passed to two monks, Puspadanta and Bhutabali, who composed the Satkhandagama, the oldest Digambara scripture. Its vast commentary, the Dhavala, and the related Jayadhavala, completed in 838 CE, survived in palm-leaf manuscripts guarded at Mudabidri in Karnataka and were only transcribed and published in the 20th century. The council story comes from Jain sources written long after the events, so its dates are traditional. But its shape is credible: it admits losses and variant readings, which later editors had no motive to invent. Scholars also find that the language and metre of texts such as the first book of the Acaranga are older than the rest of the canon, which is what we would expect if a genuinely old core was preserved and later material added around it.

chunks.heading: Jainism: 05 Evidence in stone
chunks.text: Before any Jain manuscript, there are inscriptions. In a cave at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar, King Kharavela of Kalinga had a seventeen-line Prakrit inscription carved, probably in the 1st century BCE. It opens with a salutation to the Arhats and Siddhas, the same words that begin the Jain Namokar prayer today, and records the king's gifts to ascetics. A damaged line appears to say that Kharavela brought back a 'Jina of Kalinga' carried off long before by a Nanda king; if that reading holds, Jina worship would reach back to the 4th century BCE, but scholars disagree about the passage. At Kankali Tila in Mathura, 19th-century excavators uncovered the remains of a Jain stupa with images and votive tablets dating from about the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE. The Indologist Georg Bühler noticed that the donors' inscriptions name monastic groups, the ganas, kulas and sakhas, which also appear in the list of elders in the Kalpasutra, a Svetambara text. The scripture and the stones independently record the same institutions, an encouraging sign that the tradition's memory of its own lineages is sound.

chunks.heading: Jainism: 06 The libraries of the desert
chunks.text: The Jain community built some of the finest manuscript libraries in Asia. In the 12th century King Kumarapala founded libraries at Patan, and the underground vaults of Jaisalmer, in the dry Thar desert, preserved palm-leaf manuscripts that would have rotted elsewhere. Among them is a copy of the Oghaniryukti dated 1060 CE, one of the oldest dated Jain manuscripts and among the oldest dated manuscripts of any kind from India outside the Himalaya. Copying a scripture was itself a meritorious act, and wealthy lay families commissioned richly painted copies of the Kalpasutra, many of which are now in museums. In recent decades Jain monks and scholars have catalogued these holdings, among them Muni Jambuvijaya's catalogue of the Jaisalmer collections, and many are being digitised, which will make comparison of early copies far easier. Still, the gap is real. Roughly six hundred years separate the writing down at Valabhi from the oldest surviving copies, and the oldest layers of the canon may be seven or eight centuries older than Valabhi. The manuscripts also come overwhelmingly from western India, so scholars cannot compare independent lines from different regions as they can for the Pali Canon.

chunks.heading: Jainism: 07 What is still open
chunks.text: Mahavira's dates: 527 BCE by tradition, perhaps a century later by many scholars. Whether Parshva was a historical founder whose community Mahavira reformed, as Jain sources suggest. How much of the Svetambara canon preserves Mahavira's own teaching, and how much was added before Valabhi. Whether Chandragupta Maurya ended his life as a Jain monk, as later Digambara inscriptions say. What can be said with confidence is that Jainism is among the oldest living religions of India, that its founder is attested by his rivals as well as his followers, and that its community took unusual care both to preserve its scriptures and to record honestly where the chain of memory broke. Those admissions do not weaken the tradition as a historical witness. They make it more trustworthy.

chunks.heading: Buddhism
chunks.text: Ganges plain, India Buddhism The teaching of a wandering sage of the Ganges plain, carried for centuries in memory, then written on birch bark, palm leaf and even gold. 5th century BCE. How the tradition sees its text Theravada holds that at the First Council Ananda recited the discourses and Upali the monastic rules, and that the canon was carried to Sri Lanka in Ashoka's time and faithfully kept by reciters until it was written down at Aluvihare. Pali is identified with Magadhi, the Buddha's own speech, so the canon is his word in his language. What manuscript scholarship shows Scholars see Pali as a literary Middle Indic language with western features, close to but probably not identical with the Buddha's eastern dialect. The core discourses share much with other schools' parallels and preserve early material. The text has been stable since at least the 5th century CE, but its earlier growth is inferred, and physical witnesses are late.

chunks.heading: Buddhism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Siddhartha Gautama attained awakening under a tree at Bodh Gaya and became the Buddha. Matter of faith The awakening itself is a matter of faith and inner experience. The place is historical: Bodh Gaya has been venerated at least since the Maurya period, when a stone seat (the Vajrasana) is thought to have been set up there. Majjhima Nikaya 26; Gethin 1998 Siddhartha Gautama was a real teacher who lived and taught in the middle Ganges plain. Strong evidence Nearly all historians accept this. The early discourses name real places and rulers, Ashoka honoured his birthplace about two centuries later, and rival traditions such as the Jains knew of him. No contemporary inscription or object names him. Gethin 1998; Lumbini pillar inscription He was born at Lumbini, in the Shakya lands at the foot of the Himalaya. Strong evidence Ashoka's pillar at Lumbini, rediscovered in 1896, states that the Buddha Shakyamuni was born here. Excavations under the Maya Devi temple found earlier structures, reported as pre-Mauryan (Coningham et al. 2013). Lumbini pillar inscription; Coningham et al. 2013 The Buddha lived c. 563–483 BCE, or 624–544 BCE by the Theravada reckoning. Open question Both dates come from later chronicles. Many scholars now prefer a 'short chronology' placing his death around 400 BCE, roughly 480–400 BCE for his life. The Göttingen symposium edited by Heinz Bechert reached no consensus. Bechert 1991–1997; Cousins 1996 Beings are reborn according to karma, and nirvana ends the cycle. Matter of faith A core teaching, shared in different forms with Hindu and Jain thought and set out in the Buddha's first discourse at Sarnath. It concerns what happens beyond death, so it is a matter of faith and is not rated. Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 (the first discourse) The teachings were recited together at a First Council in Rajagriha soon after the Buddha's death. Open question All the monastic codes of the early schools tell a version of this story, which suggests an old tradition. Many scholars doubt that a single meeting fixed the canon as it now stands. Cullavagga 11; Gethin 1998 The Pali Canon was first written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE. Plausible Reported by the Sri Lankan chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa), compiled in the 4th and 5th centuries CE. It fits the wider evidence that Buddhists were writing texts in Gandhara by the 1st century CE, but no manuscript of that age from Sri Lanka survives. Dipavamsa 20.20–21; Collins 1990 Buddhas appeared be

chunks.heading: Buddhism: 01 A teacher on the road
chunks.text: Around the 5th century BCE, in the river towns of the middle Ganges, a man of the Shakya clan gave up his inheritance, wandered as an ascetic and, by his own account, woke up. For some forty-five years afterwards he walked from town to town teaching what he had seen. He wrote nothing. His followers remembered his words, repeated them together, and passed them on for several centuries before anyone put them on bark or leaf. Today Buddhism has about 324 million followers by Pew Research Center's 2020 estimate, and its scriptures fill many shelves in Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan. That makes Buddhism a fascinating case for anyone who treats religious texts as historical records. It has one of the widest spreads of early witnesses of any Asian tradition, and some of its oldest manuscripts were found only in the last thirty years. He wrote nothing. His followers remembered his words and passed them on for centuries before anyone wrote them on bark or leaf.

chunks.heading: Buddhism: 02 The tradition's own account
chunks.text: Buddhist tradition tells the story this way. Soon after the Buddha's death, five hundred awakened monks met at Rajagriha. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, recited the discourses from memory, each beginning 'Thus have I heard', and Upali recited the monastic rules. The community chanted them together and so fixed them. A second council a century later settled disputes over discipline. In the Theravada account the canon then travelled to Sri Lanka with Ashoka's son Mahinda, was kept by groups of reciters, and in the 1st century BCE, when famine and war threatened the chain of memory, was written down on palm leaf at the Aloka cave, today's Aluvihare. Mahayana Buddhists add a further layer: sutras such as the Perfection of Wisdom and the Lotus Sutra, which they understand as the Buddha's deeper teaching, preserved and revealed when people were ready to receive them. These are matters of faith, and they are not weighed here. What can be weighed is the physical trail the texts left behind.

chunks.heading: Buddhism: 03 Stone before parchment: Ashoka
chunks.text: The oldest firm evidence for Buddhism is not a manuscript but stone. The emperor Ashoka, who ruled most of South Asia from about 268 to 232 BCE, cut his edicts into rocks and pillars from Afghanistan to Karnataka. In them he describes his remorse after conquering Kalinga, his support for the monastic order, and his pilgrimages. One edict, found at Bairat, recommends seven named passages of the Dhamma to monks, nuns and lay people, so recognised texts already existed. Another pillar records that he enlarged the stupa of an earlier Buddha, Konakamana. And at Lumbini, a pillar rediscovered in 1896 gives what reads like a pilgrim's certificate. When king Devanampriya Priyadarsin had been anointed twenty years, he came himself and worshipped (this spot) because the Buddha Sakyamuni was born here. (He) both caused to be made a stone bearing a horse (?) and caused a stone pillar to be set up, (in order to show) that the Blessed one was born here. In 2013 a team led by Robin Coningham reported excavations beneath the Maya Devi temple at Lumbini. Under the Mauryan brick shrine they found post-holes of an earlier timber structure around an open centre, perhaps once holding a tree, and dated it by radiocarbon and optically stimulated luminescence to the 6th century BCE. If the dating holds, the spot was sacred before Ashoka and perhaps within living memory of the Buddha. It is one well-published excavation rather than a settled consensus, but it is a striking fit between tradition and trowel.

chunks.heading: Buddhism: 04 Birch bark in a clay pot
chunks.text: In 1994 the British Library acquired a clay pot and a bundle of fragile birch-bark scrolls from the region of ancient Gandhara, in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan. Richard Salomon and colleagues identified them as Buddhist texts in the Gandhari language, written in Kharoshthi script in the first half of the 1st century CE. They were, and remain, among the oldest Buddhist manuscripts known, and among the oldest manuscripts from South Asia of any kind. More followed: the Senior collection, with sutras paralleling the Pali Samyutta Nikaya; the Bajaur collection, found in 1999; the Schøyen fragments; and the Split Collection, whose Perfection of Wisdom manuscript is radiocarbon dated to 47–147 CE. What do they show? That by the 1st century CE Buddhists in the north-west were writing their scriptures down, some two to four centuries after the Buddha by most reckonings. That these texts closely match the teachings preserved in Pali and Chinese, but not word for word: the Gandhari Rhinoceros Sutra has most of the verses of its Pali twin in a different order. And that Mahayana sutras were being copied alongside older material earlier than many scholars once assumed. Two methods date these finds. Palaeography, the study of how letter shapes changed over time, places the British Library scrolls in the early 1st century CE, supported by inscriptions on the pots. Radiocarbon dating of the bark itself, published for fragments in the Schøyen, Senior and Split collections, gives independent ranges in the 1st to 3rd centuries CE. The two methods broadly agree.

chunks.heading: Buddhism: 05 The Pali Canon: late leaves, early voices
chunks.text: The Pali Canon is the only early Buddhist canon that survives complete in an Indian language. Its physical record is late: the oldest known Pali manuscript is a fragment of monastic rules from Nepal, dated by its script to the 8th or 9th century CE, and most manuscripts from Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia were copied in the 18th and 19th centuries, because palm leaf rarely lasts longer in the tropics. Yet the commentaries of Buddhaghosa, written in the 5th century CE, quote and explain a canon almost identical to the one printed today, which suggests remarkable stability since then. Before that point the record is reconstructed by comparison. Where the Pali discourses have parallels in the Chinese Agamas, the Gandhari scrolls and Sanskrit fragments from Central Asia, the shared core is likely old. Scholars generally see the Abhidhamma and some verse collections as later additions, and Pali itself as a literary language slightly different from the eastern dialect the Buddha probably spoke. The tradition's identification of Pali with the Buddha's own speech is therefore one point where it and most scholars differ. The comparison is possible because the Buddha's words travelled in many directions at once. Translators in China began rendering Indian Buddhist texts in the 2nd century CE, and by the early 5th century they had translated whole collections of discourses and monastic codes from Indian originals now lost, belonging to schools such as the Sarvastivada and Dharmaguptaka. When a discourse appears in Pali, in a Chinese Agama and in a Gandhari scroll, with the same teaching in slightly different words, historians can be fairly confident it goes back to a period before those schools separated. When a passage appears in only one of them, it may be a later

chunks.heading: Buddhism: 06 What is still open
chunks.text: The Buddha's dates remain uncertain. Theravada reckoning puts his death in 544 BCE, older Western handbooks in 483 BCE, and many specialists now prefer a date around 400 BCE; a major Göttingen symposium in the 1990s did not settle the question. The site of Kapilavastu, his home town, is claimed by both Tilaurakot in Nepal and Piprahwa in India. The Piprahwa relic vase, found in 1898 with an inscription that many read as naming relics of the Buddha, is still debated in its date and reading; in 2025 a planned auction of gems from that find was halted after the Indian government objected, and they returned to India. A securely dated inscription or manuscript from before Ashoka would transform the debate on the Buddha's dates. Further excavation at Lumbini, Tilaurakot and Piprahwa could test the early shrine and the location of Kapilavastu. Publication of all Gandharan fragments, and more radiocarbon dates, would show how early and how widely the texts were written. The broad picture is nonetheless clear and, for a tradition that began in memory, strong. Its founder is anchored in place by an emperor's inscription within about two centuries; its scriptures appear in writing within four centuries at most; and its many versions allow scholars to see both what was faithfully kept and what grew.

chunks.heading: Confucianism
chunks.text: China Confucianism A teacher who called himself a transmitter of the ancients, and a tradition whose oldest books keep turning up, rewritten and surprising, in sealed tombs. 6th–5th century BCE. How the tradition sees its text Traditional scholarship held that the Analects was compiled by Confucius's disciples and their students soon after his death, and that it records his words faithfully. For two thousand years it was memorised by schoolchildren and examination candidates, and its wording was treated as settled from the Han onward. What manuscript scholarship shows Modern scholars see a layered book assembled over two centuries or more from many sayings collections, with the final form fixed only in the Han. Newly excavated manuscripts support early circulation of sayings but show that the selection and order varied. Since the Han, the text has been very stable.

chunks.heading: Confucianism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Heaven (Tian) entrusted Confucius with a moral mission. Matter of faith In the Analects Confucius says that Heaven produced the virtue in him (7.23; 7.22 in Legge's numbering) and that Heaven would not let the culture of Zhou perish (9.5). How Heaven acts is a religious claim and is not rated. Analects 7.23, 9.5 Human beings become good through learning, ritual and humaneness (ren). Matter of faith An ethical and spiritual teaching about human nature, developed later in different directions by Mencius and Xunzi. It concerns values, not a physical event, so it is not rated here. Analects 12.1; Mencius 2A.6 Ancestors are to be served in death as in life through sacrifice and ritual. Matter of faith A religious and moral duty central to Chinese family life for over two thousand years. Whether the dead receive the offerings is a matter of faith, and not rated. Analects 2.5, 3.12 Confucius lived c. 551–479 BCE in the state of Lu and taught a circle of disciples. Strong evidence The Zuozhuan, the Analects, Mencius and Sima Qian's Shiji all describe him. None is contemporary: the earliest date from about a century after his death. No object from his lifetime names him, but no serious scholar doubts he existed. Shiji 47; Nylan 2001 Confucius edited the Classics and wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals. Open question Mencius (4th century BCE) first says Confucius made the Annals. Most modern scholars think the Annals is a Lu court chronicle and that the Classics took shape over centuries, with Confucius at most a teacher of them. Mencius 3B.9; Nylan 2001 The Analects preserves Confucius's own words, as remembered by his disciples. Plausible Manuscripts of about 300 BCE show that collections of his sayings circulated early, but the book as we have it was compiled over two centuries or more and fixed in the Han. Some sayings are probably early, others later additions. Poli and Li 2024; Makeham 1996 The Zhou founders, King Wen, King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, established the ritual order Confucius sought to restore. Strong evidence Western Zhou bronze inscriptions name Kings Wen and Wu, and the Li gui vessel records Wu's conquest of Shang. The idealised 'golden age' portrait is Confucian; the kings themselves are historical. Li gui inscription; Shaughnessy 2006 The sage kings Yao and Shun ruled China in an age of perfect virtue. Awaiting discovery Yao and Shun appear in later Zhou texts, not in any Shang or early Zhou inscription. Some archaeologists link the large l

chunks.heading: Confucianism: 01 A transmitter, not a maker
chunks.text: Confucius did not claim to found anything. He said he was passing on what the ancients had already taught, and for two and a half thousand years his followers took him at his word. The tradition he started is sometimes called a philosophy, sometimes a religion; it has temples, sacrifices, a reverence for Heaven and a cult of ancestors, but no creed to sign and no church to join. Pew Research Center does not count Confucians as a separate religious group, because Confucian ethics and ancestral rites are woven into the lives of hundreds of millions of people who may also call themselves Buddhist, Daoist, Christian or nothing at all. The Master said, 'A transmitter and not a maker, believing in and loving the ancients, I venture to compare myself with our old P'ang.' That self-description turns out to be a good guide to the texts. The Confucian classics are layered works, gathered, edited and re-edited over centuries. What makes this tradition exciting for historians is that in the last fifty years its oldest copies have been coming out of the ground, in sealed tombs, on bamboo and silk, and they do not always say what the printed books say. Claims about Heaven, virtue and the ancestors are matters of faith and ethics and are not rated. Claims about Confucius's life, the making of the books and the events around them are rated on the evidence. The texts are scored only on how well their record survives, never on whether their teaching is true.

chunks.heading: Confucianism: 02 The man behind the sayings
chunks.text: Kong Qiu, known as Kongzi or Master Kong, was born in the small state of Lu in what is now Shandong, in 551 BCE by Sima Qian's reckoning or 552 by others. He served briefly and unhappily in government, travelled among rival courts hoping for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice, and spent most of his life teaching. He died in 479 BCE. The evidence for this life is real but indirect. The Analects, the Zuozhuan chronicle, the book of Mencius and Sima Qian's great biography, written about four centuries later, all describe him. They do not always agree, and Sima Qian's story of 3,000 students, 72 of whom mastered the arts, has the round numbers of legend. But the core of a teacher in Lu with a circle of named disciples fits everything we know of the period, and the site rates it as strong evidence. The core is secure: a teacher in Lu, a circle of disciples, and a legacy that outgrew every empire that honoured it.

chunks.heading: Confucianism: 03 How the Analects was made
chunks.text: The Analects is not a book Confucius wrote. It is a collection of short sayings and scenes, most beginning 'The Master said'. Tradition holds that his disciples compiled it; modern scholars think it grew over two centuries or more. By the Han dynasty there were three versions: one from Lu in 20 books, one from Qi in 22, and an 'Old Text' copy in 21 books, said to have been found hidden in a wall of Confucius's own house. Around the end of the 1st century BCE a tutor to the emperor, Zhang Yu, merged the Lu and Qi versions, and his composite became the ancestor of every printed Analects today. In 2022 Anhui University published a bamboo manuscript of about 300 BCE containing 25 sayings of 'Zhongni', Confucius's courtesy name. Maddalena Poli and Yumeng Li, studying it alongside a similar manuscript from Wangjiazui, found that only some of its sayings have parallels in transmitted literature, and those are scattered rather than concentrated in the Analects. The picture that emerges is of many collections of the Master's sayings in circulation, from which the Analects was one selection that won. Tsze-kung asked, saying, 'Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?' The Master said, 'Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.'

chunks.heading: Confucianism: 04 Bamboo in the tombs
chunks.text: In 1973 archaeologists opened a Han tomb at Dingzhou in Hebei, probably that of Liu Xiu, King of Zhongshan, who died in 55 BCE. Robbers had set a fire inside long ago. Among the charred objects were 620 bamboo slips carrying 7,576 characters of the Analects, about half the received text. The slips were further damaged in the 1976 Tangshan earthquake before they could be fully studied, and the text was published only in 1997. Even so, it gives us an Analects older than any other complete edition by centuries. Two more Han copies followed: one from a tomb near Pyongyang in North Korea, closely guarded and published only in part, and one from the spectacular tomb of Liu He, the deposed emperor who became Marquis of Haihun, who died in 59 BCE. Scholars have suggested the Haihun slips may preserve part of the lost Qi version, including a chapter title that the received text lacks. Three copies, buried within a few years of one another, from the Chinese heartland, the southeast and the Korean peninsula: that is an unusually rich early record. The Anhui University 'Zhongni said' manuscript (published 2022) and the Haihunhou slips (excavated 2011–2016, still being published) are changing the story of how the Analects formed. Poli and Li's 2024 study in Early China argues that 'Analects-like materials' circulated by about 300 BCE in several forms. Expect more revisions as the Haihunhou texts appear.

chunks.heading: Confucianism: 05 Did the First Emperor burn the classics?
chunks.text: Every Chinese schoolchild learns that in 213 BCE the First Emperor of Qin burned the books and in 212 BCE buried scholars alive. The story comes from Sima Qian, writing about a century later under the Han dynasty, which had every reason to paint the Qin darkly. His own account includes important limits: books on medicine, divination, agriculture and forestry were exempt, and official copies were kept in the imperial library. That library was destroyed when rebel armies burned the Qin capital in 206 BCE. Scholars such as Michael Nylan and Martin Kern have questioned how much the burning mattered. Qin and early Han writers quote the classics freely, which would be hard if they had vanished. Losses were real, and the Han spoke constantly of recovering texts from walls and old scholars' memories. The site rates the traditional story as a mixed record: an order probably existed, but the war of 206 BCE may have done more damage than the decree.

chunks.heading: Confucianism: 06 A forgery that lasted thirteen centuries
chunks.text: The most dramatic alteration in the Confucian canon concerns the Book of Documents, a collection of royal speeches and records. After the Qin, a scholar named Fu Sheng recovered 29 chapters. In 317 CE a court official, Mei Ze, presented a much longer version of 58 chapters, claiming it as the long-lost 'Old Text'. It became the official text, carved in stone and memorised for the examinations for over a thousand years. In the 17th century the scholar Yan Ruoju showed, by close study of language, quotations and anachronisms, that the extra chapters were compositions of the 3rd or 4th century CE. Most scholars were persuaded. In 2008 a looted collection of Warring States bamboo slips, acquired by Tsinghua University and radiocarbon dated to about 305 BCE, added fresh evidence: it contains a text titled 'Yin gao' that does not match Mei Ze's chapter of that name. It is a striking example of scholarship inside a tradition correcting that tradition's own text. Confucian scholars themselves exposed the forged chapters, using the tradition's own tools of close reading.

chunks.heading: Confucianism: 07 What remains open
chunks.text: How many sayings in the Analects go back to Confucius himself remains debated; E. Bruce and A. Taeko Brooks argued for strata added over two centuries, while others see a more unified early core. The full publication of the Haihunhou slips may tell us what the lost Qi version contained. And the Tsinghua and other collections with no recorded findspot, though widely accepted, remind us that the market in looted manuscripts complicates the evidence. What seems clear is that the Confucian record, like Confucius himself, is a transmitter: layered, edited and remarkably persistent.

chunks.heading: Daoism
chunks.text: China Daoism A short, enigmatic book about the Way, whose oldest copies emerged from Chinese tombs and showed the text was still taking shape. 4th century BCE onward (traditionally 6th century BCE). How the tradition sees its text Daoist tradition holds that Laozi, an elder sage of the Zhou court who was later revered as a manifestation of the Dao, wrote the book of about five thousand characters as he departed westward. Its words are recited in ritual and treated as scripture; different editions are respected rather than ranked. What manuscript scholarship shows Scholars see a text that grew in stages. By about 300 BCE parts existed in collections that differ in order and some key lines from the received text; within a century full versions circulated. Variants are meaningful but mostly modest: the book's core ideas are present in the oldest copies.

chunks.heading: Daoism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The Dao is the nameless source and pattern of all things. Matter of faith The foundational teaching of the Daodejing's first chapter and of all later Daoism. It concerns the ultimate nature of reality and is not rated. Daodejing 1, 25, 42 Living by non-forcing action (wu wei), simplicity and humility brings harmony. Matter of faith An ethical and spiritual teaching expressed through images of water, the uncarved block and the infant. It describes how to live, not a historical event, so it is not rated. Daodejing 8, 28, 37 Lord Lao, the deified Laozi, revealed a new covenant to Zhang Daoling in 142 CE. Matter of faith The founding revelation of the Celestial Masters. The revelation is a matter of faith; the existence of the movement in 2nd-century Sichuan is a historical question rated below. Kohn 2000; Kleeman 2016 Through cultivation of breath, diet, alchemy and virtue, a person may attain long life and transcendence. Matter of faith Teachings on longevity and immortality, developed by Ge Hong (c. 283–343) and later inner alchemy. The spiritual goal is not rated here. Ge Hong, Baopuzi; Kohn 2000 Laozi was a real archivist at the Zhou court and an older contemporary of Confucius. Open question Sima Qian (c. 94 BCE) could not decide between three candidates, Li Er, Lao Laizi and the Grand Historian Dan. Some scholars think a historical Lao Dan is plausible; others treat Laozi as a legendary figure attached to a compiled book. Shiji 63; Kohn 2000 Laozi wrote the Daodejing for the keeper of the western pass before vanishing. Awaiting discovery The story appears first in the Shiji, some three centuries after the setting. No early source confirms it, and the manuscript evidence points to a text assembled over time rather than written in one sitting. Shiji 63; Henricks 2000 The Celestial Masters movement arose in Sichuan in the 2nd century CE. Strong evidence Official histories describe Zhang Daoling's grandson Zhang Lu ruling a religious community in Hanzhong, and Celestial Master liturgy survives in early medieval texts. The precise date of 142 CE comes from the tradition itself. Sanguozhi 8; Kleeman 2016 The Tang emperors descended from Laozi. Awaiting discovery The Tang imperial Li family claimed Laozi (surnamed Li in the Shiji) as its ancestor and honoured him with imperial titles. The claim served political legitimacy; no genealogy links them. Kohn 2000

chunks.heading: Daoism: 01 Five thousand characters
chunks.text: The Daodejing is one of the most translated books on Earth, yet it is only about five thousand Chinese characters long. Its first lines warn that the Way cannot be captured in words, and then it spends 81 short chapters trying anyway, with images of water, valleys, infants and uncarved wood. From this small book, and from the wilder, funnier Zhuangzi, grew a whole religious tradition with priests, temples, a canon of about 1,500 texts and a pantheon of immortals. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. For historians, the Daodejing is special for another reason. Its oldest copies were not preserved by libraries but sealed in tombs, and the tombs have been opened in our lifetime. They let us watch a sacred book in the act of taking shape. Teachings about the Dao, Lord Lao and immortality are matters of faith and are not rated. Claims about Laozi's life, the dates of texts and events in Daoist history are rated on the evidence. The texts are scored only on how well their record survives, never on whether their teaching is true.

chunks.heading: Daoism: 02 Who was Laozi?
chunks.text: The name Laozi simply means 'Old Master'. Our earliest biography, in Sima Qian's Shiji of about 94 BCE, is refreshingly honest about its uncertainty. It says Laozi was Li Er, an archivist of the Zhou court whom Confucius once visited; then it adds that some say he was Lao Laizi, a contemporary of Confucius who wrote a book in 15 parts; and others that he was Dan, a grand historian of the 4th century BCE. It ends with the famous scene: seeing the Zhou in decline, Laozi rode west, and at the frontier pass the keeper Yinxi begged him to write down his teaching, which he did in two parts, of some five thousand characters, before vanishing. Modern scholars are divided. Some think a historical Lao Dan, perhaps a court ritualist, is plausible, especially since the Liji, a ritual classic, has Confucius quoting him on funeral customs. Others think 'Laozi' is a name attached to a compiled book, as happened with many early Chinese texts. The site rates Laozi's historicity as an open question: the tradition is early and widespread, but the only biography was already unsure two thousand years ago. Even the first biographer of Laozi, writing two thousand years ago, admitted he did not know who Laozi was.

chunks.heading: Daoism: 03 The tutor's tomb at Guodian
chunks.text: In October 1993, archaeologists working at Guodian near Jingmen in Hubei, after robbers had broken into a small tomb, found about 800 bamboo slips in the burial chamber. The tomb dates to around 300 BCE, before the Qin army took the nearby Chu capital in 278 BCE. A lacquer cup in the grave bears an inscription usually read as 'teacher of the eastern palace', which suggests the dead man tutored a crown prince. Among the slips were three bundles, labelled A, B and C by scholars, with material matching 31 chapters of the Daodejing, around two-fifths of the received text, in an order found in no later edition. Other bundles held Confucian writings, a reminder that the labels 'Daoist' and 'Confucian' were not yet sharply drawn. One difference caught the world's attention. Received chapter 19 tells rulers to 'abandon humaneness and cast off righteousness', words that sound like an attack on Confucian virtues. At Guodian the same passage targets knowledge, argument and artifice instead. Robert Henricks and others suggest that the sharper anti-Confucian wording was added later, as the schools became rivals. The Guodian tomb has no dated inscription. Its date comes from tomb construction, pottery and bronze types that match other Chu tombs of the late 4th to early 3rd century BCE, and from the historical fact that Chu elite burials in this area ended after the Qin conquest of 278 BCE. A date of about 300 BCE is widely accepted, give or take a few decades.

chunks.heading: Daoism: 04 Silk from Mawangdui
chunks.text: Twenty years earlier, in 1973, a family tomb of the Marquis of Dai at Mawangdui in Changsha had yielded one of the great finds of the century. Tomb 3, sealed in 168 BCE, contained a library on silk: medical texts, maps, astronomical charts and two complete copies of the Laozi. Copy A was written in an older script and does not avoid the personal name of the first Han emperor, which suggests it was copied before about 195 BCE; copy B does avoid it and is somewhat later. Both copies put the second half of the received book, the 'De' or virtue chapters, first, so that the title would be Dedaojing. The wording is recognisably the same book, but with thousands of small differences in characters and particles, and some lines that change the sense. Together with Guodian, Mawangdui shows that by the early Han the Daodejing was complete in content, but its order and precise wording were still flexible. The tombs show a sacred book that was already itself, but not yet fixed.

chunks.heading: Daoism: 05 Zhuangzi and the editor's knife
chunks.text: The Zhuangzi takes the Daodejing's paradoxes and turns them into stories: cooks who carve oxen without dulling their knives, giant birds, talking skulls, and the man who dreamt he was a butterfly. Formerly, I, Kwang Kau, dreamt that I was a butterfly, a butterfly flying about, feeling that it was enjoying itself. The Han imperial library catalogued a Zhuangzi in 52 chapters. Around 300 CE the scholar Guo Xiang cut it to 33, removing material he considered spurious or trivial. His edition was so successful that all others vanished. Short Han fragments from Fuyang and Zhangjiashan, Tang manuscripts from Dunhuang and a medieval copy kept at the Kōzanji temple in Kyoto let us check Guo Xiang's text, and they agree well. But roughly a third of the older book is gone, known only through quotations in other works.

chunks.heading: Daoism: 06 From book to religion
chunks.text: By the 2nd century CE Laozi was being worshipped. The Hou Hanshu records sacrifices to him by Emperor Huan in 165 and 166 CE, and in Sichuan a movement called the Way of the Celestial Masters traced its founding to a revelation from Lord Lao to Zhang Daoling in 142 CE. Zhang's grandson Zhang Lu ran a religious community in Hanzhong for about a quarter of a century, until he submitted to the warlord Cao Cao in 215. Official histories describe its officers, its free inns for travellers and its practice of confessing sins, one of the earliest organised religious communities in Chinese history. Over the following centuries Daoist scriptures multiplied, and scholars such as Lu Xiujing (5th century) catalogued them into a canon. The record then suffered a blow: in 1281, after court debates with Buddhists, Khubilai Khan ordered Daoist texts and printing blocks burned, sparing only the Daodejing. The Ming canon printed in 1445 preserved what survived, about 1,500 works, and remains the foundation of Daoist studies today. Two great orders carry the tradition today. The Zhengyi order, married priests who perform rituals for local communities, claims descent from the Celestial Masters. The Quanzhen order, monastic and celibate, was founded by Wang Chongyang (1113–1170) in the 12th century and is headquartered at the White Cloud Temple in Beijing. Both recite the Daodejing, and both treat the ancient book and its later scriptures as a living, ritual text rather than a museum piece.

chunks.heading: Daoism: 07 What remains open
chunks.text: Was there a historical Laozi? When did the Daodejing reach its full form, and was Guodian an early stage or a selection from an already complete book? Scholars still argue both sides of that last question: Guodian may be an anthology drawn from a longer text, or evidence of growth. The Peking University Han copy, acquired from the antiquities market in 2009, adds another witness but carries the uncertainty of any object without a recorded findspot. What the tombs have made clear is that Daoism's founding book, like the Way it describes, was fluid before it was fixed.

chunks.heading: Shinto
chunks.text: Japan Shinto A way of the kami lived through shrines, festivals and purification, whose first books were written a thousand years after its roots. Yayoi period onward; chronicles of 712 and 720 CE. How the tradition sees its text Shinto tradition treats the Kojiki as the most venerable record of the age of the kami and of the imperial line, faithfully set down from the memory of Hieda no Are. Since Motoori Norinaga, it has been read as the purest expression of ancient Japanese spirit, less coloured by Chinese learning than the Nihon Shoki. What manuscript scholarship shows Scholars read the Kojiki as an early 8th-century court compilation that preserves genuinely old myths, songs and genealogies, arranged to legitimise the ruling house. The text is well preserved in wording but survives only in copies made more than six centuries later, and parts of its reading remain disputed.

chunks.heading: Shinto: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Kami are present in nature, in sacred places and in the spirits of ancestors. Matter of faith The heart of Shinto practice, expressed through shrines, rituals and festivals rather than a written creed. As a claim about the spiritual world it is not rated. Breen and Teeuwen 2010 The kami Izanagi and Izanami brought forth the islands of Japan and many other kami. Matter of faith The creation account of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, told with several variant versions. It is sacred narrative about origins and is not rated as geology or history. Kojiki I; Nihon Shoki I The imperial family descends from the sun goddess Amaterasu. Matter of faith Divine descent is a matter of faith. Emperor Hirohito's 1946 rescript renounced the idea of the emperor as a 'living god', though the rescript's meaning is debated. The early human line is rated below. Kojiki I–II; Imperial Rescript, 1 January 1946 Purification removes pollution and restores a bright, sincere heart. Matter of faith Rituals of harae and misogi are central to Shinto worship, from shrine visits to the great purification rites held twice a year. The spiritual effect is not rated. Engishiki norito; Breen and Teeuwen 2010 Emperor Jimmu founded the Japanese realm in 660 BCE. Ruled out No state existed in Yamato in the 7th century BCE; Japan was then at the Jōmon to Yayoi transition. The date appears to have been calculated backward using the sexagenary cycle. Jimmu himself is rated below as a separate question. Nihon Shoki III; Brownlee 1997 The Kojiki preserves oral traditions that the court reciter Hieda no Are had memorised. Plausible The preface says Emperor Tenmu had Hieda no Are memorise imperial genealogies and old tales, which Ō no Yasumaro wrote down in 712. No independent record confirms the reciter, but the account fits the book's archaic language. Kojiki preface; Philippi 1968 The sacred mirror of Amaterasu is kept at the Inner Shrine of Ise. Matter of faith The mirror, one of the three imperial regalia, has never been displayed or studied. Its presence and nature are matters of faith and tradition, not open to historical checking. Nihon Shoki VI; Ise Jingū Ise's shrines have been rebuilt every 20 years since the late 7th century. Strong evidence Shrine and court records trace the Shikinen Sengū to the reign of Empress Jitō (690 or 692 CE, sources differ). The cycle was interrupted for more than a century during the civil wars of the 15th–16th centuries. The 62nd rebuilding took place in 2013. Is

chunks.heading: Shinto: 01 A religion of places before books
chunks.text: Most religions on this site begin with a founder or a scripture. Shinto begins with places: a mountain, a waterfall, an island, a great tree tied with a straw rope. It has no founder and no single sacred book. It is practised more than it is professed, through shrine visits, seasonal festivals, purification and prayers of thanks to the kami, the sacred powers present in nature, ancestors and awe-inspiring things. Shinto organisations reported about 88 million members to Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs for 2020, yet many of the same people also count as Buddhists, and in surveys few Japanese call themselves 'Shinto' at all. That makes Shinto a fascinating test case for this site's question about records. Its roots are older than writing in Japan, traced by archaeologists to the Yayoi period, when rice farming and bronze ritual objects spread across the islands. Its first books, the Kojiki of 712 and the Nihon Shoki of 720, were written by a royal court that already had a thousand years of traditions behind it. Claims about the kami, divine descent and purification are matters of faith and are not rated. Claims about emperors, dates, shrines and manuscripts are rated on the evidence. The chronicles are scored only on how well their text survives, never on whether their sacred stories are true.

chunks.heading: Shinto: 02 The two chronicles
chunks.text: The Kojiki, 'Record of Ancient Matters', opens with the age of the kami: the first deities appearing in the Plain of High Heaven, the divine pair Izanagi and Izanami bringing forth the islands, the sun goddess Amaterasu hiding in a cave and being coaxed out with a mirror and dancing. It then turns into a genealogy of rulers from Jimmu to Empress Suiko in the early 7th century. The names of the Deities that were born in the Plain of High Heaven when the Heaven and Earth began were the Deity Master-of-the-August-Centre-of-Heaven, next the High-August-Producing-Wondrous Deity, next the Divine-Producing-Wondrous-Deity. Eight years later came the Nihon Shoki, 'Chronicles of Japan', written in formal Classical Chinese for a readership that included the courts of China and Korea. It covers similar ground at greater length and, unusually, quotes alternative versions of its myths side by side, introduced with the phrase 'one document says'. For a historian that is a gift: the compilers show us the variety of traditions they were choosing from. Of old, Heaven and Earth were not yet separated, and the In and Yo not yet divided.

chunks.heading: Shinto: 03 From memory to manuscript
chunks.text: The Kojiki's preface tells how it was made. Emperor Tenmu, worried that clan records were full of errors, had a court attendant named Hieda no Are, remarkable for memory, learn the imperial genealogies and ancient tales by heart. After Tenmu's death the project stalled, until Empress Genmei ordered Ō no Yasumaro to write down what Hieda no Are recited. He presented the result in the first month of 712. Writing Japanese in Chinese characters was still an experiment, and Yasumaro mixed characters used for meaning with characters used for sound. No copy from the 8th century survives. The oldest Kojiki is the Shinpukuji-bon, copied by a Buddhist monk named Ken'yu in 1371 and 1372 and now a National Treasure kept at the Ōsu Kannon temple in Nagoya. That is a gap of about 660 years. The Nihon Shoki fares better: the Nara National Museum holds the Tanaka copy of volume 10, dated by its calligraphy to the 9th century, perhaps within about a century of the original. It has no reading marks and a few names in older forms, a sign that later copies added glosses. The oldest Kojiki is younger than the Nihon Shoki's oldest page by about five centuries.

chunks.heading: Shinto: 04 An emperor in 660 BCE
chunks.text: The Nihon Shoki dates the accession of the first emperor, Jimmu, to 660 BCE, a date still celebrated on 11 February as National Foundation Day. Historians have long noted that the year is a xin-you year in the sixty-year cycle and appears to have been chosen by counting cycles back from 601 CE, a year of reform under Prince Shōtoku. The first emperors are given reigns of many decades and lifespans over a century. Archaeology shows no kingdom in the Nara basin in the 7th century BCE. Japan was then at the transition from the Jōmon to the Yayoi period, a world of villages. The site therefore rates a realm founded in 660 BCE as ruled out by the evidence, and Jimmu's existence as awaiting discovery. That does not make the story empty. Scholars such as Kenneth Henshall suggest that the tale of Jimmu's march east from Kyushu may carry a memory of real migrations of Yayoi people, and the chronicles become steadily more reliable as they approach the 6th and 7th centuries, where they can be checked against Chinese and Korean records. The Chinese Wei zhi, written in the late 3rd century, describes a Japanese queen named Himiko and an embassy she sent in 239 CE. The Nihon Shoki quotes this Chinese record under its Empress Jingū, while Korean events it records in the same reigns fall about 120 years, two sixty-year cycles, earlier than Korean histories date them. Comparing dates with Chinese and Korean sources is how historians calibrate the chronicles.

chunks.heading: Shinto: 05 Shrines as records
chunks.text: Where the books are late, the ground speaks. On Okinoshima, a small island in the strait between Japan and Korea, excavations uncovered ritual sites used from the 4th to the 9th century, with about 80,000 offerings including bronze mirrors, iron weapons, gold rings and even Persian glass. UNESCO inscribed the island and its associated sites in 2017. They show that kami worship was a matter of state ritual centuries before the chronicles were written. At Izumo, tradition held that the great shrine once stood about 48 metres tall on towering pillars. Many doubted it until 2000, when excavators found pillar bases made of three bundled cedar trunks, each bundle about three metres across, probably from a 13th-century rebuilding. And at Ise, the shrines of Amaterasu and the food goddess Toyouke are rebuilt beside their old sites every twenty years, a custom recorded from the reign of Empress Jitō in the late 7th century. The 62nd rebuilding took place in 2013. The buildings are young; the design they preserve may be among the oldest in Japan. Ise keeps an ancient design alive by never letting the building grow old.

chunks.heading: Shinto: 06 When Shinto was remade
chunks.text: For most of Japanese history, kami and buddhas were worshipped together, often at the same sites. In the 18th century the scholar Motoori Norinaga spent 34 years on his Kojiki-den, a monumental study that set out to recover a pure ancient Japanese way free of Chinese and Buddhist influence. His work, and the nativist school behind it, helped inspire the Meiji government after 1868 to separate kami from buddhas and to create a state-supported Shinto that taught the divine origin of the emperor. After defeat in 1945, the Allied Shinto Directive ended state sponsorship. This history matters for the record, because much of what people think of as 'ancient Shinto' was organised and standardised in the modern period. Historians such as Kuroda Toshio have argued that Shinto as a distinct, separate religion took shape late. Others stress the continuity of shrines, rites and kami across fifteen centuries. The evidence supports both: old practices, newly framed.

chunks.heading: Shinto: 07 What remains open
chunks.text: Where was Himiko's Yamatai, in northern Kyushu or in the Nara basin? Who lies in the great keyhole tombs, most of which the Imperial Household Agency still guards from excavation? How much of the Kojiki's myth was ancient and how much shaped in the 7th century to support the ruling house? Opening the imperial tombs would answer more questions about early Japan than any other single step. Until then, Shinto's record rests on late manuscripts, well-dated shrine archaeology and a living practice that may be its most faithful witness of all.

chunks.heading: Christianity
chunks.text: Galilee and Jerusalem Christianity A faith centred on one life, recorded in Greek writings whose earliest surviving copies come within a century or two of their writing. 1st century CE. How the tradition sees its text Christians hold that the apostles and their companions wrote under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and that the church received rather than created the canon, recognising the books already used in worship. Many traditions teach that God has providentially preserved the text through the church, so that no doctrine depends on a disputed reading. What manuscript scholarship shows Textual scholars reconstruct the early text from thousands of manuscripts, early translations and quotations, a richer record than for any other ancient Greek book. Early copyists were not always professionals, and the 2nd century saw real fluidity. Modern critical editions such as Nestle-Aland mark the few passages that are later additions and list significant variants in the notes.

chunks.heading: Christianity: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Jesus is the Son of God, and God is one in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Matter of faith The centre of Christian belief, defined in the creeds of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381). It concerns the nature of God and is a matter of faith, not rated here. John 1:1–14; Nicene Creed Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day. Matter of faith Historians can establish that within a few years of his death, his followers proclaimed that they had seen him alive: Paul records this around 55 CE. The resurrection itself is a matter of faith. 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 (NRSV) Jesus was born of a virgin, Mary. Matter of faith Told in Matthew and Luke and affirmed in the creeds. As a miracle it lies outside what historical methods can test, so it is not rated. Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:26–38 Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher from Galilee, crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate. Established Attested by Paul's letters, the Gospels, the Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus. Almost all historians, whatever their beliefs, accept it. Tacitus, Annals 15.44; Josephus, Antiquities 18.63–64, 20.200 The four Gospels were written by Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Open question The Gospels are anonymous in their text. Papias (early 2nd century) links Mark and Matthew to named authors, and Irenaeus (c. 180) names all four. Scholars divide: many accept Mark and Luke, fewer accept apostolic authorship of Matthew and John. Eusebius, Church History 3.39; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1 Paul wrote letters to early churches within about 20–30 years of the crucifixion. Established Seven letters (Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon) are accepted as Paul's by nearly all scholars and are dated c. 50–60 CE. Six more carry his name but their authorship is debated. Ehrman 2012; Metzger and Ehrman 2005 The New Testament we read today is substantially the text first written in the 1st century. Strong evidence Thousands of manuscripts let scholars reconstruct the early text closely. Most variants are spelling or word order, but a few passages, such as Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11, are later additions to the earliest copies. Metzger and Ehrman 2005; Nestle-Aland 28th ed. (2012) Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. Matter of faith A hope about the future expressed in the creeds and in Paul's earliest letter. It is a matter of faith and cannot be tested historically. 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; Apostl

chunks.heading: Christianity: 01 A faith built on a life
chunks.text: Christianity rests on a claim about a person. Its scriptures are not mainly laws or poems but reports: letters written to young communities and four accounts of what one Galilean teacher said and did, how he died and what his followers said happened next. That makes the historical questions unusually close to the heart of the faith, and Christians have argued about them in the open for two centuries. The questions here are the same ones asked of every tradition. How does the tradition understand its texts? What survives, in what language, and how close to the first writing? And which historical claims can be checked against other evidence? Since many have undertaken to set down an orderly account of the events that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed on to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word, I too decided, after investigating everything carefully from the very first, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus. Luke's opening is itself a statement of method: sources, eyewitnesses, careful investigation. It is a good place to start.

chunks.heading: Christianity: 02 How the church understands its books
chunks.text: For Christians, the Bible has two parts. The Old Testament is the scripture of Israel, read in the light of Jesus. The New Testament gathers 27 writings from the first generations of believers: four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, 21 letters and the Revelation to John. The church teaches that these were written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and that the church recognised them because they were already read in worship and traced to the apostles. Traditions differ in the details. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include books from the Greek Old Testament, such as Tobit and the Maccabees, that Protestant Bibles leave out. The Syriac Peshitta long omitted 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation, and the Ethiopian church keeps a broader canon that includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees. The core, though, has been shared since the 4th century.

chunks.heading: Christianity: 03 The earliest pages
chunks.text: The oldest Christian writings are Paul's letters, written in Greek to communities he founded around the eastern Mediterranean between about 50 and 60 CE. In one of them he passes on a summary he says he had received, very likely within a few years of the crucifixion. For I handed on to you as of first importance what I in turn had received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures. Most scholars date Mark's Gospel to about 70 CE, Matthew and Luke to about 80–90, and John to about 90–100. None of the original documents survives; none of any ancient book does. What survives are copies, and here the New Testament is unusually rich. A scrap of papyrus the size of a credit card, P52 in the John Rylands Library in Manchester, holds a few lines of John 18. It is usually dated by handwriting to about 125–175 CE, though Brent Nongbri has shown that the handwriting alone allows a later date. By about 200 CE the evidence widens: P46, a papyrus book of Paul's letters split between Dublin and Michigan; P66, a nearly complete copy of John; and P75, holding much of Luke and John, now in the Vatican Library. In the 4th century come the great parchment Bibles, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, the second containing the oldest complete New Testament. Altogether more than 5,700 Greek manuscripts are catalogued. Most early New Testament papyri are dated by palaeography, comparing handwriting with dated documents, because radiocarbon testing would destroy precious material. Palaeography gives ranges of 50 to 100 years or more. Scholars such as Pasquale Orsini, Willy Clarysse and Brent Nongbri have argued that some famous papyri were dated too early and too precisely,

chunks.heading: Christianity: 04 Where the copies disagree
chunks.text: Copying by hand produces differences, and the New Testament's many copies record hundreds of thousands of them. Most are trivial: spelling, word order, a dropped article. A few matter, and modern Bibles mark them openly in brackets or footnotes. Mark 16:9–20. The oldest complete manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, end Mark at 16:8, with the women fleeing the empty tomb in fear. The familiar longer ending is missing there, and early writers such as Eusebius knew copies without it. John 7:53–8:11. The story of the woman caught in adultery, with the line about casting the first stone, is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Many scholars think it is an old story that found its way into John later. 1 John 5:7–8, the Comma Johanneum. A sentence naming the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit appears in Latin writers from the late 4th century and in later Latin Bibles, but in only a handful of late Greek manuscripts. Erasmus added it in 1522 and the King James Version kept it. Acts. The form of Acts in Codex Bezae is nearly a tenth longer than the other forms, with added details that may reflect a 2nd-century revision. The New Testament has more variants than any ancient book because it has more copies than any ancient book. Scholars disagree about what this means. Bart Ehrman stresses that early copyists sometimes changed the text for theological reasons. Others, such as the editors of the Nestle-Aland edition, stress how rarely those changes affect meaning and how securely the early text can be reconstructed. Both points can be true at once.

chunks.heading: Christianity: 05 Translated from the start
chunks.text: Christianity is a translated faith in a way few others are. Jesus taught mainly in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee, yet the Gospels were written in Greek. Only a few of his Aramaic words survive in the text, such as "Talitha cum" (Mark 5:41) and his cry from the cross (Mark 15:34). His teaching reaches us, from the beginning, through translation. The first Christians read the Hebrew scriptures mostly in Greek, in the Septuagint made by Jews in Alexandria. By the 2nd century the Gospels were being put into Latin, Syriac and Coptic. Jerome's Latin Vulgate, begun in 382 CE, became the Bible of the Western church for a thousand years. Erasmus printed the Greek New Testament in 1516, and the translations of the Reformation, from Luther's German (1522) to the King James Version (1611), rested on the late Byzantine Greek text he used. Modern translations rest on the older manuscripts found since then.

chunks.heading: Christianity: 06 Which books? The making of the canon
chunks.text: No council in the 1st century issued a list. Around 140 CE Marcion, whom other Christians rejected, proposed a canon of one edited Gospel and ten letters of Paul, and the wider church began to define its own. The Muratorian fragment, a list of accepted books, is usually dated to the late 2nd century, though some scholars argue for the 4th. Some writings, such as Hebrews, James, 2 Peter and Revelation, were debated for generations. In 367 CE Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, listed exactly the 27 books of today's New Testament, and councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) confirmed the list for North Africa. The canon, in other words, is a well-documented historical process, in which believers see the church recognising what God had given. Other early Christian writings were left out. In 1945 farmers near Nag Hammadi in Egypt found a jar of 4th-century Coptic books, among them the Gospel of Thomas, a collection of sayings attributed to Jesus. Greek fragments of Thomas found earlier at Oxyrhynchus date to around 200 CE. Scholars debate whether some of its sayings are as early as those in the canonical Gospels; most date the collection as a whole to the 2nd century. These finds show how varied early Christian writing was, and why the question of which books belonged mattered so much to the communities that decided it.

chunks.heading: Christianity: 07 Jesus in the historical record
chunks.text: Outside the New Testament, the earliest references to Jesus come from writers who had no reason to promote him. Josephus, a Jewish historian writing around 93 CE, mentions James as the brother of Jesus "who was called Christ"; a longer paragraph about Jesus in his work is widely thought to contain later Christian additions around an authentic core. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around 116 CE, explains who the Christians were. Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus. In 1961 archaeologists at Caesarea Maritima found a limestone block naming Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea, the clearest inscription naming him from his own lifetime. An ossuary inscribed with the name of Caiaphas, the high priest of the Gospels, turned up in a Jerusalem tomb in 1990, and an inscription at Delphi dates the Roman governor Gallio, before whom Acts sets Paul on trial, to about 51–52 CE. Together, these sources support what nearly all historians accept: Jesus lived, was baptised by John, gathered followers in Galilee, and was crucified in Jerusalem under Pilate around 30–33 CE. Other matters stay open. The birth stories in Matthew and Luke differ from each other, and Luke's census under Quirinius sits uneasily with Josephus's date of 6 CE. Miracles and the resurrection lie beyond what historians can test; they remain, as they began, matters of faith. What the historical record does show is that the faith's founding documents are close in time to their events and exceptionally well preserved.

chunks.heading: Islam
chunks.text: Arabia Islam A faith founded on a recited book, whose earliest surviving pages were written within decades of the Prophet's lifetime, perhaps within it. 7th century CE. How the tradition sees its text Muslims hold the Quran to be the word of God, revealed in Arabic and protected by God's promise (15:9). Its preservation rests first on memory, an unbroken chain of reciters back to the Prophet, checked against the written codex compiled by the Companions. The accepted readings are understood as revealed ways of reciting the same text, not as corruption.
