What manuscript scholarship shows Radiocarbon and palaeography place many Quran fragments in the 7th century, and the consonantal text of nearly all early manuscripts matches the Uthmanic standard, supporting standardisation around 650 CE. The Sana'a lower text shows that other textual forms circulated before then. Scholars still debate the Abu Bakr collection, the exact date of the archetype, and how to calibrate early radiocarbon dates.

chunks.heading: Islam: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. The Quran is the word of God, revealed to Muhammad through Gabriel (Jibril) over about 23 years. Matter of faith The foundation of Islam. Historians can study when and how the text was written down; the claim that it is God's own speech is a matter of faith and is not rated. Quran 96:1–5; 26:192–195 Muhammad is the last prophet in a line that includes Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Matter of faith Islam sees itself as the restoration of the faith of Abraham, not a new religion. Prophethood is a matter of faith; Muhammad's life as a historical person is rated below. Quran 33:40; 3:84 God has promised to protect the Quran from corruption. Matter of faith Muslims understand this verse as a divine guarantee. The historical record of the text, which can be tested, is set out in the text record below and is kept separate from this promise. Quran 15:9 Muhammad lived in Mecca and Medina and led a community of believers in the early 7th century. Established Christian writers mention him from the 630s onward, Arabic documents and coins name him by the 680s, and a dated calendar counting from his emigration is in use by 643 CE. Hoyland 1997; PERF 558 The Quran was written down and standardised under Caliph Uthman around 650 CE. Strong evidence Radiocarbon-dated manuscripts from the mid-7th century, almost all matching the Uthmanic consonantal text, fit the tradition's account well. Details of the process and its exact date are still discussed. Sadeghi and Goudarzi 2012; Déroche 2014 The Kaaba in Mecca was built by Abraham and Ishmael. Awaiting discovery Mecca's sanctuary cannot be excavated and no pre-Islamic inscription describes its founding. The tradition may preserve old memory, but no physical evidence has been found either way. Quran 2:127 Muhammad was carried by night from Mecca to Jerusalem and ascended through the heavens. Matter of faith The Night Journey and Ascension (al-Isra wa al-Miraj) are central to Muslim devotion and to Jerusalem's place in Islam. They are matters of faith, not rated here. Quran 17:1; Sahih al-Bukhari 3887 The hadith collections preserve Muhammad's words and deeds through reliable chains of narrators. Open question Muslim scholarship built a rigorous system for testing narrators. Western scholars since Goldziher and Schacht have doubted many chains; later work traces some material to the late 7th century. Reliability varies report by report. Brown 2009; Motzki 2002

chunks.heading: Islam: 01 A book meant to be recited
chunks.text: The word qur'an means recitation. Before it was ever a book, the Quran was a voice: verses spoken by Muhammad in Mecca and Medina over some 23 years, repeated by his followers, recited in prayer. Muslim tradition remembers the first words he received, in a cave above Mecca around 610 CE, as a command to recite. Recite in the name of your Lord who created. That origin shapes everything about how Muslims understand their scripture. The Quran is held to be God's own speech, in Arabic, and it lives first in memory. Children learn to recite it; many believers know the whole text by heart, and teachers pass on their recitation through certified chains that reach back, in the tradition's account, to the Prophet himself. Written copies serve the recitation, not the other way round. The same questions apply here as to every tradition. What does the tradition say about how its scripture was kept? What survives on parchment and stone, and how close does it come to the Prophet's lifetime? And what can be said about the historical Muhammad from sources outside the tradition? On several of these points, the answers are unusually strong.

chunks.heading: Islam: 02 The tradition's account of the collection
chunks.text: According to reports preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari and other collections, parts of the Quran were written down during Muhammad's lifetime by scribes such as Zayd ibn Thabit. After his death in 632, many reciters died in battle, and Umar urged Abu Bakr, the first caliph, to gather the whole text. Zayd gathered it from what had been written on palm stalks, thin stones and other materials, and from the memories of those who knew it by heart; the resulting sheets later passed to Umar's daughter Hafsa. Around 650 CE, the third caliph, Uthman, hearing that believers in different provinces recited differently, ordered a committee led by Zayd to produce standard copies from Hafsa's sheets. The copies went to cities such as Kufa, Basra and Damascus, and other codices were to be destroyed. The tradition also remembers that some Companions kept their own codices: that of Ibn Mas'ud is said to have lacked the first and last two surahs and to have differed in wording in places. Indeed, it is We who sent down the message [i.e., the Qur'an], and indeed, We will be its guardian. This is a remarkably detailed account for a 7th-century text, and it is candid about variation. It names the people involved, gives reasons, and admits that other copies once existed. That candour makes it testable.

chunks.heading: Islam: 03 Parchment and radiocarbon
chunks.text: In 2015 the University of Birmingham announced that two parchment leaves in its Mingana collection, containing parts of Surahs 18 to 20, had been radiocarbon dated at Oxford to between 568 and 645 CE with 95.4 percent probability. The range overlaps the Prophet's lifetime. The leaves belong to the same codex as sixteen leaves in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris. Birmingham is not alone. A manuscript in Tübingen (Ma VI 165), containing Surah 17:35 to 36:57, was dated in 2014 to 649–675 CE. The Corpus Coranicum project in Berlin counts more than 60 fragments, with over 2,000 folios, from before 800 CE. Their consonantal text agrees with the standard Quran with very few exceptions. Radiocarbon measures when the animal whose skin became the parchment died, not when the ink went on, and parchment could be stored for years. Specialists such as François Déroche have urged caution, noting that radiocarbon results for some dated Quran manuscripts come out earlier than their written dates. Palaeography, the study of the script and page layout, provides a second, independent check, and here it also points to the 7th century. One recent finding is quietly striking. Marijn van Putten (2019) showed that early manuscripts share the same odd spellings of particular phrases in the same places, such as a special spelling of "the grace of God" in some verses but not others. Oral copying would not preserve such quirks. They suggest that the manuscripts descend from a single written archetype, as the account of Uthman's copies describes. On the question of when the Quran's text was fixed, tradition and manuscript science point to the same few decades.

chunks.heading: Islam: 04 A text beneath the text
chunks.text: In 1972, workers repairing the Great Mosque of Sana'a in Yemen found a cache of old parchment. Among the pages was a palimpsest: a Quran whose first text had been washed off and written over. Under ultraviolet light the lower text can be read. Its upper text is the standard Quran; its lower text is not. One leaf, radiocarbon dated for Behnam Sadeghi and Uwe Bergmann (2010), gave 578–669 CE at 95 percent probability. Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi (2012) edited the lower text and found words and phrases added, missing or replaced, and surahs in an order unlike the standard one, while the verses within each surah largely match. Asma Hilali, who edited the pages in 2017, counted dozens of non-spelling variants and suggested the pages may reflect teaching or practice copies. Here the manuscript evidence and the tradition meet in an unexpected way. Muslim sources had always said that Companions' codices differed before Uthman's standard. The Sana'a lower text looks like exactly such a codex. Sadeghi and Goudarzi argued that comparing it with the standard text supports the view that the Uthmanic version preserves the Prophet's recitation with high accuracy, and that the surahs had taken their shape in his lifetime.

chunks.heading: Islam: 05 Dots, vowels and readings
chunks.text: Early Arabic writing was a skeleton. Several letters shared one shape, told apart by dots, and short vowels were not written at all. The earliest Quran manuscripts use dots sparingly. Tradition credits Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali (d. c. 688) with the first vowel marks and places a fuller system of dotting under the governor al-Hajjaj (694–714); al-Khalil ibn Ahmad (d. c. 786) created the vowel signs used today. Because the skeleton allows more than one reading in places, several recognised ways of reciting it grew up, each carried by a chain of teachers. In the 10th century the scholar Ibn Mujahid defined seven canonical readers; later scholars accepted ten. Most readings differ in small points, such as whether the opening surah calls God "King" (maliki) or "Master" (maaliki) of the Day of Judgement. Today most printed Qurans follow the reading of Hafs from Asim, fixed in the Cairo edition of 1924; the reading of Warsh from Nafi is used across much of North and West Africa. For Muslims, these readings are part of the revelation, not errors that crept in. For historians, they are a well-documented record of how a consonantal text was vocalised. Both descriptions can be held at once.

chunks.heading: Islam: 06 The hadith: sayings and their chains
chunks.text: Beside the Quran stands a second body of text: the hadith, reports of what Muhammad said and did, each with a chain (isnad) of named narrators. Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari (810–870) is said to have travelled widely, examined hundreds of thousands of reports and chosen only a few thousand for his Sahih, completed around 846. Sunni Muslims regard it, with the collection of his contemporary Muslim, as the most authentic body of hadith. Its oldest known manuscript, published by Alphonse Mingana in 1936, dates from around 970–1000 CE, and the oldest complete copy was finished in al-Andalus in 1155. The book itself is well preserved. The harder question is how far each report reaches back. Ignaz Goldziher and Joseph Schacht argued that many chains were created later to give legal opinions authority. Harald Motzki, comparing chains and wording together, traced some material to the late 7th century, and Jonathan Brown has shown how carefully Muslim critics themselves tested narrators. Muslim hadith criticism and modern historical criticism both ask the same question: who reported this, and could they have known? They differ mainly on how much trust the chains deserve. Reliability varies from report to report, which is why this site rates the collections as an open question rather than a single verdict.

chunks.heading: Islam: 07 Muhammad in the eyes of others
chunks.text: Some of the earliest references to Muhammad come from people who did not follow him. A Syriac chronicle by Thomas the Presbyter, copied in a manuscript of 724 now in the British Library, records a battle in February 634 between the Romans and "the Tayyaye of Muhammad" twelve miles east of Gaza. The Greek Doctrina Jacobi, written around 634, speaks of a prophet who had appeared among the Saracens. The Armenian historian Sebeos, in the 660s, describes a merchant named Mahmet who preached the God of Abraham to the Arabs. Documents and stones add dates. A Greek-Arabic papyrus from Egypt, PERF 558, is dated in year 22 of the new era, April 643 CE. A rock inscription near al-Hijr, signed by a man named Zuhayr, is dated to the year Umar died, 24 (644 CE). Coins struck in the 680s carry the phrase "Muhammad is the messenger of God", and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed in 691–692, bears a long mosaic inscription quoting the Quran. Say, "He is Allah, [who is] One, Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, Nor is there to Him any equivalent." In the 1970s some scholars, notably John Wansbrough and, in a different way, Patricia Crone and Michael Cook, argued that the Quran and the traditional story took shape much later than Muslims believe. Their questions sharpened the field, but the 7th-century manuscripts and inscriptions have since pushed the text back to the time tradition gives it. Debate continues over the details of Muhammad's biography, first written down more than a century after his death. On the survival of the Quran's text itself, the evidence and the tradition's account now largely agree.

chunks.heading: Sikhism
chunks.text: Punjab Sikhism A faith born in Punjab around 1500 whose Gurus compiled their own scripture, so manuscripts from their lifetimes still survive today. 15th–17th century CE. How the tradition sees its text The Gurus spoke the divine Word and took care to record it. Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth to separate authentic gurbani from imitations, and the Kartarpur volume is his original. Guru Gobind Singh completed it at Damdama and made it the eternal Guru, and the text has been kept without change since, down to the page layout. What manuscript scholarship shows Scholars agree the record is exceptionally good: manuscripts survive from within the Gurus' lifetimes, compiled by the Gurus themselves. Debates concern details, such as early drafts like MS 1245, the history of the Kartarpur volume, and the Banno additions, not the substance of the text, which is very stable.

chunks.heading: Sikhism: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Guru Nanak received the divine Word and his mission during an experience in the Vein river at Sultanpur, around 1499. Matter of faith Told in the janamsakhis, the traditional life stories of Guru Nanak. The revelation is a matter of faith. Nanak's time at Sultanpur Lodhi in the service of the Lodi administration is accepted by historians in outline. Janamsakhi traditions; McLeod 1968 The Guru Granth Sahib is the living, eternal Guru. Matter of faith The central belief of Sikh practice: the scripture is treated as a living Guru, installed, consulted and honoured. A matter of faith, not rated. The historical act of vesting guruship in the scripture is weighed separately below. Grewal 1990 Guru Nanak lived from 1469 to 1539 and founded a community at Kartarpur on the Ravi. Strong evidence The dates are traditional but widely accepted, and Nanak's own hymns survive in manuscripts copied about 30 years after his death. The janamsakhis mix legend with memory, so details of his life are less secure than the outline. McLeod 1968; Mann 1996 Guru Nanak travelled as far as Mecca and Baghdad. Open question The janamsakhis describe long journeys (udasis) east, south, north and west. Nanak's hymns show wide knowledge of Hindu and Muslim practice, but independent evidence for the western journeys is thin, and a claimed commemorative inscription in Baghdad is disputed. McLeod 1968 Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth and installed it at Harmandir Sahib in 1604. Established Supported by tradition, by the dated Kartarpur manuscript and by closely related early copies. Few ancient scriptures have their compilation so securely placed in time, by name and by place. Mann 2001; Pashaura Singh 2000 Guru Arjan was executed on the orders of the Mughal emperor Jahangir in 1606. Established Recorded in Sikh tradition and, independently, in Jahangir's own memoir, which names Arjan and describes the order against him. The motives and the manner of death are told differently in the two sources. Jahangirnama, trans. W. M. Thackston (1999) Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi, 1699. Strong evidence Central to Sikh memory and accepted by historians. Most detailed accounts of the day were written decades later, so the event is secure while particular details, such as the exact words spoken, are less certain. Grewal 1990; McLeod 1989 In 1708, before his death at Nanded, Guru Gobind Singh declared the scripture to be the Guru. Strong evidence The transfer of gurushi

chunks.heading: Sikhism: 01 A scripture edited by its prophets
chunks.text: For most of the world's scriptures, historians spend their careers trying to close a gap: centuries of silence between the founder and the oldest surviving copy. Sikhism is different. Its scripture was collected by the Gurus themselves, and manuscripts made in their lifetimes survive in Punjab today. The distance between composition and the oldest written witness is measured in years, not centuries. Few religious traditions of any age can say as much, and that makes Sikhism a valuable test case for how well written records can preserve a teaching when the teachers take charge of the writing. Sikhism is also young by the standards of this section. Its founder, Guru Nanak, was born in 1469, and the tradition took its classical form over the next two and a half centuries under ten human Gurus. Today there are about 25 to 30 million Sikhs, most of them in Punjab and across a large diaspora. The distance between composition and the oldest written witness is measured in years, not centuries.

chunks.heading: Sikhism: 02 Guru Nanak and the tradition's own account
chunks.text: Sikh tradition tells how Nanak, working as a storekeeper at Sultanpur Lodhi, went to bathe in the Vein river and disappeared for three days. He returned with a message: there is no Hindu and no Muslim, only the one God before whom all are equal. He travelled widely, sang his hymns with the Muslim musician Mardana, and in his later years settled at Kartarpur on the Ravi, where disciples farmed, worshipped and ate together in a community kitchen, the langar. Before his death in 1539 he passed the guruship not to his sons but to a disciple, Angad. Nine more human Gurus followed. These stories come to us through the janamsakhis, lives of the Guru written down from the 17th century onward. In 1968 the historian W. H. McLeod analysed them and concluded that they combine a core of probable fact with miracle stories and teaching tales. Many Sikh scholars thought him too sceptical, and the debate continues. What is not in doubt is the voice of the hymns themselves, which survive in manuscripts copied within about thirty years of Nanak's death. Ik Onkar, Satnam, Karta Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang, Gur Prasad.

chunks.heading: Sikhism: 03 A scripture that witnessed its age
chunks.text: The hymns are not only devotional poetry; some are eyewitness history. A group of Guru Nanak's compositions, known as the Babarvani, laments the violence of Babur's invasions of Punjab in the 1520s, the campaigns that founded the Mughal empire. They describe the suffering of ordinary people, including women of both Hindu and Muslim families, in a town traditionally identified as Saidpur, today's Eminabad. Babur's own memoir describes his raids into Punjab in these years, though it has a gap for part of the early 1520s, so a Mughal conqueror and a Punjabi poet describe the same era from opposite sides. The scripture is also a record of the religious landscape of north India. Alongside the Gurus it includes verses by bhagats from several centuries and backgrounds: Kabir the weaver of Benares, Namdev the tailor-saint of Maharashtra, Ravidas the leatherworker, and the Sufi Sheikh Farid, who lived about three centuries before Nanak. Its languages range from old Punjabi to Braj and the mixed idiom of the wandering saints, with Persian and Arabic words, all written in the Gurmukhi script the Gurus promoted. A separate collection, the Dasam Granth, is traditionally attributed to Guru Gobind Singh; its authorship is debated, and it does not have the status of the Guru Granth Sahib.

chunks.heading: Sikhism: 04 From pothis to Granth
chunks.text: The first great collection was made in the time of the third Guru, Amar Das, at Goindval on the Beas. The Goindval pothis, a set of manuscript volumes dated to about 1570–72, gather hymns of the first three Gurus and of several bhagats, the Hindu and Muslim saints whose verses the Gurus honoured, arranged by the musical mode in which they were to be sung. Gurinder Singh Mann's study of these volumes in the 1990s showed how much of the later scripture's structure was already in place. The fifth Guru, Arjan, completed the task. Working with the scholar and scribe Bhai Gurdas, he gathered the hymns of the first five Gurus and of saints including Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid, and arranged them by raga and author. In 1604 the finished volume, the Adi Granth, was installed in the newly built Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar, today's Golden Temple. The tradition explains his motive clearly: imitations of the Gurus' hymns were circulating, and an authorised book would separate true gurbani from false. A manuscript known as the Kartarpur Bir, kept by the Sodhi family of Kartarpur, is regarded by Sikhs and many scholars as Guru Arjan's 1604 volume. Scholars who have examined it or its photographs describe several scribal hands and corrections, which fits a working editorial copy. Related manuscripts, the older Goindval pothis and other early copies, allow its contents to be checked. Few scriptures anywhere can be compared with a copy made under the direction of the person who compiled it.

chunks.heading: Sikhism: 05 The Tenth Guru and the Guru Granth
chunks.text: The 17th century brought conflict with Mughal power. Guru Arjan was executed at Lahore in 1606, an event recorded not only by Sikhs but in the emperor Jahangir's own memoir. The ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, was beheaded in Delhi in 1675. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, created the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, at Anandpur on Vaisakhi in 1699. Around 1706, at Damdama Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh prepared a final recension of the scripture, adding his father's hymns and couplets; this Damdama recension is the text in use today. Then, in 1708 at Nanded in the Deccan, shortly before his death, he ended the line of human Gurus and vested guruship in the scripture and the community. From that moment the book was not simply a record of the Gurus' words: it became the Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib. Its standard printed form has 1,430 pages, and a copy is installed and read in every gurdwara.

chunks.heading: Sikhism: 06 What historians still debate
chunks.text: Because the record is so rich, debates focus on details that would be invisible for older scriptures. A manuscript at Guru Nanak Dev University, MS 1245, has been dated by some scholars to about 1599 and read as an early draft showing how hymns were revised before the 1604 edition; others dispute that date and interpretation, and the question sparked a heated controversy in the 1990s. The Banno Bir, a 17th-century line of copies, contains extra passages that mainstream Sikh authority rejects. The physical history of the Kartarpur volume, which has been in private hands for centuries, has also been discussed. How far the janamsakhis preserve reliable memories of Guru Nanak's travels. Whether MS 1245 and similar manuscripts are drafts of the scripture or later copies. How the Banno additions entered part of the manuscript tradition. The exact wording and circumstances of the 1708 transfer of guruship.

chunks.heading: Sikhism: 07 Why this record matters
chunks.text: Set beside the other traditions on this site, the Guru Granth Sahib is a rare case in which the tradition's own account and manuscript scholarship largely agree. Both say the Gurus composed the hymns, that they were gathered in stages from around 1570, compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 and completed by Guru Gobind Singh around 1706. Disagreements concern early drafts and later additions at the margins, not the heart of the text. Its languages and script are still read and sung every day. The later history of the text is also well documented. For about two centuries the scripture was copied by hand, and scribes in different places produced copies that differ mostly in spelling and small details. From the second half of the 19th century printed editions spread, and in the 20th century a standard page layout of 1,430 pages became universal, so that a reference to a given page points to the same words in every gurdwara in the world. Few scriptures have such a uniform modern text with such a short and visible path back to their authors. It also offers a lesson for reading older scriptures. Even here, with autograph-era manuscripts, there are drafts, variant copies and debated additions. Where older texts show larger variation after centuries of copying, that is what the Sikh case would lead us to expect, and it is a reason to value each tradition's early witnesses, not to dismiss them.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith
chunks.text: Iran and the Ottoman Empire Bahá'í Faith The youngest tradition on this site, whose founders' writings survive in their own hands or their secretaries', with almost no gap at all. 1844–1892 CE. How the tradition sees its text Bahá'ís regard the Aqdas as the charter of Bahá'u'lláh's world order. Because it was written down under his eye, reviewed by him and preserved in his lifetime, they see its text as authentic in a way that earlier scriptures, transmitted over centuries, could not be. Authentication is the work of the Universal House of Justice's Research Department. What manuscript scholarship shows Scholars agree the Aqdas is securely dated and attributed, with copies close to the author's lifetime. The main limit is access: the Haifa originals are not published in facsimile or critical edition, so independent comparison relies on copies such as the British Library manuscript, which has been described as highly accurate.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: In the text's own words
chunks.text: Each line rates only what the text itself says, not later dates, commentaries or modern identifications. Bahá'u'lláh is the Manifestation of God for this age, promised by earlier religions. Matter of faith The central belief of the Bahá'í Faith, grounded in Bahá'u'lláh's own writings and in readings of earlier scriptures. It concerns revelation and is not rated. Kitáb-i-Íqán; Kitáb-i-Aqdas The Báb was an independent Messenger of God and the herald of Bahá'u'lláh. Matter of faith Bahá'ís honour the Báb as a Manifestation in his own right. Followers of Subh-i Azal, a rival Bábí leader, read his writings differently. A religious claim, not rated. Persian Bayán; Saiedi 2008 God is one, the religions are one in origin, and humanity is one. Matter of faith The three 'onenesses' that summarise Bahá'í teaching. They concern the divine and the moral order, so they are not rated here. Gleanings CXVII; Smith 2008 Bahá'u'lláh first became aware of his mission in the Síyáh-Chál dungeon of Tehran in 1852. Matter of faith The imprisonment itself is historical: Bábís were jailed after an attempt on the Shah's life in August 1852. The experience of revelation Bahá'u'lláh later described is a matter of faith. Bahá'u'lláh, Epistle to the Son of the Wolf; Cole 1998 The Báb announced his mission to Mullá Husayn in Shiraz in May 1844. Strong evidence Early Bábí and later Bahá'í sources agree on the event and the evening of 22–23 May 1844. Its details come from followers, but the rapid rise of the Bábí movement from 1844 is well documented in Persian and European sources. Amanat 1989; MacEoin 1992 The founders' writings survive in their original form, unlike earlier scriptures. Strong evidence The Báb's and Bahá'u'lláh's writings were recorded in their lifetimes, often by their own hands or trusted secretaries, and many originals are held in Haifa. Independent scholars have limited access to those archives, and no full critical editions have been published. MacEoin 1992; Smith 2008 Bahá'u'lláh wrote to the kings and rulers of his time, calling them to justice. Strong evidence Tablets addressed to Napoleon III, Queen Victoria, Pope Pius IX, Tsar Alexander II and Nasir al-Din Shah survive in Bahá'í collections and early copies. Whether each letter was delivered is less certain; the Shah's courier Badí' was executed in 1869. Smith 2008; Cole 1998 Bahá'u'lláh's writings foretold specific political events. Matter of faith Bahá'ís read passages, such as the tablet to Napoleon III, as prophecies that were fulfilled. Whether they are prophecy is a matter of faith; the dates of the tab

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: 01 The shortest gap on this site
chunks.text: Most of the scriptures on this site cross centuries, sometimes millennia, between the moment of composition and the oldest copy we can hold. The Bahá'í Faith is different. Its founders lived in the age of steamships and consular reports; their words were written down as they spoke them, many originals survive, and the gap between composition and the oldest surviving copy is close to zero. For a project that rates texts by how well their record has been kept, the Bahá'í writings are a benchmark of what a very short gap looks like, and a reminder that a short gap does not answer every question. The Bahá'í Faith has about eight million followers according to the World Religion Database (2020) and its own governing body, the Universal House of Justice, with communities in almost every country. Its world centre is on Mount Carmel in Haifa and near Acre, in Israel, where the shrines of its founders stand amid terraced gardens inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2008. Claims about God, revelation and the station of the Báb and Bahá'u'lláh are matters of faith and are not rated. Claims about events, dates, exiles and manuscripts are rated on the evidence. The texts are scored only on how well their record survives, never on whether their teaching is true.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: 02 The Báb: a gate in Shiraz
chunks.text: On the evening of 22 May 1844, in Shiraz, a young merchant named Siyyid 'Alí-Muhammad told a visiting scholar, Mullá Husayn, that he was the Báb, the 'Gate' to the hidden Twelfth Imam expected in Shi'i Islam. His claim soon grew larger: he presented himself as the bearer of a new revelation, with new laws and a new holy book. Within a few years his followers, the Bábís, numbered by some estimates in the tens of thousands, and the Persian state and clergy moved against them. The Báb spent most of his remaining years in prison, first at Mákú and then at Chihríq in the far northwest of Iran. There he dictated a flood of writings, among them the Persian Bayán, planned in 19 sections of 19 chapters but left unfinished. His secretary, Siyyid Husayn Yazdí, wrote down the verses as he spoke, and, according to Denis MacEoin's survey of Bábí sources, that original dictation copy is now kept in the Bahá'í archives in Haifa. On 9 July 1850 the Báb was executed by firing squad in Tabriz, an event recorded by Persian chroniclers and European diplomats alike. Bábí uprisings and their suppression cost several thousand lives.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: 03 Bahá'u'lláh: prison, exile and a torrent of words
chunks.text: Among the Báb's followers was a Tehran nobleman, Mírzá Husayn-'Alí Núrí, who took the title Bahá'u'lláh, 'the Glory of God'. After Bábís attempted to kill the Shah in 1852, he was thrown into the Síyáh-Chál, an underground dungeon, where, he later wrote, he first became aware of his mission. Released and exiled, he spent the rest of his life as a prisoner of two empires: Baghdad from 1853, Constantinople and Edirne from 1863, and from 1868 the Ottoman prison city of Acre. In 1863, before leaving Baghdad, he declared to companions that he was the one the Báb had foretold. In April 1890 the Cambridge scholar Edward Granville Browne was admitted to see him at the mansion of Bahjí, near Acre, and left one of the most quoted descriptions in the study of religion. The face of him on whom I gazed I can never forget, though I cannot describe it. Bahá'u'lláh died at Bahjí in 1892. His son 'Abdu'l-Bahá, then his great-grandson Shoghi Effendi, led the community, and since 1963 it has been governed by the elected Universal House of Justice.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: 04 How the words were written
chunks.text: Bahá'u'lláh rarely wrote his major works himself. He dictated, often at great speed, to his secretary Mírzá Áqá Ján, who developed a rapid shorthand called 'revelation writing'. These drafts were then written out in fair copies, which Bahá'u'lláh reviewed and approved. Trusted transcribers such as Zaynu'l-Muqarrabín made further copies known for their accuracy. By one estimate cited in Bahá'í sources, more than 7,000 of perhaps 15,000 tablets have been collected, and the Bahá'í World Centre holds the revelation drafts and many transcriptions in the International Bahá'í Archives in Haifa. The record also includes a deliberate loss. Mírzá Áqá Ján reported that in Baghdad Bahá'u'lláh ordered a great quantity of verses destroyed and thrown into the river, because he judged that people were not ready for them. Few scriptures include a founder's own decision about what not to keep. The earth is but one country, and mankind its citizens. Here the question is not whether an original survives, but who may study it.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: 05 The Most Holy Book, from 1873 to 1992
chunks.text: The Kitáb-i-Aqdas, written in Arabic in Acre around 1873, contains the laws and institutions of the new faith. Bahá'u'lláh answered believers' questions about it in a supplementary text, and in 1890–91 had it printed in Bombay. A copy in the hand of Zaynu'l-Muqarrabín, dated January 1887, is in the British Library, which describes his copies as highly regarded for their accuracy. That gives us an independently accessible witness only fourteen years after composition. The first duty prescribed by God for His servants is the recognition of Him Who is the Dayspring of His Revelation and the Fountain of His laws. The English story is longer. Scholars Earl Elder and William Miller published an unauthorised translation in 1961 through the Royal Asiatic Society. The Bahá'í authorities issued a synopsis in 1973 and the full authorised translation, with notes and the 'Questions and Answers', only in 1992. The long delay reflects the care the community gives to authorised translation, and also shows that for most readers the text reached them through a translation more than a century after it was written.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: 06 Where the record is debated
chunks.text: A short gap does not end all debate. After the Báb's death the Bábí community divided between Bahá'u'lláh and his half-brother Subh-i Azal, whom many Bábís had recognised as leader. The two factions, Bahá'ís and Azalís, copied the same early texts and each has accused the other of suppressing or altering some writings. E. G. Browne, who corresponded with both sides, became involved in a bitter controversy over an early Bábí history. Denis MacEoin's 1992 survey lists dozens of manuscripts of the Báb's works and stresses that critical editions are still lacking. There is also the question of access. The originals held in Haifa are, in the tradition's view, the best witnesses of all; but they have not been published in facsimile or critical editions, so outside scholars cannot yet test every reading. Bahá'í scholars, and academics such as Nader Saiedi and Juan Cole, have nevertheless produced detailed studies, and the documented history of revisions, such as Bahá'u'lláh correcting Quranic quotations in the Kitáb-i-Íqán, is unusually open about how the texts were shaped. One feature of the tradition limits disputes over meaning, if not over wording. Bahá'u'lláh named his son 'Abdu'l-Bahá as the authorised interpreter of his writings, and 'Abdu'l-Bahá in turn appointed Shoghi Effendi. Their interpretations, and Shoghi Effendi's English translations, which set the elevated style most English readers know, are treated as authoritative. Historians note that this chain of appointed interpreters is itself carefully documented in the founders' wills and letters, one more way in which this young faith recorded its own formation.

chunks.heading: Bahá'í Faith: 07 What remains open
chunks.text: The Bahá'í record raises a new kind of question for this site. For ancient texts we ask whether any early copy survives. Here the early copies exist, and the open question is when they will be available for full scholarly comparison. Publication of facsimiles or critical editions of the Aqdas, the Íqán and the Bayán would allow scholars to measure the stability of the text directly, and to settle the old factional disputes. Until then, the Bahá'í writings stand as the best-documented scriptural origins on this site, recorded within living memory and still, in part, waiting to be read by outside eyes.

chunks.heading: The Earth and Moon are born
chunks.text: Precambrian · Hadean The Earth and Moon are born c. 4.567–4.4 billion years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Precambrian · Hadean The Earth and Moon are born c. 4.567–4.4 billion years ago The claim: Strong evidence A young planet was struck by another world about the size of Mars, and from the glowing debris the Moon was born. The claim on the scales The Moon formed when a Mars-sized planet collided with the young Earth. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established The giant-impact idea explains the Moon's small iron core, its dry rocks, the fast spin of the Earth-Moon pair, and the near identical isotopes of lunar and Earth rocks. Simulations since 2001 can make a Moon this way. The main puzzle is that the Moon is almost too similar to Earth, which has pushed researchers toward variants: a more violent impact, a well-mixed debris cloud, or an impactor born near Earth. Still open Theia's size, speed and birthplace are still debated, and so is the Moon's exact age, with estimates spread over more than 100 million years. A 2023 study proposed that pieces of Theia survive as two continent-sized blobs deep in Earth's mantle. That idea is new and far from confirmed. chunks.heading: The first oceans and a cool early Earth
chunks.text: Precambrian · Hadean The first oceans and a cool early Earth c. 4.4–4.0 billion years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Precambrian · Hadean The first oceans and a cool early Earth c. 4.4–4.0 billion years ago The claim: Strong evidence Zircon grains thinner than a hair hint that Earth had liquid water within a few hundred million years of its birth. The claim on the scales Liquid water existed at Earth's surface within about 300 million years of the planet's formation. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Two teams in 2001 found heavy oxygen in Jack Hills zircons about 4.4 to 4.3 billion years old, a signature of rock altered by liquid water near the surface before it melted. Later atom-probe work showed the ages are not artefacts of lead moving inside the crystals. The case still rests on rare grains from a small part of Western Australia, which is why it is strong rather than settled. Still open How large were the oceans, and was there land above them? Some researchers picture a water world with a few volcanic islands; others argue for continents and even plate tectonics by 4.4 billion years ago. The oldest grains come mostly from one Australian range, so they may not speak for the whole planet. chunks.heading: The Late Heavy Bombardment
chunks.text: Precambrian · Hadean to Eoarchean The Late Heavy Bombardment c. 4.1–3.8 billion years ago The claim: Open question. Precambrian · Hadean to Eoarchean The Late Heavy Bombardment c. 4.1–3.8 billion years ago The claim: Open question The Moon's scarred face was read as a sudden storm of asteroids. Rocks from its far side now suggest a long, slow decline instead. The claim on the scales A sudden spike of impacts, a 'lunar cataclysm', struck the inner Solar System about 3.9 billion years ago. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established The spike rests on Apollo rock ages clustering near 3.9 billion years. But the Apollo and Luna landings were all on the near side, close to the huge Imbrium basin, whose debris may have reset many of those clocks. Boehnke and Harrison (2016) showed how partial resetting of argon ages can create an illusory spike. Far-side Chang'e-6 melts published in 2026 spread over three billion years, favouring a gradual decline. Still open Was there a smaller, later bump in impacts, perhaps driven by the giant planets shifting orbits as in the Nice model, or only a smooth decline after the planets formed? How old are the big lunar basins, and how often was the early Earth hit? The answers change when life could first have settled in. chunks.heading: The faint young Sun paradox
chunks.text: Precambrian · Archean The faint young Sun paradox c. 4.0–2.5 billion years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Precambrian · Archean The faint young Sun paradox c. 4.0–2.5 billion years ago The claim: Strong evidence The young Sun shone roughly a quarter weaker than today, enough to freeze the oceans, yet the rocks record liquid water. Something kept Earth warm. The claim on the scales A stronger greenhouse, mainly carbon dioxide and methane, kept the young Earth from freezing under a faint Sun. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established The Sun's early faintness follows from well-tested stellar physics, and the rocks record liquid water, so extra warming is needed. Climate models reviewed by Feulner (2012) and Charnay and colleagues (2020) find that carbon dioxide at many times today's level, plus methane, can do the job within the limits set by ancient soils and minerals. Other factors, such as fewer clouds or less land, probably helped. Still open How much carbon dioxide was really in the air is poorly pinned down, because estimates from ancient soils and minerals disagree. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The timing fits: oxygen began rising around 2.46–2.43 billion years ago, and Warke and colleagues (2020) found this came before the most widespread Huronian glaciation. Precambrian · Late Paleoproterozoic to early Neoproterozoic The Boring Billion c. 1.8–0.8 billion years ago The claim: Mixed record For a billion years the climate barely changed and oxygen stayed low. Beneath the calm, complex cells, sex and many-celled life were quietly invented. The claim on the scales Little of importance happened on Earth during the 'Boring Billion'. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established The 'boring' label fits the climate and chemistry: carbon isotopes stayed flat, no major ice ages are known, and oxygen stayed low for hundreds of millions of years. Fossils and chemical traces show eukaryotes diversifying, the first multicellular forms, the first red algae and early evidence of sex, while supercontinents assembled and broke apart. Precambrian · Cryogenian Snowball Earth c. 717–635 million years ago The claim: Plausible Twice, glaciers reached the tropics at sea level. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established Glacial deposits formed near the equator at sea level, at the same times on many continents, and are capped by carbonates that suggest an abrupt, extreme greenhouse afterwards. A nearly frozen ocean explains these features neatly (Hoffman and colleagues, 1998 and 2017). chunks.text: Paleozoic · Early to Middle Cambrian The Cambrian Explosion c. 539–515 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Paleozoic · Early to Middle Cambrian The Cambrian Explosion c. 539–515 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence In a few tens of millions of years the seas filled with animals that could see, hunt, burrow and armour themselves. The claim on the scales The Cambrian explosion was a real burst of evolution, not just a burst in fossil preservation. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Several independent records change together. Body fossils, shelly fossils and trace fossils (burrows and tracks, which do not depend on unusual preservation) all diversify quickly and in step across many continents. Soft-bodied sites such as Chengjiang and the Burgess Shale show the same flowering among animals without shells. But molecular clocks and Ediacaran fossils point to deeper animal roots, so the explosion was of large, active, skeletal animals, not of animals from nothing. Still open Why it happened then is still debated: rising oxygen, predator and prey arms races, genetic toolkits for building bodies, and changing seawater chemistry are all candidates, probably working together. How long the fuse was is also argued. Wood and colleagues (2019) see a longer, stepwise radiation beginning in the late Ediacaran rather than one sharp burst. Paleozoic · Ordovician The Great Ordovician Biodiversification c. 485–445 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence Seas filled with reefs, shellfish and squid-like hunters, while the first tiny plants crept onto bare rock. The claim on the scales Plants were already growing on land by about 470 million years ago. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established The evidence is spores, not whole plants, but they are distinctive: thick walls of the resistant polymer sporopollenin, often in fours (tetrads), with wall structure matching that of living liverworts. They appear in Argentina around 470 million years ago and soon afterwards in many regions, in sediments laid down near land. Molecular clocks agree that land plants existed by then, and some place their origin even earlier. Still open Whether plants reached land earlier, in the Cambrian as some molecular clocks suggest, is unresolved because no fossils confirm it. What these first plants looked like is largely unknown. Also debated: whether cooling seas, rising oxygen, or even dust from an asteroid break-up about 466 million years ago helped drive the marine boom. Paleozoic · Late Ordovician (Hirnantian) The First Great Extinction c. 445–443 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence Ice spread over the South Pole, seas cooled and drained from the continents, and most species in the ocean vanished in two blows. The claim on the scales An ice age caused the first great mass extinction. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established The first and larger pulse coincides with the onset of the Hirnantian glaciation, recorded by glacial deposits in North Africa and South America, falling sea level and cooling measured in fossil shells. Models of how cooling and shrinking shelf habitat would affect marine animals reproduce much of the observed pattern (Saupe et al. 2020). But low oxygen, and possibly volcanism, clearly played roles, especially in the second pulse, so cooling was central but not the whole story. Still open A minority view argues that volcanism, warming and ocean anoxia were the main killers rather than cooling (Bond & Grasby 2020). Paleozoic · Silurian Life Climbs onto Land c. 443–419 million years ago The claim: Open question Forests were still far off, but ankle-high plants and the first air-breathing animals began to colonise the shores. The claim on the scales Animals were already living on land more than 425 million years ago. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established The key fossil, the millipede Pneumodesmus from Scotland, has spiracles, openings for breathing air, so it clearly lived on land. The problem is its age. It was first placed at about 428 million years; zircon dating in 2017 suggested about 414 million; a 2023 study argued again for about 430 million; and a 2025 review favours the latest Silurian to earliest Devonian. Older tracks hint that arthropods visited shores earlier, but visiting is not living there. chunks.text: Paleozoic · Devonian The First Forests c. 419–359 million years ago The claim: Plausible. Paleozoic · Devonian The First Forests c. 419–359 million years ago The claim: Plausible Plants grew into trees, roots cracked rock into soil, and the air began to change as the first forests spread. The claim on the scales The spread of the first forests pulled carbon dioxide out of the air and helped push Earth toward an ice age. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established The timing fits: carbon dioxide proxies fall across the Devonian and into the Carboniferous as forests with deep roots spread, and glaciation followed. Fossil soils show deeper rooting and stronger chemical weathering, and models of the carbon cycle reproduce a large drawdown when forests are added. But tectonics also changed, and some modelling (Goddéris et al. 2017) attributes most of the cooling to mountain building and rock weathering rather than to plants, so the size of the forest effect is uncertain. Still open How much carbon dioxide fell, and how fast, depends on proxies with large uncertainties. Researchers still argue about whether plants or tectonics did most of the work, and about how forest expansion connects to the ocean anoxia and extinctions of the Late Devonian. The oldest forests keep getting older as new sites are found, most recently in England in 2024. Paleozoic · Middle to Late Devonian Fish Walk Ashore c. 395–360 million years ago The claim: Plausible In weedy shallows beside the first forests, fish grew necks, wrists and fingers, and the ancestors of all land vertebrates took their first steps. Paleozoic · Late Devonian (Frasnian to Famennian, end-Devonian) The Late Devonian Crises c. 372 and 359 million years ago The claim: Open question Two waves of extinction, thirteen million years apart, destroyed the greatest reefs of the age and reset the story of backboned animals. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established The idea fits the timing: forests with deep roots expanded, releasing nutrients that could have fed algal blooms and oxygen-poor water, and black shales mark anoxia at both crises (Algeo & Scheckler 1998). But volcanism, including the Viluy traps of Siberia dated close to the Kellwasser event, cooling and glaciation, and even ultraviolet damage are strong competitors, so no single cause is agreed. Paleozoic · Carboniferous The Coal Forests c. 359–299 million years ago The claim: Plausible Steaming swamp forests buried so much carbon that they changed the air, fed giant insects, and later powered the Industrial Revolution. The claim on the scales Oxygen once reached about 35% and made giant insects possible. Paleozoic · Mississippian to early Permian The Late Paleozoic Ice Age c. 340–285 million years ago (main glacial phase) The claim: Mixed record Ice sheets came and went over the southern continents for tens of millions of years, and the tropical coal forests broke apart. The claim on the scales The collapse of the coal rainforests about 305 million years ago was a mass extinction on land. Paleozoic · Permian Pangaea and the Rise of Our Ancestors c. 299–252 million years ago The claim: Established Nearly all land joined into one supercontinent, its heart turned to desert, and the ancestors of mammals ruled the land. The claim on the scales Dimetrodon, the sail-backed 'dinosaur' of toy boxes, was more closely related to us than to any dinosaur. Weight of evidence Established Ruled out Established Dimetrodon lived at least 40 million years before the first dinosaurs. Its skull has a single opening behind each eye, the defining feature of synapsids, the lineage that leads to mammals. Its teeth came in different sizes, an early step toward our differentiated teeth. Anatomy, the fossil sequence through therapsids and cynodonts, and every modern family tree place it on the mammal side of the split with reptiles, including dinosaurs. Still open What Dimetrodon's sail was for (heat regulation, display, or both) is still debated. So is the exact pattern of Permian climate change and how strongly the harsh interior climate shaped where animals could live. The timing of the split between synapsids and reptiles has been pushed back by new trackway finds, which remain under discussion. Paleozoic · End-Permian (Changhsingian to earliest Triassic) The Great Dying c. 252 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence Siberian volcanoes poured out carbon, the oceans overheated and lost their oxygen, and most species in the sea disappeared. The claim on the scales Volcanic eruptions in Siberia caused the Great Dying. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established High-precision dating shows the main Siberian Traps activity, especially the intrusion of magma sills into carbon-rich rocks, began shortly before and overlapped the extinction (Burgess & Bowring 2015). Mesozoic · Early to Late Triassic Life Recovers from the Great Dying c. 251–230 million years ago The claim: Ruled out After the worst extinction in Earth's history, a scorched supercontinent slowly refilled with life, and among the survivors walked the ancestors of dinosaurs and mammals. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established Early dinosaurs are well dated to about 231 million years ago in Argentina, and they are a minority in those beds. Dinosaurs became dominant only later, after the Carnian crisis and especially after the end-Triassic extinction. The idea that they took over at once does not fit the record. Footprints from Poland and the Tanzanian fossil Nyasasaurus hint at dinosaur relatives about 243 to 250 million years ago, but their identity is disputed. Why recovery took so long, whether through repeated heat and carbon pulses or lingering low-oxygen seas, also remains open. Mesozoic · Late Triassic (Carnian) The Carnian Rains c. 234–232 million years ago The claim: Plausible In the middle of the dry Triassic, the skies opened for a million years or more, and dinosaurs emerged from the wetter world that followed. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established Dinosaur footprints in the Dolomites become common just after the episode (Bernardi et al. 2018), and body fossils show dinosaurs becoming more varied in the later Carnian and Norian. But early dinosaur fossils are loosely dated, and some analyses find dinosaur-line diversity rising faster at other times. The link is reasonable, not firmly established. Still open How closely the Wrangellia eruptions match the wet pulses in time, and whether there were several separate pulses, is still being worked out. Whether the rains were the decisive push for dinosaurs, or one factor among several including the end-Triassic extinction, remains debated. chunks.heading: The End-Triassic Extinction
chunks.text: Mesozoic · Triassic-Jurassic boundary The End-Triassic Extinction c. 201.5 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Mesozoic · Triassic-Jurassic boundary The End-Triassic Extinction c. 201.5 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence As Pangaea began to split, lava flooded parts of four future continents, and in the upheaval that followed, the dinosaurs inherited the land. The claim on the scales Volcanic eruptions from the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province caused the end-Triassic extinction. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established High-precision zircon dates place the oldest lava pulses at the extinction horizon, within the limits of the method (Blackburn et al. 2013). Carbon-isotope swings, a rise in carbon dioxide in fossil soils, signs of acidification and mercury spikes in many sections all fit a volcanic trigger. Gas-rich bubbles show the magma carried large amounts of carbon dioxide (Capriolo et al. 2020). No known impact matches the date. Details of the kill mechanism are still argued. Still open Which gases did the most harm, carbon dioxide warming, sulfur cooling or both, is still debated, as is how quickly the extinction unfolded; some records suggest tens of thousands of years or less. Why dinosaurs came through while their crocodile-line rivals did not remains an open question. Rift valleys opened between what are now North America, Africa and South America, filling with lakes and sediment. Then, around 201.5 million years ago, the crust gave way to magma. chunks.heading: Jurassic Giants in a Greenhouse World
chunks.text: Mesozoic · Jurassic Jurassic Giants in a Greenhouse World c. 201–145 million years ago The claim: Established. Mesozoic · Jurassic Jurassic Giants in a Greenhouse World c. 201–145 million years ago The claim: Established Long-necked sauropods, the largest animals ever to walk, browsed conifer forests as Pangaea split and warm, shallow seas crept over the land. The claim on the scales Sauropods were the largest animals ever to walk on land. Weight of evidence Established Ruled out Established Limb bones, vertebrae and complete skeletons from several continents show sauropods far larger than any land mammal, including the giant hornless rhinos of later times. Mass estimates for individual species vary widely, because the largest are known from partial skeletons, but even conservative estimates for the biggest sauropods exceed any other land animal. Only whales, supported by water, have been larger. Still open How sauropods grew so big and shed heat from such huge bodies is still debated, as are their exact masses. When exactly the Atlantic first opened, and how high Jurassic carbon dioxide rose, also carry wide uncertainty. Rifts widened into seas. The central Atlantic was born as a long, narrow gulf between North America and Africa, and shallow seas flooded large parts of Europe. chunks.heading: Feathered Dinosaurs and the First Birds
chunks.text: Mesozoic · Middle to Late Jurassic Feathered Dinosaurs and the First Birds c. 165–150 million years ago The claim: Established. Mesozoic · Middle to Late Jurassic Feathered Dinosaurs and the First Birds c. 165–150 million years ago The claim: Established Feathers came before flight, and the line between dinosaur and bird blurred so completely that birds are now counted as living dinosaurs. The claim on the scales Birds are living dinosaurs. Weight of evidence Established Ruled out Established Hundreds of anatomical features, analysed in many independent studies, place birds inside the theropod dinosaurs, close to troodontids and dromaeosaurs. Feathers, wishbones, hollow air-filled bones, brooding postures and bird-like eggs all appear in non-bird dinosaurs. Transitional fossils such as Anchiornis and Archaeopteryx fill the gap. The conclusion rests on several lines of evidence that agree. Still open Where exactly the line between bird and non-bird dinosaur falls is debated, since Anchiornis and Archaeopteryx sit close to it. How flight began, from the ground up or the trees down, and how well Archaeopteryx could fly, remain open. A 2025 study of the Chicago Archaeopteryx added new clues about its wings and feet (O'Connor et al. 2025). That same year a skeleton turned up with feathered wings, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. chunks.heading: Flowers Take Over the World
chunks.text: Mesozoic · Early to Late Cretaceous Flowers Take Over the World c. 140–90 million years ago The claim: Open question. Mesozoic · Early to Late Cretaceous Flowers Take Over the World c. 140–90 million years ago The claim: Open question Darwin called their sudden rise an abominable mystery. In some 50 million years, flowering plants went from rare newcomers to rulers of the green world. The claim on the scales Flowering plants originated long before their first fossils, in the Jurassic or earlier. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established Unambiguous flowering-plant fossils, especially distinctive pollen, begin about 135 million years ago and grow steadily more common. Some molecular clock studies put the origin near 140 million years ago (Magallón et al. 2015), close to the fossils, while others place it in the Jurassic or Triassic (Barba-Montoya et al. 2018). Claimed Jurassic flowers remain disputed. The two kinds of evidence have not yet been reconciled. Still open When and where flowering plants first evolved, and from which seed-plant ancestors, is unresolved. The Chinese fossil Nanjinganthus, described as Jurassic, is disputed. Why they spread so fast, through faster growth, insect partners or repeated doublings of their genomes, is still debated. chunks.heading: The Cretaceous Hothouse
chunks.text: Mesozoic · Mid to Late Cretaceous The Cretaceous Hothouse c. 120–80 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Mesozoic · Mid to Late Cretaceous The Cretaceous Hothouse c. 120–80 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence No ice at the poles, forests near the North Pole, and seas so high that a shallow ocean cut North America in two. The claim on the scales At its peak, the Cretaceous hothouse had no permanent polar ice sheets. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Fossil forests, polar dinosaurs and warm-water plankton at high latitudes, together with oxygen-isotope and molecular temperature records, point to warm poles and no lasting ice at peak warmth. A proposed short-lived ice sheet around 91 million years ago (Bornemann et al. 2008) has been questioned by later work (Huber et al. 2018). Small mountain glaciers cannot be excluded, but large ice sheets do not fit the evidence. Still open How high carbon dioxide rose, how hot the tropics became (some proxies suggest well above 35 °C), and why the poles were so warm with such a small pole-to-equator temperature difference are still debated. Sea-level estimates differ by more than 100 m depending on method. That was Earth for much of the mid-Cretaceous. Between about 120 and 80 million years ago, and especially around 94 million years ago, the planet ran hotter than in almost any later time. chunks.heading: Chicxulub: The Day the Dinosaurs Died
chunks.text: Mesozoic · Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary Chicxulub: The Day the Dinosaurs Died c. 66 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Mesozoic · Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary Chicxulub: The Day the Dinosaurs Died c. 66 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence A rock about 10 kilometres across struck the Yucatán, darkened the sky and ended the age of dinosaurs in a geological instant. The claim on the scales An asteroid impact was the main cause of the dinosaurs' extinction. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Iridium, shocked quartz, melt spherules and tsunami deposits sit at the same thin layer worldwide, the crater is dated to the boundary, and extinctions in well-sampled sections are abrupt at that layer. Precise dating shows major Deccan eruptions both before and after the impact, but studies combining climate models and fossil patterns find the impact best explains the extinction (Hull et al. 2020). Some researchers still give volcanism a larger role. Still open How much the Deccan Traps contributed remains debated: precise dates show major eruptions both before and after the impact (Schoene et al. 2019; Sprain et al. 2019). Whether dinosaurs were already declining beforehand, and exactly how long the darkness lasted, are also still argued. chunks.heading: Mammals Inherit the Earth
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Paleocene Mammals Inherit the Earth c. 66–56 million years ago The claim: Mixed record. Cenozoic · Paleocene Mammals Inherit the Earth c. 66–56 million years ago The claim: Mixed record With the dinosaurs gone, small mammals grew, multiplied and spread, while a giant snake hunted in one of the first true tropical rainforests. The claim on the scales Mammals only began to flourish after the dinosaurs died out. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established Jurassic and Cretaceous mammals were already varied: there were gliders, swimmers, diggers and even Repenomamus, which ate small dinosaurs. Molecular clocks suggest several modern mammal lineages split before the impact. But body size, numbers of species and ecological range jumped after it, as Corral Bluffs shows (Lyson et al. 2019), with maximum body size rising sharply (Smith et al. 2010). The claim is half right. Still open How many placental mammal lineages crossed the boundary, and how quickly the modern orders arose, is still debated between fossil and molecular evidence. Whether Titanoboa's size really records hotter tropics is contested. How tropical forests coped with such heat is also an open question. The full story 2 min read · 398 words · 0 animated drawings The morning after Snapshots from Corral Bluffs A primate relative at the dawn Tropical giants 01 The morning after In the first years after the impact, the world was dark, cold and then hot, and food webs collapsed. The mammals that survived were mostly small, able to eat insects, seeds or whatever else they found. What happened next was one of the most important radiations in the history of life, and fossil sites in the American West capture it almost step by step. chunks.heading: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Paleocene-Eocene boundary The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum c. 56 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Cenozoic · Paleocene-Eocene boundary The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum c. 56 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence In a geological blink, a vast release of carbon warmed the planet by several degrees, acidified the oceans and reshuffled life on land. The claim on the scales Humans are releasing carbon faster than during the PETM. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Modelling of how fast the carbon-isotope signal and ocean chemistry changed suggests the PETM onset took at least about 4,000 years, with release rates of no more than about 1.1 billion tonnes of carbon a year (Zeebe et al. 2016). Human emissions are roughly ten times that. One study argued for a much faster onset of about 13 years, but most researchers reject that reading. Age models still carry uncertainty. Still open The source of the carbon, whether volcanoes, methane from seafloor ice, thawing permafrost or burning peat, is still debated, as are the total amount and exact length of the onset. How ecosystems will respond to a faster, shorter human pulse is uncertain. The full story 2 min read · 401 words · 0 animated drawings A spike in the record Acid seas and dwarf horses A northern arrival Then and now 01 A spike in the record About 56 million years ago, an already warm Earth warmed sharply. In deep-sea cores, the chemistry of fossil shells shows a sudden plunge in carbon-13, the signature of a huge pulse of light carbon entering the oceans and air. Temperatures climbed by around 5 °C or more. This event, the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum or PETM, now marks the official start of the Eocene epoch. chunks.heading: Arctic Forests and the Eocene Hothouse
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Early to Middle Eocene Arctic Forests and the Eocene Hothouse c. 53–40 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Cenozoic · Early to Middle Eocene Arctic Forests and the Eocene Hothouse c. 53–40 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence Alligator relatives basked in the Arctic, a floating fern carpeted a polar sea, and early whales waded out from the shores of the Tethys. The claim on the scales The Arctic had a warm, nearly frost-free climate in the Eocene. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Alligator relatives, which cannot survive long hard freezes, lived on Ellesmere Island, alongside turtles and broad-leaved forests (Eberle and Greenwood 2012). Leaf shapes, fossil soils and Arctic Ocean temperature proxies agree on mild conditions, with winters close to or just above freezing. The Azolla blooms point to a warm, fresh surface ocean. Several independent lines point the same way. Still open How the poles stayed so warm while the tropics did not overheat still puzzles climate models, which tend to underestimate polar warmth. How much the Azolla blooms drew down carbon, and what drove the long Eocene cooling (falling carbon dioxide, changing ocean gateways or mountain building), are debated. chunks.heading: Antarctica Freezes Over
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Eocene-Oligocene transition Antarctica Freezes Over c. 34 million years ago The claim: Mixed record. Cenozoic · Eocene-Oligocene transition Antarctica Freezes Over c. 34 million years ago The claim: Mixed record Within a few hundred thousand years, ice spread across Antarctica and Earth entered the cold state we still live in today. The claim on the scales The opening of ocean gateways around Antarctica, rather than falling carbon dioxide, froze the continent. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established The gateway idea has real support: a current circling Antarctica would isolate it from warm water, and both passages opened around this time. But their exact timing is uncertain, and models find gateways alone struggle to build a large ice sheet, while falling carbon dioxide can (DeConto and Pollard 2003). Boron-isotope records show carbon dioxide declining across the transition (Pearson et al. 2009). Most recent reviews see carbon dioxide as the main driver, with gateways helping (Hutchinson et al. 2021). Still open When the Drake Passage opened deeply enough to carry a strong circumpolar current is still uncertain, with estimates spread over millions of years. How big the first ice sheet was, and why carbon dioxide fell, through weathering, carbon burial or reduced volcanism, remain debated. chunks.heading: The Age of Grass
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Miocene The Age of Grass c. 23–5.3 million years ago The claim: Mixed record. Cenozoic · Miocene The Age of Grass c. 23–5.3 million years ago The claim: Mixed record A warm world cooled, grass conquered the continents, and apes spread from Africa into Eurasia, setting the stage for our own family. The claim on the scales Falling carbon dioxide was the main reason grasslands spread in the late Miocene. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established C4 grasses have an advantage when carbon dioxide is low, and reconstructions point to a CO2 decline during late Miocene cooling (Herbert et al. 2016). But C4 grasslands took over at different times on different continents, which suggests regional drivers such as seasonal drought, fire and grazing also mattered. Falling CO2 probably set the stage; local climate and fire decided where and when grass won. Still open How low CO2 fell in the late Miocene is still uncertain, because different proxies disagree. Scientists also debate how much fire, grazing animals and monsoon changes drove the grass takeover, and why C4 grasses rose millions of years apart in different regions. A 2021 review of the epoch put carbon dioxide at roughly 400–600 ppm, similar to or above today's level, and global temperatures several degrees higher than now. chunks.heading: The First Upright Apes
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Late Miocene to Early Pliocene The First Upright Apes c. 7–4 million years ago The claim: Mixed record. Cenozoic · Late Miocene to Early Pliocene The First Upright Apes c. 7–4 million years ago The claim: Mixed record In the woods and grasslands of a drying, shifting Africa, a few apes began to walk on two legs. Why they stood up is still argued. The claim on the scales Our ancestors stood up because forests turned to savanna. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established Early hominins did begin walking upright while Africa was drying and grasslands were spreading, which fits the idea. But Ardipithecus lived in woodland, and Sahelanthropus and Orrorin come from mosaic habitats with trees and water. Bipedalism seems to have begun before open savanna dominated. Many researchers now favour variability selection: changeable, patchy environments rewarded versatile bodies that could both climb and walk (Potts 1998). Still open Whether Sahelanthropus walked upright is still argued: a 2026 study of its thigh and forearm bones reports hominin-like features, while critics read the same bones as ape-like. We also do not know which early species, if any, is our direct ancestor, or whether upright walking evolved more than once. A variable world What the newest bones say 01 Three candidates In 2001 a team led by Michel Brunet found a skull in the Djurab Desert of Chad. Nicknamed Toumaï, Sahelanthropus tchadensis is about 7 million years old, with a small, ape-sized brain but small canine teeth and a face flatter than a chimpanzee's. chunks.heading: When the Mediterranean Became a Salt Desert
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Late Miocene (Messinian) to Early Pliocene (Zanclean) When the Mediterranean Became a Salt Desert c. 5.97–5.33 million years ago The claim: Plausible. Cenozoic · Late Miocene (Messinian) to Early Pliocene (Zanclean) When the Mediterranean Became a Salt Desert c. 5.97–5.33 million years ago The claim: Plausible Cut off from the Atlantic, the Mediterranean shrank into a salt-crusted basin far below sea level, then refilled, perhaps in a flood of unimaginable size. The claim on the scales The Mediterranean refilled in a catastrophic flood through Gibraltar. Weight of evidence Plausible Ruled out Established A long erosion channel beneath the Strait of Gibraltar, a huge chaotic deposit at the foot of the Malta Escarpment and about 300 streamlined ridges on the Sicily Sill all fit a sudden, violent inflow (Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009; Micallef et al. 2018, 2025). But no single site records the flood unambiguously, and several specialist teams read the same rocks as the product of slower refilling. The megaflood is a serious candidate, not an established event. Still open How far the sea actually fell is debated: some argue for a deep, nearly empty basin, others for a shallower, partly connected sea. Critics favour repeated drying and refilling, or a gradual rise fed by rivers and the Paratethys lakes to the north-east. New drilling near the Atlantic gateways may help decide. chunks.heading: The Last Time CO2 Was This High
chunks.text: Cenozoic · Pliocene (Piacenzian) The Last Time CO2 Was This High c. 3.3–3.0 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence. Cenozoic · Pliocene (Piacenzian) The Last Time CO2 Was This High c. 3.3–3.0 million years ago The claim: Strong evidence With carbon dioxide close to today's level, the mid-Pliocene world was warmer, the Arctic was forested, and the seas stood metres higher. The claim on the scales The last time carbon dioxide was as high as today, about 3 million years ago, Earth was several degrees warmer and seas stood metres higher. Weight of evidence Strong evidence Ruled out Established Independent proxies, including boron isotopes in plankton shells, leaf pores and plant waxes, place mid-Pliocene CO2 near or below today's 420-plus ppm, while pollen, plankton and Arctic tree remains show clear warmth. Sea level is the weakest link: estimates depend on how coasts have risen or sunk since, so ranges run from about 5 to 25 m. The broad picture is robust; the exact numbers are not. Still open How much Pliocene warmth came from CO2 and how much from slower changes, such as smaller ice sheets, different ocean gateways and vegetation, is debated. Whether parts of East Antarctica's ice melted is uncertain. And today's warming is far faster than any Pliocene change, so the Pliocene shows a possible end state, not the path. chunks.heading: The Ice Ages Begin
chunks.text: Ice Ages · Late Pliocene to Early Pleistocene (Piacenzian to Gelasian) The Ice Ages Begin c. 2.7–2.4 million years ago The claim: Mixed record. Ice Ages · Late Pliocene to Early Pleistocene (Piacenzian to Gelasian) The Ice Ages Begin c. 2.7–2.4 million years ago The claim: Mixed record As great ice sheets began to grow and melt across the north, Africa dried and flickered, and our ancestors reached for stone. The claim on the scales The start of the ice ages drove the origin of our genus, Homo. Weight of evidence Mixed record Ruled out Established The timing is suggestive: the oldest Homo fossil, a jaw from Ledi-Geraru, is about 2.8 million years old, close to the onset of northern glaciation and pulses of African drying. But fossils are sparse, dates have wide error bars, and stone tools start before Homo, at Lomekwi 3.3 million years ago. Climate probably shaped the stage, yet linking one global shift to the birth of a genus remains hard to test. Still open Whether Lomekwi's artefacts are truly 3.3 million years old and deliberately made has been questioned. Who made the earliest Oldowan tools is unclear: at Nyayanga, Kenya, they lie with Paranthropus teeth. And how strongly northern ice actually changed East African rainfall is debated. chunks.text: Ice Ages · Early to Middle Pleistocene (Calabrian to Chibanian) When the Ice Ages Grew Longer c. 1.25–0.7 million years ago The claim: Open question. Ice Ages · Early to Middle Pleistocene (Calabrian to Chibanian) When the Ice Ages Grew Longer c. 1.25–0.7 million years ago The claim: Open question The rhythm of the ice changed: short, gentle cycles gave way to long, deep ice ages, as our ancestors spread and struggled across three continents. The claim on the scales Our ancestors came close to dying out about 900,000 years ago. Weight of evidence Open question Ruled out Established A 2023 genetic study (Hu et al.) inferred that the ancestors of modern humans fell to about 1,280 breeding individuals for roughly 117,000 years during the transition. A gap in the African fossil record around then fits loosely. But other geneticists argue the method can mistake population structure for a crash, and the signal is not clear in some other analyses. Humans lived on several continents then, though not all were our direct ancestors. Still open The cause of the Mid-Pleistocene Transition is unresolved: falling carbon dioxide, erosion of soft ground beneath ice sheets and changes in ocean circulation are all candidates, and they may have acted together. Early dates for controlled fire are debated, because natural wildfires can leave similar traces. The full story 2 min read · 336 words · 0 animated drawings A new rhythm Why did it change? Humans on the move Fire and a narrow squeeze 01 A new rhythm Seafloor records show a striking change between about 1.25 million and 700,000 years ago. The early ice ages were modest and regular, keeping time with the 41,000-year tilt of Earth's axis. chunks.heading: Toba: The Supereruption
chunks.text: Ice Ages · Late Pleistocene Toba: The Supereruption c. 74,000 years ago The claim: Ruled out. Ice Ages · Late Pleistocene Toba: The Supereruption c. 74,000 years ago The claim: Ruled out One of the largest eruptions of the past two million years blanketed South Asia in ash. Did it also push humanity to the edge? The claim on the scales The Toba eruption nearly wiped out humanity. Weight of evidence Ruled out Ruled out Established The idea, popularised in 1998 (Ambrose), linked Toba's volcanic winter to a genetic bottleneck in our species. Since then, sites spanning the ash layer in South Africa, Ethiopia and India show people carrying on and adapting, and Lake Malawi cores show no volcanic winter in East Africa. Bottlenecks in our genes are better explained by other events, such as small founding groups leaving Africa. Regional hardship is likely; near extinction is contradicted by the evidence. Still open How cold and how long any volcanic winter was is still modelled with wide ranges. Whether the Jwalapuram toolmakers were modern humans or another kind of human is debated. The eruption's effect on Denisovans and other Asian populations remains unknown.
